title: JGMA band boundaries use [lo, hi) where the standard prints (lo, hi]: m=1.0 and m=0.6 read the wrong row, m=1.6, standard m=10 and d=1.5 get no entry
claim: The published fine table labels its module bands 'm0.2以上0.6以下', 'm0.6をこえ1以下' and 'm1をこえ1.6以下', which read [0.2, 0.6], (0.6, 1] and (1, 1.6]. Its diameter bands are '1.5以上3以下', '3をこえ6以下', and so on. `in_band` treats every band as [lo, hi), and the test `module_bands_are_half_open` asserts the reverse of the standard: m = 0.6 goes to the upper band. The diameter bands were patched differently, by storing 1.51/3.01/6.01/12.01..., so the CSV mixes two conventions. It also leaves 0.01 mm slivers wrong and puts d = 1.5 outside coverage. On the standard scale, m = 10 gets nothing (band [6.3, 10)), m = 3.5 and d = 125 go to the upper band, although ISO/JIS tables put those boundaries in the lower band.
evidence: Probe (probes/metrology, jgma_bounds): Fine 0 at m=1.0, d=20 gives 7.1/20 (band 1 to 1.6), but the table gives 6.7/18 (band over 0.6 up to 1). Fine 0 at m=0.6 gives 6.7/18, table 6.3/18. Fine 0 at m=1.6 gives None. d=1.5 and d=1.505 give None. Standard 4 at m=10 gives None, at m=3.5 gives 9/25 where [1, 3.5] would give 7/20, and at d=125 gives 8/22 where d ≤ 125 would give 7/20. default_class(10, 400) = None, and default_class(1.6, 30) = Standard 4 although the fine table covers m = 1.6. The recorded wasm answer for the default tab (tools/wasm_boundary.json: z=9, m=1, d=9) shows tolerance fine 0 tooth_to_tooth 6.2999999999999998 / total 18; the published (0.6, 1] row at d 6 to 12 gives 6.0/18. Band labels were extracted from https://a-mec.jp/ots/cnt01_06.html (notes/metrology/amec.html).
proposal: Store bands exactly as printed (1.5, 3, 6, 12, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400; modules 0.2, 0.6, 1, 1.6; 1, 3.5, 6.3, 10; diameters 0, 125, 400, ...), with one explicit convention: `in_band = v > lo && v <= hi`, and the first band of each table also closed at lo (either a per-table `first_lo_inclusive` or an `lo_inclusive` column). Remove the +0.01 offsets and the CSV comment that explains them. Replace `module_bands_are_half_open` with `boundaries_belong_to_the_lower_band`: m=1.0 reads the 0.6 to 1 row, m=1.6 is covered, d=1.5 is covered, standard m=10 is covered.
validation: A table-driven test of every printed boundary value (each lo and hi of every band) asserting which row it reads. Re-run check_wasm.sh --write; the default tab's tooth_to_tooth must become 6.0. A law: for every (scale, grade), lookup is Some on the closed hull of the printed ranges and None just outside it.

verdict.reason: Holds as stated for the fine table. The standard-scale part rests on convention rather than a printed source. The a-mec reproduction (notes/metrology/amec.html) prints the module blocks as 'm0.2以上0.6以下', 'm0.6をこえ1以下' and 'm1をこえ1.6以下', and the diameter bands as '1.5以上3以下', '3をこえ6以下' and so on, which is (lo, hi]. jgma.rs:139 `v >= lo && v < hi` puts every printed boundary module in the upper band. The test jgma.rs:406 `module_bands_are_half_open` asserts the wrong side ('0.6 must fall in the 0.6-1.0 band'). The diameter bands were patched the other way, +0.01 on every edge (corrections.md: 'a gear of exactly 12.00 mm got no tolerance'), so the CSV now mixes two conventions. Note that m = 1.0 (the default), 0.6 and 10 are all ISO 54 series-1 modules.
verdict.evidence: My probe (probes/verify-metrology, notes/verify-metrology/probe1.txt): Fine 0 at m=0.6, d=20 gives 6.7/18 (printed [0.2,0.6] row: 6.3/18). At m=1, d=20 it gives 7.1/20 (printed (0.6,1] row: 6.7/18). At m=1, d=9 it gives 6.3/18 (printed 6.0/18). m=1.6 gives None. d=1.5 and d=1.505 give None. d=6.005 reads the lower band, 5.3/16 (printed (6,12]: 5.6/16). d=400.005 is Some, where the printed table ends at 400以下. Standard 4: m=10 gives None, m=3.5 gives 9/25 (vs 7/20 just below), d=125 gives 8/22 (vs 7/20). default_class(10,400) = None. available_classes(1.6,30) lists Standard only. tools/wasm_boundary.json records the default tab (m=1, z=9) as fine 0 '6.2999999999999998' / 18, where the printed value is 6.0/18. For the standard scale no reproduction of JGMA 116-02's main body was found. Its band edges (1/3.5/6.3/10; 125/400/800/1600/2500/4000) are the ISO 1328:1975 / GB 10095-88 scheme, which is printed '≥1~3.5, >3.5~6.3'. That, together with JIS usage (以上/をこえ/以下), supports the lower-band reading, but it is not verified from the standard itself.
verdict.proposal_note: 'The first band of each table also closed at lo' is wrong as a per-table rule. In the fine table only the m0.2–0.6 block opens with a closed band ('1.5以上'). The m0.6–1 and m1–1.6 blocks open with '3をこえ' and '6をこえ', which are open at lo. Store the printed edges (1.5, 3, 6, 12, …) and give each band a `lo_inclusive` flag as printed; do not derive the flag from band order. Amend the corrections.md 4.6.1 row, which describes the +0.01 fix as the resolution. For the standard scale, state that the (lo, hi] reading is by convention until the main body is checked.

repro.reproduction: Probe crate /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/repro-metrology-0 (src/main.rs) calls the public gear_core::jgma::{lookup, default_class, available_classes} at printed band edges and just inside them. I built it with CARGO_TARGET_DIR=.../probe-target gc ... cargo run --offline -q. The correct answers come from the published JGMA 116-02 small-module table as reproduced at a-mec.jp (notes/metrology/amec.html). I extracted its text independently. It prints the module blocks as 'm0.2以上0.6以下', 'm0.6をこえ1以下' and 'm1をこえ1.6以下', and the diameter columns as '1.5以上 3以下 | 3をこえ 6以下 | … | 200をこえ 400以下'. That means (lo, hi], with only the first block's first column closed at lo. The expected values are the CSV's own rows read under that convention. Smallest input: lookup(Fine 0, m=1.0, d=9), which is the default tab (z=9, m=1).
repro.observed:
What the code returns at each input, against the printed row:
- Fine 0, m=1.0, d=9: returns 6.3/18, which is the m1–1.6 row. The printed (0.6,1] row for d 6–12 gives 6.0/18. tools/wasm_boundary.json:3960 records the same wrong value for the shipped default: "tooth_to_tooth": "6.2999999999999998", total 18.
- Fine 0, m=1.0, d=20: returns 7.1/20. m=0.999 gives 6.7/18, and the printed row for m=1 is 6.7/18.
- Fine 0, m=0.6, d=20: returns 6.7/18. m=0.599 gives 6.3/18, and the printed row for m=0.6 is [0.2,0.6], 6.3/18.
- Fine 0, m=1.6, d=20: returns None. m=1.599 gives 7.1/20, so the printed '1.6以下' edge is dropped.
- Fine 0, m=0.4, d=1.5 and d=1.505: both return None, although the table prints '1.5以上'.
- Fine 0, m=0.4, d=3.005: returns 5.0/13, the lower band. The printed '3をこえ' band gives 5.3/16. This is the 0.01 mm sliver the +0.01 offsets create.
- Fine 0, m=0.4, d=400.005: returns 8.0/24, past the printed '400以下' end.
- available_classes(1.6, 30) lists Standard 4–12 only, with no fine grades.
- Standard scale, under the (lo, hi] convention: m=10, d=400 returns None, and default_class(10, 400) is None. m=3.5 returns 9/25, where m=3.49 gives 7/20. d=125 at m=2 returns 8/22, where d=124.9 gives 7/20.

Cause: jgma.rs:138-140 reads `/// Bands are half-open: [lo, hi)` and `v >= lo && v < hi`. The test jgma.rs:406 `module_bands_are_half_open` asserts the reverse of the printed standard. The CSV header (lines 14-18) patches only the diameter edges, by +0.01, so the table carries two conventions.
repro.note:
The fine-scale part is reproduced by execution and checked against an independent printed source. The standard-scale part reproduces as behaviour: m=10 gets no entry and the boundary values read the upper row. But whether it is wrong depends on the (lo, hi] convention, which is the ISO 1328:1975 / GB 10095 / JIS 以上・をこえ・以下 usage. JGMA 116-02's standard-scale main body was not available to confirm it.

Severity stays high:
- It silently returns a wrong tolerance for the shipped default gear (m=1).
- It shifts every boundary module up one band, and 0.6, 1 and 10 are ISO 54 series-1 modules, so these edges are the common values, not rare ones. The shift is about 5–6% in the value, or a whole band.
- At m=1.6 it drops the fine scale entirely, and at m=10 it drops every class.

Fix direction as in the ledger, with the reviewer's amendment. Store the printed edges (1.5, 3, 6, 12, …, 400; 0.2, 0.6, 1, 1.6), use `v > lo && v <= hi`, and give each band an explicit lo_inclusive flag as printed rather than one derived from band order (only the m0.2–0.6 block's d=1.5 edge and m=0.2 are closed). Remove the +0.01 offsets and the CSV comment that explains them, and replace `module_bands_are_half_open` with a test of every printed edge.

No worktree was created. The probe is at /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/repro-metrology-0, and nothing in /home/user/gearcalc was modified.

title: The contact radius for a ball on a helical gear or ring leaves out cos beta_b, so the pin bound and the verdict near the tip are wrong
claim: The ball centre is right, because inv phi uses d_p/(2 r_b cos beta_b): the offset of an involute helicoid is another involute helicoid. But the contact point lies along the helicoid normal, which sits in the base tangent plane at angle beta_b to the transverse plane. The contact roll is therefore u_c = tan phi_M − sigma·d_p·cos(beta_b)/(2 r_b); the code has u_c = tan phi_M − sigma·d_p/(2 r_b). On external helical gears the reported contact is too low, on helical rings too high. As a result `Space::seat` accepts balls whose real contact is past the tip, and `pin_diameter_range` (the bound the pin box is held to and that the UI hint states) is too large.
evidence: 3D minimum distance from the ball centre to the flank helicoid (probe helicoid_min): distance − D/2 is 1e-15 in every case, but the radius of the closest point differs from the code. z20 beta30 D1.8: true 11.636143, code 11.593929, formula with cos beta_b 11.636143. z40 beta40: 26.176955 vs 26.093801. Ring z72 beta30: 41.732043 vs 41.771600. Largest seating ball, code vs corrected: z20 beta30 3.235 vs 3.062; z12 x0.4 beta30 4.562 vs 4.075; z24 x0.3 beta35 3.233 vs 3.023; ring z72 beta30 2.3525 vs 2.3259. A 3.1487 mm ball on z20 beta30 is accepted with a stated contact of 12.5004 (tip 12.547), but its true contact is past the tip. With the one-line fix in a worktree, `cargo nextest run --workspace` gives 678/679, the only failure being the known wall-clock test. So no test checks a helical contact radius: both tangency tests are spur-only, and neither compares contact_radius with the sampled closest point.
proposal: In pin_seat: `let u_contact = phi.tan() - sigma * pin_diameter * beta_b.cos() / (2.0 * rb);`. Update the formula in the doc comment (metrology.rs:459) and in reference.md:1413. The u_contact ≤ 0 branch for sigma < 0 is then provably unreachable (tan phi plus a positive term); drop its ring arm.
validation: Extend both tangency tests to helical gears (beta 15/30/40, external and ring) with a 3D minimum distance over (roll, axial position), as in the probe's helicoid_min. Assert |dist − D/2| < 1e-9 and |radius of the closest point − contact_radius| < 1e-9. Re-run the pin-range law test, which should keep holding at both ends.

verdict.reason: The mathematics is right. The ball-centre relation (the cos β_b in inv φ) is correct: the offset of an involute helicoid is an involute helicoid. The contact, however, lies along the helicoid normal, which is inclined at β_b to the transverse plane in the base tangent plane, so its transverse roll is reduced by (D/2)cos β_b, not D/2. The code at metrology.rs:504 omits the cos β_b. I verified this independently, and a mutation run shows no test notices. I lower the severity from high because the nominal M (the number that goes on the drawing) comes from the centre and is correct. PinsOut does not carry the contact radius, so the UI never shows it. What is wrong is the validity verdict near either end and the pin_diameter_range bound, which the pin box shows and enforces. The magnitude is 2 to 12% on the upper bound for external gears at β 15 to 40°, about 0.3 to 1% for rings, and 0.5 to 2.5% (conservative) on the external lower bound.
verdict.evidence: notes/verify-metrology/helicoid2.py fits the true involute helicoid (the transverse involute rotated by ζ·tan β_b/r_b) and minimises the 3D distance from the code's ball centre, seeded near the analytic contact. A dense grid over u ≥ 0, |ζ| ≤ 2D confirms the minimum is global on the physical sheet. The distance equals D/2 to about 1e-15 in 44 cases. The closest point's radius equals rb·hypot(1, tan φ − σ·D·cos β_b/(2 r_b)) to the printed 6 decimals, and differs from the code's value: z20 β30 D1.8: true 11.636143 vs code 11.593929; z40 β40 D2.6: 27.064157 vs 26.935621; ring z72 β30 D1.5: 41.793896 vs 41.829064. Spur cases agree exactly. Wrong verdicts: z20 β30 D3.1487 is accepted with contact 12.500437 < tip 12.547005, but the true contact is 12.598189, past the tip. z24 x0.3 β35 D3.1487: code 15.898 < tip 15.949, true 16.034. Ring z72 β30 D2.3 is accepted with contact 40.593 > tip 40.569, true 40.549. Largest seating ball (pinmax.py), code vs corrected: z20 β30 3.2352 vs 3.0623 (+5.6%); z12 x0.4 β30 4.5623 vs 4.0751 (+12.0%); z24 x0.3 β35 3.2331 vs 3.0228 (+7.0%); z40 β40 2.7989 vs 2.6466 (+5.8%); z17 β15 3.6528 vs 3.5772 (+2.1%); ring z72 β30 2.3130 vs 2.2892 (+1.0%). Worktree mutation with the one-line fix: `cargo nextest run --workspace` gave 678/679, the only failure being the known wall-clock test every_search_is_quick_enough_to_type_over. Both tangency tests (tests/metrology.rs:158 and :447) are spur-only and check only the centre distance.
verdict.proposal_note: Also correct the prose at metrology.rs:496-497 ('unwrapped length r_b·tan φ, less the pin'), which states the same error in words. The claim that the ring arm of `u_contact <= 0` becomes unreachable is not new: it is already unreachable (tan φ + D/(2r_b) > 0), and the comment there says 'were it reachable'. The proposed helical tangency test must restrict the search to the u ≥ 0 sheet or seed near the contact. An unconstrained optimiser finds spurious closer points on the other involute branch (my first, unseeded run did).

title: Best k is 'contact nearest the reference circle': a hidden selection rule, different from DIN/KHK practice, that crowds shifted gears' contacts against the form circle
claim: best_span and best_span_around choose the admissible k whose contact is nearest r, whatever the profile shift. DIN 3960 and KHK place the measuring point near d + 2x·m_n, which is about the middle of the usable flank. A rule that maximises the worse of the two margins is exactly 'contact nearest (r_j + r_a)/2'. The user cannot choose k and is not shown the admissible range, unlike the pin, where the range is shown and the value is an input.
evidence: On a published drawing (a-mec.jp cnt01_02: m0.5, z18, x0) the span is given as W3 = 3.816, and the probe gives W3 = 3.8162. The tool picks k=2 (contact 4.3875; form 4.2293, tip 5.0), while k=3 contacts at 4.6392 with margins 0.41/0.36. z17 x0.8 20°: the tool picks k=2 with contact 8.402 against a form radius of 8.318 (0.08 mm margin); DIN d+2xm gives k=3, contact 8.970. Over 594 gears (z 8 to 150, x −0.4 to 0.8, alpha 14.5/20/25, beta 0/20/35) the tool's k is not the max-margin k in 296. In 175 of them the alternative more than doubles the margin. Worst: z8 alpha14.5 beta20, where the tool's k=1 contacts 0.0006 mm above the form circle and k=2 has a 0.48 mm margin.
proposal: Change the target radius in both functions from `g.r` / `mean.r` to the middle of the usable flank, `(r_j + r_a)/2`, or equivalently maximise min(c − r_j, r_a − c), taking the worst position for the eccentric case. Add an optional `teeth_spanned` to GearRequest, and report the admissible [k_min, k_max] as the pin box reports its range. Because contact radius is monotone in k, the admissible set is an interval, and the continuous optimum k* = 1 + z(u_mid − psi_b)/pi (u_mid the roll at the target radius) gives the pick as the admissible integer nearest k*. Say in reference.md which rule is used and why.
validation: A law over the shared grid: the chosen k maximises the worse margin among the admissible k, and a supplied k within [k_min, k_max] is honoured. The a-mec example must give k=3 and W = 3.816. best_span and best_span_around agree on concentric gears (they do today, 56/56).

verdict.corrected_claim: best_span and best_span_around pick the admissible k whose contact radius is nearest the reference circle, whatever x is. reference.md:1403-1405 states the rule, but the user cannot override k and is not shown the admissible range. For shifted gears this departs from the published DIN 3960 / ISO 21771 / KHK formula, which targets d + 2x·m_n and rounds in k, so the tool's k (and therefore its W) often differs from the one a drawing uses, and the tool cannot give W for the drawing's k. Neither the code's rule nor DIN's keeps the contact away from the form circle. Maximising the worse margin is a third convention, not DIN practice.
verdict.reason: The rule is real, and it differs from the standard formula on shifted gears. Two parts of the argument overreach. First, the a-mec z18 example is a tie under the standard formula (k* = z·α/π + 0.5 = 2.5), so it shows only a different tie-break, not a DIN disagreement. Second, the 296/594 statistic and the worst cases compare the code against the max-margin rule, not against DIN, and DIN's own pick crowds a flank limit about as often as the code's does. The feature gap (no k input, no admissible range shown) is sound.
verdict.evidence: Probe spans(): z18 x0 m0.5 gives the tool's k=2, W 2.3401, contact 4.3875; k=3 gives W 3.8162 (matching the drawing's 3.816) at contact 4.6392. z17 x0.8: the tool picks k=2 at contact 8.402 with form 8.318; k=3 contacts at 8.970, target r + xm = 9.3. z8 α14.5 β20: k=1 contacts 0.0006 mm above form, while k=2 has margins 0.59/0.48. Rule comparison on a spur grid (z 8 to 150, x −0.4 to 0.8, α 14.5/20/25; 315 gears): the code's k ≠ the DIN k in 191. For x = 0 alone it is 1 of 45, and that one is a rounding difference in radius vs k, so the difference is the target d vs d + 2xm. The code's k ≠ the max-margin k in 186. The chosen contact lies within 0.05 m of a limit while another k has more than 0.2 m: 15 for the code, 10 for DIN. Adding helical gears (945 gears) gives 42 for the code and 48 for DIN (DIN's helical form with /cos²β_b, written from memory).
verdict.proposal_note: Add `teeth_spanned: Option<u32>` and report [k_min, k_max]. That is the uncontroversial part. For the default, prefer the published closed form, k = z/π·(tan α_Mt/cos²β_b − 2x·tan α_n/z − inv α_t) + 0.5 with cos α_Mt = d_b/(d + 2x·m_n), clamped to the admissible interval. It is the convention drawings follow and matches the project's preference for grounded closed forms. The proposed mid-flank rule is an invented convention and would not reproduce DIN/KHK k values either. If it is wanted, expose it as a named option. Whichever rule is kept, state it once in reference.md.

title: The two JGMA scales are one ladder offset by four grades, not independent scales
claim: jgma.rs and reference.md say the fine and standard scales are 'independent', that 'no rule for choosing between overlapping entries avoids' a non-monotone merged ladder, and that the two must 'never be compared'. In the overlap (1 < m ≤ 1.6), fine grade g equals standard grade g+4 to within the band granularity. That is the documented old-to-new relation 'new JIS grade = old grade + 4' (KG Gear technical data, section 5.7). Mapping fine g to standard g+4 gives a monotone ladder.
evidence: notes/metrology (overlap at m=1.2): d=10: fine 0 6.3/18 vs S4 7/20; fine 6 45/140 vs S10 45/140. d=150: fine 0 8/22 vs S4 8/22; fine 5 40/125 vs S9 40/125. Over 12 diameters × 7 grades × 2 values, fine g / standard (g+4) has mean 0.952 (min 0.70, max 1.29), while fine g / standard g (the comparison the docs make) has mean 3.68. The grade step inside the fine table is sqrt(2) (mean ratio 1.4107).
proposal: Rewrite the module doc and reference.md#tolerance-tables: the annex (fine) uses the pre-ISO grade numbering and the main table the ISO-style numbering, offset by 4. Either show a fine class as 'Fine g (≈ Standard g+4)', or, better, bring both onto one axis (see the ISO 1328-2 finding). Rework or delete `the_two_scales_are_not_interchangeable`; its assertion is true only for same-numbered grades.
validation: A test that, in the overlap, lookup(Fine g) / lookup(Standard g+4) lies within [0.7, 1.3] for every band, as a statement of the relation rather than a threshold on it. Or, after unification, a monotonicity law along the merged axis.

verdict.corrected_claim: In the overlap (1 < m ≤ 1.6), fine grade g is close to standard grade g+4: the ratio lies within about one grade step (0.70 to 1.29). The two scales are not one ladder. The fine scale steps by √2 per grade. The standard scale steps by about 1.6 at grades 4 to 6 and about 1.25 at grades 8 to 12. The docs are right that equal grade numbers are not comparable. They overreach in saying that 'no rule for choosing between overlapping entries avoids' a non-monotone merge, because an offset of 4 roughly avoids it.
verdict.reason: The offset relation is real but approximate, and 'one ladder' is too strong. The KG catalogue's '新JIS = 旧JIS + 4' is about old JIS B 1702 / JGMA 116-01 against JIS B 1702-1/2:1998. KG calls it only a rough guide that fails at small and large tooth counts, so it is an analogy here, not evidence about JGMA 116-02's two scales. The design decision (two named scales, user picks, fine first) is still sound. Only the argument in jgma.rs:20-26 and rationale.md needs softening. The test `the_two_scales_are_not_interchangeable` asserts true facts about same-number grades and need not change.
verdict.evidence: Probe (m = 1.2 and 1.5, d = 10 to 300, grades 0 to 6; 168 ratios): fine g / standard g+4 has mean 0.942, geometric mean 0.933, min 0.70, max 1.286. Fine g / standard g (g = 4 to 6) has mean 3.62. From the CSV, standard totals at m 1–3.5, d ≤ 125 are 20, 32, 50, 71, 90, 112, 140, 180, 224: step ratios 1.60, 1.56, 1.42, 1.27, 1.24, 1.25, 1.29, 1.24. Fine totals at m 1–1.6, d 6–12 are 18, 25, 36, 53, 71, 100, 140 (about √2). kgtech.txt section 5.7: '新JIS精度等級＝旧JIS精度等級＋4（級）…おおよその目安…適用できない部分があります'.
verdict.proposal_note: Do not build a merged ladder or a monotonicity law along it: the standard scale's non-geometric step means the offset holds only within ±1 grade. A one-sentence note in jgma.rs, rationale.md and reference.md ('fine g ≈ standard g+4 within about one grade in the overlap; still two tables') is sufficient.

title: The JGMA table could be replaced or complemented by ISO 1328-2's continuous closed-form formula for the same two quantities
claim: JGMA 116-02 tabulates double-flank (両歯面) total and one-pitch composite deviations. ISO 1328-2:1997 defines the same two quantities as closed forms in the actual m_n and d: F_i'' = 3.2 m_n + 1.01 sqrt(d) + 6.4 and f_i'' = 2.96 m_n + 0.01 sqrt(d) + 0.8 at grade 5, times 2^(0.5(Q−5)). It covers grades 4 to 12, m_n 0.2 to 10, d 5 to 1000, has a stated rounding rule, and uses its tables only 'with agreement'. A formula model is continuous (the table jumps at every band edge), needs no boundary convention (the source of the high finding above), has a single grade axis (no fine/standard fork), and raises no licensing question, since a formula is a fact.
evidence: ISO 1328-2:1997 clauses 6.1, 7 and A.2/A.3, read from the public preview (notes/metrology/iso97.txt lines 259-345): 'Use the actual values of module and diameter in the following formulae'; step factor sqrt(2); 'If values are greater than 10 µm, they are rounded to the nearest integer. If less than 10 µm ... nearest 0,5 µm'. Table jumps in the current model: Fine 0 goes from 6.7/18 at m = 0.99999 to 7.1/20 at m = 1.00001; Standard 4 goes from 7/20 at d = 124.999 to 8/22 at d = 125. On the ISO axis the JGMA fine grades come out around ISO g+5.6 and the standard grades at roughly ISO grade 3.7 to 10.7 (notes/metrology/iso_vs_jgma.py).
proposal: Add `tolerance::radial_composite(Q, m_n, d) -> (F_id, f_id)` as the formula above, with a `Standard` enum {Iso1328_2, Jgma116_02}. The ISO formula is the default, unrounded, with the rounded value as an explicit option; the JGMA table stays a named lookup. The wasm summary reports which standard and grade are in force. If ISO 1328-2:2020 (classes R30 to R50) is preferred, the same shape applies: one base(m, d) times a step. Put the bounds of validity (m, d, z ranges) in Ranges, as other inputs have, and say when a gear is outside them rather than refusing silently. ISO 1328-1:2013's elemental tolerances (pitch, profile, helix, runout) are formulas of the same form and could follow on the same function.
validation: Recompute ISO 1328-2 Annex A table cells from the formula at the geometric-mean m and d with the A.3 rounding, and assert equality with a handful of printed cells (spot values, as for JGMA). Laws: continuity in m and d, and exactly sqrt(2) per grade before rounding.

verdict.corrected_claim: ISO 1328-2:1997 gives closed-form grade-5 formulas for the same two double-flank quantities, with a √2 step, grades 4 to 12, m_n 0.2 to 10 and d 5 to 1000. Its tables apply only by agreement. It could be added beside JGMA 116-02 as a second, user-selected standard. It cannot replace or unify the JGMA table, because the two standards give different numbers. The 1997 edition has also been superseded by ISO 1328-2:2020 (a different class system; scope d ≤ 600 mm).
verdict.reason: The formulas and clauses are quoted correctly (iso97.txt, clauses 6.1, 7 and A.2/A.3). This is not 'two models of one thing'. It is two standards, and a drawing names one of them. No JGMA grade maps to one ISO grade. A fine grade's total corresponds to about ISO g+5.6 but its tooth-to-tooth to about ISO g+7.5, and the standard scale drifts from about ISO g−0.3 to g−1.3. Replacing the table would therefore change answers by up to a factor of about 2 in one quantity. Making ISO the default would switch a JGMA user's standard silently. The continuity argument is valid only for the unrounded ISO formula. JGMA's band jumps belong to that standard and are not a modelling fault.
verdict.evidence: notes/verify-metrology/iso_equiv.py inverts the ISO formula at each JGMA cell's geometric-mean m and d. Equivalent ISO grade, total / tooth-to-tooth: fine 0 → 5.63 / 7.49; fine 6 → 11.58 / 13.13; standard 4 → 3.72 / 4.38; standard 8 → 8.03 / 8.38; standard 12 → 10.68 / 11.02. iso.org and BSI list ISO 1328-2:2020 as current, applicable to z ≥ 3 and d ≤ 600 mm. Its formula was not verified here (the preview PDF could not be text-extracted).
verdict.proposal_note: If adopted, add it as `Standard::{Jgma116_02, Iso1328_2}`, chosen by the user, with JGMA kept as the default where it is today. Target the current edition (2020) or label the 1997 one as withdrawn. The 'exactly √2 per grade' law holds only for the ISO formula and must not be applied to JGMA data.

title: The standard-scale transcription stops at module 10; JGMA 116-02's main body is reported to cover m_n 1 to 40
claim: The CSV and the docs give the standard scale as 'modules 1 to 10'. A review of composite gear inspection summarises JGMA 116-02 as covering normal module 1 to 40 mm and reference diameter up to 4000 mm in grades 4 to 12, with the annex covering m_n 0.2 to 1.6, d 1.5 to 400, grades 0 to 6. Gears of m ≥ 10 therefore get 'JGMA 116-02 does not cover module …', which is a claim about the standard that appears to be false. The standard-scale values themselves are not verifiable here: no public reproduction was found.
evidence: Web search result text (from a review citing JGMA 116-02: 'defines the allowable values for normal module 1 mm–40 mm, reference diameter up to 4000 mm, grade 4–12 … The annex lists … normal module 0.2 mm to 1.6 mm, reference diameter 1.5 mm to 400 mm, grade 0–6'). The CSV has 3 standard module bands (1 to 3.5, 3.5 to 6.3, 6.3 to 10). Probe: lookup(Standard 4, 12, 300) = None, lookup(Standard 4, 20, 1000) = None.
proposal: Check against the standard: transcribe the 10 to 16, 16 to 25 and 25 to 40 module bands if they exist, and correct the scope statements in the CSV header, the jgma.rs Scale docs and reference.md. Until then, the 'not covered' note should say 'not transcribed' rather than 'does not cover'.
validation: Row-count test updated to the full band count, and spot values from the printed pages.

verdict.reason: The only evidence is a web-search summary that I could not reproduce. Two Japanese and one English search found no statement of JGMA 116-02's main-body module range. Circumstantial evidence points both ways. JGMA 116-02 (1983) was 'revised to align with ISO' (gearplas.com), and its standard-scale band edges are the ISO 1328:1975 / GB 10095-88 scheme, which in those standards continues to modules 10–16, 16–25 and 25–40. That makes the scope claim plausible, but it does not establish it. What can be verified is that the code and docs assert a fact about the standard: 'JGMA 116-02 does not cover module {module}' (strings_en.toml:335), and 'modules 1-10' in the CSV header, jgma.rs:53 and reference.md:1497. That fact is not checkable from the repository.
verdict.evidence: CSV: 3 standard module bands (1–3.5, 3.5–6.3, 6.3–10) × 6 diameter bands. Probe: lookup(Standard 4, 12, 300) = None and lookup(Standard 4, 20, 1000) = None. WebSearch for 'JGMA 116-02 … 1～40 … 4000' returned only the fine-annex reproduction (a-mec) and general descriptions.
verdict.proposal_note: The cheap and safe part is to reword ui.gear_tolerance_not_covered (×5) and the scope statements to 'has no transcribed entry' until the main body is checked. Transcribing further bands needs the standard itself.

title: English tolerance-scale names reach all five languages through `Display for Class`, and Svelte hard-codes them
claim: `ui.gear_tolerance_no_entry` is filled with `.text("class", c.to_string())`, and Display writes 'Fine 3' or 'Standard 4'. The German, Portuguese and Chinese sentences therefore carry English words. The panel's class select and its readout write `"Fine" : "Standard"` literally. This breaks rule 2 (no English in gear-core) and the UI-strings rule, and check_strings.py cannot see either.
evidence: strings_zh-Hans.toml:242 'JGMA 116-02 中没有 {class} 级…' is filled with 'Fine 3'. GearPanel.svelte:532 `{c.scale === "fine" ? "Fine" : "Standard"}`, and the same at :819.
proposal: Add catalogue keys `ui.gear_tolerance_scale_fine` and `ui.gear_tolerance_scale_standard` (×5). The Note carries the scale as a key-valued field plus `.number("grade", …)`. The panel renders `t(scaleKey)`. Delete `Display for Class`, or restrict it to the CLI and keep it out of any Note.
validation: check_strings.py extended to flag string literals of capitalised words inside Svelte markup, or at minimum a grep gate for the two literals. A strings test that fires `gear_tolerance_no_entry` in every language and asserts the rendered sentence has no ASCII word outside the catalogue's own.

verdict.reason: Holds as stated. The English words are real and appear in every language, but the harm is cosmetic: two labels on every gear tab, plus one note that fires only when a stored class stops applying. That puts it at low, not medium. The Svelte half duplicates web#11.
verdict.evidence: jgma.rs:77-85: `impl Display for Class` writes "Fine"/"Standard". Its only consumer in the workspace is gear-wasm/src/lib.rs:336, `.text("class", c.to_string())`. A grep of gear-cli finds no jgma or Class use, so the Display exists only to feed a browser Note. Results: strings_de.toml:246 `Klasse {class}` becomes 'Klasse Fine 3', and zh-Hans:242 becomes 'Fine 3 级'. GearPanel.svelte:532 and :819 are `{c.scale === "fine" ? "Fine" : "Standard"}`. tools/check_strings.py only matches `"ui.…"` literals (used_keys regex), so it cannot see either path. How no_entry is reached: tab.toleranceClass persists (GearPanel.svelte:525), and changing the module then makes lookup return None for the stored class.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposed 'key-valued field' does not exist. Note::text (note.rs:388) stores a preformatted string, and t() in strings.svelte.ts:66 substitutes values verbatim, so nothing translates a value. Simplest fix with no new mechanism: split the note into `ui.gear_tolerance_no_entry_fine` and `ui.gear_tolerance_no_entry_standard`, each taking `{grade}` (×5). In the panel, write both keys literally, as `c.scale === "fine" ? t("ui.gear_tolerance_scale_fine") : t("ui.gear_tolerance_scale_standard")`. A concatenated `t("ui.gear_tolerance_scale_" + scale)` would make check_strings.py report both keys as orphans. Then delete `Display for Class`, which has no other user.

title: Eccentric pins: a space is checked against one of its two bounding teeth, and the summary's range silently leaves out refused positions
claim: `space_at(gear, i)` describes the space between teeth i and i+1 but takes tip, form and root from tooth i alone, so a pin touching past tooth i+1's tip or below its form circle is accepted. Separately, the summary reports `nominal` at start 0 and builds `around` only from the positions where `over_pins_at` returns Ok. The span, by contrast, is refused unless every position measures ('a span that can only be taken at some angular positions is not a measurement of the gear'). The same gear thus gets two different rules, and a pin the pin box marks invalid still shows a plausible range.
evidence: Probe eccentric_space_limits: the largest pin for a single space, one tooth vs both teeth, differs by up to 2.04 mm (z12 amp0.8: 6.3147 vs 4.2748), 0.91 mm (z17 amp0.8 λ0.5) and 0.43 mm (z17 amp0.4). 74 to 211 of 200·z trial (space, pin) pairs are accepted that break a neighbour's limits. The around intersection happened to coincide in the 5 cases tried. Probe eccentric_partial: z17 amp0.4, d=1.5125 measures at start 0, is refused at 2 of 17 starts, and the summary shows [18.3802, 18.6024]. z17 amp0.8 λ0.5, d=1.79: refused at 4 of 17, summary [19.2950, 19.6032].
proposal: space_at: `tip = a.ra.min(b.ra)`, `form = a.r_j.max(b.r_j)`, `root = a.rf.max(b.rf)` with a, b = tooth(i), tooth(i+1). In metrology, add one reducer, `around(gear, |start| -> Result<f64,E>) -> Result<[f64;2], E>`, that fails if any position fails. Use it for span, two pins and three pins, so the wasm loop and best_span_around's hand-rolled lo/hi/every flags go away.
validation: A law over eccentric gears: for every d, over_pins_at(start) is Ok if and only if d lies inside pin_diameter_range(space) for every space it uses; and the summary's pins value is Unavailable exactly when d is outside pin_diameter_range_around.

verdict.reason: Both halves reproduce. The pin centre lies on the bisector of two involutes of one base circle, so the pin touches both flanks at the same radius. Tooth i+1's tip, form and root limits therefore bind exactly as tooth i's do, and space_at ignores them. The auditor saw the around intersection coincide in its 5 cases. It does not always: I found a gear where the pin box's bound itself is wrong. The summary half duplicates wasm-boundary#3.
verdict.evidence: Probe /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/verify-metrology (a copy of space_at next to a both-teeth version). Largest pin per space, tooth i alone minus both teeth, max over spaces: z12 amp0.8 = 2.0400 mm (reproduces the auditor), z12 amp0.4 = 0.946, z17 amp0.8 λ0.5 = 0.912, z20 amp1 λ1 = 0.842. All of these are inside admissible_angular_shift. over_pins_at accepts 78–310 of 200·z·2 (d, start, count) triples that break a bounding tooth's limit. pin_diameter_range_around, z20 amp1 λ1: code (1.94057, 2.47268) against both teeth (1.94528, 2.47268). A pin in that 4.7 µm window shows a valid pin box and measures at every start, yet it contacts below a neighbour's form circle. Summary: for every case, a d just outside the around range gives start 0 Ok with some starts refused, and the loop at lib.rs:357-368 still prints a range. Example: z17 amp0.4, d=1.5236, Two pins, refused at 2/17 starts, shown as [18.4361, 18.6438]. The pin box is marked invalid at the same moment (GearPanel.svelte:505). best_span_around refuses the same situation (metrology.rs:586-590). No test ties over_pins_at validity to pin_diameter_range_around (tests/metrology.rs:864-990).
verdict.proposal_note: Proposing `root = a.rf.max(b.rf)` is not the drawn gear. The outline puts the root at mid-space on the envelope `mean.rf + m·Δx·cos θ` (gear.rs root_at and displacement), and that is the point where the pin's innermost point sits. max(rf) over-restricts the smallest pin: on z12 amp0.8 it raises the per-space minimum by 0.152 mm over the code, where the envelope raises it 0.083 mm. Use the envelope at the space centre: add a `Gear::space_root(i)` built on root_at at `(flank_seat(i,+1)+flank_seat(i+1,−1))/2`. Keep `tip = min(ra)` and `form = max(r_j)` as proposed. The all-positions reducer and the proposed law are sound: every space is used by some start, so all starts Ok ⟺ d inside every space's interval.

title: reference.md has the direction in which a space narrows backwards for both gear kinds
claim: reference.md:1418-1419 reads 'an external gear's space narrows outward so a larger pin rides higher, a ring's narrows inward so a larger pin sits deeper'. Both directions are inverted. An external gear's space narrows inward (which is why a larger pin rides higher), and a ring's narrows outward. The code comment (metrology.rs:462-465) and the same document at :1510 and :1600 say so correctly.
evidence: metrology.rs:462 'An external gear's space narrows *inward*, so a larger pin rides higher'. reference.md:1510 'A ring's **space** is what narrows outward'. The test `a_bigger_pin_sits_deeper_in_a_ring_and_higher_in_a_gear` passes on the code's reading.
proposal: Change it to 'an external gear's space narrows inward, so a larger pin rides higher; a ring's narrows outward, so a larger pin sits deeper', and state it once. The same fact now appears about six times across metrology.rs, the tests and reference.md; keep it in reference.md and point to it.
validation: Reading; check_doc_links.py.

verdict.reason: Both directions in reference.md:1418-1419 are inverted, and the same document says the opposite at :1510 and :1599. The formulas beside the sentence and the code are right, so this is a wrong physical explanation in the spec, not a wrong number. Low, not medium.
verdict.evidence: reference.md:1418 'an external gear's space narrows outward so a larger pin rides higher, a ring's narrows inward so a larger pin sits deeper'. The text contradicts itself under either reading of 'narrows outward': if the space narrowed going outward, a larger pin would sit deeper, as it does in a ring. Against it: metrology.rs:34, :462-465 and :484-486; tests/metrology.rs:501-502, 601 and 620; reference.md:1510 and :1599; corrections.md:432 and :506. All of these say external space narrows inward and ring space narrows outward. That makes about ten statements of one fact.
verdict.proposal_note: Fixing the sentence is enough. Keep the assertion messages in the tests, since they are diagnostics and not documentation.

title: Doc comments contradict the pin-diagnosis fix recorded in corrections.md
claim: corrections.md:605 records that a ring's bottoming is a pin too small, and that an external contact inside the base circle is a pin too small. pin_geometry's doc still says '[PinTooLarge] if contact would [fall inside the base circle]', which the code answers with PinTooSmall. between_pins' doc still says 'a pin so large it reaches the root circle'.
evidence: metrology.rs:430-431 vs pin_seat:505-510 (sigma > 0 gives PinTooSmall); metrology.rs:797-798 vs Space::seat:131 (a ring bottoms when r_m + d/2 ≥ r_f, i.e. a small pin).
proposal: Delete both '# Errors' paragraphs and link to MeasurementError, whose variant docs are correct, so the diagnosis is written once.
validation: Reading.

verdict.reason: Both doc comments still describe the behaviour that corrections.md:605 records as fixed. between_pins even keeps the exact phrase the correction quotes as the fault.
verdict.evidence: metrology.rs:430-431 (pin_geometry): 'PinTooLarge if contact would [fall inside the base circle]'. pin_seat with sigma=+1 returns PinTooSmall for `u_contact <= 0` (metrology.rs:505-510), and tests/metrology.rs:629 asserts PinTooSmall from pin_geometry. metrology.rs:797-798 (between_pins): 'a pin so large it reaches the root circle'. For sigma=−1, Space::seat flags bottoming when r_m + d/2 ≥ r_f and returns PinTooSmall (metrology.rs:128-131). corrections.md:605 quotes 'a pin so large it reaches the root' as the fault it corrected.

title: Other doc comments that disagree with their code
claim: (a) best_span_around says k is chosen by the contact nearest the pitch circle 'averaged over the revolution'; the code minimises the worst offset. (b) best_span calls the standard k formula 'a rounded empirical formula'; k = z·alpha/pi + 0.5 is the exact continuous solution for contact at the reference circle, which is the criterion this code applies. (c) pin_diameter_range says 'Sixty halvings'; the code does 64, plus up to 64 doublings. (d) The CSV header cites 'DESIGN.md 4.6.1', which does not exist. (e) The preferred-number test says '7.0 … is the only entry that is not strictly in the R40 series'.
evidence: (a) line 617 `worst_offset = worst_offset.max(...)` and line 640 `worst_offset < *w`. (e) 14 distinct CSV values are not strict R40 members: 7, 11, 12, 13, 21, 22, 24, 26, 32, 34, 36, 38, 42, 48, all of which are rounded R40 (ISO 3 R''40).
proposal: Correct each sentence. Point the CSV comment at docs/reference.md#tolerance-tables and have check_doc_links.py scan crates/**/data/*.
validation: check_doc_links.py extended to data files.

verdict.reason: All five sentences disagree with the code or the repository. Two need small refinements, given in corrected_claim.
verdict.evidence: (a) metrology.rs:596-598 says 'averaged over the revolution'. The code takes `worst_offset.max(...)` (line 617) and keeps `worst_offset < *w` (line 640), which is a minimax. (b) Setting the contact roll equal to tan α_t in W_t = r_b[2π(k−1)/z + 2ψ_b] gives k = z(tan α_t − ψ_b)/π + 1. At x=0 on spur gears this is exactly zα/π + 0.5: an exact solution for the same criterion best_span applies, rounded. It is not empirical. (c) The comment at metrology.rs:181 says 'Sixty halvings'. The code runs 64 halvings (line 200) and up to 65 doublings (lines 188-194). (d) jgma_116_02.csv:10 'see DESIGN.md 4.6.1': there is no DESIGN.md. That section is now docs/history/design-record.md:1653, a superseded record. (e) A script over the CSV finds 63 distinct values, 14 of which are not strict R40: 7, 11, 12, 13, 21, 22, 24, 26, 32, 34, 36, 38, 42, 48.
verdict.corrected_claim: (c) '… a bracket a few modules wide' is also wrong. The bracket starts at [0, r_b], with r_b ≈ z·m·cos α/2, so it is about z/2 modules wide (1,400 mm at z=3000). 64 halvings still reach sub-ulp there. (e) The 13 values other than 7.0 are all in ISO 3/ISO 497's first rounded series R'40 (1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 2.1, 2.2, 2.4, 2.6, 3.2, 3.4, 3.6, 3.8, 4.2, 4.8). 7.0 is the only value outside R'40 (it is in R''20). The comment should say 'every value is R'40 except 7.0'. The auditor's 'R''40' is the wrong series name.
verdict.proposal_note: (d) The live two-scale argument is at rationale.md:1530, so point the CSV at docs/rationale.md#the-tolerance-table-has-two-grade-scales-not-one rather than reference.md#tolerance-tables. The same dangling-source problem affects jgma.rs:165 and :368 (see missed).

title: pin_diameter_range uses its own doubling and 64-step bisection where closed forms, or solve.rs, would do
claim: CLAUDE.md says every transcendental step routes through solve.rs, but this function carries its own doubling (limit 64) and fixed 64-iteration bisection on the verdict. Each end is one monotone condition. For spur, the contact at roll u needs D = 2 r_b[tan(u + h) − u] (from phi_M = u_c + h), so D_max (u = u_a), D_form (u = u_j) and D_base = 2 r_b tan h are closed forms. The root-bottoming end and all helical ends are scalar monotone roots. The range is [max of the too-small thresholds, min of the too-large thresholds], and this also names which condition binds, which the UI could show.
evidence: Probe pin_range_checks: bisection vs closed form agree to ~1e-12. z17: max 3.764349758669691 vs 3.764349758670, min(form) 1.240556603104201 vs 1.240556603104. z20 x0.5: the minimum 0.97398 is set by the root, since the closed-form form value is 0.95912.
proposal: Give Space a method per condition: `d_at_contact(roll)` (closed form when beta_b = 0, otherwise brent from solve.rs on the corrected seat relation) and `d_bottoms()` (brent). pin_diameter_range returns a `PinRange { lo, hi, lo_binds: Form|Root|Base, hi_binds: Tip }`, with no loop counts.
validation: The existing law test (a hair inside or outside each end) still holds, and a new test asserts the spur ends equal the closed forms to 1e-12.

verdict.reason: Holds. The spur ends have closed forms that match the bisection to the last ulp, and the remaining ends are monotone scalar roots that solve.rs could take. The comment's argument for bisecting the verdict does not hold up: form, tip, root and base are the same four conditions for every kind, differing only by σ. The verdict does have one real merit: the range cannot disagree with seat(). The existing hair-width law (tests/metrology.rs:258, hair 1e-9) keeps that guarantee under per-condition solves. The finding overlaps lens-continuity#7 and lens-docs-accuracy-2#1.
verdict.evidence: In Python, z17 x0 m1 α20: D_max = 2 r_b[tan(u_a + h) − u_a] = 3.7643497586696886, against the code's 3.764349758669691 (difference 2.2e-15). D_base = 2 r_b tan h = 1.24046 < 1.24056, so the form circle binds the lower end, as the auditor says. The 'every transcendental step routes through solve.rs' claim (CLAUDE.md, solve.rs:3) is broken in more places than this one: hand-rolled bisection loops also sit at ring.rs:543, gear.rs:1119, auto.rs:2162, train/shape.rs:946, :1645 and :1667, and verify.rs:726. Cost: each space takes about 130 seat() calls (0.03 ms native).
verdict.proposal_note: Do not branch on β_b = 0 for the closed form, since rule 4 forbids that kind of branch. With c = cos β_b and d/(2r_b) = c(inv φ + h), the contact roll is one monotone relation in φ at every helix. With the current code it is u = (1−c)tan φ + c(φ − h). If metrology#1's cos β_b fix lands, it becomes u = (1−c²)tan φ + c²(φ − h). Solve that one relation for φ with newton_bracketed. At c = 1 it is linear, and the first Newton step is exact. Then d_contact(u) = 2 r_b c(inv φ + h), and the bottoming end is one more monotone root. Whichever order the fixes land in, the thresholds must use the same relation as seat(), and the hair law is what enforces that.

title: Every measurement has two copies, one on Tooth and one on Gear; the Tooth copies ship only to tests
claim: span_over_teeth, best_span, pin_geometry and over_pins (Tooth) duplicate span_over_teeth_at, best_span_around and over_pins_at (Gear); a concentric gear is a Gear with one distinct tooth. Only the Gear forms reach wasm. The copies already differ in small ways: seat index by float `round` vs integer `div_ceil`; best-k by nearest vs worst-nearest; and between_pins branches on parity although the module says parity should be 'a value of the expression'.
evidence: grep: wasm calls only over_pins_at, best_span_around, pin_diameter_range_around, between_pins and cutter_tip_width. The Tooth forms are used in tests/metrology.rs and strings.rs note firing. between_pins:809 `if ring.teeth.is_multiple_of(2) { 2 r_m } else { 2 r_m cos(pi/2z) }`.
proposal: Keep a single Gear-based API (plus Space for rings). Move the published closed forms (textbook W_k, the four M forms) into tests/metrology.rs as oracles, where several already sit inline. between_pins reuses over_pins_at's seat geometry with sigma = −1. strings.rs fires the notes through the Gear API. That removes about 120 lines and the drift.
validation: The existing 'general equals published on an evenly cut gear' tests, now comparing against inline closed forms; full suite; check_wasm unchanged.

verdict.reason: The duplication is real, and outside tests nothing in the workspace uses the Tooth copies. span_over_teeth, best_span, pin_geometry, over_pins and Space::of are called only from crates/gear-core/tests/metrology.rs and from gear-io/src/strings.rs:1298/1319, which sits inside its #[cfg(test)] module (opened at line 293). gear-wasm calls only over_pins_at, best_span_around, pin_diameter_range_around, between_pins, pin_diameter_range(Space::of_ring) and cutter_tip_width. Another auditor (ablate-features #7) found the same thing on its own. One correction: the 'copies already differ' are differences in how the code is written, not in what it computes. (z/2).round() equals z.div_ceil(2) and ((z+1)/2).round() equals (z+1).div_ceil(2) for every z below 2000. On 7,776 concentric gears (z 5-150, x -0.4 to 0.8, alpha 14.5/20/25, beta 0/15/-25/35, m 0.5/1/3, k 0.8/1/1.2), best_span and best_span_around pick the same k every time, refuse the same gears (114), and differ by at most 4.3e-16 relative. over_pins and over_pins_at differ by at most 6.6e-16 and never disagree on a verdict. between_pins does branch on parity at metrology.rs:809, against the principle the module states at :560 and :689. Two latent drifts the auditor did not name: span_over_teeth(g, 0) quietly computes k = 1 (finding 18a), where the Gear copy returns None; and best_span has a severed-tooth guard that best_span_around lacks. The guard makes no difference today, because a severed tooth has r_j = ra, so the admissible interval is empty either way (3 severed gears in the grid, both functions refuse).
verdict.evidence: grep over crates/ for callers (the only non-test hits are gear-wasm lib.rs:358, 362, 399, 411, 419, 589, 599). Probe probes/verify-metrology-b over 7,776 gears: 'same k 7662, different k 0, both refuse 114, one refuses 0; worst nominal rel 4.312e-16'; 'over_pins vs over_pins_at: worst rel 6.584e-16, verdict mismatches 0'; 'round vs div_ceil seat index disagreements for z<2000: 0'.
verdict.proposal_note: between_pins cannot literally reuse over_pins_at: a Ring is not a Gear, and the core has no seat API for rings. What it can share is the index arithmetic, taking the seat at z.div_ceil(2) and the chord as hypot(P_a - P_b), which removes the parity branch. Keep cutter_tip_width(&Tooth) and base_helix_angle(&Tooth), since wasm and other modules use them. When the tests are ported, point them at the inline closed forms (the four M forms at tests/metrology.rs:674-679 already meet the 8-ulp bound through over_pins_at, whose worst error is 6.6e-16 relative), so no oracle is lost.

title: `limits` fields are always None; tolerance limits could come from a user-entered thickness allowance in closed form
claim: Span, OverPins and BetweenPins carry `limits: Option<(f64, f64)>`, which is always None and read by nothing, waiting on JGMA 1103-01 data. The owner's rule is that what nothing reads goes. A data-free alternative follows the project's preference for rules exposed as inputs: the user enters the upper and lower normal tooth-thickness allowances (A_sne, A_sni, as in ISO 21771/DIN 3967), and the limits follow exactly. Delta W_k = A_sn·cos alpha_n. Delta psi_b = A_sn/(m_n z), so for two balls with even z, Delta M = 2 r_b·Delta psi_b/sin phi_M = A_sn·cos alpha_t/(cos beta·sin phi_M), and the odd and three-pin forms scale by the same seat factor.
evidence: All constructors write `limits: None` (metrology.rs:265, 386, 586, 717, 820); the wasm PinsOut/SpanOut do not carry them.
proposal: Either delete the fields, or add `thickness_allowance: Option<(f64, f64)>` to GearRequest and compute the limits by re-evaluating the nominal functions at the thinned and thickened tooth. That is exact, needs no derivative, and reuses thickness_mod's equivalent-shift path, since Delta x_s = A_sn/(2 m_n tan alpha_n).
validation: Finite difference: the limits equal the nominal of a gear whose thickness_mod gives the same A_sn. Delta W equals A_sn cos alpha_n to 1e-14.

verdict.reason: Every constructor writes limits: None (metrology.rs:265, 386, 586, 717, 820). Nothing reads the field except one test, tests/metrology.rs:123, which asserts s.limits.is_none() and so pins the dead state. SpanOut and PinsOut do not carry it. state.md:630 records it as reserved space. Reserving space buys nothing in Rust: adding an Option field later is a change the compiler walks you through. So under the owner's rule that what nothing reads goes, the fields should be deleted now. The documented reservation does not hold up. The data-free alternative is also right. For the span, dW = A_sn cos alpha_n holds exactly, helical gears included. dpsi_b = A_sn/(m_n z) is exact. One correction: the dM expression the finding states is first order only, not exact. Against exact re-evaluation it is off by up to 3.8% relative at A_sn = -0.031 m. The proposal's own route, re-evaluating the nominal, is exact.
verdict.evidence: Probe: over the grid, with thickness_mod moved by dk in {-0.02, -0.005, 0.01} (A_sn = pi m dk/2), |dW - A_sn cos a_n| is at most 1.748e-14 mm. The linearised 2-ball dM = A_sn cos a_t/(cos beta sin phi_M) against exact re-evaluation: worst relative error 3.813e-2. The limits grep finds no reader anywhere in crates/ or web/src.
verdict.proposal_note: If the feature is built, shift psi_b by A_sn/(m_n z) inside the existing closed forms (the span sweep, pin_seat's half_space) rather than building a new Tooth with another thickness_mod. A different thickness_mod also changes the rack's tooth, and with it r_j, so a limit could be refused where the nominal measures, and the validity verdict would drift for reasons unrelated to the allowance. Keep the validity verdict of the nominal gear, or say explicitly which gear the limits are validated against. The limits must also cross the boundary (SpanOut, PinsOut) and be shown, or the field stays dead.

title: The default pin is a fixed 1.75 mm whatever the module; the 'ideal' ball has a closed form
claim: The tab's pin default is the literal 1.75 mm, about 1.75·m for m = 1 only. Change the module and the pin stays, so a module-3 gear opens with 'pin too small'. The usual choice (KHK: the pin touching at d + 2x·m_n) is closed form for spur, D = 2 r_b[tan(u_c + h) − u_c] with u_c the roll at the target radius, and one monotone root for helical.
evidence: Probe: ideal pin touching at the pitch circle is 1.8046·m (z9), 1.7349·m (z17), 1.3147·m (z20 x0.5), 1.9368·m (z40 x−0.3) and 1.6814·m (z100). So 1.75 mm is 30% off even at m = 1 for a shifted gear, and far off at any other module.
proposal: Serve `suggested_pin` in GearSummary and RingSummary: the pin whose contact lands mid-flank, using the same target as the k rule. The tab seeds from it when the user has not typed a pin, and it can be shown beside the range as 'ideal'. Rounding to a stock pin size can be an explicit option, never silent.
validation: A law: the suggested pin's contact radius equals the target radius to 1e-12, and it lies inside pin_diameter_range.

verdict.reason: The default is the Rust literal 1.75 at gear-wasm lib.rs:1159. The tab takes it once (state.svelte.ts:138) and never rescales it with the module or the shift. Every ideal-pin number reproduces exactly from the closed form D = 2 r_b[tan(u_c + h) - u_c], with h = pi/z - psi_b, and the resulting pin contacts at r to 1e-9. At m = 3, z = 9 and at m = 2, z = 17 the default returns PinTooSmall; at m = 0.3, z = 17 it returns PinTooLarge. One correction: '30% off even at m = 1 for a shifted gear' is measured against the reference-circle target. Against the KHK d + 2xm target that the finding itself calls the usual choice, the ideal is 1.998 m for z20 x0.5 (so 1.75 is 12% small) and 1.657 m for z40 x-0.3 (6% large). The impact is limited, because the panel shows the admissible range in the hint and marks the box invalid, so the user is not misled, only made to retype.
verdict.evidence: Probe F14: z9 x0 m1 ideal 1.8046 m; z17 1.7349 m; z20 x0.5 1.3147 m (KHK target 1.9980 m); z40 x-0.3 1.9368 m (KHK 1.6568 m); z100 1.6814 m; z9 m3: range (4.267, 17.669), 1.75 mm gives Err(PinTooSmall); z17 m2: Err(PinTooSmall); z17 m0.3: Err(PinTooLarge).
verdict.proposal_note: Seeding 'when the user has not typed a pin' adds a dirty flag to the tab state. It is simpler to serve suggested_pin, computed in Rust, show it in the hint beside the range, and offer it as a one-click value. Its target must be whatever k-rule target finding 2 settles on. For helical gears and rings it must wait for the ball-contact fix (finding 1), or it inherits that error. The helical case is a monotone root and should go through solve.rs.

title: A helical span's face-width condition (b > W_k sin beta_b) is neither checked nor stated
claim: On a helical gear the anvils touch along generators inclined at beta_b, and the span can be taken only if the face width exceeds W_k·sin beta_b, plus about 3 mm for a stable reading according to KHK. The gear tab has no face width, so the tool reports spans that a narrow helical gear cannot give, without saying so. The contact radius is also a convention here: the contact is a line crossing a band of radii. The code uses the DIN transverse-section point, and the anvil-centre point lies lower.
evidence: Probe: z40 beta30: W6 = 17.079 needs b > 8.03 mm. z60 beta35: W8 = 23.618 needs b > 12.73 mm. Contact radius at the transverse point vs the anvil-centre point: 23.385 vs 22.585 (z40 beta30) and 36.286 vs 34.915 (z60 beta35). KHK tooth-thickness page: 'b min … Δb > 3 mm to make a stable measurement of W'.
proposal: Report `min_face_width = W_k·sin beta_b` in SpanOut (closed form) and say it beside the span. Where a face width is known (a train member), refuse below it. In reference.md, state which contact point the validity check uses and why.
validation: A test that min_face_width is 0 for spur and equals W sin beta_b for helical gears; and that, with a known face width, a helical span below it is refused.

verdict.corrected_claim: The face-width condition for a helical span, b >= W_k sin beta_b (the axial offset between the two anvil contacts on one common normal), is neither checked nor stated anywhere, and the tool reports spans a narrow helical gear cannot give. The finding also calls the contact radius a convention (the 'DIN transverse-section point'). It is not a convention but an error: coaxial anvils touch on a common normal whose two rolls sum to W cos beta_b, not W/cos beta_b. That error is reported separately under missed.
verdict.reason: The face-width numbers reproduce: z40 beta30 W6 = 17.0792 needs b >= 8.025; z60 beta35 W8 = 23.6182 needs b >= 12.730. A 3D computation that shares no code with the crate confirms the axial offset along the common normal is exactly W sin beta_b (12.7299). KG's technical data gives the same condition in its older W sin beta form (kgtech.txt:3602-3605). Two parts of the proposal do not apply as written. First, train members carry no metrology at all (state.md: 'the gear tab alone has ... the metrology'), so there is nowhere to 'refuse below it'. Second, KHK's '+3 mm' is a rule of thumb, which the owner allows only as an explicit user-visible option. The contact figures the auditor quotes (23.385 vs 22.585, 36.286 vs 34.915) are right, but they show a defect, not a choice of convention.
verdict.evidence: Probe F15 output; notes/verify-metrology-b/helical_span.py (independent helicoid geometry): '|PB-PA| 23.618212; axial offset -12.7299 (W sin bb 12.7299)'. No 'sin β_b' or face-width text in the metrology section of reference.md (lines 1389-1500) or in metrology.rs.
verdict.proposal_note: Report min_face_width = W_k sin beta_b on SpanOut (it is 0 for spur by value, not by branch), and use the largest W around an eccentric gear. Do not bake in KHK's +3 mm. Fix the contact radius first (see missed), because the physical placement it describes is exactly what makes W sin beta_b the right bound.

title: UI labels say 'pins' and 'composite error' where the numbers are for balls on helical gears and are double-flank tolerances
claim: The helical over-pins figure is the ball measurement. KHK: 'Helical gears can only be measured with balls', since a cylinder parallel to the axis cannot seat tangent in a helical space. JGMA 116-02's values are allowable double-flank (両歯面) composite deviations against a master gear, not 'composite error', and single-flank (tangential) composite values differ.
evidence: a-mec.jp/ots/cnt01_06.html title: '小モジュール歯車の両歯面かみあい誤差の許容量'. cnt01_03: 'ＪＧＭＡ 116-02規格での精度測定方法は、両歯面かみあい試験機を使用し'. strings_en: 'Composite error, JGMA 116-02' and 'Measurement over pins'.
proposal: Change the labels (×5) to 'Double-flank composite tolerance, JGMA 116-02' and, for beta ≠ 0, 'Measurement over balls', either as a key the summary selects or as a note. Rename CompositeError to RadialCompositeTolerance.
validation: check_strings.py.

verdict.reason: The panel heads the section 'Measurement over pins' (GearPanel.svelte:801) with rows '2 pins' and '3 pins', and heads the tolerance 'Composite error, JGMA 116-02' (:812). For beta != 0 the numbers are ball values: metrology.rs's own doc (:423-426) calls the formula 'the correct treatment for balls in a helical gear'. A cylinder parallel to the axis seats elsewhere in a helical space. The cached a-mec pages confirm the JGMA 116-02 values are double-flank quantities: '両歯面かみあい試験機を使用し両歯面全かみあい誤差と両歯面１ピッチかみあい誤差を測定' and the table title '小モジュール歯車の両歯面かみあい誤差の許容量'. All four translations inherit the imprecision (de 'Sammelfehler' / 'Maß über Rollen', where DIN would say Zweiflanken-Wälzabweichung and Kugelmaß for balls; zh '综合误差'; pt 'Erro composto'). The pin input label ('Pin / ball diameter') and the error strings ('pin or ball') are already correct.
verdict.evidence: strings_en.toml:242, 299, 329, 341; strings_de/pt/zh-Hans/zh-Hant lines 150-212; notes/metrology/amec.html and amec_03.html (the quoted text was re-extracted by this verifier).
verdict.proposal_note: Do not choose the label by beta in TypeScript. Either let the summary cross the label key (Rust decides), or use one label for every gear: 'Measurement over pins or balls', with a note that a helical gear is measured over balls. The second needs no branch at all.

title: Test gaps: helical textbook span skipped on a false ground, preferred-number check almost cannot fail, no monotonicity in module or diameter, no metrology in the golden corpus
claim: (a) span_reduces_to_the_textbook_formula skips every helical gear with the comment that the textbook form is spur-only. ISO 21771's W_k = m_n cos alpha_n[(k − 0.5)pi + z inv alpha_t] + 2 x m_n sin alpha_n holds for helical gears, and the substitute test checks only the slope. (b) The preferred-number whitelist has 66 values and the file uses 63 distinct ones, so a digit error that lands on another allowed value (28 for 26, 16 for 18) passes. (c) Monotonicity is checked in grade only; the independent reproduction shows one genuine inversion in module (fine 1, d 12 to 25: m 0.6 to 1 total 28, m 1 to 1.6 total 26), which a module and diameter law would record as a known exception. (d) No gear-cli command prints span, k, pins, pin range or JGMA, so check_golden.sh cannot detect metrology drift. Only one default gear is recorded, in wasm_boundary.json.
evidence: Probe span_checks: the code matches the ISO closed form, helical included, with worst relative error 6.511e-16 over 990 gears × k 1 to 8. Cross-check: 294/294 fine cells equal the a-mec reproduction (notes/metrology/compare_amec.py). iso_vs_jgma.py found exactly one monotonicity violation, present in both sources.
proposal: (a) Remove the `continue` so the identity is asserted on helical gears. (b) Replace the whitelist with 'every value is a rounded R40 number' computed from the series, and add module and diameter monotonicity with the single documented exception. (d) Add a `gear-cli metrology` row to COMMANDS printing k, W, contact, pin range, M2/M3 and JGMA over a small grid (spur, helical, shifted, ring, eccentric), and record it in golden.
validation: Perturbation: changing best_span's target radius, or dropping cos beta_b, must now move the golden output.

verdict.corrected_claim: (a) confirmed. (b) The whitelist (66 values, 63 used) does let a digit error that lands on another listed value pass, but it is not 'almost unable to fail': it catches 66% of single-digit substitutions and about 72% of adjacent transpositions. The proposed series-derived rounded-R40 whitelist would be weaker (94 members, 58% caught). (c) confirmed. (d) confirmed, with one addition: tools/wasm_boundary.json, checked in CI by check_wasm.sh, also records a z60 ring's between-pins and pin range. Neither the gear nor the ring there is helical or shifted.
verdict.reason: (a) The ISO 21771 helical identity holds to 6.6e-16 relative over 62,208 (gear, k) pairs, helical ones included. In a worktree with the `continue` removed, the full suite passes. The only failure was the known wall-clock test, which passes when run alone. (b) A mutation count over every cell settles the numbers below. (c) The CSV has exactly one module inversion: fine grade 1, d 12.01-25.01, m 0.6-1 reads 8.5/28 and m 1-1.6 reads 9.0/26. The a-mec reproduction has it too (compare_amec.py re-run: 294 cells, 0 differences). (d) gear-cli help lists no metrology command, `show` prints none, and tools/golden has none. The wasm record's gear is spur (z9 m1 beta0), so no helical metrology change can move any recorded output. In the same worktree I also changed the helical span contact radius in both span functions, and every test still passed.
verdict.evidence: notes/verify-metrology-b/jgma_checks.py and jgma_power.py: 'allowed 66 distinct used 63'; single-digit substitutions (11,884 mutants) caught by the whitelist 7,816 (0.658), by the existing structural checks 4,322 (0.364), by all existing checks 9,506 (0.800), and with module and diameter monotonicity plus the one known exception 10,994 (0.925). Transpositions: 459 caught, 179 pass. r40.py: a series-derived set of 94 values catches 6,903/11,884 (0.581).
verdict.proposal_note: For (b), keep the current list (or derive it from R''40 below 100 and R20 above, the precision the table actually uses) rather than widening it to 'any rounded R40'. The real gain is the module and diameter monotonicity law with the single recorded exception, which takes detection from 80% to 92.5%. For (d), the metrology row should include a helical gear, a shifted gear and a helical ring, so the ball-contact fix (finding 1) and the span-contact fix (missed) both move the corpus.

title: Small API and robustness issues
claim: (a) span_over_teeth(g, 0) silently computes k = 1 through saturating_sub but reports teeth_spanned = 0, while span_over_teeth_at(…, 0) returns None. (b) The CSV parser drops malformed rows through filter_map, and only the row-count test notices. (c) base_helix_angle(&Tooth) sits in metrology but is imported by contact.rs and strength.rs; it belongs on Tooth, as Ring::base_helix_angle does. cutter_tip_width is a property of the rack, not a measurement. (d) best_span_around scans every k over every start, O(z²), and pin_diameter_range_around recomputes identical spaces, although Gear::distinct and the monotonicity of contact in k would bound both.
evidence: Probe: span_over_teeth(k=0).nominal = 1.7561765077967066 = k=1, teeth_spanned 0. jgma.rs:113-133 `filter_map … return None`.
proposal: Make k a NonZeroU32 (or return an Option); parse the CSV strictly, panicking with the line number inside the OnceLock, or generate a const table at build time; move base_helix_angle to `impl Tooth` and cutter_tip_width next to the rack in plane.rs; limit the k scan to the admissible interval around k* and iterate distinct teeth.
validation: Full suite; the timing test.

verdict.reason: Of the four parts, (a), (b) and (c) hold as stated. Part (d) holds only in part. best_span_around is not O(z²) in practice: its inner loop breaks at the first position that refuses, so it makes about 5z calls and costs well under a millisecond even at z = 3000. The real waste is pin_diameter_range_around. On a concentric gear it bisects z bit-identical spaces, and that is most of what solve_gear costs. Some of the proposals also need correcting. Panicking in the OnceLock goes against the crate's no-panic rule. plane.rs is the wrong home for cutter_tip_width. Gear::distinct counts distinct teeth, but a pin measures a space, so it is the wrong unit to deduplicate on.
verdict.corrected_claim: (a) span_over_teeth(g, 0) returns k = 1's span but reports teeth_spanned = 0. It also never refuses any k: k = 40 on z = 17 gives 116.85 mm. span_over_teeth_at returns None in both cases. Only library code and tests can reach either function; the product goes through best_span_around, where k ≥ 1. (b) jgma.rs:113 drops any malformed CSV row through filter_map. Of the 11 jgma tests, only the cell-count test notices, and its failure message names the grade, not the line. (c) metrology::base_helix_angle(&Tooth) is really a property of the Tooth. contact.rs, strength.rs and gear-cli all call it, and Ring already has the same thing as a method. cutter_tip_width is not a measurement taken on a finished gear, yet the module doc (metrology.rs:1) lists it as one. It is the normal-plane form of the tip width that tooth::Rack::wanted_by already computes. (d) best_span_around costs O(z·(1 + number of admissible k)), about 5z calls, not O(z²). pin_diameter_range_around re-bisects all z spaces. On a concentric gear those spaces are bit-identical, and this dominates solve_gear: 3.7 ms in wasm at z = 100, 35 ms at z = 1000. On an eccentric gear every space is distinct under the current space_at.
verdict.evidence:
All numbers below come from my own probe (/home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/verify-metrology-f18, plus an earlier run in probes/verify-metrology), a worktree mutation, and a node bench against the shipped wasm.

(a) Default gear, z = 17:
- span_over_teeth(k=0) gives nominal 1.714159889184217 with teeth_spanned 0. k = 1 gives the same 1.714159889184217 with teeth_spanned 1. The cause is metrology.rs:254, `k.saturating_sub(1)`.
- span_over_teeth_at(gear, 0, 0) returns None (metrology.rs:338, `if k == 0`).
- span_over_teeth(k=40) returns 116.847 with no refusal; span_over_teeth_at(k=40) returns None.
- The only callers of span_over_teeth are best_span (k in 1..=z) and tests. wasm calls only best_span_around.

(b) Python check: all 309 data rows of jgma_116_02.csv currently parse strictly, and 7·21 + 9·18 = 309, so nothing is dropped today. Worktree mutation: I changed CSV line 95 to `...,15,5 3`. The result was 10 of 11 jgma tests passing and 1 failing, every_grade_has_the_expected_number_of_cells, with 'fine grade 3 has 20 cells, expected 8+7+6'. The contiguity test cannot notice, because it dedups diameter bands across module bands. Cargo.toml:26 says 'A calculation engine must not panic.'

(c) metrology.rs:25 is used at strength.rs:41 (a `use`), and strength.rs:556 implements ToothOutline::base_helix_angle for Tooth by delegating to it. Ring's impl (strength.rs:627) instead calls the inherent Ring::base_helix_angle (ring.rs:668). contact.rs has six path uses, and gear-cli/main.rs:2195 has one. cutter_tip_width (metrology.rs:727) is π m − s_t cos β − 2m(h_f − x) tan α_n. That equals cos β times tooth.rs:912's `w_tip = (π m_t − s_t) − 2 b_d tan α_t` with b_d = m(h_f − x). The UI shows it in the geometry list (GearPanel.svelte:687), not under measurement.

(d) Native release timings:
- best_span_around: z = 17 / 100 / 1000 / 3000 make 65 / 496 / 4,996 / 14,996 span_over_teeth_at calls (12,389 eccentric at z = 3000), taking 0.007 / 0.047 / 0.195 / 0.59 ms. Only 3 or 4 values of k are admissible.
- pin_diameter_range_around: 0.40 / 2.5 / 7.8 / 25.8 ms at z = 17 / 100 / 300 / 1000 (concentric).
- Deduplicated by the Space's bits, the concentric case has 1 distinct space out of z. The result is bit-identical, at 0.022 / 0.022 / 0.029 / 0.043 ms. At dx = 0.3 there are 17/17 and 1000/1000 distinct spaces, so deduplication saves nothing there.
- Shipped wasm solve_gear: 0.96 / 3.7 / 10.2 / 35 / 110 ms at z = 17 / 100 / 300 / 1000 / 3000.
verdict.proposal_note: (a) NonZeroU32 is heavier than needed. Either delete span_over_teeth as part of metrology finding 12, which folds the Tooth copies into the Gear API, or make it return Option<Span> by the same rule as span_over_teeth_at. (b) Do not panic in production (Cargo.toml:26). Factor out `fn parse_row(&str) -> Option<Row>`, keep the non-panicking collect, and add a test that asserts parse_row is Some for every non-comment line, printing the line number. (c) Put `pub fn base_helix_angle(&self)` on `impl Tooth` next to Ring's, and make strength.rs's Tooth impl call Tooth::base_helix_angle(self) the way Ring's does. Move cutter_tip_width to tooth.rs beside tooth::Rack, not plane.rs: plane.rs:93 says BasicRack is not the tool. Ideally make it a Rack::tip_width shared with wanted_by and ranges_at_shift, as lens-numerical-robustness finding 7 proposes, and fix the metrology.rs:1 module doc. (d) Leave best_span_around's k scan alone; bounding it saves nothing measurable. For pins, deduplicate by the Space value rather than by Gear::distinct. That makes a concentric gear one bisection, with bit-identical output. Better still, replace the 64+64 bisection with closed-form ends (lens-continuity finding 7). An eccentric gear then costs a few inv_inverse calls per space, and deduplication becomes unnecessary.

title: A contact that slides wholly off a face falls back to the unlimited tip zone: full contact ratio reported, labelled Face
claim: CrossedPath::limited_by_face returns None when the face-bounded zone is empty. PointBuilt::zone maps that None to the unbounded tip path (map_or(*path, ..)), and point_mesh_report maps it to (*path, ZoneLimit::Face). So a pair whose contact has left the face reports the tip-limited contact ratio with limit Face. Its efficiency, locking friction and rating are then computed along a zone the faces do not hold. Narrowing a face can therefore RAISE the reported contact ratio. Separately, limited_by_face skips a member whose base helix is zero (half_span None -> continue). The contact then sits in one fixed transverse plane of that member, and the code never checks whether that plane lies on its face.
evidence: Probe 'face': 17/43 pair, helix 20, shaft angle 0.5 deg, clearance 0.02. Face 12 mm gives eps 0.860 (Face); faces 8, 6, 4, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.2 mm all give eps 1.644148 (Face), which is the tip-limited value, and efficiency 0.984056 instead of 0.986593. Probe 'shift'/'shiftdbg': 17/23 at 20 deg, x1 = 1 with the solved x2 = -0.405, zero clearance. The member axial centres sit at +28.06 and -27.85 path units from the tip zone [0.97, 3.18]. limited_by_face at face 4 returns None and the train reports eps 1.2598 (Face), identical to the 30 mm face. Probe 'spur2': at 30 deg with a spur second member and 0.5 mm clearance, the contact plane is 2.38 mm from the spur's mid-plane. A 0.5 mm face on the spur still gives eps 1.114 (Tips). state.md:711-716 says such a pair reports 'a contact ratio under one'. That holds only while the contact is partly on the face.
proposal: Make an empty bounded zone a value, not an absence. limited_by_face returns Some with the zone collapsed to a point (length 0, contact_ratio 0, limit Face), or a new ZoneLimit::OffFace. PointBuilt::zone returns that bounded zone and never the tip path. For a member with |n.a_i| ~ 0, test the fixed contact plane: |dot(through - O_i, a_i)| <= b_i/2, else the zone is empty. Callers handle the empty zone under the single no-contact policy described in the separate finding on no-zone policy. Correct state.md:711-716.
validation: Law, swept over shaft angle {0.5, 5, 20, 45, 90}, shifts -1..1, clearance {0, 0.02, 0.3} and faces 0.1..60: contact_ratio is non-increasing as either face narrows, and limited_by == Tips iff the ratio equals the tip-limited one. Plus a fixture where the contact is fully off the face that asserts eps == 0. Run it against HEAD first: it fails at 0.5 deg with an 8 mm face.

verdict.reason: Holds as stated. limited_by_face returns None whenever the face-bounded interval is empty, whether the face is narrow or merely off-centre. PointBuilt::zone turns that None back into the unbounded tip path (`.map_or(*path, |(z, _)| z)`, shape.rs:2500-2505), and point_mesh_report turns it into `(*path, ZoneLimit::Face)` (shape.rs:2719-2722). Efficiency, locking friction and the rating therefore all run along the tip-limited zone, and the reported contact ratio is the full tip value. That value is at least 1, so the 'contact ratio below one' note never fires. Narrowing a face makes the ratio jump back up. Separately, half_span returns None for a member whose axial rate is zero (a spur member), and the loop `continue`s, so that member's fixed contact plane is never tested against its face. state.md:711-716 says such a pair reports 'a contact ratio under one'. That is false: at its own example (0.01 deg, 0.02 mm clearance) the crate reports 1.6439, labelled Face. That paragraph documents only the rating fallback; it does not cover the reported ratio, and it does not cover shifted pairs at ordinary angles.
verdict.evidence:
My own probe (probes/verify-crossed-worm, mode f0). The pair is 17/43 with +20 deg additional helix, Σ = 0.5 deg and 0.02 mm clearance.
- Face 16 mm: eps 1.644148, Tips. Face 12 mm: eps 0.860170, Face, eta 0.986593. Faces 10, 9, 8, 6, 4, 2 and 0.5 mm: eps 1.644148, Face, eta 0.984056/0.983968 (the tip-zone values), worst_pos -2.567 (the same as at 30 mm).
- Called directly, path.limited_by_face at face 10, 8 or 4 returns None. The zone is [-4.468, 0.386] and the member centres sit at +16.29 and +16.74.
- At Σ = 0.01 deg with faces 400, 200, 60, 30 and 10 mm: eps 1.643928, Face, in every case.

The shifted pair is 17/23 at 20 deg, x1 = 1, with x2 solved to -0.4055 and zero clearance. The centres sit at +28.06 and -27.85 against the zone [-0.535, 3.184]. Faces 8, 4 and 2 mm give eps 1.259780, Face, which is identical to the 60 mm value, and limited_by_face returns None.

The spur member case (mode f0spur): Σ = 30 deg, 17/23, second helix 1.1e-16. At 0.5 mm clearance the contact plane lies 2.379 mm from the spur's mid-plane. A face of 0.5 mm, or of 0.001 mm, on the spur still returns (1.1145, Tips).
verdict.proposal_note:
The direction is right. Two refinements:
- Do not collapse the empty zone to a 'point'. An empty interval has no location, so efficiency and locking along it are undefined. Return an explicit empty or no-contact value and route it through the same policy as a missing path, with eps 0 and the 'contact ratio below one' note.
- The zero-axial-rate member needs no tolerance or special case. Write each face bound in that member's axial coordinate, |z_i0 + s·(n·a_i)| ≤ b_i/2. This is linear in s, so intersecting the intervals handles n·a_i = 0 naturally: the whole line or none of it. The same form also replaces the division in half_span.

The monotonicity law in the validation is the right gate.

repro.reproduction:
I built a probe crate at /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/repro-crossed-worm-0 (src/main.rs) against the public API and ran it with `Z0=1 CARGO_TARGET_DIR=.../probe-target gc <probe> cargo run --offline -q`. The output is saved at /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/notes/repro-crossed-worm-0.out.
