The matrix's ISO set is taken at the tip, which is Method-C-like, not the HPSTC of Method B. For the NaN, printing '—' with the count (0 of n) keeps the golden file meaningful.

title: Meshed-planet (and Ravigneaux) sets whose three distances cannot form a triangle are solved and reported without complaint
claim: Nothing checks that a planet-planet distance can connect the two planet axes. Planet A stands at r_A (the sun-A distance), planet B at r_B (the ring-B distance), and A-B are a apart, so the set exists only if |r_A - r_B| <= a <= r_A + r_B. A set that breaks this is physically impossible, yet it is returned Ok with no note.
evidence: Probe P2: meshed_planets(24,[18,18],96,3) with the sun and ring counts changed. Case 24/97: r_A 21.02, r_B 39.48, a 18.02, so r_A + a = 39.04 < 39.48. Case 22/96: 20.02 + 18.02 < 38.98. Case 18/96: 36.04 < 38.98. All three solve_train Ok, and the only notes are part.planets_share_load_equally. The shipped 24/96 preset closes, but only just: the angle at the centre between A and B is acos((21.02^2 + 38.98^2 - 18.02^2)/(2*21.02*38.98)) = 2.9 degrees, nearly collinear. grep finds no triangle or law-of-cosines check in shape.rs, graph.rs or mod.rs.
proposal: In rate's layout pass, for each distance between two carried axes, compute cos(theta) = (r_A^2 + r_B^2 - a^2)/(2 r_A r_B) from built.running. Refuse when |cos| > 1: the input describes no shape (rule 5), so add a TrainError::PlanetsCannotMeet with the distance index. Report theta in LayoutReport as the stagger angle. Also check the tip clearance between B_j and A_(j+1), and between B and the sun, using the same station geometry.
validation: Add a law over meshed_planets and ravigneaux on a grid of sun/ring counts: every Ok result satisfies the triangle inequality on built.running, and every case that breaks it is refused. Cross-check theta by placing the axes in the plane and measuring |A-B| against the running distance.

verdict.reason: The claim holds: shape.rs builds the three distances of a meshed-planet or Ravigneaux set independently, and nothing in rate's layout pass (shape.rs:3620-3660) or anywhere else compares them. My own probe reproduces it: meshed_planets with ring 97 gives running distances r_A 21.02, r_B 39.48 and A-B 18.02, so 21.02 + 18.02 = 39.04 < 39.48. It still solves Ok. This is not new, though: docs/state.md (the residual table, about line 637, 'Two carried axes placed round the carrier') already says 'nothing checks the three form a triangle ... a layout that does not close is a fault this tool does not yet name'. The finding does not cite that entry. The documented residual gives no argument for keeping the gap, and it breaks standing rule 5 (refuse input that describes no shape). So the finding stands, but it is a known residual and does not merit high severity. The designer reaches it simply by changing the ring or sun count.
verdict.evidence: Probe /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/verify-shape-b-1: 'meshed 24/97: ... dist [Some(21.02), Some(39.48), Some(18.02)] axes [[0,1],[0,2],[1,2]]', and solve_train is Ok. The shipped 24/96 preset is exactly collinear at nominal (24 + 2*18 + 2*18 = 96), so the clearances alone decide whether it closes: 21.02 + 18.02 = 39.04 vs 38.98. The rate layout code reads only the central-to-axis distance for the radius. The gap is documented in docs/state.md: 'nothing checks the three form a triangle, and the planet-clearance layout places one axis's planets without the other's'.
verdict.proposal_note: The refusal and the stagger angle are right. Following 'find the parameter', the better long-term design makes the stagger angle theta the parameter: the A-B running distance is derived from r_A, r_B and theta, rather than a third distance closing on its own shifts. The triangle check then becomes the admissible range of theta. Whichever is done, update the docs/state.md residual row and check the tip clearance of B_j against A_(j+1) and against the sun, as proposed. Put the law over a grid of sun and ring counts, as the validation says.

title: The shipped Wolfrom preset cannot be assembled with its 3 planets at any spacing, and the note says 'sun and ring counts' about a set with no sun
claim: Preset::Wolfrom is wolfrom(18, [60, 61], 3): one planet gear meshing two held or free rings. For a single planet gear meshing rings r1 and r2, a station at angle phi exists only if (r2 - r1)*phi/(2 pi) is an integer. With a tooth difference of 1, only one station exists, so no second planet can be fitted at any spacing. The tool reports 'N planets cannot be evenly spaced: sun and ring tooth counts do not sum to a multiple of planet count'. That wording names a sun the set lacks, cites the wrong rule, and implies uneven spacing would work.
evidence: Derivation from the phase row the code documents (shape.rs:640): z_c(theta_c - phi) + z_p(psi - phi) = K (mod 2 pi) for both ring meshes with the same z_p. Subtracting the two gives (c1 - c2)*phi in 2 pi Z. With c = -60 and -61, phi must be a multiple of 2 pi. Probe P14: Wolfrom layouts [(1, 3, Some(false), Some(false), 16.338, true)], notes [planets_share_load_equally, planets_not_evenly_spaced]. The state.md:638 residual on timed planets does not help here: timing needs two gears on the planet body, and this planet has one.
proposal: (1) Ship a Wolfrom whose ring difference is a multiple of N, e.g. rings [60, 63] with N = 3, or N = 1. Keep the shape's shifts closing it, and check that the ratio docs still quote correctly. (2) Split the note: 'cannot be equally spaced' with the rule stated generically (no sun/ring wording), plus a new 'no second planet can be assembled' note where the rule admits only phi = 0. For a single-gear cluster that is gcd over the ring differences, generally the lattice rule in the next finding. (3) Update all 5 string catalogues.
validation: A law over Preset::ALL: no shipped preset raises a planets_not_evenly_spaced note. Brute-force station search (as in assembly.py) that counts how many distinct stations admit a phase, compared with the new note.

verdict.reason: The core claim holds. With one planet gear meshing rings 60 and 61, subtracting the two phase rows gives (c1 - c2)*phi in 2*pi*Z, and c1 - c2 = 1, so phi must be a multiple of 2*pi: only one station exists at any spacing. Letting the output ring turn during assembly does not help, because theta_2 is one value shared by every planet. Timing does not help either, because the planet body carries only one gear. The code's gcd rule gives 18 % 54 != 0, so the note fires, and the English catalogue's wording (sun and ring counts summing) is wrong for a Wolfrom, which has no sun, and for a stepped set. Severity is lower than claimed: the tool does warn, so the fault is a poor shipped example plus a misleading sentence, not a silent wrong answer. Proposal (1) is wrong as written. I ran wolfrom(18, [60, 63], 3) and the solve refuses: 'no profile shift brings the meshes to one axis distance'.
verdict.evidence:
Probe verify-shape-b-1 results:
- wolfrom 18 [60,61] N3: assembly Some((false,false)), notes [planets_share_load_equally, planets_not_evenly_spaced], ratio 61.
- wolfrom 18 [60,63] N3: error 'no profile shift brings the meshes to one axis distance'.
- wolfrom 18 [60,62] N2: assembly Some((true,true)), ratio 31.
- wolfrom 18 [60,61] N1: no note, ratio 61.

strings_en.toml:109 reads 'sun and ring tooth counts do not sum to a multiple of planet count'. The preset counts also appear in shape.rs:4375 and 5832, gear-cli kinematics.rs:202, arrangements.rs:1134 and tools/train_kinematics.py:658, so changing the preset moves golden and kinematics outputs.
verdict.corrected_claim: The shipped Wolfrom preset (18 / [60, 61] / 3) admits only one planet station, so it cannot be built with 3 planets. The tool warns, but with a sentence written for a simple sun-ring set, which is wrong for this set and for the stepped (Compound) set.
verdict.proposal_note: Do not ship [60, 63] with N = 3: the solve refuses it, because 1.5 modules of centre-distance difference is more than the shifts can absorb. Options that do solve are [60, 62] with N = 2 (ratio 31, assembles) or N = 1 (ratio 61, but no load sharing). Another option is a stepped-planet Wolfrom whose counts satisfy the gcd rule. Rewrite the note generically, for example 'N planets cannot be equally spaced with these tooth counts'. Add a separate 'only one planet station exists' note for the case where the congruence admits only phi = 0. Update all five catalogues, the golden corpus and tools/train_kinematics.py together.

title: The assembly rule pairs meshes across independent bodies on one planet axis, giving a false 'not evenly spaced'
claim: Shape::assembly collects every mesh from any member on the axis into one list of pairs and requires every pair to agree. That derivation holds only for gears on one rigid body (one psi). Two bodies on one carried axis each have their own psi, so meshes on different bodies impose no joint condition.
evidence: Probe P12: one carried axis with body p1 (30 teeth meshing sun 13 and ring 71) and body p2 (28 teeth meshing ring 71). Body p1 alone gives (13 + 71) % 3 = 0, which assembles, and p2 has one mesh, which always does. assembly(1) returns Some((false, false)). The pair (13,30)/(-71,28) gives 2494 % 6 = 4, so it is reported false. The panel reaches this layout: P10 shows the offer AddGear{mate: ring, on: NewBody(planet axis)} is not refused, and it adds a second body on the planet axis.
proposal: Group the pairs by planet slot (slot_of_member) before the pairwise gcd test, and AND the per-body verdicts. Simultaneous meshing stays per central member. Better still, replace the whole rule with the general congruence system (next finding), which handles this case by construction.
validation: Extend the assembly test module: two bodies on one axis with differing counts, checked against assembles_by_search run per body.

verdict.reason: In Shape::assembly, on(i) tests only whether the member's slot lies on the axis, so meshes from different bodies on one carried axis go into one pair list. The pairwise test then assumes a shared psi, and that holds only within one rigid body. The arithmetic in the probe is right: pair (13,30)/(-71,30) gives 2520 % 90 = 0, while the cross-body pair (13,30)/(-71,28) gives 2494 % 6 = 4, which yields false. The layout is reachable: the offer AddGear{mate: ring, on: NewBody(planet axis)} is not refused. The gear it adds copies the 30 teeth, which happens to agree, but the designer can then change the count. I rate it low because two independent planet gears on one pin is an unusual arrangement and the effect is a false warning, not a false assurance.
verdict.evidence: shape.rs:659-700: `let on = |i| self.axis_of_slot(self.slot_of_member(i)) == Some(axis)` with no body grouping, and the double loop over all pairs. Auditor's probe output, which I checked against the code: 'P12 assembly(1) = Some((false, false))', and 'P10 offer AddGear { mate: 2, on: NewBody(1), ring: false } refused None'.
verdict.proposal_note: Group the pairs by body (self.members[i].body) rather than by slot, and AND the per-body verdicts. The general congruence rule in finding 3 subsumes this fix, with one unknown per body. Separately, the test's assembles_by_search helper also assumes one body, so the new test must run it per body.

title: No assembly answer for meshed planets or Ravigneaux, though the condition is derivable and was brute-force verified
claim: For a replicated cluster, the unknowns are each planet body's turn W_P. Each mesh e is the congruence sum_P A[e,P] W_P = b_e (mod 1), with A[e,P] the signed count of body P's gear, b_e = z_c/N for a central mesh and 0 for a planet-planet mesh. Equal spacing holds iff y.b is an integer for every integer y with y^T A = 0. This reduces to the textbook (z_s + z_r)/N for a simple set and to the code's gcd rule for a stepped planet. For meshed planets it is (z_r - z_s)/N; for Ravigneaux it is (z_s1 + z_r)/N and (z_r - z_s2)/N. state.md says this 'condition exists there and is not written', and a test (a_planet_meshing_a_planet_has_no_answer) enshrines the None.
evidence: notes/shape-b/assembly.py computes the rule via the integer left kernel (HNF column reduction), brute-forces W on the grid k/(N*lcm) and compares with the closed forms: 60 meshed-planet, 40 Ravigneaux and 60 stepped random cases, 0 disagreements (rerun today). Probe P2: meshed planets at sun 25 / ring 96, where (96 - 25) % 3 = 2 so they cannot be spaced, report equal_spacing None and raise no note.
proposal: Make assembly a cluster rule: take all replicated axes carried by one carrier, one unknown per planet body, and build A and b as above. Decide solvability by Smith or Hermite normal form over i64: A is at most a few rows by a few columns, about 60 lines. Report it on the LayoutReport of every axis in the cluster, or better as one per-carrier layout. Remove the None arm and replace a_planet_meshing_a_planet_has_no_answer with the closed forms. Update the state.md:754 residual.
validation: Port assembly.py's brute search as a test covering simple, stepped, meshed and Ravigneaux clusters, plus two bodies on one axis. Assert the closed forms (z_r - z_s) % N and the Ravigneaux pair on the presets.

verdict.reason: This is a real gap and already a documented residual. docs/state.md ('A layout's assembly rule ... the condition exists there and is not written') and the test a_planet_meshing_a_planet_has_no_answer both record it. The documentation gives no reason to leave it unwritten, so it is not a deliberate design choice. The closed forms hold: y = (1, -1, 1) spans the left kernel for meshed planets, giving (z_r - z_s)/N, which is the textbook double-planet rule. I reran assembly.py: 160 cases, 0 disagreements. Its brute force shares the congruence model (A, b) with the rule, so it checks the lattice algebra, not the physics. The independent anchor is agreement with the textbook simple, stepped and double-planet conditions. The shipped MeshedPlanets preset reports equal_spacing None, so with sun 25 / ring 96 no warning appears.
verdict.evidence: shape.rs:676-682 returns None when the central member is carried. shape.rs:5942 asserts None for the Ravigneaux preset. The rerun of /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/notes/shape-b/assembly.py printed 'cases 160 disagreements 0'. The auditor's P14 output shows MeshedPlanets layouts (1,3,None,None,...) and (2,3,None,None,...).
verdict.proposal_note: The cluster formulation is the right unification: one unknown per planet body. It also fixes finding 2 and the single-mesh None described under missed. Keep it exact: use i64 Hermite or Smith reduction on a matrix of a few rows by a few bodies, with no floating point. The test must include a check that shares no algebra with the rule, such as the existing phase search generalised to several bodies. The rerun Python brute force shares A and b with the rule, so it cannot serve that role.

title: Reversed bending is decided by 'in more than one mesh', a topological proxy that is wrong for a gear driven, or driving, on one flank in two meshes
claim: always_reverses = meshes_of[i].len() > 1. Which flank a mesh loads depends on the sign of the torque it applies to member i, which the flow knows per case. A gear driven by two pinions (split-torque or twin-pinion drives), or a pinion driving two gears, loads the same flank in both meshes and is not reversed. It is flagged anyway, and derated under the train's switch.
evidence: Probe P1: a 60-tooth gear driven by two 20-tooth pinions, each loaded 10 Nm, with the gear reacted. Member 0 carries note gear.reversed_bending_uncorrected. With reversed_bending = true it carries gear.reversed_bending_applied, and its fatigue minimum bending width rises from 0.754 mm to 1.077 mm (x1.43, the reversed allowable). state.md's argument ('a planet's root is loaded both ways whatever the load does') holds for planets and idlers (P8 controls are correct) but is not what the code tests.
proposal: In rate, compute per case the signed torque each mesh applies to member i: the sign of c.mesh_torques[k] carried through the mesh kind's sign and the side. A member reverses in a case iff two of its non-idle meshes apply opposite signs. Replace always_reverses with that per-case value in CaseLoadings, feeding Reversal::reverses(in_case_structural, c.reverses). This moves a load fact from topology into rate, where it belongs.
validation: Law: an idler and a planet reverse in every case, a dual-driven gear and a pinion driving two gears never do, and a reversing duty reverses everything. Check with the P1 shape and the Idler, Planetary and MeshedPlanets presets.

verdict.reason: shape.rs:3373 reads `let always_reverses = |i: usize| meshes_of[i].len() > 1;`. That is a topological proxy for the flank-loading fact that docs/state.md states in physical terms ('a planet's root is loaded both ways whatever the load does'). On a planet or an idler, the torques from the two meshes about the gear's own axis have opposite signs, so the proxy is right there. On a gear driven by two pinions, or a pinion driving two gears, both meshes load the same flank. The probe's dual-drive shape is built correctly: two pinions each give +10 Nm and the gear is reacted. It gets gear.reversed_bending_uncorrected by default, and with the switch on its fatigue bending width rises by 1/0.7 (0.754 to 1.077 mm). So by default the tool shows a false statement, and with the switch on the derating is 43% too conservative.
verdict.evidence: shape.rs:3373, and gear_notes at about shape.rs:3677 calls reversal.reverses(always_reverses(i), ...). Auditor probe P1 output: 'P1 member 0 z=60 notes=["gear.reversed_bending_uncorrected"]' and 'P1 corrected member 0 notes=["gear.reversed_bending_applied"] minw_fatigue ... bending: Some(1.0772...)', against 0.7540 uncorrected, a ratio of 1.4286 = 1/0.7. Controls in P8: an idler of 25 and planets reverse, while suns and rings do not.
verdict.proposal_note: The per-case signed-torque test is right. Two of the gear's non-idle meshes applying opposite-sign torque about its own axis is exactly the physical statement in docs/state.md. Keep the note per member as an OR over cases, as now. Also check a gear whose two meshes are idle in one case and loaded in another, such as a layshaft's unselected ratio: an idle mesh should not count as either sign.

title: Tooth cycles take the max over a member's meshes, so a gear loaded on one flank by two meshes is counted half
claim: paths_seen returns max(m.paths) over a member's meshes. Its comment justifies max because a planet's two meshes 'are one path each'. But a non-replicated gear in two meshes that press the same flank has each tooth loaded twice per relative revolution. The reported cycle count is half, which is unconservative wherever the designer reads a life factor from it.
evidence: Probe P1: pinions at 3000 rpm report 209 cycles; the 60-tooth gear at 1000 rpm, meshed by both pinions on the same flank, reports 70 (one per revolution) where 139 is right. Cycles are a reported figure only (grep: nothing in gear-core reads .cycles back), so no allowable moves.
proposal: Count per flank: cycles(i) = relative revolutions x the max over its two flanks of the sum of paths of the meshes loading that flank in the case. The flank comes from the same signed-torque reading as the reversal fix. A planet then keeps 1 per flank, an idler 1 per flank, a dual-driven gear 2. Fix the paths_seen comment.
validation: Extend the tooth-cycle laws in train/mod.rs (around 9436) with a dual-drive shape: gear cycles = 2 x its revolutions; planets and idlers unchanged.

verdict.reason: wiring.rs:234-245 takes the max of m.paths over the member's meshes. The comment justifies this only for a planet ('a planet's two meshes are one path each, so the two agree'). docs/reference.md#tooth-cycles states the rule as 'once for each parallel mesh path', and a gear driven by two pinions has two parallel paths loading the same flank, so the code disagrees with its own documented rule. For the idler and the planet, max = 1 per flank is correct. In the dual-drive probe the gear turns 1000 rpm and reports 70 cycles, where the correct figure is about 139. The cycle count is reported but read by no allowable (grep finds .cycles read only in tests), so it misstates a displayed figure without moving any rating. That is why I rate it low rather than medium.
verdict.evidence: wiring.rs:241-246 is `.filter(|m| m.a == member || m.b == member).map(|m| m.paths).max()`. shape.rs:3760 computes revolutions = |t[shaft] - t[frame]| * paths_seen(i). In gear-core, .cycles is read only in train/mod.rs tests (9436, 9505, 9572, 10662, 11108). Auditor P1 output: pinion 'cycles Some(Cycles { bending: 209.0 ...' and gear 'Cycles { bending: 70.0 ...' at a 3:1 speed ratio.
verdict.proposal_note: Count by flank using the same signed-torque reading as finding 4, so that both findings share one per-case flank map: per flank, sum the paths of the meshes loading it, and take the max over the two flanks. Under a reversing duty, loaded_cycles already splits contact across flanks, so check the two rules compose. With both flanks loaded and summed per flank, a reversing duty must not double-count.

title: The reported minimum face width inverts one mesh's stress at another mesh's width, over-stating it up to 3.6x
claim: MemberRating::rated takes bending = max_k s_k(at carried_k) and width = max_k carried_k, then inverts that product. The comment says 'each figure is inverted at the width it was taken at'; the code does not do that. The correct minimum is max_k(s_k * carried_k)/allowable, valid while the answer is below every mate's width. When the governing mesh is not the widest, the product mixes two meshes. Automatic sizing is unaffected (asks runs at equal probe widths). The reported GearCase.min_face_width is wrong.
evidence: Probe P9. planetary(12,30,72,3) with all widths typed at 10 mm: planet fatigue minimum bending width 0.4513 mm. Typing only the ring at 2 mm (so a planet 0.45 mm wide would still pass) reports 1.6347 mm (3.6x), and contact goes 4.4766 to 5.1185. Line of four gears 17/25/31/43: member 1's minimum width is 8.6373 with automatic widths and 8.4256 with all typed at 10. The answer should not depend on either.
proposal: In rated(), invert each sizing mesh at its own carried_at and take the max: bending min = max_k min_face_width_bending(s_k, carried_k, allow), and likewise for contact. Drop the shared width accumulator.
validation: Law: for every preset, the member's reported min_face_width is unchanged when all mates' widths are typed at any common value at or above it, and equals the probe-pass ask.

verdict.reason: MemberRating::rated (train/mod.rs:971-981, 990-1010) takes the largest bending stress over all meshes and, separately, the largest carried_at over the meshes that size the face, then passes both to min_face_width_bending / min_face_width_contact. When the mesh with the worst stress is not the widest one, the result mixes two meshes, which contradicts the comment 'Each figure is inverted at the width it was taken at'. Because bending ∝ 1/b and contact² ∝ 1/b, s_k·carried_k and s_k²·carried_k do not depend on carried_k. So the correct minimum is max_k(s_k·carried_k)/allow, and it cannot depend on the mates' widths while the answer stays below them. The code's answer does depend on them. Automatic sizing is not affected: asks() runs rating(i, &probe_widths) with every carried_at equal to PROBE, where the product is exact.
verdict.evidence: I re-ran the auditor's probe as my own crate (probes/verify-shape-b-2). planetary(12,30,72,3), all widths 10 mm: the planet's fatigue minimum is bending 0.4513 mm, contact 4.4766 mm. Ring typed at 2 mm, sun and planet at 10: bending 1.6347 mm, contact 5.1185 mm. The planet's own bending stress is 122.61 MPa (ring mesh at 2 mm) against 33.85 MPa at 10 mm (sun mesh). 122.61×10/allow reproduces 1.6347, and the correct max(33.85×10, 122.61×2)/allow reproduces 0.4513, a factor of 3.6. Contact: 536.58² × 10 gives 5.1185, while max(501.80² × 10, 536.58² × 2) gives 4.4766. A line of four gears 17/25/31/43: member 1 gets 8.6373 with automatic widths and 8.4256 with all typed at 10, and member 2 gets 7.9929 against 7.6172.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposal is right. Accumulate bending_need = max(s_k·carried_k) and contact_need = max(s_k²·carried_k) over the loadings that size the face, and divide once, instead of calling the two helpers per mesh. In the doc on Widths/min_face_width, state the limit that the figure holds while it is at or below every mate's width, where carried = min(b, mate).

title: A point mesh's member contact stress is read at the early width while the mesh report uses the final width, so one contact gets two figures
claim: rating(i, &mesh_widths) builds point-contact Loadings from point_probes, evaluated at early_width (the box), and labels them measured_at = widths[k]. The mesh report uses rated_point at the final widths. Where a crossed member is also on a line mesh and sized larger, the two disagree. The comment 'The mesh's figure, which is the members' figure' and the cut comment 'its point contact's zone is read at the width it ends with' are therefore false for the members.
evidence: Probe P6b: crossed([17,43], 90 degrees) with a spur gear added on member 1, widths automatic, box 2 mm, final widths [2.0, 3.5254, 3.5254]. Member 0 and member 1 contact stress is 2902.238 MPa; mesh 0 p_max is 2892.964 MPa. They agree at boxes 1 and 4 only because neither patch is truncated there.
proposal: Pass rated_point into the final rating: build rating() with the patches the widths argument implies. Compute point patches only once, at final widths, since point loadings have sizes_face = false and never feed asks. point_probes can then be deleted.
validation: Law: for every point mesh and every case, the members' contact_stress equals the mesh report's max_pressure bit for bit, swept over presets plus a crossed pair with a line mesh added.

verdict.reason: The rating closure (shape.rs:3368-3431) reads the point contact's figure from point_probes, which is computed at face_of(k, early_width) (shape.rs:3358). The mesh report reads rated_point, computed at the final widths (shape.rs:3512, used at 3865). The final member rating rating(i, &mesh_widths) therefore still carries the early-width patch, labelled measured_at = widths[k]. point_probes has no other use: asks() takes a minimum width only from loadings that size the face, so a point loading's figure only ever reaches the member's contact_stress. The claim holds, but the size of the error is bounded by how much truncating the patch moves the pressure, which is small here.
verdict.evidence: Re-run of P6b, crossed([17,43], 90°) with a spur gear added on member 1, automatic widths. Box 2 mm, widths [2.0, 3.5254, 3.5254]: both members' contact stress is 2902.238 MPa, while mesh 0's p_max is 2892.964 MPa (0.32 %). At box 1 and box 4 the two agree to the digit. The code comments 'The mesh's figure, which is the members' figure' (shape.rs:3405) and 'its point contact's zone is read at the width it ends with' (shape.rs:3141) are false for the members.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposal is sound. Make rating() take the point patches as an argument (&[Option<Vec<ContactPatch>>]), pass rated_point in the final call, pass any value in the probe-pass call (it is unread there), and delete point_probes.

title: Point-mesh efficiency is taken at the early (box) width, so marking a width auto or typed at the same value changes the efficiency
claim: cut computes each mesh's efficiency from face_of(k, early_width). Rate later sizes the final width, which for a crossed member on a line mesh depends on the load. The efficiency therefore belongs to a width the result does not report, and 'inputs are the only state' is broken: the same geometry gives two efficiencies. The underlying circularity (efficiency depends on width, width on load) means the cut/rate split is not clean for point meshes.
evidence: Probe P6b, box 1: automatic widths [1.0, 3.5259, 3.5259] give mesh 0 forward efficiency 0.8429731. Typing exactly those widths gives 0.8429475. Path forward efficiency is 0.8361452 vs 0.8361198. The effect is small (about 3e-5) but it is a real discontinuity. The worm preset (P6) is immune because its width comes from recommended.
proposal: Either (a) state and apply that a crossed mesh's width is never sized by load: a member on a point mesh takes its early width and the line mesh's ask floors only the mate, or (b) iterate once: cut, rate, recompute point efficiencies at final widths, re-flow. (a) keeps the split clean and matches the existing statement that nothing rates a crossed face.
validation: Law: for every shape, solving with each automatic width replaced by Auto::fixed(result width) reproduces every mesh efficiency and path efficiency bit for bit.

verdict.reason: cut computes every mesh's sliding and at-rest efficiency at face_of(k, early_width) (shape.rs:3191-3200). early_width is the worm proportions or the manual box value. The width a crossed member finally reports, when it is also on a line mesh, is set later by that line mesh's ask. So the same geometry gives two efficiencies, depending on whether the width is automatic or typed at the value it resolved to. The same jump appears when relieved_from turns an automatic width given, seeded from the figure it showed. The worm preset is immune because its width comes from recommended.
verdict.evidence: Re-run of P6b at box 1: automatic widths [1.0, 3.5259, 3.5259] give mesh 0 forward efficiency 0.8429731 and path efficiency 0.8361452. The same widths typed give 0.8429475 and 0.8361198. At box 2: 0.8428494 against 0.8428206. At box 4: 0.8425530 against 0.8425440. P6 (worm with a spur added) gives identical efficiencies, auto or typed.
verdict.proposal_note: Option (a) is unsound. A line mesh is carried at the narrower of its two faces, min(widths[a], widths[b]) (shape.rs:3506). If the crossed member kept its box width and only the mate were floored, the line mesh would be carried at the narrow crossed width and fail its own rating. Option (b) is the right shape: after widths are settled, recompute the point efficiencies at the final faces and re-run the flow, which is linear in torque, then rate. Alternatively, state the small residual in docs/state.md with its size and sign. Either way, add the auto-versus-typed law the auditor proposes.

title: The thickness-coefficient freedom is grouped per mesh rather than per mesh group, so a shipped planetary with the ring's k typed gets an answer that depends on mesh order
claim: Presets pin the sun's k = 1.0 (arrangements.rs:750). Typing the ring's k leaves the sun given: each mesh's group sees only one given member, so the per-mesh relief is satisfied. thickness_mods then fills the planet from whichever mesh is listed first, and the internal invariant k_ring = k_planet (or, the other way round, k_sun + k_planet = 2) breaks silently.
evidence: Probe P13: planetary(12,30,72,3), ring k fixed at 1.1, relieved on that freedom: given = [true, false, true], ks [1.0, 1.0, 1.1]. With the two meshes swapped, ks [1.0, 1.1, 1.1], and the solved planet shift moves from -0.0628 to -0.2786. The module and pressure-angle freedoms a few lines below (shape.rs:4108) are already grouped per mesh group.
proposal: Group ThicknessMod as module is: one FreedomGroup per mesh_groups() component with given_at_most 1, the one just touched staying. For a component whose mesh graph has a cycle with an odd external count, k is forced to 1, so given_at_most is 0 unless the value is 1. thickness_mods is then order-independent by construction; assert it with a debug check that no mesh ends violating its rule.
validation: Law over every preset and arrangement: after relieving any member's ThicknessMod, every external mesh has k_a + k_b = 2 and every internal mesh k_a = k_b, and permuting shape.meshes leaves thickness_mods unchanged.

verdict.reason: freedoms() makes one ThicknessMod group per mesh with given_at_most 1 (shape.rs:4088-4097). The module and pressure angle, a few lines below, are grouped per mesh_groups() component. The planetary preset pins the sun's k = 1.0 (arrangements.rs:750). Relieving the ring's k leaves both the sun and the ring given: each mesh group sees at most one given member, so relief does nothing. thickness_mods() (shape.rs:1047-1078) then propagates in mesh order. Whichever given member reaches the planet first wins, and the other mesh's rule (k_a + k_b = 2 across an external mesh, k_ring = k_planet across an internal one) is silently broken. The relief laws that sweep every preset cannot catch this, because the per-mesh group is satisfied.
verdict.evidence: Re-run of P13, planetary(12,30,72,3), ring k fixed at 1.1, relieved(Some(Member(2, ThicknessMod))): given = [true, false, true], ks = [1.0, 1.0, 1.1], so the internal mesh has 1.0 ≠ 1.1. With shape.meshes swapped, ks = [1.0, 1.1, 1.1], so the external mesh has 1.0 + 1.1 ≠ 2. The solved planet shift is -0.06283 in one order and -0.27861 in the other.
verdict.proposal_note: Group per mesh_groups() component with given_at_most 1, as module is. Every preset's mesh graph is a tree, so one given k determines the whole component. The cycle case (odd external count forcing k = 1) matters only for hand-built graphs. There, thickness_mods should raise a note or refuse a contradictory given set rather than rely on a debug assertion, since rule 5 prefers saying so to failing silently.

title: A worm wheel's reported torque is the ideal read-across, 1/eta above what its teeth carry (1.62x on the worm preset)
claim: member_torque gives the driven member the driver's torque times z_b/z_a, which the comment calls 'the mesh force at its reference cylinder'. For a line contact that is exact at the pitch point. For a crossed or worm mesh, friction at the pitch point is large and the wheel's tangential force is Ft1(cos alpha_n cos gamma - mu sin gamma)/(cos alpha_n sin gamma + mu cos gamma), not Ft1/tan gamma. The reported GearCase.torque overstates the wheel's tooth load by 1/eta_mesh.
evidence: Probe P6: worm(1,40), 20 Nm, with a 40-tooth spur added on the wheel at 1:1. Wheel member torque is 800 = 20 x 40; the spur mesh downstream carries 494.4 = 800 x 0.618 (the mesh's forward efficiency 0.6180). The point contact itself is rated correctly: p.rate receives the driver torque and friction.
proposal: For a point mesh, report the driven member's torque from the screw model's normal force resolved at its own reference radius; the flow's delivered torque on that side gives the same number. Keep the driver's read-across for line meshes and say so. A shared helper removes the duplicated z_b/z_a conversion in point_contact and member_torque.
validation: Law: on every crossed or worm mesh, the driven member's GearCase.torque x paths equals the driver torque x ratio x eta in the case's direction, and matches its body's on_body when the body has no other mesh.

verdict.reason: member_torque (shape.rs:3721-3736) gives the driven member at_a·z_b/z_a for every mesh kind. For a worm or crossed mesh with friction, the driven member's tangential force at its reference radius is Fn(cos αn cos γ − μ sin γ). Its torque is therefore exactly η·(z_b/z_a)·T_driver: the friction acts at the very contact, so the wheel's teeth carry the reduced force. The comment 'the mesh force at its reference cylinder' is false for point meshes. For line meshes the read-across is the pitch-point force, a defensible convention. The per-gear case table in the UI displays this figure (TrainPanel.svelte:1252). Nothing is rated from it on a point mesh, since bending is None there and p.rate receives the driver's torque, so the error is in a displayed number only.
verdict.evidence: V1 (my addition, worm(1,40) preset alone, 20 N·m): the wheel reports torque 800.0000 and on_body 494.4369, and the mesh's forward efficiency is 0.6180461 (800 × 0.6180461 = 494.437). P6 (spur added on the wheel): the downstream spur member reports 494.437, below the wheel's 800. The wheel overstates its tooth load by 1/η = 1.62.
verdict.proposal_note: The simplest correct form: for a point mesh, the driven side's torque is (mesh torque read across) × the mesh's η in that case's direction. This is the flow's delivered torque per path, which the case already holds, so the screw model need not be called again. When the case locks (η = 0), keep the driver's pressing torque, as point_contact's comment already argues.

title: Three different rules decide what a worm thread is
claim: The three rules are: is_worm_thread (the first member of any mesh on a worm distance), member_names (the ends of the first mesh on a worm distance only), and cut's recommended widths (every point mesh on a worm distance). After AddRatio across a worm distance, the second thread gets worm proportions and is_worm_thread = true, but member_names calls it and its wheel 'Gear'.
evidence: Probe P15: after Edit::AddRatio{distance 0}, member 2 (z = 1) has is_worm_thread true and name Gear; member 3 (z = 40) has name Gear and recommended width 4.69, the wheel proportion.
proposal: Make member_names call is_worm_thread, and add an is_worm_wheel that uses the same rule. Number shared roles (Worm 1, Worm 2) as rings already are.
validation: Extend every_preset_and_arrangement_names_its_members_as_a_designer_does with a worm that has a second ratio: the name's role agrees with is_worm_thread and with recommended.is_some().

verdict.reason: The three rules differ. is_worm_thread (shape.rs:371-375) counts the first member of any mesh on a worm distance. member_names (shape.rs:731-741) names only the ends of meshes_on(d)[0]. cut's recommended (shape.rs:3131-3155) gives worm or wheel proportions to every point mesh on a worm distance. title: LayoutReport doc and note wording are stale; the load-share note is raised once per axis
claim: equal_spacing's doc says the rule is known for 'one gear on the axis meshing two central members'; it also covers stepped planets (three meshes). The note text cites the simple-set sum. A meshed-planet set is one set but gets planets_share_load_equally twice, once per replicated axis.

proposal: Rewrite the doc to match whatever rule the cluster fix lands. Raise the load-share note once per carrier. Reword the catalogue key so it is generic ('cannot be equally spaced for these tooth counts').
validation: tools/check_strings.py; a law that each carrier raises at most one load-share note.

verdict.reason: All three parts hold. (1) The LayoutReport.equal_spacing doc at shape.rs:2999-3001 says the rule covers "one gear on the axis meshing two central members". Shape::assembly (shape.rs:669-716), its own doc (shape.rs:640-667) and reference.md:1780 all state the general rule for any number of meshes (stepped planets included), so the struct doc is stale. (2) The catalogue text in all five languages (strings_en.toml:109 and the pt/de/zh-Hans/zh-Hant equivalents) gives the simple-set sum "sun and ring tooth counts do not sum to a multiple of planet count". The shipped Wolfrom preset (arrangements.rs:944, wolfrom(18,[60,61],3)) has no sun, yet it fires this note. (3) Notes are pushed once per replicated axis (shape.rs:3662-3663), so MeshedPlanets gets the identical load-share note twice.

The Wolfrom pairs are (-60,18) and (-61,18). The rule gives (-60*18+61*18) mod (3*18) = 18, which is not zero, so the verdict is 'no' and the English blames a sun the set lacks. Two axes on one carrier can have different counts, so do not just keep the first. A plain dedup of identical notes would also remove the MeshedPlanets duplicate. title: A mesh with no distance silently borrows distance 0's axial clearance and tolerances
claim: play_of, at_band and member_backlash all use shape.distance_of(k).unwrap_or(0). Either every mesh has a distance, in which case the fallback is dead and should be an invariant, or it does not, in which case the backlash is computed with another distance's tolerances.
evidence: Read. build() presumably refuses a mesh with no distance, which would make the fallback unreachable; not confirmed.
proposal: Carry each mesh's distance index in Built (it is known at build time) and index it directly. Delete the three unwrap_or(0) calls.
validation: clippy plus the existing suite. A debug_assert that every mesh has a distance.

verdict.reason: The fallback cannot fire, so the title's claim that the mesh 'silently borrows distance 0's clearance and tolerances' is wrong. Shape::build, which every cut goes through (shape.rs:3120), refuses a mesh with no distance before play_of, at_band or member_backlash is reached: `let d = self.distance_of(k).ok_or(TrainError::Wiring(super::WiringError::NotAMesh(k)))?;` at shape.rs:2838-2840. The edits' well_formed invariant (edits.rs:853-856) also refuses `mesh {k} across no distance`. What does hold is the auditor's first branch: the three unwrap_or(0) calls at shape.rs:3521, 3550 and 3566 are unreachable defaults that hide an invariant. BuiltMesh (shape.rs:2428-2432) drops the distance index build() already found, so the cut looks it up three more times by a linear search.
verdict.evidence: shape.rs:2836-2840 in build_cached; cut() calls shape.build(...) at shape.rs:3120 before the backlash closures at 3518-3574. BuiltMesh has only kind, running and contact.
verdict.corrected_claim: A mesh with no distance never reaches the rating: build() refuses it with WiringError::NotAMesh. The three distance_of(k).unwrap_or(0) calls in cut() are dead defaults that hide an invariant build() has already enforced, and they repeat a lookup build() has already done.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposal is sound: add `distance: usize` to BuiltMesh, set it from the `d` found at shape.rs:2838, and index shape.distances[built.meshes[k].distance] at the three sites. No debug_assert is needed, because build() already returns an error. This is code hygiene, not a correctness fix.

title: A still load's derived torque decides the flow direction from its stale manual value; relief's seeding locks the wrong answer in
claim: The flow-direction weight of a load with given speed 0 is `if l.torque.manual < 0.0 { -1 } else { 1 }`, read even when the torque is automatic (derived). The derived torque's manual value is a stale seed, so it decides which end drives. relieve_case writes the solved torque back into that manual value, and the next solve then reverses the flow. The wrong answer is a stable fixed point.
evidence: Probe train-mod-b `stale2`: pair [17,43]; load 1: torque given 2 N·m, speed derived; load 2: speed given 0, torque derived, seeded -5. Round 0: output reaction 4.97510 = 2·2.5294·0.98345, pinion torque 2 (correct: input drives). relieve_case seeds +4.9751. Round 1 and every later round: output 5.14396 = 2·2.5294/0.98345, pinion torque 2.0337 (output driving the input). Seeding +5 or -5 without relief shows the same split. Relief accepts this configuration (m=1: one speed given, 2+0-1 = 1 torque given).
proposal: Never read an automatic figure. For a given-speed load at 0 rpm, set the weight so that the given torques do positive work on the impending motion. Build unit_i from each still port as now. Then choose each still port's sign so that Σ_{loads with given torque} T_j·u_j > 0. Use the port's own torque sign only when that torque is given. If no given torque does work, return NothingDrives as now.
validation: New law: for every preset and every case, the solve is invariant to the manual value of any automatic figure (sweep seeds ±1, ±1e3). Also relieve_case followed by solve_train must equal solve_train, i.e. relief is idempotent on the answer. The stall pair must give output = T_in·i·η.

verdict.reason: Holds as stated. At mod.rs:4413-4419 the weight of a given-speed load at 0 rpm is `if l.torque.manual < 0.0 { -1 } else { 1 }`, and that line runs whether `l.torque.auto` is set or not. relieve_case (mod.rs:3660-3666) writes the solved torque back into `manual`, so the next solve can read the opposite sign. The effect is worse than the auditor showed: on a worm it decides whether the case solves at all.
verdict.evidence: I rebuilt the auditor's probe as probe_verify_train_mod_b_1. `stale2` (pair 17/43; input torque given +2, speed derived; output speed given 0, torque derived, seeded -5). Round 0: output 4.975099 = 2·2.5294·0.98345, i.e. the input drives. relieve_case then seeds +4.9751. Rounds 1-3: output 5.143957 = 2·2.5294/0.98345, and the pinion's torque becomes 2.03366, i.e. the output drives. The answer then stays there. New scenario `wormstale` (Worm preset, same case shape): seed +5 gives solved=false with note train.load_shared and both torques 0; seed -5 gives solved=true with output 49.44 N·m. The seed is an automatic figure the user never gave, yet it flips the verdict. Physically only the input's +2 N·m is given and the output's torque is its reaction, so the input drives and round 0 is the right answer.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposal is sound: pick each still port's sign so that the given torques do positive work, and read a port's own torque sign only when that torque is given. It does not fix a second fault in the same weight (see missed): the ±1 stands in for an infinitesimal impending speed but is added in rpm units beside real rpm. Fix both together. Make the impending motion a perturbation that only decides meshes whose relative speed from the given speeds is exactly zero; do not add it into `unit`.

Load at 2: torque Auto::automatic(seed), speed Auto::fixed(0.0). This is a stall case, output held still. I solved it for seeds ±1e-9, ±1, ±1e3. I then ran solve_train and relieve_case alternately for 4 rounds starting from seed -5. I repeated all of it on Preset::Worm.build(), using chain_ends for the ports. The reference is the ordinary driving case's path report from the same train: pair ratio -2.52941, forward η 0.98345, backward η 0.98345; worm ratio -40, forward η 0.61805, backward η 0 (self-locking). Only the input's +2 N·m is given, and the output's torque is only its reaction. So the given torque is the only thing that can do work on the impending motion, the input drives, and the correct output reaction is T_in·|i|·η_fwd.
repro.observed:
PAIR 17/43
- Negative seed (-1e-9, -1, -1e3): output torque 4.975099 = 2·2.52941·0.98345, which is correct (input drives).
- Positive seed (1e-9, 1, 1e3): output torque 5.143957 = 2·2.52941/0.98345, which is wrong (output drives the input). The error is +3.4%, i.e. 2(1-η), in the non-conservative direction for the pinion.
- Only the sign of an automatic figure the user never gave decides which answer comes out; its size plays no part (1e-9 behaves like 1e3).
- Relief from seed -5:
  - Round 0 is correct (4.975099).
  - relieve_case then writes the solved reaction back as a positive seed (4.9751).
  - Rounds 1-3 give 5.143957, and the seed settles at 5.144. The wrong answer is a stable fixed point.
- Relief keeps the toggles as they were: input torque given / speed derived, output torque derived / speed given.

WORM
- Negative seed: solved=true, output 49.44369 = 2·40·0.61805, which is correct.
- Positive seed: solved=false, note train.load_shared, both torques 0. The self-locking backward η=0 is taken as the driving direction.
- Relief: round 0 solves correctly. relieve_case seeds +49.4437, and every later round refuses the case.
- So one relief turns a correctly solved case into a refusal, permanently.

WHERE IT IS
mod.rs:4413-4419 reads `else if l.torque.manual < 0.0 { -1.0 } else { 1.0 }` without checking l.torque.auto. mod.rs:3660-3666 is relieve_case writing `l.torque.manual = (s.torque*1e4).round()/1e4` for an automatic torque.

REACHABILITY
The shipped LoadCase::back_driving gives its still load's torque, so it is not affected. The fault needs a given-speed-0 load whose torque is derived. That is an ordinary locked-output/stall case a user can build by toggling in the panel, and relief accepts it (m=1).
repro.note:
Reproduced by execution. The ledger claim and the verifier's worm extension both hold exactly.

**Severity: high.**
- It gives a wrong answer silently: 3.4% on the pair, and on a worm a correct solve becomes a refusal.
- The only input that decides it is a hidden automatic value.
- The one path that rewrites that value, relief, drives it to the wrong fixed point. The flip is not merely possible: on this worm case, relief then solve always ends at the refusal.
- Only the rarity of the configuration keeps it from critical.

**Correctness reference.** Taken from the train's own ordinary-case path efficiencies, plus the physical argument that only the given torque can do work. A tool that shares no code would be better; the check is the closed forms 2·i·η versus 2·i/η, which match to 6 digits.

**Fix direction** (as the ledger proposes):
- Never read `torque.manual` when `torque.auto` is set.
- Choose each still port's impending sign so the given torques do positive work.
- Keep that choice separate from the rpm sum `unit`, as the verifier notes.

**Laws to add:**
- Every preset and case is invariant to the seeds of automatic figures (sweep ±1e-9, ±1, ±1e3, as above).
- `solve_train ∘ relieve_case == solve_train` on the answer.

title: Path backlash min/max put every distance at the same end of its tolerance, which is not a worst-case band
claim: backlash_at sums coefficient·row_play[band] with one band index shared by every mesh: all distances at minus, all at nominal, or all at plus. An internal mesh loses play where an external one gains it, and separate distances are independent. So the reported minimum and maximum are not the extremes. The train can report positive minimum play where the parts can bind. The document states the rule ('the band being every distance at the same end of its own tolerance') but gives no argument that it is the bound.
evidence: Probe `band2`: pair 17/43 then 20/45 internal with ±0.03 mm. Train minimum 0.01612° at the ring. Independent stack (pair min / 2.25 + internal min) = -0.01859°: interference is possible and the train says it is not. The train's maximum 0.09126 equals the internal part's maximum alone, so the pair adds nothing at max. The nominals agree exactly (0.054160). Probe `band3`, pair then each preset: train min above stack min for Wolfrom (0.00128 vs 0.0), Compound (0.00245 vs 0.00157) and Planocentric (0.00781 vs 0.0); train max below stack max (0.09741 vs 0.09869, 0.18940 vs 0.19721).
proposal: Correlate only what one distance shares. Group meshes by the distance they cross (MeshReport already knows it). For each distance d, form f_d(t) = Σ_{k on d} c_k·play_k[t] and take its min and max over the three band points. Report min = Σ_d min_t f_d and max = Σ_d max_t f_d, with nominal as now. A set's sun and ring meshes share one distance and stay correlated; separate distances become a true worst-case stack. Update reference.md:2571 to match.
validation: Law: for every preset alone and every preset after a pair, the train's path band equals the sum of the parts' own bands referred through the ratio (as probe band3 computes). Law: min ≤ every one of the 3^D corner evaluations ≤ max, checked by brute force over the distances.

verdict.reason: The code does what the claim says. row_play is three points (all distances at minus, at nominal, at plus). backlash_at sums coefficient·row_play[band] with one band index shared by every mesh (mod.rs:3465-3479), and Backlash::banded takes min/max over only those three sums. Where one train has meshes on independent distances whose play moves opposite ways (external vs internal), or where the end-points are not monotone, the reported band is not the worst case. The comment at shape.rs:3543 and reference.md:2571 state the rule but do not argue it. I lowered severity from high because each mesh's own backlash (MeshReport, member_backlash) is still banded correctly and still shows the negative minimum. Only the path figure understates it.
verdict.evidence: Re-ran `band2`: pair 17/43, then 20/45 internal on its own distance at ±0.03 mm. The internal part alone reports a minimum of -0.018593° (it can bind). The train path reports minimum +0.016116° and maximum 0.091265°, which equals the internal part's maximum alone. The independent stack (pair/2.25 + internal) is min -0.018593, max 0.125973. The nominals agree exactly at 0.054160, so the referral through the ratio is right. Re-ran `band3`: Wolfrom train min 0.00128 vs stack 0.0; Compound 0.00245 vs 0.00157; Planocentric 0.00781 vs 0.0 (max 0.18940 vs 0.19721). All-external chains (Spur, Idler, Layshaft, Crossed) agree exactly, as expected when every play rises with its distance.
verdict.proposal_note: Grouping by distance is the right correction. It keeps the sun/ring meshes of a set correlated, since they share one distance, and makes independent distances stack. Within a distance take min and max of f_d over the three points, as proposed. Keep the band's endpoints labelled as a sum of per-distance extremes in reference.md. The brute-force 3^D law is cheap on the presets.

title: Tooth-cycle ceilings are taken on float products of exact ratios, so whole counts come out one high (or one per actuation high when reversing)
claim: The turns are (speed_s/speed_port)·(range/360)·actuations in f64, times paths_seen. When the exact count is an integer, rounding error puts it a few ulp above, and ceil adds a whole engagement. On a reversing duty the per-actuation ceil adds a whole actuation count.
evidence: Real code (probe `ceil`, planetary 12/16/44, 3 planets, 360°×10 at the carrier): sun non-reversing 111 (exact 44/12·10·3 = 110); reversing bending 120 (exact 110, +9%); 7 actuations gives 78 (exact 77). 12/13/38 gives 96 (exact 95). Emulation ceil_sweep.py over 33,600 sun/ring/N/range/actuation combinations: 606 mismatches, e.g. 12/32/3 at 90°×1000 reversing gives 3000 against exact 2000 (+50%).
proposal: Snap to the nearest integer before ceil: `fn ceil_count(x) { let r = x.round(); if (x - r).abs() <= 16.0 * f64::EPSILON * x.abs().max(1.0) { r } else { x.ceil() } }`. Use it in loaded_cycles for both branches. Better still, carry the exact Ratio speeds (motion_in returns Ratio) into turns, so the only float factor is range/360.
validation: Property test: for random exact ratios p/q, ranges k·360/n and actuations, loaded_cycles equals the ceil computed in Fraction arithmetic (ceil_sweep.py's reference). The existing test at mod.rs:10606 re-derives the same float formula and cannot catch this; compare it against a rational reference instead.

verdict.reason: Holds. loaded_cycles applies ceil to an f64 built as (per[s]/per[port])·(range/360)·actuations·paths_seen. When the exact count is an integer, rounding error lands it just above and ceil adds one. Because the reversing branch applies ceil per actuation, the excess there is multiplied by the number of actuations. The existing test re-derives the same float formula, so it cannot notice.
verdict.evidence: Re-ran `ceil` (planetary 12/16/44, 3 planets, sweep at the carrier). Non-reversing 360°×10: sun 111, exact 110 (Fraction: 44/12·10·3 = 110). Reversing: 120, exact 110 (+9%). 360°×7: 78, exact 77. 180°×1000 reversing: 6000 bending, where the exact per-actuation 11/2 legitimately ceils to 6, so that one is by design. 12/13/38 non-reversing gives 96, exact 95. The test at mod.rs:10606-10640 computes `each.ceil() * n` from f64 ratio products, the same arithmetic as the code under test.
verdict.proposal_note: Prefer the exact route over an epsilon snap: the snap tolerance (16·EPS) is itself a magic number. motion_in returns exact Ratio values, so form the count as ceil((p·range·act·paths)/(q·360)). The numerator and denominator are integer-valued f64s, exact below 2^53 for any integer-degree range. A correctly-rounded division of two exact values returns an exact integer quotient exactly, so ceil is then right with no tolerance. Only a non-integer range_degrees needs any care. The validation should compare against Fraction arithmetic, as proposed.

title: An intermittent duty's sweep port is never checked: out of range panics, held gives silent zero cycles, still gives a count that depends on rpm
claim: `speeds[port]` indexes with Duty::Intermittent::at unchecked, so an at beyond the train's bodies panics (a wasm trap). An at on a held body or ground gives per[port] == 0, so every member reports 0 cycles with no note. Train::hold removes the case's loads at the body but leaves the duty there, so holding a set's carrier (the default duty port) zeroes every fatigue cycle. An at on a load given at 0 rpm falls back to `unit`, whose entries mix rpm with the unit weight ±1, so the count scales with the other load's rpm.
evidence: Probe (earlier session's run, reproduced in probe_output_first.txt): pair, duty at 3 or 99 gives a panic at mod.rs:4527:36 'index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 3'. Probe `dutyheld`: duty at 0 gives cycles 0/0 on both gears, notes []. Probe `holdcarrier`: planetary 12/30/72, hold(2) and release(3) leave the duty at 2 and all three members report 0 cycles. Probe `diffstill`: ring given 0 rpm, duty at the ring, 360°×10: sun cycles 77,118 at 3000 rpm against 7,689 at 300 rpm.
proposal: Validate before counting: refuse a case whose duty port is not an open port of the train, the way LoadPort refuses loads, and reuse TrainError::LoadPort or add DutyPort. If the duty port does not turn in the case (speeds[port] == 0), give a case note ('the sweep is measured at a body that does not turn in this case') and no cycles, rather than falling back to `unit`. Make hold() move a duty at the held body to the case's reacted port, as set_duty chooses it.
validation: Law over every preset: for every body b, a case with duty at b either solves with non-zero cycles on every loaded member or carries the new note or refusal, and it never panics. Also a hold/release edit law: after any hold, every fatigue case either counts cycles or says why not.

verdict.reason: Holds, and there is a fourth route. Nothing checks the duty port: speeds[port] at mod.rs:4527 indexes unchecked, whereas load entries are refused as TrainError::LoadPort at mod.rs:4346. Train::hold (conditions.rs:1052) drops the case's loads at the held body but leaves the duty there. drop_orphans (conditions.rs:~1219) goes further and rewrites a duty at a removed body to GROUND. Both routes then count zero cycles with no note. Where the sweep body is still, the `unit` fallback mixes rpm with ±1, so the count is meaningless. Part of this overlaps edit-ops[5] and graph-ops[5] (the held/ground duty); the panic and the still-port fallback are this finding's own.
verdict.evidence: New scenario `dutyoob` (pair, fatigue duty at=3 and at=99): panic 'index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 3' at mod.rs:4527:36; the same with index 99. A wasm build traps here. `dutyheld` (duty at 0): cycles 0/0 on both gears, notes []. `holdcarrier` (12/30/72, hold(2), release(3)): the case solves, all three members report bending 0 / contact 0, and there are no notes. `diffstill` (ring given 0 rpm, duty 360°×10 at the ring): sun cycles 77,118 at 3000 rpm against 7,689 at 300 rpm, for the same geometric sweep.
verdict.proposal_note: The fixes are right. Refuse a duty port that is not an open port, as LoadPort does. Give a note when the sweep body does not turn, and never fall back to `unit` (which is in mixed units). Carry the duty along on hold. Also make drop_orphans refuse, or say something, when it grounds a duty rather than doing it silently. Deserializing a document, and the wasm boundary, should run the same check so that no JSON can trap.
