title: carrier_driven_efficiency uses |R| and is wrong for a 3K set with a negative ratio
claim: `1/(|R|(1−η₀)+η₀)` holds only for R > 0, where the held central member drives in the carrier frame. For the same Wolfrom with its rings swapped (R < 0) the correct form is `1/η = 1 + (1−R)(1/η₀ − 1)`. The function and docs/reference.md present the relation as covering 'the 3K family with the carrier driving, one central member held and the other the output', which includes the negative case. The crate's flow gets the negative case right; only the closed form offered as a design tool is wrong. Its tests (arrangements.rs:1656, 1690) use only positive ratios.
evidence: notes/kinematics-flow/cde_sign.py (independent carrier-frame power balance) and cde_mirror.py (mirror of the crate flow), Wolfrom planet 18, rings 60/61, η₀ = 0.98. Hold 60, output 61: R = 61, independent 0.454545, cde 0.454545, crate 0.454545. Hold 61, output 60: R = -60, independent 0.445455, crate 0.445455, cde(|R|) 0.458716. Rings 69/72 with planets 21/24: R = -10.5, η₀ = 0.98, independent 0.809917 against cde 0.840336 (3.0 points high). At η₀ = 0.95: 0.62295 against 0.67797.
proposal: Write it signed: η = 1/(R(1−η₀)+η₀) for R ≥ 1 and η = 1/(1+(1−R)(1/η₀−1)) for R < 0. Better, express it through Pennestrì's `power` with the carrier input, which already chooses w, and delete the separate closed form. Correct the doc sentence at reference.md:1990 to state the sign condition.
validation: Extend the_hula_efficiency_is_the_reduction_and_the_meshes to swapped-ring Wolfroms (negative R) and assert agreement with the shape's flow to 1e-9.

verdict.reason: This holds on the crate's own fixture. The 'plain' hula [19,18,18,17] used in the_circulating_power_is_the_reductions_worth has R = -8.5, and the |R| form overstates its efficiency by 1.5 points. The existing test only compares the closed form on [n+1,n,n-1,n], all with R > 0. I derived the carrier-frame balance by hand. With the output ring driving in the carrier frame, η = 1/(R(1−η₀)+η₀), valid for R > 1. With the held ring driving, η = η₀/(1 − R(1−η₀)) = 1/(1+(1−R)(1/η₀−1)), valid for R < 0. The function is test-only, but reference.md:1990 and :712 present it as the design relation for the whole family.
verdict.evidence: Probe bin cde, hula with search off, addendum 0.8, cutter 12, arranged(&[2],1,3). [19,18,17,18]: R 324, flow 0.274486, cde 0.274486. [19,18,18,17]: R -8.5, η₀ 0.991817, flow 0.927315, cde(|R|) 0.942175, negative-branch form 0.927315. [17,18,18,19]: R 9.5, flow = cde = 0.934966. [61,60,59,60]: R 3600, flow = cde = 0.097308. The only callers are arrangements.rs:1664/1693/1712 (tests), all with R > 0.
verdict.proposal_note: Prefer one signed expression: η = η₀/(η₀ + (1−η₀)·max(R,1−R)·…) is awkward, so simpler still is to derive it from Pennestrì's power() with the carrier as input, which already picks the rolling-power sign w, and delete the standalone formula. If the formula stays, add [19,18,18,17] (R = -8.5) to the_hula_efficiency_is_the_reduction_and_the_meshes, since it is already a fixture.

title: train_kinematics.py and hula_kinematics.py never read the crate, so no crate defect can make them fail
claim: CLAUDE.md lists these as 'the crate against derivations that share no code with it'. train_kinematics.py compares its rigid-body derivation with `crate_rows`, a Python restatement of the row formula ('the relation gear_core::kinematics writes, restated'), built from the script's own topology definitions. It never runs gear-cli or reads the corpus. A frame on the wrong body in shape.rs or wiring.rs, a wrong MeshKind sign, or a mis-numbered slot in an arrangement is invisible to it, and those are exactly the faults kinematics.rs:66-71 says lock-up cannot catch and 'the cross-check does'. hula_kinematics.py compares against `closed(z)`, its own Python formula. Its 'integration' (rolling(), lines 33-50) adds a θ-independent constant 200,000 times, so it is the instantaneous relation multiplied by STEPS and cannot show any position dependence. train_kinematics.py:59-62 cites it as the answer to doubts about exactly that.
evidence: Read both scripts: no subprocess, no corpus path, no gear-cli call. Ran them: all ok. In rolling(), dphi_w = -dth*e_a/(s_a*r[1]) and the phi_out increment use only constants, so the loop equals steps*constant.
proposal: Make each tool read the crate's numbers: parse tools/golden/<kinematics>.txt (as breakaway.py does with graph.txt) or run `gear-cli kinematics`, map its bodies to the script's topology by name, and compare speeds exactly as rationals (the harness prints `total ratio -43/17`). Delete crate_rows and closed() once the crate's output replaces them. For hula, either remove the pseudo-integration and say it is the instantaneous relation, or make it genuinely position-dependent (the true pitch-point geometry as the crank turns, e.g. finite tooth-contact positions) if the wobble is really worth doubting. Run the tools in CI, since they are cheap.
validation: Before trusting: in a worktree, flip a ring's sign in arrangements::wolfrom or move a mesh's frame in wiring.rs, regenerate the corpus, and confirm the rewritten tool fails. The current tools stay green under that mutation.

verdict.reason: Both scripts are self-contained. There is no subprocess, no corpus path and no gear-cli call; train_kinematics.py imports only sys and fractions. train_kinematics.py compares its rigid-body derivation with crate_rows, a Python restatement of the row formula built from the script's own topologies, so it validates the formula but not the crate's assembly (frame, MeshKind sign, slot numbering). hula_kinematics.py's rolling() adds a θ-independent increment STEPS times, so it is the instantaneous relation times a constant. train_kinematics.py:59-62 nonetheless cites it as the answer to the wobble doubt. Severity is medium rather than high: the formula check has real value, and the crate's assembly is partly held elsewhere (flow tests against Pennestrì on every arrangement, the golden corpus). tools-ci #0 reports the same thing.
verdict.evidence: tools/train_kinematics.py:69-70 imports sys and fractions only. Lines 298-322 hold crate_rows ('The relation gear_core::kinematics writes, restated'). tools/hula_kinematics.py:35-52: dphi_w = -dth*e_a/(s_a*r[1]) and the phi_out increment use only constants of z, never phi or theta. closed() at :55 is a Python Willis formula. grep for subprocess/golden/gear-cli in both scripts finds nothing (only breakaway.py reads the corpus).
verdict.proposal_note: Reading tools/golden kinematics output (or `gear-cli kinematics`) and comparing exact rationals is the right fix. Keep the derivation-versus-row comparison as a second assertion rather than deleting crate_rows: it is what checks that the row formula itself is right. For hula, delete the pseudo-integration and the docstring claim; a position-dependent check would need a real tooth-contact model and is not worth it.

title: breakaway.py is not independent of the crate: it reimplements the same 2^M search, filters and max-efficiency choice
claim: Its docstring says 'Nothing below is the crate's assignment search or its power filter'. But `efficiency()` loops itertools.product((0,1), repeat=M), writes the same 'driver whole, driven at η' per-unit torques, applies the same 'each driver works' and 'loss ≥ 0' filters, and returns max(found), which is flow.rs's algorithm line for line in NumPy. A fault in the model or its tie-break (for example choosing the wrong branch among several consistent ones) would be reproduced, not detected. It does read the crate's output from the corpus, which is good.
evidence: Side-by-side read of breakaway.py:121-158 and flow.rs:223-349. The multi-branch case is real: notes/kinematics-flow/flow_study.py found more than one consistent assignment with distinct efficiency in 5,476/18,000 Wolfrom, 5,978/18,000 hula and 9,484/72,000 compound cases. Both implementations resolve them by the same max().
proposal: Base the independent check on a different formulation. Either the carrier-frame Pennestrì/Del Castillo power-ratio method for 3K and compound sets (closed form per preset, as cde_sign.py does for the Wolfrom), or a direct quasi-static simulation that integrates the friction law with sign(v_rel) from the actual speeds rather than from assumed directions. Fix the docstring.
validation: Mutate flow.rs to take min instead of max among positive efficiencies, or to drop the loss filter, then regenerate the corpus. The current breakaway.py stays green under the second mutation if its own filter is changed the same way. An independent formulation fails.

verdict.reason: breakaway.py:121-158 is flow.rs's algorithm in NumPy: itertools.product over 2^M, driver torque whole and driven side at η, a 'works' filter, loss ≥ 0, and max(found). Its docstring (lines 16-17) says 'Nothing below is the crate's assignment search or its power filter', which is false. What is genuinely its own is the signed efficiency (output power over input power, negative where the output must be driven too), and that is exactly the breakaway question it was written for, so it still earns its place for that narrower check. A fault in the loss model or in the max tie-break would be reproduced, not detected. Severity is low, because the crate's flow is also held to Pennestrì's closed form on every arrangement in the crate's own tests.
verdict.evidence: breakaway.py:129-156 against flow.rs:223-349: the same per_unit torque (on()), the same consistency test (driving power ≤ 1e-12 with the opposite sign convention), the same loss filter, and `return max(found)` against `efficiency > b.efficiency`. The auditor's flow_study out_study.txt records multiple consistent branches in 5476/18000 Wolfrom and 5978/18000 hula cases, so the tie-break matters.
verdict.proposal_note: 'A quasi-static simulation with sign(v_rel)' does not remove the ambiguity. The direction of power across a mesh depends on torque sign as well as relative speed, which is the same non-linearity. The carrier-frame closed forms per preset are the workable independent route, as derived by hand for the 3K case in finding 3. Fix the docstring now in any case.

title: flow::solve's branch choice is 'maximum efficiency', while its comment says 'first consistent' and 'a second genuinely different one would be a finding'; multiple branches are common
claim: The comment claims two consistent assignments arise only for a zero-power mesh and 'give one answer'. Measured, a second consistent assignment with a different efficiency (always 0, torques about 10× larger, the output delivering power) exists in about 30 % of Wolfrom and hula cases. Only the max() rule excludes it. The rule is correct there but stated nowhere as the model's selection principle, and the physical criterion (a derived output absorbs power) is not what the code tests.
evidence: notes/kinematics-flow/wolfrom_case2.py, Wolfrom 18/60/61 with carrier forward: dirs (0,1) eff 0.453562 (= Pennestrì 1/(R+(1−R)η₀)) and dirs (1,0) eff 0.0 with ring torques −266.8/+265.8, both passing the consistency and loss filters. flow_study.py: 'multi' counts 5,476/18,000 Wolfrom, 5,978/18,000 hula, 9,484/72,000 compound, 2,820/72,000 Ravigneaux. No case had two distinct positive efficiencies.
proposal: State the rule in the comment and docs/reference.md: of the self-consistent flows, the one where every derived (unknown-torque) load absorbs power. Implement that as a filter, `shaft_torques[s]*speed[s] <= zero` for each derived output, keep max() only as the tie-break for vacuous zero-power meshes, and add the Wolfrom case as a test.
validation: Test: for the Wolfrom forward case the rejected branch is rejected by the new filter, not only by the max. A sweep asserting at most one consistent flow survives the filter (up to zero-power meshes) over all presets.

verdict.reason: The comment is inaccurate, and so is docs/reference.md. The code keeps the most efficient consistent assignment (`efficiency > b.efficiency`), not the first. A second, physically wrong branch really does pass both the direction filter and the loss filter in the crate's own solve. The proposal is wrong, though: the flow also serves cases where the derived body is the driver.
verdict.evidence: Probe /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/verify-kinematics-flow-2 calls the real gear_core::train::flow::solve on the Wolfrom case 18/60/61 (bodies g, carrier, ring1 held, ring2, planet; carrier torque 1). NaN efficiencies were used to allow one assignment at a time. Only (F,B) gives Ok(eff 0.453561892), which is Pennestri's 1/(R+(1-R)eta0). Only (B,F) gives Ok(eff 0.0), with ring2 power +265.84 (the output delivering power). (F,F) and (B,B) give Inconsistent. The loop runs in bit order 0,1,2,3 = (F,F),(B,F),(F,B),(B,B), so a 'first consistent' rule would return eff 0 for the Wolfrom. In practice max() is what selects the answer; it is not a tie-break. docs/reference.md:1805-1812 says the flow makes 'the same decision' as the closed form, including condition 2, 'the output has to absorb ... T_out w_out <= 0'. The flow tests no such condition: its only energy filter is total loss >= 0 (flow.rs:319-322).
verdict.proposal_note: Do not implement 'every derived (unknown-torque) load absorbs power'. When the same Wolfrom is given an absorbing output torque (-10 at ring2) with the carrier derived, the solve correctly returns eff 0.4536 with the derived carrier delivering +22.05. solve's own comment (flow.rs:217-221) says a known driver is not required. The proposed filter would reject that valid flow. What to do instead: fix the comment at flow.rs:342-346 and docs/reference.md:1805 to state the actual rule. Among the self-consistent, loss-making flows, keep the one of greatest efficiency: for a fixed given output this means the least input, and for a fixed given input the most delivered output. Name the eff-0 branch it excludes (a derived port delivering power, all of it dissipated). A test that pins the rule would help. Note that switching to 'first consistent' would already fail the Wolfrom-vs-Pennestri laws, so today the rule is protected only indirectly.

title: The flow's rank and consistency are decided with float tolerances (1e-12 absolute pivot, 1e-9 relative), unlike the exact kinematics
claim: least_squares_exact picks pivots with `v > 1e-12` (absolute, whatever the tooth-count scale) and calls a residual inconsistent above `1e-9 * scale`. Undetermined against solvable is a structural rank question, which kinematics.rs and ratio.rs argue must not be 'a rank somebody chose'. Per-unit entries are tooth counts times η (tens), so the absolute 1e-12 threshold works only by scale. ZERO = 1e-12 is written once but reused as a power threshold whose correctness depends on M and on how badly the elimination is conditioned (hula circulation is hundreds to one).
evidence: Code read. The function is named 'least_squares_exact' but is float Gauss-Jordan with a partial pivot. The structure (which bodies' torques are known, and the mesh incidence) is exactly the rowspace question System::torques already answers in rationals.
proposal: Decide Undetermined and Inconsistent once, exactly, with System::torques on the lossless rows (applied = Asked, rational). A zero or negative η does not change the incidence pattern, and η > 0 does not change the rank generically. Then run the lossy float solve only on a system already known to be square and nonsingular. Scale the pivot test relative to the row norm, and name the two tolerances with their derivation (machine epsilon × condition estimate).
validation: A law: for every preset and case, flow::Refused::Undetermined occurs exactly when the exact lossless torque solve has a residual, over all presets with η sampled in (0, 1].

verdict.reason: Partly holds. The literals are real and underived: an absolute pivot of 1e-12, a relative residual of 1e-9, ZERO=1e-12 reused as a power tolerance, and a float routine named `least_squares_exact`. But no wrong Undetermined/Inconsistent decision was shown, and the proposal rests on a false premise. A zero efficiency does change the incidence pattern (factor = max(eta,0) removes the driven member's entry), and that change is exactly what gives a locked mesh its 'holds' answer. So the lossless exact rows cannot decide consistency.
verdict.evidence: flow.rs:171 `.filter(|(_, v)| *v > 1e-12)`, :393-396 `> 1e-9 * scale`, :180 ZERO used at :309, :320, :329. Probe: a single pair (17 to 43, frame ground), wheel given -5 N·m driving along its speed, the other member free. With backward eta 0.0 the result is Ok(eff 0.0) (the mesh holds). With backward eta 0.5 or 1.0 the result is Err(Inconsistent). The auditor's law ('Undetermined exactly when the exact lossless solve has a residual') is therefore false at eta = 0. It also conflates Undetermined (rank) with a residual, which is Inconsistent. Magnitudes: per-unit entries are tooth counts of order 10-300, so rounding residue after elimination is about 1e-14, two orders below the absolute pivot. Nothing breaks at realistic counts. The threshold is still scale-dependent and untied to machine epsilon.
verdict.corrected_claim: flow::solve's rank and consistency tests use unexplained float tolerances: an absolute pivot of 1e-12, and a residual of 1e-9 relative to the right-hand side. The routine is misnamed 'exact'. They work because tooth-count entries are of order 10-300; no failing case is known. A structural decision cannot be taken from the lossless rows, because a holding mesh (eta <= 0) changes the incidence.
verdict.proposal_note: Rename least_squares_exact to something honest (e.g. `gauss_jordan`). Make the pivot threshold relative, e.g. n·eps times the largest |entry| of the column or row, and name both tolerances in a const with their derivation. If a structural rank test is wanted, compute it from each assignment's own sparsity pattern, with an entry zero exactly where its factor is zero, not from the lossless system.

title: MeshFlow::paths is written and never read by the flow
claim: The field doc says 'a torque on a central member is paths times what one instance carries', but flow::solve never reads it. The per-mesh multiplier c already aggregates all instances because the system is linear. The Flow::mesh_torques doc ('summed over its paths; what one instance carries is this over paths') is the only consumer, and it is prose.
evidence: grep for `paths` in flow.rs finds only the field and doc comments. mod.rs:4271 sets it from the wiring. Consumers of per-instance load read wiring.meshes[k].paths (shape.rs:3284), not MeshFlow.
proposal: Remove the field from MeshFlow and the test builders. Keep the per-instance division where it is done (shape.rs), with the doc saying so there.
validation: cargo build and nextest unchanged. check_golden shows no byte change.

verdict.reason: flow::solve and Flow::on_shafts never read MeshFlow::paths. The linear per-mesh multiplier already totals over the instances. The only per-instance division is in shape.rs, and it reads the wiring's count, not MeshFlow's.
verdict.evidence: grep '\.paths' in train/flow.rs finds nothing; the field appears only at flow.rs:65-68 (declaration), 428/437/543 (test constructors), and in docs at :43 and :122-124. Across the crates, MeshFlow is built only in train/mod.rs:4264-4271 (`paths: f64::from(m.paths)`) and :4295 (couplings, 1.0). Its consumers mod.rs:3358/3419 read no .paths. shape.rs:3284 divides by `wiring.meshes[k].paths`.
verdict.proposal_note: When removing it, also fix the module doc at flow.rs:43 ('a mesh is one of `paths` alike') and the mesh_torques doc at :122-124. Say there that the torque is the total over the instances, and that shape.rs divides by the wiring's count.

title: Condition order in System::solve decides overflow as well as which conflict is named, yet its docs say 'The order changes no answer'
claim: motion_in's doc says the order of conditions changes no answer, only which conflict is named. The same 9-pair system returns Err(Overflow) driven from one end and Ok from the other, so order (and structure-first absorption) changes whether an answer exists at all.
evidence: pairs.rs output: n 9, motion from input Err(Overflow); from output Ok(-502592611936843/118587876497).
proposal: Fix with the first finding (conditions first, or Bareiss). Until then, amend the doc to say the order can decide overflow.
validation: The chain law from the overflow finding, run from both ends.

verdict.reason: The claim holds, but the auditor's evidence did not show it: it compared two different problems (drive at the input vs drive at the output). Re-measured with identical conditions and only the absorb order changed, the order decides whether an answer exists at all. The production callers use the order that overflows.
verdict.evidence: Probe: a chain of n pairs 17/43, identical conditions (Ground at 0, Drive(1) at input body 1). For n=9, sys.motion(&c) (body order) returns Ok(-118587876497/502592611936843), while sys.motion_in(&c,&[1]) and the reversed order return Err(Overflow). For n=10 and n=12 the pattern is the same (body order Ok, drive-first Overflow). The doc at kinematics.rs:437 reads 'The order changes no answer.' The production callers pass the driver first: train/mod.rs:3404, 3445, 4432 (`motion_in(&c, &[from])`) and conditions.rs:468/506.
verdict.proposal_note: Changing the doc alone is the minimum fix. A better fix makes overflow independent of order: absorb conditions before structural rows, reduce fractions at each step, or use fraction-free (Bareiss) elimination. Then 'changes no answer' becomes true again, and a law can assert motion == motion_in over permutations of `first` for chains of up to ~12 pairs.

title: Train::arranged_as silently makes output = input when input == fixed
claim: `.find(..).unwrap_or(arrangement.input)` turns an invalid Arrangement (input == fixed) into a case loaded and reacted at the same body instead of refusing it. The Arrangement type admits that value.
evidence: Code read. PlanetaryShaft::other returns Option for exactly this case elsewhere (flow.rs test line 485).
proposal: Use PlanetaryShaft::other(input, fixed) and return Option<Self>, or make Arrangement constructible only through a checked constructor.
validation: A unit test that Arrangement{Sun,Sun} is refused.

verdict.reason: The claim misreads the code. With input == fixed, `find(m != input && m != fixed)` still finds a shaft, because two of the three differ from the one repeated shaft. So `unwrap_or(input)` never fires and the output is never the input. The resulting train is not silently wrong: solve_alone refuses it, because the load sits on a held body. Every caller skips input == fixed anyway.
verdict.evidence: Probe: Train::alone(planetary(20,30,80,3)).arranged_as(Arrangement{input:m, fixed:m}). Sun gives held [1], loads [(1,Load),(2,Reacted)] and Err(LoadPort{case:0}). Carrier gives held [2], loads [(2,Load),(1,Reacted)] and Err(LoadPort). Ring gives held [3], loads [(3,Load),(1,Reacted)] and Err(LoadPort). Callers such as gear-cli/src/main.rs:3370 `if input == fixed { continue; }` and the test sweeps build only distinct pairs.
verdict.proposal_note: A cosmetic tidy is possible: the `unwrap_or(arrangement.input)` in train/planetary.rs:37, and its copy in gear-cli/src/main.rs:3375-3378, are unreachable fallbacks, and `PlanetaryShaft::other(input, fixed)` already expresses the rule. The refusal would then name the arrangement rather than LoadPort. Not a correctness issue.

title: Path backlash band puts every distance at the same end of its tolerance, so it understates the band when an internal and an external mesh are on different distances
claim: The band for a path's backlash sums coefficient_k × row_play_k[band], using the same band index (all at minus, or all at plus) for every mesh. An external mesh opens as its distance grows and an internal mesh closes, so when they sit on independent distances the same-end choice lets them cancel. The reported minimum and maximum are then not the worst cases over the tolerance box. Only meshes on one shared distance (sun–planet and planet–ring on the carrier distance) really move together.
evidence: Probe mode `mixed` (probes/mesh-contact/src/main.rs, mixed_band): a 17/43 external pair on distance 0, then 20/60 pinion-in-ring on distance 1, path read from body 1 to body 3. Reported path backlash with ±0.05 on both distances: [0.003781, 0.076663]°. With ±0.05 on distance 0 only: [0.008347, 0.073423]. With ±0.05 on distance 1 only: [−0.028959, 0.109000]. Play superposes linearly through the coefficients, so the real box extremes are nominal 0.040683 + the two deltas = [−0.061296, 0.141740]°. Adding tolerance to distance 0 moved the reported minimum from −0.029 (a jam) to +0.0038 (clear). The per-mesh row_play printed for the internal mesh is [0.1005, 0.0290, −0.0439]: its maximum play is at the minus end.
proposal: Build the band over distances, not meshes. For each distance d, let Δ_d(t) = Σ_{k on d} coef_k·(row_play_k[t] − row_play_k[nominal]) for t ∈ {−, +}. Then min = nominal + Σ_d min(0, Δ_d(−), Δ_d(+)) and max = nominal + Σ_d max(0, Δ_d(−), Δ_d(+)). This is exact because each mesh's play is monotone in its own distance and meshes enter linearly. Keep row_play as it is and change only backlash_at in train/mod.rs. It needs the mesh-to-distance map (shape.distance_of), which rated parts already have.
validation: Law: widening any one distance's tolerance never narrows the path band. Brute force: on shapes with up to three independent distances, enumerate all 3^D end combinations and require the reported minimum and maximum to equal the enumerated extremes. Regression: a planetary part on a single shared distance must keep its current band (0.04172° at every tolerance).

verdict.reason: backlash_at (train/mod.rs:3464-3480) sums coefficient(k)·row_play_k[band] with ONE band index for every mesh, and coefficient() depends only on kinematics, so the path play is linear in each mesh's row play. When an internal mesh sits on a distance of its own, the same-end rule lets it cancel the external meshes, and the tolerance box's extremes are never evaluated. The rule is stated (shape.rs:3543-3546, reference.md:2571, corrections.md:398) but never argued; bored centre distances are independent tolerances. So the documentation does not make it deliberate. The effect is stronger than the auditor showed: the shipped MeshedPlanets preset has it at default tolerances and hides a zero-play assembly.
verdict.evidence: My own probe (probes/verify-mesh-contact-bands, modes `mixed`, `presets`) pins each distance to one end with asymmetric tolerances ((minus, plus) = (tol, −tol) or (−tol, tol)), so the code's own model is evaluated at every corner of 3^D. Mixed 17/43 external + 20/60 internal at ±0.05 mm: reported [0.003781, 0.076663]°, corners [−0.061296, 0.141740]°; d0-only band [0.008347, 0.073423], d1-only [−0.028959, 0.109000]. All match the auditor, and adding tolerance to d0 does narrow the band. verdict.proposal_note: The proposal is correct as written: per distance, min(0, Δ−, Δ+) keeps the nominal as a candidate, which a sun+ring distance needs. Also: (1) reword reference.md:2571, corrections.md:398 (row 4.11) and the shape.rs:3543 comment, which state the same-end rule; (2) use MeshedPlanets at its default tolerances as the regression fixture, since it fails today; (3) the global mesh-to-distance map must follow row_play's flattened part order (part index + part-local distance_of).

Code output, path 1->3 backlash in degrees as [min, nominal, max]:
- tol 0: [0.040683, 0.040683, 0.040683]
- +-0.05 on both distances: [0.003781, 0.040683, 0.076663]
- +-0.05 on d0 only: [0.008347, ..., 0.073423]
- +-0.05 on d1 only: [-0.028959, ..., 0.109000]

The independent script agrees with the code wherever the code evaluates:
- The zero-backlash distances it finds, 30.0056525206085 and 20.0, equal the solve's `nominal`.
- Its nominal path play is 0.0406834249, the same as the code's.
- Its same-end corners, (-,-) = 0.076663 and (+,+) = 0.003781, are exactly the code's reported max and min.

The true extremes over the tolerance box are the mixed corners, which the code never evaluates:
- (d0 -, d1 +) = -0.061296 deg: interference, meaning the pair jams.
- (d0 +, d1 -) = +0.141740 deg.

So the true band is [-0.0613, +0.1417] deg and the reported one is [+0.0038, +0.0767] deg. The minimum sign is wrong: a possible jam is reported as clearance. The band is also non-monotone in tolerance. Adding +-0.05 to d0 on top of d1 moves the reported minimum from -0.029 (a jam) to +0.0038 (clear).

The shipped MeshedPlanets preset shows the same thing at its default +-0.02 on its 3 distances. I read this with the verifier's existing probe verify-mesh-contact-bands in `presets` mode: reported [0.046162, 0.093401] deg, against an enumerated box of [0.000000, 0.139563] deg. That probe enumerates corners through the code's own row_play, so for this preset the check is by the code's own model rather than independent.

Cause: backlash_at in crates/gear-core/src/train/mod.rs:3466-3480 sums coefficient(k) * row_play[k][band], using one band index (0 or 2) for every mesh. shape.rs:3543-3558 (at_band) states the rule that every distance sits at the same end of its tolerance at once. That holds only for meshes on one shared distance.
repro.note:
I confirm the finding by execution and by an independent involute derivation. Every number in the ledger reproduces to 6 digits, and the independent calculation matches the code's nominal and same-end values exactly. So the per-mesh play and the kinematic coefficients are sound, and the only defect is how the band is put together.

The fix in the ledger's proposal is correct and exact:
- For each distance d, compute Delta_d(t) = sum over the meshes k on d of coef_k * (row_play_k[t] - row_play_k[nominal]).
- Then min = nominal + sum_d min(0, Delta_d(-), Delta_d(+)), and max is the same with max.
- It is exact because each mesh's j_bt is monotone in its own distance and the meshes add linearly.
- It needs a global mesh-to-distance map in row_play's flattened part order.

Use two regressions:
- This mixed 17/43 + 20/ring60 shape at +-0.05, expecting [-0.061296, 0.141740].
- MeshedPlanets at its defaults, expecting [0.0, 0.139563].

Planetary must keep 0.041724 at every tolerance, since all its meshes are on one distance.

The ledger's high severity stands. This is a user-facing band whose minimum sign decides jam against clear, and it is wrong on a shipped preset at default tolerances. It also gets narrower as a tolerance is widened.

title: Efficiency spreads the load evenly along the path (Buckingham): 12–19 % more spur loss than a static split, not documented as a bias, and blind to the overlap ratio
claim: η = 1 − µπ(1/z₁±1/z₂)(ε₁²+ε₂²)/(ε_α cos β_b) is the time average of the loss if every engaged pair always carries F/ε_α. Under that assumption the total transmitted force is n(t)·F/ε_α, so it is not held at F_n instant by instant as contact.rs:353-357 and reference.md:611 claim. Splitting the load equally between the pairs in contact, which is what statics gives for rigid teeth, gives Ohlendorf/Niemann's H_V ∝ (1 − ε_α + ε₁² + ε₂²), the loss factor ISO/TR 14179-2 uses. The helical argument at contact.rs:377-382 ('the line-length-weighted mean of |ξ| equals the plain average') holds only when the total contact-line length is constant, i.e. at integer ε_β. For a spur gear (ε_β = 0) it fails by the full 12–19 %. The model also disagrees with the LoadSharing ramp the crate offers for bending. Rule 6 requires every bias to be stated with its size and sign; this one is absent from docs/state.md.
evidence: hv.py numerically integrates µ|ξ|·share over the mesh cycle. Loss/µ for 17/43: Buckingham (the code) 0.20991, equal split 1/n 0.18012 (matches the Ohlendorf closed form to all digits), 1/3–2/3 ramp 0.16907. Ratio code/Ohlendorf: 1.165 (17/43), 1.183 (9/37), 1.188 (20/20), 1.118 (30/90). gear-cli strength 17 43 2.0 prints 98.741 % at µ 0.06, the code value; Ohlendorf gives 98.919 %. Helical 17/43 at β 15° with rigid load uniform per unit line length: loss/µ 0.17403 at ε_β 0, 0.19665 at 0.5, 0.20649 at 1.0, 0.20651 at 2.0, against the code's constant 0.20654. So the rigid model runs continuously from Ohlendorf to Buckingham as ε_β rises. Stage effect (probe `stage`, mesh loss × 0.85 ≈ Ohlendorf/Buckingham): Wolfrom 45.36 → 49.39 %, Compound 65.55 → 69.17 %, Worm 61.8 → 65.6 %, Spur 98.345 → 98.593 %. The optimum shift barely moves (probe `opt`: 17/43 Σx 1.26 under both models). Source: Fernandes et al., Mech. Sci. 6, 81 (2015), notes/mesh-contact/hv.pdf, which compares the Ohlendorf, Niemann and Buckingham loss factors, all rigid.
proposal: Replace the closed form with one model that has ε_β as its parameter: the time- and face-averaged µ|ξ|(1/r_b1 ± 1/r_b2)/cos β_b, weighted by load per unit contact-line length, with the total held at F_n at every instant (rigid teeth, uniform per unit length). At ε_β = 0 this is exactly Ohlendorf's closed form, generalised to any ε_α by the 1/n(t) split. At integer ε_β it is exactly today's expression. In between it is a short piecewise integral in closed form, or a fixed quadrature with a convergence gate. Optionally let LoadSharing::LinearRamp weight it too, so bending and efficiency share one load-sharing assumption. At minimum: switch the spur value to H_V and list the present bias in docs/state.md (+12–19 % of loss on spur, conservative on η). Apply the same weighting in screw.rs CrossedPath::efficiency, which also averages uniformly along one pair's path, so that the crossed model still converges to the parallel one as the shaft angle goes to 0.
validation: Independent check: a time-stepped simulation over one mesh cycle and the face, splitting the load in proportion to engaged contact-line length, compared to the closed form at ε_β ∈ {0, 0.3, 0.5, 1, 1.7}. Limit laws: equals Ohlendorf's (1 − ε + ε₁² + ε₂²) at ε_β = 0 and 1 ≤ ε_α ≤ 2; equals today's value at integer ε_β; continuous in ε_β. Re-run the golden corpus and look for the expected η shifts (Spur about +0.25 points, Wolfrom about +4 points).

verdict.reason: contact.rs:437 is Buckingham's H_V exactly. The paper's Eq. 4, ε_α(2k₀² − 2k₀ + 1) with k₀ = ε₁/ε_α, reduces to (ε₁² + ε₂²)/ε_α. That equals every engaged pair carrying F/ε_α at all times, so the transmitted force is n(t)F/ε_α: F only on the time average, not at every instant as contact.rs:353-357 and reference.md:611-612 claim. The equal (static, rigid) split gives Ohlendorf's (1 − ε_α + ε₁² + ε₂²), the spur case of the Ohlendorf/Wimmer H_V the FVA and ISO/TR 14179-2 line uses. The helical argument at contact.rs:377-382 needs constant total contact-line length, which holds at integer ε_β. docs/state.md's known-approximate list has no entry for this bias, and the doc calls the formula exact.
verdict.evidence: eff.py (independent time-stepped mesh cycle, 2e5 phases). Loss/μ for 17/43: Buckingham 0.20991 (simulation equals closed form), equal split 0.18012 (equals Ohlendorf's closed form); ratio 1.1654. Ratios for 9/37, 20/20 and 30/90: 1.1834, 1.1884, 1.1183. η at μ 0.06: 98.741 % (gear-cli strength 17 43 2.0 prints 98.741 %) against 98.919 %. helical.py (rigid, uniform per unit contact-line length, total F at every instant), as a fraction of Buckingham: ε_β 0 → 0.858 (= Ohlendorf), 0.3 → 0.922, 0.5 → 0.965, 0.7 → 0.989, 1.0 → 1.000, 1.5 → 0.996, 2.0 → 1.000. Ohlendorf/Buckingham over buildable jsonl pairs: external median 0.880 (0.828–1.000), internal median 0.864, so the auditor's ×0.85 stage proxy is in range. The FVA KnowledgeBase (doc.fva-service.de/80/en/root-power-loss.html) gives the Ohlendorf/Wimmer H_V = π(u+1)/(z₁u cos β_b)(a₀ + a₁|ε₁| + … + a₄|ε₂|ε₂), whose spur coefficients are Ohlendorf's.
verdict.proposal_note: (1) screw.rs CrossedPath::efficiency also averages uniformly along one pair's path, so today the two models agree as Σ → 0. Changing only the parallel one opens a seam of about 2.4e-3 in η (17/43 at μ 0.08), and the crossed.rs:1573 limit test's 5e-3 bound would not catch it; tighten that bound when both change. (2) The default μ 0.08 (arrangements.rs:30) states no source. A μ taken from ISO/TR 14179-2's μ_mz is calibrated with Ohlendorf's H_V, so document the μ and H_V as a pair. (3) Fix the 'holds the total transmitted force at F_n' prose whatever else is done. (4) For ε_β ≥ 1 the change is under 0.4 %; only spur and low-overlap helical meshes move materially.

title: Contact ratio, efficiency and load sharing use the whole tip-to-tip path even when a flank is reached past its usable end
claim: ContactPath::new limits the path only by the two tip circles. Where the mate's tip reaches past a member's junction or its base tangent point, the part of the path beyond it is not conjugate contact: no involute exists there, or it is undercut or fillet. Yet the reported ε_α, the efficiency integral, the load-share coordinate and the single-pair points all use the full tip-to-tip length. The train reports flank_interference beside the mesh, but the figures next to it describe contact that cannot happen. The automatic search refuses such meshes (auto.rs MeshTrial), so this only affects meshes whose shifts or tooth counts the user entered.
evidence: trunc.py over ext.jsonl: 4,649 of 8,767 external grid pairs with a path interfere. Reported against usable ε includes 14/30 at x −0.6/−0.3: reported 3.243, usable 0.000. 20/40 at x −0.6/−0.6: 3.229 against 0.045. Median overstatement 0.41. Internal: 17/47 at x −0.5/−0.5: 3.142 against 0.783; median 0.45. check.py confirms the path ends match independent geometry exactly (|Δ| < 1e-10), so the lengths are what the tip circles give; the error is which limits are applied.
proposal: Give ContactPath effective ends. start = max(−approach, ξ at which the mate's contact reaches member 1's usable end), where that is ξ₁ = T(r_j1, r_b1) − r_b1 tan α_w, also bounded by −r_b1 tan α_w. end = min(recess, the same for member 2, signed as conjugate_radius signs it). Keep the tip-limited ends as separate fields for the interference readout. Base ε_α, efficiency, load_fraction and the HPSTC/LPSTC points on the effective ends. With no interference the two coincide exactly, so every non-interfering answer is unchanged to the bit. ContactPath::new needs each member's FlankEnds, which the shape already has (shape.rs:2395).
validation: Law: when flank_interference is [false, false], the effective and tip ends are bitwise equal, and the whole golden corpus is unchanged. Independent check: trunc.py's usable ε over the jsonl grids must equal the new ε. Law: the effective ε never exceeds the tip ε, and it falls continuously to 0 as a shift is pushed into interference.

verdict.reason: ContactPath::new (contact.rs:77-121) limits the path by the two tip circles only. Every figure built on it (contact_ratio, the efficiency integral, load_fraction, HPSTC/LPSTC) uses that length even when Mesh::flank_interference reports the mate's tip reaching past a usable flank end. Physically, on an undercut flank the mate's tip passes through space the generating rack already cleared, so contact simply ends and the usable path is the real one. The auditor's headline example is pathological, but the effect is real on ordinary standard pairs.
verdict.evidence: trunc.py re-run reproduces the auditor's table (4,649 of 8,767 external and 2,345 of 3,400 internal pairs flagged; medians 0.41 and 0.45). The headline row, 14/30 at x −0.6/−0.3, also has bottom clearance −0.164 mm on both members and a near-zero operating angle, which is not a design anyone enters. Realistic rows from the same grid (reported against usable ε): standard 12/40 (undercut pinion) 1.567 vs 1.275; 10/40 1.542 vs 1.093; 13/40 1.578 vs 1.366; 8/200 1.609 vs 0.913, so continuous contact is claimed where it is lost. In the train, members default to no_undercut = true (mod.rs:1302), which confines the undercut case to users who switch it off. Given shifts still reach interference: 17/43 at x 0.8/0.8 solves with flank_interference [true, false] and reports ε 1.4433.
verdict.proposal_note: The effective-end construction is the right physics for an undercut flank. Where a tip reaches a fillet the cutter did not undercut, the teeth collide and no path describes the mesh, so the flag must stay primary and the truncated ε should be documented as 'the contact left on the usable flanks'. The change moves the bending load point (HPSTC) and the Hertz point, which is the strength scope's. The 'golden corpus unchanged' law holds only because every preset has flank_interference [false, false]; assert that in the test rather than assume it.

title: A band end below the base-circle limit is read as zero play, and a negative distance passes the pressure-angle guard
claim: play_of calls `l.design.backlash(a).unwrap_or(0.0)`. When the minus end of a tolerance is below the base-circle limit, CentreDistanceTooSmall becomes 0 play: a silent value where rule 5 wants a refusal or a clamp with a note. Mesh::pressure_angle_at accepts cos α ∈ [−1, 1], so a negative a_actual with |a| > a_ref cos α_t returns an obtuse angle and a large finite backlash. In shift_sum_for, `cos_w > -1.0` can never be false once a_w > 0 has been checked.
evidence: Probe `band`, 17/43 pair (running 30.0257 mm, base limit a_ref cos α = 28.19 mm). Mesh backlash with ±1 mm: [−4.1377, 0.0985, 5.5888]°. With ±5 mm: [0.0000, 0.0985, 35.1948]°, so the minimum jumps from −4.14° to exactly 0 as the tolerance widens. With ±60 mm (minus end −30 mm): [−1282.5464, …]°. Probe `backlash`: pressure_angle_at(−100) = Ok(1.8566 rad), backlash(−100) = Ok(1054.97 mm). The planetary case shows the same, e.g. [−21.78, 0.0586, 0.0586]° on the ring mesh at ±5.
proposal: In pressure_angle_at, require a_actual > 0 and c ≤ 1; return CentreDistanceTooSmall otherwise. In play_of, take the band end to the base-circle limit a_ref cos α_t (the tightest distance that has an answer) and raise a note (e.g. `mesh.band_below_base_limit`, with both distances) instead of unwrap_or(0.0). Alternatively refuse a tolerance that reaches past it. Remove the dead `cos_w > -1.0` term.
validation: Law: the band minimum is monotone non-increasing as tolerance_minus grows, with no jump. Test: a tolerance reaching the base limit yields the note and a minimum equal to backlash at a_ref cos α_t. Test: pressure_angle_at(−x) is Err for all x > 0.

verdict.reason: play_of (shape.rs:3527) maps CentreDistanceTooSmall to 0.0 play, and Mesh::pressure_angle_at (mesh.rs:296-302) accepts any c ∈ [−1, 1], so a negative distance gets an obtuse angle and a finite backlash. Both are silent substitutions that rule 5 forbids. Once a_w > 0, a_ref ≥ 0 and cos α_t > 0, the guard's `cos_w > -1.0` term in shift_sum_for (mesh.rs:172) can never be false. Severity lowered from medium: reaching the base-circle limit takes a tolerance of about 6 % of the distance (1.84 mm on the 1-module spur preset, about 0.4 mm on the 1.73 mm planocentric crank), against a 0.02 mm default. No tolerance input is validated anywhere (TrainPanel.svelte:777-778 takes any finite number).
verdict.evidence: My probe's `tolsweep` mode: Spur's mesh minimum is −6.0391° at ±1.8 mm and 0.0000° at ±1.9 mm (a jump to 'just touching' where the teeth jam by degrees); Layshaft and Idler do the same. Internal meshes lose their maximum instead: Planetary ring mesh [−6.4121, 0.0586, 0.0586]° at ±1.8, and the Wolfrom path maximum collapses to 0.0489°. Planocentric at ±5 mm (minus end −3.27 mm) returns a finite 48.2466° maximum. `negative` mode on a 17/43 Mesh: a = −30 gives α = 160.0°, backlash 190.28 mm and −1282.64°; a = −28.2 gives α = 178.5°. shift_sum_for(−100) is None only because of `a_w > 0.0`.
verdict.proposal_note: Refusing a band end that has no operating angle is simpler and truer than clamping it to the base-circle limit. Any end that far is already a jam by degrees, so the clamped value would be finite but meaningless; refusing matches rule 5 (the input describes no assembly). ring.rs described_at (ring.rs:1047-1049) has the same `(-1.0..=1.0)` guard and needs `centre_distance > 0` too. Point contacts clamp their tight end separately; see the missed finding below.

title: ring::mesh_with recomputes path length, contact ratio, operating angle and rack compatibility beside ContactPath and Mesh
claim: described_at builds its own α_w (the same as Mesh::pressure_angle_at), its own path length `T₁ − T₂ + a sin α_w` clamped with .max(0.0) (ContactPath::new returns None instead), its own contact ratio, and its own module and pressure-angle compatibility check (`>` tol on mt and α_t, while Mesh::new uses same_rack_as plus the helix sign). These are two models of one phenomenon that a test keeps in step. Their edge semantics already differ: a zero path is ε = 0 in one and None in the other.
evidence: check.py: ring_eps_vs_path |Δ| ≤ 1.23e-14 over 3,400 internal pairs, and the interference flags agree in every case. So the copy is only redundant today; it is not yet wrong. Only gear-cli (main.rs:1204) and tests call mesh_with; the train goes through Mesh, ContactPath and TipRoom::at (mod.rs:584, via mesh_at).
proposal: Make RingMesh a view built from Mesh::new(pinion, &Tooth::new(ring.params), Internal) → at(running) → ContactPath::new(pinion, ring.ra, …) → conjugate_radius for the two contact radii, plus tip_clearance, which is the one thing that is really the ring's own. Delete reference_geometry's compatibility checks and the hand-written path.
validation: The existing ring tests, which hold mesh_with against the general path, become identities. Keep their sweep as a regression. The golden `meshsweep` and `hula` outputs must be unchanged.

verdict.reason: described_at (ring.rs:1045-1098) recomputes α_w, the internal path length (with `.max(0.0)`, where ContactPath::new returns None), the contact ratio, and a rack-compatibility check that uses the transverse mt/α_t in mm/radians instead of same_rack_as's module/degrees plus the helix-sign test. Severity lowered from medium: the copy is held equal by tests and nothing gets a wrong answer today. Its only production consumer is TipRoom::at (train/mod.rs:584), which reads just tip_interference and tip_margin; the duplicated ε and the trochoid/involute flags reach only gear-cli's mesh_sweep (main.rs:1190-1218) and the ring tests.
verdict.evidence: From the code, with callers checked by grep. The auditor's check.py agreement (|Δε| ≤ 1.23e-14 over 3,400 pairs) confirms it is redundant, not wrong. Both tolerances are 1e-9 (params.rs:292), so the unit mismatch has no practical effect. ContactPath::new's doc (contact.rs:71-72) cites mesh_with's 'independently written form' as its cross-check.
verdict.proposal_note: Do not simply delete the hand-written path: it is the independent oracle ContactPath's doc leans on, and 'verify against something that shares no code' is the project's first testing rule. Move it into ring.rs's tests as the oracle. Shrink RingMesh to the tip room, which is really the ring's own, and have gear-cli's mesh_sweep read ε and the flags from Mesh, ContactPath and flank_interference.

title: Above ε = 2 the linear ramp's shares sum to more than the load (up to 1.73×)
claim: The F25 fix made each tooth's share continuous, and that closure holds. Above ε = 2, however, the shares of the pairs engaged at one instant no longer sum to 1, so the model puts more load on the mesh than is transmitted. Below 2 they sum to exactly 1.
evidence: Probe `share2`: sum of shares over engaged pairs, interior instants. ε 1.2/1.5/1.9: exactly 1.0000. ε 2.05: max 1.3413, mean 1.0169. ε 2.5: max 1.3889, mean 1.1806. ε 3.0: min 1.3333, max 1.4167. ε 3.5: min 1.40, max 1.7333.
proposal: Normalise within load_share. Compute the ramp weight w(d) for this tooth and for every engaged neighbour (d ± k for k ≥ 1, while inside [0, ε]) and return w(d)/Σw. Below ε = 2 this is bitwise the present value, because the two weights sum to 1 in the double zone and a single tooth is 1. Above 2 it conserves load.
validation: Law: Σ shares = 1 at every instant for every ε. The existing below-2 bitwise-equality test stays green. Check the out-of-band figures in state.md (the '24 % relief to 15 % increase' range) are re-measured.

verdict.reason: load_share's min-form ramp (contact.rs:892-924) conserves load only while at most two pairs are engaged. Above ε = 2 the engaged shares sum to more than 1, so the model carries more load than the mesh transmits: a statics violation, not just the uncalibrated extrapolation state.md:729-737 describes. The severity is low because LinearRamp is opt-in (LoadSharing::None is the default) and every mesh in that regime already says it is extrapolating.
verdict.evidence: share.py, my independent reimplementation over 2e5 phases: ε 1.2/1.5/1.9/2.0 sum = 1.0000; ε 2.05 max 1.3413, mean 1.0169; 2.2 max 1.3611; 2.5 max 1.3889, mean 1.1806; 3.0 min 1.3333, max 1.4167; 3.5 min 1.4000, max 1.7333. Identical to the auditor's.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposal's claim that normalising is 'bitwise the present value' below ε = 2 is false. The two ramp weights sum to 1 only to an ulp: in my reimplementation 9 %, 19 %, 29 % and 35 % of instants at ε 1.2, 1.5, 1.9 and 2.0 are not exactly 1.0, so dividing by Σw changes last bits. Either apply the normalisation only above ε = 2, where Σw differs from 1 by more than rounding, or relax the existing bitwise-equality test to one ulp. Re-measure state.md's '24 % relief to 15 % increase' figures afterwards.

title: A test's 'least shift' foil is a design whose flanks interfere, and its doc quotes it as a design
claim: an_external_pair_loses_least_well_above_its_undercut_floor filters out undercut and severed gears but not flank interference. On 17/43 its 'least' design is x = (0.05, −1.25), Σx −1.20, ε 3.04, and both flanks are reached past their usable end. The doc presents it as a design keeping 96.87 % with contact ratio 3.04, and the assertion that the best design 'gets there by shortening the path' is measured against a path that does not exist.
evidence: Probe `least` over the test's own grid: Some((0.05, −1.25, −1.2, 3.035989, 0.968681, [true, true])).
proposal: Add `m.flank_interference([a.flank_ends(), b.flank_ends()]) == [false, false]` and the bottom-clearance check to the test's filter, the same refusals as MeshTrial::efficiency. Re-quote the figures in the doc comment.
validation: Re-run the test. The foil must now be a buildable pair, and all three assertions should still hold.

Both flanks are reached past their usable end, and both tips also reach past the mate's root circle. The doc comment at contact.rs:1293-1296 quotes that foil as a design ('96.87 % at Σx = −1.20 … 3.04'). The proposal's validation is wrong, however: with the proposed filters two of the test's three assertions fail.

Probe probes/verify-mesh-contact-b6 mode `least` runs the test's own grid, filter and µ 0.08.

Test filter as written:

title: The efficiency 'verification' tests share the assumption they are meant to check
claim: 'Verified against a numerical average … to 1e-10' compares the closed form with mean_over_path(|ξ|), a uniform average in ξ, which is the very load assumption the closed form encodes. It checks the integral arithmetic, which is correct, but not the physics. No test could detect the load-distribution error in the finding above.
evidence: Both efficiency_matches_a_numerical_average_of_the_instantaneous_loss and efficiency_is_the_integral_of_the_sliding_vector average with uniform weight over one pair's path. The hv.py cycle-level simulation with statics-consistent sharing disagrees by 12–19 %.
proposal: Add a mesh-cycle simulation test. Step the phase over one base pitch, place all engaged pairs, split F by the chosen rule (1/n for rigid, or by contact-line length for helical), and integrate µΣF_k|v_s,k| against F·v_b. Reword 'verified' to say what is checked.
validation: The new test fails against the present closed form for spur gears (by about 16 %) and passes after the efficiency change.

verdict.reason: Both 'verification' tests average |ξ| (or |v_s|) uniformly over one pair's path. That is the closed form's own weighting, so they check the integral's algebra and the sliding kinematics, both of which are correct, and cannot see the load assumption. The documented claim that the /ε_α 'holds the total transmitted force at F_n' (contact.rs:353-357, reference.md:611) is true only on the cycle average.
verdict.evidence:
notes/verify-mesh-contact/eff.py simulates the mesh cycle, 2e5 phases per base pitch.
- Uniform weight 1/ε_α reproduces the code's closed form: 17/43, 0.407016 against 0.407017 per p_b.
- An equal split (1/n) reproduces Ohlendorf's (1 − ε + ε₁² + ε₂²)/2 exactly.
- Code over equal split: 1.165 (17/43), 1.183 (9/37), 1.188 (20/20), 1.118 (30/90).
- At µ 0.06 on 17/43 that is 98.741 % against 98.919 %; the golden strength_17_43_2.0 prints 98.741 %.
- Under the code's weighting the engaged pairs carry 2/ε_α = 1.23 F in double contact and 0.62 F in single contact.
- A repo-wide grep finds no test or document comparing the result with Ohlendorf, Niemann or ISO/TR 14179.
verdict.proposal_note:
The cheapest correct fix is independent of finding 1: reword contact.rs:349-357 and reference.md:608-611 to say that the check is of the integral, and that the loads sum to F only on average.

A cycle-level test should state a law of whatever sharing rule is adopted: at every phase the shares sum to 1, and the loss is the phase-average of Σ share·|ξ|. As proposed ('fails now, passes after') it is the regression test for finding 1's change, not a separate gap.

title: ContactPath accepts a member whose tip is inside its own base circle
claim: `tangent` clamps √(r_a² − r_b²) to 0, so a member with no involute at all (r_a < r_b) still gets a path, a contact ratio and an efficiency, built from the other member's end alone. Rule 5 says input that describes no shape is refused.
evidence: 90 pairs in ext.jsonl, e.g. 5/5 at x −0.6/0.6: ra1 1.040 < rb1 2.349, yet a path with ε 0.495 and η 91.9 % is returned (flagged as severed and interfering).
proposal: Return None from ContactPath::new when either tip radius is below its base radius (|r_a| < |r_b|), so that TrainError::NoContact follows. Or keep the value and raise a note, if the panel should keep showing it.
validation: The grid rows with r_a < r_b return None. No golden output moves, because no shipped preset has such a member.

verdict.corrected_claim: ContactPath::new clamps a sub-base-circle tip to its base-tangent point and returns a path, contradicting its doc ('None when either end of the path is not reached'). But only a severed tooth has r_a < r_b, and every production consumer refuses a severed member, so no such path figure reaches a user.
verdict.reason: The function-level behaviour is as described. Unsevered tips are clamped to at least r_b in both the Tooth and the Ring, and the train and the search both refuse severed members. The proposal would also make the train's refusal less accurate.
verdict.evidence:
Where r_a < r_b occurs:
- In the auditor's ext.jsonl the rows with r_a < r_b and the severed rows are the same 90 of 8,767.
- Probe mode `subbase`: an unsevered tooth at an extreme negative shift is clamped (z100 x −4.3 and −4.5: ra = rb = 46.9846 exactly) and then fails Mesh::new with OutsideInvoluteDomain.
- ring.rs:282 sets ra_min = rb(1+1e-9).

What production does with a severed member:
- Probe mode `severed`: the train returns InPart{NoRootSection} for 5/5 at x −0.6/0.6, 8/20 at −0.9/0.9 and 10/20 at −1.2/1.2 ('the tooth is too undercut to have a root section').
- The tooth also carries clamp.tooth_severed.
- The search refuses severed members through member_is_buildable (auto.rs:1022) before MeshTrial.
verdict.proposal_note:
Returning None from ContactPath::new is built at shape.rs:2886, before rating, and would turn today's accurate NoRootSection refusal into NoContact ('the teeth never contact'). That is a worse message for a tooth that has been cut away.

Better options:
- state the precondition in ContactPath::new's doc, perhaps with a debug_assert; or
- refuse a severed member at the member, under its own key.

The path-truncation issue (finding 2) is the general form of this.

title: split_residual / efficient_split: public, unused in production, and wrong under the default no_sharp_tip
claim: The doc itself says nothing in production calls these functions and that their premise dr_a/dx = m fails when no_sharp_tip is on, which it is by default. They keep ContactPath::tip_pressure_angle alive, a field only they read. For a ring that field holds π − α_a, not the 'pressure angle at the tip' its doc names.
evidence: grep shows split_residual used only in contact.rs tests, and efficient_split has one non-test mention. A ring's (rb2/tip_radius_2).acos() with rb2 < 0 exceeds π/2.

verdict.reason: `split_residual` and `efficient_split` are pub and are called only from contact.rs's tests. `tip_pressure_angle` is read only by `split_residual`. The functions' own doc says their premise fails under the shipped `no_sharp_tip` cap. For a ring the field holds π − α_a; that is harmless to the residual, which reads only its sine, but its doc misdescribes it.
verdict.evidence:
Callers:
- A workspace grep finds `split_residual` and `efficient_split` called only at contact.rs:1149, 1196, 1234 and 1272 (all tests).
- The other mentions are intra-doc links (auto.rs:1468, gear-cli main.rs:1085) and history (corrections.md:564, audit.md F64).
- `tip_pressure_angle` is read only at contact.rs:504.

title: Stale or self-contradicting prose in contact.rs and mesh.rs
claim: (a) ContactPath::new says 'at their zero-backlash centre distance', but production passes the operating mesh. (b) load_fraction says 'between one and two pairs are in contact at any moment', which is false for ε > 2 and ε < 1. (c) The '# Applied to every stage kind' heading and mesh.rs 'stage kind' use a vocabulary the graph refactor retired. (d) 'The crossed-axis version … arrives … (milestone 7, step 5)' describes the future; Contact and screw.rs exist. (e) The '/// Three-component vector helpers' paragraph sits directly above `/// One contact…`, so rustdoc joins it onto Contact's docs. (f) RAMP_MIN's rationale ('a tooth entering at its root is stiffer …, so it takes less than half') contradicts itself, since a stiffer pair takes more, and it cites 'the literature' without a source.
evidence: Read at the cited lines. The helpers' `pub(crate) fn add` follows at line 832, after Contact's impl.
proposal: (a) Say 'at the distance the mesh describes (operating in production)'. (b) Say 'a share of the pairs engaged'. (c) Say 'every mesh'. (d) Delete the paragraph. (e) Move the helper comment above `fn add`. (f) Give the real reason (tip relief and deflection lag of the entering pair) and a citation, or say plainly 'uncalibrated stand-in'.
validation: cargo doc renders Contact's docs starting with 'One contact'. check_doc_links stays green.

verdict.reason:
All six items hold.
(a) Production passes the running mesh, not the zero-backlash one.
(b) The number of pairs in contact is not bounded to one or two; load_share itself handles ε > 2.
(c) 'Stage kind' is retired vocabulary. One more present-tense instance is at auto.rs:1299 ('not a branch on the stage kind').
(d) Future tense about a milestone already delivered.
(e) rustdoc joins the helper comment onto Contact's docs.
(f) The ramp's rationale is a non sequitur and has no source.
verdict.evidence:
(a) shape.rs:2884-2890 passes `design.at(at)`, at the running distance (zero-backlash + clearance). auto.rs:1522-1526 does the same.
(d) The prophecy was in fact kept, in tests: screw.rs:1797 (cfg(test)) calls `sliding_velocity` with axis_2 = [0, sin Σ, cos Σ]. Production crossed meshes use `Contact::slip` (screw.rs:1141).
(e) `cargo doc -p gear-core` into the probe target renders Contact's description as 'Three-component vector helpers. Shared with crate::screw … One contact, as a force balance sees it'.
(f) Which pair takes less load depends on the pair's series compliance compared with the other pair's. A root-loaded tooth being stiffer than its partner does not imply that its pair takes less.
verdict.proposal_note:
(f) The 1/3 end value has a citable source: the minimum-elastic-potential load-sharing model of Pedrero, Sánchez and Pleguezuelos (Mech. Mach. Theory / Meccanica, 2013–2017). The physical reason needs no tip relief: at the path's ends one tooth of the pair is loaded at its tip, so the pair is at its most compliant.
(d) Rather than deleting the paragraph, it could be replaced with a pointer to the screw.rs test that calls the same function with the crossed axis.

title: The interference verdict is taken at the running distance, not at the tightest end of the tolerance band
claim: flank_interference is evaluated on l.operating (the running distance). An external pair's tips reach deepest at running − tol₋, and an internal pair's at running + tol₊, so a pair that is clean at nominal can foul inside its tolerance.
evidence: From the code. Not quantified: at the default ±0.02 mm the effect is tiny, but the band machinery already evaluates both ends.
proposal: Evaluate flank_interference at the tighter band end, running − σ·tol, and report that verdict (or both).
validation: A fixture placed just clean at nominal must flag at the tight end.

verdict.reason: The claim holds as stated, and it is systematic rather than 'tiny'. shape.rs:3839-3841 reads the line-contact verdict off `l.operating`, the mesh at `bm.running` (built at shape.rs:2885). The band machinery beside it (`at_band`, shape.rs:3549-3558; `Backlash::banded`, mod.rs:162) already evaluates running − tol₋ and running + tol₊, but only for play. I checked the direction by probe on every parallel-axis mesh of every preset, search off and on. External margins are least at running − tol₋ and internal margins at running + tol₊, and the margin is monotone in a, since ρ_here = a sin α_w − ρ_mate. The shift search admits a design on the same running-distance verdict (shape.rs:2251-2257 passes `mesh: &l.operating` to `MeshTrial`, whose filter is auto.rs:1257). So any search optimum that is interference-bound sits on the boundary at running and fouls at the tight end for any positive tol₋. That includes the documented 9/37 answer (reference.md table: 97.678 % at Σx = 1.4078). Nothing else in the report or the notes covers the tight end: no string names it, and the backlash band's minimum on 9/37 is exactly 0, because the default clearance equals the default tolerance. No document argues that interference should be judged at the running distance alone. reference.md:323-330 argues running against zero-backlash and never considers the tolerance. Not deliberate. Severity goes up from info because the verdict panel shows 'Interference: none' for the optimiser's own recommendation on a pair that fouls inside its stated tolerance. The depth is small (µm at module 1) and scales with the tolerance.
verdict.evidence:
Probe /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/verify-mesh-contact-f12. It rebuilds each member from `GearResult::params` (`Ring::cut_by` for rings), builds `Mesh::new(..).at(a)`, and computes the signed margin σ_i(r_i − r_j,i). Its verdict at running matched `MeshReport::flank_interference` on every mesh.

(1) 9/37, search on: x 0.6746/0.7332, running 24.2240. Margin mm: −0.00588 [running − 0.02], 0.00000 [running], +0.00631 [running + 0.02]. The report says [false, false]; the pair fouls at the minus end.

(2) Sweep over z₁ 7..20 × z₂ {20,25,30,37,43,50,60,80}, search on: 112 pairs solved. 27 of them, every interference-bound optimum (z₁ ≤ 11), sit within 1e-4 mm of the boundary at running, and all 27 foul at running − 0.02, by 0.0015 to 0.0095 mm (e.g. 11/20 −0.0095, 8/20 −0.0062, 7/80 −0.0015).

(3) Direction on internal meshes: planocentric 30/33 margin 0.02791 / 0.02217 / 0.01663 (minus / running / plus); Wolfrom with search 0.2507 / 0.2384 / 0.2263. Least at the plus end, as claimed.

(4) Cost of requiring clearance at the tight end. I searched at clearance 0, which puts the admissibility check at the default band's tight end, then pinned those shifts and rated them at 0.02. 9/37: 97.6778 → 97.6672 % (−0.0106 points), Σx 1.4078 → 1.4222, ε 1.2929 → 1.3156, margin at the tight end +3.3e-5. 8/30: −0.0087 points.
verdict.proposal_note: Changing only the report would make the tool flag its own search's answers: 27 of 112 pairs in the sweep. The same check must move into the search's filter (shape.rs:2251-2257, `MeshTrial.mesh`; auto.rs:1238-1257), which also holds `bottom_clearance`, and it tightens at the same end. That moves the reference.md 9/37 row and the goldens (tools/golden/shifts_9_37.txt and others), so the effort is M, not S. A better form than the signed rule 'running − σ·tol' is to evaluate both band ends, `at_band(k, −1.0)` and `at_band(k, 1.0)`, and fail if either fails. Every one of these quantities is monotone in a, so the two ends suffice and no sign reasoning is needed. corrections.md:601 records the bug that came from assigning a band end by reasoning. It also matters directly here: `TipRoom` on an internal pair tightens at the *minus* end, the opposite of flank interference (see missed). Apply the same rule to the point-contact verdict (shape.rs:3869, where the path is built at running) and to `CrossedTrial` (auto.rs:1193-1206). Tip-diameter tolerance is not modelled at all; that is a separate gap.

title: A path's backlash band is too narrow when it crosses independent distances whose meshes' play moves in opposite directions (MeshedPlanets reports a minimum of 0.046 deg; the true minimum is 0)
claim: backlash_at sums each mesh's row_play at one band index across every mesh, so it assumes every axis distance sits at its minus end together, then at running, then at plus. Each distance has its own tolerance and the tolerances are independent. On a path with an internal mesh (play falls as the distance grows) and an external mesh (play rises) on different distances, the true extremes need the distances at opposite ends. The reported minimum is too high and the maximum too low, in the unsafe direction: a mesh that can bind is reported as having play.
evidence: Probe train-mod-a-e (notes/train-mod-a/out) holds every shift fixed, sets each of MeshedPlanets' 3 distances to running + {-0.02, 0, +0.02} (27 combinations, clearance automatic), solves each, and reads the path's nominal play. The measured range is [-0.00000 .. 0.13956] deg; the solve reports minimum 0.04616 and maximum 0.09340. The zero case is at [-1, +1, -1]. Probe -b rebuilds the same figures from the code's own row_play and play coefficients: mesh 1's row is [0.0580, 0.0291, ~0] (falling) while meshes 0 and 2 rise. Taking min and max per distance and summing gives [0, 0.1396], which agrees. On Idler and Layshaft (all meshes external) the reported band equals the measured range, so the defect needs meshes whose play moves in opposite directions.
proposal: In backlash_at, group the meshes by the distance they sit on (shape.distance_of). For each distance d, compute S_d(t) = Σ_{k on d} coeff(k)·row_play[k][t] for t ∈ {minus, running, plus}. Report nominal = Σ_d S_d(running), minimum = Σ_d min_t S_d(t), maximum = Σ_d max_t S_d(t). Since the distances are independent, this is the exact extreme wherever play is monotone in each distance, which the 3-point sample already assumes. This also removes the Backlash::banded(0.0, 1.0, 1.0, |t| ...) construction, which uses banded only as a way to pick one of three indices.
validation: A law over every preset and arrangement: the reported band contains the path's nominal play at every corner of the tolerance box, computed as probe -e does by setting each distance and re-solving, and each band end is reached by some corner. MeshedPlanets must report minimum 0 (to 1e-9) with the shipped ±0.02 tolerances.

verdict.reason: backlash_at (mod.rs:3467-3483) sums coefficient(k)·row_play[k][band] over every mesh at one shared band index, so every distance sits at its minus end together, then its running value, then its plus end. row_play is built per mesh at its own distance's band (shape.rs:3811). The Backlash::banded doc (mod.rs:141-160) argues only about one distance carrying an internal and an external mesh (the planetary case, which the 3-point extremes handle correctly). It does not cover independent distances. I re-ran the auditor's corner sweep as my own probe, and the reported band is narrower than the reachable range, in the unsafe direction: the report says there is play where the mesh can bind.
verdict.evidence: Probe probes/verify-train-mod-a-1 (a copy of -e): the MeshedPlanets shifts are frozen, then each of its 3 distances is set to running+{-0.02,0,+0.02} (27 corners) and re-solved. The corners range from -0.00000 at [-1,+1,-1] to 0.13956 at [+1,-1,+1]. The solve reports minimum 0.04616, nominal 0.06965, maximum 0.09340. The nominal and the [1,1,1] corner (0.09340) match the report exactly, so the probe reproduces the solve's own figures. Idler reports [0, 0.15625] against a corner range of [0, 0.15625], and Layshaft reports [0, 0.19928] against [0, 0.19928]: the two agree wherever all meshes' play moves the same way. The same defect was filed independently as train-mod-b#1, mesh-contact#0 and lens-feature-gaps#0 (duplicates).
verdict.proposal_note: The per-distance fold is right, and it keeps the stationary-nominal case inside one distance. Also hoist coefficient(k, read, from) out of the band closure. Today it runs System::play once per mesh per band point, 3x the work. Compute each mesh's coefficient once and reuse it for the three bands.

repro.reproduction:
Probe crate /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/repro-train-mod-a-0 (src/main.rs), run with `CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probe-target gc <probe> cargo run --offline -q --release`. The probe runs each of Preset::{MeshedPlanets, Idler, Layshaft, Planetary} through `solve_alone(Train::alone(p.build(), 10, 1000))` and reads `backlash.forward`. It then freezes every profile shift and sets each distance to `Auto::fixed(running + {-tol_minus, 0, +tol_plus})` with the clearance automatic, which keeps the gears fixed and moves only the centres. That gives every combination of the 3^nd corners. Each corner is re-solved and its nominal path play recorded. The probe also records each distance's change alone and checks that the play adds across distances.

For the independent check, /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/notes/repro-train-mod-a-0/indep.py shares no code with the crate. It computes each mesh's spur normal backlash in closed form, j_n = (z1+z2)·m·cosα·(inv α_w − inv α) with cos α_w = a0·cosα/a, where z2 is negative for the ring. It refers that play to the carrier of the meshed-planet set with the sun and ring held. Solving the three line-of-action equations gives ω_c = (s1 − s2 + s3)/(r_bR − r_bs), where r_bR − r_bs = 36·cos20° mm. The smallest input is the shipped MeshedPlanets preset (sun 24, planets 18/18, ring 96, m 1, α 20°, running distances 21.02 / 38.98 / 18.02, tolerance ±0.02 on each).
repro.observed:
For MeshedPlanets the solve reports minimum 0.046162, nominal 0.069648 and maximum 0.093401 deg. The 27 re-solved corners run from 0.000000 at [-1,+1,-1] to 0.139563 at [+1,-1,+1].

The closed-form check reproduces all of these exactly: nominal 0.0696481, corner minimum 0.0 at (-1,+1,-1), corner maximum 0.1395630 at (+1,-1,+1). It also gives 0.0461621 with every distance at its minus end and 0.0934009 with every distance at its plus end. Those are exactly the reported minimum and maximum, which confirms that `backlash_at` (crates/gear-core/src/train/mod.rs:3467-3483) moves every distance to the same end at once, using one band index for all.

Moving one distance alone shows why:
- distance 0 (sun to planet A, external): −0.02325 / +0.02342 deg
- distance 1 (planet B to ring, internal): +0.02304 / −0.02313 deg, so it falls as the distance grows
- distance 2 (planet A to planet B, external): −0.02327 / +0.02346 deg

The play adds across distances to within 3e-17. So folding per distance (sum the minimum of each distance's three values, and separately the maximum) gives exactly the true band [0, 0.139563].

Controls, where every mesh's play moves the same way, agree with the corners exactly:
- Idler: reported [0, 0.156245], corners [0, 0.156245]
- Layshaft: reported [0, 0.199275], corners [0, 0.199275]
- Planetary (sun and ring on one distance, play stationary): [0.041724] both ways

The correct answer comes from the solve's own re-solved corners and, separately, from the closed-form derivation. The two agree to 1e-7 deg.
repro.note:
Confirmed by execution. The reported band is one third of the true width, and it is wrong in the unsafe direction. The report says the path always keeps at least 0.046 deg of play, but at a reachable tolerance corner the play is exactly zero, so the mesh can bind. It also under-reports the worst-case play by 0.046 deg.

The defect needs meshes on different distances whose play moves in opposite directions: an internal and an external mesh, as in MeshedPlanets, probably Ravigneaux and Wolfrom, and any graph train that chains a set with a parallel stage. It does not appear when every mesh is external, or when one distance carries both an internal and an external mesh.

The three distances of a meshed-planet carrier really are independent: planet A's radius, planet B's radius and the A–B spacing are three separate carrier dimensions. The nominal is correct; only the band is wrong. I keep the severity at high because this band is the figure a designer reads to rule out binding. It is not a strength or rating figure; if the plan weights those above clearance figures, medium is defensible.

The proposal in the ledger is exact for this model, and I validated it: the play adds across distances to machine precision. For each distance d, compute S_d(t) = Σ over its meshes of coeff(k)·row_play[k][t]. Then minimum = Σ_d min_t S_d, nominal = Σ_d S_d(running), maximum = Σ_d max_t S_d. Grouping uses the crate-private `Shape::distance_of` (shape.rs:560), so this belongs in the crate. Also compute `coefficient(k, read, from)` once per mesh rather than once per band point.

A regression test should assert that MeshedPlanets reports minimum ≤ 1e-9 and maximum ≈ 0.139563 deg at the shipped ±0.02 tolerances. The probe's corner sweep can serve as a law over every preset.

No worktree was created. Notes and the independent script are in /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/notes/repro-train-mod-a-0/.

title: A member's minimum face width inverts its worst stress at its widest mesh's width, not the width that stress was carried at
claim: MemberRating::rated takes bending = max_k σ_k and sizable = max_k σ_H,k, but sets width = max_k carried_at_k, then calls min_face_width_*(σ_max, width_max). The comment above says 'each figure is inverted at the width it was taken at', and the code does not do that. When a member's two meshes carry it at different widths (a planet wider than its sun), the reported minimum grows with the member's own face width, although the requirement does not depend on it. This does not affect automatic face-width sizing (in the probe pass carried_at == PROBE everywhere), but it does affect the displayed 'min face width' column (TrainPanel.svelte:1268).
evidence: Probe -w: planetary 12/30/72, sun 8 mm, ring 20 mm, planet widened from 8 to 24 mm. The planet's case-0 bending stress stays 211.549 MPa (the sun mesh at 8 mm governs). The reported bmin_F is 1.2398, 1.8598, 2.4797 and 3.7195 mm at planet widths 8, 12, 16 and 24: exactly 211.549·b_planet/1365. bmin_H reads 6.757, 10.136, 13.515, 20.272 mm. Both should stay 1.2398 and 6.757, because the governing mesh carries 8 mm whatever the planet's width. The ring, with one mesh, shows the correct behaviour: bmin_F stays 0.6971 while its stress falls with the carried width.
proposal: Fold per mesh: bending_min = max_k min_face_width_bending(σ_F,k(b_k), b_k, allow) and contact_min = max_{k sizes_face} min_face_width_contact(σ_H,k(b_k), b_k, allow). The product σ·b (or σ²·b) is width-invariant for each mesh, so the result is exact. Keep the worst-stress fold for the stresses shown. Then drop the shared `width` accumulator.
validation: A law: for any member whose meshes carry different widths, min_face_width does not change when that member's own face width grows past the narrowest mate's. It equals the asks() value from the probe pass. Rerun probe -w and expect a constant 1.2398/6.757 on the planet.

verdict.corrected_claim: MemberRating::rated inverts max_k σ_k at max_k carried_at_k, and those two maxima can come from different meshes. The displayed min face width therefore grows with the member's own width even when a narrower mate governs. Because σ_max ≥ σ_k and b_max ≥ b_k, the product σ_max·b_max (and σ_max²·b_max for contact) is always ≥ every mesh's own product. The error is therefore always an overstatement (conservative) and never unsafe. Automatic sizing is unaffected. It is still a wrong figure under rule 6.
verdict.reason: mod.rs:966-1010: bending and sizable are folded with max, and so is `width = width.max(l.carried_at)`, independently of them. The comment 'each figure is inverted at the width it was taken at' is false for a member with meshes of different widths. Re-running the auditor's probe -w reproduced every number. Severity is lowered from high because the error has a proven sign (it overstates) and touches only the displayed column, not sizing or stresses.
verdict.evidence: My rerun of probe_train_mod_a_w (output identical to notes/train-mod-a/out/probe_train_mod_a_w.txt): planet σF stays 211.549 MPa while its bmin_F reads 1.2398, 1.8598, 2.4797 and 3.7195 mm at planet widths 8, 12, 16 and 24, which is 211.549·b/1365. The correct figure is 1.2398, because the sun mesh carries at 8 mm. The ring, with a single mesh, stays at 0.6971. With the planet width automatic, the sizing gives 2.2565 = the case-1 value at 8/8, which shows asks() is correct (carried_at == PROBE there). Also filed as shape-b#6 (duplicate).
verdict.proposal_note: Folding per mesh, as max_k min_face_width(σ_k at b_k, b_k), is exact because σ·b and σ²·b are width-invariant. It also makes rated() agree with asks() by construction, so a law 'rated().min_face_width == asks() at any width' can hold it.

title: Relief counts each group on its own, so it lets through states that are over-determined as a whole; the realistic path 'pin the sun's shift, type the distance' then misses the distance
claim: Each mesh relation is declared as its own FreedomGroup, 'given ≤ entries − 1': the first mesh on a distance gets {D, x_a, x_b, C, size}, and later meshes get their absorbers. Groups that share unknowns (x_planet, D, C) are never checked together. The real condition is Hall's: every relation needs its own distinct automatic unknown. So relief accepts states where two relations compete for one unknown, and the solve then misses a given distance or refuses.
evidence: Probe train-mod-a (out/probe_train_mod_a.txt), planetary 12/30/72 preset: pin x_s (relieved with just = x_s, and nothing moves), then type D = running + 0.1 (just = D). Relief leaves D, C, x_s and x_r given with x_p as the only automatic shift: two relations, one unknown. Both groups pass their counts: group 1 has 3 of 5 given, limit 4; group 2 has 2 of 3, limit 2. The solve reports part.distance_not_reached and part.clearance_negative, and the planet-ring nominal is 21.063 against 21.225 asked. The same happens on 13/30/74.
