Tuning literals are real: hertz.rs:429 passes Tol{x_tol:1e-14,max_iter:200}; ring.rs:543-549 grows by 1.4 up to 64 times; shape.rs:946 caps at 60; shape.rs:1645/1667 caps at 40/80 with growth 1.5; shape.rs:860 brackets at 89.0. auto.rs:744-755 is two brent calls, and docs/reference.md:249-251 also still calls it 'a bracketed Newton', a stale site the auditor missed. My script notes/verify-primitives/thresh.py bisects the crate's seed with unbracketed Newton to a threshold of 73.177°. newton_div2.py against an mpmath root gives 'within 2ulp after' 3 steps at 20/30/40°, 4 at 50/55/60°, 5 at 65°, 6 at 70°, 8 at 72° and 10 at 73°, and 'left domain at step 1' from 73.3°. At 5° and 10° it never reaches 2 ulp, because of the cancellation in finding 7. involute.rs:97 still says 75°. More stale lines in the same topic: involute.rs:28 and :83 say 60° is 'the most this tool allows', while admissible_ranges uses Bound::strictly(0.0, 90.0) (auto.rs:696) and reference.md:156 says 0 < α < 90°. Rationale row #4 says 'closed-form bracket', but shape.rs:1478-1489 falls back to ±5 and widens by pull_in's doubling search (shape.rs:2345).
verdict.proposal_note: Do not add a tool that counts solver call sites. CLAUDE.md itself refuses to quote numbers that date, and a count check fails on every legitimate new solve without telling anyone whether the prose is still right. Instead: drop 'Ten' and 'none with a tuning parameter'; state the invariant, that every continuous transcendental step goes through solve.rs's two bracketed solvers (greppable, and the two predicate bisections at gear.rs:1119 and metrology.rs:200 named as the exception); and keep table rows only where a method choice needs arguing (#6, #9b, #10). Correct the divergence sentence in solve.rs:6, involute.rs:46-49 and :97, reference.md:30 and corrections.md:423 to 'about 73°', and drop the 'inside the pressure-angle range this tool allows' justification: the allowed range is (0°, 90°), and bracketing needs no measured threshold to justify it.

title: inv and inv_inverse lose relative accuracy below ~0.3 rad through cancellation; a series fixes both and makes the inverse 0–2 Newton steps
claim: inv(α) = tan α − α cancels for small α. inv_inverse's residual inv(a) − v inherits the cancellation, while the derivative tan²α → 0, so root error grows like ε/α² in relative terms. That is not inherent: α = (3v)^{1/3}(1 + …) is perfectly conditioned. Separately, the 2-term seed needs 3–5 Newton steps, and newton_bracketed spends two evaluations on bracket ends that are known in closed form (f(0) = −v).
evidence: notes/primitives/inv_acc.out (mpmath reference at 200 bits against the crate's f64 results). inv: max 2.2e12 ulp for α∈[1e-6,1e-4), 1.3e8 in [1e-4,1e-2), 1.6e4 in [0.01,0.1), 116 in [0.1,0.3), 15.6 in [0.3,0.7), ≤ 4 above. inv_inverse: 3.3e4 ulp in [1e-4,1e-2), 4.6e3 in [0.01,0.1), 43 in [0.1,0.3), 4.9 in [0.3,0.7), < 1 above 0.7. seed.py derived the Lagrange inversion α = y − 2y³/15 + 3y⁵/175 − 2y⁷/1575 − 16y⁹/202125 + …, y = (3v)^{1/3}. The code's 0.4v is exactly the 2y³/15 term, so the comment is right. Unbracketed Newton steps, code seed against 5-term seed: α=0.1: 3 vs 1; 0.3: 3 vs 2; 0.5: 4 vs 2; 0.7: 4 vs 3; 1.0: 5 vs 3. Above 1.2 rad, the seed α = atan(v + atan(v + atan(v+1))) has error ≤ 5e-4 and needs 1–4 steps. Logged calls at mesh.rs:152 average 6 evaluations. Physically negligible: the absolute error is ≤ 3e-14 rad.
proposal: In involute.rs: (1) inv(α): for |α| < 0.25, use the odd series α³/3 + 2α⁵/15 + 17α⁷/315 + 62α⁹/2835 + 1382α¹¹/155925 + 21844α¹³/6081075 (exact Taylor coefficients of tan, no fit), otherwise tan α − α. (2) inv_inverse: seed with the 5-term Lagrange series for y < ~1.0, and with the atan fixed-point for larger v. Refine with Newton on the same series-evaluated residual, keeping the bracket as the safety net. Gate the change on golden digits: expect at most last-digit moves.
validation: A test against a table of mpmath values (committed as literals, computed once) over α ∈ [1e-6, π/2 − 1e-6]: inv within 2 ulp and inv_inverse within 2 ulp everywhere. Newton step count ≤ 3 on the logged mesh.rs:152 inputs.

verdict.reason: I reproduced the accuracy measurements, and inv_from_roll behaves the same way. But nothing reads these values in relative terms: every caller uses inv α or inv⁻¹ as an absolute angle (ψ_b − inv α, cos α_w, cos φ), where the error is ≤ 2.4e-14 rad. The proposed fix is also numerically wrong as written. A 6-term Taylor series switched in below 0.25 rad is accurate only below about 0.07 rad; at the proposed cutoff it is 250,000 times worse than today. So the 'within 2 ulp everywhere' validation cannot pass with this proposal.
verdict.evidence: Probe probes/verify-primitives-b (4001-point log grid; mpmath at 200 bits; notes/verify-primitives/inv_acc.py). Worst error per range, as inv / inv_inverse / inv_from_roll in ulp: [1e-6,1e-4) 1.83e12 / 0.9 / 1.83e12; [1e-4,1e-2) 1.34e8 / 3.33e4 / 1.34e8; [0.01,0.1) 1.57e4 / 4.56e3 / 1.63e4; [0.1,0.3) 127 / 56 / 129; [0.3,0.7) 15.8 / 4.8 / 15.4; ≥0.7 ≤3.3 / <1. The largest absolute inv_inverse error is 2.4e-14 rad. series_trunc.py puts the proposed 6-term series against today's tan−α: 0.13 vs 1.2e4 ulp at 0.01, 1.9 vs 433 at 0.07, 27.7 vs 27.7 at 0.1, 2970 vs 61 at 0.15, 1.1e5 vs 20 at 0.2, and 1.6e6 vs 6.4 at 0.25. The next Taylor term, 929569/638512875·α^15 ≈ 1.4e-12 at 0.25, explains it. sympy series reversion confirms the Lagrange seed coefficients (−2/15, 3/175, −2/1575, −16/202125, 362/9384375), so the code's 0.4v is indeed the 2y³/15 term. The atan fixed-point seed error above 1.2 rad is 4.9e-4, as claimed.
verdict.proposal_note: If anything is done, keep inv as tan α − α; switching in a series adds a branch for no geometric gain. The better seed is harmless and saves 1–3 Newton steps on a microsecond solve, and it could be taken on its own. A relative-accuracy fix for inv would need a series to about α^25 to cover 0.3 rad, or a different formulation. Neither is warranted while no consumer reads relative accuracy. Any accuracy test should be absolute, e.g. |inv_inverse(inv(α)) − α| ≤ 4ε·max(α,1), not '2 ulp everywhere'.

title: The pointed-tooth roll (u − atan u = ψ_b) is an inverse involute solved by hand twice, with two different solvers
claim: tooth.rs:456 (newton_bracketed, seed (3ψ)^{1/3}) and auto.rs:744 (brent) both solve inv_from_roll(u) = ψ_b on [0, POINTED_TOOTH_MAX_ROLL = 50], which is tan(inv_inverse(ψ_b)). ring.rs:297/399 already solve the same thing through inv_inverse. That is three routes to one number, with different domain caps: roll 50 is 88.85°, while inv_inverse's ALPHA_MAX is π/2 − 1e-12.
evidence: tooth.rs:456-463: `newton_bracketed(|u| psi_b - inv_from_roll(u), |u| -(u * u) / (1.0 + u * u), 0.0, POINTED_TOOTH_MAX_ROLL, (3.0 * psi_b).cbrt(), Tol::default())`. auto.rs:744-749: `brent(|u| g.psi_b - inv_from_roll(u), 0.0, POINTED_TOOTH_MAX_ROLL, Tol::default())?`. Logged: tooth.rs:456 took 7 evaluations median over 147,910 calls.
proposal: Add `pub fn roll_of_inv(v: f64) -> Option<f64>` to involute.rs (inv_inverse(v).map(f64::tan), or a native roll-variable solve), and call it from tooth.rs:456 and auto.rs:744. Decide whether the 50-roll cap is a physical limit (then express it as an angle next to ALPHA_MAX) or drop it.
validation: Both call sites return values bit-identical to (or within 1 ulp of) today's across the golden corpus. Test: for ψ ∈ logspace(1e-9, 10), inv_from_roll(roll_of_inv(ψ)) == ψ to 2 ulp.

verdict.reason: There are three routes to one number. tooth.rs:456 solves u − atan u = ψ_b by bracketed Newton with seed (3ψ)^{1/3}. auto.rs:744 solves the same equation on the same bracket [0, 50] with Brent, from the psi_b of the Tooth it was handed, which had already solved it and not stored the result. ring.rs:297/399 reach the same relation through inv_inverse. The routes agree to rounding at real gears, so this is duplication, not a wrong answer.
verdict.evidence: tooth.rs:455-463 and auto.rs:744-749 are quoted correctly. POINTED_TOOTH_MAX_ROLL = 50 (tooth.rs:944), atan(50) = 88.85°. My probe (probes/verify-primitives-b) compared the Newton, Brent and tan(inv_inverse(ψ)) routes for ψ from 1e-6 to 31. All return Some. They differ by up to 30 ulp only near ψ≈1e-3, where u − atan u cancels. Over realistic ψ_b (z 4–120, x −0.5..1, α 14.5–30°), ra_point/r_b = hypot(1,u) from tan(inv_inverse) agrees with today's Newton to 1.38 ulp at worst.
verdict.proposal_note: Prefer tan(inv_inverse(ψ)). Its bracket is ALPHA_MAX, so POINTED_TOOTH_MAX_ROLL disappears rather than needing a ruling. A leaner alternative is for Tooth to keep the pointed radius it already computes, so addendum_for_tip_width reads g's value and does not solve again. Two fixes to the validation: expect ra_point within about 2 ulp, not bit-identical; and 'inv_from_roll(roll_of_inv(ψ)) == ψ to 2 ulp for ψ from 1e-9' cannot pass. At ψ = 1e-9, u ≈ 1.4e-3, where inv_from_roll itself loses about 1e6 ulp to cancellation. Test the round trip in absolute terms, or compare u against an mpmath table.

title: plane.rs identities and base_pitch are re-written at call sites; transverse module m/cos β is written eight times
claim: plane.rs says it replaced every hand-written copy. Some remain. screw.rs:1471 writes `(alpha_n.tan() / cos_beta).atan()` on the line before it calls plane::base_helix_angle. screw.rs:869 and shape.rs:3529 (production; shape's tests start at 4192) write π·m_n·cos α_n instead of plane::base_pitch. The transverse module `m / beta.cos()` is open-coded in eight production places, although BasicRack.mt exists. The transverse tooth thickness `m(π/2 + 2(x+x_s) tan α_n)/cos β` is written three times (tooth.rs:834, auto.rs:357, auto.rs:678).
evidence: grep over crates/gear-core/src for 'tan() / .*cos()).atan', 'PI * .*cos()', and '/ beta.cos()' (output quoted in the session). The three sites compute the same product order, so replacing them moves no digit.
proposal: Replace screw.rs:1471 with plane::transverse_pressure_angle, and screw.rs:869 and shape.rs:3529 with plane::base_pitch. Add `pub fn transverse_module(mn, beta)` and `pub fn transverse_thickness(mn, x_thick, alpha_n, beta)` to plane.rs, or build a BasicRack and read .mt, and use them at the listed sites. Add the missing companion identity tan β_b = tan β · cos α_t to the plane.rs tests.
validation: check_golden shows zero diffs, which is the gate plane.rs itself sets. A grep check in tools/ for the patterns above.

verdict.reason: The cited copies exist. screw.rs:1471 writes (alpha_n.tan()/cos_beta).atan() on the line before it calls plane::base_helix_angle. screw.rs:869 and shape.rs:3529 (production: inside pub fn rate, and shape's tests start at 4190) write π·m_n·cos α_n in base_pitch's own product order. m / beta.cos() is open-coded at eight production sites. There are also more copies than the auditor listed.
verdict.evidence: Transverse module: ring.rs:220; tooth.rs:367, 413, 895; auto.rs:117, 306, 623, 664 (plane.rs:123 is BasicRack's own). Transverse thickness: tooth.rs:834, auto.rs:357 and auto.rs:678, all as m·(π/2 + 2x tan α_n)/cos β. It appears twice more, in another product order, at ring.rs:246 and ring.rs:358 (mt·(π/2 + 2x tan α_n)); a single helper would move last digits there unless it keeps that order. gear-wasm/src/lib.rs:556 also open-codes the transverse pressure angle (see missed). The plane.rs tests already cover cos α_t cos β_b = cos α_n cos β; tan β_b = tan β cos α_t is not covered.
verdict.proposal_note: Sound. For the thickness, the private tooth.rs::transverse_thickness already exists and also applies the thickness guards. auto.rs wants the unclamped figure, so name the raw formula once in plane.rs and let transverse_thickness clamp it. Review the ring.rs sites under check_golden, not on the assumption that no digit moves. Skip the grep-pattern lint: patterns like '/ beta.cos()' have legitimate uses (tooth.rs:344's z/cos³β).

title: The pressure-angle guard is written five times, twice without its note
claim: `pressure_angle.to_radians().max(MIN_PRESSURE_ANGLE_DEG.to_radians())` appears in tool_wanted_by, three places in auto.rs, and as the noted clamp in build_with_z. The copies can disagree: build_with_z clamps on `<=` and pushes a note, the others clamp with .max and say nothing. params::thickness_shift has no copy at all (see the thickness_shift finding).
evidence: grep 'guard::MIN_PRESSURE_ANGLE_DEG' output: tooth.rs:364, 402-406; auto.rs:115, 304, 662.
proposal: Add one `GearParams::normal_pressure_angle(&self) -> (f64 /*rad, guarded*/, Option<Note>)` in params.rs, and use it at all five sites and in thickness_shift.
validation: Golden unchanged. A grep check that MIN_PRESSURE_ANGLE_DEG is read only in params.rs.

verdict.reason: The guard is written five times, and centralising it is right. Two parts of the claim are off. First, it is four copies (not two) that clamp without a note, but all four feed a Tooth whose build_with_z raises the note, so no note is lost on that path. Second, 'the copies can disagree' holds only for NaN; for every finite input `<=` and `.max` give the same angle. The larger problem the finding misses: several readers of the pressure angle never apply the guard. The guard is therefore a property of whichever path reads the input, not of the input.
verdict.evidence: Five sites: tooth.rs:364, tooth.rs:402-406 (the noted one), auto.rs:115, 304, 662. On NaN, NaN.max(0.5°) is 0.5° while `NaN <= 0.5°` is false. My probe shows Tooth::new at pressure_angle NaN keeps alpha_n = NaN, while tool_wanted_by settles its tool at 0.5°. Unguarded readers: ring.rs:218; Shape::rack_of → BasicRack::new (shape.rs:1155), which drives shift_sum_for, nominal_of and the slope in the train's shift plan (shape.rs:548, 1188, 1433, 1463); shape.rs:525 (screw); shape.rs:3526 (play); params::thickness_shift (params.rs:105). Probe at pa = 0.3°: Tooth α_n = 0.5000° with clamp.pressure_angle_raised; Ring α_n = 0.3000° with no pressure-angle note; thickness_shift at k = 1.2 gives 29.9997; and admissible_ranges(...).pressure_angle.admits(0.3) is true. That contradicts reference.md:149 ('each [bound] sits exactly where the generator's own guards begin to clamp'), since the bound is 0 and the clamp is 0.5°. In a train, a Spur preset at 1°, 0.5° and 0.3° is refused anyway (InPart NoRootSection), so the mismatch between plan and cut cannot be observed there. In the ring tab it can.
verdict.proposal_note: Put the guard in one accessor on GearParams: guarded radians plus whether it clamped. Use it in Tooth (which raises the note), Ring, thickness_shift and BasicRack::new, or wherever MemberGear builds a rack. Then either raise the admissible lower bound to MIN_PRESSURE_ANGLE_DEG so the range and the guard agree, as reference.md claims, or correct reference.md:149. The proposed grep check that MIN_PRESSURE_ANGLE_DEG is read only in params.rs is fine.

title: Error messages exist in English twice, in gear-core Display and in the catalogue, and have already drifted
claim: Rule 2 says there is no English in gear-core. Yet MeshError, TrainError, MeasurementError and EditRefused keep English Display impls 'for the CLI and for Debug' (note.rs Explain doc; rationale.md:60), alongside the catalogue sentences. The two copies already say different things. Also, Debug is derived and does not use Display, so 'for Debug' is wrong. gear-cli depends on gear-io and could render through gear_io::strings.
evidence: mesh.rs:772: `"no such gear pair: the profile shifts require the base circles to overlap"`. strings_en.toml:188: `mesh_outside_involute_domain = "profile shifts leave no operating pressure angle"`. The Incompatible, RingTooSmall and axis-distance messages are the same today, but only by hand-copying. The CLI prints `{e}` at gear-cli/src/main.rs:709, 1238 and kinematics.rs:644.
proposal: Delete the Display impls (keep std::error::Error, if needed, via a Display that prints the note key). Make the CLI print gear_io::strings::render(&e.note(), "en"). Update rationale.md:60 and the Explain doc.
validation: grep: no English string literals in gear-core/src outside tests (a check_strings-style lint). check_golden: CLI error lines change to the catalogue wording; review the diff.

verdict.reason: The drift is wider than the finding shows, and the documented exception rests on a false premise. The Display impls are said to be 'for Debug', but Debug is derived on every one of these enums. The CLI already depends on gear-io, whose catalogue renders notes. One more point makes the case stronger: in places the Display text carries detail the user-facing note drops.
verdict.evidence: Differing messages, Display vs strings_en.toml [error]/[ui]: MeshError 1 of 4 (OutsideInvoluteDomain); MeasurementError 2 of 3 (the pin messages add 'to seat on the flanks'); screw messages inside TrainError's Display 4 of 5; TrainError about 8 of 13 (NoContact, Wiring, Overdetermined, NoSuchBody, Overflow 'holds' vs 'can hold', LoadPort 'shaft' vs 'body', UnknownMaterial quoting); EditRefused 6 of 10 (edits.rs:171 vs strings_en.toml:538-547). All six enums carry #[derive(Debug)] (mesh.rs:180, train/mod.rs:1559, metrology.rs:42, edits.rs:120, screw.rs:169, wiring.rs:176). strings_en.toml:182 says 'These were `Display` impls inside `gear-core`', but they still are. rationale.md:57-60 lists ScrewError as having a Display; it has none. crossed.rs:1094 asserts `format!("{err}").contains("too thin")`, which is branching on wording, the pattern rationale.md:52-55 says was removed. tools/golden/kinematics.txt:1466, 1475 and 1542 record Display text. TrainError::note maps Wiring(_) to one key with no values (train/mod.rs:1682), so the UI cannot say which member has no teeth, while Display prints 'member N has no teeth'. EditRefused's Display is read only by tests; gear-cli/src/graph.rs:229 prints {e:?}. No `dyn Error` is used anywhere, so the Error impls can go too.
verdict.proposal_note: The render call is `gear_io::strings::Strings::english().render(&e.note())` (strings.rs:199/248), not `render(&note, "en")`. Before deleting Display, carry the index in the Wiring note (values for member or mesh, or one key per WiringError variant) and map ground to a word in `located`, so the switch loses nothing the CLI prints today. Change crossed.rs:1094 to matches!(err, TrainError::Screw(ScrewError::WormTooThin)), and switch test panics from {e} to {e:?}. Expect golden diffs on the three kinematics.txt lines. Fix rationale.md:57-60, note.rs:381-382 and strings_en.toml:182-185 at the same time.

title: Brent is used with residuals that jump to a sentinel value, collapsing it to bisection
claim: shaper::largest_tip_round's residual returns −1.0 when corner ≤ 0 or corner_angle is None, so it is discontinuous. Brent takes 44–55 evaluations there, about the log2(11.25/1e-15) ≈ 53 of pure bisection. Every other site takes 2–24. The failure is then .unwrap_or(floor). Either the root being found is the edge of the sentinel region (a wrong answer dressed as a root) or the function is badly scaled; the log cannot tell which.
evidence: sum_cli.txt: 'brent shaper.rs:450 n=4179 evals med/p99/max 44/55/55, chandrupatla 55/55/55'. A raw log line: bracket [1e-9, 11.25], root 0.3462280774297214, 44 evaluations.
proposal: Return NaN from the residual outside its domain (so brent reports failure), and shrink the upper bracket to the largest ρ where corner_angle is Some. Or, since the boundary is where the corner angle reaches zero, derive it in closed form if corner_angle is invertible.
validation: Probe: evaluate angle_at on either side of the returned boundary. It should be continuous and change sign there, not jump to −1. The evaluation count drops to ≤ 15.

verdict.reason: The evaluation count holds: the sentinel residual pushes Brent to near-bisection, while the same root with a continuous residual takes 8-12 evaluations. The finding's worry that this might be 'a wrong answer dressed as a root' does not hold. Both sentinel regions are real limits. `angle < 0` means the two corner rounds have crossed. `corner <= base` means the round's centre would have to sit inside the cutter's base circle, which the offset involute cannot reach, because its minimum radius is r_bc. In both cases the sign change is exactly at the domain edge. The root agrees with the continuous solve to within 3e-15 mm, so the only cost is about 40-60 wasted evaluations per ring build, a few microseconds. The `.unwrap_or(floor)` cannot fire: f(floor) >= 0 is checked, f(r_tip) is always -1, and the worst case of about 76 iterations is far below max_iter = 200. The proposal's first option is harmful. Returning NaN outside the domain makes brent fail at once, because f(hi = cutter_tip_radius) is evaluated at corner = 0. Every ring would then fall back to `floor` = 1e-9 m and get no fillet. The second option, shrinking the bracket to where corner_angle is Some, is circular, because that edge is the root being sought.
verdict.evidence: Probe /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/verify-primitives, run through gear_core::solve::brent with a counting closure that copies shaper.rs:432-439, compared with the unrefused angle on [floor, r_ac - r_bc]. zc=25 m=2 ha=1.25 α=20°: 51 evaluations vs 8, roots 0.7456242015140999 vs ...1026. zc=12 m=1: 54 vs 12. zc=40 m=3 x=0.3: 54 vs 9. zc=60 m=1 α=25°: 53 vs 8. Stub cutters (ha=0.5 zc=10; ha=0.4 zc=8 α=14.5°): 76 and 68 evaluations, and the boundary is r_ac - r_bc, where the continuous angle is still +1.4e-3 or +8.5e-2. So the corner=base limit binds there, and it is a real limit. The angle 1e-9 mm either side of each ordinary root is ±2e-11, which is a true zero crossing. Analytic derivative: d(angle)/dρ = -(1 - sin α_g)/r_bc, checked against central differences to 4e-11 (notes/verify-primitives/dangle.py). This proves the docstring's monotonicity claim, which is SOUND. The auditor's log sum_cli.txt shows 44/55/55 evaluations at shaper.rs:450, consistent with this.
verdict.corrected_claim: shaper::largest_tip_round solves on a residual that jumps from +0 to a -1 sentinel at the domain edge, so Brent takes 44-76 evaluations where a continuous residual takes 8-12. It also runs this solve on every ring build, including the ordinary case where the asked round fits. The root it returns is correct, since both sentinel edges are genuine limits, so the cost is only clarity and a few microseconds.
verdict.proposal_note: Do not return NaN. Solve the raw angle, without the angle<0 refusal, on [floor, r_ac - r_bc]. It is continuous and monotone there with derivative -(1 - sin α_g)/r_bc, so either use brent or use newton_bracketed with that exact derivative. If the angle at r_ac - r_bc is still >= 0, that end is the boundary. Also exit before any solve: the angle is monotone, so asked <= 0.95·boundary exactly when angle(asked/0.95) >= 0. The ordinary case then costs one evaluation, which is what the docstring's 'returns the requested round untouched' already implies. No closed form exists, since the equation mixes sqrt, acos and linear terms in r_g.

title: Bracket growth and predicate bisection are hand-rolled at least seven times, each with its own factor and cap
claim: solve.rs holds root finders but no bracket search, so callers write their own. Growth ×1.4 for 64 steps (ring), ×2 for 60 (shape:946), ×1.5 for 40 and 80 with halving on NaN (shape:1645/1667), ×2 until ln MIN_POSITIVE (hertz), ×2 for 64 (metrology). Fixed 64-step bisections on a boolean appear at metrology.rs:200 and gear.rs:1119. These are the unexplained caps and factors the audit brief asks about, and there is no shared law saying a bracket found this way really brackets.
evidence: Code quoted in the session. For example ring.rs:542-548: `let mut far = -self.mt; for _ in 0..64 { if radius_at(far) < 0.0 { ... brent(...) } far *= 1.4; }`. shape.rs:1645: `for _ in 0..40 { hi = lo + step; ... step *= 1.5; }`.
proposal: Add two primitives to solve.rs. `grow_bracket(f, from, first_step, direction, limit) -> Result<(f64,f64), SolveError>` doubles until the sign changes, halves back on a non-finite value, and stops at an explicit physical limit the caller passes (not an iteration count). `bisect_predicate(pred, lo, hi) -> f64` runs to adjacent floats, `while mid != lo && mid != hi`, rather than for 64 steps. Move the seven sites over; each keeps only its limit, stated physically.
validation: Golden unchanged or last-digit moves. Unit tests of both primitives on monotone, NaN-holed and unbracketable functions.

verdict.reason: Every cited site exists as described, and there are more than seven. Also missed: auto.rs:137-147 (×2 per step, capped by MINIMUM_SHIFT_BRACKET_STEPS = 16, a named constant with a stated argument), shape.rs:2346 pull_in (×2 from 1e-9·span, stops at the span, a physical limit), and verify.rs:726 (60-step boolean bisection). Two of the listed sites already have the form the proposal asks for: hertz.rs:418 stops at a type-derived floor, ln(MIN_POSITIVE)/2, and shape.rs:1645 at a physical reach. So 'each with its own factor and cap' is accurate, but not every cap is arbitrary. The claim that no shared law says a found bracket really brackets is weaker than stated for the grow-then-brent sites: brent itself checks the sign change and returns None. For the boolean bisections the claim holds, since monotonicity of the predicate is only asserted in prose. Related doc slip: metrology.rs:181-183 says 'Sixty halvings of a bracket a few modules wide', while the code does 64. The bracket there is also rb·2^k, which is tens of modules on a large gear, not a few.
verdict.evidence: ring.rs:542-549 grows `far *= 1.4` from -m for 64 steps. shape.rs:944-952 grows `top *= 2.0` for 60 steps. shape.rs:1645-1662 does `for _ in 0..40` with `step *= 1.5`, halving on NaN, bounded by `from + reach`. shape.rs:1667-1688 does `for _ in 0..80` with `step *= 1.5`. hertz.rs:418-426 does `lo *= 2.0` until `floor = MIN_POSITIVE.ln()/2`. metrology.rs:190-196 does `hi *= 2.0` with steps > 64 giving None. Boolean bisections: metrology.rs:200 (64), gear.rs:1119 (64), verify.rs:726 (60). Also auto.rs:140 and shape.rs:2346-2359.
verdict.proposal_note: `bisect_predicate` should not run 'while mid != lo && mid != hi'. When the boundary is at or near 0 and lo = 0, as in gear.rs:1119 when nothing beyond 0 is feasible, that loop walks hi down through every binade to subnormals, about 1075 predicate calls. At gear.rs each call is a mesh solve. Stop instead when hi - lo <= ε·(initial width), which is at most about 53 steps. The fixed 64 already approximates this, so the gain is a stated stopping rule rather than precision. `grow_bracket` has to cover both additive stepping (shape.rs:1645/1667, auto.rs:137) and geometric growth of a position (ring.rs:543, metrology.rs:193), each with a caller-stated physical limit. Keep the NaN-halving that shape.rs needs. Moving the sites over may move the last digit of Brent roots whose brackets change, so rerun check_golden.

title: Core-formatted note values cannot be localised, can print '-0.000', and readouts round in TypeScript anyway
claim: note.rs says 'a locale may decide how to write 1.234', but Note::number emits a finished string with '.', and nothing downstream re-localises it. de and pt therefore show English decimal points in notes. `format!("{:.3}", -0.0001)` gives '-0.000', and nothing prevents that for values such as overlap = −clearance (train/mod.rs:1950). Meanwhile the panel's own readouts choose decimals in TS (16 toFixed calls), so the claim that decimals are 'a judgement made where the model is' holds for notes only.
evidence: web/src/strings.svelte.ts:78-87 renders values verbatim. grep for toLocaleString or Intl.NumberFormat in web/src: none. `grep -rn toFixed web/src | wc -l` = 16. Decimals per value name across all 34 Note::number sites are consistent within each name (radius 4, ratio 3; rim ratio 2 is a different quantity).
proposal: Send numbers as {value: f64, decimals: u8} (or a typed Fixed value) and let the catalogue renderer format them with the locale's separator (Intl.NumberFormat with minimumFractionDigits = maximumFractionDigits = decimals), snapping values that round to zero to +0. Give readouts decimals from the core the same way, or state in note.rs that readouts are exempt.
validation: A strings test: a note rendered in de shows ','. A test that Note::number(−1e-9, 3) renders '0.000'.

verdict.reason: The core claims hold. Note::number emits a finished '.'-decimal string, nothing localises it, and note.rs:21 and rationale.md:47-48 ('a translator may decide how 1.234 is written') promise something this design cannot deliver. Evidence the gap is visible: the de and pt catalogues write their own figure as '1,2' (strings_de.toml:408, strings_pt.toml:409), while notes and readouts on the same page print '0.760'. Two parts are wrong or duplicated. First, the cited '-0.000' example is wrong. At train/mod.rs:1950 the value is `-clearance` inside `if clearance < 0.0`, so it is always positive and cannot print a minus sign. A site that can is shape.rs:3670, `.number("gap", l.clearance, 3)`, where clearance = 2a·sin(π/N) - d_tip is signed and moves continuously through 0. There, a gap in (-0.0005, 0) prints 'adjacent planets clear by -0.000 mm'. Second, the 'readouts round in TypeScript' part duplicates web finding 9, and the mixed-locale part duplicates web finding 10. Only the note-side promise and the -0 formatting are new here.
verdict.evidence: Probe: format!("{:.3}", -0.0001) gives "-0.000", and format!("{:.4}", -1e-9) gives "-0.0000". Node: (-0.00001).toFixed(3) gives '-0.000', so the TS readouts share the fault for signed quantities such as shifts. strings.svelte.ts:78-87 interpolates values verbatim. Nothing in web/src uses Intl.NumberFormat; the only locale call, toLocaleString at TrainPanel.svelte:409, follows the browser (web 10). The same quantity is shown at two precisions: the note prints ε_α as '0.760' (shape/mod.rs, 3 decimals) while TrainPanel.svelte:1121 prints num(r.transverse, 4) = '0.7604'.
verdict.corrected_claim: The claim that 'a locale may decide how to write 1.234' in note.rs and rationale.md cannot be honoured: Note values cross as pre-formatted '.'-decimal strings, and de/pt catalogue prose already writes '1,2'. A signed note value that rounds to zero prints with a minus sign, reachable at the planet-gap note (shape.rs:3670), not at the overlap note. The TS rounding and locale mixing are already reported as web findings 9 and 10.
verdict.proposal_note: The typed value is the right direction, but it changes the Note wire type (ts-rs binding, gear-io's renderer used by the CLI, golden outputs), so the effort is M. Take the separator from the app's language, not the browser's, e.g. Intl.NumberFormat(langCode) or a per-catalogue separator key. A cheaper interim step: in Note::number, write +0 when the value rounds to zero, e.g. `if (value * 10f64.powi(d)).round() == 0.0 { 0.0 } else { value }`, and reword note.rs/rationale.md to say values are locale-neutral until the renderer localises them. Separately, a negative 'gap' deserves wording of its own ('overlap by'), as the distance note at mod.rs:1948 already has.

title: The contact-ratio-below-one note is raised at two sites with the threshold and decimals copied
claim: MESH_CONTACT_RATIO_BELOW_ONE is pushed from line_mesh_report (train/mod.rs:472) and from the point-contact report (shape.rs:2733), each with its own `< 1.0` and `, 3)`. mod.rs:467's comment exists precisely to stop callers each remembering to raise it.
evidence: Both lines read `notes.push(Note::new(key::MESH_CONTACT_RATIO_BELOW_ONE).number("ratio", ..., 3))`.
proposal: Raise it once, in the MeshReport constructor both paths use (or a `fn contact_notes(contact_ratio) -> Vec<Note>`).
validation: Existing note-firing tests. Grep: one site per key.

verdict.reason: Both sites exist as quoted, each with its own `< 1.0` and `, 3`. They test different quantities, though: the line site tests r.transverse (ε_α), while the point site tests the zone's single contact ratio. A shared helper therefore has to take the ratio as a parameter, which is what the proposal's `contact_notes(ratio)` does. The threshold is also copied twice more in TypeScript (TrainPanel.svelte:1120 and :1127), which web finding 8 already reports. The unification is worth doing mostly because the note's meaning is currently wrong for helical line contact (see missed), and one site is where that gets fixed once.
verdict.evidence: train/mod.rs:471-472: `if r.transverse < 1.0 { notes.push(Note::new(key::MESH_CONTACT_RATIO_BELOW_ONE).number("ratio", r.transverse, 3)); }`. shape.rs:2732-2733: `if contact_ratio < 1.0 { ... .number("ratio", contact_ratio, 3)); }`. The comment at mod.rs:467-469 states the intent that no caller has to remember to raise it.
verdict.proposal_note: Put the helper beside MeshReport and give it the quantity that decides continuity, not always ε_α (see the missed finding on helical wording). Otherwise the unification cements the helical mis-statement.

title: inv_inverse doc omits the v > ~1e12 refusal and has a malformed link line
claim: inv_inverse returns None for v > inv(ALPHA_MAX) ≈ 1e12 (unbracketed), not only for v < 0 as the doc says. Lines 38-39 contain two link targets run together without separator text, and cite a 'planetary ring-gear search' that is now the shape's.
evidence: newton_bracketed on [0, ALPHA_MAX] with f(ALPHA_MAX) = tan(π/2−1e-12) − ALPHA_MAX − v < 0 for v > ~1e12 returns None at solve.rs:161. Doc text: '(docs/reference.md#primitives\n/// docs/reference.md#planetary-sets)'.
proposal: State both refusals, and fix the citation to the current caller (mesh::operating_angle via Mesh::new, ring.rs:297/399, metrology.rs:489).
validation: check_doc_links.

verdict.reason: inv_inverse returns None for v >= inv(ALPHA_MAX) ≈ 9.998e11 and for non-finite v. The doc names only v < 0. The two doc paths at lines 38-39 run together with no separator. Both anchors resolve, so check_doc_links is right to pass and the fault is only presentation. The justification 'a negative argument means ... a centre distance smaller than the base circles permit' covers only mesh.rs:152. The other callers pass other quantities: ring.rs:297 passes -ψ_b (a pointed ring tooth), ring.rs:399 passes half_pitch - ψ_b (space closure), and metrology.rs:489 passes a pin-seat target. The 'planetary ring-gear searches' sentence is history. More wrong statements sit next to it; see missed.
verdict.evidence: Probe: inv(ALPHA_MAX) = 9.998498896126417e11. inv_inverse(9.9e11) returns Some(1.5707963267938865). inv_inverse(1e12), inv_inverse(1e13), inv_inverse(inf) and inv_inverse(NaN) all return None. involute.rs:52 reads `if v < 0.0 || !v.is_finite() { return None; }`.

title: The search reports 'no solution' when admissible designs exist, because the feasible region is narrower than one grid step
claim: Search::maximise only walks from points the opening 13-point-per-axis sweep found admissible. If no grid point lands inside the admissible region, it returns None. chosen_at then reports Searched::FoundNothing ('no solution within the admissible range; shifts remain unaltered') and falls back to the settled shifts, which are often inadmissible themselves. The box is per member (searchable_shift), but pair constraints inside it (contact ratio, flank interference, bottom clearance, root round) can leave a sliver thinner than the grid step. F52's fix (the box made the caller's) therefore does not close the fault it names: 'a resolution had become a feasibility test'.
evidence:
Shipped search vs a dense brute force over the same objective (Shape::trial_efficiency):
(a) pair 7/40, both root radii 0.10/0.15/0.17/0.18: shipped FoundNothing at every value. A 500x500 brute force over x1∈[0.3,1.0], x2∈[-0.3,1.2] finds 14/719/1268/1644 admissible points, best (0.7802,0.903) η=0.9735433. Search::refined(4) finds η=0.97354 at ρ≥0.15.
(b) 7/40 at clearance 0.08: shipped FoundNothing. refined(4) gives (0.6331,0.8405) η=0.97387; a 420² brute force over [-0.5,1.6]² finds 131 admissible points. At 0.075 the shipped search chose η=0.97382, so the answer drops off a cliff.
(c) 9/37 at a given distance: at 24.27 mm the feasible window in the free shift is [0.6186,0.6575] and the search chose. At 24.28 the window is [0.6319,0.6538] (width 0.022) and at 24.29 it is [0.6452,0.6502] (width 0.005). The grid step is 0.0314, and both give FoundNothing. A 20000-point brute force finds η=0.97675481 and 0.97674518.
In (a)-(c) the fallback shifts themselves fail the search's own admissibility test (trial_efficiency None). For comparison, hula d=1 and d=3 and 9/37 at eps_min≥1.36 are genuinely infeasible (brute count 0), so the note is right there.
proposal: Make 'found nothing' a claim the search has checked. Target shape: the trial returns Result<f64, Violation>, where Violation is a continuous non-negative residual. It is the largest normalised constraint violation among (floor − x), (ε_min − ε_α), the interference overlap along the path, the negative bottom gap, (ρ − ρ_max) and the tip-foul overlap. MeshTrial/CrossedTrial already compute each of these before returning None. Run a feasibility phase first: if the sweep finds no admissible point, run the same pattern walk minimising Violation from the least-violating grid points, stopping when it reaches 0 or when the step falls below resolution. Report FoundNothing only if the minimum violation is still > 0. Migration: (1) change MeshTrial::efficiency/CrossedTrial::efficiency to return the violation beside None; (2) make maximise take objective -> Result<f64,f64>; (3) chosen_at unchanged apart from the type.
validation: A law over a sweep of inputs (root radius 0.08-0.4, clearance 0-0.2, a given distance stepped to the edge of reach, eps_min) on 7/40, 9/37 and 17/43: FoundNothing only where a brute grid at the search's resolution finds no admissible point, and otherwise the result is admissible and within 1e-5 of the brute best. Before merging, run it against HEAD and confirm it fails on 7/40 ρ=0.15 and 9/37 a=24.28.

verdict.reason: The finding holds as stated. Search::maximise (auto.rs:1757-1928) only walks from sweep points the objective admitted, and returns None when none is admitted. chosen_at (shape.rs:1924) then falls back with Searched::FoundNothing. A pair is a single part, so solve_train reaches this path directly. The fallback shifts are themselves inadmissible. F52's closure is therefore partial: the box is now the caller's, but pair constraints inside it (contact ratio, flank interference, bottom gap) can still leave an admissible sliver thinner than one grid step, and the grid then decides feasibility. Severity lowered to medium: this happens only near the edge of feasibility, and the user is shown a note, although the note is false.
verdict.evidence:
Re-run in my own worktree test (release build, same objective as chosen_at: plan -> sized -> closed -> trial_efficiency). Brute force was 301x301 over each member's searchable_shift rectangle, plus a local refine.
(a) 7/40, both root radii rho: at 0.10, 0.15, 0.17 and 0.18 shipped gives FoundNothing, with fallback x=[0.7748,0] (etc.), trial=None. Brute finds 20/723/1365/1763 admissible points, best (0.781,0.903) eta=0.973545. refined(4) finds it at rho>=0.15. At rho=0.19 shipped chooses (0.7800,0.9036).
(b) 7/40 clearance: at 0.08 shipped gives FoundNothing (fallback [0.5905,0], None) while brute finds 1560 points, best 0.973872. At 0.09 it is also FoundNothing, with 464 points and 0.973927. At 0.075 shipped chose 0.973820.
(c) 9/37, given distance, free pinion box (0.4736,0.85) with a grid step of 0.0314. From an 8000-20000-point 1-D brute force: 24.27 has window [0.6186,0.6575] and the search chose. 24.28 has [0.6319,0.6538], 24.285 has [0.6385,0.6520] and 24.29 has [0.6452,0.6502]; all three give FoundNothing, with fallback [0.741,0.741] and trial=None, while brute best is 0.9767548, 0.9767502 and 0.9767452. 24.295 and 24.30 are genuinely empty (brute count 0).
verdict.proposal_note: The violation-residual feasibility phase is sound. It needs a stated normalisation for residuals in different units: mm for gaps, contact ratio, and the signed flank relation sigma_i(r_i - r_j,i) that reference.md already writes. A cheap interim for 1-D boxes (given distances): when the sweep admits nothing, re-sweep at doubling scan down to `resolution`, which costs at most about 850 evaluations. A residual would also let the note name the binding constraint (see the missed Planetary-preset item).

title: When one of several independent components finds nothing, its members are left at the box midpoint and reported as 'Chose'
claim: With more than one search component, `at` starts at the midpoint of every coordinate's box. A component whose maximise returns None leaves its coordinates at that midpoint. Meanwhile `any` becomes true as soon as any other component succeeded, so the round returns Some(at). The result is Searched::Chose, with shifts for the failed component that nobody chose, that were never judged admissible, and that equal neither the settled shifts nor any fallback. No FoundNothing note is raised.
evidence: Probe probe_component_partial_failure: compound train 17→43=17→43 (gears 1 and 2 on one body, two distances, so two components), search on, mesh 1 min_contact_ratio set to 1.9 or 2.5. Result: how=Chose, shifts [0.4946, 0.762, 0.4278, 0.425]. The settled shifts are [0.0057, 0, 0.0057, 0]. mesh0 η=0.98488 and mesh1 trial_efficiency=None. (0.4278, 0.425) is exactly the midpoint of the sum box (~0.853) and the division box (~0.003) mapped back to shifts. At eps2=1.2 both components choose [0.4946,0.762] as expected.
proposal: Track success per component. For a component whose maximise returns None, put its coordinates back to the fallback: the values whose place() gives the settled shifts, or the closure the fallback path would use. Carry a per-component Searched, and report FoundNothing (with the note) when any asking component found nothing, ideally naming the part or mesh. Simplest form: initialise `at` from the coordinates of `settled`, not from box midpoints, and set how = FoundNothing if any component failed.
validation: Unit law in shape.rs tests: for every preset and for a two-component compound train, make one component infeasible (eps_min = 3). The other component's shifts must equal what it chooses alone, the infeasible component's shifts must equal its settled shifts, and searched() must be FoundNothing.

verdict.reason: The mechanism is real. In the multi-component branch (shape.rs:1882-1900), `at` starts at box midpoints, a component whose maximise returns None keeps them, `any` becomes true, and the result is Chose with shifts nobody chose and no note. The auditor's reproduction is not a production path, though. solve_train splits a compound 17->43=17->43 into two parts before chosen_at runs. I solved it through solve_train with eps2=2.5: part 2 correctly falls back to [0.0057,0] and carries part.optimiser_found_nothing. The branch is reached in production only by a single part with two or more meshes on a held distance (given or tip-sized) whose free members are disjoint. Examples are a layshaft with its distance given, a hula at its sized crank, or a set with a given distance. There it is silent, as claimed.
verdict.corrected_claim: Within one part whose meshes share a held (given or tip-sized) distance, and so split into several search components, a component whose search finds nothing is left at its box midpoint and reported as Chose, with no note. Example: the shipped Layshaft preset with its distance given. Trains whose components are separate parts (e.g. a compound shaft between two distances) are not affected, because solve_train searches each part alone and notes FoundNothing correctly.
verdict.evidence: My probe v10: compound 17/43 + 17/43 through solve_train with mesh 1 eps_min 2.5 gave shifts [0.4946,0.7620,0.0057,0.0000] and part notes [[],["part.optimiser_found_nothing"]], which is correct. Calling chosen_at on the whole shape reproduces the auditor's [.., 0.4278, 0.4250] (Chose), but production never does that. My probe v11: Preset::Layshaft (1 part, 1 distance, 3 meshes), search on, distance fixed at 31.156 mm, meshes[2].min_contact_ratio = 2.5. solve_train shifts are [0.5026,0.7779,0.7604,0.5202,0.4250,0.8555]. 0.4250 is the midpoint of member 4's box [0,0.85] and member 5 reaches. trial_efficiency for mesh 2 is None, part notes are [[]] (no FoundNothing), and chosen_at.how is Chose. The whole-shape fallback, closed(plan,&[]), would have given the even split [0.6403,0.6403].
verdict.proposal_note: Two corrections to the proposal. First, 'initialise at from settled' does not reproduce the fallback. At a given distance, closed() with a non-empty free vector gives the reaching member the whole sum: member 4 at 0 and member 5 at about 1.28, outside its 0.85 bound. The whole-shape fallback (closed(plan,&[])) divides the sum evenly. So initialise the failed component's coordinates from closed(plan,&[]) mapped to Sum/Division/Own. Second, 'report FoundNothing when any component found nothing' is the rule docs/corrections.md:583 records as tried and rejected: a hula whose optimiser moved one mesh reported nothing to choose. Keep Chose for the part and name the failed mesh instead, either with a mesh-level note or with Searched carrying the failed meshes. The validation law should use a single part with a held distance (e.g. the layshaft with a given distance), since the two-distance compound never reaches the branch through solve_train.

title: The opening sweep is exponential in the number of free shifts: 3.6 s for a five-gear line
claim: maximise sweeps (scan+1)^dof = 13^dof points and walks 3^dof−1 directions per step. A chain of meshes whose members share axes becomes one component, so every free shift of a line is one search. The keystroke budget test (every_search_is_quick_enough_to_type_over, 200 ms) covers only a pair, a set and a hula, so this is untested. Offers and the dry-run preview solve trains repeatedly, which multiplies the cost.
evidence: Probe probe_line_cost, release build, native (wasm is slower). With search on, all members free: line [17,43] 9.9 ms; [17,29,43] 126 ms; [17,23,29,43] 437 ms; [17,23,29,31,43] 3.58 s. Each extra gear multiplies the cost by roughly 3-13x, consistent with 13^dof × 3^dof. A user can build such a line with the panel's 'gear meshing any gear' edit.
proposal: Use the structure the objective already has: it is a product of per-mesh efficiencies, and each factor depends only on its own mesh's two members, plus the absorbers on shared distances. For a chain (the general case of meshes joined through shared members) maximise the log-sum by block coordinate ascent over meshes: optimise each mesh's (sum, division) with the others fixed and sweep the chain until nothing moves. For a tree of meshes, use dynamic programming over a discretised shared member. Either way the cost is linear in mesh count. As a stop-gap, cap the sweep at a fixed point count (e.g. a Sobol/Halton set of ~13² points whatever dof is) and keep the walk.
validation: Extend every_search_is_quick_enough_to_type_over with lines of 3, 4 and 5 gears and a layshaft with every shift free. Check the new search against the current one on those lines (same η to 1e-5, or better) and against a coarse 3-D brute force on the 3-gear line.

verdict.reason: The cost claim holds, and my measurement makes it stronger: a shipped preset exceeds the keystroke budget by an order of magnitude. The grid is (scan+1)^dof. Every member of a line, and the three meshes of a layshaft on one automatic distance, form a single component. every_search_is_quick_enough_to_type_over times only a pair, a set and a hula. One detail is wrong. offers.rs never solves; it applies edits on a copy. preview.rs does solve before and after (2 solves per hover), so the multiplier comes from the preview only. The wording 'members share axes' should be 'members are in two meshes, or meshes share an automatic distance' (search_components). Severity stays medium because the optimiser is opt-in, but switching it on for the Layshaft preset costs about 2 s native per edit, and more in wasm.
verdict.evidence: Release build on a loaded machine, chosen_at timed on shape.rs's own path. Lines [17,43] 17 ms, [17,29,43] 159 ms, [17,23,29,43] 701 ms, [17,23,29,31,43] 5.86 s. The auditor measured 10/126/437/3580 ms; same growth. Every shipped preset with set_search(true): Spur 12 ms, Idler 147 ms, Layshaft 1.90 s (roles [Free,Free,Absorbs(0),Free,Absorbs(1),Free], dof 4), Worm 4 ms, Crossed 31 ms, Planetary 0.4 ms (FoundNothing, see missed), Wolfrom 35 ms, Compound 357 ms, Planocentric 4 ms, MeshedPlanets 426 ms. A layshaft with three ratios took 22.3 s. At dof 5 the sweep admitted 75,686 of 371,293 grid points, so the sweep, not the walk, dominates.
verdict.proposal_note: Block coordinate ascent 'per mesh' is not valid as stated for components joined by an absorber on a shared automatic distance. The layshaft's three meshes are one component because they share a distance, not a member, so the objective does not separate by mesh. Moving one block at a time can also stall at a constraint corner, which is the reason maximise walks all 3^dof-1 directions (auto.rs:1774). Dynamic programming over a discretised shared member is exact for chains of held distances. For the stop-gap, capping the sweep is not enough: the 3^dof-1 compass stencil also exhausts each walk's budget at dof>=3 (see missed). Cap the sweep's point count, and walk the 2*dof axis directions plus the Sum/Division diagonals the coordinates already expose, rather than the full stencil.

title: The chosen shifts jump by 0.2-0.9 module under continuous input changes, because the search picks between ridges that differ by about 1e-5 of efficiency
claim: The efficiency surface over the shifts has several near-equal ridges. Their efficiencies differ by 1e-6 to 4e-5, far below what the friction model can resolve (it states ±10% in µ is worth four orders more). Taking the argmax makes the recommended gear geometry jump discontinuously as an input moves. Part of this is intrinsic: the dense brute force jumps too. Part is grid-anchor artefact: the grid starts at box.0, so changing any input that moves a box end (root radius, working depth, floor) moves the grid, and with it which ridge is found. Either way, the user is shown visibly different gears for differences no model here can tell apart.
evidence: probe_continuity (41-step sweeps, pair, search on). 9/37 clearance 0.175→0.18: shifts (0.6442,0.8498)→(0.4741,0.7995), η 0.97821→0.97826. 9/37 helix: at β=11.5° the search gives (0.4413,0.6516) while brute gives (0.6591,0.7761), and at β=12° brute gives (0.4377,0.6493), so the true argmax itself jumps 0.22 module in pinion shift over 0.5°. 17/43 min tip width 0.30→0.325: (0.4946,0.7620)→(0.7207,0.8491), which the brute force confirms, with Δη=2e-5. 9/37 min tip width 0.0375→0.05: 0.2004 jump. 7/40 root radius: 0.90 jump at 0.1875, which is the FoundNothing edge. working_depth 1.0 moves 9/37's answer from (0.6746,0.7332) to (0.6829,0.6941) only by moving the box floor (see the working-depth finding). µ does not move the answer at all (0.03-0.12: identical shifts), so the objective is purely geometric.
proposal: Pick from the near-optimal set rather than taking the bare argmax, and expose the tolerance as a user-visible option: 'efficiency tolerance', default e.g. 1e-4, which is still two orders below µ's uncertainty. Among admissible points with η ≥ η_max − tol, pick the one that maximises a continuous secondary criterion with a single optimum. Examples: the largest minimum constraint margin, meaning the most room to the nearest wall (this also fixes the rounding finding); or the shifts closest to the undercut floor / the standard distance. Implement it as a second pattern walk on −distance subject to η ≥ η_max − tol. Report which constraint is active at the answer.
validation: Continuity law: sweep clearance, helix, tip width and root radius finely on 9/37, 17/43 and 7/40. Between consecutive steps that both choose, the chosen shifts may move by at most K·Δinput, with K stated; any exception must coincide with a feasibility change. The efficiency must still be within tol of a dense brute force.

verdict.reason: The jumps are real and are mostly intrinsic to taking the argmax over near-equal ridges. The auditor says so, and a dense brute force jumps at the same inputs. Only the helix case is partly a search artefact, and that belongs with finding 4. The argument that the gaps are 'far below what the friction model can resolve (±10% µ)' is the wrong justification. µ scales every candidate's loss alike and cannot reorder ridges; I confirmed µ does not move the argmax at all. The valid argument is fidelity of the geometric loss model: Δη of 2e-5 on a loss of 1.5% is a 0.13% relative difference in the path integral, which the load-sharing and uniform-µ model cannot rank. The proposed ε-optimal selection does not deliver continuity. The ε-optimal set itself gains and loses whole components as inputs move, so the answer still jumps, only at different inputs, and the proposal adds a user-facing tolerance. Severity lowered to low: the objective is honoured to 2e-5 and no wrong design results.
verdict.corrected_claim: The recommended shifts jump by 0.2-0.9 module under small input changes because the objective has near-equal ridges (Δη ~1e-6 to 4e-5), which is inherent to an argmax on this surface. Only a minor part is grid-anchoring artefact (e.g. 9/37 helix 11-11.5°). µ has no effect on which ridge is chosen.
verdict.proposal_note: If continuity is wanted, the options that actually help are a tie-break that is continuous on each ridge together with hysteresis against the previous answer, or showing the near-equal alternatives. A selection rule alone cannot make an argmax over a disconnected set continuous. If the tolerance is added, justify it by the loss model's relative fidelity, not by µ.

title: The convergence gate passes only on its fixtures: off-default and 7/40 surfaces miss the 1e-5 claim, and the search takes the lower ridge (F53 closure partial)
claim: the_search_is_converged_not_budgeted asserts |η(refined(3)) − η(shipped)| < 1e-5 only on 14 default pairs. Default 7/40 and ordinary off-default inputs exceed it, and in those cases the shipped search sits on a lower ridge: exactly what F53 records as closed. The gate cannot fail for the reason it exists, because its fixture list decides whether it passes.
evidence:
Shipped vs refined(k) vs brute force (probe_refined_vs_shipped_off_default, probe_pair_brute_force, probe_brute_sweeps):
- 7/40 default: shipped (0.6538,0.6995) η=0.97324304; k3 0.97325378 (+1.07e-5, above the gate's 1e-5); brute 0.97325391 (+1.34e-5, 0.07 module away in x2).
- 9/37 clearance 0: shipped 0.97646225 vs k3 0.97649894 (+3.7e-5); x2 0.797 vs 0.682.
- 9/37 β=11.5°: shipped (0.4413,0.6516) 0.97658526 vs k3 (0.6649,0.7495) 0.97659436 (+9.1e-6), a different ridge 0.22 module away.
- 9/37 β=11°: +1.2e-5 vs brute; 9/37 clearance 0.03: +5e-6.
At defaults the gate's claim holds (most pairs ≤1e-9 vs brute).
proposal: Make the gate a sweep rather than a list. Include 7/40 and, for three pairs, sweep clearance (0-0.2), helix (0-25°) and tip width. Assert against a dense brute force, not refined(3) (refined(k) moves both ways). Either fix the search (multi-start from every local grid maximum, not the 2 best plus extremes; or the ε-optimal selection in the discontinuity finding) or state the measured bound honestly.
validation: The new gate must fail on HEAD (7/40 default gap 1.34e-5 > 1e-5) and pass after the change.

verdict.reason: Confirmed with the gate's own statistic: forward efficiency from solving the fixed-shift stage, refined(3) against shipped. Default 7/40 and 9/37 at clearance 0 would fail the 1e-5 bound. The gate's convergence claim holds only on its fixture list. The auto.rs doc (1643-1645), 'A pair's is converged ... by at most 4.1e-7 and every shift by less than one step of resolution', is stale even on the gate's fixtures. Two parts are not supported. (1) 'F53 closure partial': F53 is the division search at a given distance. In that setting the shipped search matches a 1-D brute force to within 5e-6 across full sweeps, except where finding 0's FoundNothing bites. The lower-ridge gaps shown here are in the free 2-D search, a different setting from F53's. (2) 'The gate cannot fail for the reason it exists' is overstated: it is a regression canary on its fixtures and would fail if the search regressed on them.
verdict.corrected_claim: The convergence gate's 1e-5 claim holds only on its 14 default fixtures. Default 7/40 (1.07e-5), 9/37 at clearance 0 (3.67e-5) and 9/37 at β 11° (1.04e-5) exceed it, with the shipped search on a lower ridge. auto.rs:1643's '4.1e-7, every shift within one resolution step' is stale (9/20: 3.3e-6, and x2 moves 0.040). F53's own case (the division at a given distance) remains closed.
verdict.evidence: Probe v12, using the gate's exact measure (solve_preset(...).meshes[0].efficiency.forward): 7/40 default gives shipped 0.973243044 and refined(3) 0.973253777, diff 1.073e-5, which fails; 9/37 clearance 0 gives 0.976462252 and 0.976498940, diff 3.669e-5, which fails. Probe v4/v3 (trial objective): 9/20 has r3-shipped 3.26e-6 with shipped (0.7544,0.6502) and r3 (0.7619,0.6102); 9/37 β=11° 1.04e-5 (brute 1.18e-5); 9/37 β=11.5° 9.1e-6 (brute 1.14e-5). Probe v9 (F53's setting): given distance swept over 41 steps on 9/37 [23.3,24.28], 7/40 [23.6,24.4] and 17/43 [30,30.9], against an 8001-point 1-D brute force. No gap above 5e-6 anywhere (7/40 worst 6.7e-9, 17/43 worst 3.3e-9), except 9/37 at 24.28, where the search returns FoundNothing (finding 0).
verdict.proposal_note: If the gate asserts against a brute force, state the brute force's resolution: at 7/40 my 301² brute force gave a gap of 1.08e-5 where the auditor's gave 1.34e-5, both just above 1e-5, so the verdict depends on the reference. Correct auto.rs:1643-1645 in the same change.

title: The recommended shifts sit exactly on a hard wall: rounded to the 3-4 decimals a designer would copy, they are inadmissible
claim: The pattern walk accepts any strictly better admissible point, so the optimum is driven onto the constraint boundary to within the step. On 9/37 that boundary is flank interference, where the wheel's tip reaches the pinion's usable-flank end. If a designer types the displayed shift back in, the search's own test refuses it, and the fixed solve's MeshReport.flank_interference flags it.
evidence: probe_rounded_answer: 9/37 exact (0.674559163, 0.733205004) admissible; rounded to 4 dp inadmissible; 3 dp inadmissible; 2 dp admissible. 7/40: 3 dp inadmissible. probe_why_even_split_refused at (0.6746,0.7332): interf=[true,false], eps=1.2928, bottom=[0.135,0.066]. 17/43, 12/29 and 9/20 survive rounding.
proposal: Hold hard constraints with a stated margin in the search only: require the admissibility residual ≥ the effect of one resolution step (x ± resolution must stay admissible), or snap the answer inward to the resolution grid. Report the active constraint and its margin with the answer. Preferably use the ε-optimal / largest-margin selection proposed under discontinuity.
validation: Law: for every preset and the brute-force pairs, the chosen shifts rounded to Search::resolution (1e-3) are admissible, and solving them with search off gives flank_interference [false,false].

verdict.reason: The claim is confirmed, and the UI makes it directly reachable. TrainPanel.svelte:1814 shows an automatic field as Number(computed.toFixed(4)). Line 1849 seeds manual from exactly that value when the auto switch is turned off, 'so what the reader saw is what they now hold'. On 9/37 with search on, switching both shifts to manual gives (0.6746, 0.7332). That point is past the flank-interference wall, and the panel then shows ui.train_interference_flank for the design the tool just recommended. Physically the overshoot is about 1e-5 module, so this is a self-consistency defect, not a real interference. Hence medium.
verdict.evidence: Probe v5 (release). 9/37 exact (0.674559163, 0.733205004) is admissible. At 4 dp (0.6746,0.7332) it is inadmissible, and the build's operating.flank_interference is [true,false]. At 3 dp (0.675,0.733) it is inadmissible with [true,false]. At 2 dp it is admissible. The wall is 1.1e-5 in +x1 from the answer. 7/40 (0.653821,0.699474) survives 4 dp but fails 3 dp (flank [true,false]); its wall is 5.7e-5 away. 17/43, 12/29, 9/20, 13/31 and 10/51 survive 4, 3 and 2 dp. If only one member is switched to manual, the other stays searched and moves off the wall, so the defect needs both switched.
verdict.proposal_note: Backing off the wall by one resolution step (1e-3 module) is the cleanest fix: it makes any rounding to 3 or more decimals safe and costs at most about 1e-5 of η here. Keep the margin in Rust. The alternative of seeding manual with the unrounded value in the panel would contradict the panel's stated rule of seeding the digits shown.

title: working_depth moves the search's floor, but the search's buildability test ignores it and reads undercut at the full dedendum
claim: shift_asked computes the floor at working_depth (minimum_profile_shift(base, h_w)). member_is_buildable also demands !tooth.undercut, and the tooth reads undercut for the tool actually used, at the dedendum. When h_w < h_f the two are different questions. The doc says they are 'that one question asked twice' (auto.rs:1014), which is true only when h_w = h_f. Consequences: with the search on, working_depth has no effect on what is admissible and only moves the grid anchor. With the search off, the automatic 'no undercut' shift at h_w gives a tooth the search itself calls undercut.
evidence: probe_working_depth, 9/37: floors 0.4736 (default h_w = h_f = 1.25), 0.2236 (h_w=1.0), 0.0236 (h_w=0.8). The pinion at its own floor with the default mate: trial_efficiency Some(0.97646) at default, None at h_w=1.0 and 0.8. Search-on answers: default (0.6746,0.7332), h_w=1.0 (0.6829,0.6941), h_w=0.8 (0.6660,0.7721). These differ only because the box's lower end, and so the grid, moved.
proposal: Decide what working_depth means and read it once. If 'no undercut within h_w' is the control, member_is_buildable should ask x ≥ floor and nothing more of undercut: drop the !tooth.undercut term, or ask the tooth for undercut at h_w through a Tooth method taking the depth. If the form flag must win, working_depth cannot lower the floor and the control should be removed. In both cases, make the doc at auto.rs:1010-1017 say which.
validation: Law: for z=7..20 and h_w∈{0.8,1.0,h_f}, the pinion at exactly its search floor with a non-interfering mate is admissible to the search (member_is_buildable true). A test that the search-on answer changes monotonically, not arbitrarily, with h_w.

verdict.reason: Holds, and the finding misses the most direct cause. Three pieces of code disagree. (1) MemberGear::shift_asked floors the search at automatic_profile_shift(base, working_depth) (train/mod.rs:1261,1275). (2) member_is_buildable also demands !tooth.undercut (auto.rs:1019-1022), and Tooth::new decides that flag at the dedendum the tooth is actually cut to (tooth.rs:479-481). (3) Shape::trial_efficiency passes `self.members[i].gear.dedendum`, not the working depth, into undercut_bound (shape.rs:2230-2235). So even the numeric floor inside the objective is taken at h_f. Result: with h_w < h_f the tooth flag and the h_f floor decide what is admissible, and h_w only lowers the box's lower edge. With h_w > h_f the h_w floor is not enforced for paired members at all. Their box is the Sum/Division hull (shape.rs:1820-1833), which leaves admissibility to the objective, and the objective reads h_f. The search then returns shifts below the floor the control asks for. With the search off, the settled shift is x_min(h_w), and the tooth built there is flagged undercut. So the control means one thing with the search on and another with it off. auto.rs:1012-1014 calls these 'one question asked twice'. That is true only at h_w = h_f.
verdict.evidence: Worktree test vasb::f6_working_depth (notes/verify-auto-search-b/f9_f6.txt), pair z/40 with search on. At 9/40: h_w=0.8/1.0/1.25 give floors 0.0236/0.2236/0.4736, all against x_min(h_f)=0.4736. The pinion at its floor has tooth.undercut=true, member_is_buildable=false and trial None at 0.8 and 1.0. Search-on answers are [0.6573,0.7819], [0.6685,0.7316] and [0.6682,0.7316], with η 0.9769491 / 0.9769501 / 0.9769495; only the grid moved. With the search off the settled pinion is 0.0236 / 0.2236, and its tooth is undercut (true). h_w=1.5 > h_f: 9/40 has floor 0.7598 but the search chose 0.6629. 12/40 has floor 0.5844 but chose 0.4579. Both are below the working-depth floor, and no note is raised. Where the floor is an Own coordinate's box edge (a set's sun, or a free member whose mate is given), h_w > h_f does bind. So 'no effect on what is admissible' is exact only for paired members.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposal is incomplete. Dropping `&& !tooth.undercut`, or asking the tooth at h_w, is not enough: shape.rs:2233 must also pass `self.members[i].gear.working_depth.resolve(dedendum)`. Otherwise the objective's floor stays at h_f and the h_w > h_f violation remains. The recommended form: in member_is_buildable, keep only `profile_shift >= floor - 1e-12`, since minimum_profile_shift already solves for the tool Tooth gets, so at h_w = h_f the flag and the floor are one comparison. Then pass the working depth at shape.rs:2233 and in the Decided::Absorbed arm. The law test must include h_w > h_f: the chosen shift is at least floor(h_w) for every member, paired or not.

title: A second, unshipped pair search (shifts_for_efficiency/Bounds/Pinned/free maximise) is what three tests gate; Freedoms is unused; the shape re-implements Pinned
claim: No production caller in any crate uses auto::shifts_for_efficiency, Bounds, Pinned, sides, member or the free fn maximise. Freedoms<N> has no caller at all, not even a test. Production searches through Shape::chosen_at, which re-implements Pinned::place and Pinned::box_of as Coordinate::{Own,Sum,Division} (shape.rs:1820-1856); the comment at shape.rs:1790 even points at `auto::Pinned::place`. the_search_beats_a_scan_of_the_same_interval (train/mod.rs), the_shifts_it_chooses_are_the_ones_that_lose_least and the pinned-shift test (auto.rs) exercise the unshipped copy. Their comments claim to guard 'the path a given centre distance takes', which in production is chosen_at's Reaches role. Two implementations of one idea is the place CLAUDE.md rule 4 says two answers disagree.
evidence: grep over crates/ for shifts_for_efficiency|Pinned {|Bounds {|Freedoms|auto::maximise: only auto.rs definitions and tests plus train/mod.rs:5242-5288 (a #[cfg(test)] region). The shape's search is shape.rs:1717-1934; its box formula at shape.rs:1824-1833 duplicates auto.rs:1437-1440.
proposal: Delete Freedoms, shifts_for_efficiency, Bounds, Pinned, sides, member and the free maximise, along with their doc prose (auto.rs:1336-1620). Rewrite the three tests against arr::pair(..).set_search(true) and Shape::shifts_at, with a pinned distance for the given-sum case. Keep one statement of the sum/division coordinates in shape.rs (or move Coordinate to auto.rs as the only copy).
validation: cargo nextest run passes. The retargeted scan test must fail if chosen_at's Reaches branch is broken (e.g. mutate place() to swap members) and pass on HEAD.

verdict.reason: A grep over crates/, tools/ and web/ confirms the dead code. Freedoms has only its definition (auto.rs:936-990). shifts_for_efficiency, Bounds, Pinned, sides and member are used only by auto.rs tests and train/mod.rs:5231-5316, which is #[cfg(test)]. The free fn maximise (auto.rs:1614) has no caller at all; the shape calls Search::maximise directly (shape.rs:1893,1902). The shape's Coordinate::Sum/Division place and box formulas (shape.rs:1820-1856) are Pinned::place/box_of's (None,None,None) case written again. shape.rs:1790 still cites `auto::Pinned::place`. The finding understates two things. First, the_search_beats_a_scan_of_the_same_interval cannot fail on the fault it names: removing `.max(resolution)` from the walk's first step (auto.rs Search::maximise) leaves it, and all 604 tests, passing. Second, the production given-distance path does not work like the unshipped copy. Pinned::box_of narrows a free shift to what keeps its partner in range. chosen_at uses the free member's whole searchable interval, so the test's premise ('pin a centre distance and the box is a fraction of a module wide') does not describe production. More stale references: gear-cli/src/main.rs:1542 ('the only command that drives auto::shifts_for_efficiency'; it drives the shape through solve), contact.rs:495, auto.rs:817 and 855, docs/reference.md:766 ('The searches share auto::maximise') and :781 ('auto::Freedoms is the one mapping'). The free maximise's doc (auto.rs:1599-1612) describes coordinate descent 'on each axis in turn', which Search::maximise explicitly does not do ('Every direction, not one axis at a time'). Search::effort (auto.rs:1750) also has no caller.
verdict.evidence: grep 'shifts_for_efficiency|Pinned {|Bounds {|Freedoms|maximise(' finds only definitions and tests. Mutation (env-gated, worktree): walk step = spacing*first_step without .max(resolution). The full gear-core suite passes 603/604; the one failure is the timing test under load, which passes when rerun alone. the_search_beats_a_scan_of_the_same_interval passes. vasb::f7_given_distance_box, 9/37 with search on at a given distance: at 24.28, 24.285 and 24.29 mm the shape reports FoundNothing (note part.optimiser_found_nothing), while shifts_for_efficiency with Pinned{sum} and the same floors finds [0.6535,0.8284], [0.6517,0.8368] and [0.6494,0.8457].
verdict.proposal_note: Do not delete everything as is. Pinned::box_of's pinned-sum case is the one idea production lacks: it intersects the free member's interval with (sum − partner interval). Port it into chosen_at's box for a Free member whose mesh partner Reaches (shape.rs:1765-1781) first. It is what reaches 9/37 at 24.28-24.29 mm, where the shape now finds nothing. Also add a direct unit test on Search::maximise with a 1-D box narrower than scan·resolution/first_step (under 0.096) and its optimum between grid points; nothing gates that line today. Delete Search::effort with the rest. Fix the doc references listed in the reason, including reference.md:766 and :781 and main.rs:1542.

title: The search floor max(x_min, 0) is a hidden rule of thumb, justified by a search defect
claim: The floor for a chosen shift is max(x_min, 0), so turning on 'no undercut' also forbids the optimiser any negative shift on a gear that is nowhere near undercut. That is a second constraint bundled into the first. The recorded justification is that flooring at the true minimum 'let the hula stage's split walk out to −1.79 and come back with less drive efficiency than it started with'. A search that returns a worse answer from a larger admissible set has failed to find the optimum; that is a reason to fix the search, not to shrink the set.
evidence: pair.rs:30-43 and reference.md:845-855 argue it only by the hula anecdote, and the hula stage type no longer exists. In the sweeps here (pairs at defaults and given distances) chosen members stayed well above 0, so the 0 floor rarely binds. It binds when a given distance below standard makes a chosen member want a negative shift.
proposal: Floor the search at x_min (the undercut question alone). If 'do not thin a tooth that needed no help' is wanted, expose it as its own mesh option ('non-negative shifts') rather than inside no_undercut. Rerun the hula-family search at x_min to confirm the current search does not regress.
validation: For pairs at given distances 0.5-1.5 modules below standard: the search with floor x_min has η ≥ that with floor max(x_min,0) (a larger set can only help an optimum), checked against brute force.

verdict.reason: The core claim holds. max(x_min,0) is a non-negativity rule bundled into no_undercut, and its recorded justification is a defect in the search's structure. Two supporting statements are wrong, and both in a direction that understates the problem. (a) 'the 0 floor rarely binds' is false. With the optimiser off, which is the default, divide_shift_sum floors both members at max(x_min,0) (shape.rs:1374-1377). So every pair whose pinion needs shift is refused its own standard centre distance: the X-zero x1 = −x2 design becomes 'no admissible shifts reach'. It also binds on hula wobble gears (3 of 4 sit at 0.0) and on the shipped worm. There the floor costs 0.49 points of efficiency, because a negative wheel shift does help, contrary to 'a wheel shift buys a worm nothing' (crossed.rs:1499). (b) The hula anecdote is not stale. It reproduces on arrangements::hula today, but through the sized-distance/division alternation in chosen_at (three rounds, each searching at a distance the previous round sized), not through the search itself. So the proposal as written regresses the hula family. Also, the floor is not applied uniformly: a member the plan makes Reaches gets x_min through Decided::Absorbed, which makes the result depend on member order (see missed).
verdict.evidence: Worktree env toggle VAS_FLOOR_XMIN sets the chooser's floor (shift_asked.search_floor and undercut_bound Chosen) to x_min; notes/verify-auto-search-b/f8.txt. Given distances, search off, HEAD vs x_min: 9/37 at 23.00 mm gives (0.4736,0) with clearance −0.4433, notes distance_not_reached and clearance_negative, vs (0.4736,−0.4935) with clearance 0.02 and η 0.97371, neither tooth undercut. 17/43 at std: not reached vs (0.0057,−0.0057). 41/43 at std−0.5: η 0.98670 not reached vs 0.98894 reached. At std−1.5, 17/43, 23/61, 31/37 and 41/43 give Err(NoRootSection) at HEAD but are reached at x_min. With the search on, x_min is never worse on any pair or given distance tried. Worm(1,40), search on: HEAD [0,0] with objective 0.61805; x_min [0,−1.034] with 0.62297. Hula drive η: [19,18,17,18] 0.3089 → 0.2832, [31,30,29,30] 0.2078 → 0.2058. Mesh products also fall, so a larger set gives a worse answer. Under x_min, 8 tests fail: the four hula recorded-figure tests, a_distance_the_shifts_cannot_reach_is_said_out_loud, a_manual_centre_distance_ignores_the_clearance, the_optimiser_reaches_a_crossed_pair_by_its_own_mesh (wheel −1.034), and a_larger_root_round_holds_the_shift_down (sum moved 0.0012, one resolution step).
verdict.proposal_note: Flooring choosers at x_min fixes the pair refusals and the order dependence, but it needs two things with it. (1) Fix the sized-distance alternation (shape.rs:1872-1924) so the hula does not regress: search the crank jointly, or keep the round whose final objective is best rather than the last. (2) Rewrite the tests listed above, which encode the floor's refusals as geometry. If a non-negative rule is wanted as a strength proxy, make it an explicit per-member option with its own note. Keep the settled (search-off) automatic value as its own question: automatic_profile_shift's inv α_w argument concerns both members sitting at x_min, which divide_shift_sum's projection already avoids.

title: Search's doc says the set search is not converged (2.4e-4, 0.30 module) and gives the pair figure as 4.1e-7; both are stale
claim: auto.rs:1639-1656 says a set's search 'moves η₀ by up to 2.4e-4, with the sun's shift 0.30 modules away … No budget fixes that' and points to F50 for 'what is to be done'. F50 is closed and sets now converge. The same paragraph gives the pair's figure as 4.1e-7, while the test comment at train/mod.rs:5620 gives 3.3e-6 (9/20).
evidence: set_brute.txt / guards_099.txt: 7 sets (11/14, 11/17, 11/18, 13/25, 17/17, 24/18, 19/21), shipped vs 150² brute gap within −1.3e-5…+4.6e-6 (shipped usually better), shipped vs refined(3) ≤1.2e-6. The audit ledger records F50 closed.
proposal: Replace the 'What checking it found' section with the current measured statement: pair worst X, set worst Y, and the gate that holds each. Drop the history and point once to docs/corrections.md.
validation: check_doc_links; the numbers are taken from the gate's own printed worst.

verdict.reason: Re-measured with the gate's own scoring at Search::SHIPPED vs Search::refined(3). The auto.rs:1639-1656 paragraph is stale on both sides. The pair's worst is 3.26e-6 (9/20), not 4.1e-7. 'Every shift by less than one step of resolution' is false: 9/20's shifts move 0.040, forty steps. Sets have converged: the worst over the 30 fixtures is 1.06e-6 (13/14), and the largest sun-shift change is 0.0044, not 2.4e-4 and 0.30. The diagnosis 'the difference is coordinates rather than effort' is also contradicted by F50's own closure ('So it was never coordinates').
