If arcs are adopted, replace the chords: the file already carries bulges, so the CAD-compatibility risk is the same one the tip and root arcs already take. First the instrument has to change: `worst_deviation` (outline.rs:486-497) treats every bulged span as concentric with the axis, so it cannot judge a flank arc. It needs a true point-to-arc distance. A cheaper intermediate that needs no new entity: place the involute's chords by inverting the closed-form ∫√(κ/8tol)ds. That removes the 1.2-1.5x dyadic overhead but saves only vertices.

title: The feasibility edge in `amplitude_for_throw` is bisected (64 solves) where a closed form exists
claim: OutsideInvoluteDomain fires when inv α_t + 2 x_sum tan α_n/Σz < 0 at the binding tooth. x_k = x̄ + Δx cos(2π min(k, z−k)/z) is linear in Δx, and its extreme cos is −1 for even z and −cos(π/z) for odd z (the sign flipped for an internal Σz). So Δx_max = (x̄ + x_s + x_mate + inv α_t·Σz/(2 tan α_n))/|cos_min| in closed form. The 64-step bisection over `throw()` finds the same number, plus the CentreDistanceTooSmall edge, numerically.
evidence: The code bisects `throw(mid).is_ok()` 64 times. `centre_profile_of` returns OutsideInvoluteDomain only from `operating_geometry(...).ok_or(..)` per tooth, which is the inequality above.
proposal: Compute Δx_max from the closed form. Evaluate `throw` there once to catch CentreDistanceTooSmall, and bisect only when that fires. The wall-clock test `solving_an_amplitude_is_quick_enough_to_type_over` then becomes unnecessary.
validation: Law: the closed-form Δx_max equals the current bisection result to 1 ulp across a grid of z, x̄, mate and kind; throw(Δx_max·(1+1e-12)) fails.

verdict.reason: The closed form exists and matches. The auditor's formula is right for an external pair, and the internal case holds with the binding tooth at cos = +1. On a grid of 553 First-side pairs (z 5-100, mate 12-150, x̄ from −0.5 to 0.8, external and internal), the involute-domain edge binds in 478, the admissible ceiling in 75, and CentreDistanceTooSmall in none. The closed form agrees with the crate's 64-step bisection within 3 ulps (max relative 4.7e-15). Three parts of the proposal and validation do not hold. (1) "Equals the bisection to 1 ulp" fails: it is up to 3 ulps. In 86 of 478 cases the closed-form value is itself 1-3 ulps past the floating-point edge, so `throw(closed)` fails. "Evaluate once and bisect only when that fires" would then fall back to the full bisection about 18% of the time, for rounding and not for CentreDistanceTooSmall. (2) The claim that the wall-clock test then becomes unnecessary is wrong. Brent still calls `throw` many times. The test's stated purpose (gear.rs:1320-1326) is to catch gears being built inside that loop, which was 102 ms, and a closed-form edge does not remove that risk. (3) The saving is real but sub-millisecond. Measured native release: 352 µs (z17/z43) and 830-1240 µs (z41/z40, the timing test's own case, which does bisect), against 23-53 µs for small-z cases whose ceiling is feasible and skip the bisection. It is a legitimate closed-form-over-iteration simplification, which the owner's goals favour; low.
verdict.evidence: Probe mode throw/time: /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/notes/verify-gear-outline-c/throw.txt (`cases 553: ceiling binds 75, domain binds 478, CDTS binds 0; worst rel diff closed vs bisect (non-ceiling) 4.73e-15`; 86 lines `throw(closed) ok=false ... ulps 1|2|3`) and time.txt (`z17 zm43 x0: feasible-at-ceiling false ... each 351.846µs`; `z12 zm150 x0.8: feasible-at-ceiling true ... each 52.705µs`). gear.rs:937-941 is the only source of OutsideInvoluteDomain in the loop. auto.rs:630 already computes the same extreme `c_lo = cos(2π⌊z/2⌋/z)` for the ceiling.
verdict.corrected_claim: With v₀ = inv α_t + 2·x_sum(Δx=0)·tan α_n/Σz (the mean pair's inv α_w, signed Σz) and κ = 2·sign_e·tan α_n/Σz, the domain edge is Δx_max = v₀ / max(−κ, −κ·c_lo), with c_lo = cos(2π⌊z/2⌋/z). One expression covers both kinds and both sides; the internal pinion binds at k = 0. It matches the bisection within 3 ulps. In floating point it can land 1-3 ulps infeasible, so an implementation needs a rounding step and not a single evaluation. The wall-clock test stays useful.
verdict.proposal_note: Take dx = min(ceiling, v₀/max(−κ, −κ c_lo)), then step down with next_down while `throw(dx)` fails. At most about 3 steps were needed in 478 cases. Keep bisection only as a guard for a failure that is not rounding. Share the fold's extreme cos with `admissible_angular_shift` (auto.rs:630) through one helper. Keep `solving_an_amplitude_is_quick_enough_to_type_over`. Write the law as: throw(dx_closed) is ok, and throw(next_up(dx_closed)) fails or dx_closed == ceiling. Do not require bit equality with the bisection.

title: shifts and crossed headers print 'mu 0.06' while the figures below are at the preset's mu 0.08
claim: shifts_report and crossed_report print a hard-coded 'mu 0.06' in their headers. The shapes they solve carry the preset friction, FRICTION = (0.08, 0.16), so every efficiency in those tables is at mu = 0.08. The corpus has recorded the wrong label since the default moved (docs/state.md:237 records the move from 0.06 to 0.08). A label is not a number, so check_golden cannot notice it going stale.
evidence: Independent mpmath calculation (notes/gear-cli/eta.py) for 9/37 at x1 = 0.4736, x2 = 0: eta = 0.975610 at mu 0.08 and 0.98171 at mu 0.06. The golden file prints 97.561 %, i.e. mu 0.08. Probe: arr::pair meshes[0].sliding_friction = 0.08, static 0.16. Crossed 45/45: 84.216 % printed, while the closed form gives about 84.3 % at mu 0.08 and 88 % at 0.06.
proposal: Print the friction the mesh actually carries (stage.meshes[0].sliding_friction) instead of a literal, in both headers. Grep the CLI for other literal restatements of core defaults ('module 1', 'alpha 20') and replace each with the value read off the shape.
validation: After the change the headers read 'mu 0.08'. Rerun eta.py and see it agree with the printed eta at the printed mu. Add a CLI unit test that the header's mu equals the value in arr::pair's mesh.

verdict.reason: Both headers print a literal 'mu 0.06', but every mesh the arrangements build carries FRICTION = (0.08, 0.16). The printed efficiencies are at 0.08. It is a mislabel, not a wrong number, so low severity rather than medium.
verdict.evidence: main.rs:1568 `println!("pair z {z1}/{z2}  module 1  alpha 20 deg  mu 0.06\n")` and main.rs:3537 `mu 0.06` sit in the header strings. arrangements.rs:30 has `const FRICTION: (f64, f64) = (0.08, 0.16);`, and arrangements.rs:436-441 applies it to every mesh; crossed_report builds from worm_stage, which is arr::worm. The golden files shifts_9_37.txt:1 and crossed_17_23_90.txt:1 both read 'mu 0.06'. Independent crossed-helical closed form at beta1 = beta2 = 45 deg, alpha_n = 20 deg, eta = cos(beta1 + rho')/cos(beta1 - rho') with rho' = atan(mu/cos alpha_n): mu 0.08 gives 0.843 and mu 0.06 gives 0.880. The printed 84.216 % therefore matches 0.08. The auditor's probe (probes/gear-cli) also printed 'mesh fr 0.08 0.16' for arr::pair. state.md:237 records the default moving from 0.06 to 0.08.
verdict.proposal_note: Read the value off stage.meshes[0].sliding_friction as proposed. Also see the missed item: `gear-cli worm` has its own `let mu = 0.06` (main.rs:3144), which is the same stale default used as a number, not only as a label.

title: GearCase::torque doc and reference.md say the driven member's torque is cut by the mesh loss; the solve and its own test say it is not
claim: The doc says a member at the far end of a mesh 'carries the load referred by the ratio and cut by the loss the mesh takes carrying it'. The code reports the driver's torque referred by the ratio with no loss; only the body's delivered torque is cut. The test a_self_locking_worm_reports_the_load_it_reacts states the uncut rule, and the output follows it. For a worm this is a large difference. `wormstage 1 40 7 2` prints 'wheel 80.0000 Nm' beside 'efficiency 61.805 %', but the wheel shaft receives 2 × 40 × 0.618 = 49.4 N·m. `gear-cli worm` on the same worm prints 'wheel torque 54.953 Nm at mu 0.06'. A reader of the panel or the CLI would take the 80 N·m (62 % high) as the wheel torque.
evidence: train.txt part 1: gear 2 T = 5.0588 = 2 × 43/17 exactly, not × 0.98345. Part 2: gear 1 = 4.9751 = 5.0588 × 0.98345 (upstream loss only), and the reacted body is −11.626 = 2 × 6.0317 × 0.96375. The test at mod.rs:4992 says 'a member's torque is the torque its teeth carry, the driver's read across the mesh, whether or not the mesh passes any of it on'.
proposal: Either correct the doc and reference.md to state the rule actually used (driver's torque referred frictionlessly; delivered torque is on_body / the case's body torque) and rename or label the field ('tooth-load torque'), or report the torque the flank force puts about the member's axis. For a worm that is F_n(cos α_n cos γ − μ sin γ) r2, and it would stop presenting T1·i as the wheel torque. The CLI's wormstage column should print on_body beside torque.
validation: A law over every preset: for each driven member, torque × η_mesh equals the torque the flank delivers (on_body for a single-gear body), and the doc sentence states the same thing.

verdict.reason: The GearCase::torque doc and reference.md say the far member's torque is 'cut by the loss the mesh takes'. The solve reports the driver's torque referred by the ratio with no loss, and the test at mod.rs:4992 states that rule. The docs contradict the code. For a spur gear the uncut figure is the normal-force moment F_n·r_b2, which is the right tooth load for rating. For a worm the reported 'wheel 80 N·m' is not a physical torque on the wheel at all: the flank force delivers T1·i·eta = 49.4 N·m. The rating itself is not affected, because the point-contact rate calls s.normal_force(torque, on, friction, drive), which converts from the given side with friction. So the fault is in the doc and the display, not the stress.
verdict.evidence: train.txt part 1 gear 2 T 5.0588 = 2 × 43/17 exactly, not × 0.98345. Part 2 gear 1 is 4.9751 = 5.0588 × 0.98345, and gear 2 is 11.8637 = 4.9751 × 31/13 uncut. wormstage_1_40_7_2.txt prints 'wheel 80.0000' beside 'efficiency 61.805 %'. The doc at mod.rs:1331-1335 and reference.md:2925-2928 both say 'cut by the loss'. shape.rs:2589 and :2604 derive the rating force through normal_force(torque, on, friction, drive).
verdict.proposal_note: Correcting the two doc sentences is the minimum. Also label the displayed field as a tooth-load (frictionless referred) torque, or print on_body beside it in the CLI and the panel, especially for point contacts. Do not change what the rating consumes: normal_force already accounts for friction and the side.

title: loadcase's 'shared' column re-implements worst_over_cycle without its candidate points, so it always under-reads (c) below (b)
claim: Column (c), 'the worst point once sharing is applied', is a 401-point uniform sweep in the CLI. Under LinearRamp the share is exactly 1 on the plateau and at most 2/3 off it, so here the true maximum is at HPSTC and (c) = (b) exactly. The CLI sweep never lands on HPSTC and reports c < b on every row. So the '(c) vs (a)' column and its difference from '(b) vs (a)' are sampling error presented as a model difference. The core's worst_over_cycle already includes 0, ε, HPSTC and min(ε, 1) as candidates.
evidence: Golden rows: 17:17 b 2.9927, c 2.9923; 17:43 b 2.8386, c 2.8345; 12:30 x+0.4 b 2.3537, c 2.3481. c < b in all six rows, although load_share = 1 at HPSTC (contact.rs:897) and RAMP_MAX = 2/3 (contact.rs:870) makes c ≥ b.
proposal: Compute (c) with strength::bending_section_shared(&g1, eps, LoadSharing::LinearRamp) and its factor × share, and delete the CLI sweep. Also fix the command summary, 'a stage's two load cases side by side' (main.rs:436): it prints three load positions for six meshes, not load cases.
validation: After the change c ≥ b holds on every row (c == b where the plateau governs), and the rows equal what the train's LinearRamp rating reports for the same mesh.

verdict.reason: The CLI's (c) is a 401-point sweep with no HPSTC candidate. Under LinearRamp the share is 1 on the plateau, where the bending factor peaks at HPSTC. Off the plateau the share is at most 2/3, and 2/3·a < b in every row. So the true (c) equals (b), and the printed c < b is sampling error. The core's worst_over_cycle seeds exactly the missing candidates and uses the same DolanBroghamer factor. Severity is low: the harness-only output is quoted nowhere in docs/.
verdict.evidence: main.rs:2952-2959 is the uniform `for i in 0..=400` sweep. strength.rs:1488 has `let mut samples = vec![0.0, eps_n, highest_single_pair(eps_n), eps_n.min(1.0)];` and strength.rs:1512 uses the DolanBroghamer factor. Every golden loadcase row has c < b, e.g. 12:30 x+0.4 with b 2.3537, c 2.3481. contact.rs:869-870 sets RAMP_MAX = 2/3, and 2/3 × 3.2063 = 2.14 < 2.3537. main.rs:436's summary 'a stage's two load cases side by side' describes neither the three columns nor the six meshes. grep of docs/*.md for 'loadcase' finds no citation.
verdict.proposal_note: bending_section_shared works on the virtual spur and the eps it is handed, so for these spur rows it should reproduce (b) exactly. If the rows ever grow a helix, check that (a) and (b) are taken in the same plane.

title: The internal-mesh interference instrument (roll_pair, Boundary, flatten) lives in the CLI with no test, unlike verify.rs
evidence: grep for 'bulge.atan' finds only main.rs:843. The golden meshsweep and hulasweep outputs are the only record (least clearance −0.00001 mm). main.rs has 0.9 % test coverage. The CLI tests module contains only the two dispatch-table tests.
proposal: Move flatten into gear_core::outline as a public densify(outline, per_arc) (or arc_points), and move Boundary and roll_pair into gear_core::verify as `internal_mesh_clearance(ring, pinion, a, phases, steps) -> {best_phase, least, at}`. Keep the CLI as the printer. Add tests: the control (40/20 and 60/20, standard) gives least ≥ −10·TOL; a pair deliberately built at a − 0.05 mm gives least < −0.01 (the gate must be able to fail); and densify's points lie on the arc to 1e-12.
validation: The new tests. Mutating the crossing test, for example by dropping the dedup, must make the control report fouling. The golden meshsweep and hulasweep text must be unchanged.

verdict.reason: The instrument does live only in the CLI with no unit test, and its tolerances are unexamined. The golden meshsweep and hulasweep outputs do pin its output as a change detector, so 'untested' overstates it. The sharper, confirmed point is that the instrument is never shown able to fail. Both recorded cases report 'touching'. The hula case cannot be driven into fouling through the CLI either: the gap argument is overridden by the tip-sized offset, so every value gives the same pair. That makes it a gate never seen to fail (CLAUDE.md testing rule 5). It also means reference.md:1647-1651's claim ('tips foul at 134 deg ... until the far-side gap reaches about a quarter of a module ... verified by rolling', hulasweep) cannot be reproduced with the harness as it stands.
verdict.evidence: main.rs:832-1000 holds flatten, Boundary (BUCKETS 3600, ±30-bucket search) and roll_pair. The CLI's tests module has only the dispatch-table tests (main.rs:3683). Running `gear-cli hulasweep 18 0`, `... 0.1` and `... 0.2` each prints 'gap asked X got 0.2779 mm ... least clearance -0.00001 mm (touching, as a mesh does)'. The golden hulasweep_18_0.25 and meshsweep_60_20_0.8 are both 'touching'. The command table's summary default '(18, 0.2)' (main.rs:605-606) disagrees with the recorded case 'hulasweep 18 0.25'.
verdict.corrected_claim: The internal-mesh containment instrument is pinned only by golden text, has never been exercised on a fouling pair, and cannot be via hulasweep, because the requested gap does not change the pair rolled. reference.md's verification claim for the 134 deg tip fouling therefore has no reproducible evidence.
verdict.proposal_note: Moving it into gear_core::verify is reasonable. The essential part is a negative fixture: a pair rolled at a reduced axis distance, or a hula with the tip-sized crank offset overridden, must report least < -0.01. hulasweep should also be able to roll a pair at a fixed offset so the reference.md claim can be regenerated.

title: hulaband is a 12,780-solve grid search in the CLI whose grid-quantised optimum is quoted in reference.md
claim: hula_band searches addendum ∈ {0.8, …, 0.4}, cutter ∈ {10, 14, 20, 28} and x on a 0.05 grid from −1.5 to 2.0, and fixes the clearance and tolerances at 0.02·m. It applies an admissibility predicate of its own (ε ≥ 1, teeth_clear, as_asked). Its own comment says every winning row 'sits on the constraints, at ε ≈ 1.00 with the tip margin at zero'. So the documented efficiencies are wherever the 0.05 grid last touched an active bound: a record of where the sweep stopped, which is what CLAUDE.md's testing rule 3 warns against. It is a second optimiser beside the core's maximise, and nothing tests it.
evidence: The golden hulaband_18 x column is all multiples of 0.05 (+0.80, +0.65, −0.15, …). ε in the rows is 1.0005 to 1.4239. The corpus d = 1 row has x +0.00 at cutter 14 and ε 1.0005, i.e. on the ε = 1 bound.
proposal: For each (addendum, cutter), bracket the admissible x-interval by bisecting on each active constraint (ε = 1, tip_margin = 0) with solve.rs's root finder, then take the better endpoint or the interior maximum by golden section. Better still, express it as a use of the core's search with the ring shift free and the constraint set it already knows. State the discrete addendum and cutter lists as the designer's catalogue in the docs, not as literals.
validation: Refining the grid step (0.05 → 0.01 → 0.002) must no longer move the reported efficiency. The winning point satisfies an active constraint to within 1e-9.

verdict.reason: I reproduced the grid exactly with a probe that replicates hula_band through the public API, then refined the step. Rows d = 2, 4 and 6 move when the x step goes from 0.05 to 0.01, so the documented figures record where the grid stopped. The function's own comment ('every row below sits on the constraints, at eps ≈ 1.00 with the tip margin at zero') is also false for d ≥ 5, where eps is 1.11 to 1.42.
verdict.evidence: Probe notes/verify-gear-cli-1 (probes/verify-gear-cli-1), gap 0.30·m, clearance and tolerances 0.02·m, the same admissibility as main.rs:1154-1157. At step 0.05 it reproduces golden hulaband_18: d=2 x 0.80, cutter 10, h 0.7, eta 58.849 %. At step 0.01: d=2 x 0.84, eta 59.645 % (+0.80 points, ε 1.0349). d=4 moves from x -0.15 at 93.962 % to x -0.12 at 94.071 %. d=6 moves from x -0.75 at 94.611 % to x -0.78 at 94.680 %. d=1 does not move (33.397 %, x 0, ε 1.0005). reference.md:2018-2027 quotes 58.9 / 94.0 / 94.6, which would read 59.6 / 94.1 / 94.7. The comment at main.rs:1093-1095 conflicts with the golden eps column: 1.1115, 1.3153, 1.3067, 1.2914, 1.4239 for d = 5 to 9.
verdict.proposal_note: Bracketing each active constraint with solve.rs is sound where the objective is monotone up to the bound. For d ≥ 5 the optimum is apparently interior in x (ε well above 1), so a golden-section or Brent maximisation inside the admissible interval is needed too. Correct the doc comment either way.

title: The 'regression canary' `strength` hand-assembles a second rating pipeline that is not the product's configuration
claim: strength_report builds Tooth, Mesh::new, ContactPath, bending_section, bending_stress and contact_stress itself, at x = 0, zero clearance and b = 10 mm. A 17-tooth pinion in the product is lifted by no_undercut to x = 0.00566, and the pair runs at +0.02 mm clearance. So the canary's σ_F 66.8 / 56.0 and σ_H 692.7 are not what the app shows for that pair (66.5 / 56.1 / 691.3). Nothing asserts that the two pipelines agree. The CLI also re-derives the rim rule inline, as RimSupport::external(s, g.ra − g.rf), instead of calling ToothOutline::rim_support.
evidence: Probe (probes/gear-cli) of arr::pair 17/43, face fixed 10, shifts fixed 0, T = 2. Defaults: σ_F 66.508 / 56.079, σ_H 691.30, pitch 629.41. With no_undercut = false and clearance 0: 66.791 / 55.999, 692.65, 629.91 and ε 1.62110, which is the canary to every printed digit. So the two agree when configured identically, and differ at the product's defaults.
proposal: Make `strength` solve arr::pair through Train::alone, with its departures from the defaults (no_undercut off, clearance 0, fixed face) written as explicit shape edits and printed in the header. Print the extra primitive figures (Y_F, axial, K_f) from GearResult or from a public accessor for the rating's section. Replace the inline Y_B with g.rim_support(s).
validation: The golden strength file is unchanged after the rewrite, which proves the configuration is equivalent. Add a nextest test asserting that the hand-assembled figures equal the shape's for the canary pair.

verdict.reason: It is true that `strength` assembles Tooth, Mesh, ContactPath and bending_section itself, at x = 0 and zero clearance, and that no test ties it to the shape's rating. It is not a second model, though. The auditor's own probe (re-run) shows the shape reproduces the canary to every printed digit when configured the same way, so the two use the same primitives. Isolating the model from product-default drift (no_undercut, clearance, friction) is a defensible property for a model canary, and state.md:206-221 uses it that way. What does not hold up is state.md:243's claim that 'Load cases moved neither canary ... which is the check that a case was added rather than substituted'. The strength canary never passes through the train or a load case, so for it that check is vacuous. The inline RimSupport::external(s, g.ra - g.rf) duplicates the one-line Tooth::rim_support (strength.rs:566), a trivial duplication.
verdict.evidence: Re-running probe_gear_cli (probes/gear-cli) on arr::pair 17/43, face 10, x fixed 0, no_undercut false, clearance 0 gives sF 66.7906 / 55.9991, sH 692.65, pitch 629.91, eps 1.62110, matching strength_17_43_2.0.txt. At clearance 0.02 it gives 67.43 / 56.77 / 692.12. main.rs:2207-2222 builds the teeth by hand, main.rs:2302 uses RimSupport::external(s, g.ra - g.rf), and strength.rs:566-567 is the same expression.
verdict.corrected_claim: The strength canary is a primitives-level canary that agrees with the shape's rating when the configuration matches. No test asserts that agreement, and state.md claims the canary as evidence about train/load-case changes it cannot see.
verdict.proposal_note: Keep the canary's isolation from product defaults, or route it through Train::alone with every departure pinned and printed as proposed; both are acceptable. The cheap, essential part is a nextest law asserting the hand-assembled figures equal Train::alone's for the canary configuration, plus correcting state.md:243-246.

title: `verify 100` records only z = 3 gears, and misses the grid's actual worst case
claim: verify's loop nests z outermost, with 6 × 3 × 2 × 3 = 108 cases per z, and stops at `limit`. So the corpus case `verify 100` checks only the 3-tooth member. The full grid's worst deviation is at z = 31 and larger, and its only non-zero penetration is at z = 47. A regression in the cut of any realistic gear is outside the corpus.
evidence: `gear-cli verify 109` gives the same output as 100 (z = 3). Full `gear-cli verify` (1080 cases, about 65 s): worst deviation 6.150734e-4 at z=31 x=−0.5 a=14.5 b=0 rho=0, and penetration 2.05e-15 at z=47, against the recorded 5.710682e-4 at z=3 and penetration 0.
proposal: Make the limit a stride instead of a prefix: take every ⌈N/limit⌉-th case of the flattened grid, or shuffle deterministically. Alternatively record `verify` at a stride that reaches every z in about 10 s.
validation: The recorded worst case changes from z = 3, and every z in the grid appears among the checked cases (print the covered z-set).

verdict.reason: The corpus half holds. verify nests z outermost at 6×3×2×3 = 108 cases per z, so `verify 100` only ever runs z = 3. I re-ran both: `verify 109` prints exactly what `verify 100` prints, and the full grid (1080 cases) has its worst deviation 6.150734e-4 at z=31 x=-0.5 a=14.5 b=0 rho=0 and its worst penetration 2.05e-15 at z=47. Two parts are overstated. First, the claim that a regression in any realistic gear's cut is 'outside' what is checked: crates/gear-core/tests/rack_simulation.rs::profile_is_bounded_from_both_sides_by_the_cutter runs the same 1080-case grid in the suite and asserts penetration <= 1e-12 and deviation < 1e-3 on every case. So what is missing is only the corpus's change detection (a move that stays under the 1e-3 bound, which has 40 % headroom), not correctness gating. Second, the full run took 38 s here, not about 65 s. I did not check the claim that z=47 has the only non-zero penetration: the command prints only the worst case.
verdict.evidence: main.rs:2573-2610, loop `'outer: for z in [3u32,5,...]` with `if n >= limit { break 'outer; }`. My run of `gear-cli verify`: `1080 cases / worst penetration 2.053913e-15 mm z=47 x=+0.5 a=20 b=20 rho=0.38 / worst deviation 6.150734e-4 mm z=31 x=-0.5 a=14.5 b=0 rho=0`, real 0m37.9s. `gear-cli verify 109` is identical to golden verify_100.txt. rack_simulation.rs:29-37 builds the same grid through `Grid`, and lines 39-80 assert on every case.
verdict.corrected_claim: The golden record `verify 100` covers only z = 3, so it cannot detect a change in the cut at any other tooth count. The suite does gate all 1080 cases against fixed bounds (penetration 1e-12, deviation 1e-3), so this is a gap in change detection, not in correctness.
verdict.proposal_note: The full grid costs 38 s in release, and the command is already marked slow, so the simplest fix is to record `verify` in full instead of adding a stride. A stride of ceil(1080/100) would also work, but it fixes which combinations are sampled. Separately, the CLI writes the grid out by hand a second time (main.rs:2573-2577 against rack_simulation.rs:29-37). Moving the grid into gear_core::verify as a public function would give both one source.

title: `dump` is a dead command: its reference (tools/dump_ref.py) no longer exists, and it is recorded as a bare hash
claim: dump exists 'so the port can be compared point by point against the Python reference' tools/dump_ref.py, which is absent from the repository. Its only consumer is the golden corpus, as a sha256 of 10.9 MB printed at 17 significant digits. That flips on any last-bit change (libm, FMA, operation order) and says nothing about what moved. Its own Digest reason says every figure in it is printed elsewhere.
evidence: find over the whole tree finds no dump_ref*, and grep finds no reference to 'gear-cli dump' in the docs or tools.
proposal: Delete the command and its golden file. If a full-profile record is still wanted, record a summarised figure (for example the max |Δr| between consecutive builds, or a coarse-precision sample) instead of a hash.
validation: check_golden.sh still passes with 31 outputs, and CLAUDE.md and state.md do not mention dump.

verdict.reason: The stale reference is confirmed. The doc comment names tools/dump_ref.py, which does not exist, and `git log --all -S dump_ref` shows it was never in the repository after the initial import. handoff_inbound has no script that prints this grid. 'Dead' is wrong, though. Among the golden files, dump is the only record of sampled half-profiles over the grid (z up to 60, helix -30, both tip radii). Every other profile record is a single gear (dxf 17 0.2) or a count (sweep). Deleting it removes the corpus's only bit-level detector of profile change across the grid. The objection that it 'flips on any last-bit change' is its purpose as a change detector, and check_golden.sh records that determinism was measured across debug and release builds. The actual defects are the stale comment and a diff that cannot be read.
verdict.evidence: main.rs:2519-2520: `/// Emit the same case grid as tools/dump_ref.py so the port can be compared point by point against the Python reference`. `find . -name 'dump_ref*'` finds nothing. golden/dump.txt: `sha256 33ce...  3564 lines, 10891502 bytes`. The golden list has no other multi-gear profile record.
verdict.corrected_claim: dump's doc comment points at a reference script that does not exist, and its golden record is an unreadable hash. The command is still the corpus's only full-grid, bit-level profile change detector, so it is not dead.
verdict.proposal_note: Do not delete it without a replacement. Rewrite the doc comment to say what the command is for now. Then either keep the hash or replace it with a readable summary per case: max r, min r and a few sampled points at around 9 significant digits. That gives a diff that says which gear moved. If the goal is to shrink the corpus, drop the full-precision point dump and record the per-case scalar header lines ('S' rows) in full: 1188 short lines, readable and still sensitive.

title: `trainfile` duplicates `convert`'s five figures and is weaker than gear-io's own round-trip test; it writes a fixed /tmp path
claim: trainfile round-trips in memory, then writes /tmp/gear-cli-train.toml only to delete it. Concurrent runs race, and the 'wrote /tmp/…' line is part of the golden output. It declares 'the file is the train' from five figures, so a lost field that moves none of them passes. gear-io's a_train_of_every_preset_round_trips_unchanged asserts text equality, which is stronger. The five rows are the same figures `convert` prints.
evidence: The golden trainfile.txt and convert.txt contain identical figure rows (708.235294118, 4.235880399, −841.196877739, 0.593868228, 0.064023422). train.rs:550 has assert_eq!(text, to_toml(&back)).
proposal: Fold into `convert` (or keep trainfile only as 'write the elevation drive to PATH'), and compare to_toml(back) == text as well as the figures. Never write a default /tmp file.
validation: The corpus loses one file. A deliberately dropped field (for example a material override in the writer) is reported by the harness.

verdict.reason: Every part holds. train_file_report writes /tmp/gear-cli-train.toml when no path is given and then deletes it (main.rs:1367-1377), and the 'wrote /tmp/…' line is in golden trainfile.txt. The five compared figures are the same five that convert_report prints, from closures copied verbatim (at_end, total and the rows loop, main.rs:1391-1425 against 1486-1508). The golden rows are identical. A text round trip of this exact drive is already asserted in gear-io: a_file_written_as_stages_is_refused_by_name_and_converts does `assert_eq!(text, to_toml(&from_toml(&text)...))` on the converted elevation drive, and convert's golden line 'and it writes the file the tool writes of the drive now' establishes that the converted document writes the same text as elevation_drive(). So trainfile's five-figure comparison is weaker than checks that already exist. The concurrency race is real but mostly harmless: two runs write and delete the same fixed path.
verdict.evidence: golden/trainfile.txt line 1: `wrote /tmp/gear-cli-train.toml  (695 lines, 11138 bytes)`. Rows 708.235294118 / 4.235880399 / -841.196877739 / 0.593868228 / 0.064023422 appear in both trainfile.txt and convert.txt. gear-io/src/train.rs:646-647 asserts the text round trip of the converted drive.
verdict.proposal_note: Folding trainfile into convert is right. If a 'write the drive to PATH' command is kept, make PATH required. A dropped field is already caught by gear-io's text-equality test, so the harness does not need to repeat that check.

title: Positional arguments that fail to parse silently become defaults; error paths exit 0; broken pipe panics
claim: arg() maps a parse failure to the default, so `strength 17 abc` reports 17/43 and `shifts epicyclicx` reports 9/37, with no warning. An unknown command, an unknown material and 'no geometry' all eprintln and exit 0. `train bogus` runs the default train. `| head` panics with 'failed printing to stdout: Broken pipe'. `hulasweep 18 0.2 5` panics on an index out of bounds. `show 0`, `show 17 nan` and `show 17 inf` panic inside gear-core (gear.rs:564, empty half-profile), since Gear::new does not refuse z = 0 or a non-finite shift.
evidence: Ran each: exit=0 with the default's header for the parse failures. exit=101 with the gear.rs:564 'range start index 1 out of range' panic for show 0 / nan / inf. main.rs:1247 index panic for hulasweep mesh 5.
proposal: Make arg() return Result and print 'argument N: cannot parse {s:?} as {type}'. Make run return Result<(), String>, with main exiting 2 on a usage error and 1 on a failed solve. Reject a mode string that is not a listed one. Clamp or validate the hulasweep mesh index. Separately, make Gear/Tooth construction refuse z = 0 and a non-finite shift (Rule 5) instead of panicking.
validation: A CLI unit test runs each bad invocation through the dispatch and asserts an Err. Rerunning the probes above gives a message and a non-zero exit, not a panic.

verdict.reason: I reproduced every item. `strength 17 abc` prints the 17/43 default with exit 0. `shifts epicyclicx` gives output identical to `shifts 9 37` (diff empty), exit 0. `train bogus` is identical to `train`, exit 0. `bogus` prints 'unknown command' with exit 0. An unknown material prints 'no material named…' with exit 0. `hulasweep 18 0.2 5` panics at main.rs:1247 'index out of bounds: the len is 4 but the index is 10'. `show 0` and `show 17 nan` both panic at gear-core/src/gear.rs:564:44 'range start index 1 out of range for slice of length 0'. `gear-cli dump | head -1` panics with 'failed printing to stdout: Broken pipe', exit 101. The core half matters more than the CLI half. Tooth::new/Gear::new accept teeth = 0 and a non-finite shift, and Gear::outline then panics. The wasm entry points gear_profile and solve_gear pass JSON params straight to Gear::new (resolved_params only handles the eccentric throw). So a JSON request with teeth 0 plausibly reaches the same panic in the browser. That is plausible from the code; I did not run it. Tooth::tool_wanted_by guards with `params.teeth.max(1)` (tooth.rs:359) while build uses the raw count (tooth.rs:348), so even the guard is applied inconsistently.
verdict.evidence: main.rs:351-353, `args.get(n).and_then(|s| s.parse().ok()).unwrap_or(default)`. Exit codes captured above. gear.rs:557-565 slices `&r[1..]` on an empty half-profile. tooth.rs:348 against tooth.rs:359. gear-wasm/src/lib.rs:656-704: no validation of teeth or finiteness before Gear::new.
verdict.proposal_note: Keep the core fix separate from the CLI cleanup and treat it as the higher priority: refuse z = 0 and non-finite inputs where GearParams enters the core, or in resolved_params at the wasm boundary. Rule 5 says to refuse input that describes no shape at all. The CLI changes are cheap hygiene.

title: check_golden.sh aborts silently when a recorded command fails
claim: Under `set -euo pipefail`, a case whose binary exits non-zero (a panic, status 101) ends the script right at `"$bin" $case >"$out" 2>&1`. Its stderr went into the scratch file, which the EXIT trap deletes. So a red run prints nothing about which case failed or why.
evidence: Reading the script: the loop body has no `|| true` and no status capture, and the trap removes $scratch. `hulasweep 18 0.2 5` shows that a case can exit 101.
proposal: Capture the status (`"$bin" $case >"$out" 2>&1 || { echo "gear-cli $case exited $?"; tail -5 "$out"; status=1; }`) and carry on to the diff, so the panic text also shows in the diff.
validation: Temporarily add a panicking case in a worktree: the script names it and exits non-zero after the diff.

verdict.reason: Confirmed by reading. The script runs under `set -euo pipefail`, and the loop line `"$bin" $case >"$out" 2>&1` has no status capture, so a non-zero exit ends the script there. The panic text went into $out, inside $scratch, which the EXIT trap `rm -rf "$scratch"` deletes. Nothing is printed except make's or CI's bare non-zero status. No golden case panics today, but hulasweep with a bad mesh index shows a recorded command can exit 101, and a regression panic in any recorded case would be reported silently.
verdict.evidence: tools/check_golden.sh:36 `set -euo pipefail`, :79 `trap 'rm -rf "$scratch"' EXIT`, :100 `"$bin" $case >"$out" 2>&1` with no `||`.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposal is sound. Record the exit status in the output file as well (`echo "exit $?" >>"$out"`), so the diff shows it and a change to a command's exit status is itself detected.

title: Small formulas the CLI computes itself, each a second or untested implementation
evidence: Read at the cited lines. worm 1 40 7 90 prints 3487.4 MPa and 54.953 N·m, while wormstage 1 40 7 2 prints 3376.1 MPa for the same worm and torque, because μ differs (0.06 literal against 0.08 preset).
proposal: Read η₀, the residual and the ratio products from the core: the path's or part's figures, the LayoutReport or DistanceReport, and kinematics' exact ratio. Build the `worm` contact section through the worm preset (or delete it in favour of wormstage) so there is one answer per worm. Add a core helper, Cutter::fitting(ring_teeth), and use it in all three places. Print d1 as z1·m_n / sin γ with m_n read from params.
validation: The golden files are unchanged except the worm contact lines, which then equal wormstage's. grep finds no efficiency product and no ω·r arithmetic left in main.rs.

verdict.reason: Most items are accurate as descriptions, but several are mischaracterised. Confirmed: η₀ is computed as the product of forward mesh efficiencies at three sites (main.rs:125, 187, 1736). The worm's d1 is printed as `starts.max(1)/sin γ` (main.rs:3083): the module is implicitly 1 (params.normal_module defaults to 1), and `.max(1)` is unreachable because Screw::new refuses starts == 0 (screw.rs:219) and the function returns before this line. The sliding speed at a literal 3000 rpm is computed by hand: my probe shows the core's MeshCase sliding_velocity is 370.317 mm/s at 1000 rpm, and ×3 = 1110.95 matches the printed 1111.0. The `worm` command uses a literal mu 0.06 and fixed materials. Corrected: (a) the two 'residuals' are not one figure written two ways. The SetView one (main.rs:124) is the closure residual including the clearance. The planetary column (main.rs:3320) is |n0 − n1|, which equals a residual only when the clearance is zero. The command runs at zero clearance, so today both read about 0, but the planetary column is mislabelled in general. (b) The hulaband 'rule' (main.rs:1125) is a filter inside a search over cutter sizes, not a sizing rule. Only 702 (ring−5, floor 4, capped at the stocked cutter) and 1199 (ring−5, floor 6) are two inconsistent sizing rules. (c) The difference between worm's 3487.4 and wormstage's 3376.1 MPa is mostly μ, but not entirely: the two run at different distances (23.7073 against 23.7273 mm, from wormstage's clearance). Scaling 3487.4 by (49.44/54.95)^(1/3) gives 3366, not 3376.1. (d) The hula ratio products are documented at main.rs:145 as counted from the teeth on purpose, and are harmless as display.
verdict.evidence: main.rs:124 `((n0 + d.clearance) - (n1 - d.clearance)).abs()` against main.rs:3320 `(d.nominal[0] - d.nominal[1]).abs()`. golden planetary_17_17_3.txt residual column is 0.0e0 at zero clearance. main.rs:702 against 1199. Probe (probes/verify-gear-cli-2): worm preset at 1000 rpm gives mesh sliding_velocity 370.317 and wheel on_body 49.4437. The worm golden shows a 23.7073 axis distance and wormstage's shows a = 23.7273.
verdict.corrected_claim: The harness duplicates η₀ three times, hand-computes sliding speed and d1 (with an implicit m_n = 1 and an unreachable .max(1)), rates the `worm` contact at a literal μ = 0.06 that differs from the preset's, and has two inconsistent default shaper-sizing rules (702 and 1199). The planetary command's 'residual' column is |n0 − n1|, which is a closure residual only at zero clearance. That is a latent mislabel, not a second formula for one figure.
verdict.proposal_note: Harness-only duplication does not break Rule 1, which concerns TypeScript. Prioritise the items that can give a wrong-looking number: the planetary residual label and the worm/wormstage divergence. The planetary column should print the DistanceReport's own residual (running − nominal per mesh), which is the SetView formula. For the worm, make `worm` read μ from the worm preset's mesh so the two commands agree, or drop its contact section. Making `Cutter::fitting` a core helper would put a rule of thumb (ring−5) into gear-core. If it goes there, it should be a stated, user-visible default, not a hidden constant.

title: The corpus prints roundoff and Debug names, which will make cosmetic diffs
claim: Residuals are printed at {:.1e}, so 3.6e-15 and 0.0e0 are in the planetary and planetstage files. Signed zeros are printed as '-0.00000' (12 lines in kinematics.txt, 1 each in train, meshsweep and hulasweep). An operation reordering that moves nothing physical will therefore diff. Roles, presets and errors are printed through {:?} and lower-cased, so renaming a Rust variant diffs the 600 KB graph file. Each of these trains a reader to --write without looking.
evidence: grep over tools/golden: 3.6e-15 in 6 lines. '-0.00000' counts as listed. graph.rs formats format!("{:?}", s.role) and `refused: {e:?}`.
proposal: Print residuals as '< 1e-12' or as a count of ulps against the distance. Normalise −0 (add 0.0 or format through a helper). Print roles and errors through their catalogue keys or Display, as graph.rs already does for notes (n.key).
validation: Reorder a sum in a worktree, for example the residual's terms: no golden diff results.

verdict.reason: Two of the three parts hold: residuals are printed at {:.1e}, so floating-point roundoff reaches the corpus, and signed zeros print as -0.00000. The third part does not hold as a nuisance. BodyRole and Preset are serde `rename_all = "snake_case"` types that cross the wasm boundary, so renaming a variant already changes the bindings, the wasm record and TrainPanel. A golden diff at the same moment is consistent, not cosmetic. graph.txt also contains no `refused:` line today, so the `{e:?}` branch at graph.rs:229 prints nothing into the corpus.
verdict.evidence: planetary_17_17_3.txt:10 prints residual `3.6e-15` beside `0.0e0` rows. planetstage_24_18_60_3.txt:23-24 print `3.6e-15`. main.rs:124 is `residual: ((n0 + d.clearance) - (n1 - d.clearance)).abs()` and main.rs:3320 is `(d.nominal[0] - d.nominal[1]).abs()` printed as `{:>10.1e}`. `grep -c -- -0.00000` finds kinematics 12, train 1, meshsweep 1 and hulasweep 1. The train.txt case is `(min -0.00000, ...)` on a backlash minimum, which may be a tiny negative value rather than a signed zero; either way it is cosmetic. `grep -c 'refused:' tools/golden/graph.txt` = 0. Roles in graph.txt: fixed 651, free 948, load 333, reacted 333, all one-word variants, where Debug-lowercase equals the serde name. BodyRole at train/mod.rs:3758-3764 carries `serde(rename_all = "snake_case")`.
verdict.corrected_claim: The residual columns print roundoff at {:.1e}: 3.6e-15 against 0.0e0 in 6 lines across planetary_17_17_3, planetstage_24_18_60_3 and planetstage_12_30_72_3. Signed zeros print as -0.00000 in 15 lines. A reordering that changes nothing physical can therefore diff these outputs. Printing roles and presets through Debug is a lesser point: a variant rename is already a boundary change. The real hazard there is a multi-word variant, where Debug-lowercase (`meshedplanets`) differs from the serde name (`meshed_planets`) the rest of the tool uses.
verdict.proposal_note: For residuals, print against a relative threshold, e.g. `closes` when |r| < 1e-12·a and the value otherwise. Do not print a ulp count: that is still roundoff and still moves. Normalise -0 with one helper (`v + 0.0`) used by every fixed-point print in the harness. For roles and presets, print through the serde snake_case name (serde_json::to_value or a small `as_str`), not a Display impl: no catalogue key exists for BodyRole, and the snake_case name is what the boundary already carries.

title: Wrong or stale prose in the harness: orphaned doc comments, a stale shifts comment, 'spur' for helical parts, audit-history counts
claim:
Five problems:
(1) The doc comments of train_report ('milestone 6's gate') and train_file_report ('Write a geartrain out as TOML…') sit stacked on elevation_drive; neither function has its own.
(2) The shifts comment says that with the optimiser off 'the shifts stay at their undercut floor, and the clearance is not read at all'. The rows show x2 moving (0.4239 at 23.8226; 0.7039 / 0.7039 at 24.2240), and the note targets 23.0000 = 23.02 − clearance.
(3) kind_name prints every non-worm pair as 'spur', so train.txt has 'part 2 spur … beta 15 deg'.
(4) Comments count recurrences inconsistently ('a third time', 'six times', 'sixth-recorded', 'eight times', 'the ninth time this audit').
(5) 'milestone 5' in strength_report's doc.
evidence: Read at the cited lines. The golden shifts_9_37 'optimiser off' rows and train.txt line 'part 2  spur  z 13/31  beta 15 deg'.
proposal: Move each doc comment onto its own function. Rewrite the shifts comment to say what the solve does: below the floor's distance it refuses and runs at the given distance, with the clearance read; above it the shifts reach with an even division. Name the kind from the shape (worm, crossed, helical, spur: helix ≠ 0 or angle ≠ 0). Replace the history counts with a single pointer to the corrections.md entry.
validation: cargo doc shows the right text on each function. The train corpus prints 'helical' for part 2 (a deliberate golden change).

verdict.reason: All five points check out at the cited lines. One correction on (3): kind_name also labels a non-worm crossed pair `spur`, because print_point_pair receives kind_name's output at main.rs:1963. So a crossed helical pair in a train would print `part k  spur ... lead angle`.
verdict.evidence: (1) main.rs:1283-1290 put `A two-stage geartrain... milestone 6's gate` and `Write a geartrain out as TOML...` directly above `/// **The elevation drive**` and `fn elevation_drive()`. `fn train_file_report` (1349) and `fn train_report` (1772) have no doc comments. (2) main.rs:1642-1646 say `the shifts stay at their undercut floor, and the clearance is not read at all`. But shifts_9_37.txt:27-28 show x2 at 0.4239 at 23.8226 and 0.7039/0.7039 at 24.2240. Line 22's note targets 23.0000 for a 23.0200 distance, so the clearance is read. (3) main.rs:2128-2132 is `Some(d) if d.worm => "worm", _ => "spur"`. train.txt:34 reads `part 2  spur  z 13/31  beta 15 deg`, and train_toggles.txt:21 reads `part 1  spur ... beta 30 deg`. (4) main.rs:1682 `eight times`, 1917 `a third time`, 3494 `six times`, 3581 `sixth-recorded`, 3626 `ninth time`. (5) main.rs:2180 `the whole of milestone 5`.
verdict.proposal_note: For (3), derive the name from what the shape already knows. Use the distance's worm flag and angle, with the member helix (e.g. from the solved pair): worm, crossed (angle ≠ 0), helical (β ≠ 0), spur. Rule 4 argues for a single word such as `pair` plus the printed beta. That would drop the branch entirely and makes the golden change once. For (4), delete the counts rather than re-pointing them. docs/corrections.md already holds the history, and CLAUDE.md asks that each thing be said once.

title: A crossed pair whose first member is spur (β1 = 0) is refused as 'worm too thin', while β1 = 1e-6 builds
claim: Screw::new refuses sin γ1 = z1·m_n/d1 ≥ 1. With β1 = 0 the first member is a spur gear, d1 = z1·m_n and sin γ1 = 1 exactly, so a spur gear crossed with a 5° helical is refused. The same pair with the hands swapped (β2 = 0) builds, and β1 = 1e-6 builds with d1 = 17.000. The `crossed 17 43 5` table's first row reads '— no such pair' where the limit is a real design. CLAUDE.md rule 4 says 'a spur gear is helical at β = 0'.
evidence: Probe: β1 = 0 gives Err(Screw(WormTooThin)); β1 = 1e-6 gives d1 17.000000000000004, d2 43.1643, a 30.3378. The golden row at β1 = 5, β2 = 0 builds at d2 = 43.0000.
proposal: Refuse only sin γ1 > 1 (strictly, or with a relative tolerance). At sin γ1 = 1, take the limit instead of dividing by cos γ1: axial module, lead and the sliding terms go to their β → 0 forms, as the β2 = 0 end already does.
validation: `crossed 17 43 5` builds its β1 = 0 row, and that row equals the β1 = 1e-9 row to 1e-6. A continuity law in screw.rs as β1 → 0⁺.

verdict.reason: The discontinuity is real, and wider than stated. It is also a documented, tested and explained choice. The user does not see 'worm too thin': the catalogue message is 'the first member has no lead angle; put the helical member first and the spur one second', which obeys rule 5's 'say so'. crossed.rs:1153-1196 argue the ordering and test that it is refused. On the merits the argument is weak. The only quantities that are singular at γ1 = 90° are the lead and the axial module, and those are worm-only readings: shape.rs:3150-3170 reads axial_module only when `distances[d].worm`. A spur gear crossed with a helical one is a real design. Which member comes first is a labelling artefact of Screw, not a property of the pair, and it breaks rule 4 (a spur is helical at β = 0) and the continuity goal. The refusal is not limited to β1 = 0: in floating point it covers β1 up to about 1e-7°. So the auditor's validation, which asks for the β1 = 1e-9 row, would itself be refused. And the auditor's 'take the limit' fix, done naively, would produce NaN: Screw::normal_module() recovers m_n as axial_module·cos γ1 (screw.rs:862), which is ∞·0 at γ1 = 90°, and normal_base_pitch uses it (screw.rs:869).
verdict.evidence: Probe /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/verify-gear-cli-3 (arr::crossed([17,43],Σ), shifts 0, face 10, with_first_helix(β1), then screw(0) and solve_alone). At Σ=5, β1 = 0, 1e-12, 1e-9 and 1e-7 deg all give Err(Screw(WormTooThin)). β1 = 1e-6 deg gives d1 17.000000000000, d2 43.164252935, a 30.087783005, axial module 4.7e7, p_bn 2.952131434, solve ok. At Σ=30, β1 = 0 and 1e-9 are refused, 1e-6 builds, and β1 = 30 (β2 = 0) builds with d2 = 43.000. screw.rs:229-231 is `if sin_gamma_1 >= 1.0 { return Err(ScrewError::WormTooThin) }`. strings_en.toml:194 holds the message above. The golden crossed_17_43_5.txt:4 reads `0.0  5 — no such pair`.
verdict.corrected_claim: A crossed pair is refused whenever its first member's helix is within about 1e-7° of zero, a spur first member included. The same pair with its members swapped builds. The refusal is explained to the user and tested as deliberate, but the only quantities that are singular there (lead and axial module) are worm-only readings that a crossed gear pair never uses. So the refusal comes from Screw's member ordering, not from the geometry.
verdict.proposal_note: Do not simply relax `>=` to `>`. At sin γ1 = 1, normal_module() = axial_module·cos γ1 gives ∞·0 = NaN, and that flows into normal_base_pitch. Better: (a) store m_n in Screw and return it directly from normal_module(). (b) Make lead/axial_module well-defined at the limit, either Option<f64> (None for a member with no lead) or f64::INFINITY, which is the true limit, with worm_length/wheel_face_width only ever called on worm distances as now. (c) Or have Shape::screw hand Screw whichever member has sin γ < 1 as 'first' when the distance is not a worm. Then refuse only when both members would be spur, which is the parallel case AxesAreParallel already covers. After the change, retire or invert the test `a_crossed_axis_spur_pair_puts_the_spur_member_second`'s 'refused, not fudged' block. Add a continuity law as β1 → 0⁺ (β1 = 0 against 1e-6 deg) on d2, a, sliding ratio and efficiency.

title: No CLI command prints metrology or JGMA tolerances; they are in no golden record except one wasm probe
claim: The CLI touches gear_core::metrology only for base_helix_angle, and never touches jgma, shaper-cut external gears, or auto::admissible_ranges. Span, over-pins and tolerance grades therefore sit outside check_golden. They are recorded only by tools/wasm_boundary.json, for a single gear (1 'span', 1 'over_two_pins'). The project has two change-detector corpora with different coverage and no statement of which covers what.
evidence: grep across the CLI sources: metrology 1, jgma 0, shaper 0, auto 0. grep of the wasm record: a single span and a single over_two_pins.
proposal: Add a `measure [z] [x] [helix] [grade]` command that prints the span, the over-pins figures and the JGMA grade tolerances over a small grid, recorded in full. Or state in CLAUDE.md's check table that the wasm record is the corpus for metrology.
validation: Perturb a JGMA table entry or the pin-tangency tolerance in a worktree: check_golden shows a diff.

verdict.reason: It is true that no CLI command prints span, over-pins or JGMA tolerances, so check_golden does not watch them. The claim overstates the gap in two ways. First, auto::admissible_ranges is recorded: the wasm record carries `ranges` for solve_gear and for every solve_train member. The wasm record also carries a JGMA `tolerance` result and `available_classes`, not only span and pins. Second, both corpora are change detectors, and metrology has a dedicated integration suite of independent checks that a golden row would add little to: the textbook formula, consecutive spans differing by one base pitch, the caliper reading off the drawn teeth, and the pin checks. The real residual gap is narrower. The JGMA tables are checked at spot values and by structural laws: monotone in grade, total above tooth-to-tooth, preferred numbers, cell counts. An entry off the spot list can be mistyped to another preferred number that keeps the order, and nothing fires.
verdict.evidence: `grep metrology|jgma|shaper|admissible_ranges crates/gear-cli/src/*.rs` finds only `use gear_core::metrology::base_helix_angle` (main.rs:2195). The wasm record's out/solve_gear/ok has span {teeth_spanned 1, nominal 1.602}, over_two_pins {nominal 11.2577}, tolerance {class fine/0, tooth_to_tooth 6.3, total 18}, available_classes and ranges. solve_train members carry ranges too. crates/gear-core/tests/metrology.rs has span_reduces_to_the_textbook_formula (55), consecutive_spans_differ_by_one_base_pitch (93), the_span_is_what_a_caliper_reads_off_the_drawn_teeth (773) and others. jgma.rs has 11 tests, including spot_values_match_the_printed_tables (200) and tolerances_grow_with_grade_within_every_band (518).
verdict.corrected_claim: The JGMA tolerance tables are guarded by spot values and structural laws only, and no change detector records them in full. So a mistyped entry off the spot list that keeps the tables' order goes unnoticed. Span and over-pins are covered by independent integration tests, and admissible ranges by the wasm record, so neither is a real gap.
verdict.proposal_note: A `measure` command sampling a small grid covers only the cells it samples. A full-table check closes the gap: a golden `jgma` dump of every (scale, grade, module band, diameter band) cell, or a test that compares a checked-in transcription (e.g. a TOML or CSV next to the source table) cell by cell. A CLAUDE.md sentence on which corpus covers what is cheap and worth adding either way.

title: Near-self-locking (0.8) and low-efficiency (0.5) warning thresholds are unexposed rules of thumb
claim: For a point contact, the notes that tell a designer the mesh is close to self-locking or close to not driving forward fire when the static friction exceeds 0.8 of the locking threshold. The low-efficiency note fires below 50 % forward efficiency. Both are bare literals inside point_mesh_report. Neither is documented in docs/ or exposed as an input. A line contact never gets the low-efficiency note.
evidence: shape.rs:2700: `} else if threshold > 0.0 && static_friction > 0.8 * threshold {`. shape.rs:2709: `if m.efficiency.forward < 0.5 {`. grep for 0.8 or 0.5 near 'lock' in docs/reference.md, rationale.md and state.md finds nothing. strings_en.toml:139 says 'close to self-locking ... near threshold of {threshold}' and never states the 20 % margin. Those two lines are the only uses of MESH_NEAR_SELF_LOCKING and MESH_LOW_EFFICIENCY.
proposal: Name both values: `const NEAR_LOCKING_MARGIN: f64 = 0.8` and `const LOW_EFFICIENCY: f64 = 0.5`, each with a doc comment giving its rationale. Better, since the margin is in effect an allowance for how uncertain the estimated μ is, make it a field on the mesh or train (for example `locking_margin`, default 0.8) and say it in the note: 'within {margin} % of the threshold'. Document both in reference.md beside self-locking. Decide deliberately whether a line contact should also raise the low-efficiency note.
validation: A test that sets static μ just below and just above margin × threshold and sees the note flip. check_strings passes once the new placeholder is added to all five catalogues.

verdict.reason: The 0.8 near-locking margin is a bare literal that was never argued, as claimed. The 0.5 is different: the note's own sentence fixes it ('most of the input becomes heat' means below 50 %), and it matches the classical fact that a single-thread worm that self-locks runs below 50 % forward. So it is a named quantity waiting for a const, not a rule of thumb. The margin is also partly visible already, because the note prints both μ and the threshold, so a reader can see the ratio. That leaves the 20 % itself, which is chosen by feel and appears in no document. Raising the low-efficiency note only for point contacts agrees with its wording ('limits a crossed-axis stage'), but it is still a branch by contact kind.
verdict.evidence: shape.rs:2700 `} else if threshold > 0.0 && static_friction > 0.8 * threshold {` and :2709 `if m.efficiency.forward < 0.5 {`. grep of docs/*.md for the near-locking margin finds nothing. reference.md:1016-1026 documents only the locking thresholds. strings_en.toml:139/141 say 'near threshold of {threshold}' and print both numbers. reference.md:1935 ties 'below half efficiency forward' to self-locking.
verdict.corrected_claim: The 0.8 near-locking margin is an undocumented rule of thumb chosen by feel. The 0.5 low-efficiency threshold is defined by its note's wording and needs only a named constant. Whether the low-efficiency note should also apply to a line contact is a separate, minor consistency question.
verdict.proposal_note: Name both values. Document the margin in reference.md beside 'locked backwards', framed as an allowance for uncertainty in the static μ. Making it a per-mesh input is probably over-engineering, since the note already prints μ and the threshold. A cheaper step is to state the ratio μ/threshold in the note.

title: Preset friction (sliding 0.08, static 0.16) has no source, yet decides the self-locking verdict
claim: Every preset mesh gets sliding μ 0.08 and static μ 0.16 from one constant whose only comment is 'the set's'. The static value, a flat 2× the sliding one, is what the self-locking and break-away figures are judged against. The material library carries a Basis and a note for every non-datasheet value; these friction coefficients carry neither.
evidence: arrangements.rs:30: `const FRICTION: (f64, f64) = (0.08, 0.16);`. docs/ mentions μ = 0.08 only as the value used in worked examples (reference.md:1162, 2063) and never gives a source for 0.16 or for the factor of 2. The near-locking note compares `static_friction` against the threshold (shape.rs:2700).
proposal: Put the default friction in one documented place: either beside the material basis, where friction becomes a material-pair property with a Basis::Estimated note, or as a named `DEFAULT_FRICTION` with a cited source for the sliding value and an argued ratio for static/sliding. In the panel, mark the value as estimated the way material values are.
validation: check_strings and the materials law ('every non-datasheet value carries a note') extended to friction.

verdict.reason: The default friction pair is one constant with a meaningless comment ('the set's'). No document gives a source for sliding 0.08 or for static = 2× sliding. The static value decides the preset worm's headline verdict: a probe of arr::worm(1,40) gives lead angle ≈ 8.21°, so the backward threshold is cos20°·tan8.21° ≈ 0.136. Static 0.16 lies above it and the mesh reports mesh.self_locking. Sliding 0.08 alone would not lock it. rationale.md:924 presents 'The default worm stage is self-locking' as the handbook answer, but that answer rests on the unsourced factor of 2. The values are editable panel inputs (TrainPanel.svelte:673-674), so the estimate is visible, but it carries no basis, unlike every material value.
verdict.evidence: arrangements.rs:29-30 `/// Sliding and static friction every mesh here runs with — the set's.` `const FRICTION: (f64, f64) = (0.08, 0.16);`. Probe (probes/verify-lens-magic-numbers-1): worm(1,40) gives sliding 0.08, static 0.16, mesh notes ["mesh.self_locking"], efficiency 61.8 % forward / 0 backward. The default brass-on-steel worm and the default POM/PA materials would have quite different friction.
verdict.proposal_note: The minimum is to rename the constant (DEFAULT_FRICTION), add a sentence citing a source for lubricated steel sliding μ, argue the static/sliding ratio in rationale.md#two-friction-coefficients, and state that the worm preset's self-locking verdict depends on it. Making friction a material-pair property is the larger change and would touch the mesh's input model.

title: Rule 1 broken: the eccentric-gear mate's tooth count (43) is typed in TypeScript
claim: A new gear tab seeds its mate as `{ teeth: 43, profile_shift: 0 }` in TypeScript. Every other field of the tab comes from the core's `defaults()` (d.params, d.pin_diameter, d.chord_tolerance, ...), and GearTabDefaults has no mate. The panel also picks the number of profile sample points (600) in TypeScript.
evidence: state.svelte.ts:147: `mate: { teeth: 43, profile_shift: 0, internal: false },`. Right beside it, `pinDiameter: d.pin_diameter` and `chordTolerance: d.chord_tolerance` come from the core. GearPanel.svelte:250/253: `ringProfile(ringRequest, 600)` and `profile(request, 600)`. CLAUDE.md rule 1: 'A default is one of those numbers'.
proposal: Add `mate: MateRef` to GearTabDefaults in gear-wasm and have the TS copy `d.mate`. Move the profile point count into Defaults as well (for example `profile_points`), or derive it in the core from the chord tolerance, which the outline already does for DXF.
validation: grep web/src for literals that are not layout. tools/check_bindings.sh --write, then npm run check.

verdict.reason: The mate's tooth count of 43 is an engineering default typed in TypeScript, against CLAUDE.md rule 1 ('A default is one of those numbers'). GearTabDefaults (gear-wasm lib.rs ~1150) carries pin_diameter, chord_tolerance and eccentric_throw but no mate, so the core cannot own the value. The 600 points per tooth in GearPanel.svelte:250/253 is a weaker case. It is a drawing's sampling density, closer to the view state the same file exempts ('a view has no engineering default'), though deriving it from the chord tolerance would still be cleaner.
verdict.evidence: web/src/state.svelte.ts:147 `mate: { teeth: 43, profile_shift: 0, internal: false },` sits beside `pinDiameter: d.pin_diameter`. gear-wasm lib.rs:1152-1162 builds GearTabDefaults with no mate field. GearPanel.svelte:250 `ringProfile(ringRequest, 600)` and :253 `profile(request, 600)`.
verdict.proposal_note: Add `mate: MateRef` to GearTabDefaults, which is the rule-1 fix. The profile point count is optional, and moving it into the defaults would only move a display constant. If it moves at all, derive it from the chord tolerance.

title: Load-case defaults written twice in gear-wasm, and kept in the boundary rather than the core
claim: The shipped train's load cases (ultimate 0.1 N·m at 30,000 rpm, back-driving 3.0 N·m, fatigue 0.02 N·m at 30,000 rpm) are literals in `defaults()`. The add-a-case edit repeats the same pairs (0.1, 30,000) and (0.02, 30,000), commenting that they are 'the shipped train's'. Nothing ties the two sites together, so changing one leaves the other stale. Related: the continuous-duty default of 1,000 h exists only inside `set_duty`, with no `Duty::continuous()` constructor. The UI's face-width seed is 5 mm (UI_SEED) while the core presets seed 10 mm, so the panel and the CLI/golden corpus start from different trains. The harness passes the hula stage 2.0 N·m and 1,000 rpm as a literal five times.
evidence: lib.rs:1175 `LoadCase::ultimate(input, output, 0.1, 30_000.0)`, :1177 `LoadCase::fatigue(input, output, 0.02, 30_000.0)`, :1576 `CaseKind::Ultimate => (0.1, 30_000.0)`, :1577 `CaseKind::Fatigue => (0.02, 30_000.0)`. conditions.rs:1162 `runtime_hours: 1000.0`. arrangements.rs:723/726 and mod.rs:1310 give face width 10.0; lib.rs:1142 gives `const UI_SEED: f64 = 5.0`. main.rs:706, 1146, 1235, 1696, 1754 each call `solve_hula(&stage, 2.0, 1000.0, &lib)`.
proposal: In gear-core, add `impl CaseKind { pub const fn default_load(self) -> (f64, f64) }`, or a `LoadCase::shipped(kind, input, output)`, and `Duty::continuous()` with the 1,000 h as a named constant. Have both wasm sites and set_duty call them. Settle the face-width seed once in the core, as the preset's value or a named `SEED_FACE_WIDTH`, and delete UI_SEED, or say in the core why the UI differs. Give the CLI a single `HULA_LOAD` constant.
validation: A test that `fresh_case(kind)` equals the matching case of `defaults().train`, torque and speed included. check_wasm.sh --write records no change to the answers.

verdict.reason: Confirmed: the load pairs (0.1, 30 000) and (0.02, 30 000) are written twice in gear-wasm (defaults() and apply_edit's AddCase) with nothing tying them together. wasm_probe records add_case, but its figures come from the second site, so a change to defaults() alone would pass unnoticed. The 1000 h continuous duty exists only in set_duty. Its doc comment says it is 'the same numbers a fresh case starts with', but a fresh case starts intermittent and has no hours, so the comment is inaccurate. The 2.0 N·m / 1000 rpm hula load repeated five times in the CLI is harness-only and minor. The face-width sub-claim is a deliberate, argued divergence: lib.rs:1128-1142 explains that the panel wants automatic widths with a 5 mm fallback for when the toggle is off, and a test holds it (lib.rs:2878-2907). What remains open is why the core presets are fixed at 10 mm instead. That is a real but separate question, not a duplication.
verdict.evidence: gear-wasm lib.rs:1175/1177 `LoadCase::ultimate(input, output, 0.1, 30_000.0)`, `LoadCase::fatigue(input, output, 0.02, 30_000.0)`. lib.rs:1576-1577 `CaseKind::Ultimate => (0.1, 30_000.0), CaseKind::Fatigue => (0.02, 30_000.0)`. conditions.rs:1146-1165 set_duty doc says 'seeded from the same numbers a fresh case starts with ... or a thousand hours' with `runtime_hours: 1000.0`. mod.rs:2767 Duty::intermittent carries no hours. main.rs:706,1146,1235,1696,1754 `solve_hula(.., 2.0, 1000.0, &lib)`.
verdict.corrected_claim: The shipped load-case figures are duplicated in gear-wasm with no test linking the two sites. The continuous-duty 1000 h has no constructor, and set_duty's doc comment wrongly says the hours come from a fresh case. The UI's 5 mm automatic face-width seed is a documented, test-held choice and not a duplication.
verdict.proposal_note: Put `CaseKind::default_load()` (or `Train::fresh_case(kind)` without torque and speed) in gear-core, and have both wasm sites call it. Add `Duty::continuous()` with a named hours constant and fix the doc comment. Leave UI_SEED as it is unless the core presets move to automatic widths too.

title: MemberGear::default repeats GearParams::default by hand (17 teeth, addendum 1, dedendum 1.25, root 0.38)
claim: The basic-rack proportions are written in two structs. For the pressure angle the project has already fixed this: shape.rs:93-98 follows it from GearParams::default ('said once'). Teeth, addendum, dedendum and root radius were not given the same treatment.
evidence: params.rs:78-84 `pressure_angle: 20.0, teeth: 17, ... addendum: 1.0, dedendum: 1.25, root_radius: 0.38`. mod.rs:1300-1308 `teeth: 17, ... addendum: 1.0, ... dedendum: 1.25, root_radius: 0.38`. shape.rs:97 `Auto::automatic(GearParams::default().pressure_angle)`.
proposal: Build MemberGear::default from `let p = GearParams::default();`, taking teeth, addendum, dedendum and root_radius from `p`. Keep the train-only fields (min_tip_width 0.1, face width 10) as named constants with a sentence each.
validation: Existing tests and the golden corpus are unchanged, which is a pure refactor. Add a test that MemberGear::default's rack equals GearParams::default's.

verdict.reason: MemberGear::default restates GearParams::default's teeth 17, addendum 1.0, dedendum 1.25 and root_radius 0.38 by hand. shape.rs:93-98 already follows the pressure angle from GearParams::default ('said once'). No test ties the two defaults together, so changing one leaves the other stale without any failure.
verdict.evidence: params.rs:74-86 `teeth: 17, ... addendum: 1.0, dedendum: 1.25, root_radius: 0.38`. train/mod.rs:1297-1318 `teeth: 17, ... addendum: 1.0, ... dedendum: 1.25, root_radius: 0.38`. shape.rs:97 `Auto::automatic(GearParams::default().pressure_angle)`.
verdict.proposal_note: This is a pure refactor and the golden corpus should not move. Also give min_tip_width 0.1 and the face-width 10 a sentence each.

title: Worm preset: 7 mm written four times, and the helix formula assumes module 1 (NaN above 7 starts)
claim: `worm()` seeds the helix as `acos(starts/7.0)`, which is cos β₁ = z₁·m/d₁ with m = 1 fixed silently, and sets the diameter to 7.0 again two lines later. worm_and_pair and ScrewParams::default repeat 7.0. `pair()` likewise seeds the pitch diameter as f64::from(teeth), which is again m = 1. The public `worm(starts, …)` gives a NaN helix for starts > 7, and all of these go wrong without warning if the Builder's module stops being 1.
evidence: arrangements.rs:712 `let helix = (f64::from(starts) / 7.0).acos().to_degrees();`, :715 `pitch_diameter = Auto::fixed(7.0)`, :792 `pitch_diameter = Auto::fixed(7.0)`. screw.rs:120 `worm_pitch_diameter: 7.0`. Builder::new(1.0) appears at arrangements.rs:143, 212, 299 and 772.
proposal: Add `const WORM_PITCH_DIAMETER: f64 = 7.0;` (with a sentence on why) and a `PRESET_MODULE` constant. Compute the helix as `(z1 * module / d1).clamp(-1, 1).acos()` from the shape's own module and diameter. Have ScrewParams::default use the same constant.
validation: A test that worm(s, z) with a module other than 1 has helix and diameter consistent through Shape::with_first_diameter.

verdict.reason: Confirmed, and the consequence is worse than 'NaN helix'. The seed is `(starts/7).acos()`, which assumes m = 1 and d = 7. arr::worm(17,23), used by tests crossed.rs:357 and :670, gets NaN in both members' helix boxes (Auto{auto:true, manual:NaN}). with_first_helix does not clear the wheel's NaN. The solve does not read the manual value while the box is automatic, so figures come out correct (`gear-cli wormstage 8 40 20` solves fine). But the shape cannot survive the project's own JSON: serde_json writes NaN as null, and deserialising it back fails. worm_and_pair repeats the fixed 7 mm but sets no helix seed at all, so the two worm builders seed differently.
verdict.evidence: arrangements.rs:712 `let helix = (f64::from(starts) / 7.0).acos().to_degrees();` and :715/:792 `Auto::fixed(7.0)`. screw.rs:120 `worm_pitch_diameter: 7.0`. Probe (probes/verify-lens-magic-numbers-1): `worm(17,23) helix boxes: Auto { auto: true, manual: NaN } Auto { auto: true, manual: NaN }`. After with_first_helix(45), the wheel is still NaN. Serialising worm(17,23).with_first_helix(45.0) and reading it back gives `Err("invalid type: null, expected f64 at line 1 column 1230")`, where worm(1,40) round-trips Ok. worm(7..12, 40) solved alone gives Err(Screw(WormTooThin)).
verdict.proposal_note: Clamping the cosine to [-1,1] would give a 0° seed for starts·m > d, which is a legal but meaningless value, so it is better to seed only where z₁·m < d₁. The better fix is to compute the seed from the shape's own module and the diameter constant, shared with worm_and_pair and ScrewParams::default. Add a test that every arrangement's shape round-trips through serde_json, which would have caught the NaN.

title: The shipped 0.02 mm clearance and tolerance are written nine times in arrangements.rs
claim: `push_distance`, `pair` and `planetary` each spell out 0.02 for the clearance, tolerance_plus and tolerance_minus. The Builder's doc comment speaks of 'the shipped 0.02 mm' as if it were one value.
evidence: arrangements.rs:461-464, 674-676 and 757-759 all contain `0.02`.
proposal: Add `const SHIPPED_CLEARANCE: f64 = 0.02;` and `const SHIPPED_TOLERANCE: f64 = 0.02;` (in mm), or a `Distance::shipped(axes, angle)` constructor, and use it at all three sites.
validation: Golden corpus unchanged.

verdict.reason: All nine literals are there, and the finding is stronger than stated: six of the nine do nothing. `pair()` builds through `line()` and `planetary()` through `epicyclic()`. Both add their distances with `Builder::distance` -> `push_distance`, and the shape starts with no distances (`Shape::default` has `distances: Vec::new()`). So the first distance already gets `clearance: Auto::fixed(0.02)` and `tolerance_plus/minus: 0.02` from `push_distance`'s `like.map_or(...)` fallback. The three assignments at 674-676 and again at 757-759 write back the values already there.
verdict.evidence: arrangements.rs:454-466: push_distance takes `like = self.distances.first()`, which is None for the first distance, giving clearance `Auto::fixed(0.02)` and tolerances 0.02. arrangements.rs:296-310: line() is Builder::new, then `.distance([k-1,k])` per mesh, then `b.build()`, and build (110-118) only touches module/pressure-angle auto flags. arrangements.rs:267/275: epicyclic also goes through `b.distance`. arrangements.rs:674-676 and 757-759: `shape.distances[0].clearance = Auto::fixed(0.02); ...tolerance_plus = 0.02; ...tolerance_minus = 0.02;`, the same values again.
verdict.corrected_claim: The shipped 0.02 mm clearance and ±0.02 mm tolerance are real values in only one place, push_distance's fallback (arrangements.rs:461-464). The six assignments in pair() (674-676) and planetary() (757-759) repeat values push_distance has already set and have no effect.
verdict.proposal_note: Delete the six redundant lines in pair() and planetary(). Name the fallback in push_distance (e.g. `const SHIPPED_CLEARANCE_MM: f64 = 0.02; const SHIPPED_TOLERANCE_MM: f64 = 0.02;`) and point the doc comments at lines 33 and 452 to it. Also fix the doc comment on pair() ('one distance with the running clearance and the tolerance band a pair ships with'), which implies pair sets them itself. Expected result: golden corpus and nextest unchanged.

title: Seeded values are rounded to 1e-4 absolute, so small torques lose precision
claim: When relief turns an automatic value into a given one, the seed is `(v*1e4).round()/1e4`, which is four decimal places whatever the size of the quantity. The comment says 'to the digits they saw', but the panel shows torque at 3 or 4 decimals, speed at 0 or 1 and figures at 3, so the rounding is tied to no display precision. For a derived torque of order 1e-4 N·m the relative error is large.
evidence: mod.rs:3661 `l.torque.manual = (s.torque * 1e4).round() / 1e4;`. At the fast end of a 1:40 step-up with the shipped 0.02 N·m fatigue input and η ≈ 0.87, the derived torque is about 0.000437 N·m, which seeds as 0.0004 (-8.5 %). 0.00015 seeds as 0.0002 (+33 %). TrainPanel.svelte uses num(…,4) for torques, num(…,1) for speeds and n = toFixed(3) for figures.
proposal: Round to significant figures, e.g. `fn seed(v) { if v == 0 {0} else { let k = 10f64.powi(SEED_DIGITS - 1 - v.abs().log10().floor() as i32); (v*k).round()/k } }` with `SEED_DIGITS = 6`. Or seed the unrounded value and let the panel's formatting decide what is shown. Use one helper for all three sites.
validation: A law: seeding and then re-solving changes any derived figure by less than 1e-5 relative, across the presets under a step-up case.

verdict.reason: The mechanism is as described: three sites round the seed to 1e-4 absolute (mod.rs:2359, 3661, 3664), so a small derived torque loses relative precision when it is made given. But the claim that the rounding is 'tied to no display precision' is wrong for torque. The panel shows every derived or case torque with num(…,4) (TrainPanel.svelte:161, 806, 1014, 1252), so 1e-4 is exactly 'the digits they saw', as the comment says. The real defect is that both the display and the seed use a fixed absolute number of decimals: a 0.000437 N·m torque shows as 0.0004 and seeds as 0.0004. Toggling it from derived to given therefore moves the load by -8.5 %, which is a small discontinuity. Speeds (shown at 0-1 dp) and figures (shown at 3 dp) are seeded more finely than displayed, which does no harm. The example scale is reachable: the shipped fatigue case is 0.02 N·m (gear-wasm lib.rs:1177), and 0.02/40·0.87 ≈ 4.35e-4.
verdict.evidence: mod.rs:3661 `l.torque.manual = (s.torque * 1e4).round() / 1e4;`; mod.rs:2344-2346 doc says 'to the digits they saw'; TrainPanel.svelte:1014 `{num(row.torque, 4)}`, :806 `{num(x.torque, 4)}`; :373 given torque shown with num(…,3); gear-wasm lib.rs:1177 `LoadCase::fatigue(input, output, 0.02, 30_000.0)`.
verdict.corrected_claim: Seeds are rounded to four absolute decimals, which does match the panel's four-decimal torque display. Both the display and the seed therefore lose relative precision on small torques, and turning a derived torque of order 1e-4 N·m into a given one shifts it by up to tens of percent.
verdict.proposal_note: Change the seed and the display together, or 'what they saw' stops holding. Put one `seed()` helper in Rust that rounds to N significant figures and use it at all three sites. Have the panel show torques to the same significant figures (a formatting choice, which is allowed in TS). Alternatively, seed the unrounded value. That removes the jump entirely, but only at the cost of the documented copy-what-you-saw intent, which is an owner call.

title: Two thresholds for one question, whether a mesh carries power (1e-12 in flow, 1e-9 in groupings)
claim: The flow treats a mesh's power as zero when it is at most `ZERO·P_in` (1e-12). The groupings call a mesh idle when its normalised power is below 1e-9. A mesh carrying between 1e-12 and 1e-9 of input is non-idle to the flow and idle to the grouping. The flow's pivot threshold (flow.rs:366, `*v > 1e-12`) is absolute and ignores both ZERO and scale, while the consistency check two dozen lines below it is relative (`1e-9 * scale`).
evidence: flow.rs:172 `const ZERO: f64 = 1e-12;`. flow.rs:366 `.filter(|(_, v)| *v > 1e-12)`. flow.rs:395 `> 1e-9 * scale`. groupings.rs:242 `p.is_some_and(|p| p < 1e-9)`, where p is mesh_powers, already divided by p_in (flow.rs:333).
proposal: Export one `pub(crate) const IDLE: f64` from flow.rs, justified by the round-off of the rowspace solve (about m·ε·cond). Use it in groupings. Scale the pivot threshold by the column's largest entry (a relative pivot).
validation: A law: every mesh groupings calls idle has |mesh_power| ≤ IDLE and is a branch in flow's assignment. Sweep all presets and arrangements.
