verdict.reason: The literals are as quoted: ZERO = 1e-12 relative to input power (flow.rs:172, used at 300/313/323), the absolute pivot filter `*v > 1e-12` (366), the residual check `1e-9 * scale` (395), and groupings' `idle = p < 1e-9` on mesh_powers normalised by p_in (groupings.rs:242, flow.rs:333). They are not quite 'two thresholds for one question'. The flow never classifies a mesh as idle. Its ZERO decides whether an assumed direction is vacuously consistent and whether a body's power counts as in or out, while the groupings decide how to display a mesh. What is true is that both mean 'this power is round-off', both are unexplained literals, and they differ by three orders of magnitude. No preset was shown where they disagree, and in exact arithmetic an idle branch carries exactly 0 power, so the gap only matters in the round-off regime. The pivot filter is absolute, but the matrix entries are tooth counts and efficiencies of order 1-100 in every shape, so it cannot bite in practice.
verdict.evidence: flow.rs:172 `const ZERO: f64 = 1e-12;` with doc 'relative to the powers in play'; flow.rs:298-301 consistency `p.abs() <= ZERO * input_power || p > 0.0`; flow.rs:366 `.filter(|(_, v)| *v > 1e-12)`; flow.rs:395 `> 1e-9 * scale`; groupings.rs:242 `let idle = |p: Option<f64>| p.is_some_and(|p| p < 1e-9);`.
verdict.corrected_claim: flow.rs and groupings.rs each hard-code their own round-off tolerance for 'this power is nought' (1e-12·P_in versus 1e-9·P_in), with no shared constant or stated derivation. The flow's pivot filter is an absolute 1e-12 while its residual check is relative. No observable disagreement has been demonstrated.
verdict.proposal_note: Export ZERO from flow.rs as `pub(crate)` and use it in groupings. The two are on the same scale, since mesh_powers is already divided by p_in. Make the pivot test relative to the column's largest entry. A law that 'every mesh the groupings call idle has |power| ≤ ZERO·P_in' is cheap to add over the presets.

title: The shift-floor check in auto.rs uses 1e-12 and skips compat::SAME_SHIFT (1e-9), which Tooth::undercut uses
claim: member_is_buildable's comment says the numeric test and the form's `undercut` flag are 'that one question asked twice'. They use different slack: `x >= f - 1e-12` against `undercut = x < x_min - SAME_SHIFT (1e-9)`. For a shift in (f − 1e-9, f − 1e-12) the tooth reports no undercut and member_is_buildable rejects it. params::compat was written to end exactly this kind of divergence.
evidence: auto.rs:1021 `profile_shift >= f - 1e-12 && !tooth.undercut`. auto.rs:1507 `x[i] < f - 1e-12`. tooth.rs:481 `let undercut = x < x_min - compat::SAME_SHIFT;`. params.rs:304 `SAME_SHIFT = SAME_RACK` (1e-9). mod.rs:1255 has another 1e-12 slack, on the addendum clamp.
proposal: Replace both 1e-12 values in auto.rs with compat::SAME_SHIFT. Add a `compat::SAME_LENGTH_MODULES` for the addendum clamp, or reuse SAME_RACK.
validation: A test at x = f − 5e-10: tooth.undercut is false and member_is_buildable is true.

verdict.reason: The slack mismatch is real. member_is_buildable tests `profile_shift >= f - 1e-12 && !tooth.undercut`, and Tooth::new sets `undercut = x < x_min - compat::SAME_SHIFT` with SAME_SHIFT = SAME_RACK = 1e-9. Where floor == x_min, a shift in (x_min - 1e-9, x_min - 1e-12) has no undercut flag but is still rejected. That happens for Decided::Absorbed, and for Decided::Chosen when x_min > 0 (pair.rs:37 and 49: the floor is max(x_min, 0)). It can only be reached through rounding, for example an absorbed shift that closes a set's distances landing a few ulps under x_min, so the consequence is small. Still, params::compat exists precisely so that the flag and its numeric counterpart use one slack. The doc comment's 'that one question asked twice' is also only true when floor == x_min. When the floor is max(x_min, 0) > x_min, the numeric test asks a stricter question than the form's flag. mod.rs:1255 `used < asked - 1e-12` is a different question: a report flag on the addendum clamp.
verdict.evidence: auto.rs:1020-1021 `floor.is_none_or(|f| tooth.params.profile_shift >= f - 1e-12 && !tooth.undercut)`; auto.rs:1507 `x[i] < f - 1e-12`; tooth.rs:481 `let undercut = x < x_min - compat::SAME_SHIFT;`; params.rs:304 `pub const SAME_SHIFT: f64 = SAME_RACK;`; train/pair.rs:37,49 the floor is `max(x_min, 0)` for a chooser.
verdict.proposal_note: Use compat::SAME_SHIFT in both auto.rs sites; the pre-filter at 1507 has to match the check it anticipates. Reword member_is_buildable's comment: the two tests coincide only when the floor is x_min, and the numeric one is the chooser's stricter max(x_min, 0) otherwise. Leave mod.rs:1255 alone, or give it SAME_RACK only for uniformity; it is a separate report flag.

title: The pointed-tooth radius is solved twice, with its own bracket constant, though it is the inverse involute
claim: The pointed tooth is `ψ_b = u − atan u`, that is `inv(atan u) = ψ_b`, so `u = tan(inv_inverse(ψ_b))`. Tooth::new solves it with newton_bracketed on [0, POINTED_TOOTH_MAX_ROLL = 50]. addendum_for_tip_width solves the same equation again with brent on the same bracket. involute::inv_inverse already provides a seeded, safeguarded inverse for exactly this. The constant 50 exists only to bracket the duplicate solves.
evidence: tooth.rs:456 `newton_bracketed(|u| psi_b - inv_from_roll(u), ..., 0.0, POINTED_TOOTH_MAX_ROLL, (3.0 * psi_b).cbrt(), ...)`. auto.rs:744 `brent(|u| g.psi_b - inv_from_roll(u), 0.0, POINTED_TOOTH_MAX_ROLL, ...)`. involute.rs:20 `inv_from_roll(u) = u - u.atan()`.
proposal: Add `Tooth::pointed_roll(&self) -> Option<f64> { inv_inverse(self.psi_b).map(f64::tan) }`, or store `u_point` on the Tooth once. Use it at both sites and delete POINTED_TOOTH_MAX_ROLL.
validation: Golden corpus unchanged to the recorded digits. The existing tip-cap and tip-width tests pass.

verdict.reason: This holds as stated. Tooth::new solves `psi_b = u - atan u` with newton_bracketed on [0, 50], and addendum_for_tip_width solves the same equation again with brent on the same bracket. It uses the same g.psi_b, and the root is never stored on the Tooth, which is why the second solve is needed. Since inv_from_roll(u) = inv(atan u), the root is tan(inv_inverse(psi_b)), and inv_inverse already provides the seeded, safeguarded solve. POINTED_TOOTH_MAX_ROLL is used only at these two sites (grep: tooth.rs:460, auto.rs:747, definition tooth.rs:944). The swap cannot change results: inv_inverse returns None for psi_b < 0, just as a bracket with no sign change does. The cap at 50 only mattered for psi_b > 50 - atan 50 ≈ 48.4 rad, which is impossible for a half-tooth angle.
verdict.evidence: tooth.rs:455-462 `newton_bracketed(|u| psi_b - inv_from_roll(u), ..., 0.0, POINTED_TOOTH_MAX_ROLL, (3.0 * psi_b).cbrt(), ...)`; auto.rs:744-749 `brent(|u| g.psi_b - inv_from_roll(u), 0.0, POINTED_TOOTH_MAX_ROLL, Tol::default())?`; involute.rs:20 `u - u.atan()`, involute.rs:50 inv_inverse on [0, π/2 - 1e-12].
verdict.proposal_note: The simplest version stores `u_point: Option<f64>` on Tooth once, taken from `inv_inverse(psi_b).map(f64::tan)`, and reads it in addendum_for_tip_width. That removes one solve per candidate in searches and removes the constant. Check that the golden corpus is unchanged to its recorded digits; the root may move by ulps.

title: Eleven hand-written bracket-growing and bisection loops, five growth factors, six caps
claim: solve.rs says two bracketed solvers handle every transcendental step. Before those solvers, the crate hand-writes a bracket search again at each site: growth ×1.6 or ×1.4 (tooth), ×1.4 (ring), ×2 (metrology, hertz, auto, shape, pull_in), ×1.5 with NaN halving (shape); caps of 200, 64, 16, 60, 40 and 80. The predicate bisection is written three times (64, 64 and 60 halvings). Every cap is tolerated by feel, and each site carries its own failure handling: auto.rs silently returns x0 when no bracket is found.
evidence: tooth.rs:50-65 (`BASE_CROSS_GROWTH 1.6`, `CROSSING_GROWTH 1.4`, `MAX_STEPS 200`). ring.rs:548 `far *= 1.4` in `for _ in 0..64`. metrology.rs:193-195 `hi *= 2.0; if steps > 64`. gear.rs:1119 `for _ in 0..64`. verify.rs:726 `for _ in 0..60`. auto.rs:165 `MINIMUM_SHIFT_BRACKET_STEPS = 16`, auto.rs:152 `.unwrap_or(x0)`. shape.rs:946 `for _ in 0..60 { top *= 2.0 }`, 1645 `for _ in 0..40`, 1667 `for _ in 0..80`, 1661/1687 `step *= 1.5`.
proposal: Add two helpers to solve.rs: `expand_bracket(f, from, first_step, growth) -> Option<(f64,f64)>`, which grows geometrically until the sign changes or the bracket stops being finite, capped by the exponent range (about 2100 doublings) rather than a chosen count; and `bisect_by(pred, lo, hi) -> f64`, run to adjacent floats with `while hi - lo > ulp` instead of a fixed 60/64. Migrate site by site. Each migration is behaviour-preserving wherever the old cap was not binding.
validation: Golden corpus unchanged. A unit test that expand_bracket finds a root at 1e-300 and at 1e+300 scales. The existing tests of each site.

verdict.reason: The loops exist as cited, with the factors and caps quoted, and a shared `expand_bracket` and `bisect_by` in solve.rs would be a reasonable consolidation. But 'every cap is tolerated by feel' overstates it. hertz.rs:418 grows until `f64::MIN_POSITIVE.ln()/2`, a floor taken from the type. shape.rs:1645 stops at a geometric reach (`mt·|z_sum|`), and a NaN halving policy is part of its logic. gear.rs:1119's 64 halvings are documented as running to the representable limit. The auto.rs `.unwrap_or(x0)` fallback is silent, as claimed, but with 16 doublings of a module (±65,536 modules) against an admissible range a few modules wide, it cannot be reached in practice. The proposal's cap of about 2100 doublings from the exponent range also removes the cap's second job: bounding the cost of a failing search whose predicate builds a tooth or re-solves room_at over a train.
verdict.evidence: tooth.rs:50-66 BASE_CROSS_GROWTH 1.6, CROSSING_GROWTH 1.4, MAX_STEPS 200; ring.rs:543-549 `for _ in 0..64 { ... far *= 1.4 }`; metrology.rs:191-205 doubling capped at 64 then a 64-step bisection; gear.rs:1119 64 halvings; hertz.rs:417-425 type-derived floor; auto.rs:139-147,165 MINIMUM_SHIFT_BRACKET_STEPS = 16 with `.unwrap_or(x0)`; shape.rs:946 `for _ in 0..60 { top *= 2.0 }`, shape.rs:1645/1667 40/80 steps with `step *= 1.5` and NaN halving; verify.rs:726 60 halvings.
verdict.corrected_claim: About ten sites hand-write bracket growth or predicate bisection, with site-specific growth factors and iteration caps. Several caps are unexplained (tooth 200, ring 64, metrology 64, shape 60/40/80, auto 16). Others have a stated basis (hertz's type-derived floor, shape's geometric reach). A shared bracket-expansion and bisection helper in solve.rs would remove most of the literals.
verdict.proposal_note: Keep a per-call evaluation budget in the helper. Do not rely only on the exponent range, since the predicates are expensive and the budget is what bounds a failing search. The helper must support a NaN-means-step-back policy, or shape.rs's walks cannot migrate. In auto.rs, a failed bracket should return None or a note instead of x0, or be shown to be unreachable and turned into an expect with that argument.

title: The N·m to N·mm factor is written inline as 1000 or 2000 at four sites
claim: The torque-to-force conversion (torque in N·m, radii in mm) is written as a bare 1000.0 or 2000.0. check_units polices angle units but not this one.
evidence: strength.rs:1267 `1000.0 * self.torque / g.r`. contact.rs:763 `1000.0 * torque / arm.abs()`. screw.rs:527 `2000.0 * torque / self.worm_pitch_diameter`.
proposal: Add `pub const MM_PER_M: f64 = 1000.0;` in one module, for example plane.rs or a new units.rs. Write the screw case as `2.0 * MM_PER_M * torque / d`.
validation: A grep gate in check_units.py for `1000.0 \* .*torque`. Golden corpus unchanged.

verdict.reason: The factor is real and written inline, but the count is wrong and one of the sites already explains itself. It appears at five production sites, not four: strength.rs:1267 and :1279, contact.rs:763, and screw.rs:527 and :528. It also appears in a test at screw.rs:1624. strength.rs:1262-1263 already documents it: 'The 1000 converts N·m to N·mm, because every length in this crate is millimetres.' contact.rs and screw.rs do not. It is a unit conversion, not a tolerance chosen by feel, so this is naming hygiene rather than a risk to correctness.
verdict.corrected_claim: The N·m to N·mm conversion is written as a bare 1000.0 or 2000.0 at five production sites (strength.rs:1267 and 1279, contact.rs:763, screw.rs:527 and 528). Only strength.rs's doc comment explains it.
verdict.evidence: A grep over gear-core for 1000.0 and 2000.0 found the five sites above. Every other hit is a test LoadCase speed (1000 rpm) or a runtime_hours value. strength.rs:1262 reads '`F_t = 2000 T / d = 1000 T / r`. The 1000 converts N·m to N·mm'.
verdict.proposal_note: A better fix than a constant plus a grep gate is one function, e.g. `plane::force_from_torque(torque_nm, arm_mm) -> f64 { 1e3 * torque_nm / arm_mm }`, called by all five sites. The screw sites would pass d/2. The conversion then lives in one place and the grep gate is unnecessary. A related inline unit factor sits at train/mod.rs:4539: `speeds[s] * 60.0 * runtime_hours` (min/h).

title: Edits refuse fewer than 4 teeth, require a ring 2 teeth larger, and default a sun to 6 teeth: all unexplained, and the 4 does not match the core's floor of 1
claim: The graph's edits refuse a count below 4 (written three times) and a ring less than zp + 2 (written three times), and they size an unconstrained sun at max(zp, 6). No comment gives a reason for any of these. admissible_ranges gives teeth ≥ 1, so a gear the panel accepts when typed is refused when it is added. central_teeth also measures the carrier radius and the fit in normal modules, which is consistent only while every gear on the planet axis has the same helix.
evidence: edits.rs:417 `if f - f64::from(zp) < 4.0 => return Err(EditRefused::NoRoom)`. edits.rs:419 `f64::from(zp.max(6))`. edits.rs:429 `if ring { f64::from(zp) + 2.0 } else { 4.0 }`. edits.rs:491 `if z < 4.0 || (ring && z < zm + 2.0)`. auto.rs:697 `teeth: Bound::between(Some(1.0), None)`.
proposal: Name `MIN_ADDED_TEETH` and `MIN_RING_DIFFERENCE`, each with its argument (for the ring margin, what fails at a difference of 1: planocentric sets run at 1–3 with shift, so say why 2). Derive or cite 6. Better, take the floor from admissible_ranges, or from minimum_profile_shift's feasibility, so the edit and the panel give the same answer.
validation: An edit law: every count the edit refuses as NoRoom is also outside admissible_ranges or fails to solve.

verdict.reason: The claim holds, and a probe makes it stronger. The floor of 4 is not the core's floor (admissible teeth ≥ 1), and it is not the solve's floor either: 2- and 3-tooth pinions solve against some mates. The zp+2 ring floor has no stated argument. Its own neighbouring comment (edits.rs:421-428) says a ring one tooth too large at a planocentric's carrier radius has nowhere to close, yet the floor forces exactly that at Δz = 1. The helix side-claim is also accurate. carrier_radius (edits.rs:293-308) computes (zc±zp)·m_n,c/2 and central_teeth divides by the mate's m_n, but the true radius uses transverse modules. The fit is exact only when the mate's helix equals the helix of the (p, c) mesh it reads.
verdict.evidence: Probe probes/verify-lens-magic-numbers-3 (Train::alone plus solve_train): pair 2/3, 2/4, 3/3, 3/4, 3/6, 2/100, 3/100, 2/400 and 3/400 all solve; 2/6, 2/10, 3/10 and 3/30 give NoContact. So 4 is not the solve's minimum, which depends on the mate. edits.rs:417 `(false, Some(f)) if f - f64::from(zp) < 4.0 => return Err(EditRefused::NoRoom)`, :419 `zp.max(6)`, :429 `if ring { f64::from(zp) + 2.0 } else { 4.0 }`, :491 `if z < 4.0 || (ring && z < zm + 2.0)`, auto.rs:697 `teeth: Bound::between(Some(1.0), None)`. On the ring floor: planocentric(18,19) with AddGear{mate:0, on:NewBody(0), ring:true} is accepted and adds a 20-tooth ring, then the train fails with InPart{cause: NoCommonDistance}. The shape solves Δz = 1 rings elsewhere (the hula 17/18, and the test a_four_tooth_planocentric_is_sized_by_its_tips).
verdict.proposal_note: The law proposed in validation would currently fail in both directions. The edit refuses counts that solve (3 against a large mate), and it accepts a ring that does not solve (the Δz = 1 case). A better rule: size the central from the fit and let the solve decide, with preview.rs's dry run reporting why the edited train does not solve. Refuse NoRoom only where the fit gives no count ≥ 1 of the right kind. If floors are kept, derive them. For a sun, use the smallest count that has contact against the mate at its automatic shift. For a ring, use the fit itself, never max(fit, zp+2).

title: The lean past the tip-clearance root is 1e-9 mm absolute, not 'the solver's own tolerance' as its comment says
claim: The comment says the root is leaned toward the clear side 'by the solver's own tolerance'. Brent's tolerance is 2ε|x| + 5e-16, about 4e-14 at 100 mm. The lean is a fixed 1e-9 mm, about 25,000 times larger at 100 mm, and a different claim again at 1 mm and at 1 m.
evidence: shape.rs:1700 `hi.min(e + 1e-9)`. solve.rs:87 `tol1 = 2.0 * f64::EPSILON * b.abs() + 0.5 * tol.x_tol` with x_tol = 1e-15.
proposal: Lean by the solver's actual tolerance, `4.0 * f64::EPSILON * e.abs() + Tol::default().x_tol` (or step to the next representable value until `room_at >= 0`). Or keep 1e-9 as a named, relative `1e-9 * e.abs()` and correct the comment.
validation: A test that `room_at(e) >= 0` after the lean, at distances of 1 mm and 1,000 mm.

verdict.reason: The comment says 'by the solver's own tolerance', but the code leans by a fixed absolute 1e-9 mm. Brent's termination half-width is 2ε|b| + 0.5·x_tol, about 4.5e-14 mm at 100 mm, so the lean is some 2e4 times the tolerance. The literal also disagrees in kind with its neighbours in the same function, which scale relatively: shape.rs:1677 `1e-12 * from.abs().max(1.0)` and :955 `floor * (1.0 + 1e-9)`. Physically 1e-9 mm is negligible, so this is doc accuracy and a magic number, not a wrong answer. An absolute lean only fails to move e above about 1e7 mm, where 1e-9 falls below one ulp, which is unrealistic.
verdict.evidence: shape.rs:1697-1701: '// Lean to the clear side of the root by the solver's own tolerance' followed by `hi.min(e + 1e-9)`. solve.rs:87 `let tol1 = 2.0 * f64::EPSILON * b.abs() + 0.5 * tol.x_tol;` and solve.rs:38 `x_tol: 1e-15`.
verdict.proposal_note: The cleanest fix removes the constant. Brent keeps a bracket [b, c] with f(b) and f(c) of opposite sign, so a variant that returns the endpoint on a requested side (e.g. `brent_side(f, lo, hi, tol, want_nonneg)`) gives a root with room ≥ 0 by construction, with no lean and no literal. Failing that, step with f64::next_up until room_at(e) ≥ 0, bounded by hi.

title: Shape bracket fallbacks: ±5 modules of shift when the admissible range is open, and 89° as the top of the helix bracket
claim: When no mesh bounds a shift and admissible_ranges returns an open side, the search bracket falls back to ±5 modules. That figure has no source and does not appear in admissible_ranges. When a straight-tooth distance must grow with the helix, the brent bracket's top is 89°, though the comment says the distance grows 'without bound below ninety'. A target that needs more than 89° gets None with no explanation.
evidence: shape.rs:1479 `lo = lo.max(range.min.unwrap_or(-5.0));`. shape.rs:863 `crate::solve::brent(|b| at(b) - target, 0.0, 89.0, ...)`.
proposal: For the shift, use the same bound the undercut and pointed-tip limits give: admissible_ranges should always close both sides, or return None so the search does not start. For the helix, run the expanding-bracket helper toward 90° (for example 90 − 2^-k), or name `MAX_SEARCH_HELIX_DEG` and raise a note when it binds.
validation: A test with a target distance reachable only above 89° (large z, small module) that either solves or reports the named limit.

verdict.reason: Half of this is wrong. The ±5-module shift fallback is unreachable: admissible_profile_shift always returns `Bound::between(Some(min), Some(max))` (auto.rs:371), so `range.min.unwrap_or(-5.0)` and `range.max.unwrap_or(5.0)` never take their defaults. That makes the ±5 dead code, not a live magic number, and the proposal to make admissible_ranges close both sides is already true. The 89° bracket top is confirmed. A straight-tooth target needing more than 89° (target over reference distance above 1/cos 89° ≈ 57.3) fails with a misleading NoContact error rather than naming the limit, contradicting the comment's 'without bound below ninety degrees'. In practice no designer asks for a helix near 89°.
verdict.corrected_claim: The ±5 shift fallback at shape.rs:1479-1480 is dead, because admissible_profile_shift always closes both sides. It should be removed or made unrepresentable (ShiftRange::bound as a closed pair), not given a source. The 89° top of the helix bracket at shape.rs:863 is real. A given running distance more than about 57.3 times the straight-tooth reference distance fails as InPart{cause: NoContact}, with no note naming the helix limit.
verdict.evidence: auto.rs:371 `bound: Bound::between(Some(min), Some(max))`, with min and max computed unconditionally at auto.rs:344-345. Probe: pair(20,40), m = 1, shifts fixed at 0, clearance fixed at 0, distance fixed at 30·k. k = 1, 1.2, 3, 20, 50 and 57 all solve (the helix is sized). k = 58 and k = 70 give `InPart { part: 0, cause: NoContact }`, and 1/cos 89° = 57.29.
verdict.proposal_note: For the shift, delete the fallback: if Bound stays optional there, use `if let (Some(a), Some(b))`, or change ShiftRange::bound to a closed interval. For the helix, when brent returns None because at(89) < target, raise a note or error naming the helix bound instead of letting NoContact surface later. An expanding bracket toward 90° buys little, because the tooth is meaningless there.

title: The worm wheel's face-width cap is attributed to the wrong source
claim: The comment calls b₂ = 2m√(q+1) 'capped at 0.67 d₁' 'two statements from the same source' (BS 721). RoyMech gives the 2m√(q+1) under BS 721 and the '≤ 0.67 d₁' under its AGMA section. MITcalc/ČSN states the cap as 0.75·d_a1 for z₁ < 4 and 0.67·d_a1 for z₁ ≥ 4, which is on the tip diameter and not d₁. The worm length (11 + 0.06 or 0.09 z₂)·m_x does match MITcalc.
evidence: WebFetch of roymech.org/Useful_Tables/Drive/Worm_Gears: 'About 2.m √(q+1)' and, in the AGMA section, 'not to exceed 0,67 . d 1'. MITcalc search result: '[z1<4] b2=0.75·(1+2/q)·d1, [z1>=4] b2=0.67·(1+2/q)·d1'. crossed.rs:135 `recommended.min(0.67 * worm_pitch_diameter)`.
proposal: Correct the attribution to BS 721 for the width and AGMA for the cap. Or, if ČSN is meant to be followed as it is for the length, use 0.75/0.67·d_a1 by number of starts and say so.
validation: Recompute the worm preset's wheel face width under both readings and record it in the golden corpus.

verdict.reason: The misattribution is confirmed from both sources, and it reaches the screen. RoyMech lists 'About 2.m √(q+1)' as BS 721's effective face width, and '0,67 . d1' under its AGMA section as a cap on the effective width used for rating. MITcalc gives the ČSN width as b2 = 0.75(1+2/q)d1 for z1 < 4 and 0.67(1+2/q)d1 for z1 ≥ 4. Since (1+2/q)·d1 = d1 + 2m_x = d_a1, those are 0.75 or 0.67 times the tip diameter, and they are a recommended width, not a cap. The same wrong attribution sits in docs/reference.md:1076 and in the UI note strings_en.toml:385 ('per BS 721 convention', and presumably its four translations), so it is shown on screen. Also, the worm length is attributed to 'DIN/ČSN practice' (crossed.rs:105, reference.md:1075), but MITcalc gives (11 + c·z2)·m_x as ČSN only. For DIN it gives a geometric chord, L = √((de2/2)² − (a − da1/2)²).
verdict.evidence: WebFetch of roymech.org/Useful_Tables/Drive/Worm_Gears: BS 721 section 'b a = Effective face width of worm wheel. About 2.m √ (q +1)'; AGMA section 'b a = Effective face width of gearwheel = actual face width. but not to exceed 0,67 . d 1'. WebFetch of mitcalc.com/doc/gear4/help/en/gear4.htm: ČSN 'b2=0.75 • (1 + 2 / q) • d1' (z1<4), 'b2=0.67 • (1 + 2 / q) • d1' (z1≥4); DIN 'L=((de2 / 2)^2 -(a - da1 / 2)^2)^0.5' and 'b2<=b2max=2*((dm1/2)^2-(a-de2/2)^2)^0.5'. crossed.rs:122-135 and docs/reference.md:1076.
verdict.proposal_note: Fix the attribution in all three places (crossed.rs:121-130, reference.md:1075-1076, strings_*.toml train_note_wheel_width ×5): the width to BS 721, the cap to AGMA (as the effective-width limit for rating), the length to ČSN. Beyond that, the DIN forms MITcalc quotes are closed-form geometric chords of the wheel tip circle against the worm tip. They would replace two tabulated rules of thumb with geometry the crate already has (a, d_a1, d_e2), in line with the project's closed-form goal. That would also partly answer the 'does not derive that zone' residual.

title: train_kinematics.py and hula_kinematics.py never read the crate; 5 of 6 'independent verification' scripts cannot fail on a crate defect
claim: CLAUDE.md lists the six scripts as 'the crate against derivations that share no code with it'. train_kinematics.py compares its rigid-body rows against `crate_rows()`, a Python re-transcription of `z_a(w_a−w_f)+z_b(w_b−w_f)=0`, and never runs gear-cli or reads a corpus file. hula_kinematics.py compares its integration against its own `closed()` ("R = z2 z4 / D -- what the crate reports"), again without reading the crate. iso_6336_3_stack.py asserts what the tool applies ('applies neither f_ε nor Y_β', 'the crate uses z/cos³β') without reading it. crossed_path.py and worm_flank_curvature.py print for comparison by eye. Only breakaway.py reads crate output (tools/golden/graph.txt). A sign or frame error in kinematics.rs therefore leaves train_kinematics.py green, which is exactly the fault its docstring says it exists to catch. corrections.md:656 says `train_kinematics.py` 'holds that no figure moved', which it cannot do.
evidence: `grep -n 'subprocess|golden|CORPUS|open(' tools/{train,hula}_kinematics.py` finds nothing. The only imports are sys, math and fractions. Ran all six scripts in `nix develop`: each exits 0 in about 3.0–3.7 s wall time, most of it nix develop start-up. corrections.md:405 measures that the check fails on a 'flipped tangent or a mis-framed row', but that mutates the Python and not the crate. The golden corpus already has the numbers these scripts could read: tools/golden/kinematics.txt prints each path's ratio and each slot's speed per case, and tools/golden/hula_18_0.2.txt prints `ratio 324 / 1`.
proposal:
Follow breakaway.py's pattern and parse committed corpus output rather than a transcription:
- train_kinematics.py: for each topology it builds, read the matching section of tools/golden/kinematics.txt (or run `gear-cli kinematics`) and compare every slot speed and the path ratio against the rigid-body solve. Keep `crate_rows()` only as a secondary check, or delete it.
- hula_kinematics.py: compare the integration against the ratio `gear-cli hula` prints for each arrangement. A `gear-cli hula --counts a/b/c/d` form may be needed.
- iso_6336_3_stack.py: read Y_β, f_ε and z_n usage off `gear-cli strength` output, or say plainly in the docstring that it is an analysis and not a check, and move it out of CLAUDE.md's verification row.
Then add all six to CI as one step: `nix develop -c bash -c 'for s in ...; do python3 tools/$s.py || exit 1; done'`, about 20 s.
validation: In a worktree, flip the sign in kinematics.rs's mesh row, or swap the frame coefficient, and run `gear-cli kinematics > tools/golden/kinematics.txt`. The rewritten train_kinematics.py must fail; today it passes by construction.

verdict.reason: Holds for the two scripts that present themselves as checks on the crate. It is overstated for the other three, which say openly that they are compared with the crate by hand, and CLAUDE.md's CI column already marks the whole row 'no — by hand'. train_kinematics.py compares its rigid-body rows only against crate_rows(), which is a Python copy of the kinematics.rs formula. So a sign or frame error written into kinematics.rs itself cannot fail it, and that kind of error is exactly what its docstring says it exists to catch. hula_kinematics.py compares its integration against closed(), which is labelled 'what the crate reports' and is also a Python copy. corrections.md:656 says the script 'and the corpus hold that no figure moved', but only the corpus can do that. The crate's kinematics is not left unguarded: shape laws test it against Pennestri/Willis closed forms, and the golden corpus records the ratios. That is why the severity is medium rather than high.
verdict.evidence: The only imports in tools/train_kinematics.py are sys and fractions (lines 69-70). In tools/hula_kinematics.py they are math, sys and fractions (28-30). Neither script calls subprocess, opens a file or reads the golden corpus. crate_rows() at train_kinematics.py:303 re-writes z_a(w_a-w_f)+z_b(w_b-w_f)=0. hula_kinematics.py:55 is closed(z) with the docstring 'R = z2 z4 / D -- what the crate reports'. The other three say it themselves: iso_6336_3_stack.py:24-25 'The crate's own figures come from `gear-cli strength`, and the two are compared by hand', crossed_path.py:13 'the crate is never consulted' and :381 points the reader to `gear-cli crossed 17 23 90`, and worm_flank_curvature.py builds its own surface. breakaway.py:43 reads tools/golden/graph.txt. The numbers the scripts could read are already in the corpus: tools/golden/kinematics.txt prints 'path b1 -> b2 ratio -2.529412' and 'total ratio -43/17'.
verdict.proposal_note: Parsing tools/golden/kinematics.txt and hula_18_0.2.txt (or crossed_17_23_90.txt for crossed_path's contact ratio) follows breakaway.py's pattern and is the right fix. Adding the scripts to CI only helps once each one asserts against crate output: crossed_path and worm_flank_curvature have nothing to fail on today apart from their internal self-checks. The simplest honest fix for iso_6336_3_stack.py is to call it an analysis rather than a verification. Also correct corrections.md:656 so it credits the corpus alone.
verdict.corrected_claim: train_kinematics.py and hula_kinematics.py compare their independent derivations against Python copies of the crate's formulae, never against crate output, so a defect written into kinematics.rs leaves them green. That contradicts their docstrings and corrections.md:656. iso_6336_3_stack.py, crossed_path.py and worm_flank_curvature.py say openly that the comparison is by hand, which CLAUDE.md's CI column also records. The claim holds for them only in that the row heading 'the crate against derivations' overstates what they do.

title: check_figures matches a bag of numbers: swapped rows and swapped pinion/wheel figures pass
claim: Each documented number only has to appear somewhere in the union of the tagged commands' output, at the document's precision. A figure attributed to the wrong row, the wrong member or the wrong command is not detected, and neither is any figure that happens to equal another printed value. In practice the gate checks that a number exists, not that the document says what it means.
evidence:
Worktree runs of tools/check_figures.py:
- F1, 97.678→97.679: exit 1 (caught).
- F2, swapping 97.561 (9/37) and 98.345 (17/43) between rows at reference.md:640-641: exit 0.
- F4, canary `σ_F 66.8 / 56.0` → `56.0 / 66.8` at state.md:201: exit 0.
- F6, prose 98.488→98.489: exit 1.
A ±1-last-digit perturbation of each documented figure also finds 2 of 50 strong and 18 of 47 weak figures still matched by some other output value (notes/tools-ci/figstrength.py), e.g. reference.md:638 `1.4626` and reference.md:2021 `99.982`. Only 8 blocks and 98 figures are command-gated; `--list` reports 63 paragraphs of strong figures ungated.
proposal: Require each table row's strong figures (≥2 decimals) to appear as an ordered subsequence of one tagged command's number stream. A prototype (notes/tools-ci/rowcheck2.py) passes 15 of the 17 currently gated rows. The two exceptions are the reference.md:640-641 rows, whose columns are in a different order from the output; reorder those columns to match `gear-cli shifts`, or give the marker an explicit `unordered` flag with a reason. Keep the bag rule only for prose blocks. Also drop the dead `if text.strip() and text.strip() in output: pass` branch (check_figures.py:399-402).
validation: Rerun mutations F2 and F4 with the new rule and both must fail. F0 must stay green after the two rows are reordered. Add these mutations as a self-test: a small fixture .md plus a fake command output, run by the script under `--self-test` in CI.

verdict.reason: The code works exactly as described. The outputs of all tagged commands are joined into one string, and each documented number only has to equal, at the document's precision, some number anywhere in that string. The docstring admits that low-precision figures are only weakly pinned. It does not admit that a figure can sit in the wrong row, column or member and still pass. This gate is a canary for doc drift rather than a gate on correctness, so medium fits better than high.
verdict.evidence: check_figures.py:425 builds `output = "\n".join(run(c, cache) for c in commands)`. :433 builds `have = numbers(output)`. :441 tests `any(at(v, decimals) == want for v, _, _ in have)`. The block at reference.md:634-635 is tagged with both `gear-cli shifts 9 37` and `shifts 17 43`. I ran the harness: '97.561 %' appears only in the 9/37 output and '98.345 %' only in the 17/43 output, so the auditor's row swap F2 passes. At state.md:201, '66.8 / 56.0' → '56.0 / 66.8' passes on the same logic. Lines 399-402, `if text.strip() and text.strip() in output: pass`, are dead code as claimed.
verdict.proposal_note: Use an ordered-subsequence match per table row against one command's number stream. The two shift rows need their columns reordered: the output order is Σx, …, ε, η, while the document puts η first. Alternatively allow an explicit per-block 'unordered' flag. The self-test fixture is worth adding, because this project records gates that could not fail.

title: `figures-by-test` blocks can drift from their test: the gate only checks that the name exists
claim: 9 blocks are 'gated by a named test', but the named tests hold their own literal copy of the table (`(12_u32, 144.0, 98.85, 37.9), ...`) and never read the document. check_figures only checks that `fn name(` appears in some .rs file, so an edit to the document's table goes unnoticed. The docstring calls this 'a different gate'. It gates code against the test's literal, not the document against the code.
evidence: Mutation F3 changed reference.md's `| 144 | 98.85 % | 37.9 % |` to `39.9 %`, and tools/check_figures.py exited 0. The test at arrangements.rs:1399 hard-codes `37.9`. TESTS.search() at check_figures.py:147 is a plain substring search over all crate text, so a comment containing `fn name(` would satisfy it too.
proposal: Have each by-test test read its table from the document: `include_str!("../../../../docs/reference.md")`, find the block after its marker and parse the rows. flake.nix's srcFor must then keep docs/*.md for the nix test sandbox; add `|| builtins.match ".*/docs/[^/]*\\.md$" path != null`. Alternatively, have the test print the table and gate it as `figures-verbatim`, removing the duplicate literal either way. At minimum, check_figures should require `#[test]` directly above `fn name(`.
validation: Mutation F3 must make `cargo nextest run the_documented_tables` fail, and a green run must still pass.

verdict.reason: The named tests hold their own literal tables and never read the document. check_figures only checks that the text `fn <name>(` appears somewhere in the crate. A document edit therefore goes undetected, while a code change is caught against the test's copy. The docstring's words 'a different gate' are true for code against the test, and misleading for the document against the code. The severity is low because this only affects doc-drift detection on 9 blocks.
verdict.evidence: arrangements.rs:1399-1405 hard-codes `(12_u32, 144.0, 98.85, 37.9), (18, 324.0, 99.18, 27.4), ...`, and reference.md:1924-1930 has the same table as a separate copy. check_figures.py:355-363 runs only `TESTS.search(f"fn {name}(")`. There are 8 by-test markers, at reference.md:1158, 1924, 1944, 1965, 2065, 2088 and 2116 and state.md:186.
verdict.proposal_note: Reading docs/reference.md from a gear-core test with include_str! ties the core crate to the docs and requires a change to the nix source filter. A cheaper route with no Rust or nix change: check_figures extracts the body of the named test fn and requires every number in the tagged block to appear, at the document's precision, among the numeric literals in that body. That turns the pointer into a real document-to-test check. The better long-term fix is a harness command that prints the table, gated as `figures:`, so only one copy of the literal exists.

title: check_wasm does not measure the shipped module, and its entry-point grep misses three common export forms
claim: The script says 'the module measured here is the module people download'. It is not. The shipped `.wasm` is built by crane inside the nix sandbox, with vendored paths and store hashes rewritten to `eeee…`, while check_wasm builds its own copy with dev-shell cargo. The coverage claim ('a new entry point cannot arrive untested') depends on `grep -A2 '^#\[wasm_bindgen\]$' | sed 's/^pub fn …'`, which does not see `#[wasm_bindgen(js_name = …)]`, an entry whose `pub fn` is 3 or more lines below the attribute, or `pub async fn`.
evidence: sha256 of `nix build .#wasm`'s gear_wasm_bg.wasm is cb698405… at 1,543,846 bytes. build_wasm.sh in the dev shell gives 76562036… at 1,542,209 bytes, identical for the web and nodejs targets, which does confirm the script's claim that the target only changes the wrapper. `strings` shows panic-location paths `/nix/store/eeee…-vendor-cargo-deps/…/toml-1.1.5` in one and `/home/user/.cargo/registry/src/…` in the other. Appending three such exports to a copy of lib.rs: the grep pipeline still lists 23 and finds 0 of the 3 new ones.
proposal: (a) In CI, probe the shipped artifact. Give check_wasm a `--module <path>` option, run it on `$(nix build .#wasm --print-out-paths)/gear_wasm_bg.wasm` and diff that against the record, keeping the unoptimised-versus-optimised law on the dev build. Better, make the probe a flake check (`checks.wasm = runCommand … node wasm_probe.mjs ${self.packages.wasm}`), so it runs on exactly what ships. (b) Take the export list from the module itself: in wasm_probe.mjs, `Object.keys(await import(glue)).filter(k => typeof m[k] === 'function')`, or read gear_wasm.d.ts. That is what wasm-bindgen actually exported.
validation: Add a `#[wasm_bindgen(js_name=x)]` fn in a worktree and the check must fail. In CI, assert that the module the probe ran has the same sha256 as the one in `result/`.

verdict.reason: The export grep does have the hole described. I reproduced it: `#[wasm_bindgen(js_name = ...)]`, a `pub fn` two or more lines below the attribute, and `pub async fn` are all missed. The 'shipped module' part is overstated. flake.nix runs the same tools/build_wasm.sh, with the same rust-toolchain.toml toolchain (flake.nix:34-40), the same `--profile wasm` and the same wasm-opt flags. By the auditor's own evidence the bytes differ only in embedded panic-location paths, which do not affect computation. What remains is wording: 'the module people download' should read 'a module built by the shipped recipe'.
verdict.evidence: I copied lib.rs and appended a `#[wasm_bindgen(js_name = fooBar)] pub fn foo_bar`, a `#[wasm_bindgen]` with two doc lines before `pub fn baz`, and a `#[wasm_bindgen] pub async fn qux`. The pipeline `grep -A2 '^#\[wasm_bindgen\]$' | sed -n 's/^pub fn .../p'` still lists 23 names and none of the three new ones. The flake's installPhase is `BUILD_WASM_SKIP_CARGO=1 BUILD_WASM_MODULE=... bash tools/build_wasm.sh "$out"` (flake.nix:118-122). I did not rebuild .#wasm to recheck the sha256 values.
verdict.proposal_note: (b) is the valuable part: take the list of exports from the generated glue, `Object.keys(require(glue)).filter(k => typeof m[k] === 'function')`, or from gear_wasm.d.ts. That is the authority and needs no regex. (a), running the probe as a flake check on self.packages.wasm, is sound but optional. Asserting that the sha256 matches the result/ build will not work, because the embedded paths differ by construction.

title: npmDepsHash trap is avoidable: importNpmLock builds a byte-identical site
claim: The documented trap (any package-lock.json change breaks only `nix build .#web`, because a fixed-output hash sits beside the lockfile) is self-inflicted. nixpkgs' `importNpmLock` reads the lockfile's own integrity hashes, so no second hash exists to go stale.
evidence: In the worktree I replaced `npmDepsHash = "sha256-…";` with `npmDeps = pkgs.importNpmLock { npmRoot = ./web; }; npmConfigHook = pkgs.importNpmLock.npmConfigHook;` and ran `nix build .#web`: exit 0 in 19.8 s. `diff -r` against the current site's output /nix/store/r2qk0l2h…-gears-web-0.3.0 reported IDENTICAL. The pinned nixpkgs (26.11) has `importNpmLock`.
proposal: Apply those two lines in flake.nix's webFor, then delete the trap paragraph in docs/state.md:40-45 and the 'fixed-output hash' clause in CLAUDE.md:167.
validation: `nix build .#web` gives the same output as today, byte for byte. Bump one devDependency in package-lock.json without touching flake.nix and the site still builds.

verdict.reason: The trap is avoidable with importNpmLock, as the finding says. The pinned nixpkgs provides it, and every entry in the lockfile carries the integrity and resolved fields that importNpmLock needs. I did not repeat the build to check byte identity (that would mean a nix build under the user's memory caution), so that part rests on the auditor's run, which is plausible because the dependency set is the same. The severity is low: this is CI ergonomics, costing one red build per lockfile change.
verdict.evidence: `nix eval` over the flake's nixpkgs input shows `? importNpmLock` = true, version 26.11.20260629. A Python scan of web/package-lock.json finds 0 non-link packages without integrity+resolved. flake.nix:133 has `npmDepsHash = "sha256-vqmk..."`. The trap paragraph is at docs/state.md:39-45, and CLAUDE.md:167 has the matching clause.
verdict.proposal_note: When deleting the CLAUDE.md clause, keep 'the site — `flake check` does not cover it', because that part stays true. Only the fixed-output-hash half goes. Also update the state.md paragraph rather than deleting it outright, because its first sentence ('nix flake check is not all of what CI runs') still holds.

title: check_doc_links: the promised 'heading with no referrer' report does not exist, and whole classes of dead pointer pass
evidence:
Worktree mutations:
- a) .rs pointer to a missing heading: exit 1 (caught).
- b) `[x](nosuch.md)`: exit 0.
- c) `#worth-doing-next_typo`: exit 0.
- c2) uppercase anchor: exit 0.
- d) `docs/history/audit.md#no-such`: exit 0.
- e) broken pointer in tools/check_units.py: exit 0.
- e2) the same in flake.nix: exit 0.
- f) new heading nothing points at: exit 0.
- h2) a working GitHub `#…-1` link: exit 1 (false positive).
The gate's own docstring examples `docs/rationale.md#the-lewis-parabola` and `#one-hob-one-setting` do not resolve (links_wide.py). The gate prints '83 documentation pointers', which counts distinct pairs; ci.yml:53 says '389 of these', and the docstring says '175 across 32 sections'.
proposal: Implement the claimed reverse check or delete the claim. Match anchors with `#([^)\s`'\"]+)` and compare the whole anchor. Check file existence for every `(…\.md)` link and every `docs/…\.md` mention, including history/. Scan `git ls-files` rather than hand-picked globs, excluding web/src/wire. Skip fenced lines in anchors(). Give duplicate headings GitHub's `-1`, `-2` suffixes. Report both occurrences and distinct pointers. Share one SOURCES function with check_strings.py (both currently glob web/src non-recursively).
validation: Rerun mutations a–h2: every dead pointer must fail, and h2 must pass. The current tree stays green, apart from fixing the two docstring examples.

verdict.reason: Every mechanism claimed checks out on reading the code. The reverse check promised in the docstring does not exist: `used` is only counted. A link to a .md file with no anchor is never checked, because CROSS requires '#'. LINK's `[a-z0-9-]+` has no boundary, so an anchor is truncated at '_' or an uppercase letter. `docs/history/...` cannot match. tools/, flake.nix and .github are not scanned. Duplicate-heading suffixes are not modelled. Several classes are latent today, though: I found no duplicate headings, no headings inside fences, no nested web/src sources apart from generated wasm .d.ts, and no truncated pointers. So the severity is low. There are real dead pointers now: the two docstring examples and a dead README link in corrections.md, which I list under missed.
verdict.evidence: tools/check_doc_links.py:58 has `LINK = re.compile(r"docs/([a-z0-9_-]+)\.md#([a-z0-9-]+)")` and :61 has `CROSS = ...#([a-z0-9-]+)\)`. The docstring at :25-27 promises 'a renamed heading with no referrer is reported', and nothing compares `used` with the headings. Running the script prints '83 documentation pointers', a count of distinct pairs, while ci.yml:47 says '389' and the docstring says '175'. My wider scan over `git ls-files` found about 380 occurrences. The rationale.md anchors that exist are 'the-lewis-parabola-over-the-30-tangent' and nothing containing 'hob', so the docstring's examples at :19 and :55 are dead. My wider scan also found docs/corrections.md:608 `[README.md](README.md)`, which resolves to the nonexistent docs/README.md.
verdict.proposal_note: Implementing 'every heading must have a referrer' would fail on most headings, because many sections are legitimately unreferenced. Delete that docstring claim rather than implement it. The other fixes are cheap and right: whole-anchor matching, a file-existence check for anchorless links resolved relative to the linking file, scanning git ls-files, and printing both counts.

title: check_units misses unit-silent pub angles in tooth.rs and the parameter-level ambiguity it was written for
claim: Rule 1 says every angular field states its unit, but `looks_angular` only matches `angle` or `alpha|beta|gamma|sigma`, and FIELD only matches `pub `, not `pub(crate)` or private fields, and only f64 or Auto/Option<f64>. The public fields `Tooth::psi_p`, `psi_b` ('Half tooth angle at the base circle'), `theta_a` and `theta0` state no unit, while `Ring::psi_b` says radians. Rule 2 (no name in both units) is violated at parameter level, which the motivating bug (`least_distance_lead_angle`'s parameter) belongs to: `helix` is radians in screw.rs:1466 (`helix.cos()`) and degrees in gear-cli kinematics.rs:76 `pair(z1, z2, helix)`. `push_distance(axes, angle)` has no suffix at all.
evidence:
Worktree mutations of check_units.py:
- u1) `pub foo_angle: f64` with no doc: exit 1 (caught).
- u2) `pub theta_x`: exit 0.
- u3) `pub(crate) pressure_angle`: exit 0.
- u4) private field: exit 0.
- u5) `pub helix`: exit 0.
- u6) `pub lead_angle: f32`: exit 0.
- u7) `pub alpha: Vec<f64>`: exit 0.
- u8) a degree field whose doc says 'In degrees, converted to radians': classified radians, a false 'both units' report.
The widened scan (notes/tools-ci/units_wide.py) lists 26 silent fields and struct-literal lines, including the four tooth.rs pub fields. grep finds 24 fn parameters with angular names and no _rad/_deg suffix.
proposal:
- Widen the name rule to `(angle|helix|lead|(alpha|beta|gamma|sigma|theta|psi|phi|delta)(_|\d|$))` and the visibility rule to any field (`^\s*(pub(\([a-z]+\))? )?name: …`). Also accept f32 and containers.
- Add a parameter pass: every fn parameter with an angular name must end in `_rad` or `_deg`, or appear in an allowlist of Greek names whose fn doc says radians.
- When a doc names both units, classify by the first unit word, or require exactly one.
- Longer term, `struct Deg(f64)` and `struct Rad(f64)` newtypes at the public API would make the question a type error rather than a regex.
validation: Mutations u2–u7 must fail. Fixing the tooth.rs docs (radians) and renaming the screw.rs parameter to `helix_rad` makes the tree green.

verdict.reason: The gap in the checker is real. FIELD (check_units.py:38) matches only `pub name:`, and looks_angular (:57) matches only 'angle' or alpha/beta/gamma/sigma. So the radian fields Tooth::psi_p, psi_b, theta_a and theta0 (tooth.rs:151,153,167,192) pass unchecked with no unit in their docs. But no present wrong answer comes out of it, and part of the proposal is wrong. `lead` is a length: screw.rs:140 says 'how far a point on the thread advances per worm revolution, mm', and train/mod.rs:1416 says 'Lead, mm'. Adding `lead` to the angular pattern would demand an angular unit of a length, which is the exact thing the NOT_ANGLES comment warns against. A widened pass also flags names that already carry `_rad`/`_deg` (shaft_angle_rad, helix_deg), so the suffix has to count as stating the unit. The `helix` parameter clash (screw.rs flank_curvature in radians, gear-cli kinematics.rs pair() in degrees) is real, but these are private fn parameters in different crates. It is naming hygiene, not a demonstrated bug.
verdict.evidence: I copied the checker to notes/verify-tools-ci-2/wide.py, widened the visibility rule to pub(crate) and private fields, and added theta|psi|phi|delta|helix|lead. It reports 27 silent names. Among them are tooth.rs:151/153/167/192, mesh.rs:143-144 alpha_t/alpha_n, metrology.rs:470/472 and tooth.rs:828/887/888. Among the false positives are screw.rs:140 and :265 `lead` (mm), train/mod.rs:1416 `lead` (mm), and every `*_rad` and `helix_deg` name. Some matches are fn-parameter lines picked up by the field regex.
verdict.corrected_claim: check_units.py sees only `pub` f64 fields whose names contain 'angle' or alpha|beta|gamma|sigma. Radian fields named psi_*/theta_* (four pub fields in tooth.rs, and private alpha_t/alpha_n in mesh.rs, among others) and every fn parameter go unchecked. No unit mismatch is shown today.
verdict.proposal_note: Leave `lead` out of the angular pattern: it is a length throughout the crate. Treat a `_rad`/`_deg` suffix as a stated unit. Check the psi/theta/phi/delta names by the doc rule rather than by a new parameter pass, since fn parameters have no doc comment above them to read. The Deg/Rad newtype is the durable fix, but it is a large API change. Weigh it against how rare this fault has been (one recorded case).

title: CI's tests job holds id-token: write while running npm ci and project code, contradicting its own comment
claim: `tests` declares `permissions: id-token: write`, so every step (npm ci's install scripts, build scripts, tests) can request an OIDC token for the repository. The deploy job's comment says '…mint an OIDC token, and nothing that runs project code should be able to'. With `determinate: false` the nix-installer-action does no FlakeHub login, so nothing in `tests` needs the token.
evidence: ci.yml lines 17-20: `permissions: id-token: write, contents: read`. ci.yml:134-135: 'it publishes, so it can write Pages and mint an OIDC token, and nothing that runs project code should be able to'. ci.yml:25-29: `determinate: false`. `upload-pages-artifact` needs no id-token.
proposal: Set the tests job to `permissions: contents: read` only.
validation: CI stays green. The upload-pages-artifact and deploy steps still work, since deploy keeps its own `id-token: write`.

verdict.reason: The tests job grants id-token: write (ci.yml:18-20). Nothing in the job uses it: determinate: false turns off the FlakeHub login, no cache action is present, and upload-pages-artifact needs no OIDC. The permission dates from the initial import (commit 34d3be4), when a Determinate cache was probably in use. It was never removed when the cache was dropped. It contradicts the job's own comment at ci.yml:136-138. I rate it low rather than medium because the job has no pages: write, deploy runs behind the github-pages environment, and fork PRs never get OIDC tokens. The real exposure is a same-repo npm ci install script minting a repo OIDC token, which matters only if some cloud trusts this repo's tokens.
verdict.evidence: ci.yml:16-20 `tests: permissions: id-token: write, contents: read`. ci.yml:30 `determinate: false`. ci.yml:136-138 '...mint an OIDC token, and nothing that runs project code should be able to'. `git log -S'id-token: write'` shows it added in 34d3be4 (initial import) and untouched in dda39e6, which only added deploy's copy.
verdict.proposal_note: Set `permissions: contents: read` on tests, as proposed. It is safe and a one-line change.

title: Repo-wide `concurrency: group: pages` serialises every run and lets pushes on one branch cancel pending runs on another
claim: The concurrency group is workflow-level, fixed to `pages`, and applies to every push, pull_request and workflow_dispatch on every ref. GitHub keeps at most one pending run per group and cancels the older pending one when a newer run queues, regardless of `cancel-in-progress: false` (which only protects the in-progress run). A PR's check can therefore be cancelled by an unrelated push, and all CI runs repo-wide wait on each other, at about 5 minutes or more each. `on: push` with no branch filter together with `pull_request` also runs every same-repo PR twice, and both runs share that one group.
evidence: ci.yml:3-13. The comment states the intent: 'the published site should end up at the newest commit that passed'. That intent is about deploy only. My confidence is medium because the cancellation behaviour comes from GitHub's documented concurrency semantics and could not be reproduced here.
proposal: Move `concurrency: {group: pages, cancel-in-progress: false}` onto the `deploy` job. Give the workflow `concurrency: {group: ci-${{ github.ref }}, cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}}`. Restrict `push` to `branches: [main]`, which is where the only deploy happens, and let pull_request cover the rest.
validation: Push to two branches in quick succession: both runs complete, and deploy still serialises on main.

verdict.reason: The concurrency block is workflow-level with a fixed group `pages` (ci.yml:11-13), and the triggers are push with no branch filter plus pull_request (:3-6). Under GitHub's documented semantics a group holds one running and one pending run, and a newly queued run cancels the pending one. cancel-in-progress: false protects only the running one. So every run on every ref serialises, and a PR check can be cancelled as 'pending' by an unrelated push. The comment at :8-10 states a deploy-only intent. Impact is small for a single-author repo, hence low.
verdict.evidence: ci.yml:3-13 as quoted. deploy (ci.yml:143-150) is the only job that needs serialising, and it is already gated by `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`. The cancellation semantics come from GitHub's documentation and were not reproduced here.
verdict.proposal_note: Moving `concurrency: {group: pages, cancel-in-progress: false}` onto the deploy job and using a per-ref group for the workflow is right. Restricting `push` to main is a separate trade-off: this owner works on long-lived branches (train-as-graph, audit-ablation) and may rely on push CI without opening a PR. Either keep push unfiltered with a ref-scoped group, or confirm that PRs are always opened before restricting.

title: Doctests and rustdoc intra-doc links are never checked: 22 broken links
claim: `cargo nextest` does not run doctests, and check_bindings' `cargo test … export_bindings` filters them out, so the 4 doctests (elliptic::r_f, elliptic::r_d, hertz::elliptical_contact, lib.rs) never run in CI. Nothing runs rustdoc either, so ``[`Item`]`` links in doc comments rot unseen. They are the code-to-code equivalent of the pointers check_doc_links guards.
evidence: `cargo test --workspace --doc` in the worktree: 4 passed. `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --document-private-items` gives 22 `unresolved link` warnings. Among them are auto.rs:1032 [`crate::Ring`], mesh.rs:765, gear.rs:255 [`Tooth::profile`], wiring.rs:87 [`Wiring::mounts`], mod.rs:268 [`kinematics::System::play`], and links to `minimum_profile_shift`, `stated_helix`, `always_given` and `super::member_inputs`, none of which exist under those names. There are also 25 'public documentation links to private item' warnings and 2 redundant explicit links (notes/tools-ci/rustdoc.txt).
proposal: Add `doc = craneLib.cargoDoc (commonArgs // { inherit cargoArtifacts; RUSTDOCFLAGS = "-D rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links"; cargoDocExtraArgs = "--workspace --no-deps --document-private-items"; });` and `doctest = craneLib.cargoDocTest (commonArgs // { inherit cargoArtifacts; });` to flake checks. Fix the 22 links first.
validation: `nix flake check` fails on a deliberately broken ``[`NoSuch`]`` link and passes once the 22 are fixed.

verdict.reason: I reproduced the finding. The flake checks have no doc or doctest derivation. nextest skips doctests. check_bindings' `cargo test ... export_bindings` filter excludes them. Rustdoc reports exactly 22 unresolved intra-doc links. About half of them are genuinely stale names, where the item no longer exists: stated_helix, always_given, super::member_inputs, Wiring::mounts, Loading::for_cases, Tooth::profile (profile lives on Gear and Ring, not Tooth), ToothOutline::rim_support as a path, Self::span. The rest point to items that exist but are out of scope for the link (minimum_profile_shift, Train::relieve_case, kinematics::System::play). This is stale prose of the kind check_doc_links guards for docs/, so it fits the project's goals. The 4 doctests pass today.
verdict.evidence: In a worktree at HEAD, `cargo test --workspace --doc` reports 4 passed: elliptic::r_f, elliptic::r_d, hertz::elliptical_contact and lib.rs. `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --document-private-items` gives 22 'unresolved link' warnings (the list is in notes/verify-tools-ci-2/rustdoc.txt): auto.rs:1032, gear.rs:255, mesh.rs:765, metrology.rs:747, strength.rs:331, tooth.rs:324, outline.rs:3, conditions.rs:162, pair.rs:99, wiring.rs:87 and :308, mod.rs:268/740/912/1118/1711/2073/2225/2804, gear-wasm lib.rs:1419/1473, and gear-io dxf.rs:35. It also gives 22 'public documentation ... links to private item' warnings, not the 25 the finding states. `grep -n 'doc' flake.nix` finds no cargoDoc or doctest check.
verdict.proposal_note: Adding craneLib.cargoDoc with RUSTDOCFLAGS='-D rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links' is right. The private-item warnings are expected under --document-private-items and should stay allowed. The doctest check is cheap, but only 4 doctests exist, so its value is small.

title: Four boundary types are still hand-mirrored in TypeScript, outside check_bindings
claim: check_bindings exists so that no hand-written copy of the boundary drifts. Still hand-written: `Note`, which duplicates the generated web/src/wire/core/Note.ts; `LanguageOption`, which Rust builds with ad hoc `serde_json::json!` so no type exists; and `TrainDocument` and `Imported`, which are gear-io types in a crate with no `typescript` feature. A renamed field in any of these compiles on both sides and breaks at run time.
evidence: strings.svelte.ts:80 declares `export interface Note { key: string; values: Record<string,string> }`, while wire/core/Note.ts is generated with the same shape. lib.rs:920 builds `json!({"code", "name", "english": l.english_name})`. core.ts:580-591 declares `TrainDocument` and `Imported`, and gear-io's Cargo.toml has no ts-rs.
proposal:
- Import `Note` from ./wire.
- Add a `#[derive(Serialize, TS)] struct LanguageOption` in gear-wasm and serialise that instead of json!.
- Add an optional `typescript` feature to gear-io (ts-rs on TrainDocument and Imported, export_to "io/"), include it in check_bindings.sh's feature list, and add `io` to the barrel loop.
validation: check_bindings.sh --write generates the three new files, the hand-written interfaces are deleted, and `npm run check` passes. Renaming `english_name`'s JSON key then fails svelte-check.

verdict.reason: Confirmed, and the finding undercounts. Note is hand-declared at strings.svelte.ts:80 while wire/core/Note.ts is generated with the same shape. LanguageOption (strings.svelte.ts:23) mirrors a json! literal at gear-wasm lib.rs:920. TrainDocument and Imported (core.ts:580, :588) mirror gear-io types, and gear-io has no ts-rs dependency (only gear-core and gear-wasm Cargo.toml carry it). The same holds for every private request type in gear-wasm: TrainEdit (lib.rs:1544, a snake_case enum mirrored by hand at core.ts:809), EditRequest, RelieveRequest, RelieveCaseRequest, AdoptRequest, PreviewRequest and OffersRequest are all written in TS as inline object literals, e.g. core.ts:680 `{ shape: train.shape, just, figures }`. I rate it low because check_wasm's probe executes the entry points, which catches some request drift, though not a field the TS side sends and serde ignores.
verdict.evidence: web/src/strings.svelte.ts:80-83, web/src/wire/core/Note.ts, web/src/core.ts:580-591 and :809-812, crates/gear-wasm/src/lib.rs:919-921 and :1542-1554. `grep ts-rs crates/*/Cargo.toml` finds only gear-core and gear-wasm.
verdict.proposal_note: Extend the fix to the request types. Add `cfg_attr(feature = "typescript", derive(TS))` to TrainEdit and the *Request structs in gear-wasm, and import them in core.ts. TrainEdit is the most drift-prone of all: a sum type with a rename rule, hand-written. Re-exporting Note from ./wire costs one line and should be done first.

title: Every script that 'builds, never merely finds' the binary ignores CARGO_TARGET_DIR
claim: check_golden.sh, check_figures.py, build_wasm.sh and check_wasm.sh run `cargo build`, which honours CARGO_TARGET_DIR, and then read `$root/target/...`. With CARGO_TARGET_DIR set, they run whatever stale binary or module sits in ./target, or fail with 'not built'. That is exactly the stale-binary fault each docstring says it fixed ('Built every time, never merely found'). The same path logic is written four times.
evidence: check_golden.sh:65 `bin="$root/target/release/gear-cli"` after `cargo build … --bin gear-cli`. check_figures.py:115-122 returns `ROOT/'target'/profile/'gear-cli'`. build_wasm.sh:48 `module=${BUILD_WASM_MODULE:-$root/target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/wasm/gear_wasm.wasm}`. check_wasm.sh:78 hard-codes the same path. In this audit I had to symlink the worktree's target/ to CARGO_TARGET_DIR for the scripts to work at all.
proposal: One helper, tools/cargo_artifact.sh <cargo args>, that runs `cargo build --message-format=json-render-diagnostics … | jq -r 'select(.reason=="compiler-artifact" and .executable!=null).executable'`, or for the wasm cdylib the `filenames[]` ending in .wasm. All four scripts call it. Also accept `GEAR_CLI=<path>` so CI can pass `result/bin/gear-cli` from the nix build it has already done and skip the dev-shell release build.
validation: Run each script with CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/elsewhere and an empty ./target: each must build and use the fresh artifact.

verdict.reason: I confirmed this by reading the code. check_golden.sh:65 and check_figures.py:115-122 run `cargo build` and then read `$ROOT/target/<profile>/gear-cli`. build_wasm.sh:48 and check_wasm.sh:78 hard-code `$root/target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/wasm/gear_wasm.wasm`. Under CARGO_TARGET_DIR, the build goes elsewhere and the script reads a stale or missing artifact, which is the stale-binary fault their docstrings claim to have closed. A further inconsistency: check_wasm.sh:78 ignores BUILD_WASM_MODULE even though build_wasm.sh honours it, so the 'before' and 'after' halves of the differential could come from different modules. check_figures.py's profile choice also prefers debug whenever only a debug binary exists, while check_golden's full run insists on release. Neither the dev shell nor CI sets CARGO_TARGET_DIR, so the default workflow is unaffected, hence low.
verdict.evidence: tools/check_golden.sh:65 `bin="$root/target/release/gear-cli"`. tools/check_figures.py:118-122 build, then `return ROOT / "target" / profile / "gear-cli"`. tools/build_wasm.sh:48. tools/check_wasm.sh:78. `grep -rn CARGO_TARGET_DIR tools flake.nix` finds nothing.
verdict.proposal_note: Parsing --message-format=json needs jq, and jq is not on the host PATH. A simpler fix: read the directory once with `cargo metadata --format-version 1 --no-deps` (in Python, json.loads; in shell, `python3 -c` or `${CARGO_TARGET_DIR:-$root/target}`), and have check_wasm.sh use the same BUILD_WASM_MODULE default as build_wasm.sh.

title: CI compiles the workspace about 7 times; cheap gates run after the 5-minute build
evidence: Read ci.yml and flake.nix. check_golden measured at 62.7 s. The three cheap gates run in under 1 s each.
proposal:
Make every gate a flake check, so `nix flake check` is CI and the CLAUDE.md warning can go:
- `checks.golden = runCommand` running check_golden with `GEAR_CLI=${self.packages.default}/bin/gear-cli` (needs the GEAR_CLI override above, plus tools/ and docs/ in its src).
- The same shape for check_figures, check_units, check_doc_links, check_strings, validate_dxf and the by-hand scripts, which need only python3 and numpy.
- `checks.web = self.packages.web`.
The workflow reduces to `nix flake check -L` plus the npm typecheck and bindings. Until then, move the three dependency-free gates to the top of the job.
validation: `nix flake check` fails on each of the mutations in this report. CI wall time drops by about the release gear-cli build and the check_bindings compile.

verdict.reason: The claim matches ci.yml and flake.nix. `nix flake check` builds native release deps, packages.default (which contains bin/gear-cli), clippy and the nextest build. `nix build .#web` builds the wasm deps and the module separately. The dev-shell steps then compile again: check_bindings runs `cargo test` with the typescript features in the debug/test profile, `npm run check` runs build:wasm in the wasm profile, and the golden step does `cargo build --release --bin gear-cli`. check_golden.sh:67 also builds the binary itself, so that explicit CI line is redundant twice over. The dependency-free gates (doc links at ci.yml:50, strings at :55, units at :94) come after flake check and web. The timing is off: with `nix develop` overhead the three cheap gates take 3.2 to 5.2 s each, not under 1 s. The argument is unaffected.
verdict.evidence: Read ci.yml:39-117 and flake.nix:162-195. Timed `nix develop -c python3 tools/check_{doc_links,strings,units}.py`: 5.21 s, 3.20 s and 3.32 s. check_golden.sh:67 runs `cargo build "${profile[@]}" ... --bin gear-cli`, and check_figures.py:118 does the same, so the ci.yml:85 build only warms the cache.
verdict.proposal_note: Moving the three cheap gates to the top of the job costs nothing and should be done first. The full flake migration is sound for the Python gates and golden/figures, given GEAR_CLI pointing at ${self.packages.default}. Two caveats. check_bindings and `npm run check` need a crane test derivation with the typescript features and a buildNpmPackage check respectively, so they are not free. And the by-hand scripts are deliberately by-hand (CLAUDE.md marks them 'no'); some are slow, e.g. hula_kinematics integrates 200 000 steps per row, so putting them in `flake check` changes the stated policy and needs its own decision.

title: docs/state.md's 'Running it' list omits check_units, check_wasm and validate_dxf, and says 'run all four'
claim: CLAUDE.md:180 records two red builds caused by naming fewer checks than CI runs ('the five omitted check_units.py'), and tells the reader to run everything the table marks yes. docs/state.md:40-58 still says 'Before pushing, run all four' and lists nine tools, without check_units.py, check_wasm.sh or validate_dxf.py. That is the same omission, and state.md:151 even says CLAUDE.md's table is 'the exhaustive list'.
evidence: Read docs/state.md:30-58 and compared it with the CI steps and CLAUDE.md:160-176.
proposal: Replace state.md:40-58 with one line pointing to CLAUDE.md#which-check-catches-what, or, once the flake finding is done, with `nix flake check`. Delete the 'run all four' sentence.
validation: `grep -n 'check_' docs/state.md` shows no second, partial list.

verdict.reason: docs/state.md:38-44 says 'Before pushing, run all four', meaning nextest, flake check, web build and npm check. The list at :48-56 omits check_units.py, check_wasm.sh and validate_dxf.py, and check_units is exactly the omission CLAUDE.md:180 records as causing a red build. state.md:154 does name CLAUDE.md's table as the exhaustive list, but only 100 lines later and not at the partial list itself. The two documents also disagree on the cost: state.md:38 says the reading 'has cost one red build', CLAUDE.md says 'the second red build'. The harm is a red CI run, not a wrong answer, so low rather than medium.
verdict.evidence: sed -n 28,62p docs/state.md: the block lists check_bindings, check_doc_links, check_strings, check_golden, check_figures and npm check, and nothing else. grep for check_units/check_wasm/validate_dxf in docs/state.md finds no hit in that section.
verdict.proposal_note: Replace the whole block, prose and list, with a pointer to CLAUDE.md#which-check-catches-what. The rationale for the npmDepsHash trap can stay as one sentence, since CLAUDE.md's table row already carries it.

title: Lints: `expect`, `panic`, `unreachable` and float equality are uncounted; many allow attributes are no-ops
claim: The workspace sets `unwrap_used = warn` ('A calculation engine must not panic'), and all four crates inherit it, with `--deny warnings` in the flake. That part is sound. But `.expect()` is the same panic with a message and is unlinted: 20 production sites, one in gear-core (arrangements.rs:221), plus `unreachable!` at shape.rs:1852. 7 strict float `==`/`!=` in gear-core are unmarked, e.g. gear.rs:389 `r == g.rf` identifies root-arc points by exact equality. About 13 `#[allow(clippy::cast_precision_loss)]` and one `too_many_lines` allow suppress lints that pedantic=allow already turns off, so they are dead. `unsafe_code` is only `warn`.
proposal: Enable `expect_used`, `panic`, `unreachable` and `float_cmp` (warn) for non-test code, with `#[expect(clippy::…, reason = "…")]` at each of the roughly 28 sites, so every intended panic or exact compare is named and counted. Set `unsafe_code = "forbid"`. Convert all `#[allow(...)]` to `#[expect(...)]`: the unfulfilled_lint_expectations lint will then flag the dead ones for deletion. Do not enable indexing_slicing or cast_precision_loss workspace-wide.
validation: `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` is green with the new lints, and adding a bare `.expect()` in gear-core fails it.

verdict.corrected_claim: `expect_used`, `panic`, `unreachable` and `float_cmp` are not linted. The extra-lint run finds 20 `.expect()` calls: 1 in gear-core (arrangements.rs:217-221), 3 in gear-io and 16 in the gear-cli harness. It also finds 1 `unreachable!` (shape.rs:1852), 0 production `panic!` and 7 strict float compares, all deliberate sentinels. The dead-allow count is understated. There are 58 `#[allow(clippy::cast_precision_loss)]` attributes across 16 files, plus 3 `too_many_lines`, and all of them are no-ops because `pedantic = allow`. The finding says about 13. `too_many_arguments` is in clippy::all, so those allows are live. The code has no `unsafe`, and `unsafe_code = forbid` builds cleanly even for wasm32 with wasm_bindgen expansions.
verdict.reason: The core claim holds. The counts are re-derived from the auditor's clippy_extra.txt and grep. The 'about 13' is wrong: grep finds 58 cast_precision_loss allows, e.g. verify.rs 9, matrix.rs 9, shaper.rs 7, gear.rs 6, contact.rs 6. Most `.expect()` sites are in the dev harness, where the 'calculation engine must not panic' argument is weaker, so the lint belongs at least on gear-core, gear-io and gear-wasm. I checked that forbidding unsafe does not break the wasm build.
verdict.evidence: `grep -rn 'allow(clippy::cast_precision_loss' crates | wc` gives 58. `CARGO_TARGET_DIR=... RUSTFLAGS='-F unsafe_code' cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p gear-wasm` exits 0. clippy_extra.txt lines 387, 773 and 1147-1671 list the expect and unreachable sites. The float_cmp sites (auto.rs:1849, gear.rs:147, gear.rs:389, hertz.rs:402, planetary.rs:270, tooth.rs:705, edits.rs:438) each compare a value with itself or with a value copied from the same computation.
verdict.proposal_note: Converting to `#[expect]` works on toolchain 1.96.1 and would flag all 58+3 dead allows, so deleting them outright is simpler. For gear-cli, a crate-level `#![allow(clippy::expect_used)]` with a reason is more honest than 16 per-site expects. The `unreachable!` at shape.rs:1852 could be removed by iterating the coordinate pairs structurally rather than by a flat index.

title: validate_dxf covers one external gear; ring DXF export has no independent reader; expected radii are hand-typed in YAML
claim: The only independent DXF read is `dxf 17 0.2 0.001`. `export_ring_dxf`, the internal gear, goes out only through wasm and is never parsed by ezdxf or checked structurally. An undercut pinion (e.g. 9 −0.3, where the flank runs below the base circle) is not exercised either. The expected radii `--root 7.45 --tip 9.7 --base 7.987387276680222 --pitch 8.5` are engineering numbers typed into ci.yml.
evidence: ci.yml:115-119, and `gear-cli help` has no ring-dxf command. The radii are correct: 8.5−1.25+0.2, 8.5+1+0.2 and 8.5·cos20°. The bulge rule `bulged == 3*teeth` in validate_dxf assumes the external form.
proposal: Add a `gear-cli dxf --ring z x tol` (or `ringdxf`) subcommand. Have validate_dxf take `--teeth --shift --module --pressure-angle` and compute the reference radii itself from the closed forms, so CI passes only design inputs. Run it over three cases (17/0.2, 9/−0.3, ring 60/0) in the CI step, with the ring expectations adjusted for tip inside root.
validation: A worktree mutation that flips the ring outline's winding or drops its BLOCKS section must fail the new case.

verdict.corrected_claim: Only one DXF, the external 17-tooth x=0.2 case, is read back by an independent parser in CI, and no ring DXF is ever read by ezdxf. The ring export is not unchecked, though. gear-io's `the_file_meets_the_r2000_minimum` (dxf.rs:627-647) runs the full R2000 section, table and ownership gate on `ring_to_dxf` for a 60-tooth ring. `a_rings_dxf_carries_its_rim_as_a_construction_circle` (dxf.rs:898) checks the rim circle, and wasm_probe records the ring export. So a dropped BLOCKS section is already caught for rings. What is missing is an independent geometric read of the ring outline (winding, radii, periodicity) and of an undercut pinion. The existing tool already handles the undercut pinion.
verdict.reason: 'Never parsed by ezdxf' is right; 'never checked structurally' is wrong. The proposal's validation mutation, dropping BLOCKS, already fails a Rust test. I exported `gear-cli dxf 9 -0.3 0.001` and it passes validate_dxf with every check, including 27 bulges and periodicity. Adding that case is a one-line CI change that needs no new tool. The radii in ci.yml are not a rule-1 violation, which is about TypeScript. For an independent check, an expectation derived outside the code under test is the right thing, though computing it in the Python from z, x, m and α reads better.
verdict.evidence: crates/gear-io/src/dxf.rs:627-647 loops over two gear_to_dxf outputs and `ring_to_dxf(&Ring::cut_by(&GearParams{teeth:60,..}, &Cutter::default()), ..)`. `validate_dxf.py g9.dxf --root 2.95 --tip 5.2 --base 4.228616793536588 --pitch 4.5 --teeth 9` prints 'all checks passed'. The radii were derived as r−1.25m+x, r+m+x and r·cos20°.
verdict.proposal_note: Split the work. (1) Now: add the 9/−0.3 case to the CI step, and let validate_dxf derive its reference radii from --module, --shift and --pressure-angle. (2) A ring case needs a `gear-cli dxf` ring mode, plus validate_dxf changes: clockwise or hole winding, tip inside root, the rim as a construction circle, and a bulge count set by the ring's form. Make the mutation that validation is judged against a flipped winding or a wrong bulge, not a dropped BLOCKS section.

title: check_golden --fast silently passes if --golden-cases fails
claim: The case list comes from process substitution `< <("$bin" --golden-cases)`, whose exit status `set -e` does not see. If the binary fails there, `cases` is empty. The full mode still fails, because diff -r of the store against an empty scratch differs, but `--fast` loops over nothing and prints 'all unchanged' with exit 0.
evidence: Read check_golden.sh:79-90 and 134-150.
proposal: Capture first with `list="$("$bin" --golden-cases)"`, which set -e catches, then `[[ -n $list ]] || { echo 'no cases' >&2; exit 1; }`, and read from the variable.
validation: Make `--golden-cases` exit 1 in a worktree; `check_golden.sh --fast` must fail.

verdict.reason: I reproduced it in a scratch copy of the script with a stub gear-cli whose `--golden-cases` exits 1. `--fast` printed 'SKIPPED 0 slow commands ()' and '32 recorded outputs, all unchanged' and exited 0. The full mode exited 1. The same mechanism does more damage under `--write`: the empty case list reaches `rm -f "$store"/*.txt` before `cp "$scratch"/*.txt` fails, so the committed corpus is deleted and the script exits 1. git can recover it, but the fault is destructive.
verdict.evidence: Fake root at /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/notes/verify-tools-ci-3/fakeroot. The stub printed 'boom' to stderr and exited 1. `bash tools/check_golden.sh --fast` gave exit 0 with 'all unchanged'. After `bash tools/check_golden.sh --write`, `cp: cannot stat '/tmp/tmp.../*.txt'`, exit 1, and `ls tools/golden | wc -l` gave 0.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposed capture fixes both modes. Also refuse `--write` when the scratch directory is empty, and move the `rm -f` after a successful build of the scratch set, e.g. `cp` into a fresh directory, then swap.

title: Stale or inaccurate statements in build and CI comments
claim:
Each of these no longer matches the code or the gate:
- gear-wasm's description says 'three functions'; there are 23.
- check_figures._bin says 'CI builds debug'; CI builds release (ci.yml:99).
- check_strings says 'Run by hand'; it runs in CI.
- flake.nix:43 says 'Anything else added under a data/ directory is picked up automatically'; only *.csv is (plus *.toml via crane), so a .json or .txt data file would vanish from the sandbox.
- .cargo/config.toml says `jobs = -1` means 'all available cores'; it means all but one.
- The deploy comment says 'the four consistency checks'; there are seven.
- ci.yml says '389 of these' pointers; the gate reports 83 distinct.
- state.md:166 says hula_kinematics runs 'on one arrangement'; it runs 32 rows (16 arrangements × 2 differences).
- cargoNextest's `partitions = 1; partitionType = "count"` restate the defaults.
- .cargo aliases t/c/b/r duplicate cargo's built-ins.
evidence: I read each file and compared it with the gate output: 83 pointers, and 32 'ok' rows in hula_kinematics.out.
