- Through the train, the bending stress stays continuous up to the refusal (330.07, 331.51, 334.77 MPa over x = −0.336 to −0.3425). There the discontinuity is ok→Err, not the 34 % drop, so the drop is visible only through the standalone `bending_section_shared` API and the paths that use it.
- Automatic shifts (no_undercut, or the search) keep away from interfering candidates. So the defaults are exposed only when a user fixes a shift or the tooth count is small enough that x=0 interferes, as with 9 teeth.

**The fix proposed in the ledger is the right one.** Cap each path end at the conjugate of the mate's `FlankEnds::junction`, report the d_Nf-limited ε, and raise a Note carrying the interference depth. The independent rack-simulation script in notes/repro-lens-continuity-0/indep.py can serve as the external check on the capped ε: it agrees with the crate-junction-capped ε to 0.007 at x=0 and to 0.003 at x=−0.3.

title: Crossed pair whose face misses the contact falls back to the full, face-unlimited path (ε, η and σH reported for teeth that never touch)
claim:
`CrossedPath::limited_by_face` returns None when the face-bounded zone closes entirely. Both callers then substitute the unbounded tip-limited path:
- `PointBuilt::zone` (`.map_or(*path, |(z,_)| z)`), which feeds efficiency, locking friction and the single-pair contact ratings;
- the report (`.unwrap_or((*path, ZoneLimit::Face))`), which feeds `contact_ratio`.
So narrowing the face past the point where the contact slides off it makes ε jump from 0 back to the full tip-limited value, and no 'contact ratio below one' note fires. The comment beside it says the opposite ('No zone at all is a contact ratio of nought'), which holds only when `p.path` itself is None.
evidence:
Probe at the Screw level, 17/43, Σ=0.5°, β₁=β₂=0.25°, 20 µm clearance (crossed_face_0.5.txt): the axial centres of the contact sit ±1535.7 path-units (≈6.3 mm axially) off each gear's mid-plane, and the zone is [−2.52, 2.21]. Face 12.786 mm: Tips-limited, ε=1.6013. Face 12.402 mm: `limited_by_face` = None, yet the fallback reports ε=1.6013 and η=0.987644, down to a 0.4 mm face.
Through the train (worktree test, `arr::pair` at angle 0.5°, clearance 0.02, both faces b; train_crossed_face.txt):
- b=17: limited=Tips, ε=1.5992, η=0.983601.
- b=16, 14, 6: limited=Face, ε=1.5992, η=0.983601, below_one_note=false, pmax rising 552 → 902 MPa.
The true ε falls from 1.60 to 0 inside a window about 2·sin β_b·L ≈ 0.04 mm wide. Below it the report is exactly the pre-correction answer that corrections.md 4.5.1 and rationale.md:1197 say was fixed ('A designer now gets these teeth will not touch as built').
proposal:
Treat a closed zone as what it is.
- In the report: `contact_ratio = 0.0`, `limited_by = Face`, and raise `MESH_CONTACT_RATIO_BELOW_ONE`, or better a dedicated 'contact is off the face' note carrying the axial offset (|axial_centre| − b/2) as its value.
- In `PointBuilt::zone`: return None for a closed zone, not `*path`. Efficiency then falls to the pitch-point form as the existing fallback, or better, the mesh is flagged as not transmitting.
- Rate contact at no single-pair points.
Remove the misleading comment. Longer term, make `limited_by_face` total: return an empty zone [c, c] with length 0 rather than None, so no caller can substitute anything.
validation: Law: along any sweep of face width at fixed geometry, the reported contact ratio is non-decreasing in b and equals min(tip-limited ε, face-limited ε). It reaches 0 exactly when the zone closes and never exceeds the value at a wider face. Add the Σ=0.5°, 20 µm, b ∈ {17, 16.9, …, 6} sweep as a test. It fails on HEAD at b=16.

verdict.reason: The code is as described. PointBuilt::zone (shape.rs:2500-2504) uses `.map_or(*path, |(z, _)| z)`. The report (shape.rs:2717-2720) uses `.unwrap_or((*path, ZoneLimit::Face))`. So when limited_by_face returns None (screw.rs:944-946, a closed zone), both substitute the full tip-limited path. The report then says limited_by=Face with the tip-limited contact ratio, and MESH_CONTACT_RATIO_BELOW_ONE cannot fire. The comment at 2715 ('No zone at all is a contact ratio of nought') covers only p.path == None. state.md:711-717 does record that the rating falls back to the tip-limited zone near parallel. It also says 'the reported zone then says face and a contact ratio under one', which is false once the zone has closed. Its argument ('neither is a number a designer should read at that angle') is weak: the fallback reaches ordinary face widths at half a degree, and the answer given is the pre-correction one that rationale.md:1197 says was fixed. Severity is medium rather than high because it takes a shaft angle of roughly 1° or less.
verdict.evidence:
Code read at shape.rs:2500-2504, shape.rs:2713-2731 and screw.rs:922-956. I re-ran the Screw-level face sweep (probe-target/debug/crossed face 0.5 0.02, 17/43, m_n 1):
- Full path: eps 1.6013, zone [-2.52, 2.21], axial centres ±1535.7 path-mm.
- b=12.786: Tips, eps 1.6013.
- b=12.402 and below: limited_by_face=None, and the fallback still gives eps 1.6013, eta 0.987644.
The centres scale as 1/sin²Σ: 1535.7 at 0.5°, 38393 at 0.1°, 95.97 at 2°. So the closed-zone case reaches face widths above 3 mm for any Σ ≲ 2°. The auditor's train-level sweep (train_crossed_face.txt) shows limited=Face, eps=1.5992, no below-one note, for b=16..6.
verdict.proposal_note: Making limited_by_face total, returning an empty zone of length 0 rather than None, is the cleanest fix. Every caller then reads a contact ratio of 0 and the existing below-one note fires with no new branch. Once it is fixed, state.md:714-717 needs rewriting: the sentence claiming a contact ratio under one is reported is currently false.

title: Given-distance shift search jumps basins and staircases: 2 µm of distance moves the division by 0.17 module for a 1e-6 change in η
claim: With the axis distance given, the pair has one free number (the division at fixed sum), yet the answer is found by the coordinate/pattern search `Search::maximise` at resolution 1e-3. The objective along the division is flat to about 1e-6 between widely separated divisions, and it has two local optima: the undercut floor and an interior point. So the chosen gears jump discontinuously as the distance moves continuously, and between jumps x1 moves in quanta of about 0.00196 (non-monotone), not continuously.
evidence:
Probe shifts.rs, 9/37, search on, a from 23.000 to 24.400 in 0.002 steps (shifts_9_37_a.txt).
- a=23.990: x1=0.473568 (floor), x2=0.632270, ε=1.341810, η=0.9764662.
- a=23.992: x1=0.642178, x2=0.466189, ε=1.282718, η=0.9764670.
That is Δx1=+0.169 and Δx2=−0.166 (visibly different gears), ε down 4.4 %, η up 8e-7. Between 24.0 and 24.15, x1 steps 0.646099 → 0.648060 → … → 0.702956 and back down to 0.693153 in quanta of 0.00196, while x2 absorbs the rest continuously.
proposal: For a one-dimensional bounded division, replace the pattern search with an exact piecewise solve. The candidates are the bounds of the admissible interval (each a bracketed root of its own constraint: floor, interference, bottom clearance, ε_min, tip cap onset) and the stationary points of the closed-form loss on each smooth piece (`split_residual`, or a corrected version of it for the tip cap). Take the best candidate. That yields a continuous (piecewise-smooth) answer to machine precision. Where two candidates are within a stated tolerance in η (say 1e-5, surfaced as an option), break the tie by a stated secondary rule, e.g. the larger ε or balanced specific sliding, so the geometry does not flip on noise. Keep `maximise` for the genuinely multi-dimensional sets.
validation: Law: along any continuous sweep of the given distance, x1(a) and x2(a) are continuous except where the documented tie-break switches, and each such switch is reported. Check against a brute-force dense 1-D scan (1e-6 step) that the exact solve finds η ≥ the scan maximum − 1e-9 at every a.

verdict.reason: Both observations reproduce, but the claim mixes an inherent effect with an artefact of the search. The basin jump at a≈23.991 is a genuine change of global maximiser: the interior basin is higher by 8e-7 in eta. Any exact solver that maximises eta alone would jump there too, so it is a discontinuity of the objective's argmax, not of the search. Only a stated tie tolerance or secondary rule, which the proposal does include, removes it. The staircase of x1 in quanta of about 0.00196 (≈2^-9), non-monotone in a, is the pattern search's resolution. The eta it costs is of order 1e-6, e.g. 24.274 → 24.276: eta 0.9767594 → 0.9767547 while a increases. Real, but numerically tiny.
verdict.corrected_claim: With the distance given, the division is found by the pattern search at a resolution of about 2e-3, so x1(a) is a non-monotone staircase: continuity is lost to the search's grid, at a cost in eta of about 1e-6. The larger jump near a=23.991 is a genuine switch between two near-equal optima (Δeta 8e-7). An exact solve keeps that jump unless a tie tolerance and a secondary criterion are stated and exposed.
verdict.proposal_note: An exact 1-D solve over the division, with the admissible interval's ends as bracketed roots and stationary points of the loss, is sound and matches the owner's closed-form preference. The tie tolerance must be surfaced as a user-visible option, not buried as a constant, or it becomes a new magic number.

title: When the shift search finds nothing admissible it falls back to an equal split that violates its constraints and beats the constrained answer next to it
claim: When the admissible set empties at the edge of the distances a pair can reach, `fallback` builds `closed(plan)`: a default division (x1=x2 here) chosen without the admissibility the search enforces (cut as asked, bottom clearance, flank interference, ε ≥ 1.2). The design therefore jumps at that edge, and the fallback beats in η the constrained answer just before it, i.e. it reads as better while being inadmissible. The only signal is `part.optimiser_found_nothing`.
proposal: Make the fallback the least-violating point, continuous with the admissible set's last member. Minimise the largest normalised constraint violation (or maximise the smallest margin) over the same division, with the same exact 1-D machinery as the finding above, and report which constraint could not be met, with its shortfall, in the note's values. Failing that, at least fall back to the division the search last found admissible and name the binding constraint.
validation: Law: across the edge of the admissible distance range, the chosen division is continuous, and η never increases when entering the infeasible region. The note carries the binding constraint's key and shortfall. Test: the 24.270–24.290 sweep above.

verdict.reason: The fallback closure (shape.rs:1730-1751) calls self.closed(plan, &[], helix), which divides the sum by the default rule and checks none of the search's admissibility conditions. At the edge of the reachable distances the answer therefore jumps to an equal split that beats the last admissible answer on eta only because it breaks a constraint. The fallback also interferes: the pinion's flank_interference turns true, which is the condition the search refuses (corrections.md:584). reference.md's promise that the solve 'falls back to what the constraints imply' is not met here.
verdict.evidence:
Probe sweep, 9/37, search on:
- a=24.278: x1=0.653941, x2=0.825272, eps=1.308428, eta=0.9767549, interf [false,false], no notes.
- a=24.280: x1=x2=0.740934, eps=1.270945, eta=0.9768965, interf [true,false], notes [part.optimiser_found_nothing].
So in 2 µm of distance eta rises by 1.4e-4 and flank interference appears.
verdict.proposal_note: Simplest acceptable fix: fall back to the least-violating division, found with the same 1-D machinery as finding 2, and put the binding constraint's key and shortfall in the note. Under finding 0's fix the fallback's interference will also lower its eps, so the fallback's eta 'advantage' partly disappears. Keep the two fixes consistent.

title: Hula/planocentric tip sizing allows the tip circles' crossing margin to reach exactly zero; the asked clearance governs only the far-side gap
claim: The room the automatic distance is sized to is `min(far_gap − asked, tip_margin)`: the asked clearance is subtracted from the far-side gap but not from the tips' crossing margin. Whenever the crossing binds, which is every asked clearance below about 0.27 mm on the 18-tooth hula, the design is built with the two tips exactly grazing where their circles cross, with no tolerance. The clearance input then stops having any effect (a plateau), and no note says the crossing is at zero.
evidence: gear-cli hula 18 c for c from 0.05 to 1.20 (hula_clearance.txt). For c ≤ 0.26 every output is identical: offset 0.746026 mm, η 31.310 %, x 0.4519, ε 0.9735. The run at c=0.1 prints 'far-side gap 0.2779 mm' and 'tip false (+0.0000 deg)', i.e. the tips touch at the crossing. For c ≥ 0.29 the far gap binds and everything moves smoothly. The kink at about 0.27 is a legitimate active-set switch; the zero margin is not.
proposal: Give the crossing its own clearance. Either convert the asked clearance to a pinion-rotation angle at the crossing (clearance / (r_tip · sin of the crossing angle)) and size to `min(far_gap − c, tip_margin − c_θ)`, or expose a separate 'tip crossing clearance' input with a documented default. Report which of the two bound the distance (the 'held open by' line already names the mesh; add the condition).
validation: Law: at every asked clearance c > 0, the built design has far_gap ≥ c and a crossing margin ≥ c_θ(c) > 0, and the outputs change strictly with c. Test over the hula and planocentric presets at c ∈ {0.02, 0.1, 0.5}.

verdict.reason: tip_room (shape.rs:1538-1546) returns (t.far_gap - asked).min(crossing), and the crossing margin carries no allowance. The sizer drives the minimum to zero, so whenever the crossing binds the built design has its tips meeting exactly at the crossing. The asked clearance then has no effect at all. The comment at shape.rs:~1568 says each distance 'opens out to the least at which every tip clears by what was asked', which is not what the code does for the crossing. The Distance::tip_clearance doc (shape.rs:274-280) defines the input as a far-side gap only, so the plateau is 'as documented', but a margin of exactly zero is not a clearance. It is also not deliberate in any argued sense: reference.md only says 'held to nought'.
verdict.evidence:
gear-cli hula 18 c:
- c = 0.05, 0.1 and 0.26: all identical. Crank offset 0.746026 mm, efficiency 31.310 %, far-side gap 0.2779 mm, 'tip false (+0.0000 deg)' on the binding mesh.
- c=0.28: offset 0.746668, far gap 0.2800, tip +0.0230 deg.
- c=0.30: offset 0.752769, tip +0.2363 deg.
- c=0.50: offset 0.812697, tip +1.9593 deg.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposed conversion c/(r_tip·sin(crossing angle)) needs deriving. The margin is in pinion-rotation angle, and the gap that matters is the distance between the two tip corners at the crossing, so the cleanest form measures that gap in mm (or converts c at the pinion's tip radius, c/r_a1) and compares it with the same asked c. That keeps one clearance input rather than adding a second. Also report which of the two conditions bound the distance.

title: The 'where closed form is impossible' inventory is stale: it lists ten solves and one search; the crate has about 25 root finds, two quadratures, two bisections and three searches
claim: rationale.md says: 'Ten scalar solves… Everything else in the crate is algebraic — except one search'. solve.rs and CLAUDE.md say: 'Two bracketed root finders. Every transcendental step routes through them'. Both are false today. Row #2 says 'Newton, analytic ds/dr' but the code is two Brent solves.
proposal: Regenerate the table from the code, one row per call site, with columns: what is solved, method, bracket source, why no closed form, and the gate that checks it. Name the quadratures and searches in the same table. Move the two hand-rolled bisections into solve.rs (a `bisect_predicate(f: Fn(f64)->bool, lo, hi)`), so 'every transcendental step routes through solve.rs' is true. Better still, add a check (grep in tools/ or a test) that fails when `brent`, `newton_bracketed` or a `for _ in 0..` halving loop appears at a site the table does not list, as `check_wasm.sh` does for entry points.
validation: The new tools check fails on HEAD (at least 14 unlisted sites) and passes after the table is regenerated. `check_doc_links` still passes.

verdict.reason: The inventory is stale on all three counts. rationale.md:412-427 lists ten solves and 'one search'. Row #2 says Newton, but the code is Brent. solve.rs:3 and CLAUDE.md say every transcendental step routes through the two solvers, yet there are hand-rolled bisections. This is documentation accuracy, not a wrong answer, hence low.
verdict.evidence: grep of production call sites finds about 28 brent/newton_bracketed calls against the table's ~11 rows. Among them: auto.rs:146, 366, 744, 755 and 842; screw.rs:454 and 1230; shaper.rs:450; gear.rs:1137; contact.rs:534 (efficient_split); shape.rs:860, 959 and 1695; strength.rs:688, 725 and 735; ring.rs:545 and 568; tooth.rs:456, 604, 630, 689 and 708. auto.rs:744-755 (tip radius for a tip width, row #2) is two brent calls, not Newton. There are hand bisections at gear.rs:1119 and metrology.rs:200, both `for _ in 0..64`, and bracket-growth loops at shape.rs:946, 1645 and 1667.
verdict.proposal_note: A grep gate would need an allow-list keyed by function, not by line, or it will churn. The two predicate bisections (gear.rs:1119 and metrology.rs:200) look for a feasibility boundary rather than a root of a smooth function, so a `solve::bisect_predicate` is a fair home for them. Separately, auto.rs:744's u_point solves psi_b = u - atan u, which is inv(alpha)=psi_b with u=tan alpha. It can use inv⁻¹ (#1) directly instead of a separate Brent.

title: `split_residual`, `efficient_split` and `ContactPath::tip_pressure_angle` are production-dead
claim: The closed-form stationary condition for the shift division, and its bracketed solver, are called only by their own tests in contact.rs. auto.rs documents that the search deliberately does not use them. The `tip_pressure_angle` field of every ContactPath exists only to feed `split_residual`.
evidence: grep over the workspace, docs, web and tools: `split_residual` has production uses only at contact.rs:504/533, and tests at 1149/1272. `efficient_split` is used only in tests (contact.rs:1196, 1234) and in a doc link at gear-cli/src/main.rs:1085. `tip_pressure_angle` is read only at contact.rs:504.
proposal: Either wire them in as the exact 1-D division solve (see the shift-search finding), corrected for the tip cap as audit F64 describes, or delete all three with their tests, per the project's rule that what nothing reads goes.
validation: cargo build and nextest pass after deletion; or, if wired in, the continuity law of the shift-search finding passes.

verdict.reason: Holds as stated. A grep over crates, docs, web and tools finds `split_residual` called only by `efficient_split` (contact.rs:533) and contact.rs's own tests (1149, 1272). `efficient_split` is called only in tests (1196, 1234) and is named in prose at gear-cli main.rs:1085. `ContactPath::tip_pressure_angle` is read only at contact.rs:504. The code says this itself: contact.rs:492 has a heading 'Nothing in production calls this', and auto.rs:1467-1475 says the search does not use it. So the facts are admitted, and the only question is whether keeping the code is a sound deliberate choice. It is not, for three reasons. (1) By its own doc (contact.rs:471-489) and audit F64, the residual is wrong on the shipped default: `no_sharp_tip` changes dr_a/dx to about 0.47 m, and the solver misses by a third of the interval wherever the cap is active. (2) The public function therefore gives a wrong best division for default gears, and nothing warns a caller. (3) state.md:1168-1178 lists the exceptions to 'what nothing reads goes', and this is not one of them. The argument for keeping it, 'a derived and checked fact about the model', would be served as well by a test-only helper. The field also costs every ContactPath a `tip_pressure_angle` computed at contact.rs:115 that nothing uses.
verdict.evidence: grep -rn 'split_residual|efficient_split|tip_pressure_angle' finds only contact.rs:39,40,115,469,499,504,520,529,533 (definitions, their docs and their internal use) plus tests at 1112-1272; auto.rs:1468 (doc); gear-cli main.rs:1085 (doc); docs/history/audit.md:479,1257; docs/corrections.md:564. contact.rs:492-497: '# Nothing in production calls this ... The audit's record says what wiring it in would take and why that was weighed and not taken.' audit.md:1254-1258 records the wiring as 'Weighed and not taken'.
verdict.proposal_note: Prefer deleting over wiring the code in. Wiring it in was weighed in audit.md Phase 4 and not taken: it means five bracketed solves per piece, plus the dr_a/dx correction, to replace a cheap 1-D search. To keep the derivation, move `split_residual` into contact.rs's `#[cfg(test)]` module (it could take the tip angles as arguments so the field can go), delete `efficient_split` and `ContactPath::tip_pressure_angle`, and fix the prose references at auto.rs:1467-1475 and gear-cli main.rs:1084-1085 so check_doc_links stays green. corrections.md:564 is a historical record and needs no edit.

title: The pin-diameter range is bisected on a verdict although each end has a closed form
claim: The smallest and largest pins that seat are found by 64 halvings of `seat(d).err()`, after a doubling walk. For the involute contact limits (contact at the form radius, contact at the tip), the two seating conditions are inv α_M = K + D/d_b and tan α_M = tan α_c + D/d_b. Subtracting them gives α_M = tan α_c − K exactly, so D = d_b (tan α_M − tan α_c) in closed form, with no iteration. The bisection is exact to the mantissa but hides which condition binds, and it costs about 130 `seat` calls per space, multiplied by z in `pin_diameter_range_around`.
evidence: Derivation above (inv α = tan α − α). The code comment justifies bisection by 'which condition binds at each end is exactly what differs between an external gear, a ring and a helical one'. That is a reason to evaluate each closed-form candidate and take max/min, not to bisect.
proposal: Compute each limit's candidate diameter in closed form: contact at r_j, contact at r_a, and pin bottoming on the root (also closed form, since the pin centre is at a known radius). Take the interval they bound. Keep the bisection only as a test oracle.
validation: Agreement with the current bisection to 1e-12 mm over tests/metrology.rs's grid for external, ring and helical cases.

verdict.corrected_claim: The closed form exists only for a spur space's two contact limits: with β_b = 0, subtracting the two seat equations gives φ = u_lim + σ·h and D = σ·2r_b(tan φ − u_lim). My probe reproduces the bisection's ends to about 1e-15 mm on an external space and on a ring. With β_b ≠ 0 the pin term carries 1/cos β_b in the inv equation and not in the contact equation (nor with the same factor once the separately reported cos β_b contact fix is applied), so the two equations no longer cancel to a closed form. What remains is a transcendental equation in φ, of the form k·tan φ − φ = c, which needs a 1-D root. The bottoming limit is not closed form either: r_M = r_b/cos φ and D are coupled through inv φ, so 'the pin centre is at a known radius' is false. The proposal's validation (helical and ring cases to 1e-12 with no iteration) cannot pass as written. The cost argument is weak too: pin_diameter_range measured 15-30 µs per space in release, so about 1.5 ms for a 100-tooth gear in `pin_diameter_range_around`.
verdict.reason: I re-derived the relations from pin_seat (metrology.rs:481, 504) and probed `pin_diameter_range` against the closed form on hand-built `Space`s. Spur external, root 18.5: bisection (2.216289183563717, 3.9526306128788935) against closed (2.216289183563719, 3.952630612878889). Spur ring: agreement to 1e-15. Helical β_b = 0.3: bisection (2.111166, 3.724988), while the spur closed form gives (2.216289, 3.952631), so no closed form exists there. Root 20.35, where bottoming binds: the lower end is 3.0325, which neither contact limit gives. So the bisection on the verdict covers three kinds of condition (closed form, transcendental contact, transcendental bottoming) with one robust mechanism at negligible cost. The documented reasoning mostly holds: this is deliberate, with a small missed opportunity for spur.
verdict.evidence: Probe /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/verify-lens-continuity-2 (first version of src/main.rs), output: 'bb=0 sign=1 root=18.5 bisect=Some((2.216289183563717, 3.9526306128788935)) closed(form)=2.216289183563719 closed(tip)=3.952630612878889 t=31µs'; 'bb=0.3 sign=1 ... bisect=Some((2.111166180454185, 3.7249882847671625)) closed(form)=2.2162...'; 'bb=0 sign=1 root=20.35 bisect=Some((3.0325257389220877, 3.95...))'; 'bb=0 sign=-1 ... bisect=Some((1.0278552970899275, 1.9276553148567266)) closed(form)=1.027855297089932'.
verdict.proposal_note: Do not replace the bisection. If which condition binds matters to the UI, return it alongside the range: evaluate `seat()` just inside each end and report which check fired. Two small true defects exist here. The doc at metrology.rs:181 says 'Sixty halvings' while the loop runs `0..64` (metrology.rs:199). The helical contact radius these bounds rest on omits cos β_b, which another lens has already reported (metrology finding 1, lens-docs-accuracy-2 finding 0). My independent ball-on-helicoid computation confirms that: β_b = 0.3, D = 3.5, true contact radius 21.86317 against the code's 21.83171.

title: The parallel-axis efficiency is the first-order linearisation while the crossed one is the exact balance, so the Σ → 0 limit carries an O(μ²) seam
claim: `contact::efficiency` is 1 − μπ(1/z₁+1/z₂)(ε₁|ε₁|+ε₂|ε₂|)/(ε cos β_b), linear in μ. `CrossedPath::efficiency` integrates the exact pointwise force balance. They meet at Σ → 0 only to O(μ²). The exact parallel average has a closed form: the pointwise η(ξ) is a ratio of linear functions of ξ on each side of the pitch point, so its mean is elementary (log terms). No quadrature is needed and the seam would vanish.
evidence: crossed_sigma.txt, 17/43, μ=0.06: the crossed path η at Σ = 0.01° / 0.001° is 0.98751528 / 0.98751530; the parallel spur is 0.98740560. The gap is 1.10e-4 (documented in rationale.md:862 as the linearisation's residual). The trapezium quadrature converges cleanly: 64 samples 0.98751426, 2048 samples 0.98751528, 200k samples 0.98751530.
proposal: Replace the linearised parallel formula with the exact mean of the pointwise balance in closed form: integrate (a − bξ)/(c + dξ) over approach and recess separately. The crossed path at small Σ could then be held to it bit-for-bit in the limit. Optionally give the crossed path a closed form in the same way (the pointwise loss is a rational function of s with a |·| kink at the pitch point), replacing the 2048-point trapezium and the Brent-over-quadrature locking friction.
validation: Law: |η_crossed(Σ→0) − η_parallel| < 1e-9 for μ ∈ {0.02, 0.06, 0.1} over 14 tooth pairs. The closed form reproduces the 200k-point trapezium to 1e-12.

verdict.reason: Reproduced independently. For spur the pointwise force balance is η(ξ) = (1 + μσρ₂/r_b2)/(1 + μσρ₁/r_b1), where σ = sgn ξ, ρ₁ = r_b1·tan α + ξ and ρ₂ = r_b2·tan α − ξ. Linearised in μ, it gives exactly the code's 1 − μπ(1/z₁+1/z₂)(ε₁²+ε₂²)/ε. Each side of the pitch point is (A − Bξ)/(C + Dξ), whose integral is elementary: −(B/D)ξ + ((A + BC/D)/D)·ln(C + Dξ). For 17/43 at 20°, standard proportions, μ = 0.06, the closed form gives 0.987515299615, matching adaptive quadrature to 12 digits and the auditor's crossed Σ→0 value of 0.98751530. The linear formula gives 0.987405604352, a gap of 1.097e-4. Across μ = 0.02, 0.06, 0.1 and 0.3, gap/μ² stays at 0.032, 0.031, 0.029 and 0.024, so the gap is genuinely O(μ²). The linearisation understates η (a conservative bias) by about 1e-4 at μ = 0.06 and 2.2e-3 at μ = 0.3. The bias is recorded only as a seam (rationale.md:861-864; reference.md table 'efficiency | first order in μ'), not with its size and sign in state.md as rule 6 asks. The existing test (screw.rs ~2620-2650) accepts a 2e-4 gap, so it would not notice a change of that order.
verdict.evidence: Script /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/notes/verify-lens-continuity-2/eff.py, output: 'mu=0.06 closed=0.987515299615 quad=0.987515299615 linear=0.987405604352 gap=1.097e-04 gap/mu^2=0.0305'; 'mu=0.3 closed=0.939189781575 ... linear=0.937028021760 gap=2.162e-03'. contact.rs:414-439 is the linear formula; screw.rs:1170-1190 is the 2048-point trapezium over Contact::efficiency.
verdict.proposal_note: The closed form needs care with numerics. As μ→0, D = μσ/r_b1 → 0 and the ln form cancels catastrophically, so write it with ln_1p(Dξ/C)/D, or with its series below a stated threshold derived from f64::EPSILON rather than chosen by feel. In the approach piece at large μ, 1 − μρ₁/r_b1 can reach 0 (pointwise locking), where the log argument goes non-positive; that must be refused or reported the way the crossed path's locking is. Drive::Backward swaps approach and recess, as the current function does. A ring (negative signed r_b2) and a rack (r_b2 → ∞, B → 0) must go through the same expression, and the latter is fine. Three knock-on effects: `split_residual` is derived from the linear integrand; the golden corpus and reference tables move by about 1e-4 per mesh; and the 'never locks' reading for line contact (reference.md ~1171) could then become a threshold from the same balance, removing the second seam that table records. A closed form for the crossed path also looks possible but is a separate derivation; keep the trapezium as its oracle until then.

title: Small hard-coded brackets and nudges in the train solves
claim: The helix-for-distance solve brackets at a literal 0..89.0°. The tip-room root is nudged by a literal +1e-9 mm 'the solver's own tolerance', which is not the solver's tolerance (Tol x_tol is 1e-15 plus relative). least_distance_lead_angle uses 1e-9 / 1e-12 bracket insets and a 1e-12 right-angle test that picks the closed form, so there is a closed-form/solve seam at Σ=90° ± 1e-12.
evidence: Source reads at the listed lines.
proposal: Bracket the helix at the helix guard constant the params already define (|β| < 90°, `guard::`), and derive the nudge from the Tol actually used (e.g. `2·f64::EPSILON·|e| + tol.x_tol` in the direction of increasing room). For Σ=90° there is no need to branch: the Brent solve reproduces cbrt to 1e-15. Keep the closed form as a test oracle only.
validation: Existing tests pass. A sweep of Σ through 90° ± 1e-10 shows no step in the least-distance lead angle.

verdict.corrected_claim: The literals exist and are unexplained. At shape.rs:863 the helix-for-distance bracket's upper end is 89.0°. If a target needs more helix than that, the solve returns None and the parallel mesh is left without a sized helix; that is harmless in practice, since the distance at 89° is 57× the straight one, but it is an unstated cap. At shape.rs:1697-1700 the comment says the +1e-9 nudge is 'the solver's own tolerance'. It is not: Brent's tolerance is 2·EPS·|b| + 0.5·1e-15, about 1e-14 mm at these distances, so the comment is inaccurate and the nudge is a feel number. The Σ = 90° branch in `least_distance_lead_angle` (screw.rs:436-438) is redundant, since the Brent solve gives the same answer. Two parts of the finding are wrong. There is no measurable closed-form/solve seam: probing Σ = 90° ± {5e-13, 1e-12, 2e-12, 1e-10} rad, γ varies linearly and continuously, and the only artefact is a flat of width ±5e-13 rad worth at most 4e-13 rad in γ. And the proposal's 'helix guard constant the params already define' does not exist: `params::guard` holds cutter-depth, thickness and fillet fractions only, and params.rs:112 says the helix is deliberately not guarded there.
verdict.reason: I re-read the three sites and Tol (solve.rs:35-41; brent's tol1 at solve.rs:87), and probed Screw::least_distance_lead_angle through 90°. The dγ/dΣ-scaled differences (3.6e-13 at 1e-12, 3.6e-11 at 1e-10 for 1/40) show no step. grep for a helix guard found none.
verdict.evidence: Probe output (verify-lens-continuity-2, second main.rs): 'z=1/40 dSigma=-1e-12 gamma-closed=3.596e-13', 'dSigma=-5e-13 gamma-closed=0e0', 'dSigma=1e-12 gamma-closed=-3.597e-13', 'dSigma=1e-10 gamma-closed=-3.596e-11'; the pattern is the same for 3/30 and 17/23. shape.rs:1697-1701 reads: '// Lean to the clear side of the root by the solver's own tolerance ... hi.min(e + 1e-9)'. solve.rs:38 has 'x_tol: 1e-15'.
verdict.proposal_note: Drop the Σ = 90° branch, or keep it: either is fine, and the closed form is a better test oracle than a production branch. For the tip-room nudge, the clean fix is a bracketed solver variant that returns the end of its final bracket on the requested sign side (it already holds a and b with opposite signs), so no nudge is needed. `2·EPS·|e| + x_tol` does not guarantee room_at ≥ 0 either. For the helix bracket, no guard constant exists to reuse. Either state 89° as a named constant with its reason, or bracket to just below 90° by growing toward it as `size_reaching` does, and report the unreachable target rather than falling back silently. shape.rs:955/957 has similar `floor*(1+1e-9)` insets that deserve the same treatment.

title: Eccentric-gear play rewrites the backlash law without the kind's sign: internal pairs report play and interference swapped
claim: centre_profile_of computes sinusoid_backlash as `2·fit·(inv α_actual − inv α_ideal)`, a hand copy of Mesh::backlash that omits the `kind.sign()` factor. On an internal mesh every sample therefore has the wrong sign: slack is reported as interference and interference as slack. The UI flags the minimum in red as interference.
evidence: Probe (probes/lens-unification): z=20, x=0.2, Δx=0.3. For each tooth k, Mesh::new(tooth_k, mate, kind).backlash(fit_k) was compared with CentreProfile.sinusoid_backlash, after checking that commanded[k] equals the per-tooth Mesh a_w to 1e-9. External vs a 40-tooth mate: both [-0.003568, +0.003659], identical. Internal vs a 60-tooth ring: centre_profile [-0.008590, +0.009076], Mesh::backlash [-0.009076, +0.008590]. The worst interference (9.08 um) is reported as 8.59 um, and the positions are swapped. The only tests (gear.rs:2022, gear-wasm lib.rs:2140) assert just that the range straddles zero, and only on External. gear-wasm reaches the internal case through eccentric_mate (lib.rs:934-944).
proposal: Delete the hand-written acos/inv lines, gear.rs:986-999. For each position build the operating pressure angle through the one law: a free fn `mesh::backlash_at(kind, a_ref, alpha_t, alpha_w_ideal, a) -> Result<f64, MeshError>` that Mesh::backlash also calls, i.e. `kind.sign()*2a(inv α(a) − inv α_ideal)`. Or build the Mesh for tooth k and call .backlash(fit). Keep the RingTooSmall and domain errors as they are.
validation: New law in gear.rs tests over both kinds, both MeshSide values, and Δx in {0.05, 0.2, 0.4}: sinusoid_backlash equals [min, max] of Mesh::new(tooth_k, mate, kind).backlash(fit_k) to 1e-12. Run it against HEAD first; the Internal rows must fail.

verdict.reason: The claim holds as stated. gear.rs:999 computes `j = 2.0 * fit * (inv(alpha_actual) - inv(alpha_ideal))` with no `kind.sign()`, while Mesh::backlash (mesh.rs:349) applies `self.kind.sign()`. The function computes `sigma` at line 907 and uses it for the sums, but not here. I rebuilt the evidence with my own probe. On External the two agree to the printed precision. On Internal every row comes out negated, and the ends of the range swap. The web panel does reach this case: gear-wasm's eccentric_mate (lib.rs:645) builds MeshKind::Internal when `mate.internal`, and GearPanel.svelte:781 colours the minimum as interference. I lowered the severity from high to medium: the range is nearly symmetric, so the reader sees about 5% less worst-case interference and the ends in the wrong places, not a wildly wrong figure. The existing tests cannot catch it. They check only External and only that the range straddles zero (gear.rs:2022, gear-wasm lib.rs:2140).
verdict.evidence: Probe /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/verify-lens-unification-1 (src/main.rs): z=20, x=0.2. For each tooth k, Mesh::new(g.tooth(k), mate, kind).backlash(fit_k), after asserting that m.a_w equals commanded[k] to 1e-9. External vs z=40, dx 0.05/0.2/0.3: identical, e.g. dx=0.3 gives [-0.003568, 0.003659] both ways. Internal vs z=60: dx=0.05 gives centre_profile [-0.0002280, 0.0002302] vs Mesh [-0.000230, 0.000228]; dx=0.2 gives [-0.003717, 0.003857] vs [-0.003857, 0.003717]; dx=0.3 gives [-0.008590, 0.009076] vs [-0.009076, 0.008590].
verdict.proposal_note: Prefer the simpler form of the proposal: build `Mesh { a_w: ideal, alpha_w: α(ideal), ..}` once, or use a mesh built from `sign_e`/`sign_m`, and call `.backlash(fit)`. That also removes the second hand-written acos/domain check. Watch the MeshSide::Second case: Mesh::new expects the ring second, so building from `(mate, tooth)` needs the sign handled, not only the order. Add the proposed law over both kinds and both sides.

title: A mesh listed ring-first is silently wired as external: wrong motion ratio and a misleading refusal
claim: Shape::kind_of recognises an internal mesh only as (a = gear, b = ring). (ring, gear) returns None. Shape::wiring then maps None to MeshKind::External, under a comment saying only 'two rings in mesh' reach it. So a legitimate internal mesh stored with its members the other way round gets the external sign in the kinematic row. The motion is wrong with no error, and the solve refuses with an unrelated reason.
evidence: Probe: Preset::Planetary.build(), then a/b swapped on the sun-planet/planet-ring mesh whose b is the ring, so meshes go from [(0,1),(1,2)] to [(0,1),(2,1)], then Train::alone(..).motion(). As built, total = 7/1. Ring-first, total = -5/1, with no error. solve_train returns InPart{part:0, cause: NoCommonDistance}, not NotAMesh or anything about order. Nothing in Shape or gear-io normalises the order: only arrangements.rs:430 swaps when building a list, and a hand-written graph document or a future edit can store either order.
proposal: Make the kind a property of the pair, not of the order. Minimal fix: kind_of returns Internal for (false,true) or (true,false) on a parallel distance, and every consumer that assumes b is the ring (Mesh::new, ContactPath::new, TipRoom::at, build_cached) reads the pair through a `ring_side(k)` accessor that swaps. Alternatively normalise the order once, in Shape deserialisation and in Shape::apply. Wiring must never default: replace `.unwrap_or(MeshKind::External)` with a WiringError::NotAMesh(k). The structural fix is the signed tooth count in the Tooth/Ring finding below, where the sign travels with the member and order cannot matter.
validation: Law over every preset and arrangement: swapping a and b of every mesh leaves Train::motion's speeds and every PathReport ratio, efficiency and play identical. Plus a negative fixture: two rings in mesh returns WiringError::NotAMesh.

verdict.corrected_claim: The mechanism is real: kind_of (shape.rs:470) matches only `(false,true)`, and wiring (shape.rs:4150) turns None into External, so a ring-first mesh gives a wrong motion without any error. It can only be reached through a hand-written or hand-edited geartrain document (gear-io's HEADER says 'Editing this file by hand is expected'). Every in-code path that creates a mesh normalises the order (arrangements.rs push_mesh:430, which edits.rs uses at 394/520/562) or copies an existing order (graph.rs). What the user sees is a refusal with a misleading reason (NoCommonDistance), not a wrong ratio, because solve_train refuses and gear-wasm exposes no separate motion(). The 'wrong motion ratio' exists only inside the core and in the harness.
verdict.reason: I re-ran the auditor's probe: as built, meshes [(0,1),(1,2)] give motion 7/1 and the solve succeeds. Ring-first, [(0,1),(2,1)] gives motion -5/1 and solve Err(InPart{part:0, cause: NoCommonDistance}). The wiring comment says only 'two rings in mesh' reaches the default, which is wrong. build_cached (shape.rs:2834) would refuse with NotAMesh, but the plan fails first with the unrelated NoCommonDistance.
verdict.evidence: Probe bin src/bin/swap.rs in /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/verify-lens-unification-1 prints 'ring first: meshes [(0, 1), (2, 1)] motion Some(Ratio { num: -5, den: 1 }) solve Some(InPart { part: 0, cause: NoCommonDistance })'. gear-io/src/train.rs:360 from_toml deserialises Shape directly and calls only `relieved`, which does not normalise. grep shows no `.a =`/`.b =`/swap of mesh members in edits.rs, conditions.rs or graph.rs.
verdict.proposal_note: Normalising once at the boundary is lower risk than letting kind_of accept both orders, because more than 15 consumers (shape.rs:596-1801, 2836, Mesh::new's `p2` = ring, ContactPath, TipRoom) assume b is the ring. Put the normalisation in gear-io's `relieved()` and in the wasm train-request entry, or in a Shape method both call. Then make `wiring` refuse rather than default: `kind_of(k).ok_or(NotAMesh)`, which changes wiring() to return a Result. A two-ring mesh should get its own refusal key.

title: The rack-cut/shaper-cut split: two tooth types, three dispatch layers, a fake Tooth for every ring, and no shaper-cut external gear
claim: docs/rationale.md states 'the rack is the shaper at z_c → ∞' and 'a ring is a gear with a negative tooth count'. Neither holds in the types. Tooth (rack-cut, external) and Ring (shaper-cut, internal) are separate structs with parallel machinery: involute_at, trochoid_at, solve_junction, sections, sample_section, profile, virtual_spur, flank_ends. Their guards are separate too: transverse_thickness vs the ring's space clamps, and severed vs self-crossing. The split is re-dispatched three times: BuiltMember {Rack, Ring} (shape.rs:2365, 8 match sites), auto::Cut {ByRack, Pinned, ByShaper} (auto.rs:1068, 10 arms), and ToothOutline with two impls (strength.rs:508/573). The cut simulation is written twice as well (check_cut vs check_ring_cut). 'Is internal' is inferred from 'has a cutter' (`members[i].ring: Option<Cutter>`, kind_of at shape.rs:470), so an external gear cut by a pinion cutter cannot be stated, although ShaperCut supports MeshKind::External and only tests use that path (shaper.rs:485, equivalent_to_rack). Every ring member on every search trial also builds a full rack-cut Tooth::new of the ring's parameters ('as_gear', shape.rs:2805). Its form is never read: only params, mt, alpha and x_thick reach Mesh::new.
evidence: Function lists of tooth.rs, ring.rs and shaper.rs (grep). The as_gear consumers are all member a (never the ring) or params-only: shape.rs:2851, 2887, 3192, 3317, 3392, 3844. The ShaperCut::equivalent_to_rack callers are all tests (shaper.rs:552-857). The auto::Cut methods flank_ends, tip_radius and root_radius duplicate BuiltMember's (shape.rs:2378-2400) one for one. ring.rs:1143 and mesh.rs:838 build a 'ring_as_gear' Tooth to reach Mesh::new. The acceptance criteria differ between the two: member_is_buildable checks undercut, severed and root-round fit, while ring_is_cut_as_asked refuses any clamp at all (auto.rs:1018 vs 1057).
proposal: Target: one `Tooth` generated by one `Tool { depth, tip_round, kappa }`, where kappa = σ/r_c is the signed pitch curvature of the cutter and kappa = 0 is the rack exactly. Write the shaper corner centre in κ-safe form so the rack is the value at 0 and not a limit: R_c sin(sκ) with R_c = 1/κ − b, and r_c(1 − cos sκ) = 2 sin²(sκ/2)/κ, using sinc-style helpers. Carry the workpiece sign σ (ring = −1) on the member, i.e. a signed tooth count, and derive MeshKind from the product of the two signs. Migration: (1) add GearParams-level `Rack`/`MeshRack` data so Mesh::new takes the rack and signed counts, not &Tooth, which removes as_gear and its per-trial Tooth::new; (2) move Ring onto the ShaperCut generator behind Tooth's API (σ = −1) and delete RingMesh (see its own finding); (3) make the rack path the κ = 0 value of the same trochoid, bit-checked against today's Tooth; (4) collapse BuiltMember, auto::Cut and the ToothOutline impls into one type, keeping Cut::Pinned as a flag; (5) expose an optional cutter on any member, so a cluster gear cut by a shaper becomes an input (a feature). Risk: high. tooth.rs's four 'looks wrong but is not' items and the fillet cap must survive, so gate each step with the existing rack-simulation, shaper-convergence and golden checks.
validation: Step 3: bit-identical profiles, clamps and ratings on the whole tests/common grid and the golden corpus at κ = 0. Existing shaper convergence tests (first order in 1/z_c) turned into equality at κ = 0. check_cut and check_ring_cut merged, then run over both σ and several κ. Relief and arrangement sweeps unchanged. Timing: every_search_is_quick_enough_to_type_over should get faster, since the redundant Tooth per ring per trial is gone.

verdict.corrected_claim: The generation duplication is real. Tooth and Ring carry parallel machinery, the rack/shaper split is dispatched three times (BuiltMember shape.rs:2365, auto::Cut auto.rs:1068 whose flank_ends/tip_radius/root_radius mirror BuiltMember's one for one, and ToothOutline strength.rs:508/573), and check_cut/check_ring_cut (verify.rs:129/540) are two simulations. Every ring cut in build_cached (shape.rs:2808-2811) also builds a full rack-cut `Tooth::new(p)` as `as_gear`. Only its params, mt and alpha are ever read, via Mesh::new/x_thick (mesh.rs:745), ContactPath and TipRoom as member a. An external gear cut by a pinion cutter cannot be stated: `members[i].ring: Option<Cutter>` doubles as 'is internal', and ShaperCut::equivalent_to_rack has only test callers. But 'neither rule holds in the types' overstates it. rationale.md scopes 'a ring is a gear with a negative tooth count' to *meshing* relations ('Every internal meshing relation is the external one under that sign'), and it documents the rack/shaper generation split as deliberate with a stated trigger ('What would change this: a second shaper-cut member', rationale.md ~1010).
verdict.reason: Every factual sub-claim I checked holds: the grep of ShaperCut callers, the as_gear readers (shape.rs:2851, 2887, 3192, 3317, 3392, 3844 are all member a or params-only), the auto::Cut arms, and the Tooth::new-does-not-alter-params check (tooth.rs:425 reads params and stores them unchanged). The framing as a violation of the doc's rule is only half right. The owner's goal of one model per phenomenon does argue against the documented deferral: the doc's trigger (a second shaper-cut member) is exactly the missing feature. So the unification is a legitimate high-effort refactor, but not a correctness defect.
verdict.evidence: shape.rs:2365-2410 (BuiltMember and its matches), shape.rs:2808-2815 (`as_gear: Tooth::new(p)` per ring per cache miss), mesh.rs:247-288 (Mesh::new reads g2 only through params and x_thick), auto.rs:1088-1121 (Cut arms), shaper.rs:485 plus callers at 552-857 all inside `#[cfg(test)]` (line 532), rationale.md:80 and ~1005-1020.
verdict.proposal_note: Stage it by risk. Step 1 alone, letting Mesh::new take (GearParams-level rack, signed counts) so BuiltMember::Ring no longer needs `as_gear`, is small, removes a per-trial Tooth::new and loses nothing. Steps 2-5 (the κ-parameterised single generator) are a redesign that must preserve tooth.rs's four 'looks wrong but is not' items and bit-identity at κ=0. Only commit to them together with the feature they enable (a shaper-cut external member). Otherwise it is a large rewrite against a documented, reasoned deferral.

title: RingMesh is a second internal-mesh model; production reads only its tip clearance
claim: ring::mesh_with / mesh_at / described_at recompute, for an internal pair: the reference geometry (via operating_geometry again, with its own compatibility check), the operating angle (cos α' = a_ref cos α_t / a' written again), a contact ratio from the textbook internal formula, the conjugate radii, and trochoid/involute interference. All of these already come from Mesh, ContactPath and MeshReport::flank_interference. Production (TipRoom::at) keeps only tip_interference and tip_margin; the rest feeds gear-cli meshsweep and tests. The main cross-check test compares described_at, which itself calls mesh::conjugate_radius, against Mesh::contact_radius_at, i.e. the general form against itself.
evidence: TipRoom::at (train/mod.rs:584) maps a RingMesh to {tip_interference, tip_margin, far_gap}. The TipRoom doc (mod.rs:549) says the other two interferences 'are every mesh's… answered in two places' and were already moved. ring.rs:1047-1089 re-derives α' and the contact ratio. The test at ring.rs:1121 compares values both produced by conjugate_radius.
proposal: Reduce ring.rs's mesh API to `pub fn tip_clearance(ring, pinion, a) -> f64` (the one internal-only question, ring.rs:940), and have TipRoom::at call it directly. Delete RingMesh, mesh_with, mesh_at, reference_geometry and described_at. Port gear-cli meshsweep to Mesh::new + ContactPath + flank_interference, which is what a train reports. Replace the self-comparison test with a comparison of tip_clearance against the cut simulation's outlines (verify::contact_phase_from_outlines already exists).
validation: The golden corpus for meshsweep/hulasweep may change only in field sourcing; every number must match to its printed precision. The tip-margin tests at ring.rs:1893-1966 keep passing against tip_clearance.

verdict.reason: Production reaches ring::mesh_at only through TipRoom::at (train/mod.rs:584), which keeps tip_interference, tip_margin and a far_gap it computes itself. The rest of RingMesh (alpha_w, contact_ratio, the two conjugate radii, trochoid/involute flags) feeds only gear-cli mesh_sweep (main.rs:1192) and tests. described_at (ring.rs:1041) re-derives cos α' = a_ref cos α_t / a' and its own compatibility check (reference_geometry, ring.rs:1020) beside Mesh::new/pressure_angle_at. The cross-check test at ring.rs:1121 is circular: its doc says mesh_with uses 'the internal relation written out here', but described_at calls crate::mesh::conjugate_radius (ring.rs:1060-1063), and Mesh::contact_radius_at calls the same function (mesh.rs:578). mesh.rs:568's '[verified: it reproduces ring::mesh_with's two readings to the bit' is circular for the same reason. The only independent content left in described_at is the textbook internal contact-ratio formula, which ContactPath already provides.
verdict.evidence: ring.rs:997-1107 read in full. train/mod.rs:579-589. `grep ring::mesh_with|mesh_at|described_at|RingMesh` outside ring.rs gives only doc comments plus train/mod.rs:584 and gear-cli main.rs:1192.
verdict.proposal_note: Keep the one independent check the module still offers: turn the self-comparison test into a comparison of ContactPath's contact ratio against the textbook internal formula (a written-out closed form), or against verify's outline-based contact phase, before deleting it. The meshsweep golden line prints contact ratio, alpha_w and three flags, so re-source them from Mesh/ContactPath/MeshReport and confirm the recorded output does not move.

title: The line-contact play re-derives angular_play by hand, and hides a failed backlash as zero
claim: mesh.rs documents angular_play as 'one function rather than a formula written once per stage kind'. play_of's Line arm nevertheless writes `backlash(a)·|Σz|/a + 2π·slide/p_bn`, with p_bn = π m_n cos α_n typed out instead of plane::base_pitch, and β_b recomputed. The Point arm calls p.angular_play. The two are the same law: with j_n = j_t cos α_wt cos β_b, 2π j_n/(z p_bn) = j_t/r_w. So they agree today, but as two copies. Separately, `.backlash(a).unwrap_or(0.0)` turns a distance below the base-circle limit (MeshError::CentreDistanceTooSmall) into 'zero play' inside a tolerance band, where it should be a refusal or NaN.
evidence: shape.rs:3524-3540 read directly. The algebraic identity was checked by hand above. The Mesh::angular_backlash doc (mesh.rs:405-418) states the same j·|Σz|/(a z) relation that the arm re-multiplies by z.
proposal: Give LineBuilt an `angular_play(a, axial, z)` that mirrors PointBuilt's: normal gap = design.backlash(a)? · cos α_t(a) · cos β_b + axial · sin β_b, then mesh::angular_play(gap, z, plane::base_pitch(m_n, α_n)). play_of then becomes one call on BuiltContact with no match. Propagate the error: a band end below the base-circle limit should be reported (NaN or a note), not read as 0.
validation: Law: for every preset, row_play from the new LineBuilt::angular_play equals the current value to 1e-12 at all three band points. Negative fixture: a tolerance_minus that crosses the base-circle limit yields a note or NaN, not 0.

verdict.reason: play_of's Line arm (shape.rs:3524-3533) writes `backlash(a)·|Σz|/a + 2π·slide/p_bn`, with `p_bn = π m_n cos α_n` typed out and β_b recomputed, while the Point arm calls mesh::angular_play through PointBuilt::angular_play (shape.rs:2631). I checked the identity independently. p_bn = p_bt cos β_b and cos α_wt = a_ref cos α_t / a with a_ref = m_t|Σz|/2, so 2π(j_t cos α_wt cos β_b)/(z p_bn) = j_t|Σz|/(a z). Times z this gives the row form, so the two arms are one law written twice. `.unwrap_or(0.0)` turns CentreDistanceTooSmall into zero play: a line mesh reads negative backlash just above the base-circle limit and exactly 0 just below it, a discontinuity. tolerance_minus is unbounded (grep: no validation, only defaults of 0.02). Reaching the limit takes about 3.6 mm on the default 17/43 m=2 pair, but only tenths of a mm on a few-tooth-difference internal (hula-like) mesh, so it is rare but reachable. Severity is low.
verdict.evidence: shape.rs:3517-3542, mesh.rs:224-238, and the algebra above. `grep tolerance_minus` over gear-core finds no bound anywhere (arrangements.rs:464, shape.rs:284, 3553, 3569).
verdict.proposal_note: Before unifying, decide the sign convention, because the two arms differ today beyond their form. The Point arm floors the separation at zero (`(a - s.centre_distance).max(0.0)`, shape.rs:2638), while the Line arm reports negative play as interference; see the missed item. Surface an out-of-domain band end as a note, not NaN, because Backlash::banded feeds straight into rendered degrees.

title: English lives in gear-core twice: Display impls restate the catalogue in other words and carry detail the Note drops
claim: Rule 2 says every word lives in strings_<code>.toml. Yet TrainError, MeshError, MeasurementError and EditRefused each carry a hand-written English Display 'for the CLI and Debug'. TrainError's Display restates every ScrewError message inline instead of delegating, as its note() does. The texts disagree: ScrewError::WormTooThin reads 'the first member has no lead angle: given a diameter, the worm is too thin … put the helical member first and the spur one second' in Display but 'the first member has no lead angle; put the helical member first and the spur one second' in the catalogue. The Note also drops information the Display keeps: TrainError::Wiring(_) becomes the generic ERROR_TRAIN_WIRING, while Display names the member or mesh (WiringError index). So the browser user gets less than the CLI user.
evidence: Read train/mod.rs:1660-1780 and mesh.rs:750-780. Compared strings_en.toml:186 and :194 and :200 with the Display arms. No test ties the two, and check_strings.py covers only `ui.` keys.
proposal: Delete the English Display bodies in gear-core. Implement Display generically as `self.note().key` plus values (still useful for Debug), and have gear-cli render errors through gear_io::strings::Catalogue::for_language("en"), the path the browser takes. Put the WiringError index into the note (`.count("member", i+1)` / `.count("mesh", k+1)`), with keys error.train_wiring_no_teeth / _no_common_frame / _not_a_mesh / _not_a_coupling in all five catalogues. The golden corpus records CLI error text, so re-record it deliberately.
validation: gear_io::strings' 'fire every note' test then covers every error variant. Add a test that renders every TrainError variant through the English catalogue and asserts no {placeholder} is left and the index appears where one exists. `grep -n 'impl std::fmt::Display' crates/gear-core/src` should then show only Ratio and jgma::Class.

verdict.reason: TrainError (train/mod.rs:1712), MeshError (mesh.rs:766), MeasurementError (metrology.rs:748) and EditRefused (edits.rs:171) each have an English Display in gear-core, against rule 2. TrainError's Display restates each ScrewError message instead of delegating, and the texts differ from strings_en.toml: screw_worm_too_thin (line 194) is the short form, Display the long one; screw_axes_are_parallel ('a worm stage needs non-parallel shafts') differs from Display ('parallel axes: … a parallel pair is a spur stage'); train_no_contact 'never contact' differs from 'never come into contact'. The Note drops information Display keeps: `Self::Wiring(_) => ERROR_TRAIN_WIRING`, a generic text whose English does not even mention the NotAMesh or NotACoupling causes. The catalogue's own [error] header (strings_en.toml:181-184) says 'These were Display impls inside gear-core', which is stale: they still are. gear-wasm never uses these Display impls (its `e.to_string()` calls are on serde/toml/gear-io errors), so only the CLI and Debug read them.
verdict.evidence: train/mod.rs:1666-1790 read in full. strings_en.toml:180-203. `grep 'impl std::fmt::Display' gear-core/src` gives mesh.rs:766, metrology.rs:748, jgma.rs:77, train/edits.rs:171, train/mod.rs:1712, plus ratio.rs:204 (`impl fmt::Display`).
verdict.proposal_note: Sound. When rendering the CLI through Catalogue 'en', keep Debug derived rather than hand-written, since Debug already carries the structure. Also put the part index of InPart in the note (mod.rs:1693 drops it on purpose for the wire, but the CLI prints it). Re-record the golden corpus deliberately.

title: The power flow enumerates 2^M direction assignments over the whole train: exponential time, and a u32 shift that wraps at 32 meshes
claim: flow::solve runs a least-squares solve for every one of the 2^M assignments of mesh power direction and keeps the best. It is called once per case over the whole train, and again for paths. So solve time doubles with each mesh, which contradicts rule 3 ('a full train solve is microseconds'). The loop bound is `1u32 << m`: overflow checks are off in the release and wasm profiles, so from 32 meshes the shift wraps and only one assignment is tried (unreachable today only because 2^31 solves never finish). The comment says 'the first consistent one is the answer' but the code keeps the highest-efficiency one.
evidence: Probe, native release, Train::chained(n × Preset::Planetary) with one fatigue case. Meshes: 12 → 15.0 ms, 14 → 73 ms, 16 → 334 ms, 18 → 1.66 s, about 4.6× per two meshes. wasm opt 'z' runs about 1.6× slower (Cargo.toml profile note), so about 2.7 s per keystroke at 18 meshes. A spur chain stays near 1 ms to 13 meshes, so the growth is where Backward assignments are needed. No mesh cap exists (no match for MAX_MESH or meshes.len() > in the crate).
proposal: Infer the directions, then verify, instead of enumerating. (1) Solve the ideal flow (η = 1; the rowspace solve already exists) and take each mesh's direction from the sign of its driving power. (2) Solve the lossy system once with those directions and run the existing consistency and loss checks. (3) Enumerate only the meshes whose ideal power is within ZERO·P_in (idle or near-circulating), plus any mesh that fails the check, which is 2^k with k usually 0. Keep full enumeration as a test oracle (cfg(test)) for small M. Use u64 and refuse M > 20 with a note if the fallback ever needs more. Fix the 'first consistent' comment or the selection rule so they agree.
validation: Law over every preset, arrangement, both load directions and locked/self-locking worms: the inferred flow equals the enumerated flow (directions, factors, shaft torques, efficiency, mesh_powers) to 1e-12. Timing test: 9 chained planetary sets (18 meshes) solve in under 5 ms. Pennestrì η₀^w and hula laws unchanged.

verdict.reason: Holds as stated. flow::solve loops `for assignment in 0..(1u32 << m)` (flow.rs:223) and runs a Gaussian elimination for every assignment, with no early exit. It is called once per case (mod.rs:4486) and four more times per path (`flowing` at mod.rs:3497-3505: moving and resting, both directions). With overflow checks off in release and wasm, `1u32 << 32` masks to `1 << 0`, so at 32 meshes the loop tries one assignment. The comment at flow.rs:342-345 says 'the first consistent one is the answer', but the code keeps the highest-efficiency one (`efficiency > b.efficiency`). One detail of the evidence is wrong: a spur chain does not stay near 1 ms. It grows too, about 1.7x per mesh, because the loop always enumerates every assignment.
verdict.evidence: My own probe (/home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/notes/verify-lens-unification-2/timing_probe.rs), native release, one fatigue case, the machine shared with other builds. Chained Preset::Planetary, meshes then ms: 2 0.30, 4 1.03, 6 2.94, 8 8.46, 10 24.8, 12 90.7, 14 363, 16 1639, 18 7892, about 4.5x per two meshes, i.e. 2^M. Chained Preset::Spur: 1 0.14, 2 0.22, 3 0.47, 4 0.85, 5 1.52, 6 2.63, 7 4.44, 8 7.30 ms. flow.rs:11 states '2^M assumptions' openly, but no document names the cost and nothing caps M. Cargo.toml [profile.release]/[profile.wasm] set no overflow-checks, so they are off.
verdict.proposal_note: The inference-then-verify plan is sound, with one caveat. The current selection rule keeps the most efficient of several consistent assignments. When a worm locks, or a mesh carries near-zero or circulating power, more than one assignment can be consistent with different efficiencies, and the ideal-sign assignment need not be the most efficient. The fallback enumeration must therefore cover every mesh whose ideal power is near zero or whose η in one direction is 0 or non-finite, and the equality law against the full enumeration must include the self-locking worm presets and the back-driven cases. Replace `1u32 << m` with a checked u64 bound in either case.

title: Two efficiency models for one phenomenon: a first-order-in-μ loss for line contacts, the exact force balance for point contacts
claim: A parallel mesh's efficiency is 1 − μ·mean|v_s|/(v_b cos β_b), the power loss linearised in μ (contact.rs:414). A crossed mesh's is the path average of ContactPoint::efficiency, the exact friction balance (screw.rs:1176), which already applies to parallel axes: contact.rs's sliding vector and ContactPoint are written for any axis pair. The two meet at Σ → 0 only to O(μ²) (rationale.md:862 measures the gap falling linearly with μ). They differ in kind, too: the line model has one value both directions and never locks; the balance is directional and has a threshold. A train mixing both carries two conventions in one flow. In addition, a crossed mesh whose zone vanishes falls back to the pitch-point formula (shape.rs:2489), which is a third reading and not the zone average's limit when the contact is off the pitch point (shifted pairs).
evidence: contact.rs tests efficiency_is_the_integral_of_the_sliding_vector and efficiency_matches_a_numerical_average_of_the_instantaneous_loss both check the linearised form against a linearised numeric average, not the balance. reference.md:1166 lists 'efficiency: first order in μ' as a recorded seam. The rule-6 size and sign of the linearisation bias are not stated in state.md (grep 'lineari' finds only corrections.md:430 and rationale.md:1046, both about ring roots).
proposal: Make the zone-averaged ContactPoint::efficiency the one model for every mesh. A line contact samples its transverse path of contact; the sliding and the normal are already general. Keep the closed form as the law it reduces to at first order in μ, in tests. Replace the pitch-point fallback for an empty crossed zone with the balance at the zone's collapse point, or report no efficiency. At minimum, record the linearisation's size and sign in docs/state.md per rule 6.
validation: Law: the balance-average efficiency minus the closed form is O(μ²) (the ratio of gaps at μ and μ/2 tends to 4) on a grid of spur and helical pairs. At Σ = 0.01° the point and line efficiencies agree to 1e-6, where today the tolerance is 2e-3. The Pennestrì and hula laws re-run with the new η₀.

verdict.corrected_claim: The two efficiency models do coexist, and they differ at O(μ²). The gap is about 0.01 points (98.787 % against 98.777 % at Σ = 0.02°; the closed form is the lower, conservative one). The rule-6 record of that size and sign is missing from docs/state.md; it appears only in screw.rs and crossed.rs test docs, rationale.md:860-864 and corrections.md:448. The unification itself is not clearly worth making. The linear closed form carries the closed-form optimality condition used by the efficiency search (contact.rs:440ff, efficient_split). The O(μ²) law the validation asks for already exists as a test (screw.rs the_friction_balance_meets_the_parallel_model_at_its_limit). The 'third reading' fallback is the same balance evaluated at the pitch point, and it fires only when there is no path of contact at all (PointBuilt::zone returns None only when self.path is None).
verdict.reason: The factual core is right: contact.rs:414 is first order in μ and symmetric in direction, screw.rs uses the exact balance, and shape.rs:2482-2493 falls back to the pitch-point formula. But the finding's evidence says only linearised-against-linearised tests exist, and it misses the screw.rs test that already asserts the balance-minus-closed-form gap shrinks with μ and falls below 1e-3 of the loss. Making the zone-averaged balance the one model for line contacts would replace a closed form (and its analytic shift-division optimum) with sampling, which cuts against the closed-form goal, to recover about 0.01 points. The documented choice that a line contact never locks (reference.md:1171-1176) holds up: the first-order model says nothing about locking. The part that should be acted on is the rule-6 record in state.md.
verdict.evidence: screw.rs:2568-2640 (test asserts the share strictly decreasing over μ ∈ {0.12, 0.06, 0.03, 0.01, 0.003} and < 1e-3); crossed.rs:990-1045 (parallel + 2e-4 allowance, balance 'a hundredth of a point above'); grep -n -i efficien docs/state.md finds no linearisation entry in 'Known-approximate'; contact::efficiency is used by auto.rs:1271 and 2800 (search objective) and train/mod.rs:5732; shape.rs:2499-2504 zone() is None only when path is None.
verdict.proposal_note: Keep the closed form as the line-contact model. Add one bullet under state.md 'Known-approximate': 'Parallel-axis efficiency is first order in μ: it sits about 0.01 points below the exact friction balance at μ = 0.06 on 17/43, and the gap is O(μ²); conservative.' If an exact parallel figure is ever wanted, the instantaneous exact spur/helical balance integrates in closed form (a log term), which keeps a closed form. The zone average is not needed for that.

title: The rating's line/point seams are a discontinuity at Σ = 0 (peak pressure 3-6 %, pitch pressure 0.5-3 % with friction)
claim: Line and point contacts are rated through two pipelines. The line is rated once at a probe width and scaled per case, with the flank load as the transverse projection and single-pair bounds one transverse base pitch in along the path. The point is rated case by case, with the flank load from the friction balance and single-pair bounds one normal base pitch in along the line of action. A designer turning a shaft angle from 0 to 0.01° sees the peak pressure step by 3-6 % and, at μ = 0.08, the pitch pressure step by 0.5-3 %. The test asserts the seam exists, so it is recorded rather than closed.
evidence: the_two_contacts_report_one_patch_at_the_limit (train/mod.rs:6141-6185) asserts (l.max_pressure − p.max_pressure)/l.max_pressure > 3e-2 with a 6e-2 tolerance, and a friction gap in 0.005..0.03. reference.md:1152 tabulates 1.5 % and 5 %.
proposal: Pick one convention per quantity and use it for both contacts. Flank load: the balance's F(±n̂ + μv̂) for both, which also makes the line rating direction-aware. Single-pair zone: one definition in terms of contact spacing measured along the direction the path is parameterised in, applied to both. The probe-and-scale shortcut can stay for line contacts where it is exact (the power split is linear in torque) but should read the same force.
validation: The seam test is inverted to 'closes': at Σ = 0.01° every MeshReport field meets the line value to 1e-3, and the peak pressure is continuous across Σ = 0 on a sweep Σ ∈ {0, 1e-3, 1e-2, 0.1}°.

verdict.corrected_claim: Two seams are real at Σ → 0: peak pressure about 5 % and pitch pressure about 1.5 % at μ = 0.08. Both are already recorded with size and sign in docs/state.md:700-710 ('the parallel figure is the higher on both') and reference.md:1150-1170, as rule 6 asks. The pitch-pressure seam is Coulomb friction's own discontinuity at zero slip, not a convention to unify: at Σ = 0.01° there is a real (tiny) lengthwise slip, so μF_n acts in a definite direction; at Σ = 0 the pitch point has no slip and the friction force is anywhere in its cone. Only the peak-pressure seam, a transverse against a normal base-pitch definition of the single-pair point, is a convention that one definition could close.
verdict.reason: The finding reads the test correctly. But it presents as open what the docs record with size and sign, and its flank-load proposal is ill-posed. Applying F(±n̂ + μv̂) to a line contact needs v̂, which is undefined at the parallel pitch point where sliding is exactly zero. So the proposal would not make the line rating continuous there: it would import the discontinuity into every parallel rating. It would also depart from the ISO 6336-2 convention of rating contact stress without friction. The Σ → 0 limit is also where the point model is known to be degenerate (state.md:711-717: at 0.01° the contact slides 95 mm off the face), so continuity across Σ = 0 is not a meaningful user path.
verdict.evidence: train/mod.rs:6105-6185 (test tolerances: peak within 6e-2 and > 3e-2, friction gap within 0.005..0.03); docs/state.md:700-710; reference.md:1152-1170; shape.rs:2482-2493.
verdict.proposal_note: Drop the flank-load unification. If anything is changed, define the single-pair point for both contacts as one contact spacing along the path parameterisation (the normal base pitch along the line of action projects onto the transverse path as p_bn·cos β_b, against p_bt = p_bn / cos β_b, hence the cos² β_b). Keep the seam test as a recorded seam until that is done.

title: The admissible-range bounds hand-copy the tooth's clamp rules
claim: The reference tooth thickness `m(π/2 + 2(x+x_s) tan α_n)/cos β` is written in tooth.rs:834, auto.rs:357, auto.rs:678 and ring.rs:246 (plus ring.rs:358 for the cutter). The fillet-fit cap `w_tip cos α_t/(2(1 − sin α_t))` and 0.95·min(b_d, ρ_fit) are written in tooth.rs:906-916 and again in auto.rs:679-685. The thickness bounds in admissible_profile_shift (auto.rs:311-312) are the inverse of transverse_thickness's clamps. They agree today, but as copies.
evidence: Probe: admissible_ranges().root_radius.max against the bisected threshold at which Tooth::new raises clamp.fillet_capped, over 10 cases (z 8-40, x −0.3 to 1.5, β 0/20°, a shallow cut at x = 1.22 and 1.4, dedendum 3). Every case agrees within 4e-17. So this is duplication, not a wrong answer.
proposal: Expose the rules once, on the tool: `GearParams::reference_thickness(x)` (transverse, with x_s), and `Rack::fillet_cap(params, st, bd) -> f64`, called by Rack::wanted_by and by ranges_at_shift. Also `Tooth::thickness_at(radius)` carrying σ, so auto.rs:737 and auto.rs:358-363 stop re-deriving 2r(ψ_b − inv) and Ring::tooth_thickness_at becomes the σ = −1 value.
validation: The probe's equality made a permanent law in auto.rs tests (bound equals clamp threshold) over the tests/common grid, including eccentric gears. The golden corpus unchanged.

verdict.corrected_claim: The copies are real, and they already disagree in one corner. auto.rs:676-685 computes the fillet cap from the uncapped bd = m(dedendum − x), while Rack::wanted_by (tooth.rs:896-905) first caps bd at MAX_CUTTER_DEPTH_FRACTION_OF_R·r. Whenever the dedendum exceeds 0.9 r/m, admissible_ranges().root_radius.max is therefore tighter than the tooth's actual clamp threshold. That condition itself lies outside the dedendum's own admissible range, so the error is conservative and flagged alongside, but it is exactly the drift the duplication risks.
verdict.reason: All the cited sites were re-read: tooth.rs:834 and auto.rs:357/678 and ring.rs:246 each write m(π/2 + 2(x + x_s) tan α_n)/cos β; the fillet-fit cap and 0.95·min(bd, ρ_fit) are written in tooth.rs:906-916 and auto.rs:679-685; auto.rs:311-312 invert transverse_thickness's clamps (checked algebraically: st ≤ MIN·m ⇔ π/2 + 2x tan α ≤ MIN cos β, and st_max = FRAC·π·m_t ⇔ ≤ FRAC·π). The auditor's agreement reproduces on in-range inputs, including shallow cuts, where admissible_ranges handles d_shared. It does not hold where the tooth caps bd.
verdict.evidence: Probe /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/notes/verify-lens-unification-2/root_radius_probe.rs bisects the root_radius at which Tooth::new fires clamp.fillet_capped and compares it with admissible_ranges(p, 2.0).root_radius.max. Agreement within 4e-17 for z17 x0/1.22/1.24/1.4, z8 x0.5, z30 b20, z40 x1.5 b20, z20 x1.249, z6, z4. Disagreement: z2 x0 d1.25 bound 0.4483 against threshold 0.6211 (tooth bd/m = 0.90); z2 x0.3 bound 0.4483 against 0.4730; z3 x0 d2.0 bound 0.0780 against 0.3989 (bd/m = 1.35); z3 x0.2 d1.6 bound 0.2755 against 0.3002.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposal is right, and the shared helper must take the bd after the tooth's depth clamps. Better still, have Rack::wanted_by and ranges_at_shift call one function (bd_clamped, st) → ρ_cap, so the depth clamp cannot be omitted again. Add the equality law over the tests/common grid, including tooth counts 1-3 and out-of-range dedenda, not only the auditor's ten in-range cases.

title: Remaining rule-4 residue: integer and pair rules re-matched on MeshKind
claim: shape.rs:689 matches External => 1 / Internal => −1 by hand, which mesh.rs:88 says must go through MeshKind::signed ('a caller turning sign() into an integer is a second place the convention could be written down'). shape.rs:1056 writes the thickness-mod pair rule as `Internal => x, _ => 2 − x`, which is `1 + σ(1 − x)`. shape.rs:1465 re-derives the involute-domain bound inv α_t/(2 tan α_n) that operating_geometry enforces. shape.rs:1617 re-derives the base-circle limit a_ref cos α_t, with an unexplained (1 + 1e-6).
evidence: Read at the cited lines. The matches.txt inventory lists the MeshKind matches in production: shape.rs:676, 689, 1002, 1056.
proposal: `kind.signed(i64::from(teeth))`; `MeshKind::mate_thickness_mod(k) = 1 + σ(1 − k)` next to sign(); `mesh::min_shift_sum(alpha_t, alpha_n, sum_z)` and `mesh::base_circle_limit(mt, alpha_t, sum_z)` in mesh.rs, used by shift_sum_for, pressure_angle_at and the two shape.rs sites. The 1e-6 becomes a named step next to pull_in's.
validation: Relief laws and every_arrangement_of_a_set_solves unchanged. grep 'MeshKind::Internal =>' in production returns only mesh.rs.

verdict.reason: All four sites read as claimed. shape.rs:689-692 matches External => 1 / Internal => -1 by hand, while MeshKind::signed (mesh.rs:98-103) exists and its doc explicitly forbids a second copy. shape.rs:1056-1059 writes the mate rule `Internal => x, _ => 2 - x`, which equals 1 + σ(1 − x). shape.rs:1463-1464 re-derives the involute-domain floor −inv α_t·Σz/(2 tan α_n) ≤ Σx that operating_geometry (mesh.rs:151-152) enforces implicitly through inv_inverse. shape.rs:1617-1621 rewrites the base-circle limit a_ref·cos α_t with an unexplained `* (1.0 + 1e-6)`.
verdict.evidence: Read at shape.rs:670-695, 1045-1062, 1450-1475, 1600-1625 and mesh.rs:70-110, 141-176. kind_of (shape.rs:470-480) returns None for crossed meshes and for a ring-first mesh, which the `_ =>` arm silently treats as external in the thickness rule.
verdict.proposal_note: When moving the thickness rule to MeshKind, keep what happens to the None (crossed) arm explicit. Today a crossed mesh gets 2 − x through the wildcard, and `kind_of(k).map_or(2 - x, |k| k.mate_thickness_mod(x))` would keep that without hiding it. For the 1e-6 floor, prefer asking pressure_angle_at / shift_sum_for for the smallest admissible distance over a named relative epsilon.
