title: The map says every transcendental step goes through solve.rs; several hand-rolled searches do not
claim: CLAUDE.md, on solve.rs: 'Two bracketed root finders. Every transcendental step routes through them'. Several code paths run their own searches instead. There are fixed 64-step predicate bisections for the pin-size range (metrology.rs:200) and the eccentric amplitude (gear.rs:1119). There are bracket-growing walks with literal caps and growth factors: ×1.4 up to 64 times (ring.rs:543), ×2 up to 60 times (shape.rs:946), and a 1 % step growing ×1.5 up to 40 times outward, 80 inward, floored at 1e-12 (shape.rs:1640-1690).
evidence: The loops are quoted at the locations listed. Some of these are bisections on a boolean verdict, which brent cannot take, so the claim is too strong rather than the code wrong. The bracket-growing, though, is written four times with four different constants.
proposal: Add `solve::bracket_outward(f, from, step, grow, limit) -> Option<(f64, f64)>` and `solve::bisect_predicate(pred, lo, hi) -> f64` to solve.rs, and route the four walks and two bisections through them. Name each cap by what it bounds (e.g. 'a pinion leaves its ring within two reference distances'). Then the map's claim becomes true.
validation: The golden corpus and the suite are unchanged bit for bit. grep for `for _ in 0..` outside solve.rs, elliptic.rs and the tests returns only non-search loops.

verdict.reason: CLAUDE.md:62's 'Every transcendental step routes through them' is too strong, but less so than claimed. Every bracket-growing walk the finding cites ends in solve::brent (ring.rs:545, shape.rs:959, shape.rs:1694), so the root step does route through solve.rs. Only the bracket search is written by hand. The pure predicate bisections do bypass solve.rs: metrology.rs:200 (together with its own ×2-up-to-64 growth at :191-197, which the finding missed) and gear.rs:1119. The finding's count 'four times with four different constants' is wrong the other way: hand-grown brackets appear about nine times. They are tooth.rs:594 and :618 (named constants in a `search` module), auto.rs:136-144 (MINIMUM_SHIFT_BRACKET_STEPS, ×2), hertz.rs:420 (×2, with a floor derived from the type), ring.rs:543 (×1.4, 64), shape.rs:946 (×2, 60), shape.rs:1645 and :1667 (1 %, ×1.5, 40/80, 1e-12), shape.rs:2356 pull_in (×2 from 1e-9 span), and metrology.rs:191. They range from named and argued constants (tooth.rs, hertz.rs) to bare literals (ring.rs 64/1.4, shape.rs 60, 40/80/1.5/0.01/1e-12).
verdict.evidence: Ran `grep -n 'for _ in 0\.\.\|\*= 2\.0;\|\*= 1\.[0-9]\|0\.5 \* (lo + hi)'` over gear-core/src, then read each hit in context: metrology.rs:185-215, gear.rs:1105-1135, ring.rs:530-550, shape.rs:930-965, shape.rs:1630-1700, shape.rs:2345-2360, hertz.rs:410-430, auto.rs:130-150 and tooth.rs:585-625.
verdict.corrected_claim: Every root closes in solve::brent or newton_bracketed. The bracket around it, though, is grown by hand at about nine sites with different growth factors and caps, several of them bare literals. Two predicate bisections (metrology.rs:200, gear.rs:1119) do not route through solve.rs at all. CLAUDE.md:62 should say 'every root', not 'every transcendental step', or solve.rs should own the bracket and predicate bisection too.
verdict.proposal_note: A solve::bracket_outward helper is a good unification. It has to cover the variants actually present: a walk that halves on NaN (shape.rs:1645-1690, pull_in), a cap given as a distance rather than a count (shape.rs reach), and a type-derived floor (hertz.rs). tooth.rs's `search` constants show the naming to copy. 'Bit for bit unchanged' is only expected if each site keeps its own step sequence. A shared growth factor would move roots within brent's tolerance and could move the golden corpus.

title: state.md figures and descriptions left over from retired solvers
claim: Three statements describe solvers or presets that no longer exist. (a) There is one objective: `trial_efficiency`, the product of every mesh's efficiency, maximised over the whole box or per component (shape.rs:1877-1902, 2206-2210). There is no per-kind objective or per-kind variable set. (b) No hula preset exists (CLAUDE.md says so, and arrangements::hula has no Preset). The harness never prints 0.998/0.996. verdict.evidence: state.md:486-488: 'The spur pair, the planetary set and the hula stage each have their own free variables and their own objective over one shared search'. shape.rs:1877 `let objective = |v, only| ... self.trial_efficiency(...)` is the only objective. Drop the sentence; the over-prediction table in the same bullet (0.06 % at 0.999 ... 29.4 % at 0.5) already gives the size. For (c), timings are not deterministic, so check_figures cannot gate them. title: state.md says gear.rs is the only place a gear is drawn
claim: The Layout table says '`Gear` — the assembly, and the only place a gear is drawn.' The ring tab is drawn by `Ring::profile` (ring.rs:827) through `ring_profile_impl`, and DXF output goes through outline.rs.
evidence: lib.rs:605-611: `ring_of(&req).profile(points_per_tooth)`, where ring_of returns a `gear_core::ring::Ring`.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. A ring is drawn by its own code: `Ring::profile` (ring.rs:827, a separate half-profile mirror-and-replicate loop) and `Ring::outline` (outline.rs:250-263, `impl crate::ring::Ring`). title: A broken link from corrections.md to README.md, invisible to check_doc_links
claim: `[README.md](README.md)` in docs/corrections.md resolves to docs/README.md, which does not exist. check_doc_links only matches links with an `#anchor` (the LINK and CROSS regexes), so a file-only link to a missing file, or a link to ../CLAUDE.md, is never checked. That is weaker than CLAUDE.md's 'every pointer into the documents resolves'.
evidence: A script over README, CLAUDE and the docs checking every `](path)` link's file found exactly this one missing target.
proposal: Fix the link to ../README.md. Extend check_doc_links to resolve every relative markdown link's file, anchor or not, and to accept README.md and CLAUDE.md as targets.
validation: Run the extended checker against the pre-fix tree: it must fail on corrections.md:608.

verdict.reason: This holds exactly. docs/README.md does not exist, and check_doc_links' regexes only match links that carry an `#anchor`, so a file-only link is never resolved. An independent scan of every `](path)` in docs/*.md, README.md and CLAUDE.md, plus every `docs/*.md|html` mention in crates, web/src, tools and docs, finds this one missing target and nothing else.
verdict.evidence: docs/corrections.md:608 `| [README.md](README.md) |`. `ls docs` shows bending-check.html, corrections.md, history, rationale.md, reference.md, state.md. tools/check_doc_links.py:56 `LINK = re.compile(r"docs/([a-z0-9_-]+)\.md#([a-z0-9-]+)")` and :59 `CROSS = re.compile(r"\]\((?:\./)?([a-z0-9_-]*)(?:\.md)?#([a-z0-9-]+)\)")` both require '#'. The CROSS character class also excludes '.' and '/', so `../CLAUDE.md#x` is not matched either.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposal is sound. When extending the checker, also allow `../` paths (CROSS currently cannot match them) and non-.md targets such as bending-check.html.

title: The untested-modules paragraph leaves train/pair.rs unaccounted for
claim: 'Eight modules carry no #[cfg(test)] module … and seven of them are covered from somewhere else: … the first, third and fourth, … params.rs, and … the last three.' In the listing order that is metrology, tooth, verify, params, conditions, wiring and planetary. The fifth, train/pair.rs, is never said to be covered or not.

By subtraction it is marked as the one module covered from nowhere else. The paragraph never names it or gives a reason, though. That implied claim is also doubtful: the coverage notes put pair.rs at 95% of its lines reached, with only line 113 uncovered, through shape.rs's search (undercut_bound at shape.rs:2230) and mod.rs's shift_asked (mod.rs:1260). So the fault is an unstated and probably stale exception, not an arithmetic gap.

That implied claim looks stale, since shape.rs's shift search and mod.rs's shift_asked reach pair.rs at 95% line coverage. Move arranged_as next to Train::arranged in mod.rs, or gate it to the harness. Keep crossed.rs as a test module (e.g. train/tests/crossed.rs) with the worm proportions moved to arrangements::worm. It holds ShiftAsked, Decided and undercut_bound, which wrap auto.rs's automatic_profile_shift and minimum_profile_shift, and nothing in it concerns a pair. train/planetary.rs is 44 non-blank lines holding one method, Train::arranged_as, used by gear-cli main.rs:3382 and by tests in shape.rs and mod.rs. train/crossed.rs's production code is the proportions module (lines 98-137), called only from shape.rs:3161,3167, and #[cfg(test)] starts at line 139 of 1968. title: An empty package-lock.json is committed at the repo root
claim: The root has a package-lock.json with no packages (`"packages": {}`). It was committed in an unrelated core commit (9bd0358), has no root package.json, and is read by nothing: flake.nix hashes web/package-lock.json.

title: Worm friction is a constant 0.08/0.16; AGMA 6034 gives 0.04–0.06 at the canary's sliding speeds, so forward efficiency is understated by 8–14 points and no starting efficiency is reported
claim: Every mesh, the worm included, runs at FRICTION = (0.08, 0.16) whatever the sliding speed or materials. For steel on bronze, AGMA 6034's standard friction falls steeply with sliding speed: mu = 0.103·exp(−1.185·v^0.45) + 0.012, with v in m/s, and 0.150 at rest. The tool therefore understates running efficiency substantially and says nothing about starting efficiency, which is what sizes a motor for a worm.
evidence: `gear-cli train mixed` reports a worm sliding speed of 439.2 mm/s and efficiency 61.805 %. /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/notes/lens-standards/worm.py uses the same 8.2132° lead angle and alpha_n = 20°, and reproduces the tool's own table (mu 0.06 gives 68.69 % against the tool's 68.691 %). With AGMA 6034 friction: at 0.439 m/s, mu = 0.0574 and forward efficiency 69.6 %; at 1.111 m/s (the `worm` command's 3000 rpm), mu = 0.0417 and 76.0 %. At rest the AGMA mu of 0.150 gives a starting forward efficiency of 46.4 %, which is never reported. For parallel steel meshes the constant is reasonable: ISO/TR 14179-2 (Schlenk) mu_m for 17/43, m = 2, 50 N·m, 1500 rpm, VG100 at 70 °C, Ra 0.8 comes out at 0.071.
proposal: Make the friction coefficient of a crossed mesh an Auto input. Automatic means AGMA 6034's mu(v_s) (or ISO/TR 14521's mu_0T for the chosen lubricant), evaluated at each case's sliding speed, which the solve already computes per case. Its note should name the source and the material pairing it holds for. Keep an explicit number as the manual value. Report starting efficiency (forward, at the static coefficient) beside running efficiency. Record in state.md the size and sign of the constant-0.08 default against AGMA 6034 at the canary.
validation: A test reproducing AGMA 6034's efficiency at three sliding speeds. The canary moves from 61.805 % toward about 69.6 % at its case speed. worm.py serves as the independent check.

verdict.reason: The numbers reproduce, but the framing overstates the problem. Friction is not fixed in the model. `sliding_friction` and `static_friction` are per-mesh inputs that the panel shows. (0.08, 0.16) is only the shipped default, the same for every mesh kind. AGMA 6034's curve is for a hardened, ground steel worm on a bronze wheel. The canary's wheel is Brass C360, which is outside that scope, so '8-14 points understated' is a statement about a different drive. What holds: a speed-independent default is used for crossed meshes; state.md gives no size or sign for it against any published curve; forward starting efficiency is never reported (rationale.md says 'the static figure is never itself reported').
verdict.evidence: `crates/gear-core/src/train/arrangements.rs:30` `const FRICTION: (f64, f64) = (0.08, 0.16);`. `web/src/TrainPanel.svelte:673-674` has numberFields for `m.sliding_friction` and `m.static_friction`. I re-ran `notes/lens-standards/worm.py` and checked the AGMA 6034 conversion from ft/min to m/s (0.110·196.85^0.45 = 1.183; 10 ft/min = 0.0508 m/s). It gives AGMA μ(0.439 m/s) = 0.0574, forward efficiency 69.63 %; μ(1.111) = 0.0417, 75.98 %; static μ = 0.150, 46.39 %. `gear-cli train mixed` gives a worm efficiency of 61.805 % and sliding 439.2 / 0.0 / 351.4 mm/s by case. `gear-cli worm`'s table at μ 0.06 gives 68.691 %. `gear-cli wormstage` names the materials: 4340 Hardened Steel worm on a Brass C360 wheel. rationale.md:918-919: 'the static figure is never itself reported — its only job is the sign'.
verdict.corrected_claim: The shipped default friction (0.08 sliding / 0.16 static) is one constant for every mesh kind and does not depend on sliding speed. For a steel worm on a bronze wheel at the canary's 0.44 m/s, AGMA 6034 gives μ ≈ 0.057, so the default understates forward efficiency by about 8 points (61.8 % against 69.6 %). The default's size and sign against any published curve appear nowhere in state.md, and forward starting efficiency is not reported. Both coefficients are user-editable per mesh.
verdict.proposal_note: An automatic μ(v_s) has a real architectural cost. Mesh efficiency is currently computed in `cut`, 'everything no load moves' (shape.rs), and a path's efficiency is one figure per path. Speed-dependent friction makes efficiency a per-case quantity, which moves it into `rate` and multiplies the path report. AGMA 6034 also applies only to a bronze wheel. Any Auto must be named as that curve, with its material scope stated, and must fall back to the manual value for other pairings (brass, polymer, steel/steel). The cheaper first step: a state.md Known-approximate entry giving the default's size and sign against AGMA 6034 at the canary, plus reporting the forward efficiency at the static coefficient as a starting efficiency.

title: The 8.2° default worm is reported as 'cannot be back-driven' (0.000 %); practice says a worm at 8–10° back-drives under vibration, and the rationale's 'the answer a handbook gives' is the reverse of the handbooks
claim: The back-driving figure is decided only at a static coefficient of 0.16, and the running back-driven efficiency is never shown. At 8.2°, the threshold is cos alpha_n·tan gamma = 0.1327–0.1356. The 17 % margin rests entirely on the assumed 2:1 static-to-sliding ratio. Once the mesh moves (vibration, shock), the AGMA 6034 coefficient of 0.04–0.09 back-drives it at 33–69 %. A designer who treats the worm as a brake would be acting on a verdict that the published guidance explicitly warns against.
evidence: `gear-cli wormstage` prints 'efficiency 61.805 % forward / 0.000 % backward (cannot be back-driven)' and '! self-locking: static μ 0.160 against a threshold of 0.1327'. rationale.md:923: 'The default worm stage is self-locking, which is the answer a handbook gives.' The running back-driven efficiency at the tool's own 0.08 is 40.5 % (worm.py). With AGMA friction it is 33 % at 0.05 m/s, 57 % at 0.44 m/s and 69 % at 1.1 m/s. Machine Design ('Self-locking worm gears: fact or fiction?'): a worm at 8–10° 'cross[es] from self-locking into back-drivable as soon as ambient vibration is present'; a 5° worm with static 0.13 stops self-locking if mu drops to 0.08; AGMA recommends a brake rather than relying on self-locking.
proposal: Report back-driving in two parts: breakaway at rest (static) and running back-driven efficiency (sliding), with the lead angle and the friction angle at both coefficients. Rename the verdict: 'statically self-locking at mu_s = x; back-drives at y % once moving; do not rely on this as a brake (AGMA)'. Fire the near-locking note on the dynamic threshold as well. Fix rationale.md:925.
validation: A law: for lead angle gamma with tan gamma > mu_sliding/cos alpha_n, the running back-driven efficiency is positive and is reported. A canary line for the 8.2° worm shows about 40 % running back-driven at mu = 0.08.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. The verdict 'cannot be back-driven' rests entirely on the default static coefficient of 0.16, which is 1.21 times the 0.1327 threshold. The running back-driven efficiency is computed and then clamped to zero by `once_moving`, so it is never shown. The rationale's 'the answer a handbook gives' is not supported: common guidance puts reliable static self-locking below roughly 5° of lead and treats 5-10° as unreliable under vibration. The near-locking note fires only when the mesh is *not* locked (`else if`), so a locked mesh never hears how close it is. I rate this medium rather than high because the note does print both the static μ and the threshold, and the static coefficient is an editable input with a UI hint.
verdict.evidence: `gear-cli wormstage`: 'efficiency 61.805 % forward / 0.000 % backward (cannot be back-driven)' and '! self-locking: static μ 0.160 against a threshold of 0.1327'. worm.py: back(0.08) = 40.52 %; threshold cos α_n·tan γ = 0.1356 at the pitch point. shape.rs:2697-2705: `if *locked.get(drive) { notes.push(said(is_locked)); } else if threshold > 0.0 && static_friction > 0.8 * threshold {...}`. rationale.md:923-925: 'The default worm stage is self-locking, which is the answer a handbook gives.' contact.rs:307 `once_moving` is the clamp.
verdict.proposal_note: Report the running back-driven efficiency, at sliding friction, beside the at-rest verdict: the solve already has it as `self.sliding[k]` before `once_moving`. Reword the self-locking note so it says the lock is static only and can be lost under vibration, and fix rationale.md:925. Keep the core free of English (rule 2): the running figure should cross as a note value, not as prose.

title: A worm's reported contact stress is a crossed-helical point-contact peak, about 3.7× ISO/TR 14521 / DIN 3996's mean contact stress for the same drive; wear and temperature, which the rationale names as how worms fail, are not computed
claim: The worm is rated as a cylindrical wheel with point contact. Worm-gear practice uses an enveloping (throated) wheel with line contact, rated by ISO/TR 14521 / DIN 3996 method B: sigma_Hm = (4/pi)·sqrt(p*_m·T2·10^3·E_red/a^3). The two differ by a factor that no document states. The rationale also says worm stages 'fail by wear and heat far more often than by tooth breakage', and neither is computed. ISO/TR 14521's scope covers wear, pitting, worm deflection, tooth breakage and temperature. This overlaps the crossed-worm auditor's cylindrical-wheel finding; what is new here is the size against the standard.
evidence: The worm stage reports 'contact 3376.1 MPa' at 2 N·m (`gear-cli wormstage`); `gear-cli worm` reports 3487.4 MPa at a wheel torque of 54.95 N·m. ISO/TR 14521 method B for the same drive (worm.py: T2 = 49.4 N·m, a = 23.73 mm, E_red = 141 622 MPa from the library's steel and brass, p*_m 0.9–1.1) gives sigma_Hm = 875–967 MPa, a ratio of 3.5–3.9. state.md 'Not built' lists the enveloping wheel's zone but gives no size for the stress difference. Nothing reports a wear rate or an oil or flank temperature.
proposal: Either (a) implement ISO/TR 14521 / DIN 3996 method B for a distance marked `worm`: mean contact stress, wear intensity and sump-temperature safety, as the explicit user-visible 'worm rating (ISO/TR 14521 B)' with its empirical parameters named; or (b) at minimum, have the worm rating state in state.md and in a note on every worm mesh that the figure is a cylindrical crossed-helical peak, with its measured ratio to sigma_Hm. Keep the point-contact figure for true crossed helical pairs.
validation: Reproduce a published ISO/TR 14521 or DIN 3996 worked example (for instance a KISSsoft or DIN 3996 annex example) to its printed sigma_Hm. A law that the point-contact and sigma_Hm figures converge only where the wheel is cylindrical.

verdict.reason: The ratio is real, but it is not an error in the figure. The crate deliberately models a cylindrical wheel: reference.md#crossed-axes says 'both flanks as involute helicoids on cylinders, and nothing here throats anything' (see also corrections.md:446). For that geometry the point-contact peak is the right answer. The 3.5-3.9× ratio against ISO/TR 14521 σ_Hm is the expected gap between point contact on a cylindrical wheel and line contact on an enveloping wheel, compounded by comparing a peak with a mean, so it is not a defect in the rating. What holds: nothing tells a designer that the figure cannot be compared with worm-gear allowables. Those are calibrated on σ_Hm of enveloping bronze wheels. The difference is not sized anywhere; state.md's not-built row names only the enveloping wheel's zone. rationale.md:911-913 says the stage reports 'what a worm stage is actually limited by' and then names wear and heat, neither of which is computed.
verdict.evidence: I re-ran worm.py: σ_Hm = 875/922/967 MPa for p*_m 0.9/1.0/1.1 at T2 = 49.44 N·m, a = 23.73 mm, E_red = 141622 MPa. `gear-cli wormstage`: contact 3376.1 MPa. `gear-cli worm`: peak 3487.4 MPa at 54.953 N·m. state.md:629: 'The enveloping (throated) wheel's zone of action | The cylindrical one is derived ... reports it as a floor'. Nothing states the stress's size. rationale.md:911-913 is quoted above. A grep of docs for 14521/3996/wear-rate/temperature finds nothing.
verdict.corrected_claim: The worm's contact figure is a correct point-contact peak for the cylindrical wheel the crate explicitly models. It is about 3.7× the ISO/TR 14521 method-B mean stress of an enveloping wheel on the same drive, and no document states this ratio or warns that the figure cannot be compared with worm-gear allowables. The rationale's claim that the stage reports what a worm is limited by (wear and heat) is inaccurate, because neither is computed.
verdict.proposal_note: Option (b) is the one consistent with the no-correction-factors policy and should come first: a state.md entry with the measured ratio, and a rewording of rationale.md:911-913. Option (a), implementing ISO/TR 14521 method B, brings in p*_m, wear intensity and thermal empirics. Under the owner's goals those are acceptable only as an explicitly named, user-visible rating, and they need an enveloping-wheel geometry that the crate does not have.

title: Equal planet load sharing (K_gamma = 1) is disclosed by direction only; its size, 1.0–1.61 in AGMA 6123 and about 2 for four rigid planets at the tool's own tolerances, is recorded nowhere, and the argument for declining it does not apply
claim: Each planet mesh is rated at mesh_torque/N exactly. The rationale says the remedy 'is a mesh-load factor of exactly the kind refused above'. It is not: K_gamma is not half of a calibrated set balanced against sigma_lim. It is a statically indeterminate share that follows from planet position error and mesh stiffness. The omission is unconservative (bending in proportion, contact as the square root), and state.md's Known-approximate list, which rule 6 says must carry size and sign, has no entry for it.
evidence: shape.rs:3289: `(c.mesh_torques[k] / paths(k)).abs()`. The note in strings_en.toml:108 fires, but gives no size. AGMA 6123 Table 8 gives K_gamma from 1.0 to 1.61 by planet count, application level and mount flexibility. With the tool's default distance tolerance of ±0.02 mm and an ISO 6336-1-order mesh stiffness of about 20 N/(mm·µm) at b = 10 mm (200 N/µm per mesh), a 10 µm position error puts about 2000 N of redistribution against about 83 N per planet in a light set (sun torque 2 N·m, z_s = 12, m = 1, N = 4). A rigid set of four or more therefore rides on two planets.
proposal: Add K_gamma as an explicit per-replicated-axis input, default 1, and apply it to the most-loaded instance's pressing torque, so that sharing becomes a stated user choice. Offer an 'estimate' option that fills it from AGMA 6123's table, labelled as such. Add a state.md Known-approximate entry: 'unconservative, 0–61 % on planet mesh load (AGMA 6123), larger for N ≥ 4 without a floating member'. Fix the rationale's argument.
validation: A law: with K_gamma = k, every planet-mesh bending stress scales by k and contact by sqrt(k), and the flow's totals are unchanged.

verdict.reason: Each planet mesh is rated at the flow's mesh torque divided by the number of instances, which is exactly K_γ = 1. state.md records the assumption only in a 'declined' table, with a direction and no size, even though rule 6 asks for size and sign. The rationale's argument is that K_γ is 'a mesh-load factor of exactly the kind refused above'. That does not follow from its own criteria. K_γ is not in the refused list (rationale.md:580), is not half of a calibrated pair, and dropping it is unconservative, which are the tests rationale.md:608-612 uses to admit exceptions. One caveat: a computed K_γ would need a mesh stiffness c_γ, and that is itself an empirical ISO 6336-1 figure. The auditor's 'about 2 for four rigid planets' treats the ±0.02 mm distance clearance, a backlash input, as a planet position error, so it is illustrative rather than measured.
verdict.evidence: shape.rs:3288-3289: `let pressing_torque_at_a = |k: usize, c: &super::CaseLoad| -> f64 { (c.mesh_torques[k] / paths(k)).abs() };`. rationale.md:1608-1612: 'Real sets need a floating member, and the remedy is a mesh-load factor of exactly the kind refused above.' state.md:618: '| **Equal planet load sharing** | The remedy is a mesh-load factor of the kind above. ...|' appears outside the Known-approximate list, with no size. strings_en.toml:108 gives the planets_share_load_equally text, also with no size. The arithmetic checks: 2 N·m / 6 mm = 333 N, ÷ 4 = 83 N per planet.
verdict.proposal_note: An explicit per-replicated-axis K_γ input with default 1 fits 'estimates only as user-visible features'. An 'estimate from AGMA 6123' option must be labelled as a population table. The size quoted in state.md should cite the standard's K_γ range, not the backlash-clearance calculation.

title: Fatigue cases count tooth cycles precisely, but no rating reads them: the allowable ignores life, and a material's fatigue figure has no cycle count
claim: `allowable()` returns `fatigue_allowable` for every fatigue case whether it has 1e4 or 1e9 cycles. The cycle count is computed per member with considerable care (docs/reference.md#tooth-cycles) but only displayed. The material values are quoted at unstated or differing lives: 4340 annealed 'does not state the cycle count', Delrin at 1e7. state.md:1055-1060 itself records that ISO 6336-3 5.4.4.3's limited-life law needs only 'two stress numbers and a cycle count, all of which this tool has'. The error goes both ways: conservative for short-duty steel actuators, unconservative for polymers run past the chart's 1e7 (polymers have no endurance limit).
evidence: `gear-cli train mixed`, case 3 (1000 h): cycles 1.440e8 on the pinion, judged against the same 750 MPa a 1e4-cycle duty would be. The ISO 5.4.4.3 exponent for 4340H with the library's own ultimate/fatigue pair: exp = 0.4037·log10(1365/750) = 0.105, so the allowable at N = 1e5 is 750·(3e6/1e5)^0.105 = 1072 MPa (43 % above the constant) and reaches static at about 1e4. The Delrin entry is a 1e7 chart reading applied to 1.4e8 cycles in the same case.
proposal: Add `fatigue_cycles` (the life at which fatigue_allowable holds) to each material, with a basis. In `allowable()` take the case's cycle count and interpolate between ultimate (at 1e3, say) and fatigue (at its N) with the ISO 5.4.4.3 power law. For polymers, continue the slope past N, or refuse to extrapolate and say so. Expose the law as a train-wide switch that is on by default and named, so it is not a hidden rule of thumb.
validation: A law: the allowable is monotone non-increasing in cycles, equals the ultimate at or below the lower knee and the fatigue value at N. The canary's case 3 is unchanged for steel at 1.44e8 if N ≤ 3e6 and the curve is flat beyond.

verdict.reason: The facts hold: `allowable()` ignores cycles, and the cycle count is only displayed. But the proposed remedy conflicts with a documented decision whose argument holds. rationale.md ('The S-N curve was withdrawn') notes that two points on a fatigue curve do not exist for six of the eight materials. ISO 6336-3 5.4.4.3's exponent is defined on σ_FP,stat, a tooth's static bending strength, and only for steels and irons. Feeding it the library's tensile *yield* (for example 1365 MPa for 4340H) as σ_FP,stat, and extending it to polymers, would be the invented curve the rationale refuses, dressed in the ISO name. Two things hold. Materials do not record the life at which their fatigue figure applies (4340 annealed: 'the source does not state the cycle count'; Delrin: 10^7). And nothing flags a case whose cycles exceed that life, which is unconservative for polymers and has no size or sign in state.md.
verdict.evidence: mod.rs:2718-2723: `pub fn allowable(material: &Material, kind: CaseKind) -> f64 { match kind { CaseKind::Ultimate => material.ultimate_allowable.value, CaseKind::Fatigue => material.fatigue_allowable.value } }`. materials_default.toml:48 ('does not state the cycle count'), :62 (ultimate is 'Tensile yield strength'), :100 (Delrin 'at 10⁷ cycles'). `gear-cli train mixed` case 3: cycles 1.440e8 against the same 750 MPa. The auditor's arithmetic checks: 0.4037·log10(1365/750) = 0.105; 750·30^0.105 = 1072.
verdict.corrected_claim: Tooth cycles are computed but no rating compares them with anything. A material's fatigue allowable carries no life at which it holds, so a case whose cycles exceed the life of the allowable's source (for example a polymer past its 10^7 chart point) is judged without warning. That is unconservative, and state.md gives it no size.
verdict.proposal_note: Add an optional `fatigue_cycles` field with a basis to each material, and a note when a case's cycles exceed it. That discloses the gap without inventing a curve. If a limited-life law is added at all, it should be off by default and restricted to materials that carry a σ_FP,stat defined as ISO defines it, not the tensile yield.

title: The reported efficiency is mesh friction alone; ISO/TR 14179's load-independent and bearing losses are left out and not disclosed in state.md
claim: The paths' 'efficiency' is labelled and documented as the train's, but it contains only the load-dependent tooth loss (ISO/TR 14179's P_VZP). Churning and windage (P_VZ0), bearing losses (P_VLP, P_VL0) and seals (P_VD) are left out. The sign is optimistic; the size is comparable to the mesh loss at rated load and dominant at part load. On a Wolfrom, which reference.md:720-727 presents as where shift optimisation is 'decisive', planet bearing losses in the carrier frame are amplified by the same 1/[R(1−eta0)+eta0] as the mesh loss. No Known-approximate entry states any of this.
evidence: grep over docs for 'bearing|churn|windage|seal|14179' finds nothing relevant. loss.py, for 17/43, m = 2, b = 20, 50 N·m, 1500 rpm: the tool's mesh loss is 1.672 % (131 W). Four deep-groove bearings with 25 mm bore (M = 0.5·mu·F·d, mu = 0.0015) add 12.9 W (0.16 %) load-dependent loss alone. Seals and splash typically add tens of watts each, so the true total runs about 0.3–1 point above what is reported. Planet bearing loss per planet mesh is about 2·mu_b·(r_bore/r_p), roughly 0.15–0.25 % of rolling power, which the Wolfrom amplifies like eta0.
proposal: Add a state.md Known-approximate entry: 'efficiency is tooth friction only; bearings, seals and churning omitted; optimistic; typical 0.3–1 point on a stage at rated load, more at part load, amplified by the ratio in a Wolfrom'. Rename the readout to 'mesh efficiency'. Optionally add an explicit per-body bearing friction input (a torque, or mu_b·F_r·d/2) that the flow already has a place for, as a per-body loss.
validation: The docs-link check for the new entry. If the bearing input is built, a law that a zero bearing input reproduces today's figures to the bit.

verdict.reason: Nowhere do the documents say that the path and train efficiency exclude bearing, seal and churning losses, and there is no Known-approximate entry. The path readout is labelled plainly 'Efficiency'. The size estimates are rough, but their sign (optimistic) is certain. The auditor's bearing figure reproduces.
verdict.evidence: A grep of docs/*.md for bearing, churn, windage, seal, 14179 and load-independent finds only an unrelated corrections.md hit. strings_en.toml:449 `train_efficiency = "Efficiency"`. I re-ran loss.py: mesh loss 1.672 % (131 W) and a load-dependent bearing loss of 12.9 W (0.164 %) for 17/43, m = 2, 50 N·m, 1500 rpm.
verdict.proposal_note: Do not rename the path readout to 'mesh efficiency': strings_en.toml:476 already uses 'Mesh efficiency' for the per-mesh figure, and the two would collide. Add the state.md entry, and use a label such as 'tooth efficiency', or add a note on the path. A per-body loss input for bearings is sound and fits the flow's per-body structure.

title: Defaults written in absolute mm (tip land 0.1 mm, clearance 0.02 mm, tolerance ±0.02 mm, planet gap 0.3 mm) do not scale with module, and at the shipped defaults the band's tight end has zero backlash
claim: Addendum, dedendum and root round are in modules, but these defaults are in mm, so their meaning changes with module. The minimum tip land of 0.1 mm is 0.1·m at m = 1, half Niemann's s_an ≥ 0.2·m (0.4·m case-hardened), and 0.02·m at m = 5, effectively a pointed tooth. Distance clearance 0.02 mm with tolerance ±0.02 mm makes the minimum backlash exactly zero at any size. ISO/TR 10064-2 / AGMA 2002 give j_bn,min = (2/3)(0.06 + 0.0005·a + 0.03·m_n): about 0.07 mm for the default m = 1, a = 30 pair, and 0.19 mm at m = 5, a = 150. Backlash can also only come from the axis distance (state.md:750-755 holds the thickness coefficients to sum to 2), whereas DIN 3967 / ISO 21771 practice sets it with thickness allowances on both gears.
evidence: `gear-cli train`: 'backlash at b3 0.07280 deg (min -0.00000, max 0.14599)'; hula: 'min 0.000000'. MemberGear::default has min_tip_width: 0.1 ('Minimum transverse tooth tip width, mm'). push_distance uses clearance Auto::fixed(0.02) and tolerance_plus/minus 0.02. No document justifies any of the four values (grep for 'tip width' in rationale finds only the solver table).
proposal: Express min_tip_width, clearance, tolerances and min_planet_clearance in modules (defaults of about 0.25·m tip land, and a clearance giving the ISO/TR 10064-2 j_bn,min), or make the clearance's automatic value the ISO/TR 10064-2 minimum, named as such in its note. Offer a pure thickness allowance (both gears thinned, the sum below 2) as the standard way to take backlash off a fixed housing distance, with backlash and tips read from the equivalent thickness shift the crate already has.
validation: A law: scaling every length input by s scales every length output by s, which fails today because of the mm defaults. A test that the default pair's minimum backlash is at least j_bn,min.

verdict.reason: Every cited literal is there, and the zero-backlash result reproduces. Distance.clearance is the radial opening of the zero-backlash distance (shape.rs:270-273, nominal_of(running, clearance)). The shipped clearance is Auto::fixed(0.02) and the shipped tolerances are 0.02/0.02 (arrangements.rs:461-464, 674-675, 757-758), so the tight end of the band is nominal + 0.02 - 0.02 = 0 at every module. MemberGear::default has min_tip_width: 0.1 (mod.rs:1306) next to addendum, dedendum and root radius given in modules. default_planet_clearance() is 0.3 mm (shape.rs:89-91). A grep of rationale/state/reference for 'tip width', '0.1 mm', '0.02 mm' and 'three tenths' finds uses of these values but no argument for any of them. The j_bn,min formula checks: (2/3)(0.06+0.0005*30+0.03*1) = 0.070 mm and (2/3)(0.06+0.075+0.15) = 0.190 mm. The claim that backlash comes only from the axis distance holds, but its citation is wrong: the passage is docs/state.md:764-770 ('A mesh's two thickness coefficients are one number said twice ... so it is not offered'), not 750-755.
verdict.evidence: `gear-cli train`: 'backlash at b3 0.07280 deg (min -0.00000, max 0.14599) at b1 0.43912 deg (min -0.00000, max 0.88059)'. arrangements.rs:461 `clearance: like.map_or(Auto::fixed(0.02), |d| d.clearance)`, :463-464 tolerance 0.02/0.02. mod.rs:1306 `min_tip_width: 0.1`. shape.rs:89-91 `fn default_planet_clearance() -> f64 { 0.3 }`. state.md:764-770 explains why a thickness allowance is not offered. Even the default pair's maximum play, about 0.05 mm normal, is below the 0.07 mm j_bn,min.
verdict.proposal_note: 1) The ISO/TR 10064-2 / AGMA 2002 j_bn,min table is written for industrial coarse-pitch drives (m_n of about 1.5 and up). At the default m = 1 it is an extrapolation. If it becomes the clearance's automatic value it is a rule of thumb, so it has to be named in a note and shown as an option, as the owner's goals require. 2) min_planet_clearance is a physical gap between planet tips, and it can reasonably stay absolute. The tip land and the backlash band are the defaults whose meaning changes with module. 3) A scaling law would also have to scale every other mm default, for example face_width Auto::fixed(10.0), so write it over explicitly scaled inputs rather than over defaults. 4) Offering a thickness allowance means lifting the documented k1 + k2 = 2 rule (state.md:764). Its backlash is closed form, j_t = (2 - k1 - k2)·πm/2 in the transverse plane, and the tips already read x + x_s, so the stated blocker is small.

title: GearCase.torque is documented as 'cut by the loss' but carries the lossless driver torque read across; a worm wheel shows 199 N·m while its shaft carries 123 N·m
claim: The public field doc says a far-end member 'carries the load referred by the ratio and cut by the loss the mesh takes carrying it that way, which for a locked mesh is nought'. The code (shape.rs:3722) computes the driver's pressing torque × z_b/z_a with no loss and never zero. The two members' 'torques' on one free body therefore do not balance, and a worm wheel's shown torque exceeds its real torque by 1/eta. Its real tooth force is T2/r2 with T2 = eta·i·T1.
evidence: `gear-cli train mixed`, case 1: spur wheel T 5.0588 = 2·43/17 exactly (lossless), while the worm on the same body shows 4.9751 = 5.0588·0.98345. Worm wheel T 199.0040 = 4.9751·40, against body b3 reacted −122.9936 N·m (ratio 1.62 = 1/0.618). Case 2, where the doc promises 'nought' for a locked mesh: worm T 0.0150 = 0.6/40.
proposal: Decide which quantity the field is. If it is the tooth force, compute a crossed mesh's driven-side force from its friction balance (F_t2 = T2/r2 with the mesh's eta), which is the physically carried force, and fix the doc. If it is the shaft torque, use on_body. In either case make the doc and the code say the same thing, and have the panel label the column accordingly.
validation: A law: on a free body the members' carried torques, each read the documented way, sum to the body's on_body figure. A worm-wheel test asserting T_wheel = eta·i·T_worm.

verdict.reason: The public doc at mod.rs:1332-1336 says a far-end member's torque is 'cut by the loss ... which for a locked mesh is nought'. The code at shape.rs:3722-3741 takes pressing_torque_at_a × z_b/z_a with no η and never returns zero, and its own comment says the loss belongs to the body's figure. The doc and the code disagree. Worse, the code comment's justification ('the mesh force at its reference cylinder') fails for a crossed mesh. With friction the wheel's tangential force is F_n(cos α_n cos γ − μ sin γ), which equals η·i·T1/r2, not i·T1/r2. So a worm wheel's 'Torque' column overstates what its teeth carry by 1/η. The panel shows the field in a column labelled only ui.train_torque (TrainPanel.svelte:1238, 1252).
verdict.evidence: `gear-cli train mixed`, case 1: part 1 gear 2 T 5.0588 = 2·43/17 (lossless), while part 2's worm on the same free body b2 reads 4.9751 = 5.0588·0.98345. Wheel T 199.0040 = 4.9751·40, against body b3 reacted −122.9936 N·m: 199.004/122.994 = 1.618 = 1/0.61805, the printed worm efficiency. Case 2 (self-locking, load on the wheel): worm T 0.0150 = 0.6/40, not the documented nought. shape.rs:3722-3726 comment: 'A member's torque is the torque its teeth carry — the mesh force at its reference cylinder ... What a member's body delivers, η less on the driven side, is the body's figure'.
verdict.proposal_note: The fix with least churn is to make the doc match the code: 'the driver's torque referred by the tooth ratio, lossless — the force the teeth press with'. On a line-contact mesh this is right, because both flanks share one normal force. For a crossed/worm mesh the lossless referral is not the wheel's tooth force, so either take the driven member's figure from the screw model's own force balance or label the figure as referred and lossless. The balance law in the proposal ('members' carried torques sum to on_body') only holds if the field becomes the shaft-side figure. Pick the definition first and then write the law for it.

title: Polymer gears are rated with 23 °C properties and no tooth temperature (VDI 2736), and nothing in the docs says so
claim: Five of the eight shipped materials are thermoplastics, quoted at 23 °C / 50 % RH. VDI 2736-2 rates polymer gears only after computing flank and root temperature from power, friction, speed and housing, because their strength and modulus fall steeply with temperature (roughly 30–50 % from 23 °C to 80 °C for POM and PA). The tool has power, speed and friction per case but no temperature. This is unconservative for any running polymer gear, and neither state.md nor the library header records it with size and sign.
evidence: grep over docs for 'temperature|23 °C|polymer|VDI' finds only rationale.md:1605, which cites VDI 2736-2 as paywalled. The library header states conditioning at 23 °C and never mentions service temperature. Case speeds (e.g. 3000 rpm) and mesh power losses are already computed per case.
proposal: Add a state.md Known-approximate entry (unconservative; size from the CAMPUS multipoint strength–temperature curves the entries already cite). Then add a per-case ambient temperature and the VDI 2736-2 tooth temperature estimate as an explicit option, with the material allowables taken from a temperature table where the datasheet provides one.
validation: Reproduce a VDI 2736 worked example's tooth temperature. A law that at ambient temperature and zero power the rating is today's.

verdict.reason: Five of the eight shipped materials are polymers: POM Delrin 100P, PA6, PA6 GF30, PA GF50 and PA GF70. The library header quotes the polyamides conditioned at 23 °C / 50 % RH (materials_default.toml:17-21) and says nothing about service temperature. A grep of docs/*.md and crates/*/src for temperature, thermal, VDI, polymer and °C finds only rationale.md:1605 (VDI 2736-2 as paywalled) and contact.rs:368 (μ depends on temperature). The Known-approximate list in state.md has no entry for the rating of a running polymer gear, although the project's rule 6 requires every known bias to be written down with size and sign. The direction (unconservative) is certain, since polymer modulus and strength fall monotonically over 23-80 °C. The quoted 30-50 % size is plausible from datasheets, but I did not reproduce it.
verdict.evidence: materials_default.toml:17-21 ('The polyamides are quoted CONDITIONED, at 23 °C and 50 % relative humidity'). The entries are at :90 POM, :118 PA6, :131 PA6 GF30, :144 PA GF50 and :157 PA GF70. There is no temperature input anywhere in gear-core (grep). state.md:640 onward (Known-approximate) has no such entry.
verdict.proposal_note: Split the proposal. The state.md entry is effort S and should happen now. A VDI 2736-2 tooth-temperature model is effort L and depends on empirical heat-transfer and housing coefficients, which is the kind of calibrated rule of thumb rationale.md#no-isoagma-correction-factors resists. If it is built it must be an explicit, named option. The cheaper route uses what the library already has: a material 'condition' is its own entry (header lines 13-15), so elevated-temperature entries such as 'POM Delrin 100P, 80 °C' from the CAMPUS multipoint data would let a designer rate at service temperature with no thermal model.

title: No scuffing, micropitting or dynamic-load check, and speed enters no rating
claim: Case speeds are inputs and are carried to every member, but no stress or check depends on them. ISO/TS 6336-20/21 (flash and integral temperature scuffing), ISO/TS 6336-22 (micropitting) and K_v (ISO 6336-1) are the checks a designer expects at speed. The rationale's refusal of K factors (calibrated sets) does not apply to scuffing, whose flash-temperature model (Blok) is mechanics plus an explicit mu and a thermal contact coefficient. The strength auditor reported the omitted K factors; the scuffing and micropitting gap, and the fact that speed is read by nothing, are what is added here.
evidence: grep for 'scuff|flash|micropit' in docs and code finds nothing. `gear-cli train mixed` rates cases 1 and 3 (3000 and 2400 rpm) with identical sigma_F and sigma_H (750.0 / 2308.6), so speed has no effect.
proposal: List the three in state.md 'Not built' with the reason. If built, start with Blok's flash temperature along the path the crate already has (sliding speed, Hertz half-width, load share at each point), exposed as an explicit check with its thermal parameters as inputs.
validation: Blok flash temperature against a published ISO/TS 6336-20 example. A law that the flash temperature is zero at the pitch point.

verdict.corrected_claim: Neither scuffing (ISO/TS 6336-20/21, Blok flash temperature) nor micropitting (ISO/TS 6336-22) is built, and neither is listed under 'Not built' or 'Decided, not pending' in state.md. K_v, by contrast, is deliberately declined along with the other ISO/AGMA factors (rationale.md:580, state.md 'Decided, not pending'), and that argument holds as documented. Speed does not enter any stress. It does enter each case's tooth-cycle count (case 3: 2400 rpm × 60 × 1000 h = 1.44e8 cycles, shown in the panel's cycles column), and a worm's sliding speed is reported. No allowable reads either, because a per-material S-N curve is also declined.
verdict.reason: The scuffing and micropitting gap is real and undocumented: a grep for scuff, flash and micropit over docs and code finds nothing. 'K_v is a check a designer expects' re-litigates a documented decision without taking on its argument (validated band, balance as a set), so that part does not stand. 'Speed enters no rating' overstates: speed feeds the reported cycle count. The evidence is right that sigma_F and sigma_H are identical at 3000 and 2400 rpm.
verdict.evidence: `gear-cli train mixed`: case 1 at 3000 rpm and case 3 at 2400 rpm both give sigma_F 750.0 and sigma_H 2308.6. Case 3 prints 'cycles 1.440e8 / 1.440e8' = 2400·60·1000. rationale.md:580 lists K_v among the declined factors. crossed.rs:83 mentions K_v only as not admissible. The worm prints 'sliding 439.2 / 0.0 / 351.4 mm/s by case'.
verdict.proposal_note: Add scuffing and micropitting to state.md's Not-built table, each with its reason. A Blok flash-temperature check fits the crate's style: it is mechanics along the path contact.rs already has, it needs explicit μ and thermal inputs, and it is zero at the pitch point. Leave K_v where the rationale put it unless that argument is taken on directly.

title: Path backlash band is not the worst case when external and internal meshes sit on independent distances
claim: backlash_at sums every mesh's referred play at one shared band index: all distances at minus, all at nominal, or all at plus. It then takes the extremes of those three. A larger distance opens an external mesh and closes an internal one, so when the two are on different distances the true minimum (externals at minus, internals at plus) is none of the three points. The reported minimum is too high and the reported maximum too low. The planetary case is right only because its sun and ring meshes share one distance.
evidence: Probe /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/lens-feature-gaps/src/main.rs, default ±0.02 mm on every distance, forward path. Spur then planocentric: all tolerances on gives min 0.007809 / nom 0.099657 / max 0.189396 deg. Only distance 0 on gives 0.095762–0.103571. Only distance 1 on gives 0.003895–0.193291. The worst case built from each distance's own extremes is 0.000000–0.197206: the train binds, and the tool says 0.0078° of play. Idler then planocentric reports 0.015625–0.189396 against a true 0.000000–0.205021. Spur then planetary matches exactly (0.041724–0.052880), because distance 1 contributes nothing there. The code closes over the band with Backlash::banded(0.0, 1.0, 1.0, |t| band index from the sign of t), a fake nominal used only to index the bands.
proposal: Group row_play by the distance each mesh runs on, since meshes on one distance are correlated. For each distance d, compute the referred play P_d(b) = Σ_{k on d} |coef_k| · row_play_k[b] for b in {minus, nominal, plus}. Report nominal = Σ_d P_d(nom), minimum = Σ_d min_b P_d(b), maximum = Σ_d max_b P_d(b). Delete the banded(0,1,1) indexing trick and give Backlash a constructor from (nominal, min, max) sums. Optionally add an RSS (statistical) band beside the worst case as a labelled option.
validation: A law over every pair of presets in `graph`: the band equals the sum of one-distance-at-a-time bands, which is what the probe computes, and it contains every one of the 3^D corner combinations evaluated by brute force. Spur then planocentric must report min ≤ 0 (binding). The planetary-only figures must be unchanged.

verdict.reason: backlash_at (train/mod.rs:3467-3482) calls Backlash::banded(0.0, 1.0, 1.0, ...) only to get three indices, then sums every mesh's row_play at one shared index. Every distance is taken at the same end at once. A larger distance opens an external mesh and closes an internal one, so when they sit on different distances the true extremes are none of the three points. The reference admits this in one clause ('the band being every distance at the same end of its own tolerance', reference.md:2571) but gives no argument for it, and the fields are called minimum and maximum. The default distance tolerance is already ±0.02 mm, so the default Spur+Planocentric chain reports 0.0078 deg of minimum play on a train that binds at the worst-case corner.
verdict.evidence: Re-ran /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/lens-feature-gaps and reproduced every figure. Spur+Planocentric: all distances ±0.02 gives min 0.007809 / nom 0.099657 / max 0.189396. Distance 0 alone gives 0.095762-0.103571. Distance 1 alone gives 0.003895-0.193291. Summed per-distance worst case is -0.000000 to 0.197206. Idler+Planocentric reports 0.015625-0.189396 against a true 0.000000-0.205021. Spur+Planetary is unchanged at 0.041724-0.052880 because distance 1 adds nothing on that path. The reported min 0.007809 equals nominal + 0.003914 (external at plus) - 0.095762 (internal at plus), which is the all-plus point.
verdict.proposal_note: Grouping by distance and summing each distance's min/max over its three points is correct. Meshes on one distance stay correlated, which keeps the planetary stationary-point behaviour. Also rewrite reference.md:2569-2571, which documents the current same-end rule. member_backlash (shape.rs:3557) is per mesh and already correct; keep it.

repro.reproduction: Probe crate /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/repro-lens-feature-gaps-0/src/main.rs (public API only; no worktree was created). It chains presets with Train::chained, sets every distance to ±tol (TOL env var, default 0.02 mm, which is also the default tolerance), and reads paths[0].backlash.forward. The check does not rely on the band-summing code under test. It evaluates every one of the 3^D corners through the tool's own geometry (play_of, i.e. l.design.backlash(a)). For a corner vector s it sets tolerance_plus[d] = s[d]*tol and tolerance_minus[d] = 0, so the solve's "plus" band point is that corner exactly and no linearity assumption is needed. The smallest input is [Spur, Planocentric] at the defaults ±0.02 mm, forward path b1->b4. Run it with: CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probe-target /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/gc /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/repro-lens-feature-gaps-0 cargo run --offline -q
repro.observed:
Spur+Planocentric at ±0.02 mm: the tool reports min 0.007809 / nom 0.099657 / max 0.189396 deg. The brute force over 9 corners gives a true min of 0.000000 at [d0 -, d1 +] and a true max of 0.197206 at [d0 +, d1 -]. The reported min is exactly the all-plus corner [1,1] (0.007809) and the reported max is the all-minus corner [-1,-1] (0.189396).

Idler+Planocentric (3 distances, 27 corners): reports 0.015625-0.189396, true 0.000000 at [-1,-1,+1] to 0.205021 at [+1,+1,-1].

Spur+Planetary: reports 0.041724-0.052880, and the brute force matches exactly. On this path the sun and ring meshes share distance 1 and their contributions cancel, so distance 1 changes nothing (all corners over d1 are identical).

Single-distance presets (Spur alone, Planocentric alone): reported equals brute force.

Per-mesh row_play confirms the textbook mechanism. On the external spur mesh play is [0, 0.0292, 0.0586] over [-, 0, +]: it opens as the distance grows. On the internal planocentric mesh it is [0.0992, 0.0501, 0.0]: it closes as the distance grows. So the worst corners set the two distances at opposite ends, and the shared-index code in backlash_at (train/mod.rs:3467, Backlash::banded(0.0,1.0,1.0,...)) never evaluates those corners.

At ±0.03 mm there is no clamping and the error persists. Spur+Planocentric reports min -0.038868 against a true -0.050582, and max 0.233436 against a true 0.245150.

The linear per-distance sum from the ledger's proposal matches the brute force to 6 digits in every case: for Spur+Planocentric, 0.099657 - (0.099657-0.095762) - (0.099657-0.003895)... gives 0.000000, and the max gives 0.197206.
repro.note:
Confirmed by execution, and the corners were evaluated through the full geometry, not by adding up per-distance results. The error has a consistent direction that is not conservative: the band is always too narrow at both ends. On the minimum side it equals the sum of every distance's contribution that the shared index sets at the wrong end. With the defaults that is about 0.004-0.016 deg, roughly 4-8% of nominal play. It flips the qualitative answer: the default Spur+Planocentric chain reports 0.0078 deg of play at worst case when the true worst case is zero backlash.

I rate it medium rather than high. The magnitude at the defaults is small next to the band width, and at the default clearance the true worst case is contact at zero play, not interference. But it is a wrong figure on a headline output, it grows with every independent distance on a path, and the fix is small.

The proposal is right as stated. Group by distance, keeping meshes on one distance correlated (this preserves the planetary cancellation and its stationary nominal). Then report min = Σ_d min_b P_d(b), max = Σ_d max_b P_d(b), nominal = Σ_d P_d(0). Remove the banded(0,1,1) indexing trick, and rewrite the "every distance at the same end" sentences at shape.rs:3543-3548 and docs/reference.md ~2569-2571.

A law would catch a regression: brute-force the 3^D corners the way this probe does (tolerance_plus = s*tol, tolerance_minus = 0) over preset pairs, and assert the band equals their extremes. member_backlash, which is per mesh, is sound. So are the single-distance and shared-distance (planetary) paths. The probe shows no clamping of negative play.

title: No contact-fatigue allowable: Hertz pressure is judged against a tensile/flexural fatigue figure
claim: `allowable(material, Fatigue)` returns material.fatigue_allowable for both the bending and the contact rating, and the library carries no σ_Hlim. The comment at train/mod.rs:2497 ('the fatigue allowable is a flank figure') and rationale.md:1268 ('a flank pressure against a fatigue figure that was derived for flanks') are false for every entry. 4340 carries a 'Published fatigue strength' of 330 MPa. POM's 35 MPa is 'flexural fatigue … ASTM D671 … fully reversed'. The polyamides carry 0.30 × ultimate. Contact face width goes as (σ_H/allowable)², so an allowable 2–3× too low (steel contact endurance is typically 2–3× its bending endurance) sizes the contact face 4–9× too wide. That is the 'order of magnitude' (8.5 mm against bending's 0.9 mm) used to justify leaving contact off by default.
evidence: train/mod.rs:2718–2723: `pub fn allowable(material, kind) { Ultimate => ultimate_allowable, Fatigue => fatigue_allowable }`. Every call site is the same for contact and bending (the bending_allowable wrapper only adds the reversal). min_face_width_contact = evaluated_at·(stress/allowable)². The library notes are quoted above. For through-hardened alloy steel near 200–220 HB, ISO 6336-5 contact limits are about 600–700 MPa against the 330 used here, a width ratio of about 4.
proposal: Add `contact_fatigue_allowable: Value` (σ_Hlim, with a basis and note like every other value) to Material and the TOML. Make the rating read a per-rating allowable: a `Rating::{Bending, Contact}` × `CaseKind` table, one function. Where no published contact figure exists, ship it as `estimated` with the class rule stated in the note, as the polyamide fatigue figures already are, and keep the contact ratings off until each figure has a basis. Correct the two false sentences. Re-derive the 'dominates' measurement with the new column before keeping the default-off argument. Five catalogues gain one label.
validation: A test that no rating passes a bending allowable to a contact width: the contact width must move when only contact_fatigue_allowable is overridden, and not otherwise. Corpus diff on every contact width. The existing test that every non-datasheet value carries a note covers the new column.

verdict.reason: allowable() (train/mod.rs:2718-2723) serves bending and contact alike. The contact width at mod.rs:1006-1010 is inverted against material.fatigue_allowable. The library holds no contact figure: every fatigue_allowable is a bending or tensile fatigue value (4340 'Published fatigue strength', hardened 4340 '0.5 x UTS' endurance ratio, brass '0.30 x UTS', POM 'flexural fatigue ASTM D671 fully reversed', polyamides '0.30 x ultimate'). So the comment at mod.rs:2497 ('the fatigue allowable is a flank figure') and rationale.md:1268-1269 ('a fatigue figure that was derived for flanks') are false for all eight entries. min_face_width_contact goes as (sigma/allowable)^2 (strength.rs:1910-1912), so an allowable 2x too low sizes the width 4x too wide. The 8.5 mm vs 0.9 mm 'dominates' measurement that justifies default-off is inflated by that factor.
verdict.evidence: materials_default.toml:51,64,85,100,128,141,154,167 quoted above. mod.rs:1002-1010: bending uses reversal.bending_allowable, contact uses allowable(self.material, c.kind), which is the same fatigue_allowable field. strength.rs:1911: evaluated_at * (stress/allowable).powi(2). The width ratio (sigma_Hlim/sigma_bend)^2 of about 4 for through-hardened steel rests on typical ISO 6336-5 values the auditor cited. I did not re-verify the exact sigma_Hlim figures, but the direction and the order of the effect follow from the formula.
verdict.proposal_note: A separate contact_fatigue_allowable column with its own basis fits the material-data convention. Where no source exists it should ship as 'estimated' with its rule in the note, or be absent. The ultimate-contact case has the same problem (a tensile yield against a Hertz pressure) and could take the same column family. Re-measure the 'dominates' claim before keeping the default-off argument.

repro.reproduction: Probe crate /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/repro-lens-feature-gaps-1 (src/main.rs), run through gc against the public API: gear_core::train::arrangements::pair([17,43]), Train::alone(&shape, 2.0 N·m, 0), solve_alone with gear_io::materials::default_library(). The member material is set to "4340 Hardened Steel" or "4340 Steel", and material_overrides.fatigue_allowable is either left at None or set to a flank figure. Each gear's min_face_width.{bending, contact} is read in both cases. Cross-check: `gear-cli strength 17 43 2.0 ["4340 Steel"|"POM Delrin 100P"|"PA6"]`, which prints "b_min against fatigue" from the same field (gear-cli/src/main.rs:2354, min_face_width_contact(cs.worst, B, mat.fatigue_allowable.value)).
repro.observed:
Gear 0 at 17/43, 2 N·m, b = 10 mm, fatigue case (sigma_F 67.15 MPa, sigma_H 690.77 MPa):
- Hardened 4340, library values (fatigue 750): bending b_min 0.8953 mm, contact b_min 8.483 mm. These are the "8.5 mm against 0.9" behind the default-off argument at train/mod.rs:2499-2501.
- Same material with fatigue_allowable overridden to 1088 MPa (AGMA 2001 grade 1 Sac at 400 HB): contact 4.031 mm, which is 8.483·(750/1088)² exactly. Bending also moves, 0.8953 → 0.6172, which is 0.8953·750/1088.
- Annealed 4340 (fatigue 330): bending 2.035 mm, contact 43.82 mm. Overridden to 682 (Sac = 2.22·217 HB + 200): contact 10.26 mm, and bending drops to 0.985 mm.
The ultimate case does not move under any fatigue override. It is judged separately against the tensile ultimate_allowable, which is the same class of mismatch.

So the one Value (Material::fatigue_allowable, material.rs:260) is used for both the root rating and the Hertz rating. The contact width is its inverse square, and the bending width its inverse. No input, override included, moves the contact allowable without also moving the bending allowable. The panel's override cannot express "flank limit X, root limit Y". The library carries no contact figure: its eight fatigue entries are a tensile/rotating-bending endurance, 0.5×UTS, 0.30×UTS, POM "flexural fatigue ASTM D671 fully reversed", and polyamides "0.30 × ultimate". The comment "the fatigue allowable is a flank figure" (train/mod.rs:2497) and the rationale.md:1268 phrase "a fatigue figure that was derived for flanks" are therefore false for every entry.

What is correct, from an independent source that shares no code: AGMA 2001-D04 / 2101-D04 grade 1 through-hardened steel gives Sac = 2.22·HB + 200 MPa for contact and Sat = 0.533·HB + 88.3 MPa for bending. That puts contact about 3.3× bending at 217 HB. At 217 HB (annealed 4340), Sac is 682 against the 330 used, so the contact width is inflated by (682/330)² = 4.3× (43.8 mm against 10.3 mm). For the hardened entry (AGMA caps at 400 HB), Sac is about 1088 against the 750 used, so the width is inflated by 2.1× (8.48 mm against 4.03 mm). ISO 6336-5 alloy through-hardened MQ (about 1.313·HV + 373, roughly 900 MPa near 400 HV) gives a similar 1.4-2.1×.

Re-judged "dominates": with a flank figure on the reference train, contact asks about 4.0 mm (AGMA) to about 5.9 mm (ISO MQ) against bending's 0.9 mm. That is 4-6×, not "an order of magnitude". Contact still governs, so the default-off decision now rests on a factor about half the size its prose states. The ledger's "4-9× too wide" holds for the annealed entry (4.3×). For the hardened entry, which is the reference and default material, it is only about 2×.
repro.note:
Severity stays high. Every contact rating and every contact-sized automatic width in the tool is off by a factor of 2-4× in width for the steels, and the plastics have no defensible flank figure at all (PA6's 12 MPa gives a 189 mm contact width in `gear-cli strength 17 43 2.0 PA6`). The error is structural: the Overrides type offers no way to express a separate flank limit, so a designer cannot work around it either. Contact ratings are off by default, and that limits the blast radius but does not remove it: the fatigue-contact width and stress are still computed and shown.

The fix proposed in the ledger is sound. It is a contact_fatigue_allowable column (and a contact ultimate column, or a documented absence of one) with basis and note, a matching Overrides field, and allowable() keyed by rating as well as kind. Its validation test is exactly what this probe does, turned into a law: an override of the contact column moves only min_face_width.contact, and an override of the bending column moves only min_face_width.bending. On today's code that test fails, because bending moves 0.8953 → 0.6172 when only a flank figure is meant.

Also to correct: train/mod.rs:2497-2501 and rationale.md:1266-1269. I did not re-derive exact ISO 6336-5 coefficients; the AGMA figures come from the D04 formulas cited below. No worktree was created; the probe crate and its notes directory are under /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit.

Sources: [ANSI/AGMA 2001-D04](https://wp.kntu.ac.ir/asgari/AGMA%202001-D04.pdf), [ANSI/AGMA 2101-D04 preview](https://webstore.ansi.org/preview-pages/AGMA/preview_ANSI+AGMA+2101-D04.pdf), [Engineers Edge AGMA contact stress table](https://www.engineersedge.com/gears/agma_allowable_contact_stress_15854.htm)

title: Fully-reversed fatigue data treated as one-directional, then derated again for reversal
claim: REVERSED_BENDING_FRACTION is described as the fraction of the one-directional allowable that survives full reversal. The library's figures are themselves fully reversed data: POM states 'fully reversed', and a MakeItFrom 'fatigue strength' is rotating bending at R = −1. A one-directional tooth root is therefore judged against an R = −1 figure, conservative by roughly 1/0.7. A reversed root with the switch on is derated a second time. rationale.md:1502 says 'an allowable measured under fully reversed loading' would replace the fraction; the library already holds exactly that.
evidence: Goodman with the library's own ultimate: the one-directional allowable is 2σ_eσ_u/(σ_u+σ_e). 4340 annealed (σ_e = 330, UTS 690) gives 446 MPa against the 330 used, 26 % low. POM (35, UTS ≈ 70) gives about 47 against 35. The reversed case uses 0.7·330 = 231, where the data's own R = −1 value of 330 was already the reversed figure. Bending face width scales as 1/allowable, so a widened face of about +35 % one-directional, and +43 % more on a reversed root.
proposal: Record each fatigue value's stress ratio in the TOML (`fatigue_ratio = -1 | 0`, required, basis-noted). Derive the other ratio with a single stated mean-stress rule (Goodman on the material's own ultimate), shown on the material card as a derived value, as reversed_bending_allowable already is. That replaces the constant 0.7 with the material's own figures, so the derate is no longer a population constant. Verify the R of the 4340 source before shipping.
validation: A law: for R=-1 data the reversed allowable equals the stored value, and the one-directional allowable is at least the stored value. Corpus diff on bending widths. Cross-check the Goodman result against ISO 6336-5's 0.7 convention, which it should reproduce to within about 5 % for steels.

verdict.reason: REVERSED_BENDING_FRACTION = 0.7 (material.rs:150-165) is ISO 6336-5's convention for turning a pulsating (R=0) sigma_Flim into an alternating one, and it is applied to fatigue_allowable. The library's fatigue figures are fully reversed data: POM states 'fully reversed'; the hardened-4340 figure is the classical rotating-bending 0.5 x UTS endurance ratio, and the file says the temper matches 'the published R = -1 fatigue work'. A one-directional root is therefore judged against an R=-1 figure, and a reversed root with the switch on is derated again. Neither bias appears in state.md with its size and sign, which rule 6 requires. state.md:1064-1080 records the 0.7 and Annex B's Y_M without noting that the data's stress ratio differs from ISO's. The source of 4340 annealed's 330 MPa does not state its stress ratio ('does not state the cycle count'), so that entry's R is inferred, not given.
verdict.evidence: Goodman one-directional maximum = 2*sigma_e*sigma_u/(sigma_u+sigma_e). 4340 annealed (330, UTS 690) gives 446.5 MPa, ratio 0.739. Hardened 4340 (750, UTS 1500) gives 1000, ratio 0.75. POM (35, yield 71) gives 46.9. rationale.md:1502 says an allowable 'measured under fully reversed loading' would replace the fraction, and POM's already is one.
verdict.proposal_note: Goodman needs the tensile ultimate. The steels' ultimate_allowable is yield (ultimate_measure = "yield"; UTS appears only in the note), so 'Goodman on the material's own ultimate' would silently become Soderberg. Either add the UTS as a value or state that the rule is Soderberg on yield. Making fatigue_ratio required breaks every user library; take a default with a note instead, or version the library schema. At minimum, record the bias with its size and sign in state.md now.

title: Backlash band ignores tooth-thickness tolerance, the dominant source of minimum backlash
claim: The only band on a mesh's play is the centre-distance tolerance (tolerance_plus/minus on Distance). In practice the minimum backlash is set mostly by the upper tooth-thickness deviations (DIN 3967 / ISO 21771 A_sne, T_sn). The 'Not built' row declines tooth-thickness tolerance because the JGMA 1103-01 table is unavailable, but the designer can type their own allowance with no table at all. The model already turns a thickness change into play exactly: thickness_mod is an equivalent shift x_s = π(k−1)/(4 tan α_n).
evidence: row_play = [-1,0,1].map(|t| play_of(k, at_band(k,t))), where at_band moves only the distance. No member field carries a thickness deviation. docs/state.md:629 cites the table's unavailability as the reason.
proposal: Add per-member upper and lower thickness deviations (mm, normal plane, default 0) and fold them into play_of as the equivalent shift delta already defined by thickness_shift. Take each mesh's band as the extreme of the distance and thickness corners, which is linear so the corners suffice. Distances must still be grouped as in the backlash-band finding. JGMA 1103 can later supply defaults without changing the model.
validation: A closed-form check: Δj_t = (Δs_1+Δs_2)/cos α_wt·... against the involute backlash law on a spur pair. The band must widen by exactly the thickness corner at zero distance tolerance. The corpus should be unchanged at zero deviation.

verdict.reason: The only band on play is the distance tolerance. row_play at shape.rs:3811 is [-1,0,1] through at_band, which moves only the distance. No member field carries a thickness deviation; only the nominal thickness_mod exists (params.rs:42, thickness_shift at :104). state.md:630 and reference.md:1487 decline min/max because the JGMA 1103-01 table is unavailable. That argues against shipping default allowances, not against a designer-typed deviation. The same input would also fill metrology's reserved tolerance band (metrology.rs:229, :778), which the proposal does not mention.
verdict.evidence: grep finds no thickness tolerance or deviation field in crates/; state.md:630 reads 'Tooth thickness tolerance (JGMA 1103-01) | Unavailable. Min/max on span and over-pins only; the result types carry the space'. shape.rs:283-284 shows the tolerances exist only on Distance.
verdict.proposal_note: Garbled validation formula: a normal-plane thickness change Δs_n on the reference circle changes the normal (base-tangent) backlash by (Δs_n1 + Δs_n2)·cos α_n. Its transverse circumferential equivalent on the operating circle follows via cos α_wt and cos β_b. Fold one pair of upper/lower deviations into both the play band and the metrology min/max (span, over-pins), so one input serves both and fills the space the result types reserve. Play is linear in thickness, so adding the thickness extremes to each distance group's extremes is exact.

title: One mesh-stiffness model from the exact profile would replace the uncalibrated ramp and make TE and tip relief askable
claim: rationale.md:752 declines a stiffness model because it 'would drag in tooth and rim stiffness, deflection under load and manufacturing deviation — none of them available'. On its merits the argument is weak. Tooth and rim compliance follow from geometry plus E and ν, all of which the crate holds: the exact involute+trochoid profile, rim thickness and the material. They can be computed with the potential-energy (Timoshenko cantilever) integrals over the generated profile plus a foundation term. Manufacturing deviation is exactly what the JGMA grades and a profile-modification input would supply. With k(ξ) per pair, load sharing follows from compatibility, Σ F_i = F with F_i/k_i + e_i(ξ) equal, which is closed form at each position. The same solve gives loaded static transmission error, the effect of tip relief (e_i), and the mesh stiffness a resonance disclosure needs. LoadSharing is already the enum seam.
evidence: LoadSharing has one variant, LinearRamp (1/3 to 2/3, 'explicitly uncalibrated'). load_share takes only (d, ε), so it cannot see the tooth. hertz.rs's EllipticalContact::approach exists 'not used by any rating'. state.md 'Worth doing next' already names 'a calibrated mesh-stiffness model, which would replace the load-sharing ramp'. No transmission error, profile modification or dynamic output exists anywhere (grep).
proposal: Add `LoadSharing::Compliance`. (a) `strength::tooth_compliance(tooth, ξ)`: the bending, shear and axial-compression energy integrals along the generated profile (a quadrature over the tooth's own sampled centreline), plus a fillet-foundation term. Weber's half-plane is closed form; label Sainsot's variant as a fit if used. (b) The Hertz line term via Weber's contact formula. (c) Per mesh position, solve the n-pair compatibility in closed form, with optional per-member tip relief (amount and start roll) as e_i(ξ). Outputs: share(ξ), loaded TE peak-to-peak, mean stiffness c_γ. Keep LinearRamp, so the change is a new parameter value rather than a new branch. load_share's signature must widen to take the pair, which touches only contact.rs and the bending sweep.
validation: Against published data that shares no code. The ISO 6336-1 single-tooth stiffness c' ≈ 14 N/(mm·µm) and mesh stiffness c_γ ≈ 20 for standard steel spur teeth (the formula's own band). Cornell (1981) compliance curves. A law: shares sum to 1 at every ξ. At zero relief the share is continuous at single-pair boundaries once stiffness ramps. A high-contact-ratio case must not reproduce the ramp's unconservative 1/3 relief without cause.

verdict.corrected_claim: The rationale's reason for declining a stiffness model overstates it. Tooth and rim compliance do follow from the generated profile, rim thickness, E and ν, all of which the crate holds; only manufacturing deviation and alignment are unavailable. But this is already listed in state.md 'Worth doing next' (line 1179). The rationale measures that sharing moves ordinary worst-case bending by 0.0-0.2% because the single-pair boundary governs. So the payoff for current ratings is confined to virtual contact ratio ≥ 2, where the ramp's roughly one-third relief is already flagged by mesh.load_sharing_out_of_band. The rest (TE, tip relief, mesh stiffness) is new scope, XL effort.
verdict.reason: 'LoadSharing has one variant' is wrong: it has None (the default) and LinearRamp (contact.rs:937-948). The claim that the argument is weak holds for tooth and rim stiffness only. 'Manufacturing deviation' is not supplied by JGMA grades in a form that yields e_i(ξ) without assuming a realisation. A potential-energy (Weber/Cornell) model is itself uncalibrated against measurement, with known scatter against FE, so it runs into the rationale's own objection about authoritative-looking numbers unless it is validated against published c'/c_γ data, as the auditor's validation suggests.
verdict.evidence: contact.rs:937-948; rationale.md:746-751 and 764-770 (the 0.0-0.2% measurement and the exact single-pair argument); rationale.md:781-786 (the ε ≥ 2 disclosure); state.md:1179-1180 (already a listed next step).
verdict.proposal_note: If built, add it as a third LoadSharing value and gate it against ISO 6336-1 c' ≈ 14 and c_γ ≈ 20 N/(mm·µm) for standard steel spur teeth before exposing it. Keep TE and tip relief as a separate later step; they are new outputs, not a fix.

title: Crowning is one argument away: lengthwise_curvature is the unifying parameter and is hard-wired to zero
claim: contact_stress takes lengthwise_curvature, and its doc says it is 'positive only for crossed axes or crowning'. Every production call passes PARALLEL_AXES = 0.0. A lead crown of height C over face b gives each member 1/R_L ≈ 8C/b², summed across the pair. Passing that value makes the existing max(elliptical, line) rule rate a crowned pair with no new branch. Crowning also shifts face load distribution, and bending does not see that. A contact-only crown is an honest first step if the notes say so.
evidence: grep: PARALLEL_AXES is used at shape.rs:3318 and :4513, the only line-contact call sites. hertz.rs's elliptical solution already goes continuously to line contact at 1/R_L → 0 (strength.rs:1848 comment, test stress_rises_monotonically_with_lengthwise_curvature_and_returns_to_the_line).
proposal: Add `crown_height: f64` (mm, default 0) on MemberGear. Compute 1/R_L = Σ 8C_i/b_i² per mesh and pass it for PARALLEL_AXES. Add a note that bending face-load distribution is not modelled. Add one label ×5 and one field on the gear card.
validation: At C = 0 the corpus is unchanged bit for bit (it passes through the existing zero). As C grows, contact stress rises monotonically (the existing test's law) and matches a hand Hertz point-contact calculation at a crown large enough that the ellipse sits inside the face.

verdict.reason: Every production call passes PARALLEL_AXES = 0.0 (shape.rs:3318, :4513; other uses are tests). contact_stress's doc names crowning as a use of lengthwise_curvature, and at 0 the elliptical term vanishes exactly, so C = 0 is bit-identical. A circular crown of height C over face b has R = (b²/4 + C²)/(2C), about b²/(8C), and the pair's relative lengthwise curvature is the sum of both members' (both convex). So the mechanics of the proposal are right.
verdict.evidence: grep of PARALLEL_AXES and lengthwise_curvature: only shape.rs:3318/4513 in production. strength.rs:1672-1680 and 1768-1790 describe the zero as a value of the general model and crowning as a positive case. Test stress_rises_monotonically_with_lengthwise_curvature_and_returns_to_the_line is at strength.rs:2877.
verdict.proposal_note: Crowning exists to tolerate misalignment and lead error, and the tool models neither. A crown input would therefore only ever raise the reported contact stress and show no benefit, which misleads in the opposite direction. The note must say so, or the feature should wait for a misalignment input (face-load factor) that crowning then relieves. Near where the ellipse meets the face ends, the max(elliptical, line) rule under-reports, as its own doc admits; say that in the note too.

title: Specific sliding is closed form from what the mesh already has, and is not reported
claim: Specific sliding ζ_1(ξ) = 1 − (ω_2 ρ_2)/(ω_1 ρ_1), where ω_2/ω_1 = z_1/z_2 and ρ_i = Mesh::curvature_radii(ξ). It is the classical criterion for wear, scuffing risk and plastic gears (6 of the 8 library materials are polymers), and the classical shift-balancing objective beside the efficiency the search already maximises. Neither the core nor the UI reports it.
evidence: grep for 'specific sliding' finds nothing in crates or strings. curvature_radii(xi) exists, and sliding_velocity exists for the crossed case.
