(4) amplitude_for_throw reusing OutsideInvoluteDomain for a negative target is documented in its # Errors section and is harmless. ring::mesh_with returning Option already has a bit-for-bit cross-check against Mesh (mesh.rs:568).
verdict.evidence: Read mod.rs:1560-1700 (enum, From<MotionError>, Explain) and mod.rs:1712-1768 (Display with member/mesh indices). Read wiring.rs:177-192 and edits.rs:121-185. Grepped MotionError::Empty: produced only at mod.rs:3209 (solve_alone) and conditions.rs:387. Read gear.rs:1040-1110.
verdict.proposal_note: Do the cheap, concrete fixes rather than the full Refusal struct: give error.train_wiring (or one key per variant) the index as a value, and have TrainError::Display delegate to the note so the English says only what the note says. Give EditRefused an Explain with error.edit_* keys. Map MotionError::Empty to its own key. Flattening every enum into a single struct would lose the typed matches that tests and callers use (e.g. matches!(e, TrainError::InPart{..})) and gains little.

title: Zero face width is rated to silent nulls, while a negative one is refused as 'no contact'
claim: A given face width of 0 passes and yields null bending, contact and min-face-width figures with no note. reference.md says a null is allowed only at a field named as being able to have none. A face width of -11 is refused as error.train_no_contact. The same input axis gives a kind-jump at 0, and neither answer names the face width.
evidence: Probe diff, Spur /shape/members/0/gear/face_width/manual 0: 16 fields → null, notes unchanged. Train sweep: -11 → ERR error.train_no_contact.
proposal: Refuse a given face width ≤ 0 through the input gate, with the field named.
validation: Covered by the gate's per-field law.

verdict.reason: Reproduced. A face width of 0 on the Spur preset solves with 16 extra nulls: min_face_width becomes {bending:null, contact:null}, with no note. A face width of 1e-9 solves normally. -1e-9 and -11 are both refused as error.train_no_contact, 'the teeth never come into contact'. So the output changes kind at 0, and two different kinds happen either side of it. The 0 case breaks reference.md:3117-3124, which allows a null only at a field that can have none. The negative case is the same misuse of NoContact for a non-contact cause that TrainError::NoContact's own doc (mod.rs:1566-1572) says was removed for two other causes.
verdict.evidence: Probe probes/verify-lens-errors-policy-3: fw=10 and fw=1e-9 give nulls 20; fw=0 gives nulls 36 with min_face_width nulls; fw=-1e-9 gives ERR error.train_no_contact. Source: shape.rs:3314-3322 maps contact_stress's None (non-positive width) to TrainError::NoContact via ok_or.
verdict.proposal_note: Refusing a given width of 0 or less with the field named is right. Also stop contact_at mapping a width refusal to NoContact: give it its own variant or key that names the member, so the refusal says what is wrong.

title: Dead fallbacks that would silently read distance 0 or zero play
claim: Inside rate, `shape.distance_of(k).unwrap_or(0)` (three times) and `w.frame(j).unwrap_or(GROUND)` are unreachable today, because cut() already refuses a mesh with no distance (shape.rs:2839). If that invariant ever broke, they would pick another distance's clearance and tolerance, or book torque on ground, silently. `l.design.backlash(a).unwrap_or(0.0)` reports zero play where the band's distance falls below the base-circle limit, which is a pair that cannot assemble, not a pair with no play.
evidence: Code read. distance_of is None only for a mesh across no distance, which build refuses as Wiring(NotAMesh).
proposal: Store the resolved distance index on the built mesh (BuiltMesh.distance) when cut() finds it, and read that; delete the three unwrap_or(0). Make play_of return Option and let Backlash::banded carry None for an end that cannot assemble.
validation: No behaviour change on the corpus (check_golden). Add a unit test with a tolerance_minus large enough to cross the base-circle limit: the band's minus end is None, not 0.

verdict.reason: The three shape.distance_of(k).unwrap_or(0) calls and w.frame(j).unwrap_or(GROUND) are unreachable, as claimed: cut() refuses a mesh with no distance with Wiring(NotAMesh) at shape.rs:2839. The play fallback is live and produces a measurable discontinuity: the band's minimum backlash jumps from strongly negative (interference) to exactly 0 once the minus end crosses the base-circle limit.
verdict.evidence: Probe on the Spur preset (17/43, m=1), sweeping distances/0/tolerance_minus: 1.8 gives backlash minimum -6.039 mm (member 0); 1.9 gives 0.0 exactly; 2.5 and 5.0 give 0.0. Mesh::backlash (mesh.rs:349) returns Err(CentreDistanceTooSmall) below rb1+rb2 ≈ 28.19 mm, and shape.rs:3531 reads l.design.backlash(a).unwrap_or(0.0).
verdict.proposal_note: Storing the distance index on BuiltMesh is a sound cleanup. For play, None or a note at the band end is better than 0. A band end below the base-circle limit is deeper interference than any negative figure, so 0 has the wrong sign as well as the wrong size.

title: Case edits never refuse, while graph edits do, and a fresh case's figures are duplicated
claim: Train::set_duty on an out-of-range case silently does nothing, while every graph edit refuses NoSuchIndex. apply_edit's AddCase arm hard-codes (0.1, 30_000.0) and (0.02, 30_000.0), a second copy of the literals in defaults_impl. set_duty also hard-codes `runtime_hours: 1000.0`.
evidence: conditions.rs:1149-1151 (`let Some(c) = ... else { return; }`); lib.rs:1580-1583 against lib.rs:1164-1168.
proposal: Make set_duty return Result<(), EditRefused> with NoSuchIndex. Move the fresh-case torque and speed (and the continuous-duty hours) to named constants on LoadCase in gear-core, read by both defaults and AddCase.
validation: The existing a_refused_edit_changes_nothing law extended to case edits with a bad index.

verdict.reason: Train::set_duty returns silently on an out-of-range case (conditions.rs:1149-1151). apply_edit's AddCase arm (gear-wasm lib.rs ~1580-1583) repeats the (0.1, 30_000.0) and (0.02, 30_000.0) literals from defaults_impl (lib.rs:1175-1177). runtime_hours: 1000.0 appears at one production site only, is documented in set_duty's doc, and is a user-editable seed, so it is unnamed rather than duplicated. Neither literal breaks rule 1, since both are in Rust. The panel presumably only sends valid case indices, so a user cannot see this.
verdict.evidence: Read conditions.rs:1144-1165, lib.rs:1160-1180 and lib.rs:1570-1586. Grep of runtime_hours in production code: only conditions.rs:1162 and a fixture at lib.rs:1714.
verdict.proposal_note: Put the fresh-case torque and speed on LoadCase or CaseKind as associated constants in gear-core, so defaults and AddCase read the same value. Also see missed: Edit::Release has the same silent no-op, while Edit::Hold refuses.

title: Train panel inputs commit any finite value: a fractional tooth count breaks the boundary, and bounds are typed as HTML attributes
claim: `finite()` writes 2.5 into a u32 field (teeth, planet count, cutter teeth). serde then refuses the whole request, and the panel shows ui.train_boundary_failed ('The calculation could not be run: invalid type…'). That is the defect path, reached by a typo. `min="1"`/`min="0"` are bounds written in TypeScript (rule 1) and do not stop typed values. A chord tolerance of 0 (allowed by min=0) silently falls back to the 1 µm default (gear.rs:612) with no note.
evidence: Code read. The wasm-boundary results record serde type errors crossing as thrown strings. GearPanel instead gates commits through validate() and a Rust Bound.
proposal: Give the train panel's number fields the gear tab's path: commit only when the core's Bound (member ranges, plus the new mesh and axis ranges) admits the value, and show the validation string otherwise. Delete the HTML min attributes. Refuse a chord tolerance ≤ 0 in the same way, or note the fallback.
validation: npm run check. A Playwright or wasm_probe step typing 2.5 teeth, expecting a validation message and no boundary failure.

verdict.reason: TrainPanel's finite() (TrainPanel.svelte ~404) commits any finite number, including 2.5 into teeth, cut.teeth and axis.count, which are u32 in Rust. serde_json refuses a float for a u32, and solveTrain's catch (core.ts:768-790) reports ui.train_boundary_failed, whose own comment says that path is for 'nothing a designer typed'. The min="1" attributes (lines 834, 1356) are bounds typed in TypeScript and do not stop typed input. Line 1366 (gear.teeth) has none, so 0 there reaches the WiringError path. A chord tolerance of 0 (GearPanel.svelte:548, min="0") falls back to DEFAULT_CHORD_TOLERANCE. That fallback is documented in the core (gear.rs:597-600), but no note is shown to the user.
verdict.evidence: Code read of TrainPanel.svelte lines 404, 834, 1356 and 1366, core.ts:765-790 and gear.rs:588-616. It is standard serde_json behaviour that 2.5 into u32 fails with 'invalid type: floating point'.
verdict.proposal_note: The GearPanel validate()/Bound path is the right model. For count fields, the minimum fix is to refuse a non-integer before committing, since integrality is not an engineering number. Better, have the wasm boundary report a malformed count as a refusal note instead of a thrown failure.

title: `z < 4.0` in fitted_teeth is not NaN-safe before an `as u32` cast
claim: If span is NaN (a transverse module of ∞/∞ at a 90° helix, which the train accepts today), `z < 4.0 || …` is false, and `z as u32` gives 0. The edit then adds a gear with no teeth instead of refusing NoRoom.
evidence: Code read. The train sweep shows helix 90° is accepted when set manually (Spur/Crossed helix_angle/manual=90, OK). NaN as u32 is 0 in Rust.
proposal: Write `if !(z >= 4.0) || …` (or check `!z.is_finite()` first). Better, rely on the input gate refusing |β| ≥ 90°.
validation: A unit test calling Edit::AddGear on a shape whose helix is 90° expects Err(NoRoom) or the gate's refusal, never a zero-tooth member.

verdict.reason: The stated mechanism is wrong. In f64, cos(90° in radians) is 6.1e-17, not 0, so at a 90° helix the transverse module is finite and the ratio in fitted_teeth is finite. The probe shows helix 90, module 1 sizing the added gear correctly at 17 teeth. A NaN needs normal_module/cos to overflow to infinity, i.e. an absurd module of about 1e292 or more. With module 1e300 at 90°, AddGear does add a 0-tooth member, and the next solve then refuses it through WiringError::MemberWithoutTeeth, so the result is not silent in the end.
verdict.corrected_claim: fitted_teeth's `z < 4.0` guard is not NaN-safe. A NaN span arises only when the transverse module overflows to infinity (module ≳ 1e292 at a helix near 90°). It then adds a 0-tooth gear, which the next solve refuses as a wiring error. A very large finite z likewise saturates `as u32` to u32::MAX.
verdict.evidence: Probe on Spur with AddGear{mate:1, on:NewBody(0)} and {mate:0, on:NewBody(1)}: helix 90, module 1 gives teeth [17,43,17] and [17,43,43]; helix 90, module 1e300 gives teeth [17,43,0].
verdict.proposal_note: The one-character fix `!(z >= 4.0)` is still worth making, together with a guard on z > u32::MAX. The real remedy is refusing a non-finite or absurd module and |β| ≥ 90° at the input.

title: params.rs says root_radius is in normal modules, but the rack multiplies it by the transverse module
claim: The struct doc says 'addendum, dedendum and root_radius are multiples of the normal module', and the field doc repeats that 0.38 is the ISO 53 rack. Rack::wanted_by uses `params.root_radius * mt`, and the Ranges bound divides by m_t, so a helical gear's tip round is 1/cos β larger than the documented reading.
evidence: tooth.rs:919 `let mut rho = params.root_radius * mt;`; auto.rs:704 `(rho_max / mt)`; reference.md's table also says '/m_t'.
proposal: Decide which is meant. If the ISO 53 normal-plane radius is intended, use m (normal) at tooth.rs:919 and auto.rs:704, and state the transverse-section curvature explicitly. Otherwise fix params.rs's doc to 'root_radius in transverse modules'. Either way, one sentence in one place.
validation: A helical law: the rack tip round seen in the normal plane equals root_radius·m_n (or ·m_t, as decided), checked with verify.rs's cut simulation at β=30°.

verdict.reason: The mismatch is real. params.rs:8 says root_radius is a multiple of the normal module, and tooth.rs:918 multiplies it by m_t (auto.rs:704 and reference.md:163 divide by m_t to match). But neither half of the proposal is right, because the input has two readings in the code, not one. (1) The strength path's Tooth::virtual_spur (tooth.rs:338) rebuilds the gear at helix 0, where m_t = m_n. So the bending fillet is cut with 0.38·m_n in the normal plane, which is ISO 53 and matches the doc. (2) The drawn transverse profile uses a transverse circle of radius 0.38·m_n/cos β. The exact transverse section of a normal-plane round is not a circle. Stretching the normal rack by 1/cos β along the pitch line makes it an ellipse, 0.38 m/cos β across and 0.38 m deep. I computed this: at β=30° the ellipse's curvature radius at the tip is a²/b = 0.507 m, the m_t circle's is 0.439 m, and the m_n circle's is 0.38 m. The flank tangency height is 0.250 m for the ellipse, 0.269 m for the m_t circle and 0.233 m for the m_n circle. So the code's m_t circle is the better of the two circle approximations. Switching tooth.rs:918 to m_n, as proposed, moves the drawn fillet further from the true section. Relabelling the input 'transverse modules' would mis-describe an ISO 53 input that the strength path reads correctly as normal. Neither approximation is written down, against rule 6. verify.rs:302 builds its simulated cutter from the same transverse circle (g.rho), so the 'independent' rack check cannot see this on a helical gear.
verdict.evidence: tooth.rs:918 `let mut rho = params.root_radius * mt;` with mt = m/beta.cos() (tooth.rs:896). auto.rs:704 `(rho_max / mt)`. reference.md:163 `ρ ≤ 0.95·min(b_d, ρ_max)/m_t`. tooth.rs:338-344: virtual_spur sets helix_angle 0.0, so its Rack uses root_radius·m_n. verify.rs:302 draws the cutter tip as `g.rho*a.cos()` circle arcs. The ellipse-vs-circle comparison is in notes/verify-lens-errors-policy-4/round.py. At β=20/30/35°, ellipse tip curvature radius is 0.430/0.507/0.566 m against the m_t circle's 0.404/0.439/0.464 m. No document mentions an elliptical section or this approximation (grep for 'ellip' in tooth.rs, gear.rs, verify.rs, reference.md and state.md finds only the virtual-gear pitch ellipse).
verdict.corrected_claim: root_radius is the ISO 53 normal-plane round, and the strength path (virtual spur) reads it that way. The transverse profile generator (and verify.rs, which shares its cutter) models the normal round's section as a transverse circle of radius root_radius·m_t, but the true section is an ellipse (semi-axes ρ m_n/cos β and ρ m_n). That is an approximation, stated nowhere, whose fillet error grows with β: tip curvature radius 0.439 against the true 0.507 m at 30°, and flank tangency about 0.02 m high. params.rs says 'normal' with no hint of this.
verdict.proposal_note: Do not switch tooth.rs:918 to m_n; that makes the drawn fillet worse. Do not relabel the input as transverse; it is correctly normal for strength. Either generate the transverse tip round as the stretched normal circle (an ellipse: parametrise the normal arc and scale x by 1/cos β; the trochoid envelope code takes any tip curve that has a normal) and give verify.rs the same exact section, or keep the circle and write one sentence in params.rs and one row in state.md giving the approximation's size and sign. The proposed validation is not independent while verify.rs shares the circle; check against an analytic stretched-circle rack instead.

title: Only unwrap is linted; expect, panic and slice indexing are not, which is how gear.rs:564's panic got through
claim: The workspace denies `unwrap_used` ('A calculation engine must not panic') but not `expect_used`, `panic`, `unreachable`, `indexing_slicing` or `string_slice`. All 7 production expect/assert/unreachable sites are safe today, but the one reachable panic found is a slice.
evidence: Cargo.toml:15-27; prod.py over non-test code finds 7 sites in core/io, all over compiled-in data or fixed preset lists. The Gear::profile panic is `&r[1..]`.
proposal: Add `expect_used = "warn"` with `#[allow]` plus a reason at the 4 compiled-in-data sites, and `panic`/`unreachable` likewise. Turn on `indexing_slicing` per module where indices come from deserialized data (train/*, gear.rs), fixing sites or allowing them with a reason.
validation: cargo clippy --all-targets -- --deny warnings stays green after the allows.

verdict.reason: These parts hold. Only unwrap_used is denied (Cargo.toml:26-27). I confirmed the gear.rs:564 panic with a probe: Gear::new at teeth=0 or module=0, then .profile(64), panics with 'range start index 1 out of range for slice of length 0'. clippy::indexing_slicing would flag that site. The proposal's main part is impractical. With -W indexing_slicing -W string_slice -W expect_used -W unreachable -W panic on the gear-core, gear-io and gear-wasm libraries, clippy reports 796 'indexing may panic' and 10 'slicing may panic' sites. 660 of them are in train/*, 378 in shape.rs alone, and 15 in gear.rs. Allowing each one with a reason would bury the single live site. The 4 string_slice hits in strings.rs:267-280 are false positives: they slice at byte positions returned by find('{') and find('}'), which are ASCII boundaries. The cheap part does hold. There are 5 expect/unreachable sites (arrangements.rs:217, shape.rs:1852, materials.rs:80, strings.rs:200 and 225) and no panic!. Linting expect_used and unreachable with a reasoned allow at each is consistent with the 'must not panic' comment. The root cause of the gear.rs:564 panic is missing input validation rather than a missing lint, and rule 5 already says to refuse input that describes no shape (finding 9 in this lens).
verdict.evidence: Probe crate probes/verify-lens-errors-policy-4: z0 and m0 both panic at gear.rs:564:44 'range start index 1 out of range for slice of length 0'. Clippy run in a detached worktree, output saved at notes/verify-lens-errors-policy-4/clippy.txt: 'gear-core (lib) generated 814 warnings'. By kind: 796 indexing, 10 slicing, 4 string, 3 expect on a Result, 1 expect on an Option, 1 unreachable. By file: shape.rs 378, train/mod.rs 69, graph.rs 53, arrangements.rs 48, edits.rs 37, kinematics.rs 34, and so on.
verdict.corrected_claim: The workspace lints only unwrap_used. expect_used and unreachable would catch 5 production sites cheaply. indexing_slicing would catch the one reachable panic, but only among about 806 sites in library code (660 in train/*), so it cannot be switched on usefully module by module.
verdict.proposal_note: Adopt expect_used and unreachable = 'warn', with #[expect(..., reason = ...)] at the 5 sites. Do not adopt indexing_slicing for train/* or gear.rs. Fix the actual gap instead: refuse teeth=0, module<=0 and non-finite inputs at the Gear/Tooth constructor or the wasm boundary (rule 5). Add a property test that feeds degenerate GearParams (0, negative, NaN, 90° angles) through every public entry point and asserts it does not panic. That test would have caught gear.rs:564 and catches future sites whatever the lint set.

title: An external gear with k above 2 − 4·h_f·tan α_n/π is drawn with flanks crossing the space centreline, often with no note, and admissible_ranges admits it
claim: For an external gear cut by a rack, the rack tooth that generates the space has normal tip width w = π·m − k·π·m/2 − 2·h_f·m·tan α_n. The shift x cancels, and z and β do not enter. When w < 0 (k > k_max = 2 − 4·h_f·tan α_n/π) no rack can reach full depth. Tooth::new builds the profile anyway: rho_fit = 0, rho = MIN_FILLET, theta0 = ac/r > π/z, so the root arc is negative and the two fillets of a space cross its centreline. Where the root_radius asked is 0, no clamp fires, so nothing is said. admissible_ranges reports thickness_mod ∈ (0, 2) for every gear.
evidence: (1) Widening geometry_laws::grid() by `.thickness_mod(THICKNESS_MODS)` (0.7/1.0/1.3), with the code otherwise unmutated, fails fillet_cap_guarantees_a_nonnegative_root_arc ('root arc is negative (1.0519718839953214 > 1.0471975511965976) at z=3 x=-0.5 rho=0.38') and radius_is_monotone_and_theta_stays_in_the_half_pitch. (2) Probe, 4374 gears (the grid × k): 471 have theta0 > half_pitch. At α = 25°, k = 1.3 it is 12/12 at every z from 3 to 200 and every x from −0.5 to 0.9, with about 6 of 12 carrying no note; the profile's θ overshoots the space centreline by 0.033 mm at k = 1.3 and 0.19 mm at k = 1.5 (m = 1). (3) The threshold is exact: at k_max ± 0.002 the result is 0/12 vs 12/12 for (α, h_f) = (20°, 1.25) → 1.4207, (25°, 1.25) → 1.2578, (20°, 1.0) → 1.5366 and (14.5°, 1.25) → 1.5884, and admissible_ranges().thickness_mod.max = 2.0 in every case. (4) corrections.md:506 records the same fault on a ring (a space closing on itself, 'an inverted spur at the bottom of every space, in an outline bound for a DXF') and its guard; the external side has none.
proposal: Treat w_tip ≤ 0 as the space closing before the tool's depth, the exact mirror of the ring guard. Either (a) truncate the root where the rack's flanks meet, i.e. the tool depth becomes (π·m_t − s_t)/(2·tan α_t) below the rolling line, and raise a keyed note such as `clamp.space_closed` with the radius; or (b) cap the thickness. Add the closed-form bound to admissible_ranges: thickness_mod.max = 2 − 4·(h_f − x_eff-independent)·tan α_n/π, i.e. from w_tip = 0 with the dedendum asked, so the panel refuses what cannot be cut. Share one w_tip helper between tooth.rs:912 and auto.rs:679, which today duplicate the formula. Then add `.thickness_mod(THICKNESS_MODS)` to geometry_laws::grid() permanently.
validation: The widened geometry_laws grid passes. A new law: for every gear in the grid × k ∈ {0.6..1.8}, either theta0 ≤ half_pitch or a keyed note fires. admissible_ranges' thickness_mod.max equals the closed form to 1e-12 and a gear just inside it has w_tip > 0. rack_simulation, with k added to its grid, still shows zero penetration.

verdict.reason: I reproduced it independently. tooth.rs:912 computes w_tip = (π·m_t − s_t) − 2·b_d·tan α_t. With s_t = m(π/2 + 2(x + x_s)tan α_n)/cos β and b_d = m(h_f − x), both x and β cancel, so w_tip ∝ π − kπ/2 − 2h_f·tan α_n, which is zero at k_max = 2 − 4h_f·tan α_n/π. Above k_max, rho_fit becomes 0 and theta0 goes past half_pitch, so the root arc runs backwards and the two fillets cross the space centreline. If root_radius is 0, then rho = rho_cap = 0 and nothing fires. If root_radius > 0, the only note is clamp.fillet_capped, which names the wrong cause. auto.rs:699 still reports thickness_mod ∈ (0, 2). The case is reachable in ordinary use: corrections.md cites a planetary stage at k = 1.4, and at α = 25° that is above k_max = 1.258. I rate it medium rather than high: k above about 1.26–1.59 is unusual, and at the default ρ = 0.38 a (misleading) note does fire. The fault is still a silently self-intersecting DXF outline when ρ = 0.
verdict.evidence: Probe /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/verify-lens-tests-geometry-1 (mode f0) builds z ∈ {5, 17, 60} × x ∈ {−0.3, 0, 0.5} × ρ ∈ {0, 0.38} at k_max ± 0.002. Results: α20/h_f1.25 k_max = 1.4207, below 0/18, above 18/18, 9 of those silent; α25/1.25 k_max = 1.2578, 0/18 vs 18/18, 9 silent; α20/1.0 k_max = 1.5366, same; α14.5/1.25 k_max = 1.5884, same. admissible_ranges thickness_mod.max = Some(2.0) in every case. At α = 25°, z = 17, ρ = 0: k = 1.3 gives theta0 = 0.188694 against half_pitch = 0.184800, an overshoot of 0.028 mm at r_f = 7.25 with clamps = []. k = 1.5 gives 0.162 mm, also with no clamps. The ring has the mirror guard (ring.rs:403, CLAMP_RING_SPACE_CLOSED); the external gear has none.
verdict.proposal_note: Prefer option (a). A rack whose tooth comes to a point before reaching depth still cuts a gear, just with a pointed-rack root: tool depth b_d = (π·m_t − s_t)/(2·tan α_t) with ρ = 0. Rule 5 therefore says clamp and say so, with a key such as clamp.space_closed carrying the radius. Refusing through admissible_ranges would refuse a cuttable gear. If a range bound is added anyway, the proposal's formula is garbled ('h_f − x_eff-independent'). The correct bound is k_max = 2 − 4·h_f·tan α_n/π. It is independent of x, z and β only while neither dedendum clamp (MIN_CUTTER_DEPTH / MAX_CUTTER_DEPTH_FRACTION_OF_R) fires, so derive it from the clamped b_d. Sharing a w_tip helper between tooth.rs:912 and auto.rs:679 is right: the two copies are identical today.

title: The rack simulation builds its cutter from the Tooth's own derived rack, so it cannot detect a misplaced or mis-sized rack; its grid never turns module, k, dedendum or addendum
claim: cutter_sdf reads g.alpha_t, g.mt, g.rf, g.rho and g.ac, all computed by Tooth::build_with_z. check_cut therefore proves that the profile is the envelope of the rack the Tooth believes cut it. It does not prove the rack is the one GearParams describes: its depth from the dedendum, its fillet from root_radius and the cap, its thickness from k. The module doc calls it 'the definitive check … Together they pin the profile down uniquely'. The grid holds module = 1, k = 1, h_f = 1.25, h_a = 1 fixed.
evidence: verify.rs:42-66 uses only Tooth fields. Mutation M15 (the fillet cap computed from the k = 1 thickness, tooth.rs:912) passed all 645 tests, including rack_simulation; only the golden sweep aggregate moved (18572 → 24872 clamped). The rack sim itself measures worst penetration 2.05e-15 mm and worst deviation 6.15e-4 mm (limit 1e-3), so it is tight on what it checks.
proposal: Give verify a `Rack::from_params(&GearParams)` built only from the inputs (the ISO 53 rack: h_a, h_f, ρ = root_radius·m_n, s = π·m/2 at the datum line, shifted by x·m radially and x_s tangentially), with no clamps, and use it in cutter_sdf for cases where no clamp fired. Cases where a clamp fired should assert the clamp key instead. Widen the rack grid with module (0.5, 12), thickness_mod (0.7, 1.3), dedendum (1.0, 1.4) and addendum (0.8), sampling if cost matters. State in the module doc what the check proves.
validation: Re-run M15 and M1 (rho·m instead of rho·m_t) against the new check: both must fail. The existing 1080-case grid still shows penetration ≤ 1e-12.

verdict.reason: This part holds: cutter_sdf (verify.rs:42-66) builds the cutter only from Tooth fields (alpha_t, mt, rf, rho, ac). check_cut therefore proves that the profile is the envelope of the rack the Tooth derived, not that this rack is the one GearParams asks for. The module doc's 'definitive… pin the profile down uniquely' overstates this. This part does not hold: nothing else pins the rack's sizing. tests/regression.rs:250-256 checks rf, st and rho against fixtures from the independent Python reference implementation. geometry_laws' module-scaling law checks rf, rho, st, bd, bc and ac scale exactly with m over k ∈ {0.8, 1, 1.2}. geometry_laws:171 holds k equal to an equivalent shift. The M15 escape has a different cause than the finding says: at k = 1, M15 is the identity, so it survives because no grid turns k in a region where the fillet cap binds, not because the rack simulation refers to itself.
verdict.evidence: verify.rs:42-66 reads g.alpha_t, g.mt, g.rf, g.rho and g.ac only. tests/regression.rs:250-256 closes rb, ra, rf, st, rho, l, r_j and theta0 against reference fixtures. tests/geometry_laws.rs:600-625 is the module-scaling check over thickness_mod [0.8, 1.0, 1.2] for rf, rho, st, bd, bc and ac. The rack_simulation grid (rack_simulation.rs:30-38) turns only teeth, shift, α, β and ρ.
verdict.corrected_claim: The rack simulation checks the envelope against the Tooth's own rack, and its doc overstates what it proves. Rack sizing is pinned elsewhere only at k = 1 and only where no fillet cap binds, so a fault in the cap's k-dependence (M15) goes undetected. The gap is the k × fillet-cap-binding region, not the rack simulation as such.
verdict.proposal_note: The cheaper, sharper fix is to add k (for example 0.7 and 1.3) to a grid where the fillet cap binds: small z, large ρ, and the rack-sim or fillet-cap laws. Also restate the verify.rs and rack_simulation.rs module docs as 'the profile is the envelope of the rack it records'. Rack::from_params in verify would re-derive Rack::wanted_by's un-clamped arithmetic as a second copy. That is acceptable as a test oracle, but only if it is written from ISO 53 directly and not transcribed from wanted_by.

title: The outline breaks its stated chord tolerance by up to 4.07×, and its test bound of 3.0 records where a sweep stopped
claim: The module doc says 'the outline is within 1 µm of the true curve', and DEFAULT_CHORD_TOLERANCE is argued as finer than JGMA's tightest 5 µm. Subdivision stops when the MIDPOINT sagitta is within tolerance, which is not the chord's worst deviation. The test concedes 2.7× in its own table and asserts r ≤ 3.0, turning only teeth and shift.
evidence: Probe using the test's own worst_deviation method (a nearest-segment distance, so a lower bound) at tolerance 1e-3 over z {5, 9, 17, 43} × x {−0.3, 0, 0.4} × β {0, 25} × ρ {0, 0.38} × m {1, 5}: worst 4.07× at z=5 x=−0.3 β=0 ρ=0.38 m=5, then 3.30× at z=9 x=0 β=25 ρ=0 m=1, with 32 cases above 1.5×. Both of the first two exceed the test's own 3.0 bound; the test's grid never reaches them.
proposal: Make the tolerance a bound. In subdivide, test the sagitta at t = 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4 of each span, split while any exceeds tol, and require at least a small minimum depth on each flank. Alternatively bound the deviation from the curvature, max over the span of |κ|·L²/8. Then assert worst_deviation ≤ tol·(1 + reference error) over a Grid that turns module, helix, root_radius and thickness_mod. Correct the doc if a residual factor remains.
validation: worst_deviation/tol ≤ 1.05 on the widened grid at 1e-2, 1e-3 and 1e-4. Vertex count grows by less than about 2× (measure it). validate_dxf.py stays green.

verdict.reason: Reproduced, and it is worse than reported. outline.rs:72-93 stops subdividing on the midpoint sagitta alone, and the module doc (outline.rs:5-11) promises 'within 1 µm of the true curve'. Using the test's own worst_deviation, the ratio reaches 4.65× at 1e-4 on z = 5. The test's own convergence claim (ratio ≤ 1.4 at 1e-4) fails on z = 9, where it measured 3.42 at m = 5 with ρ = 0. The worst points sit at the root end of the trochoid (r ≈ r_f), where the curvature changes too fast for a midpoint check. The test's 3.0 bound and 1.4 convergence bound record where a z ∈ {9, 17, 43}, x-only sweep stopped. The absolute error is a few µm, below JGMA grade 0's 5 µm only by luck, but the stated contract is broken.
verdict.evidence: Probe mode f2 covers 288 cases: z {5, 9, 17, 43} × x {−0.3, 0, 0.4} × β {0, 25} × ρ {0, 0.38} × m {1, 5} × tol {1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4}. Worst ratios: 4.646 (z5 x0 β25 ρ0 m5 at 1e-4), 4.195 (z5 x−0.3 ρ0 m5 at 1e-2), 4.068 (z5 x−0.3 ρ0.38 m5 at 1e-3, the auditor's case, reproduced exactly), and 3.417 (z9 x0 ρ0 m5 at 1e-4). 20 cases exceed 3 and 147 of 288 exceed 1.5. Mode f2b puts the worst points just above r_f: 7.5427 vs r_f 7.5422, 4.7541 vs 4.7500, 101.2518 vs 101.25. Even non-undercut z43 m5 at 1e-3 gives 1.76×.
verdict.proposal_note: Checking the sagitta at 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4 is still a heuristic: a span whose curvature is concentrated near one end can slip past all three. A rigorous stop exists because both curves have closed-form curvature. The involute's radius of curvature is r_b·u, and the trochoid's is tooth.rs rolling_curvature_radius. Split while L²/(8·ρ_min over the span) > tol. ρ_min is monotone on each section, so the endpoint values bound it. Then the test can assert ratio ≤ 1 + (reference error) on a grid that turns m, β, ρ and k. Measure the vertex growth before choosing.

title: The bending rack-limit tests use tolerances 10⁴× looser than the law they could assert
claim: form_factor_converges_to_the_rack_limit checks z = 4000 against the closed form to 5e-3 absolute, but the O(1/z) residual there is already 3.3e-3. A limit error of about 1.7e-3 on one side (8.3e-3 on the other) passes, and so does any error that vanishes as 1/z. The parabola test allows 1e-2 against an actual gap of 4.6e-4, so an error of up to 0.44 % passes. Only α and ρ are turned: x = 0, h_a = 1 and h_f = 1.25 are fixed, though the rack limit is closed-form in all of them.
evidence: Probe: Y_F(z) at α=20°, ρ=0.38 is 2.286318 (z=60), 2.076254 (1000), 2.066465 (4000), 2.064020 (16000). Two-point Richardson in 1/z gives 2.06320398 (4000), 2.06320503 (8000), 2.06320528 (16000). The independent closed form (bending.rs rack_limit, reimplemented in Python) gives 2.0632053659, which agrees to 8e-8. The parabola extrapolates to 2.1587998 against its closed form 2.1588065.
proposal: Replace the absolute check at z = 4000 with Richardson extrapolation of (s_Fn/m, h_Fe/m, Y_F) from z = 8000 and 16000, asserted equal to the rack limit to 1e-6, and keep the monotone approach. Generalise rack_limit to shift and depth (datum-line thickness π/2 + 2x·tan α, working depths h_a + x and h_f − x) and sweep x ∈ {−0.3, 0, 0.5}, h_f ∈ {1.0, 1.4}, h_a ∈ {0.8, 1.0}.
validation: The new assertions pass at 1e-6 on current code. Deliberately perturbing TANGENT_ANGLE_DEG by 0.1° or the flank-normal load angle by 1e-3 rad makes them fail, where the 5e-3 check does not.

verdict.reason: The numbers hold. Y_F at z = 4000 is 2.066465 against the closed form 2.0632054, a 3.26e-3 residual inside a 5e-3 tolerance. Two-point Richardson from 8000/16000 gives 2.0632053 (9e-8 off). The parabola test's 1e-2 is also loose. Where the claim overreaches: 'any error that vanishes as 1/z passes' is inherent to any rack-limit test, Richardson included. An error in a curvature-dependent term vanishes in the limit by definition, so the proposal cannot close that part. The validation step is also partly wrong. tests/bending.rs:14 imports TANGENT_ANGLE_DEG from the crate and rack_limit uses it (line 36), so perturbing that constant moves the implementation and the reference together, and no tightening would catch it.
verdict.corrected_claim: The z = 4000 absolute checks (5e-3; parabola 1e-2) are about 10³–10⁴ times looser than a Richardson-extrapolated check could be, and only α and ρ are swept. A limit-level error of up to about 1.7e-3 in Y_F would pass. Errors that vanish in the rack limit are outside what any rack-limit test can see.
verdict.proposal_note: The Richardson residual on s and h is already 5–7e-7, so a 1e-6 tolerance leaves under 2× margin. Use 1e-5, or three-point extrapolation. To make the tangent-angle constant testable, write 30° literally in the test's rack_limit, citing ISO 6336-3, instead of importing TANGENT_ANGLE_DEG. Generalising to x, h_a and h_f is sound.

title: extremes::addendum_and_dedendum_bound_each_other asserts a tautology, and nothing pins the addendum floor
claim: `assert!(a <= -dedendum + 1e-9 || a > -dedendum)` is true for every non-NaN a. The companion test the_geometric_bounds_are_exactly_where_the_generator_starts_clamping checks only `lo + eps` (tip above root) and never the far side, so a floor that is too high passes. The addendum floor, a user-visible input bound, is therefore unpinned.
evidence: Mutation M13, `let above_root = -0.5 * p.dedendum;` at auto.rs:670: 645/645 nextest pass, and check_golden --fast reports all 32 outputs unchanged.
proposal: Replace line 181 with the law the comment states: addendum.min == max(−dedendum, (r_b(1 + TIP_ABOVE_BASE_FRACTION) − r)/m − x) to 1e-12. In the bounds test, assert both sides as the dedendum and fillet parts already do: at lo − eps the tooth either has ra ≤ rf or fires a named clamp, and at lo + eps it does neither. Also add a k ≠ 1 case and a helical case to its case list.
validation: M13 fails the new test, and so does the mirror mutation `-1.5 * p.dedendum`.

verdict.reason: extremes.rs:181, `a <= -d + 1e-9 || a > -d`, is true for every non-NaN a. The bounds test (extremes.rs:106-118) checks only lo + eps. Its cases all use h_f = 1.25, where the base-circle term binds (z = 17 gives above_base ≈ −0.51, z = 9 gives ≈ −0.27), so the −dedendum branch of auto.rs:670 is never the active floor in any case that makes a real assertion. The one loop where it binds (d = 0.5 at line 181) asserts the tautology. M13 (−0.5·d) therefore survives by construction. The consequence is limited to a UI input bound, since admissible_ranges feeds only the panel's limits, hence low severity.
verdict.evidence: Read extremes.rs:100-118 and 168-189 and auto.rs:669-671. For the default z = 17, α = 20°: r_b = 7.9874, so above_base = (7.9874·(1 + 1e-9) − 8.5)/1 − 0 = −0.5126. That is above −1.25, −1.0 and −2.0, so the base term binds for every dedendum in the loop except 0.5.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposal's second half ('at lo − eps the tooth either has ra ≤ rf or fires a named clamp') cannot pass for base-bound cases as the code stands. tooth.rs:471, `ra = ra.max(rb·(1 + TIP_ABOVE_BASE_FRACTION))`, raises the tip to the base circle without pushing any note. Either add a clamp note there (see missed) or assert ra == r_b(1 + f) at lo − eps for base-bound cases. The exact-law replacement for line 181 is sound.

title: No test in the suite pins the contact modulus of two different materials; the one that claims to asserts a tautology
claim: contact_modulus_is_symmetric_and_between_the_two_single_material_values asserts `ab < contact_modulus(&b,&b) * 2.0 && ab > 0`. Since 1/E*_ab = c_a + c_b > c_b = 1/(2·E*_bb), that holds for any positive compliances. The comment ('must sit below the softer material's own like-on-like value') and the name ('between') state stronger properties than are asserted. Every other nextest case uses like-on-like materials.
evidence: Mutation M4, contact_modulus = 1/(2·max(c_a, c_b)), which is right for identical materials and wrong for any pair: 645/645 nextest pass. Only the golden corpus (train_mixed.txt, σ_H 4574.4 → 3806.7 MPa) sees it.
proposal: Assert the exact law: 1/E*_ab = ½(1/E*_aa + 1/E*_bb) to 1e-15 relative, i.e. E*_ab is the harmonic mean, so min(E*_aa, E*_bb) < E*_ab < max(...). Add a steel-on-polymer value checked against the textbook form E* = [(1−ν₁²)/E₁ + (1−ν₂²)/E₂]⁻¹, computed by hand in the test.
validation: M4 fails the new test.

verdict.reason: material.rs:459 asserts ab < 2·E*_bb, and 2·E*_bb = 1/c_b > 1/(c_a + c_b) = ab for any positive c_a, so it is a tautology. The accompanying comment is worse than 'stronger than asserted': it is false. E*_ab sits below the softer material's like-on-like value only when c_a > c_b. For a stiff mate (steel on polymer, the very case the test builds), E*_ab > E*_bb. The '* 2.0' was presumably added to make that false statement pass. The other callers (crossed.rs:377, shape.rs:4501, gear-cli) use contact_modulus itself as the reference, so they cannot see a wrong formula. Only the golden corpus does, and the corpus runs in CI, hence low severity. I accepted the M4 result without re-running it: it follows algebraically, since 1/(2·max(c_a, c_b)) equals E*_bb for a steel/polymer pair, which is < 2·E*_bb and symmetric.
verdict.evidence: Read material.rs:404-405 and 446-461. Algebra: 1/E*_ab = c_a + c_b and E*_bb = 1/(2c_b). The test pair is steel E = 190000, ν = 0.29 (c_a = 4.82e-6) against b with E = 3000, ν = 0.37 (c_b = 2.88e-4). That gives E*_ab = 3416 > E*_bb = 1738, contradicting the comment. grep shows every other nextest use recomputes contact_modulus instead of checking it.
verdict.proposal_note: The harmonic-mean identity 1/E*_ab = ½(1/E*_aa + 1/E*_bb) is exact and independent of the implementation's arithmetic. Assert it, plus one hand-computed steel/polymer value, and correct the comment to 'between the two like-on-like values (their harmonic mean)'.

title: The JGMA transcription checks cannot see a wrong cell that stays a preferred number and stays monotone in grade, and one cell breaks monotonicity across module bands
claim: The three checks (cell counts, preferred numbers, monotone in grade) plus four spot values admit any single-cell error that keeps its neighbours in order. The table also has one more ordering the checks do not state, non-decreasing with module band at fixed grade and diameter, and exactly one cell breaks it: fine grade 1, d 12.01–25.01 has total 28 at m 0.6–1.0 against 26 at m 1.0–1.6. The 28 equals the next diameter band's value (line 54), which looks like a copy slip.
evidence: Mutation M5 (line 95, fine g3 m0.6–1 d12.01 t2t 15 → 14): 645/645 pass and golden is unchanged. Python over the CSV: 0 violations of diameter monotonicity, 1 of module monotonicity (the cell above). Grade-to-grade ratios cluster tightly: standard grades 4–7 about 1.41 and 8–12 about 1.25 (a Renard step), a stronger law than monotonicity.
proposal: Check lines 53 and 59 against the standard's page. Add laws for monotonicity in module band and diameter band, with any genuine exception listed along with the page it was read from. Add a grade-ratio law per scale (each step within the Renard ratio's rounding band, e.g. 1.25 ± 0.04 or 1.41 ± 0.06 as measured per scale), which catches a single wrong cell in one direction or the other.
validation: M5 fails the ratio law (15 → 14 changes the g2→g3 and g3→g4 ratios out of band). The module law fires on line 53 until it is resolved.

verdict.reason: There is a real test gap. The structural checks (cell counts, preferred numbers, monotone in grade, total > tooth-to-tooth, contiguous coverage) plus four spot values cannot see a single wrong cell that stays a preferred number and stays in grade order. The M5 mutation (fine g3 m0.6-1 d12.01 t2t 15 -> 14) keeps 14 in the ALLOWED list and between g2=10 and g4=24, so no check fires. The module-band breach is also real: exactly one cell. But the 'copy slip' hypothesis is refuted. I rendered the source PDF, which is on disk outside the repo at /home/user/gears/docs/JGMA 116-02 1983.pdf (a 2010 xlsx-derived compilation), and compared every cell of both pages with the CSV: all 618 values match. Page 1, grade 1, m 0.6-1.0, d 12.01-25.00 prints 8.5 / 28, and m 1.0-1.6 at the same diameter prints 9 / 26. The anomaly is in the source, not the transcription. The proposed ratio law is also wrong as written. Measured grade-step ratios on the fine scale span 1.18-1.67 (e.g. fine g0->g1 total 1.25-1.56, g3->g4 t2t 1.53-1.67), so a band of 1.25±0.04 or 1.41±0.06 fails the faithful data. A per-step band fitted to the data is the 'bound recording where the sweep stopped' that the project's testing rule 3 rejects.
verdict.evidence: python over crates/gear-core/data/jgma_116_02.csv: 0 diameter-monotonicity breaches; 1 module breach, 'fine 1 0.6 12.01 tot 28.0 -> 26.0' (CSV lines 53 and 59). Per-step ratio ranges: fine (0,t2t) 1.200-1.294, (0,tot) 1.250-1.556, (1,tot) 1.300-1.538, (3,t2t) 1.529-1.667, (4,tot) 1.250-1.562; standard (4,tot) 1.556-1.636, (7..11) 1.244-1.286. pdftoppm on the PDF: page 1 grade 1 row 'total' reads 20 20 22 25 28 28 30 32 | 22 25 28 28 30 30 34 | 25 26 30 32 32 34, identical to the CSV; page 2 (standard 4-12) identical too. Under M5 the ratios would be 1.4 and 1.714; the latter is outside the measured fine g3->g4 range, so only a data-fitted band would catch it.
verdict.corrected_claim: The transcription checks cannot see a wrong cell that stays a preferred number and stays in grade order. The table has one cell (fine g1, m 0.6-1.0, d 12.01-25.00, total 28) that breaks module-band monotonicity against m 1.0-1.6 (26). That cell matches the source page exactly, so it is a feature (or error) of the source, not a copy slip.
verdict.proposal_note: Add module-band and diameter-band monotonicity laws, with this one cell listed as a known exception that cites page 1 of the source and says it is faithful. Drop the Renard-band ratio law: it fails real fine-scale data, and a fitted band would break rule 3. The strongest guard against a future single-cell edit is double entry, not a statistical law: a second, independently typed copy of the table (or a digest of it) kept in the test and compared cell by cell with the CSV. The rationale already says the CSV ships with 'three transcription checks'. That count is itself stale, since jgma.rs also has total>t2t and coverage checks.

title: auto::the_sharp_rack_reproduces_the_classical_tooth_count_rule never calls the crate
claim: The test bisects on z using its own copy of the x_min formula ('so the test shares no algebra with the implementation'). It shares no code at all, so no change to Rack::undercut_shift or minimum_profile_shift can make it fail. It checks the design document's numbers against a formula written in the test.
evidence: auto.rs:2160-2183: the closure builds GearParams but computes x_min inline, and no crate function is called on the result.
proposal: Bisect on the crate's own reading: minimum_profile_shift(&p, working_depth).with_cutter_radius (or Rack::undercut_shift) crossing zero at the continuous z. Better still, assert the closed form z_min = 2(h − ρ(1 − sin α))/(m·sin²α) against the crate to 1e-12, and the integer boundary (x_min > 0 at z = 17, < 0 at 18 for the sharp rack).
validation: Mutating undercut_shift (e.g. dropping the ρ term) fails the new test.

verdict.reason: The test builds a GearParams per bisection step but only reads the defaults' pressure_angle and module from it. It computes x_min with its own inline formula and calls no crate function. Only a change to GearParams::default() could make it fail. Its docstring says it pins 'the tooth-count thresholds in the design document', but 17.10 / 21.37 / 12.82 appear only in docs/history/design-record.md (superseded, governs nothing), not in reference.md or rationale.md. So it checks a retired document against a formula written in the test. The formula it duplicates is otherwise very well held. Dropping the ρ term in Rack::undercut_shift made about 30 tests fail, including regression::matches_the_reference_implementation (which pins l), auto::tests::minimum_shift_matches_the_closed_form_and_the_cutter_helps and geometry_laws::flank_and_fillet_meet_exactly. So the test's loss costs little, and severity is low.
verdict.evidence: auto.rs:2157-2188: the closure computes `x_min = working_depth - (rho + sa * (r * sa - rho)) / p.module` inline, and `p` is used only for `p.pressure_angle` and `p.module`. grep for 12.82/21.37/17.10 finds them only in docs/history/design-record.md. Worktree mutation `(self.depth - (sa*(r*sa)))/module` in tooth.rs:869-873: 30+ failures across gear-core; the test in question was not among them.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposal is sound. The simplest form: assert the crate's minimum_profile_shift(&p, h).sharp_rack and .with_cutter_radius at z = 17 and 18 (sign change) against the closed form z_min = 2(h − ρ(1 − sin α))/(m sin² α) with ρ in rack units. Alternatively delete the test and its reference to 'the design document', since the numbers now live only in the history record.

title: The span test skips every helical case on a false premise, so a helical span's absolute value is pinned only code against code
claim: span_reduces_to_the_textbook_formula skips every β ≠ 0 case ('The textbook form is stated for spur gears'). But W_k = m_n·cos α_n[π(k − 0.5) + z·inv α_t] + 2x·m_n·sin α_n is the ISO 21771 helical form. consecutive_spans_differ_by_one_base_pitch pins only differences, and the_general_span_is_the_published_one compares span_over_teeth_at with span_over_teeth, both the crate's own.
evidence: The code is correct: cos β_b·r_b = m_n·z·cos α_n/2 reduces metrology.rs:252-256 exactly to the ISO form. Probe over β {0, 15, −25, 40} × x × k × z × k_span: worst relative disagreement 4.4e-16. So the defect is the skip and its comment.
proposal: Delete the `if p.helix_angle != 0.0 { continue; }` and correct the comment. The grid already turns β ∈ {0, 15, −25}.
validation: The test passes at 1e-14 with helical cases included; mutating inv(α_t) → inv(α_n) in both span routes now fails it.

verdict.reason: The skip rests on a false premise: the formula the test writes is the ISO 21771 helical form, with m_n, cos α_n and z·inv α_t. With the skip removed, the test passes over the grid's β ∈ {0, 15, −25}, worst 5.5e-16 relative. Golden outputs contain no span, so the helical absolute span has no independent value check. One qualification, not a refutation: the helical span is still held indirectly. The consecutive-span law pins the cos β_b·r_b factor through p_bn. the_general_span test checks span_over_teeth against span_over_teeth_at, which reads each tooth's psi_b rather than st/r + 2 inv α_t. And the helical regression fixtures pin st, rb and α-derived values. So a wrong answer would have to get past several routes. Deleting three lines and fixing a comment is still clearly right.
verdict.evidence: tests/metrology.rs:66-68 skip. Worktree with the skip removed: `cargo nextest run -p gear-core span_reduces` -> 'worst relative span disagreement with the textbook form: 5.526e-16 ... 1 passed'. grep -il span tools/golden/* returns nothing. metrology.rs:337-359: span_over_teeth_at uses gear.tooth(j).0.psi_b, a separate route from metrology.rs:252-256.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposal's validation ('mutating inv(α_t) -> inv(α_n) in both span routes') is not a clean mutation: span_over_teeth_at has no inv term and reads psi_b from the tooth. The simple validation is that inv(α_t) -> inv(α_n) in span_over_teeth alone already fails the_general_span test on helical cases and, once the skip goes, this test too.

title: Stale and fused prose in the integration tests
claim: (a) regression.rs says 'these eight cases' and fixtures() has seven. (b) geometry_laws.rs:677-699 is the doc comment of only_an_undercut_tooth_can_be_severed, left above a_tooth_called_unsevered_is_not_severed_at_a_finer_scan, so rustdoc and readers see two docstrings fused. (c) That test says 'The interval the crate scans, sampled a hundred times finer' and its failure message says 'the 2000-point scan missed a crossing', yet the crate now solves dθ/ds = 0 (tooth.rs:647-660), and 40 000/2000 is 20×, not 100×. (d) It also says 'the same shape as only_an_undercut_tooth_can_be_severed above', which is actually below it.
evidence: Read regression.rs:41-233 (7 Fixture literals). geometry_laws.rs:677-723 and 758-777; tooth.rs:647-665.
proposal: Say 'seven' (or add an eighth fixture, see the helical fillet finding). Move lines 677-699 onto only_an_undercut_tooth_can_be_severed. Reword (c) to 'a dense scan of the interval the solve brackets' and '…the solve missed a crossing'. Fix 'above'.
validation: Read-through; cargo doc shows one docstring per test.

(a) regression.rs:6 says 'these eight cases', but fixtures() has seven Fixture literals (lines 44, 71, 98, 125, 152, 179, 206; the eighth 'Fixture {' at line 21 is the struct definition).
