Make cmp_checked #[cfg(test)] or delete it together with its test. Keep distinct_teeth: the zero-shift cost law at gear.rs:2623 uses it, so #[cfg(test)] is enough. Its doc should also stop claiming 'one tooth generated' is the whole cost (see missed).

title: Two note renderers: the Rust fill() that the strings laws test, and a TypeScript regex the user actually sees
claim: gear_io::strings::Catalogue::render/fill (reached only from gear-cli and tests) and strings.svelte.ts `template.replace(/\{(\w+)\}/g, …)` implement the same grammar separately. The 'fire every note' law runs the Rust one. They agree on every placeholder shipped today (all match \{\w+\}), but nothing holds the TS renderer to the Rust one.
evidence: `grep -ohP '\{[^}]*\}' strings_*.toml | grep -vP '^\{\w+\}$'` finds nothing, so the renderers agree today. render has 12 CLI uses, 4 test uses and 0 wasm uses.
proposal: Either add a check (in check_strings.py) that every placeholder matches \{\w+\}, pinning the shared grammar, or have wasm render notes, a `render_notes` entry or rendered strings in results, and drop the TS renderer.
validation: A catalogue entry with `{a-b}` fails check_strings.py.

verdict.reason: The TS renderer that users see and the Rust fill() that the laws exercise are two separate implementations, and nothing ties them together. They agree on today's catalogues but differ on grammar at the edges.
verdict.evidence: web/src/strings.svelte.ts:68 uses `template.replace(/\{(\w+)\}/g, ...)`. crates/gear-io/src/strings.rs:263 fill() accepts any text between '{' and the next '}'. They differ on (a) a placeholder name outside [A-Za-z0-9_], such as '{a-b}' or a non-ASCII name: Rust fills it and TS leaves it standing; (b) '{{x}}': Rust takes the name '{x' and leaves '{{x}}', while TS fills the inner '{x}'. `grep -ohP '\{[^}]*\}' strings_*.toml | grep -vP '^\{\w+\}$'` prints nothing, so they agree today. gear-cli and gear-wasm contain 12 `.render(` calls, and 0 of them are in gear-wasm. every_placeholder_is_a_value_the_core_supplies checks placeholder names against what the core supplies, which would require the core to name a value 'a-b' before a divergence could ship. The window is real but narrow.
verdict.proposal_note: The cheapest pin is one Rust test in gear-io/src/strings.rs asserting that every '{...}' in every catalogue matches ^\{[A-Za-z0-9_]+\}$ and that '{{' never occurs. That keeps the check beside the laws, where the other placeholder tests are, rather than in check_strings.py. Rendering in wasm is not worth it: ui.* strings are filled by the front end in any case.

title: Feature ablation: the eccentric gear is the costliest feature per user (about 1,010 lines plus about 3,000 lines of dependent tests) and never reaches a train
claim: The angular shift (Δx) accounts for about 549 code + 463 comment lines in gear.rs, auto.rs, metrology.rs and gear-wasm (Sinusoid, Variation, PerToothClamps, CentreProfile, amplitude_for_throw, the *_at/_around metrology, admissible_angular_shift, eccentric_mate). 42 test fns (about 3,011 lines) name it, and the single-gear panel refers to it 44 times. Every train member is built with `angular_shift: 0.0` (shape.rs:1027), so the feature exists only in the single-gear tab and its DXF export.
evidence: specs/eccentric.out from feature_cost.py. grep angular_shift in train/ gives exactly one hit, the zero at shape.rs:1027.
proposal: No removal proposed; this is the figure the owner needs for a keep-or-cut decision. If kept, consider making the eccentric data a separate optional result of the single-gear tab, so Gear::new at Δx=0 does no per-tooth work and GearSummary does not carry per-tooth ranges.
validation: Not applicable (cost estimate).

verdict.reason: The production cost is plausible and the train never builds an eccentric gear. The test-cost figure is inflated, the finding leaves out that the feature is already hidden behind developer mode, and half of the proposal is already true.
verdict.corrected_claim: The angular shift costs roughly 550 code and 460 comment lines of production (gear.rs, metrology *_at/_around, auto.rs, gear-wasm) and about 30 of its own test functions in gear.rs/auto.rs/tests/metrology.rs. It is reachable only from the single-gear tab in the hidden developer mode (docs/state.md:500-505, rationale 'Unfinished work is knocked for, not switched on'), and every train member is built at angular_shift 0.0 (shape.rs:1027). At Δx=0, Gear::new already generates only one distinct tooth, but it cuts that tooth twice (see missed).
verdict.evidence: feature_cost.py's list of '42 dependent tests' counts screw.rs:2857/2963, which only write `angular_shift: 0.0` in a GearParams literal (screw.rs:2877, 2983), and metrology tests on evenly cut gears that would simply call the scalar API. Its 'prod dependant' list includes gear-io strings.rs:263 fill, which has nothing to do with the feature (a name-match false positive). The docs state the gating: 'The type appears in a gear tab's list only in the developer mode ... ten clicks inside four seconds' (state.md:500-502). The test an_ordinary_gear_still_generates_one_tooth (gear.rs:2623) and a probe both give distinct_teeth()==1 at Δx=0. rationale.md:83 and :1063 record that 'a concentric gear is an eccentric one at Δx = 0', a deliberate application of rule 4.
verdict.proposal_note: 'Make Gear::new at Δx=0 do no per-tooth work' is already nearly true: one tooth is generated, and the only extra work is an O(z) seat vector plus a duplicate cut of the mean tooth. Splitting eccentric results into a separate optional result would bring back the branch that rule 4 removed. For a keep-or-cut decision, the relevant fact is that the feature is developer-only and unmeasured, not that it misses the train.

title: Power-flow solve is 2^M over the whole train's meshes: seconds at 16-18 meshes, and it runs on every keystroke
claim: flow::solve tries every one of 2^M direction assignments. M is every mesh and coupling of the whole train, since solve_parts builds one list across all parts. Each assignment does an O(bodies·M + rows·M²) elimination and allocates several Vecs. solve_parts calls it once per load case and four times per path (moving and resting, each way). Cost therefore doubles with each mesh added anywhere in a train, and a chain of presets becomes unusable at about 12-16 meshes.
evidence: Native release (probe `chain`): spur chains of 1/2/4/6/8 pairs take 79/383/929/3269/9112 µs. Planetary chains of 1/2/4/6/8 sets (2/4/8/12/16 meshes) take 232 µs / 994 µs / 11.1 ms / 114 ms / 2.38 s. Mixed chains of 4/6/8 presets (7/10/15 meshes) take 6.7 ms / 30 ms / 788 ms. 6 meshed-planet sets (18 meshes) take 10.5 s. Instrumented at 8 planetary sets: 6 flow::solve calls totalling 2.09 s, of a 2.38 s solve. Shipped wasm in node: mix4 14.6 ms, mix6 50.9 ms, mix8 1206 ms per solve_train. Seeded prototype (worktree; patch in notes/lens-performance/instrumentation.patch): directions from the lossless flow, then flip the meshes whose driving power has the wrong sign, up to 2M+2 rounds. Run inside every flow::solve of the whole gear-core suite (604 tests, all passing), it never disagreed with the enumeration in efficiency (1e-12) or shaft torques (1e-9) where both found an answer. It failed to find one in 26 calls, every one locked (enumeration η = 0 with backward drivers) or Inconsistent. It also agreed on mix 3/5/6/7, planetary 6, meshed 4 and spur 8 chains. Flow time with it: 8 planetary sets 2.09 s → 72 µs; 6 meshed sets → 93 µs; 32 meshes → 98 µs.
proposal: Replace the enumeration with a seeded fixed point. (1) Solve the lossless flow (every factor 1), which needs no assignment. Set each mesh's driver from the sign of its driving power. (2) Solve with loss, flip every mesh whose driving power is negative beyond ZERO, and repeat until consistent. Bound the rounds at M. (3) Only if that fails (locked meshes, η ≤ 0 one way), enumerate the subset of meshes that can lock or whose power is within ZERO of nought, holding the rest at their seeded direction. That is 2^L with L the lockable meshes, which is one per worm. (4) Keep full enumeration only behind a test-only function, as the oracle. Also hoist the per-assignment allocations (directions, factor, rows) out of the loop. Expected: flow cost from 2^M·poly(M) to about 2-3 eliminations, i.e. a 29,000× speed-up at 16 meshes.
validation: A law run over every preset, every arrangement, and chains up to 8 presets in both directions and at static friction: the seeded solve equals the enumeration (efficiency to 1e-12, shaft torques to 1e-9, same locked verdict). Plus a test holding a 16-mesh chain's solve under a ceiling. The existing Pennestrì law (flow.rs the_per_mesh_flow_is_pennestri_on_a_simple_set) must keep passing unchanged.

verdict.reason: flow::solve loops `for assignment in 0..(1u32 << m)` over every mesh of the whole train (flow.rs:223). It is called per case in solve_parts and four times per path in paths_of (moving and resting, each way, mod.rs:3420 via `flowing`). I measured the cost independently and it doubles with each mesh. The module doc (flow.rs:11) states `2^M` as a design where M was a stage's count. The train-as-graph refactor made M the whole train's, and no document took that change into account.
verdict.evidence: My own release probe (probes/verify-lens-performance-1). Synthetic series chain through flow::solve directly, η=0.98: m=10 took 2.35 ms, m=16 277 ms, m=20 6.04 s, each giving the correct 0.98^m. solve_train on chained planetary sets: 4 sets (8 meshes) 9.5 ms, 6 sets (12) 112 ms, 8 sets (16) 2.19 s. A mix chain of 6 presets (10 meshes) took 25.6 ms.
verdict.proposal_note: The seeded approach (directions from the lossless power signs, then flip until consistent) is the standard Pennestrì/Laus way of determining directions and is sound. Two points to keep: the current code picks the *highest-efficiency* consistent assignment, so the seeded solve needs a law confirming it reaches the same one; and near-zero-power or lockable meshes must fall back to a bounded enumeration over those meshes only. Keep the full enumeration as a test oracle, as proposed. The flow.rs module doc also needs rewording, since it presents 2^M as the method.

repro.reproduction:
Probe crate /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/repro-lens-performance-0 (src/main.rs), built in release through gc against the public gear-core API. There are three modes.
(1) No arguments. It calls `train::flow::solve` directly on a synthetic series chain of m external 20:20 meshes, η=0.98 both ways, driven at body 1 (with BACK=1 it is driven at the far end instead). It then runs `solve_train` on `Train::chained` of n `Preset::Planetary` sets with one `LoadCase::ultimate(chain_ends, 10 N·m, 1000 rpm)`.
(2) Numeric arguments (`-- 4 16 32 33`) run the synthetic chain alone at those m.
(3) `env PLAN=1 SPUR=8,16,17` runs `solve_train` on 8, 16 and 17 chained planetary sets (16, 32 and 34 meshes, 0 couplings). It compares each path's forward and backward efficiency with the single set's value raised to the power n.
Smallest input showing the cost: `flow::solve` on 16 meshes. Smallest input showing the wrong answer: 32 meshes driven backward (synthetic), or 16 chained planetary sets through `solve_train`.
How the correct values are known: a series chain of lossy meshes, or of identical planetary sets joined output to input, has overall efficiency equal to the product of its stages' efficiencies. For the synthetic chain that is exactly 0.98^m, whatever the code does. For the planetary chain it is η_set^n, and the code itself matches that product to 1e-15 for n ≤ 8.
repro.observed:
COST, reproduced. Synthetic `flow::solve` alone, native release:
- m=4: 23 µs
- m=8: 488 µs
- m=12: 12.0 ms
- m=14: 56 ms
- m=16: 277 ms
- m=18: 1.33 s

The time doubles with each mesh, and every answer equals 0.98^m exactly.

`solve_train` on n chained planetary sets (2n meshes):

| n | meshes | time | efficiency | η_set^n |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2 | 222 µs | 0.97682 | 0.97682 |
| 2 | 4 | 915 µs | | |
| 3 | 6 | 2.9 ms | | |
| 4 | 8 | 8.1 ms | | |
| 5 | 10 | 24.6 ms | | |
| 6 | 12 | 92.5 ms | | |
| 7 | 14 | 360 ms | | |
| 8 | 16 | 1.68 s | 0.828914 | 0.828914 (to 2e-15) |

Up to 16 meshes the answer is correct but exponentially slow. This matches the ledger's figures (2.38 s) and the verifier's (2.19 s) to within machine noise. The shipped wasm is opt-level "z" and slower still.

NEW, AND WORSE THAN COST: a silent wrong answer at 32 or more meshes. `flow.rs:223` loops `for assignment in 0..(1u32 << m)` and tests `assignment & (1 << k)`. The release and wasm profiles inherit release, so overflow checks are off and the shift count is masked mod 32:
- m=32: `1u32<<32` gives 1, so only the all-Forward assignment is tried.
- m=34: the shift gives 4, so only 4 assignments are tried.

Synthetic chain, m=32 and 33:
- driven forward: returns the right 0.98^m in about 15 µs, because assignment 0 happens to be the answer.
- driven backward (BACK=1): returns `Err(Inconsistent)`, where the answer is 0.98^32 = 0.52388.

Through the public `solve_train`:
- 16 planetary sets (32 meshes): finishes in 0.75 s, faster than 8 sets. Forward efficiency is 0.6870988 (correct). Backward efficiency is 0.0, where η_bwd^16 = 0.686088. The case is reported `solved: true`.
- 17 sets (34 meshes): forward and backward are both 0.0, where the expected values are 0.67117 and 0.67012. The case comes back `solved: false`.

So a train past 31 meshes is reported as locking or unsolvable. No error or note says anything was skipped. A 31-mesh train would instead run 2^31 eliminations, which is hours. In the dev and test profiles the same shift would panic.

Incidental, not in scope: a chain of 12 spur pairs gives a path with efficiency None and a case not solved. At 14 pairs the train is refused with "the tooth counts along the shaft line multiply past what an exact ratio holds", which is i128 ratio overflow. Spur chains therefore cannot reach the regime above; planetary chains can.
repro.note:
Severity stays high. The ledger's claim reproduces as stated: exponential cost in the whole train's mesh count, 1.7 s at 16 meshes natively, run once per case and four times per path on every solve. Answers below 32 meshes are correct.

The re-judgment adds a correctness defect the ledger and the verifier did not report. The enumeration's `u32` bitmask wraps at 32 meshes. From there `flow::solve` silently searches only a truncated set of assignments and reports efficiency 0 (locks) or an unsolved case for a train that is perfectly efficient. Two facts point the same way: the result is wrong exactly when the solve suddenly becomes fast, and no guard names the limit.

This strengthens the proposal. The seeded fixed point from the lossless power signs removes both the cost and the bitmask. It also needs the oracle law the verifier asked for, that it reaches the enumeration's highest-efficiency assignment. Whatever enumeration survives (the lockable subset L, or the test-only oracle) must use a bound-checked count such as u64 with an explicit refusal above a stated L, never `1u32 << m`.

Suggested extra validation: a law that a backward-driven synthetic series chain at m = 32 and 40 gives 0.98^m. It fails today with Inconsistent.

No worktree was created. The probe and its notes are in /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/repro-lens-performance-0. Locations: /home/user/gearcalc/crates/gear-core/src/train/flow.rs:223 (the loop) and the `1 << k` test inside it; profile inheritance at /home/user/gearcalc/Cargo.toml:33 and :64.

title: `1u32 << m` wraps at 32+ meshes: silently wrong efficiency (false self-locking) and false refusals in release
claim: `for assignment in 0..(1u32 << m)` and `assignment & (1 << k)` overflow once m ≥ 32. In release and wasm (no overflow checks), the shift is masked. At m = 32 only assignment 0 (all Forward) is tried, and at m = 34 only 4 assignments, with bits aliased. So back-driving comes out 0 (self-locking) or the case is refused. A debug or test build panics instead. Nothing bounds M or reports that the model's limit was reached.
evidence: Release probe, chain of 16 planetary sets (32 meshes): path 1->47 efficiency forward 0.6871, backward 0.0, and the solve takes 0.8 s instead of the years 2^32 would need. With the complete seeded solve, the same train gives backward 0.6861. At 8 sets the enumeration gives backward 0.8283, so 0.0 is an artefact. A chain of 17 sets (34 meshes): both cases unsolved with note train.load_shared (Refused::Undetermined); seeded gives backward 0.670 (forward is a separate pivot issue, see the least_squares_exact finding).
proposal: The seeded solve (previous finding) removes the enumeration from production. Whatever enumeration survives, as fallback or test oracle, must use a u64 bound checked against M (`assert!(m < 64)`) or iterate over a `Vec<bool>` counter. It must refuse by name (a Refused::TooManyMeshes carried as a note) rather than mask. The fallback subset L must also be capped, with a note when exceeded.
validation: A unit test with m = 32 and 33 synthetic series meshes (flow::MeshFlow chain, η = 0.98 both ways): efficiency equals 0.98^m both ways. It fails today (backward 0.0). Run under both debug and release profiles.

verdict.reason: The shift wraps in release as described, and the answer comes back silently wrong: a path's backward efficiency reads 0.0, which is self-locking, or the case is refused as load_shared. Severity is lower than claimed because only trains of 32 or more meshes hit it. At 31 meshes the same loop would run for hours first, so a real user meets a hang well before they meet the wrap. It is still a silent wrong answer with no limit reported.
verdict.evidence: Release probe, synthetic series chain with η=0.98. m=32: forward Ok(0.52388), backward Err(Inconsistent), in 12 µs. m=33 and m=34 give the same: backward refused where 0.98^m is expected. Chain of 16 planetary sets (32 meshes): path 1->47 efficiency forward 0.6871, backward 0.0, solve 1.0 s, against 0.8283 backward at 8 sets. 17 sets (34 meshes): forward 0.0, backward 0.0, case solved=false with note train.load_shared.
verdict.proposal_note: Once finding 0's seeded solve is in, any remaining enumeration (the fallback over lockable meshes, or the oracle) needs an explicit cap with a named refusal carried as a note. A u64 bound on its own only moves the cliff.

title: Exact kinematics overflows at 9 chained spur pairs and is reported as 'case underdetermined' while the train still shows a ratio
claim: Ratio::checked_add forms `self.den * other.den` without dividing by gcd(b, d). Reduced-row elimination over i128 therefore overflows on trains whose answer fits easily, and whether it overflows depends on the order conditions are absorbed. The case loop in solve_parts maps any error from motion_in (including Refusal::Overflow) to `determined = false`, which emits TRAIN_CASE_UNDERDETERMINED with short = 0. The designer is told the case is short of a speed when it is fully determined. Train::motion (ground first) succeeds, so the headline ratio is shown beside cases that say they cannot solve, and the train reports no path. per_tooth and motion_from also swallow the error via `.ok()`.
evidence: Probe `kin`, chain of 9 Spur presets: motion_in with first=[driver] gives Err(Overflow); first=[ground] gives Ok(unique, -2.36e-4); Train::motion() gives Ok(-502592611936843/118587876497). solve_train gives paths=0, both cases solved=false with note train.case_underdetermined{short: 0}. Same for 10 and 12 pairs; 8 pairs solve (ratio 1675.5). With checked_add changed to `g = gcd(b,d); a·(d/g) + c·(b/g) over (b/g)·d` (worktree), 9, 10 and 12 pairs solve (ratios -4238.14, 68585.8, η 0.861/0.819), and the failure moves out to between 12 and 16 pairs.
proposal: (1) In ratio.rs, make checked_add cancel by gcd of the denominators, as checked_mul already cancels across. (2) In solve_parts' given_speeds loop, match `Err(Refusal::Overflow)` separately and raise the existing 'ratio too large to hold exactly' refusal (the one Train::motion raises) instead of TRAIN_CASE_UNDERDETERMINED. Do the same for per_tooth and motion_from. (3) Consider solving each case's motion by one reduction of the structural rows reused across conditions (see the paths_of finding), which also removes the order-dependence.
validation: A test chaining 9-12 Spur presets: every case solves and the path ratio equals (43/17)^n exactly. A test on a train built past i128: the case note is the too-large refusal, not underdetermined. A law: for every preset chain, motion_in agrees on the answer for every order of `first`.

verdict.reason: Reproduced exactly. Whether motion_in overflows depends on the order conditions are absorbed. The case loop's `_ => determined = false` (mod.rs:4437) turns Err(Overflow) into TRAIN_CASE_UNDERDETERMINED with short=0, while Train::motion (ground-first) still reports the ratio. Ratio::checked_add (ratio.rs:136) forms den·den without cancelling first, although checked_mul's own comment explains that cancelling is what keeps elimination inside i128. motion_from and per_tooth in paths_of also discard the error with `.ok()?`, so the path simply vanishes.
verdict.evidence: Release probe on chains of Spur (17/43) pairs. n=8: all three orders give Ok, with value 5.97e-4. n=9: motion_in(first=[driver]) = Err(Overflow), while first=[0] and first=[] give Ok(unique, -2.3595e-4). n=10 behaves the same. solve_train at n=9 and n=12 gives no paths and a case note train.case_underdetermined{short: 0}, while t.motion() = Ok(-4238.14) and Ok(68585.8).
verdict.proposal_note: Do all three parts. The gcd cancellation is standard (Knuth's add) and cannot change any exact result. Surfacing Overflow as the existing ERROR_TRAIN_OVERFLOW note, not 'underdetermined', is the actual correctness fix, because the gcd change only moves the threshold.

repro.reproduction: Probe crate /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/repro-lens-performance-2/src/main.rs (release build, public API only). It builds `Train::chained(vec![Preset::Spur.build(); n], ...)` with the ultimate and fatigue LoadCases on `chain_ends()`, for n = 1..16. For each n it prints `t.motion()`, `system().motion_in(c, &[driver])` and `motion_in(c, &[0])`, then `solve_train`'s path count, the first path's ratio and each case's notes. It also calls `Ratio::checked_add` on its own with 1/(3*2^62) + 1/(5*2^62). The correct answer comes from something that shares no code with the crate: the chain of 17/43 pairs is exactly (-43/17)^n, and Python's `fractions.Fraction` gives 4238.144967116917 for n=9, 10720.013740354552 for n=10 and 68585.83185437912 for n=12. To test the fix I made a second worktree probe (repro-lens-performance-2-fixed) with only `checked_add` changed to cancel by gcd(b, d). I ran it, then removed the worktree.
repro.observed:
On HEAD a2f2234:
- n=1..8: everything agrees. At n=8 the path ratio is 1675.5456846741297 = (43/17)^8.
- n=9..13: `Train::motion()` returns the exact ratio, e.g. n=9 gives Ok(-502592611936843/118587876497), which is exactly -43^9/17^9. `motion_in(first=[0])` gives Ok(unique). `motion_in(first=[driver])` gives Err(Overflow). `solve_train` returns Ok with paths=0, and both cases come back solved=false with the note `train.case_underdetermined {short: "0"}`. So the designer is told the case is short of a speed, with a count of zero, on a fully determined train. The largest exact value is 43^13 ≈ 1.7e21, far inside i128 (about 1.7e38).
- n=14..16: `motion()` and `solve_train` both return Err(Overflow). That is the honest refusal, so the misreport occurs only in the window where the ground-first order survives and the driver-first order does not.
- `Ratio::checked_add(1/(3*2^62), 1/(5*2^62))` returns None, but the exact sum is 1/(15*2^59), and its denominator (8.6e18) fits.

With only the gcd-cancelling `checked_add` in the worktree:
- The isolated add returns Some(1/8646911284551352320).
- n=9..12 all solve, with path ratios -4238.144967116917, 10720.013740354552, -27115.33 and 68585.83185437914. These match (43/17)^n to the last digit or two.
- n=13..16 still show exactly the same misreport, now with `motion()` Ok for every n up to 16. The case loop in train/mod.rs (~4431-4437, `_ => determined = false`) still turns Err(Overflow) into TRAIN_CASE_UNDERDETERMINED with short=0.

So the gcd change moves the threshold from 9 to 13 pairs. The real correctness fix is to report Overflow as the existing too-large refusal, which also still fixes the order dependence.

One small ledger slip: the evidence says "9, 10 and 12 pairs solve (ratios -4238.14, 68585.8 ...)". 68585.8 is the n=12 ratio. The n=10 ratio is 10720.01.
repro.note: I downgrade severity from high to medium. No number shown is ever wrong. A determined case is refused, and the refusal text is wrong: it says underdetermined with short=0, while motion()'s exact ratio is still available. That misleads, and it is internally inconsistent, but it only shows on large reductions: 9 or more chained 17/43 pairs, or presumably earlier on trains with large coprime tooth counts. Part (1) of the proposal is standard, and I verified it cannot change an exact result: n=1..8 are unchanged, and n=9..12 now equal (43/17)^n. Part (2) is required, because even after (1) the misreport persists for n=13..16 while motion() succeeds. Part (2) is the fix that removes the bug class; (1) only delays it. A suitable test is a chain of 13 Spur presets on the gcd-fixed tree: today it gives case_underdetermined{short:0} and paths=0, while motion() is Ok. Probe crates are left at /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/repro-lens-performance-2 and repro-lens-performance-2-fixed. The worktree /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/wt/repro-lens-performance-2 has been removed.

title: Shift search is a 13^dof grid plus 3^dof−1 directions: a searched Layshaft is 2.2 s native / 3.9 s wasm per keystroke, and its timing gate skips it
claim: Search::maximise sweeps a full (scan+1)^dof = 13^dof grid, then pattern-walks along all 3^dof − 1 directions with a budget of 2,000 per walk. Objective calls grow as 13^dof: a dof-4 search is about 46k calls, and dof 5 would be about 400k. The search runs inside `cut` on every solve_train, i.e. on every keystroke, including edits (a torque, a speed) that cannot move the geometry. every_search_is_quick_enough_to_type_over says it gates 'All three, because the point is the slowest one', but it times only a pair, a planetary set with two shifts freed, and the hula. The slowest shipped presets are ungated.
evidence: Instrumented maximise, preset with set_search(true), calls per search: Spur dof 2 = 1,967; Crossed dof 2 = 1,934; Wolfrom dof 2 = 990; Idler dof 3 = 12,344; Compound dof 3 = 8,728; Layshaft dof 4 = 46,251 (13^4 = 28,561 of them the sweep); MeshedPlanets dof 4 = 45,850. Per call 8-50 µs. Native searched solve_train: Idler 151 ms, Compound 331 ms, MeshedPlanets 574 ms, Layshaft 2.26 s. Shipped wasm in node: Spur 115 ms, Idler 277 ms, Compound 446 ms, MeshedPlanets 508 ms, Layshaft 3,922 ms.
proposal: (1) Replace the full grid with a fixed-size space-filling sample (a Sobol or Halton set of scan²·k points, or the 2-D grid over the two most influential coordinates). Replace the 3^dof direction set with a positive spanning set of 2·dof (MADS/GPS with rotated orthogonal bases). That keeps diagonal moves at constraint corners without enumerating all of them. Cost becomes linear in dof. (2) Memoise each part's cut on its own inputs (next finding), so a load edit never reruns a search. (3) Extend every_search_is_quick_enough_to_type_over to every preset with set_search(true), one ceiling per preset. Or better, one budget in objective calls (deterministic, no wall clock) per dof, which cannot flake on a loaded machine.
validation: the_search_is_converged_not_budgeted, run for the new sampler over every preset and the existing 30-set and 14-pair studies: optimum objective within its stated tolerance of Search::refined(k) and of the current grid's answer. The golden corpus shows no moved figure beyond that. A deterministic call-count law: calls ≤ C·dof·budget.

verdict.reason: The cost structure is as described: a (scan+1)^dof grid and 3^dof−1 directions (auto.rs:1775-1830). The timing gate covers only a pair, one planetary set and the hula, and its doc still speaks of 'stages' and 'All three'. The claim overstates one thing: this does not run on every keystroke by default. The optimiser is off by default (the gate's own doc says 'nothing pays this unless it was asked for'), and it runs per keystroke only once the designer turns the per-mesh search toggle on in the panel. Once it is on, it does rerun on every input, including load edits.
verdict.evidence: Release probe, Train::alone per preset after set_search(true), one solve_train each: Spur 9.9 ms, Idler 127 ms, Layshaft 1.68 s, Worm 6.7 ms, Crossed 38 ms, Planetary 1.1 ms, Wolfrom 27 ms, Compound 276 ms, MeshedPlanets 341 ms. Planocentric failed to solve at all (see missed). The gate is at mod.rs:9994-10044.
verdict.corrected_claim: When the designer switches the search on, the shift search costs 13^dof grid points plus 3^dof−1 walk directions and reruns on every input. A searched Layshaft takes about 1.7 s native per solve, and Compound and MeshedPlanets about 0.3 s. every_search_is_quick_enough_to_type_over gates none of the dof≥3 presets, and its doc text ('All three', 'Each stage') is stale.
verdict.proposal_note: The deterministic call-count budget is the better gate: it cannot flake, and it removes the known coverage-instrumentation failure of the wall-clock test. A sampler change must be held to the_search_is_converged_not_budgeted on every preset. The gate should also sweep every preset with search on, which would have caught the Planocentric refusal reported in missed.

title: The panel solves synchronously on the main thread on every input; the 'microseconds' premise of that decision is false
claim: `const result = $derived(solveTrain(tab.train, ...))` recomputes on every change to the train, with no debounce, no worker and no latest-wins. Hovering an offer runs previewEdit, which is two more full solves. rationale.md justifies this with 'A full geartrain solve is microseconds, so it runs on the main thread … No worker, no async, no loading states', and CLAUDE.md rule 3 repeats it. Measured, the premise does not hold. Any train past about 5 presets, or any searched multi-mesh preset, freezes the tab for longer than a frame per keystroke.
evidence: Shipped wasm (node, web/src/wasm/gear_wasm_bg.wasm), solve_train: Spur 0.95 ms, Idler 1.33, Layshaft 2.07, Worm 3.60, Crossed 3.13, Planetary 1.28, Wolfrom 1.45, Compound 1.87, Planocentric 5.75, MeshedPlanets 1.59; mix2 1.98 ms, mix4 14.6 ms, mix6 50.9 ms, mix8 1,206 ms. Searched Layshaft 3.9 s. Native preview of each of the 10 train-level offers on a 6-preset mix: mean 163 ms per hover.
proposal: First fix the algorithmic hot spots (seeded flow, search sampler, backlash reuse). Then move the wasm module into a dedicated Web Worker with latest-request-wins: post {seq, train}; drop replies whose seq is stale; keep the last good result on screen with a 'computing' mark. The core stays pure, and 'inputs are the only state' is untouched, because the worker is a transport. Also add a per-part cut memo keyed by the part's serialised shape and library (an LRU of a few entries inside gear-wasm), so edits that move no geometry skip cut and search. Reword rationale.md#… and CLAUDE.md rule 3 to state measured budgets (e.g. 'a lone preset is 1-6 ms in the browser') instead of 'microseconds'.
validation: A node benchmark in tools/ (next to wasm_probe.mjs) recording solve_train time per preset and for mix4/mix6 chains, with a ceiling in CI. Manual: typing into a 6-preset train keeps input latency under 50 ms.

verdict.reason: TrainPanel.svelte:103 derives solveTrain synchronously on every change. Offers.svelte:69 runs previewEdit on hover, which solves both trains (preview.rs). There is no worker or debounce anywhere in web/src (grep finds none). rationale.md:1771 and :65 and CLAUDE.md rule 3 rest this on 'a full solve is microseconds'. My native timings alone refute that for anything past a lone preset: a 6-preset mix takes 25.6 ms, 8 planetary sets 2.2 s, and a searched Layshaft 1.7 s. wasm runs slower still.
verdict.evidence: Code: web/src/TrainPanel.svelte:102-104 `const result = $derived(solveTrain(...))`; web/src/Offers.svelte:69 `const preview = $derived(... previewEdit(...))`; web/src/core.ts:768 is a synchronous JSON call into wasm. My native measurements are above. I did not re-time the wasm numbers.
verdict.proposal_note: Fix the algorithms first (findings 0, 2, 3 and 5): with the flow seeded, lone presets and moderate chains are back to about a millisecond and the synchronous design largely holds. A worker with latest-wins is still worthwhile as insurance, and the hover preview should at least be debounced. The rationale text should state a measured budget, not 'microseconds', and the argument for 'inputs are the only state' does not depend on that word.

title: paths_of recomputes each mesh's play coefficient three times, each a full exact re-reduction of the whole system
claim: backlash_at passes Backlash::banded a closure that sums coefficient(k, read, from) over every mesh. banded calls it at 3 band points, and coefficient does not depend on the band. Each coefficient is System::play, which re-absorbs every structural row from scratch in exact i128 rationals, with gcd per operation, before adding conditions. So a path costs 2 directions × 3 bands × M full exact reductions. Likewise per_tooth rebuilds the whole system per member, and motion_from and each case's motion re-reduce the same structural rows.
evidence: Instrumented paths_of, 16 planetary sets (32 meshes, 50 bodies), flow already cheap: backlash 707 ms and per_tooth 145 ms of a 1.55 s paths_of (≈3.7 ms per exact solve). At 8 sets: backlash 54 ms, per_tooth 12 ms. Memoising the coefficients once per (read, from) (worktree) gives 8 sets 58.6 → 18.1 ms, 16 sets 692 → 374 ms, identical backlash output.
proposal: (1) Hoist the coefficient out of banded: `let c: Vec<f64> = (0..M).map(|k| coefficient(k, read, from)).collect();` and sum `c[k] * play[band]`, which is exact and 3× cheaper. (2) Add a kinematics API that reduces the structural rows once (a `Reduced` kept on System), then absorbs conditions on a clone. motion_in, play and the per-case motions then reuse it. (3) Compute all M play right-hand sides in one elimination: augment with M columns (the mesh unit vectors), giving every coefficient in one pass. (4) Compute per_tooth by the same cached reduction, or by rank-one update of the one row whose count changes.
validation: Existing path/backlash laws and the golden corpus (backlash figures unchanged to the printed digits). A unit law that System::play via the cached reduction equals the current one exactly (Ratio equality) for every preset and chain. Timing ceiling on a 16-mesh chain.

verdict.reason: backlash_at hands Backlash::banded a closure that calls coefficient(k, read, from) for every mesh at each of the three band points (mod.rs:3459-3483). coefficient does not depend on the band, so two thirds of the System::play reductions are redundant. per_tooth rebuilds the system per member through system_counting (mod.rs:3437-3456). I read both in the code. The cost matters only on large trains, and there it is dwarfed by finding 0 until that is fixed, so low to medium.
verdict.evidence: mod.rs:3468 `Backlash::banded(0.0, 1.0, 1.0, |t| { ... row_play.iter().enumerate().map(|(k, play)| coefficient(k, read, from) * play[band]).sum() ...})`; banded (mod.rs:162) calls `angular` three times. I did not re-time the auditor's 707 ms at 32 meshes.
verdict.proposal_note: Step (1), hoisting the coefficients into a Vec before banded, is a one-line change with the same result in exact arithmetic and should go in regardless. Steps (2) to (4), a cached reduction and multi-RHS play, are larger kinematics API changes and are worth doing only if profiling after finding 0 shows them dominant.

title: The wasm ships every string catalogue twice (172 KB, 11% of the payload) because LANGUAGES is a `pub const`
claim: `pub const LANGUAGES: &[Language] = &[… include_str!(…) …]` is a const, so each use site instantiates its own copy of the slice and its string data. The five TOML catalogues appear twice in the shipped module's data segments. Making it `static` leaves one copy.
evidence: Exact byte search of web/src/wasm/gear_wasm_bg.wasm (1,542,209 B): strings_en/de/pt/zh-Hans/zh-Hant.toml each found 2 times, materials_default.toml once; duplicate bytes 172,291. twiggy shows two data segments of 186,121 and 175,523 B, each holding catalogue text. Worktree build with `pub static LANGUAGES` and `fn en() -> &'static str { LANGUAGES[0].source }`: wasm-opt -Oz output 1,524,869 → 1,352,334 B (−172,535), gzip 571,279 → 517,651 B.
proposal: Change `pub const LANGUAGES` to `pub static LANGUAGES`, and replace `const EN: &str = LANGUAGES[0].source` with a function or its own include_str!. Consider also shipping each catalogue as its own lazily fetched asset generated from the TOML at build time. The UI shows one language at a time, which would take out about another 135 KB.
validation: tools/check_wasm.sh (answers unchanged) and a size assertion in it: no catalogue's bytes appear more than once in the module (the same Python count as above).

verdict.reason: Reproduced. The shipped module holds each of the five string catalogues twice. Rebuilding through tools/build_wasm.sh with `pub static LANGUAGES` (and `EN` made a fn) leaves one copy each and takes off 172.5 KB raw and 53 KB gzip. The fix is two lines and changes no behaviour.
verdict.evidence: Byte count over web/src/wasm/gear_wasm_bg.wasm (1,542,209 B): strings_en/de/pt/zh-Hans/zh-Hant.toml each found 2 times, materials_default.toml 1 time. In a worktree, a baseline build through tools/build_wasm.sh (wasm profile, wasm-opt -Oz) came out at 1,542,209 B, the same as the shipped file. With strings.rs:101 `pub const` changed to `pub static` and strings.rs:135 `const EN` changed to `fn en() -> &'static str { LANGUAGES[0].source }`, it came out at 1,369,675 B, catalogues 1 each. gzip -9 went from 567,980 to 514,503. The auditor's absolute sizes differ a little (their baseline was 1,524,869) but the delta agrees: -172,534 B.
verdict.proposal_note: The static change is safe as stated. Lazily fetching the catalogues is a separate, larger design change: every Note is rendered through the core's catalogue, so a missing language has to fall back cleanly. Keep it apart from the two-line fix. A size assertion in check_wasm.sh (no catalogue appears twice) is a good gate.

title: Typed TOML deserialisation monomorphs are ~257 KB of the wasm; the JSON deserialisers for the same types are already there
claim: toml::from_str::<TrainDocument> and ::<MaterialLibrary> instantiate toml's ValueDeserializer for every nested type of a Train and a Material. twiggy attributes 254 KB to toml. serde_json::from_str::<TrainDocument> and ::<MaterialLibrary> already exist in the module (export_train and export_materials take JSON). Parsing TOML untyped (toml::Table) and handing it to the existing JSON deserialiser removes the typed toml instantiations.
evidence: twiggy top/monos on an unstripped wasm-profile build: toml ≈ 254,450 B shallow (the largest single items are ValueDeserializer::deserialize_any/struct monomorphs of 5-19 KB each; monos: 107,906 B across deserialize_any variants and 63,250 B across deserialize_struct). Worktree on top of the static fix: `let table: toml::Table = toml::from_str(src)?; serde_json::from_str(&serde_json::to_string(&table)?)` in both from_toml functions gives 1,352,334 → 1,095,475 B (−256,859), gzip 517,651 → 441,897 B. Cumulative with the static fix: −28% raw, −23% gzip.
proposal: In gear-io, parse to toml::Table, then deserialise the typed document with serde_json (serde_json::from_value, or the string form if that is smaller, measured). Map errors to a key path with serde_path_to_error, so a type error still names where it is (train.shape.members[0].module), and keep toml's own error for syntax. Check that TOML integers into f64 fields and datetimes behave as before: none of the documents use datetimes.
validation: gear-io's round-trip and negative-fixture tests (each malformed document still refused, with the path in the message). The corpus of shipped TOML documents imports byte-identically to JSON before and after. tools/check_wasm.sh.

verdict.corrected_claim: The size saving is real: routing both from_toml functions through toml::Table and serde_json (string form) takes 264 KB raw / 76 KB gzip off the module, on top of the static fix. The naive swap loses diagnostic quality, though. An import error then gives the JSON-string position ('at line 1 column 3564') of a string the user never saw, and for a type error it loses the TOML line/span and the field name. That fails gear-io's a_field_the_shape_no_longer_has_is_refused_and_named. The saving is only kept without that regression if serde_path_to_error (or similar) is added, a new dependency that is not in Cargo.lock.
verdict.reason: Measured. The byte saving holds. The error-message trade-off is concrete and not free: one existing test fails without the extra dependency. The payload is downloaded once and cached, so this is a size-versus-diagnostics trade rather than a defect. Low.
verdict.evidence: Worktree built through tools/build_wasm.sh. Static fix: 1,369,675 B / 514,503 gz. Plus serde_json::from_value(to_value(table)): 1,179,434 / 461,958. Plus serde_json::from_str(to_string(table)): 1,105,908 / 438,307. cargo nextest -p gear-io on the swapped code: 40/41 pass. train::tests::a_field_the_shape_no_longer_has_is_refused_and_named fails with the message 'invalid type: floating point `1.0`, expected struct Auto at line 1 column 3564', which no longer names `module` and points into the intermediate JSON. The auditor also missed a third typed site, train.rs:423 `toml::from_str::<StagedDocument>` in convert(). It is CLI-only, so it does not reach the wasm.
verdict.proposal_note: Add serde_path_to_error (vendoring it touches the Nix fixed-output hashes) and prefix the path to the message. Keep TrainError::Parse carrying toml's own error for syntax, and add a variant for type errors, since TrainError::Parse(toml::de::Error) cannot honestly hold a serde_json error. Also check non-finite floats: TOML allows inf/nan and JSON does not. None of the shipped documents use them, but a hand-edited file could, and it would get a new, confusing refusal. Alternative: do the conversion only in gear-wasm, so the native CLI keeps toml's precise errors.

title: preview re-solves the unedited train on every hover and fully rates both trains to read one path
claim: preview(before, after) calls solve_train on both. The panel already holds `before`'s result from its own solve, and preview reads only its first path and its error. Every hover therefore costs two full solves, including the ratings nothing reads.
evidence: Native probe `offers`: mean preview per train-level offer 1.6 ms (1 preset), 4.2 ms (2), 33 ms (4), 163 ms (6 mixed presets). Each is ≈ 2 × solve_train of that size.
proposal: Give preview the before-train's headline path as an argument, which preview_edit's request can carry from the panel's last result. Or cache the last before-result in gear-wasm keyed by the train's JSON. For `after`, add a paths-only solve (motion, cut, flow, paths_of) that skips `rate`, since preview reports no rating.
validation: preview.rs's laws unchanged (same notes). A test that preview with a supplied before-path equals preview computing it.

verdict.corrected_claim: preview() does solve_train both trains in full and reads only paths.first() and after's error, so re-solving `before` on every hover is redundant. But preview is not ≈2 × solve_train of the train's size. The edited train (usually with a preset added) dominates, and the redundant `before` solve is roughly 7-40% of a preview's time. Skipping `rate` for `after` is not behaviour-preserving: rate() can return TrainError (e.g. NoContact at shape.rs:2563), and preview reports after's error as `unsolved`.
verdict.reason: The structure is confirmed. The size of the waste and the safety of the second half of the proposal are not as stated.
verdict.evidence: preview.rs:110 `let (was, now) = (solve_train(before, lib), solve_train(after, lib));`. Only `first()` and `now.err()` are read (lines 118, 159). Native probe (probes/verify-lens-performance-2, release, 6 non-refused Train-level offers each), before-solve / mean preview / mean after-solve: n=1: 72 us / 1,171 / 1,058. n=2: 637 / 3,058 / 2,282. n=4: 8,002 / 20,621 / 14,659. n=6: 30,287 / 136,718 / 100,947. So preview ≈ before + after, with after 3-15× before. shape.rs:3250 `pub fn rate(...) -> Result<ShapeResult, TrainError>`.
verdict.proposal_note: Passing the before-result's headline path (or caching it keyed on the train) is safe and cheap, but saves only the smaller half. A paths-only solve for `after` must keep rating errors visible, or `unsolved` goes silent on an edit that would leave an unrateable train. At minimum run `cut` and the contacts' construction. Most of the hover cost is the 2^M flow (lens-performance #0), not preview's structure.

title: default_library() re-parses the material TOML on every wasm call that sends no library
claim: solve_train_impl, preview_edit_impl and the others call gear_io::default_library() when `materials` is null, which is the panel's default (TrainPanel passes undefined unless a library was imported). That parses the 11 KB TOML each time.
evidence: Native: default_library() 55 µs, against Spur solve_train 78 µs. Wasm (node): default_materials() 0.369 ms (parse + JSON). Spur solve_train with materials=null 0.781 ms vs materials sent 0.660 ms, i.e. about 0.12 ms and 15% of a lone preset's solve on each keystroke.
proposal: Cache it: `static DEFAULT: OnceLock<MaterialLibrary>` in gear-io, with default_library() returning a clone, or a `&'static` borrowed accessor for callers that only read.
validation: Existing materials tests; a wasm probe timing solve_train(materials=null) ≈ solve_train(materials=sent).

verdict.reason: Every entry point that takes an optional library reparses the compiled-in TOML when none is sent, and the panel sends none by default.
verdict.evidence: gear-wasm/src/lib.rs:835, 1391 and 1621 each do `req.materials.unwrap_or_else(gear_io::default_library)`. materials.rs:79 parses DEFAULT_TOML on each call. TrainPanel.svelte:104 and :332 pass `undefined` unless library.origin is set. Native probe: default_library() takes 50.6 us, against a 72 us lone-Spur solve_train.
verdict.proposal_note: A `static DEFAULT: OnceLock<MaterialLibrary>` works on wasm32-unknown-unknown. Returning `&'static MaterialLibrary` avoids the clone for the three callers that only borrow. It matters only for the lone-preset case: in a 6-preset train, 50 us is noise.

title: least_squares_exact's absolute pivot floor 1e-12 refuses long trains' flows as 'load shared'
claim: A pivot is accepted only if |entry| > 1e-12, an absolute number. The matrix entries are torque coefficients that scale with products of tooth-count ratios along the train. Driving a reduction train from its input, the coefficients shrink by the stage ratio per stage, and past about 1e-12 total the column is taken as empty, giving Refused::Undetermined, shown as TRAIN_LOAD_SHARED. The consistency tolerance 1e-9·scale is likewise chosen by feel. Both tolerances are inside the model rather than relative to the rows.
evidence: Chain of 17 planetary sets (ratio 2.3e14, 7 per set): with the seeded solve (so the 2^M wrap is not involved), the forward path efficiency is 0.0 and both forward cases are refused with train.load_shared. The backward direction, whose coefficients grow instead, solves (η 0.670). 7^-17 ≈ 4e-15 < 1e-12.
proposal: Scale the pivot test to the column (or row) norm: `|a_ij| > ε · max_i |a_ij|` with ε a named constant tied to f64 precision (e.g. 64·f64::EPSILON). Equilibrate rows first, since each row is a body's balance in its own torque scale. Make the consistency test relative to the row's norm, not to max rhs.
validation: A law: scaling every tooth count of a train by k (same ratios) or chaining up to 20 stages leaves the flow's solvability unchanged. The 17-set chain solves forward at η ≈ 0.977^17 per set's efficiency.

verdict.corrected_claim: Reproduced in HEAD without any seeded solve, using a chain of spur pairs (M ≤ 17, under the u32 wrap). Forward is refused Undetermined at 10/70 × 17 (ratio 2.3e14) and 10/100 × 15 (1e15). Backward solves every one of these to η^n. The mechanism is not that the raw entries scale with the ratio (every raw entry is a tooth count times η). Partial pivoting picks the larger driven-side entry in each column, so the input row's remaining entry shrinks by η·zn/zd per column (fill-in), and the last pivot drops under the absolute 1e-12 floor (smallest pivot 4.2e-13 at 10/70 × 17). The problem is a scaling artifact: the torque-unit matrix has cond 1.9e14, while the same system scaled on both sides to mesh power has cond 19. It only bites at total ratios around 1e14, which no real train reaches.
verdict.reason: The defect is real but only reachable at absurd ratios. The mechanism is misdescribed, and the proposed remedy would not cure it.
verdict.evidence: Worktree test calling flow::solve on n spur pairs (za 10, zb 70/100, η 0.98, frame GROUND, Asked::through), results: n=14 both directions Ok. n=15 10/100 fwd Err(Undetermined), bwd Ok(0.7386). n=16 10/100 fwd Err, 10/70 Ok. n=17 both fwd Err, bwd Ok(0.7093). Python (notes/verify-lens-performance-2/chain.py): minimum partial-pivot magnitude 3.1e-2, 1.4e-5, 6.3e-9, 2.9e-12, 4.2e-13 at n=4, 8, 12, 16, 17. Min pivot / column max 4.2e-14 at n=17. Matrix cond 1.9e14 at n=17. With rows × body speed and columns ÷ (za·ω_a), cond is 19.3 at n=17 and 30.7 at n=30. The auditor's own 17-planetary-set scenario (M=34) cannot run on HEAD as described: `1u32 << 34` wraps (lens-performance #1).
verdict.proposal_note: A pivot test relative to the column max (|a| > 64ε·max|a_col|) does not fix this. At n=17 the ratio is 4.2e-14, which passes 64ε≈1.4e-14 only narrowly, and it fails again a stage or two later. Row equilibration alone does nothing, since the rows are already evenly scaled. The cure is two-sided scaling to power units: unknown p_k = c_k·z_a·(ω_a − ω_frame), and each known body's row multiplied by its speed where that is nonzero. The entries then become ±1 and ±η, and a fixed relative tolerance means something. Bodies at rest with known torque need their row left in torque units. Tie this to lens-performance #0: a per-path/seeded solve could take unknowns in the order power reaches them, which is triangular and needs no pivoting.

title: flow.rs says the first consistent assignment is the answer; the code keeps the most efficient one
claim: The comment reads 'Otherwise the first consistent one is the answer, and a second genuinely different one would be a finding worth a test.' The code is `if best.as_ref().is_none_or(|b| efficiency > b.efficiency) { best = Some(flow) }`, which takes the maximum efficiency over all consistent assignments and never flags a second genuinely different one.
evidence: flow.rs lines 342-347 as quoted.
proposal: Decide which is meant and say it once. If several consistent assignments can differ (the locked cases in the suite are where they can), either debug_assert that they agree or state why the most efficient is the physical one. With the seeded solve this comment belongs on the fallback.
validation: A debug-only check in the oracle enumeration that all consistent assignments give one efficiency within ZERO, run over the suite.

verdict.reason: Confirmed, and it matters more than the finding says. Genuinely different consistent assignments occur all the time in the suite, and the max-efficiency tie-break decides the hula/Wolfrom results. The comment at flow.rs:342 and docs/reference.md:1805-1812 ('Two conditions decide it') both say the choice is unique, and neither states or argues the rule the code actually uses.
verdict.evidence: Instrumented flow::solve in a worktree to log every consistent assignment whose efficiency differs from the kept one by more than 1e-9, then ran the full gear-core suite (605 pass). 671 disagreements across 26 tests, e.g. a_path_holds_at_rest_where_no_mesh_does: '0 vs 0.4190 dirs [Backward, Forward] vs [Forward, Backward]' with both meshes at η≈0.995 both ways, so neither is self-locking and both branches pass the sign and energy conditions. Mutating the tie-break to first-consistent (`if best.is_none()`) fails 7 tests: hula::the_hula_efficiency_is_the_reduction_and_the_meshes, the_documented_tables_are_the_ones_this_code_prints, the_four_hula_studies_are_the_ones_this_code_prints, the_circulating_power_is_the_reductions_worth, a_higher_reduction_costs_efficiency, shape::hula_recorded::the_harness_hula_is_what_the_corpus_recorded, and a_path_is_what_it_crosses::every_preset_in_every_pair_is_the_path_across_it_alone.
verdict.proposal_note: A debug_assert that all consistent assignments agree would fire across the suite, so don't add one. Instead state the rule and its physical argument once, in reference.md next to the two conditions: of several self-consistent branches, the one delivering the most power to the output is kept, and say why that branch and not the 0-output 'all lost' one. Then fix the flow.rs comment to point there. Better still, find a third condition that rules out the 0-efficiency branch on physical grounds (it has the output absorbing nothing while the input delivers, all of it dissipated at non-locking meshes), so the selection is a law and not an ordering. The hula tests already hold the behaviour.

title: The Cargo.toml wasm-profile table and the 'microseconds' claims are stale
claim: The table under [profile.wasm] records payload 1,209,487 B and solve_train 0.273 ms at opt 'z', and argues that 'z' costs 0.1 ms against a 16.7 ms frame and that 'nothing here is near a budget'. The shipped module is 1,542,209 B (+27%). A lone preset solve is 0.8-5.8 ms in wasm, and a 6-preset train is 51 ms, over three frames. The table does not say which train it timed, so it cannot be re-measured, and tools/check_figures.py does not guard it.
evidence: ls -la web/src/wasm/gear_wasm_bg.wasm = 1,542,209 B. Node timings above.
proposal: Either drop the table or have a tool regenerate it: add the size and a named-train solve time to tools/check_wasm.sh's recorded output, and tag the block so check_figures.py holds it. Replace 'microseconds' with the measured figure and the train it was measured on.
validation: tools/check_figures.py fails when the payload or timing moves beyond a tolerance.

verdict.reason: The facts hold. The shipped payload is 1,542,209 B, while the Cargo.toml table records 1,209,487 B at opt "z". Its gzipped size is 567,980 B (gzip -9), against 427,195 B in the table. Both timing columns are well off. Nothing guards the table: tools/check_wasm.sh prints the unoptimised-to-optimised byte counts but never compares or records them, and tools/check_figures.py globs docs/*.md and docs/*.html, not Cargo.toml. The 'microseconds' wording is right only for the smallest train. The default two-gear train solves in 95 µs natively, but a train of a few presets takes milliseconds to tens of milliseconds, so the rationale.md:1771 argument ('runs on the main thread ... no worker') rests on a false premise. That part overlaps lens-performance finding 4, which makes the same point about rationale.md:1771. Finding 12's own contribution is the stale Cargo.toml table and the CLAUDE.md:54 and rationale.md:66 wording.
verdict.evidence: sha256 of web/src/wasm/gear_wasm_bg.wasm is 76562036..., identical to four independent audit rebuilds, so the size is the reproducible HEAD build: 1,542,209 B, and gzip -9 gives 567,980 B. Cargo.toml:56-58 records opt "z" at 1,209,487 / 427,195 B, solve_train 0.273 ms, solve_gear 0.058 ms. I timed the shipped wasm in node with the web glue and initSync (notes/verify-lens-performance-3/t.mjs, median of 30). Default train through solve_train: 0.853 ms. solve_gear default: 0.330 ms. Lone presets: spur 0.73, idler 1.13, layshaft 1.95, worm 2.74, crossed 2.88, planocentric 4.10 ms. Default pair with presets inserted by edit_train: +planetary 2.2 ms, +wolfrom 7.9 ms, +layshaft 28.1 ms. The same trains solved natively (probe probe_verify_lens_performance_3, --release, gear_core::train::solve_train only): 0.095, 0.783, 3.278 and 14.212 ms. So 'microseconds' holds natively for the default pair alone, and the 4-part chain takes 28 ms in wasm, over one 16.7 ms frame. The Cargo.toml comment says neither which train it timed nor on which runtime, so it cannot be re-measured. I did not reproduce the auditor's 6-preset 51 ms figure, but my 4-part measurement supports its direction.
verdict.proposal_note: Do not put wall-clock times under check_figures with a tolerance: they depend on the machine, and the project already has one timing test that fails under instrumentation (every_search_is_quick_enough_to_type_over). title: Dolan–Broghamer bending factor goes negative/inf/NaN when the load point is low; a train reports negative bending stress and negative min face width, with no note
claim: `bending_factor(DolanBroghamer)` returns `(Y_F − axial_compression)·K_f`, and `K_f = H + (t/ρ)^L·(t/h)^M` with `h = moment_arm`. Nothing requires h > 0 or `Y_F > axial_compression`. When the unshared load point `d = ε_n − 1` sits low on the flank, which a high transverse contact ratio does (ε_α ≈ 2.3-2.7, plausible with a long-addendum mate), three things follow. The compression term exceeds the bending term, so the tensile-fillet stress comes out negative. As h → 0, `K_f` → ∞. For h < 0, `powf` gives NaN. The train rates with this model, `min_face_width_bending` then goes negative, and no note fires: the `ε_n ≥ 2` band note fires only when load sharing is on (`train/mod.rs:767`).
evidence:
Wild train fuzz, 20,000 cases: 36 NaN, 10 negative and 2 −inf member bending stresses.

Replays (JSON saved in notes/lens-numerical-robustness):
- **train_6199.json** — `pair([318,71])`, m = 8.8135, α = 20°, face 12.207 mm, 1 N·m, sharing off.
  - Member 0: x = −0.3356, h_a = 1.5232. Bending +0.01657 MPa.
  - Member 1: x = +0.5211, h_a = 1.0, h_f = 0.9114, ρ = 0.139, `min_tip_width` 0.494. Bending **−0.000941 MPa**, `min_face_width.bending` **−8.4e-6 mm**.
  - ε_α = 2.286.
- **train_1181.json** — `planocentric(52,56)`: the ring's bending is **−10.87 MPa** and its min face width **−0.265 mm**, at ε_α = 2.656.

`strength::bending_section` on member 1 alone: the moment arm falls from 12.09 mm at ε = 1.2 to 0.98 mm at ε = 2.2856 (form factor 0.121), and the section is `None` beyond about 2.5. The same form factor 0 or NaN shows up in 635 + 282 of the single-gear fuzz cases.

The load location matches ISO's own formula: its outer point of single-pair contact is also `(ε_αn − 1)·p_bn` from the tip, and ISO corrects ε_αn ≥ 2 with `Y_DT`, which this project declines (docs/state.md:965). So the defect is the model's arithmetic, not the choice of point.
proposal:
Make the section's validity explicit in one place, `finish`/`bending_factor`. A section with `moment_arm ≤ 0` is not a bending section, so `root_section_with` returns `None` there, just as it does for an unusable tooth. For Dolan–Broghamer, rate the **governing** fillet rather than the tensile one alone: `max(Y_F − a, Y_F + a)`, or `|Y_F − a|` if only the tensile fillet is modelled. Document which one is chosen.

Where the load point is low enough that `(t/h)^M` exceeds the fit's published range, raise a note (e.g. `strength.load_point_outside_fit`) with ε_n formatted, rather than returning a number. Fire that note from `Bending::new` whenever `eps_n ≥ 2`, whatever the sharing model, since the unshared convention is equally outside its argument there.

Migration: add the guard, add the note key to the 5 string catalogues, and regenerate the golden corpus.
validation: A law over every preset and every arrangement, with the addendum swept from 1.0 to 1.8 so ε_α passes through 1.5-3.2: every `GearCase::bending_stress` is `None` or finite and > 0, and every `min_face_width.bending` is `None` or > 0. Replay train_6199.json and train_1181.json as regression fixtures. Run the new law on the unfixed code first and watch it fail.

verdict.reason: I reproduced it independently. The mechanism is exactly as claimed: at a high contact ratio the unshared load point d = ε_n − 1 falls low on the flank, the moment arm shrinks, Y_F drops below the axial-compression term, and at the same time K_f = H + (t/ρ)^L (t/h)^M blows up. The Dolan–Broghamer factor goes negative and so does min_face_width.bending. No note fires, because Bending::new sets out_of_band only when sharing is on (train/mod.rs:767, `!matches!(model, LoadSharing::None) && eps_n >= 2.0`). title: NaN bending stress at a pointed tip: Lewis tangency has a trivial root at the vertex, and the sharing sweep and candidate reduce latch onto the first NaN
claim:
When the load point is the tip of a pointed tooth (`clamp.tip_capped_pointed`), X = 0 and Y = y_v there. So the Lewis condition `X·Y' + 2X'(y_v − Y) = 0` holds trivially at the vertex, and brent on the flank can return the vertex itself: root chord 0 and moment arm 0, which makes `Y_F` equal 0/0 = NaN, or 0 with `K_f = ∞`.

The load-sharing sweep always samples d = 0, the tip, first. `best.is_none_or(|..| weighted > w)` accepts that NaN as the first best, and every later `weighted > NaN` is false, so the NaN is never replaced. The Lewis `reduce(|a, b| if b.ff > a.ff {b} else {a})` is likewise order-dependent when a candidate is NaN. The result is `Some(NaN)` bending stress in the train, which crosses the boundary as JSON `null`, and the panel shows it blank.
evidence:
Repro (probe `src/bin/repro_tip.rs`): `arrangements::pair([12,40])`, both members `no_sharp_tip = false`, addendum 1.6, pressure angle fixed at 25°, member 0 profile shift fixed at 0.5, `meshes[0].load_sharing = LinearRamp`, `Train::alone(shape, 50.0, 3000.0)`.
- With sharing on, member 1's bending stress is `[Some(NaN), Some(NaN)]` and the JSON carries 4 extra nulls.
- With sharing off, the same member gives 1897.1 MPa.
- A second geometry, x = 0.7, h_a = 1.5, α = 28°, shows the same NaN.

Single-gear fuzz calling `root_section(t, t.u_tip)` on unsevered pointed teeth: 900 ISO factors NaN, 618 Dolan–Broghamer factors +inf, 282 root chords 0.
proposal:
1. In `root_section_with`'s flank search, exclude the vertex. Bracket the flank below the load point (`flank_hi = min(flank_hi, load_roll − δ)`, with δ derived from the tolerance), or reject any tangency whose `X` is ≤ `f64::EPSILON·r`.
2. Make every max/min selection NaN-safe and order-independent. `worst_over_cycle` skips non-finite `weighted`; the Lewis candidates are filtered to `form_factor.is_finite() && form_factor > 0` before `reduce`, using `f64::total_cmp`.
3. A tooth whose tip is pointed has no load-bearing tip, so sampling the sweep at d = 0 on such a tooth should either be skipped or rated at the last point with a finite chord.
validation: The repro pair above gives finite, positive bending with sharing on and off, and sharing on is within the documented 0-0.2 % of sharing off below ε_n = 2. Law: for every `Tooth` with `clamp.tip_capped_pointed` and any roll in `flank_bracket`, `root_section` is `None` or has a finite form factor > 0 and root chord > 0. Fuzz 10k pointed teeth.

verdict.reason: The NaN, its cause and the latch all hold. At d = 0 on a pointed tip, the flank tangency lands on the vertex with chord 0 and arm 0, and `is_none_or(|w| weighted > w)` never replaces a NaN best. But the vertex is not an isolated trivial root that excluding one point would cure. It is the end of a genuine 1/d divergence: as the load approaches a pointed apex, the inscribed Lewis parabola tangent to the flank shrinks, and Y_F ∝ m/p → ∞. Proposal items 1 and 2 (skip non-finite values, bracket the flank below the load point) would turn the NaN into a finite answer that depends on the sample count, far above the true root rating. Only item 3 addresses the defect.
verdict.corrected_claim: On a tooth whose tip is capped pointed, the load-sharing sweep samples load points at and near the apex. There, the Lewis flank tangency lies next to the load, root chord and moment arm → 0, and the form factor diverges like 1/d. At d = 0 exactly it is 0/0 = NaN, which latches as the sweep's best and reaches the train as Some(NaN), sent as JSON null. Skipping the NaN would not fix it: the maximum then grows without bound as SHARING_SAMPLES rises.

title: A rack whose tip width is ≤ 0 still cuts to its full dedendum: root too deep, negative cutter tip width reported, 0-mm pin 'measures', no note, bound admits it
claim:
`Rack::wanted_by` computes `w_tip = (π m_t − s_t) − 2 b_d tan α_t`. When `w_tip ≤ 0` it sets `rho_fit = 0` and floors the round at 1e-9·m, but it never limits the depth `b_d` to where the rack's flanks meet, `(π m_t − s_t)/(2 tan α_t)`. A physical cutter cannot cut below its own point.

The tooth is then built with a root circle deeper than any tool can reach, and a trochoid generated by corners on the wrong side of the crossing. Consequences:
- The space at the base circle has negative width, i.e. adjacent flanks cross above the form circle.
- `pin_diameter_range` returns a lower bound of 0, because a zero-diameter pin 'seats' at the crossing.
- `cutter_tip_width` is negative, and the gear summary sends it to the panel.
- The only note raised is `clamp.fillet_capped`.
- `admissible_ranges` bounds the dedendum at [−1, 0.9r/m] and the pressure angle at (0°, 90°), so nothing tells the user.
- `verify::cutter_sdf` builds its wedge from the tooth's own `ac`/`rf` with `x1 = ac`, `x2 = pitch − ac`. For a pointed rack `x1 > x2`, the wedge is inverted, so the independent instrument inherits the defect and cannot catch it.
evidence:
Probe `src/bin/repro_rack.rs`, `GearParams::default()` with `teeth: 40, pressure_angle: 35.0`:
- Rack tip width −0.1797 m; the pointed-rack depth is 1.1217 m, but r − r_f = 1.2500 m (0.128 m too deep).
- Half space at base −0.0501 rad; pin range (0.0508, 4.36) mm; clamps only `clamp.fillet_capped`; dedendum bound [−1, 18].
- The same gear at z = 100 gives pin range (0.0, 3.90).
- At 30° and 32° the rack still has positive width, yet the space at base is already negative.

Gear fuzz: 3,721 of 30,000 cases report a negative cutter tip width. 2,039 report a pin range starting at exactly 0. Of the first 218 zero-pin cases, 203 have π/2 − 2h_f·tan α < 0, and the other 15 all have `thickness_mod` 1.13-1.18, whose thicker tooth makes the true `w_tip` negative too.

`verify::check_cut` on the 35°/z40 gear reports penetration 0 and deviation 2.2e-4 mm (baseline for a 20° gear: 8.7e-7), so it does not flag this. Nothing in docs/ mentions a pointed tool.
proposal:
Treat a pointed cutter as a guard in the one tool construction, following rule 5 (clamp and say so). In `Rack::wanted_by`:

```
b_d_max = (π m_t − s_t) / (2 tan α_t)
if bd > b_d_max { bd = b_d_max·(1 − ε); push CLAMP_DEDENDUM_POINTED_TOOL(radius) }
```

The round is then forced to `MIN_FILLET` as now.

Mirror the same bound in `ranges_at_shift` as the dedendum maximum. Better, have `ranges_at_shift` call the same `Rack::wanted_by` arithmetic, so there is one expression instead of the copy at auto.rs:679.

In verify.rs, build the reference cutter from `GearParams` (module, α, dedendum, root_radius) rather than from the tooth's derived `ac`/`rf`, and refuse (`None`) a wedge with `x1 ≥ x2`, so the instrument shares no code with what it checks.

New note key in all 5 catalogues.
validation: Law over the gear grid, α = 10-35° and h_f = 0.8-1.7: for every gear, `cutter_tip_width ≥ 0`, `pin_diameter_range` lower bound > 0, and `r − r_f ≤` the pointed-rack depth + m·x. The independent check, rebuilt from the params, reports zero penetration on the clamped tooth. Run the new check against current HEAD first; it must fail on 35°/h_f 1.25.

verdict.reason: The core claim holds. Rack::wanted_by never bounds the depth b_d at the depth where the rack flanks meet, so with w_tip < 0 the root is cut deeper than any tool can reach. The only note is clamp.fillet_capped, and verify builds its wedge from the tooth's own rf, ρ and ac, so it inherits the defect. The ranges_at_shift copy of the w_tip/rho_fit arithmetic (auto.rs:~679) duplicates tooth.rs:~912. Some of the evidence is wrong, though. 'Space at base negative at 30° and 32° while the rack is still positive' is not a defect: there r_b (17.32, 16.96) < r_f = 18.75, so the half-space at the base circle measures involutes extrapolated below the root. That also removes the claim that flanks 'cross above the form circle' as a consequence in general. Severity: 35° with a 1.25 dedendum is uncommon but admitted, and the panel does show a negative cutter tip width, so medium rather than high.
verdict.corrected_claim: When the rack's tip width is ≤ 0 (for example 35° with h_f 1.25), the tooth is still generated to the full dedendum. The root lies 0.128 m below the depth a pointed rack can reach, and the trochoid comes from corners past their crossing. The cutter tip width is reported negative, the pin range can start at 0, and nothing but clamp.fillet_capped is said. The independent check shares the tooth's derived tool and cannot see it. The negative 'space at base' at 30° and 32° is an artefact of r_b < r_f, not a symptom.
verdict.evidence:
Probe repro_rack, run by me:
- 35°/z40: rack tip width -0.1797 m; pointed-rack depth 1.1217 m against r − r_f = 1.2500 m; clamps [fillet_capped]; pin range (0.0508, 4.36).
- 35°/z100: pin range (0.0, 3.90).
- 30°/z40: w_tip +0.127 m, half-space at base -0.0145, but r_b 17.32 < r_f 18.75.

tooth.rs:~899–925: `bd` is capped only by MIN_CUTTER_DEPTH and MAX_CUTTER_DEPTH_FRACTION_OF_R. verify.rs:43–47 takes yb = g.rf + g.rho, x1 = g.ac, x2 = pitch − g.ac from the tooth.
verdict.proposal_note: The clamp belongs in wanted_by as proposed, but the bound must be the depth at which the tip round of radius MIN_FILLET still fits, not the exact crossing times (1−ε), which is another feel-chosen epsilon. Collapsing auto.rs's copy into a call to the Rack arithmetic is the better half of the proposal. For verify, rebuilding the wedge from GearParams alone is right, but it will then disagree with every clamped tooth (fillet cap, depth caps), so it needs the clamp record to know which differences are intended.

title: Heavily undercut teeth: the flank-to-fillet junction lies above the tip, so the profile and DXF outline extend outside the tip circle (verify shows 0.06-0.73 mm cutter penetration)
claim:
`solve_junction` finds the trochoid/involute crossing without bounding it by the tip. Before the tooth severs, there is a band of negative shift where the crossing radius r_j exceeds the tip radius r_a, so u_j > u_tip. `sample_section(Involute)` then lerps from u_tip up to u_j, and the half-profile climbs from the tip circle out to r_j before the trochoid comes back down. The drawn tooth, `Gear::outline` and the DXF export all carry material outside the addendum circle, and radius is not monotone, which CLAUDE.md states as the profile's invariant.

The tooth is neither flagged severed nor clamped. `admissible_profile_shift` admits the band: for the standard 20° gear the minimum is −2.13 at every z.
evidence:
Minimal repro: `GearParams { teeth: 17, profile_shift: -1.5, ..Default }` (20°, h_a 1, h_f 1.25, ρ 0.38). u_j = 0.2004 > u_tip = 0.0562 and r_j − r_a = 0.146 mm. `verify::check_cut` penetration **6.31e-2 mm** (the contract is 0).

Fuzz case gear 1302: m = 3.440788, α = 14.580153°, z = 9, x = −0.685214, β = 6.845211°, h_a = 0.540009, h_f = 1.477107, ρ = 0.372547, tm = 1.198174. r_a = 15.0951 mm but the outline's maximum radius is **16.1532 mm**; check_cut penetration **0.729 mm**. The inputs are within `admissible_ranges` (x ∈ [−2.60, 2.12], addendum ≥ 0.537).

The standard-gear sweep (`src/bin/junc.rs`) puts the band before severing at 20°:
- z = 10: x −1.089 to −1.16
- z = 17: x −1.375 to −1.70
- z = 25: x −1.668 to −2.16

464 of 30,000 random gears hit it, with an overshoot up to 0.47 modules.
proposal:
Close the gap in the tooth construction. In `build_with_z`, after `solve_junction`, if `r_j ≥ r_a` the flank has been consumed entirely. Solve (brent) for the trochoid parameter `s_a` where `trochoid_at(s).0 = r_a` on `[s_j, s_b]`, set `s_j = s_a`, `u_j = u_tip` (the involute section is empty), set `theta_a` from the trochoid at `s_a`, and push a clamp note (e.g. `clamp.flank_consumed`). Downstream code already handles an empty involute through the severed branch's pattern; alternatively make `sections()` omit `Involute` when `u_j ≥ u_tip`.

Bound `admissible_profile_shift`'s minimum at the shift where r_j = r_a, found by bisection on the same flag as the severing bound.
validation: Law over the geometry grid `tests/common` builds, extended into negative shifts down to the admissible minimum: for every unsevered tooth `u_j ≤ u_tip`, `half_profile` radius is monotone, and the outline's maximum radius ≤ r_a·(1 + 1e-12). `verify::check_cut` penetration is 0 on z17 x−1.5 and on gear 1302. Run it on HEAD first: it fails.

verdict.reason: I reproduced it independently. Before the tooth severs there is a band of negative shift in which solve_junction's crossing lies above the tip (u_j > u_tip). The half-profile then climbs past r_a, radius is not monotone (the stated invariant), the outline and DXF carry material outside the tip circle, and verify reports penetration. No clamp note fires. At h_a = 1 the case sits inside admissible_ranges: at x = −1.5 the addendum minimum is (r_b − r)/m − x ≈ 0.987 < 1, and the shift minimum is −2.13.
verdict.proposal_note: The fix in build_with_z (cap the junction at the tip, an empty involute section, a note) is sound. The note must fire exactly where u_j crosses u_tip, so that the outline is continuous in x through the band edge: at x = −1.375 the overshoot is already 0.0008 mm, so the switch changes the outline continuously. Bounding admissible_profile_shift at that crossing is optional once the clamp exists; rule 5 favours clamping and saying so over narrowing the range.

repro.reproduction:
The smallest demonstration uses the built harness and nothing else: `/home/user/gearcalc/target/release/gear-cli show 17 -1.5` (z 17, 20°, standard rack h_a 1, h_f 1.25, ρ 0.38) prints "tip radius 8.000000" and "junction r 8.146181" with "severed false". The flank-to-fillet junction is 0.146 mm above the tip circle.

Probe crate /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/repro-lens-numerical-robustness-3 (public API: Tooth::new, half_profile, Gear::outline, gear_io::dxf::gear_to_dxf with its LWPOLYLINE parsed back, verify::check_cut, admissible_ranges). It sweeps z17 over x and runs fuzz gear 1302.

Independent check: /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/notes/repro-lens-numerical-robustness-3/sim.py. It is a brute-force envelope simulation of rack generation written from scratch in numpy: the cutter tooth is a shrunken trapezoid dilated by ρ, the gear is rolled through 24,001 phases, and the tooth half-width at each radius is found by bisection. It shares no code with gear-core. Its input is the probe's dump of the z17 x −1.5 half-profile (z17_x-1.5.csv in the same folder). No worktree was created.
repro.observed:
z17, 20° standard rack, from the probe:

| x | u_j | u_tip | ra | max radius (half-profile = Gear::outline = DXF) | check_cut penetration | clamps |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| −1.30 | 0.1787 | 0.2323 | 8.2000 | 8.2000 | 0 | none |
| −1.37 | 0.1864 | 0.1898 | 8.1300 | 8.1300 | 0 | none |
| −1.375 | 0.1870 | 0.1864 | 8.1250 | 8.1258 | 3.8e-4 mm | none |
| −1.40 | — | — | 8.1000 | 8.1298 | 1.39e-2 mm | none |
| −1.50 | 0.2004 | 0.0562 | 8.0000 | 8.1462 | 6.31e-2 mm | none |
| −1.60 | — | — | 7.9874 | 8.1631 | 7.74e-2 mm | none |
| −1.70 | — | — | 7.9874 | 8.1805 | 8.85e-2 mm | none |
| −1.75 | — | — | — | — | — | clamp.tooth_severed |

- **Radius is not monotone.** From −1.375 onward the half-profile has radius-increasing steps: 2 of them at −1.375, 16 at −1.5, 20 at −1.7.
- **The input is admissible.** admissible_ranges gives x_min = −2.1304 at z17.
- **Fuzz gear 1302** (m 3.440788, α 14.580153°, z 9, x −0.685214, β 6.845211°, h_a 0.540009, h_f 1.477107, ρ 0.372547, k 1.198174): ra = 15.0951, but the outline and DXF reach 16.1532 mm. Penetration is 0.729 mm, and the only note is clamp.fillet_capped.

The envelope simulation (z17 x −1.5) confirms this independently:
- Below ra, the code's trochoid matches the simulation to within 1e-7 mm at every radius tested from 5.78 to 7.92 mm. So the construction is right except in this band.
- Of the 29 code profile points above ra (up to 8.1462), 15 lie inside the swept cutter. The rest lie outside the turned blank, which by definition ends at r_a. The true tooth has no material there.

A second wrong answer the claim did not state: the tip land. The code's θ_a = 0.022639 rad, taken from the involute at u_tip, but no involute exists there. The simulation's true half-width at r_a is 0.034800 rad (the trochoid meets the tip circle directly). So the tip land is 0.362 mm (2·r_a·θ_a) where it should be 0.557 mm, about 35% too narrow. Anything that reads 2·r_a·θ_a gets it wrong in this band: the tip-width addendum at auto.rs:2229, the test at train/mod.rs:9682, the outline's tip arc at outline.rs:224–226, and verify's exemption of the tip arc at verify.rs:135.

The band begins where u_j crosses u_tip, between x = −1.37 and −1.375, and the overshoot there is only 8e-4 mm. So a clamp that fires exactly at that crossing keeps the outline continuous, as the verdict says.

Related, seen in passing: from x = −1.6 on, ra shows 7.9874 = r_b while the nominal is 7.9. tooth.rs:471 raises it silently with `ra.max(rb*(1+TIP_ABOVE_BASE_FRACTION))` and no note. At x = −1.6, h_a = 1 is below the addendum minimum ((r_b − r)/m − x ≈ 1.087), so this is outside the admissible range and not part of the finding. Still, it is a silent clamp, which goes against rule 5.
repro.note:
Severity stays high. For admissible inputs, with a standard rack at x = −1.5 and no note, the tool exports a CAD outline (Gear::outline and DXF) with material up to 0.15 mm (standard gear) or 1.06 mm (fuzz gear 1302) outside the tip circle. That breaks the stated invariant of monotone radius, and verify's zero-penetration contract fails. It also misreports the tip land by about 35%, which feeds the tip-width addendum. It goes unnoticed because the `gear-cli verify` grid and the tests/common grid do not reach this negative-shift band before severing.

The proposed fix is confirmed in principle by the simulation: the true profile below the tip is exactly the code's trochoid. In build_with_z, when r_j ≥ r_a:
- solve the trochoid for r = r_a on [s_j, s_b];
- set s_j to that parameter, u_j = u_tip (an empty involute section), and θ_a from the trochoid at that point;
- push a clamp note.

The validation law (u_j ≤ u_tip, monotone radius, outline max ≤ r_a·(1+1e-12), zero penetration on z17 x −1.5 and gear 1302) should also assert θ_a against the trochoid's angle at r_a (0.034800 rad for z17 x −1.5). Otherwise the tip land error survives a fix that only trims the overshoot.
