It never builds a Train, LoadCase or CaseLoad, so it cannot move when load cases change, and citing its stillness as 'the check that a case was added rather than substituted' proves nothing for it. Only the wormstage canary goes through Train::alone.
evidence: state.md:243-246: 'Load cases moved neither canary, three times ... which is the check that a case was added rather than substituted for the first.' main.rs:2184-2320 has no Train in strength_report.
proposal: Restrict the sentence to the wormstage canary, or give the strength canary a train path, e.g. a nextest law asserting that Train::alone(arr::pair 17/43, x 0, no_undercut off, clearance 0, b 10) reproduces its figures.
validation: Documentation reads true against the code, and the added law fails if the train rating diverges from the primitives.

verdict.reason: strength_report builds Tooth and Mesh directly and never touches Train, LoadCase or CaseLoad. Load-case changes cannot move it, so its stillness is no check that a case was added rather than substituted. Only the wormstage canary goes through the train.
verdict.evidence: awk over fn strength_report: Tooth::new (lines 25, 30), Mesh::new (35, 98), and no Train, alone or solve_train. state.md:243-246: 'Load cases moved neither canary, three times ... which is the check that a case was added rather than substituted for the first.' No nextest law ties Train::alone(pair 17/43) to the canary's figures. The nearest is gear-wasm a_train_of_two_presets_crosses_the_boundary, which uses 17/43 but does not assert σ_F 66.8/56.0. The probe's pair through Train::alone gives bending 67.15/56.85, not the canary's 66.8/56.0, because its settings differ.
verdict.proposal_note: Restricting the sentence is the S-effort fix. If a train-path law is added, its settings must be chosen to match strength_report's (clearance, shifts, width). The probe's defaults give 67.15/56.85 against the canary's 66.8/56.0, so an unmatched law would pin different figures.

title: A gear's reported torque is not cut by loss, contrary to its doc and docs/reference.md
claim: Two places say that GearCase::torque on the member at the far end of a mesh is 'the load referred by the ratio and cut by the loss the mesh takes carrying it that way, which for a locked mesh is nought': the field's doc comment (mod.rs:1331-1335) and docs/reference.md#trains (2925-2928). The code does something else. Member torque is the driver's torque referred by the ratio with no loss applied, and only the body's figure (`on_body` and SlotCase torques) is cut by the loss. The test a_self_locking_worm_reports_the_load_it_reacts (mod.rs:4986-5010) states the implemented convention: 'a member's torque is the torque its teeth carry, the driver's read across the mesh, whether or not the mesh passes any of it on … it is the body's figure, not the gear's'. So the field doc and the reference contradict the tested behaviour. The harness then shows both conventions under one name: `wormstage 1 40 7 2` prints wheel 'torque Nm 80.0000' beside 'efficiency 61.805 %', while `worm 1 40 7 90` prints 'wheel torque 54.953 Nm' (T·i·η).
evidence: Probe /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/verify-gear-cli-2 (Train::alone at 2 N·m, 1000 rpm). pair [17,43]: member 1 torque 5.058824 (= 2·43/17 exactly), on_body 4.975099 (= ×0.98345, the mesh's forward η). worm(1,40), d1 7: member 1 torque 80.000000, on_body 49.443687 (η 0.61805). crossed [17,23] 90°: member 1 torque 2.705882, on_body 2.278785. With a locked mesh the member torque is not nought either (the worm test asserts worm torque = wheel/ratio whether or not the mesh locks).
proposal: Rewrite the GearCase::torque doc and the reference.md paragraph to state the implemented convention: 'the torque its teeth carry, the driver's referred by the ratio, before the mesh's loss; what its body delivers, cut by that loss, is on_body / the case's body torques'. Note in docs/state.md that bending on a driven member is therefore rated at the lossless tooth load, with its size and sign (+1.7 % torque on a 17/43 spur, +62 % on the 1/40 worm; a conservative direction, per Rule 6). Label the harness columns to match ('tooth torque' against 'delivered').
validation: Re-run the probe: the documented definition must predict member torque = driver torque × |ratio| and on_body = that × η. check_doc_links and check_figures stay green.

verdict.reason: The GearCase::torque doc (mod.rs:1331-1335) and reference.md:2925-2928 describe a member torque cut by the mesh's loss, nought when the mesh locks. The code and the test comment at mod.rs:4986-5010 do something else: the torque is the driver's referred by the ratio, and only on_body is cut. reference.md contradicts itself, since line 2824 says 'the torque its teeth carry'. corrections.md:400 records the change: 'the wheel's torque is the load its teeth carry ... 80 N·m on the shipped stage where 49.4 was the shaft's delivered torque'. corrections.md:551 is the older historical row this superseded and is fine as history.
verdict.evidence: Re-ran probes/verify-gear-cli-2. Worm: member 1 torque 80.000000, on_body 49.443687 (η 0.61805). Pair 17/43: 5.058824 (= 2x43/17), on_body 4.975099 (x0.98345). Crossed: 2.705882, on_body 2.278785. Golden wormstage shows wheel 80.0000 next to worm's 'wheel torque 54.953 Nm'.
verdict.proposal_note: Rewrite the field doc and reference.md:2925 as proposed; that part is right. The suggested state.md bias entry is not. The torque 'before the loss' is not an overestimate of the tooth's normal load. T2/r_b2 = T1·i/r_b2 = T1/r_b1, which is the driver's normal force, the force that actually presses both teeth. The loss comes out of the friction component, not the normal load, and contact was 'taken on the flank force all along' (corrections.md:400). So the +1.7 % and +62 % are not a rating bias on bending or contact. Describe it as the tooth (normal-force) torque, not as a conservative error. At most, record that the friction force's own bending contribution is not modelled.

title: The cutter-check grid is written twice: in gear-cli verify and in rack_simulation.rs
claim: gear-cli verify hand-nests the same 1080-case grid that the suite builds through tests/common::Grid: tooth counts 3..47, shifts -0.5..0.9, three pressure angles, helix {0, 20}, tip radius {0, 0.25, 0.38}. The two are kept in step only by hand. If one changes, the harness and the suite silently check different gears. The CLI copy also defines the golden `verify 100` prefix problem.
evidence: main.rs:2573-2577 `for z in [3u32,5,8,9,11,13,17,23,31,47] / for xi in [-5,-2,0,2,5,9] / for an in [14.5,20,25] / for beta in [0,20] / for rr in [0,0.25,0.38]` against rack_simulation.rs:31-36, the same values through Grid.
proposal: Expose the grid once, as gear_core::verify::cutter_grid() -> Vec<GearParams>. Use it from rack_simulation.rs and from gear-cli verify, and record the full `verify` in the corpus (38 s release, already marked slow).
validation: `gear-cli verify` still reports 1080 cases with the same worst figures (6.150734e-4 at z=31), and the suite's gate test is unchanged.

verdict.reason: The two grids hold the same values, written twice: z {3,5,8,9,11,13,17,23,31,47}, shifts xi*0.1 (which Python confirms equal the literals -0.5, -0.2, 0.2, 0.5, 0.9 exactly), angles {14.5, 20, 25} (PRESSURE_ANGLES), helix {0, 20}, root radius {0, 0.25, 0.38}. Only hand discipline keeps them in step. verify.rs sits in the library so the CLI can sweep it (CLAUDE.md), so a library-level grid function fits.
verdict.evidence: main.rs:2573-2577 nested loops. rack_simulation.rs:29-37 Grid::new().teeth(...).shifts(&[-0.5,-0.2,0.0,0.2,0.5,0.9]).pressure_angle(PRESSURE_ANGLES).helix_angle(&[0.0,20.0]).root_radius(&[0.0,0.25,0.38]). tests/common is integration-test only, so the CLI cannot call Grid.
verdict.proposal_note: Put cutter_grid() in gear_core::verify and call it from both places. The iteration order may differ between the two (the Grid's order against the nested loops). Only the 'verify 100' prefix recorded in the corpus depends on that order, so either keep the CLI's order or re-record the prefix.

title: A worm arrangement with more starts than its 7 mm diameter allows (starts > 7 at module 1) produces a Shape that cannot be read back from JSON
claim: arr::worm(starts, z) with starts > 7 leaves NaN in the automatic helix boxes, and with_first_helix keeps it on the other members. serde_json writes NaN as null, and deserialising that into f64 fails. Such a shape can be saved but not reopened. No test round-trips arrangement shapes, so nothing notices.
evidence: Probe probes/verify-lens-magic-numbers-1: worm(17,23).with_first_helix(45.0) serialises, and reading it back gives Err("invalid type: null, expected f64 at line 1 column 1230"). worm(1,40) round-trips Ok. Only code paths reach it (crossed.rs tests, and the CLI's worm/wormstage with a starts argument). The panel's Preset::Worm is worm(1,40).
proposal: Seed the helix only where z₁·m < d₁, otherwise leave the default. Separately, add a law that every Preset::ALL shape and every arrangements:: builder output round-trips through serde_json unchanged. More broadly, consider refusing non-finite values in Auto's manual field at serialisation time.
validation: The new round-trip law fails on worm(17,23) before the fix and passes after it.

verdict.reason: worm() seeds helix = acos(starts/7). For starts > 7 that is NaN, and the wheel's automatic 90 - NaN keeps it. with_first_helix fixes only member 0. serde_json writes NaN as null and refuses it on reading back. Only code reaches this: crossed.rs tests build worm(17,23) as a crossed pair. Preset::Worm is worm(1,40), and the CLI calls take starts from arguments.
verdict.evidence: Re-ran probes/verify-lens-magic-numbers-1: worm(1,40) round-trips Ok; worm(17,23).with_first_helix(45.0) gives Err('invalid type: null, expected f64 at line 1 column 1230'). arrangements.rs:712 `(f64::from(starts) / 7.0).acos()`; 725 `wheel.helix_angle = Auto::automatic(90.0 - helix)`.
verdict.proposal_note: Seed the helix from the diameter actually used, clamped: acos(min(1, z1·m/d1)). A crossed pair should be built with arr::crossed rather than worm(17,23), and the tests at crossed.rs:357 and 670 changed to match; they currently lean on worm() for a shape that is not a worm. Add the round-trip law over Preset::ALL and every builder, as proposed.

title: set_duty's doc says continuous hours come from 'the same numbers a fresh case starts with', but a fresh case has no hours
claim: The doc comment says both duty seeds are the fresh case's numbers. A fresh case is always Duty::intermittent (25°, 1000 actuations) with no runtime hours, so the 1000 h is set_duty's own literal.
evidence: conditions.rs:1144-1147 '/// seeded from the same numbers a fresh case starts with: a thousand sweeps of 25°, ... or a thousand hours.' and :1162 `runtime_hours: 1000.0`. mod.rs:2936-2947 LoadCase::ultimate uses Duty::intermittent(output) only.
proposal: Add Duty::continuous() with a named hours constant and a sentence explaining why 1000 h, and fix the comment.
validation: Read the code; a unit test that set_duty(c, false) equals Duty::continuous().

verdict.reason: The doc comment says both seeds are a fresh case's numbers. A fresh case (fresh_case -> LoadCase::ultimate/fatigue) only ever starts with Duty::intermittent, so the continuous 1000 h is a literal belonging to set_duty alone. The comment is inaccurate and the literal has no stated reason.
verdict.evidence: conditions.rs:1144-1147 '/// seeded from the same numbers a fresh case starts with: a thousand sweeps of 25°, ... or a thousand hours.'; conditions.rs:1161-1163 `super::Duty::Continuous { runtime_hours: 1000.0 }`; mod.rs:2763-2773 has only `Duty::intermittent`, with no continuous constructor; the same 1000.0 is written again in a test at mod.rs:10582.
verdict.proposal_note: Duty::continuous() with a named, justified hours constant, plus the corrected comment, is right. The test at mod.rs:10582 should call it too, so the figure is written once.

The comment at the second site says they are 'the shipped train's', but nothing ties the two together, so changing one leaves the other stale.

verdict.evidence: gear-wasm/src/lib.rs:1175 `LoadCase::ultimate(input, output, 0.1, 30_000.0)`, :1177 `LoadCase::fatigue(input, output, 0.02, 30_000.0)`; :1573 `// The figures a fresh case starts at are the shipped train's.` :1576-1577 `CaseKind::Ultimate => (0.1, 30_000.0), CaseKind::Fatigue => (0.02, 30_000.0)`. No gear-core constant holds them.

title: Adding a ring on a planet at a Δz=1 carrier radius is accepted but gives a train that cannot solve
claim: central_teeth sizes a ring as max(fit + zp, zp + 2). At a planocentric's Δz = 1 carrier radius this forces a ring two teeth larger than the planet, which cannot close at that radius (the comment at edits.rs:421-428 itself says so). The edit is accepted and the train then fails.
evidence: Probe probes/verify-lens-magic-numbers-3: planocentric(18,19) solves OK. After Train::edit(Edit::AddGear{mate:0, on:Place::NewBody(0), ring:true}), the members are [(18, ext), (19, ring), (20, ring)] and solve_train returns Err(InPart { part: 0, cause: NoCommonDistance }). planocentric(30,33) with the same edit gives a 32-tooth ring and solves.
proposal: Either refuse with NoRoom when no ring count other than one already taken can close at the fit (fit ≤ 1 with the only Δz = 1 count taken), or drop the zp+2 floor and use the fit, moving by a tooth only as `taken` requires. Also check offers.rs so the add is not offered where it would be refused or would fail.
validation: A test in edits.rs: planocentric(18,19) with AddGear ring on the central axis is refused NoRoom, or the edited train solves. every_add_on_every_preset_solves already sweeps presets, but none has Δz = 1, so add the hula or planocentric(18,19) to its sweep.

verdict.reason: Reproduced, and the failure is wider than Δz = 1. For every planocentric with Δz ≤ 2 that I tried, the ring add on a new body is accepted and also offered without refusal, and the edited train then fails NoCommonDistance. The floor zp+2 in central_teeth stops the 'move down a tooth' rule that the adjacent comment argues for. At Δz = 1 there is no smaller ring count at all, so that comment's claim 'a tooth smaller always has [somewhere to close]' does not hold there. The edited train fails whole (the preview does report why it would not solve, which limits the harm), but it breaks the rule that an offered edit leaves a solving train.
verdict.evidence: Probe probes/verify-last-7 (Train::alone + Edit::AddGear{mate:0,on:NewBody(0),ring:true} + solve_train): plano 18/19 -> teeth [(18,ext),(19,ring),(20,ring)] Err(InPart{part:0,cause:NoCommonDistance}); 20/21 -> 22, same Err; 30/31 -> 32, same Err; 30/32 -> 33, same Err; 18/20 -> 21, same Err; 30/33 (the shipped preset) -> 32, Ok. Train::offers(Target::Member(0)) lists AddGear{mate:0,on:NewBody(0),ring:true} with refused = None in every case. edits.rs:414-415 `(true, Some(f)) => (f + f64::from(zp)).max(f64::from(zp) + 2.0)`; :429 `let floor = if ring { f64::from(zp) + 2.0 } else { 4.0 };`.
verdict.corrected_claim: For any planocentric whose carrier radius fits Δz ≤ 2 (18/19, 20/21, 30/31, 30/32 and 18/20 all tested), the ring add on a new body is offered unrefused, is accepted, and gives a train that fails NoCommonDistance. At Δz = 1 no other ring count exists. At Δz = 2 the zp+2 floor stops the one-tooth-smaller move to zp+1, and the only larger count (zp+3) needs a distance tighter than its reference.
verdict.proposal_note: Lower the ring floor to zp+1. Once the fitted count is taken, refuse with NoRoom when no count ≥ zp+1 other than the taken one can close at the carrier radius (check with the same operating-angle test the solve uses: cos α_w = a₀ cos α / a must lie in (0,1)). The refusal is then in the edit, so offers.rs reports it with no change. Add planocentric(18,19) and (30,32) to the every_add_on_every_preset_solves sweep.

title: The smallest pinion count that solves is not monotone in the mate's count
claim: A 2-tooth pinion solves against 3, 4, 100 and 400 teeth but fails with NoContact against 6 and 10. A 3-tooth pinion solves against 3, 4, 6 and 100 but fails against 10 and 30. If contact ratio falls monotonically with smaller pinions, the solvable set should not have holes like this. It may come from the automatic shift or thickness choice switching regimes.
evidence: Probe probes/verify-lens-magic-numbers-3: pair([z, m]) via Train::alone plus solve_train. OK: 2/3, 2/4, 3/3, 3/4, 3/6, 4/6, 4/10, 2/100, 3/100, 2/400, 3/400. NoContact: 2/6, 2/10, 3/10, 3/30, 2/30.
proposal: Sweep z1 in 2..6 against z2 in 3..400 and record where NoContact appears together with the automatic shifts chosen. If the holes come from the shift rule switching (undercut bound vs thickness), say so in state.md. Otherwise find the branch that makes contact disappear.
validation: A sweep test that, for fixed z1, solvability in z2 is an interval or has a documented reason.

verdict.reason: There are no scattered holes. For each small pinion, solvability in z2 is one contiguous band of failures with a solvable range on each side. Instrumenting the solve shows the cause is flank or tip interference, not an absence of contact: at every failing mesh the path's approach end runs past the pinion's interference point (approach > r1·sin α_w). contact_stress then gets a negative curvature radius at ξ = −approach, returns None, and shape.rs:3322 turns that into TrainError::NoContact, which reads 'the teeth never contact'. The failure is therefore physical, but it is refused with a false message. The model already has a way to report interference (MeshReport::flank_interference) and a note for contact ratio below one, so rule 5 (clamp or say so, rather than refuse input that describes a shape) points at a note rather than a refusal. Solvability is not monotone because the mate's automatic shift falls to 0 at large z2 while the pinion keeps its undercut shift: toward the rack limit that shift keeps the mate's tip line at the pinion's interference point, and mid-size mates overshoot it.
verdict.evidence: Sweep, z2 = 3..400: z1=2 fails NoContact at z2 = 5..36 only; z1=3 fails at 7..98 only; z1=4 fails at 9 only; z1=5,6 never fail. I added an eprintln at shape.rs's two NoContact sites in a throwaway worktree (since removed); every failure came from contact_stress (shape.rs:3322), never from ContactPath::new. Examples: 2/5 approach 0.9496 > r1 sin α_w 0.8926; 2/36 0.45668 > 0.45544; 3/7 1.1667 > 1.1104; 4/9 1.29952 > 1.29767. Neighbours that solve: 2/4 ε 0.716, x = 0.938/0.766; 2/37 ε 0.724, x = 0.938/0.000; 4/10 ε 0.968. strength.rs:1856-1860 `at(0.0)?`, `at(lo)?`, `at(hi)?` with mesh.rs:634 `if rho1 <= 0.0 || s * rho2 <= 0.0 { return None; }`.
verdict.corrected_claim: For a fixed small pinion (z1 = 2..4), the pairs that fail form one contiguous band of mate counts (z1=2: 5..36; z1=3: 7..98; z1=4: 9). Each failure is tip-into-root (flank) interference, where the mate's tip passes the pinion's interference point. contact_stress reports it as None and the train refuses it as NoContact, 'the teeth never contact', which is false: the teeth do contact, too deep.
verdict.proposal_note: Give the pinion-interference case its own TrainError, or better, per rule 5, rate the contact over the part of the path that lies outside the interference points and raise the mesh's interference note, rather than aborting with NoContact. Then add a law that NoContact is raised only when ContactPath::new finds no path.

title: docs/corrections.md links to a README that is not beside it
claim: The table row at corrections.md:608 starts with `[README.md](README.md)`. The link resolves relative to docs/, and there is no docs/README.md, so the link is dead on GitHub. check_doc_links cannot see it because its CROSS pattern requires a '#anchor'.
evidence: `ls docs/README.md` gives 'No such file or directory'. The only README is at the root (`git ls-files | grep -i readme` gives README.md). A scan over every tracked file for `](x.md)` links whose target does not exist relative to the linking file found only this one.
proposal: Change it to `[README.md](../README.md)`. Extending check_doc_links to test file existence for anchorless links (finding tools-ci #5) would have caught it.
validation: Once fixed, the relative path `docs/../README.md` exists, and an extended check_doc_links run over the tree reports no dead file links.

verdict.reason: docs/corrections.md sits in docs/, which has no README.md, so the relative link `README.md` is dead. check_doc_links' CROSS regex requires a '#anchor', so an anchorless link to a file is never checked.
verdict.evidence: `ls docs` -> bending-check.html corrections.md history rationale.md reference.md state.md (no README.md); `git ls-files | grep README` -> README.md (root only); corrections.md row `| [README.md](README.md) | **`README.md` said the harness prints ε = 1.777921670 ...`; tools/check_doc_links.py:59 `CROSS = re.compile(r"\]\((?:\./)?([a-z0-9_-]*)(?:\.md)?#([a-z0-9-]+)\)")` requires '#'.
verdict.proposal_note: Changing it to ../README.md is right. Also let check_doc_links resolve anchorless `](x.md)` links, relative to the linking file.

title: Every gear-wasm request type, TrainEdit among them, is hand-mirrored in TypeScript as an inline literal
claim: The response types cross through ts-rs, but the private Deserialize request types in gear-wasm do not: AdoptRequest, RelieveRequest, RelieveCaseRequest, TrainEdit (a `#[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]` enum), EditRequest, PreviewRequest and OffersRequest. The TS side builds their JSON as untyped inline object literals. If a field is renamed in Rust, the TS literal still compiles and serde then ignores or rejects the field at run time. check_bindings cannot see it.
evidence: lib.rs:1542-1548 `#[derive(Deserialize)] #[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")] enum TrainEdit { Graph(..), AddCase(..), Duty { case, intermittent } }` has no TS derive. core.ts:809-812 hand-writes `{ graph: Edit } | { add_case: CaseKind } | { duty: { case: number; intermittent: boolean } }`. core.ts:680 `relieve(JSON.stringify({ shape: train.shape, just, figures }))` and core.ts:853 `wasm_offers(JSON.stringify({ train, at }))` are inline literals.
proposal: Add `#[cfg_attr(feature = "typescript", derive(TS), ts(export, export_to = "wasm/"))]` to each request type, and make each pub, or pub(crate) if ts-rs allows it. Regenerate with check_bindings.sh --write, and type each call in core.ts with the generated request type (e.g. `const req: RelieveRequest = {...}`). Delete the hand-written TrainEdit union.
validation: Rename TrainEdit::Duty's `intermittent` field in Rust, run check_bindings.sh --write, and confirm that `npm run check` fails at core.ts's editTrain caller.

verdict.reason: The finding holds. gear-wasm's request types AdoptRequest (lib.rs:1338), RelieveRequest (1451), RelieveCaseRequest (1489), TrainEdit (1544), EditRequest (1551), PreviewRequest (1608) and OffersRequest (1650) are private and derive only Deserialize, with no cfg_attr TS. The response types and GearRequest, RingRequest and TrainRequest do derive TS. core.ts hand-writes the TrainEdit union at 809-812 and builds every request as an inline literal (680, 711, 816, 832, 853). It is worse than the finding says, because every one of these callers swallows the error in a bare catch (relieveTrain returns, offersAt returns [], previewEdit returns null, editTrain returns null unless the message starts with 'ui.'). A renamed field therefore fails silently in the UI rather than loudly. tools/wasm_probe.mjs is a third hand-written copy of the same shapes (lines 104, 151-155, 278). check_wasm would catch a rename only if nobody updated the probe, and it says nothing about core.ts.
verdict.evidence: grep of lib.rs: 'Deserialize' at 1337/1450/1488/1542/1550/1607/1649 with no cfg_attr, against the cfg_attr(feature="typescript", derive(TS)) blocks on GearRequest (27), RingRequest (438) and TrainRequest (743). core.ts:809 `export type TrainEdit = | { graph: Edit } | { add_case: CaseKind } | { duty: { case: number; intermittent: boolean } };`. core.ts:680 `relieve(JSON.stringify({ shape: train.shape, just, figures }))` sits inside `try {...} catch { return; }`.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposal is sound: follow the pattern GearRequest and TrainRequest already use. ts-rs needs the types reachable from the export, and pub is the simplest way. Edit, CaseKind, Freedom, Figure and Target already cross, so the generated request types compose. Annotate each call in core.ts (`const req: EditRequest = {...}`) so a rename becomes a type error. wasm_probe.mjs stays untyped JS; its drift is caught by running it.

title: check_golden.sh --write deletes the whole corpus when the case list is empty
claim: If `gear-cli --golden-cases` fails or prints nothing, `--write` runs `rm -f "$store"/*.txt` and then fails on `cp "$scratch"/*.txt`. That leaves tools/golden empty and the script exits 1.
evidence: Fake-root reproduction in /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/notes/verify-tools-ci-3/fakeroot with a stub binary that exits 1 on --golden-cases. After `check_golden.sh --write`, `cp: cannot stat .../*.txt`, exit 1, and tools/golden held 0 files where it had held 32.
proposal: Capture the case list with `list=$("$bin" --golden-cases)` so set -e sees the failure, and fail if the list is empty. In write mode, verify the scratch set is non-empty before removing the store, or write to a new directory and swap it in.
validation: The stub-binary reproduction leaves tools/golden intact and exits non-zero in --fast, full and --write modes.

verdict.reason: This reproduces as described, and there is a second consequence the finding does not name. The case list is read by `done < <("$bin" --golden-cases)` (line 92), and set -e does not see a failure inside a process substitution. An empty or failed list gives an empty cases array. In --write mode, `rm -f "$store"/*.txt` (122) runs, then `cp "$scratch"/*.txt` fails, and the corpus is gone. In --fast mode it is worse: the comparison loop at 138 runs zero times, status stays 0, and the script prints 'tools/golden: 32 recorded outputs, all unchanged'. That is a vacuous green. Full check mode is safe: `diff -r` of 32 files against an empty scratch fails. CI runs the full mode (ci.yml:86), so CI is not affected. The corpus is git-tracked, so the --write damage can be undone with git.
verdict.evidence: `bash -c 'set -euo pipefail; a=(); while read -r x; do a+=("$x"); done < <(false); echo "survived, n=${#a[@]}"; for e in "${a[@]}"; do :; done; echo loop-ok'` prints 'survived, n=0' then 'loop-ok'. check_golden.sh:114-125 (write) and 135-150 (fast compare over cases only). .github/workflows/ci.yml:86 runs `tools/check_golden.sh` without flags.
verdict.proposal_note: Capture the list first with `list=$("$bin" --golden-cases)`, which set -e checks, then `[[ -n $list ]] || { echo 'harness listed no golden cases' >&2; exit 1; }`, then read from `<<<"$list"`. That one guard covers --write, --fast and full mode. Also check `(( ${#cases[@]} ))` after filtering, so --fast cannot pass vacuously.

title: More stale counts and comments in the tool configs
claim: check_doc_links.py's docstring says the code carries '175 of them across 32 distinct sections'. The gate now reports 83 distinct pointers, and grep finds 178 `docs/*.md#` occurrences in code. It is a dated count of the kind CLAUDE.md says belongs nowhere but state.md. Separately, `.cargo/config.toml` `[term] verbose = false` carries the comment 'Show warnings during compilation (not just errors)'. `verbose` does not control warnings, and false is the default.
evidence: `tools/check_doc_links.py` prints '83 documentation pointers, all resolving'. `grep -rn 'docs/[a-z_]*\.md#' crates tools web/src ... -o | wc -l` gives 178. sed -n 20,40p .cargo/config.toml shows the verbose comment.
proposal: Remove the number from the check_doc_links docstring. Delete the `[term] verbose` line and its comment, since it restates the default, or correct the comment.
validation: Reread both files; check_doc_links stays green.

verdict.reason: Both parts hold, and there is more in the same file. The check_doc_links docstring's '175 of them across 32 distinct sections when this was written' is explicitly dated, so it is history rather than a false present claim, but it is still a dated count (and repeated as 'all 175') of the kind CLAUDE.md sends to state.md. In .cargo/config.toml, `[term] verbose = false` is commented 'Show warnings during compilation (not just errors)'. That is wrong: term.verbose controls verbose command output, not warnings, and false is the default. The same file has two more misleading entries. `[build] jobs = -1` is commented 'Use all available cores', but in Cargo a negative jobs value means logical CPUs plus that value, so -1 is all cores but one. And `color = "auto"` is the default.
verdict.evidence:
tools/check_doc_links.py:3-5 'The code carries a lot of these -- 175 of them across 32 distinct sections when this was written ... breaks all 175 silently'. .cargo/config.toml: '[build]
# Use all available cores for parallel compilation
jobs = -1' and '[term]
# Show warnings during compilation (not just errors)
verbose = false
color = "auto"'. Cargo documentation for build.jobs: 'If negative, it sets the maximum number of parallel jobs to the number of logical CPUs plus the provided value.'
verdict.proposal_note: Drop the numbers from the docstring and keep the reason ('a lot of these, and nothing checked them'). In .cargo/config.toml, delete `verbose = false` and `color = "auto"` with their comment, since both are defaults. Either correct the jobs comment to 'all cores but one' or delete the key, if all cores was the intent.

title: Unshifted and moderately shifted small pinions report contact ratio, efficiency and ratings on a path that starts inside the base circle, with no note
claim: Finding 0 is written as an edge effect near x1 ≈ -0.34. The same fault misrates every fixed-shift pair with flank interference, including the plain unshifted 9/37. The reported eps (1.519) is about 50% above the usable eps (1.0025), and the path is taken to start 0.97 mm past the pinion's base tangency point. The only signal is the flank_interference field; no Note is raised.
evidence:
Probe (verify-lens-continuity-1, 'on' mode), 9/37 standalone:
- x=0.0: eps 1.5190, capped 1.0025, rho1_start -0.967 mm.
- x=0.2: eps 1.4359, capped 1.1770.
- x=0.4: eps 1.3676, capped 1.3588.
- x=0.45: interference clears; eps 1.3524 = capped.
proposal: This is the same fix as finding 0: limit the path at each member's junction conjugate. In addition, raise a Note when flank_interference is true, carrying the radial depth, so the figures cannot be read without the warning.
validation: Law: for every fixed-shift pair over z1 = 5..20 and x1 in [-0.6, 1.0], the path start satisfies rho1 >= sqrt(r_j1² - r_b1²) and rho2 >= sqrt(r_j2² - r_b2²). On the unshifted 9/37 the eps is 1.00 ± 1e-3.

verdict.reason: The numbers reproduce exactly, but this is not a separate finding. It is the verified, broadened form of lens-continuity#0: that finding's verifier already reported the unshifted 9/37 figures (eps 1.519 against 1.0025 usable, rho1_start -0.967 mm, onset clearing at x≈0.45) in its corrected_claim, and already proposed a Note for flank interference. It should be merged into #0, not counted twice. One correction: 'the only signal is the flank_interference field' understates what the UI does. TrainPanel.svelte:1198-1208 shows 'ui.train_interference_flank' naming the member, styled class:warn. What is missing is a core Note, and with it any signal in the harness, the corpus or a non-panel consumer. I independently confirmed that ContactPath::new (contact.rs:77-110) takes tip-to-tip tangent lengths and never limits them at a junction. An independent hand check for unshifted 9/37 at m=1: a·sinα = 7.8666, sqrt(19.5²−17.384²) = 8.834, so rho1_start = −0.967, which is inside the pinion's base circle.
verdict.evidence:
Probe /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/verify-last-8 ('on' mode), standalone 9/37:
- x=0: eps=1.5190, capped=1.0025, rho1_start=−0.9673, interf [true,false].
- x=0.2: eps 1.4359, capped 1.1770.
- x=0.4: eps 1.3676, capped 1.3588.
- x=0.45: interf clears; eps 1.3524 = capped.
Through the train (arr::pair, search off, x1 fixed; 'tp' mode):
- x=0: ok, eps=1.4992, sF=185.45, interf [true,false], notes=[].
- x=0.2: ok, eps 1.4173, notes=[].
verdict.corrected_claim: This is the same fault as lens-continuity#0, which covers the whole interfering range, not only x1≈−0.34. On unshifted 9/37 the reported eps is 1.519 against 1.00 usable, and the path starts 0.97 mm inside the pinion's base circle. The panel does show a warn-styled flank-interference line, but the core raises no Note, so the harness, the corpus and a non-panel consumer carry the misrated figures with no warning.
verdict.proposal_note: Merge into lens-continuity#0 and implement its fix: limit each path end at the conjugate of the other member's junction, which is ISO 21771's d_Nf-limited eps_alpha. Add a Note keyed on flank interference that carries the depth, so the warning is in the core, not only in the panel.

title: The parallel-axis efficiency is documented as 'exact' and its μ² seam as falling 'linearly with μ', but the formula is linear in μ
claim: The doc of `contact::efficiency` ends its sliding argument with '|ξ|(ω₁+ω₂) is the whole sliding magnitude ... so this formula is exact rather than conservative'. The formula is only the first-order expansion in μ of the pointwise force balance, and it understates η by about 0.03·μ² on 17/43 (1.1e-4 at μ = 0.06, 2.2e-3 at μ = 0.3), which is conservative. rationale.md says the residual was 'identified by watching the gap fall linearly with μ', and in the same sentence calls it O(μ²). The absolute gap scales as μ²; only its share of the loss scales as μ. The bias's size and sign are not recorded in state.md, which rule 6 of CLAUDE.md requires.
evidence: eff.py in /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/notes/verify-lens-continuity-2 gives gap/μ² of 0.0317, 0.0305, 0.0293 and 0.0240 at μ = 0.02, 0.06, 0.1 and 0.3. The exact mean of the pointwise balance (closed form, matching quadrature to 1e-12) is 0.9875153 at μ = 0.06, against the linear 0.9874056. The sentence at contact.rs:406: 'so this formula is exact rather than conservative'.
proposal: In contact.rs, say the formula is exact in its sliding (nothing lengthwise is missing) but first order in μ, understating η by O(μ²), about 1e-4 at μ = 0.06 on 17/43. In rationale.md, reword to 'the gap's share of the loss falls linearly with μ, so the gap itself is O(μ²)'. Add the size and sign to state.md's list of known biases, or remove the bias by adopting the closed-form exact mean (finding lens-continuity 8).
validation: check_doc_links and check_figures stay green. If the closed form is adopted, the linear formula becomes the μ→0 limit, and a test can assert (η_exact − η_linear)/μ² converges to a constant as μ→0.

verdict.reason: I re-derived the pointwise force balance independently: T_i = N(r_bi + sμρ_i), with s = sign(ξ) forced by the energy balance ρ1ω1 − ρ2ω2 = ξ(ω1+ω2). The uniform path mean of η_exact = (1+sμρ2/rb2)/(1+sμρ1/rb1) on 17/43 exceeds the code's linear formula by 0.0317μ², 0.0305μ², 0.0293μ² and 0.0240μ² at μ = 0.02, 0.06, 0.1 and 0.3. At μ = 0.06 that is 0.9875153 exact against 0.9874056 linear, matching the finding digit for digit. The linear formula is conservative (it understates η), so contact.rs:405-406 'exact rather than conservative' is wrong as written. 'Exact' was meant of the sliding kinematics, but the sentence reads as a claim about the formula. rationale.md:863-864 says 'the gap fall linearly with μ (0.0153 → 0.00047)'. The source, design-record.md:4196, shows those numbers are the gap/loss ratio, so the rationale sentence misdescribes its own figures. reference.md:1166 does say 'first order in μ', so part of the record is correct, but state.md carries no size and sign. There is also an error the finding misses. The same doc (contact.rs:361-365) says forward and backward efficiency 'are equal ... and physically it should be'. That holds only at first order: in the exact balance, backward drive (η = (1−sμρ1/rb1)/(1−sμρ2/rb2)) is lower by 2.0e-5 at μ=0.06 and 5.6e-4 at μ=0.3 on 17/43. The symmetry is an artefact of the linearisation.
verdict.evidence:
Script /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/notes/verify-last-8/eff.py (scipy quad, split at the pitch point). Its output rows are μ, exact, linear, gap/μ²:
- 0.02: 0.99581454, 0.99580187, 0.03168
- 0.06: 0.98751530, 0.98740560, 0.03047
- 0.10: 0.97930237, 0.97900934, 0.02930
- 0.30: 0.93918978, 0.93702802, 0.02402
Forward minus backward exact: 2.03e-5 at μ=0.06, 5.58e-4 at μ=0.3.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposal holds as written. Also correct the 'Forward and backward efficiency are equal ... physically it should be' paragraph: say they are equal at first order in μ and differ at O(μ²), by 2e-5 at μ=0.06 on 17/43. If the closed-form exact mean is adopted instead, the two directions separate by that amount, which is physical, and every recorded efficiency in the corpus will move by about 1e-4.

title: Crossed-axis play floors at zero below nominal while parallel-axis play goes negative: two conventions for one backlash band
claim: For a line contact, a band end inside the zero-backlash distance reports negative backlash (interference), through Mesh::backlash's signed law. For a point contact (worm or crossed pair), PointBuilt::angular_play clamps `(a - s.centre_distance).max(0.0)`, so the same minus-tolerance end reports exactly 0. It also returns 0.0 when contact_normal() is None. The test comment justifies the floor with 'closing it below nominal cannot make the backlash negative, because the flanks would simply touch'. That reasoning does not hold for a centre distance imposed by a housing: a closer imposed distance is interference, as on parallel axes. The backlash band's minimum therefore means 'interference' on one kind of mesh and 'at least zero' on the other.
evidence: shape.rs:2631-2641 `let separation = 2.0 * (a - s.centre_distance).max(0.0) * n[0].abs();`. crossed.rs:476-500 is a test asserting minimum == 0.0 at tolerance_minus 0.05. Mesh::backlash (mesh.rs:349) is signed and documented 'negative means the teeth interfere — on both kinds of mesh'.
proposal: Drop the `.max(0.0)` so the crossed band reports signed play: a negative minimum is interference, as on parallel axes. Replace `return 0.0` for a missing contact normal with a refusal or a note. Update the crossed.rs test to assert minimum < 0 when tolerance_minus > clearance. Do this together with the play_of unification (lens-unification finding 4), so one BuiltContact::angular_play serves both arms with one sign convention.
validation: Law over every crossed arrangement: row_play at the minus band end is negative exactly when tolerance_minus exceeds the clearance, matching the parallel-axis behaviour on the same shapes. The golden corpus shows the changed minima for worm cases.

verdict.reason: The code reads as claimed. PointBuilt::angular_play (shape.rs:2631-2641) computes `2.0 * (a - s.centre_distance).max(0.0) * n[0].abs()`, while the line arm of play_of (shape.rs:3524-3531) uses the signed Mesh::backlash, documented 'negative means the teeth interfere — on both kinds of mesh' (mesh.rs:341-343). The band's minimum end (at_band with t<0) therefore reads interference as negative on a parallel mesh and as 0 on a worm or crossed pair. crossed.rs:476-503 pins the floor with a test whose reasoning ('the flanks would simply touch') holds for a free distance but not for one a housing imposes, which is what a tolerance band describes. In a train mixing a worm and a pair, one path's play sums the two conventions. The only law over bands (mod.rs:8744-8776) checks order and opening, so it would pass with either convention. The `return 0.0` for a missing contact normal is probably unreachable: contact_normal is None only at sinΣ≈0 or nx²≤0, and a point contact exists only on an angled distance. It is still a silent 0 where a refusal belongs. The strings catalogue already has 'clearance_negative' for a running distance inside the zero-backlash one, so interference is a condition the tool already names.
verdict.evidence: shape.rs:2638 `let separation = 2.0 * (a - s.centre_distance).max(0.0) * n[0].abs();`. shape.rs:2633-2635 `let Some(n) = s.contact_normal() else { return 0.0; };`. crossed.rs:500 `assert_eq!(...forward.minimum, 0.0, "tighter than nominal is contact")`. mesh.rs:349-355 signed backlash. screw.rs:692-700, the conditions for a None contact normal.
verdict.proposal_note: Drop the .max(0.0) and change the crossed.rs test to assert minimum < 0 when tolerance_minus exceeds the clearance. Replace `return 0.0` with an expect-free refusal, or build the normal once when the PointBuilt is made, so it cannot be missing. Doing this together with the play_of unification is sensible, but it does not depend on it.

The durable fix is to make each Display impl print its note's key and values, or to have the CLI render notes through gear-io's English catalogue. Either removes the second copy of English that has already drifted, and it satisfies rule 2 literally.

title: A member on a body the graph does not list is refused as a wiring fault (NoCommonFrame), not as a missing body
claim: A train file whose member names an unlisted body loads without complaint. solve_train then refuses it as InPart{part:0, cause: Wiring(NoCommonFrame(0))}, which points the designer at frames rather than at the dangling body index.
evidence: probe verify-graph-ops-1 `doc member` (Planetary+Spur, members[0].body=99, round-tripped through to_toml/from_toml): from_toml Ok, solve_train Ok(Err("InPart { part: 0, cause: Wiring(NoCommonFrame(0)) }")).
proposal: Fold this into the Train::check validator from finding 1. Every member's body must be listed, refused as a structural key (e.g. NoSuchBody) before any part is built.
validation: A document with members[0].body out of range is refused at from_toml with the structural key, not a wiring error.

verdict.reason: I reproduced it by re-running probe verify-graph-ops-1 with `doc member` (Planetary+Spur, members[0].body = 99, round-tripped through to_toml/from_toml). from_toml returns Ok. solve_train returns InPart { part: 0, cause: Wiring(NoCommonFrame(0)) }, which blames frames rather than the dangling body index. from_toml → relieved() does no index validation, and the solve fails on the first frame lookup. Only a hand-written or corrupted file can reach this; the panel's edits cannot. The same probe's `doc mesh` case (meshes[0].a = 99) is worse: it panics with an index out of bounds at from_toml and at solve_train. That is presumably the 'finding 1' the proposal folds this into.
verdict.evidence: Probe output: 'member: from_toml Ok(Ok(()))', 'member: solve Ok(Err("InPart { part: 0, cause: Wiring(NoCommonFrame(0)) }"))', 'mesh: from_toml Err("index out of bounds: the len is 5 but the index is 99")'. gear-io/src/train.rs:359-362 parses and then only relieves.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposal is right: one structural validator run at from_toml (and at the wasm boundary), before any part is built. It should check every index the document holds, not just member.body: member body, mesh endpoints, body axis, axis carried_by, coupling ends, holds, load-case bodies and duty.at. Each should be refused by a catalogue key.

title: corrections.md row says a hula's wobble body is 'no port now', and the code and reference.md say it is a port; the reversal has no row
claim: docs/corrections.md records as the current state that a shaft on a carried axis 'is no port now, whatever its count'. Shape::ports makes every non-replicated body a port, including an orbiting one, and says so ('an orbiting port is a port'), and reference.md agrees. The correction was later reversed and no row records the reversal. The history is instead a parenthetical inside shape.rs's doc comment.
evidence: corrections.md:648: '...and a hula's wobble body was a port | ... A shaft on a carried axis orbits and nothing can be attached to it: it is no port now, whatever its count'. Probe: arrangements::hula(..).ports() = [1,2,3,4] with body 4 the wobble body (members on bodies [4,4,2,3], axis 1 carried by body 1).
proposal: Add a corrections.md row after 648 recording the reversal: a case now declares what it reacts, so an orbiting port no longer gets reacted by default and is a port again. Move shape.rs's '(For a while ...)' parenthetical into that row. Fix row 648's closing clause so it does not read as current.
validation: check_doc_links passes. A reader comparing corrections.md, reference.md#ports-and-bodies and Shape::ports finds one statement.

verdict.reason: corrections.md:648 ends with 'it is no port now, whatever its count'. The code contradicts that. Shape::ports (shape.rs:4175-4177) filters only on !replicated(s), and its own doc comment says 'an orbiting port is a port'. reference.md 'Ports and bodies' lists 'a single orbiting member, a hula's wobble body' as a port. No corrections.md row records the reversal: grep for 'orbiting' and 'wobble' finds only rows 644 and 648. The history sits only in shape.rs's '(For a while a body on a carried axis was no port ...)' parenthetical. That is the kind of self-referential history a doc comment should not carry.
verdict.evidence: docs/corrections.md:648 quoted. shape.rs:4165-4177 (the doc comment, and ports = (1..=bodies).filter(!replicated)). docs/reference.md 'Ports and bodies' paragraph (around line 2681). grep -n -i 'orbiting\|wobble' docs/corrections.md returns only 644 and 648.
verdict.proposal_note: Adopt the proposal. The new row should cite reference.md#load-cases, since the reason is that a case now declares what it reacts. Replace the parenthetical in shape.rs with a pointer to that row.

title: Shape::ports' doc says a hula's wobble body has four gears on it; it has two
claim: The comment reads 'a hula's wobble body is the same body with four gears on it'. The hula has four members in all: two wobble gears on the wobble body, plus the grounded gear and the output on their own bodies.
evidence: Probe: hula([100,31,30,101],[1,1]).members bodies = [4,4,2,3]. arrangements.rs:488-490: 'Members: the two wobble gears, then the grounded gear and the output'.
proposal: Change it to 'a hula's wobble body, one body carrying both wobble gears'.
validation: Read against arrangements::hula's doc.

Its doc comment says 'Members: the two wobble gears, then the grounded gear and the output'. So the wobble body carries two gears, and the part has four in all. shape.rs:4168's 'the same body with four gears on it' is wrong on either reading.
verdict.evidence: arrangements.rs:488-490 (doc) and :508 (epicyclic call with one planet list of two gears). shape.rs:4167-4168.
verdict.proposal_note: Fold this into the rewrite of the same comment from index 2, e.g. 'a single orbiting member — a hula's wobble body, one body carrying both wobble gears'.

title: A point-contact mesh's efficiency is taken at the pre-sizing width, but it is rated at the sized width
claim: For a point-contact (crossed or worm) mesh, efficiency depends on the face-limited contact zone (BuiltContact::Point uses p.zone(face)). cut() computes it at early_width, which is the worm-proportion width or the box value. rate() rates the same mesh at final_width, and final_width is load-sized whenever the member also sits in a line mesh with an automatic width. The flow and the reported efficiency then describe a narrower or wider zone than the one rated and drawn. No preset has a member in both a line mesh and a point mesh, but a graph edit (a gear meshing a crossed mate and a parallel mate) can create one.
evidence: shape.rs:3086-3089 early_width = recommended.map_or(manual, |r| resolve(r)). shape.rs:3193 bm.efficiency(a, mu, face_of(k, early_width)). shape.rs:3487-3503 widths: on_a_line(i) makes the width max(line ask, recommended) resolved, which differs from early_width when the width is automatic. shape.rs:3513 point_contact(k, face_of(k, final_width)). shape.rs:2487-2491 shows point-contact efficiency uses zone(face). Found by reading the code; not run.
proposal: Either (a) state and test that a point-contact member's width is never load-sized (make widths[i] = early_width(i) for any member in a point mesh and say so), or (b) after sizing, recompute point-mesh efficiencies at final_width and re-solve the flow once, reporting whether it changed. (a) is one line and keeps the flow single-pass.
validation: Build a graph where one automatic-width gear meshes a parallel mate (line) and a crossed mate (point). Assert that the efficiency reported for the point mesh equals bm.efficiency at that mesh's rated faces. This fails today if the line ask moves the width.

verdict.reason: I ran it; the finding had only read the code. The Crossed preset plus AddGear meshing member 1 on a new axis gives member 1 a crossed (point) mesh and a parallel (line) mesh. I loaded the case from the crossed input through to the new gear and set every width to automatic. Member 1 is load-sized to 0.0968 mm (at 1 N·m) or 1.936 mm (at 20 N·m). The crossed mesh's efficiency is still reported at the early width of 10 mm: 0.842553 forward. The same train with every width fixed at the solved values reports 0.843034 (1 N·m) or 0.842875 (20 N·m). Two trains with identical geometry therefore report different efficiencies, and the flow and path figures follow the wrong one. The size is small, about 3e-4 to 5e-4 absolute, because the zone saturates once the faces pass about 4 mm on this preset. The comment at shape.rs:3147-3148 says 'its point contact's zone is read at the width it ends with'. That holds for rated_point (3513) but not for the efficiency (3193), so the comment overstates what the code does.
verdict.evidence: Probe /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/verify-last-9 output. 'Crossed+pair tq1: widths [10.0, 0.0968, 0.0968] eff (0.842552983848133, 0.8425359359131874)'. 'frozen: ... eff (0.8430338393117085, 0.8430499900859635)'. At tq20: 0.84255 vs frozen 0.84288. At tq200 the width is 19.4 mm, past saturation, and the two agree. Face sweep on Crossed alone: w=0.5 gives 0.843003, w=4 gives 0.842553, and w≥4 is flat. Worm: w=4 gives 0.620696, w≥10 gives 0.618046 (efficiency is not monotone in width). shape.rs:3193 uses early_width, 3487-3503 load-sizes widths where on_a_line, and 3513 uses final_width for the patches.
verdict.proposal_note: Proposal (a) is wrong for this case. Pinning a point-mesh member to early_width also un-sizes a member the designer asked to have sized for its line mesh, so the line mesh would be rated at an unrequested width. Prefer (b): after sizing, recompute efficiencies for point meshes whose member width changed. Re-solve the flow once, or iterate to a fixed point, since the change is tiny and the iteration converges immediately. Or at least correct the comment at shape.rs:3147-3148 so it says the efficiency is read at the pre-sizing width, and record the size and sign in docs/state.md as rule 6 asks. The validation test in the finding is right and fails today: build that Crossed+pair train and freeze its widths.

title: The English catalogue's screw_axes_are_parallel still names the retired 'worm stage'
claim: Stage types were retired in the train-as-graph refactor, but the refusal a user reads for parallel axes on a crossed mesh still says 'a worm stage needs non-parallel shafts'. The CLI Display adds 'a parallel pair is a spur stage'.
evidence: strings_en.toml:197 screw_axes_are_parallel = "a worm stage needs non-parallel shafts"; mod.rs:1742-1743.
proposal: Reword it in all five catalogues and in the Display, for example 'a crossed mesh needs non-parallel axes'.
validation: tools/check_strings.py; gear_io::strings firing test.

Stirnradstufe', 'estágio de sem-fim ... estágio de dentes retos', '蜗杆级 ... 直齿级'). The TrainError Display (mod.rs:1740-1743) says the same. 'Stage' no longer names anything the user sees. title: DXF reference circles of an eccentric gear come from Tooth::new, not the gear's mean tooth; they disagree with the drawn outline's tool and with the panel
claim: gear_to_dxf draws the outline through Gear::new(params), which cuts every tooth, the mean tooth included, with one common tool. The r/rb/ra/rf reference circles, however, come from the Tooth its callers build with Tooth::new(params), which is cut by the tool the mean tooth alone would want. For an eccentric gear (angular_shift ≠ 0) the root circle in the DXF therefore differs from the rf the gear panel quotes (solve_gear_impl uses Gear::new(..).mean()) and from the tool depth the outline was cut with.
evidence: A release probe comparing Tooth::new(p) with Gear::new(p).mean() at module 1 gives: z=6, x=0.5, Δx=0.8: rf 2.250 vs 2.150 mm. Worst over the admissible Δx range (auto::admissible_angular_shift): z=7 x=0 0.43 mm, z=8 x=0.5 1.075 mm, z=10 x=0.5 1.525 mm. Concentric gears agree exactly. dxf.rs:124-126: `Gear::new(gear.params).outline(..)`, `&[gear.r, gear.rb, gear.ra, gear.rf]`.
proposal: Change the signature to `gear_to_dxf(gear: &Gear, opts)`: take the outline from `gear.outline(tol)` and the circles from `gear.mean()`. Have export_dxf_impl and gear-cli's dxf build a Gear. Add a gear-io test that parses the DXF of an eccentric gear (for example z=6, x=0.5, Δx=0.8) and checks that its root circle equals Gear::new(p).mean().rf.
validation: The new test fails on HEAD (2.25 vs 2.15) and passes after the fix. check_golden shows no diff for the concentric dxf command. validate_dxf.py stays green.

verdict.reason: gear_to_dxf takes a &Tooth, draws the outline through Gear::new(gear.params), and takes the four reference circles from the Tooth it was given. Both callers, export_dxf_impl (gear-wasm lib.rs:706) and gear-cli dxf (main.rs:2621), build that Tooth with Tooth::new(params). Gear::new instead cuts its mean tooth with the gear's common tool (gear.rs:207, `Tooth::cut_by(params, tool)`), and solve_gear_impl quotes the panel's figures from that mean tooth. So the rf in the DXF of an eccentric gear is not the rf of the outline it sits beside.
verdict.evidence: I reproduced it with a release probe (probes/verify-last-10). For z=6, x=0.5, dx=0.8: Tooth::new rf = 2.2500 against Gear::new(p).mean().rf = 2.1500, while ra agrees (4.4526). The DXF's CIRCLE radii are [3.0, 2.819.., 4.4526.., 2.25], so it carries the Tooth's 2.25. The concentric cases z=17 x=0 and z=10 x=0.5 dx=0.3 agree exactly. No gear-io test sets angular_shift (grep of dxf.rs and the tests finds none).
verdict.proposal_note: The proposal is right. Taking &Gear (outline from gear.outline, circles from gear.mean()) also removes the second Gear::new inside gear_to_dxf.

title: Thickness relief allows one given k per mesh, not per mesh group, so a planetary set's k can break its invariant with a mesh-order-dependent planet k
claim: The relief group for thickness_mod is declared per mesh (given_at_most 1 over {m.a, m.b}). A sun and a ring share no mesh, so both can stand given after relief. thickness_mods() then fills the auto planet from whichever mesh comes first in the list and leaves the other mesh violating k_ring = k_planet. The result depends on mesh order, and nothing is reported.
evidence: Probe on Preset::Planetary: sun Auto::fixed(1.1), ring Auto::fixed(1.0), then relieved(Some(Freedom::Member(2, ThicknessMod))). The auto flags come back [false, true, false] and thickness_mods() = [1.1, 0.9, 1.0]. After `meshes.swap(0,1)` the same shape gives [1.1, 1.0, 1.0]. solve_train on the relieved train succeeds and notes only part.planets_share_load_equally. The existing test one_thickness_modification_satisfies_both_invariants (shape.rs:5364) only ever gives one member.
proposal: In Shape::freedoms, replace the per-mesh thickness groups with one group per Shape::mesh_groups() component: given_at_most 1, automatic_at_most = the group's size, order = its members. Update the shape.rs:173-176 doc comment to match, and make rationale.md:69-72 accurate ('at most one k per meshing group is given; the rest follow'). Add a relief law: after relieved(), for every mesh, k_b == mate(k_a) holds exactly.
validation: The new law fails on HEAD for the Planetary, Wolfrom and MeshedPlanets presets when two members are given, and passes after the change. The relief idempotence and every-preset relief laws in train/mod.rs stay green. check_golden and check_wasm show no diff, since the default presets give no k.

verdict.reason: Shape::freedoms (shape.rs:4088-4097) pushes one FreedomGroup per mesh, {m.a, m.b}, each with given_at_most 1. A sun and a ring share no mesh, so relief lets both stand given. thickness_mods() then fills the planet from whichever mesh the propagation loop meets first and leaves the other mesh breaking its rule. Nothing reports it. The field doc at shape.rs:173-176 ('given on one member of a mesh ... relief keeps it so') and rationale.md:69-72 ('one stored k fixes all three') both promise what the code does not deliver.
verdict.evidence: Probe on arr::planetary(24,18,60,3): all k automatic, then sun Auto::fixed(1.1) and ring Auto::fixed(1.0), then relieved(Some(Member(2, ThicknessMod))). Auto flags come back [false, true, false] and thickness_mods = [1.1, 0.9, 1.0]: the internal rule k_ring = k_planet is broken. After s.meshes.swap(0,1), the same inputs give [1.1, 1.0, 1.0]: the external rule is broken instead. It depends on mesh order. solve_alone succeeds both times, and the only note is part.planets_share_load_equally. The existing test one_thickness_modification_satisfies_both_invariants gives only one member a k.
verdict.proposal_note: Using one group per mesh_groups() component is the right unit, since thickness_mods propagates only across meshes, and mesh_groups (shape.rs:1087) is exactly the union-find over meshes. The proposed law 'after relieved(), k_b == mate(k_a) for every mesh' still has a hole. In an odd cycle of external meshes (three gears pairwise in mesh, which the graph's edits can build), a single given k != 1 cannot satisfy every mesh. The law should therefore also run over an edited triangle, and where the component's mesh graph has an odd external cycle, the solve should either refuse or note it.

title: Five places still say ShaperCut refuses an oversized tip round; the code now caps it
claim: The refusal was recorded as a fault and replaced by a cap, but the map's 'looks wrong and is not' caution, README, state.md, the UNFIRED evidence in strings.rs and a comment inside shaper.rs still describe the refusal. CLAUDE.md and README tell a maintainer not to tidy behaviour that no longer exists. state.md and strings.rs use it as the reason `clamp.ring_fully_filleted` never fires.
evidence: shaper.rs:154 reads: '**The round is capped, not refused.** ... Refusing here instead made one input give a fillet on an external gear and *no fillet at all* on a ring'. `largest_tip_round` (shaper.rs:431-459) returns min(asked, 0.95·boundary), and ring.rs:426-428 reports the cap with a note. corrections.md:454 records 'A tip round too large for a shaper's tip **refused** the tool' as a fault. Yet CLAUDE.md:232 says '`ShaperCut` refuses a tool it cannot hold rather than clamping it.' README.md:170 says '`ShaperCut` refuses that tool rather than clamping it.' state.md:783 and strings.rs:1609 say '`ShaperCut` already refuses a tool whose rounds overlap'. shaper.rs:406-409, in `corner_angle`, says 'Refused rather than clamped, because which of the round, the addendum and the tooth count to give up is the designer's call', which is the very argument shaper.rs:161-165 rebuts.
proposal: Rewrite CLAUDE.md item 4 and README item 4 to say the round is capped to 95% of the largest that fits, and reported (corrections.md:454). In state.md:783 and strings.rs:1609, restate the shadowing hypothesis: the cap keeps the cutter's own rounds from overlapping, which may be why the ring's rounds never meet. The next search should re-test that. In shaper.rs:405-409, say that after `largest_tip_round` a negative angle can arise only for a degenerate corner (the floor case), not as a designer's choice.
validation: grep -rn 'refuses.*tool\|refuses that tool\|Refused rather than clamped' CLAUDE.md README.md docs crates returns nothing that contradicts shaper.rs:154. A worktree test that passes a tip round larger than fits to ShaperCut::new gets Some with tip_round below the one asked.

verdict.reason: ShaperCut::new now caps an oversized tip round: largest_tip_round returns min(asked, 0.95*boundary).max(floor). The comment at shaper.rs:154-165 says 'capped, not refused' and rebuts the old argument for refusing, and corrections.md:454 records the refusal as a fault. Yet CLAUDE.md item 4, README item 4, state.md:783-784 and the UNFIRED evidence in strings.rs:1609-1611 still say ShaperCut refuses such a tool. corner_angle's comment (shaper.rs:405-409) still gives the very argument the comment above rebuts. None of this changes an answer, so the severity is low rather than medium. It still misleads, and CLAUDE.md's 'looks wrong and is not' list is exactly the text maintainers are told to trust.
verdict.evidence: shaper.rs:154 reads '**The round is capped, not refused.**'. shaper.rs:405-409 reads 'Refused rather than clamped, because which of the round, the addendum and the tooth count to give up is the designer's call.' CLAUDE.md:231-232 reads '`ShaperCut` refuses a tool it cannot hold rather than clamping it.' README reads '`ShaperCut` refuses that tool rather than clamping it.' state.md:783 and strings.rs:1609 read 'ShaperCut already refuses a tool whose (own) rounds overlap'. Two refusals do remain in ShaperCut::new (corner_radius <= 0 or NaN, and corner_angle None at the floor), so 'refuses a tool it cannot hold' is still true for a degenerate corner. It is not true for the oversized round the README's own example describes.
verdict.proposal_note: Keep the shadowing hypothesis in state.md and strings.rs, but restate it: the cap to 95% of the fitting round keeps the cutter's own rounds from meeting, which may still shadow clamp.ring_fully_filleted. The 71,750-case search rests on whichever version of the crate it ran against, so it should be re-run or dated. In corner_angle's comment, say that a negative angle is the bracket's signal for largest_tip_round and refuses only at the floor.

title: contact::sliding_velocity and sliding_at are test-only, and their docs claim a unification production does not use
claim: sliding_velocity's doc says a worm's non-vanishing pitch-point sliding 'arrives here as a value of this function rather than as a separate screw-gear formula'. Production never calls it. screw.rs:246-249 computes the sliding with its own closed form, sqrt(1 - 2k cos Σ + k²). The only callers of sliding_velocity and sliding_at are test modules: contact.rs after line 950, and screw.rs:1797, which is inside screw's #[cfg(test)] starting at line 1494. sliding_at's doc also promises a crossed-axis version 'with the screw geometry it needs (milestone 7, step 5)', and that never arrived.
evidence: `grep -rn 'sliding_velocity(\|sliding_at' crates` finds contact.rs:604 (the definition), 657 (sliding_at calling it), 1409-1624 (tests), and screw.rs:1797 (tests). No gear-cli or gear-wasm use. screw.rs:246 carries the comment 'Sliding at the pitch point ... v_s = (1 − k cos Σ) ŷ + k sin Σ ẑ'.
proposal: Either make screw.rs compute its sliding through sliding_velocity, the one-model reading, or state plainly that sliding_velocity is the independent vector instrument that screw.rs's closed form is checked against, and move both functions to testing.rs or gate them #[cfg(test)]. Delete the 'crossed-axis version arrives' paragraph.
validation: A grep of non-test callers matches the doc's claim, and nextest still passes.

verdict.reason: Every call to sliding_velocity and sliding_at is inside a #[cfg(test)] module: contact.rs's test module runs from line 950 to the end of the file (1861), with calls at 1409-1624, and screw.rs's test module starts at 1494, with the call at 1797. Production computes the screw sliding with its own closed form (screw.rs:246-249). So the doc's claim that a worm's pitch-point sliding 'arrives here as a value of this function rather than as a separate screw-gear formula' is false. So is sliding_at's promise of a crossed-axis version at 'milestone 7, step 5'.
verdict.evidence: `grep -rn 'sliding_velocity\|sliding_at' crates` finds only the definitions (contact.rs:604, 637), calls in test modules (contact.rs:1409-1624, screw.rs:1797), and doc links (contact.rs:404, 550, 628). The gear-cli, gear-wasm and train hits are a different field named sliding_velocity, filled from ScrewMesh's sliding_ratio (shape.rs:2754). docs/history/design-record.md:4306 records the intended role: 'screw.rs's closed form against contact::sliding_velocity built from two axes and two speeds ... 1e-10 relative'. That is, it is the independent instrument.
verdict.proposal_note: Take the second option, since the design record already says the function is the independent check. Rewrite its doc as the vector instrument the screw closed form is held to, and delete the milestone paragraph. If both functions move under #[cfg(test)] or into testing.rs, the production intra-doc links at contact.rs:404 and :550 must be reworded too, or rustdoc will warn on broken links. Leaving the functions pub is also defensible, since they are the parallel-axis sliding model of record for the contact tests.

title: reference.md's over-pins prose has the direction each space narrows backwards
claim: reference.md says 'an external gear's space narrows outward so a larger pin rides higher, a ring's narrows inward so a larger pin sits deeper'. Both directions are reversed. An external gear's space narrows inward toward the root, and a ring's space narrows outward. The code comment beside the same formula says the opposite of the document, and the code is correct. The document's own sentence is self-inconsistent too: a space narrowing outward would make a larger pin sit deeper, not ride higher.
evidence: reference.md:1418-1419: 'an external gear's space narrows outward so a larger pin rides higher, a ring's narrows inward so a larger pin sits deeper'. metrology.rs:462-464: 'An external gear's space narrows *inward*, so a larger pin rides higher … A ring's space narrows *outward*'. ring.rs:378 and reference.md:1510/1600 agree with the code: 'A ring's space narrows outward'.
proposal: Swap the two words in reference.md:1418-1419: 'an external gear's space narrows inward so a larger pin rides higher, a ring's narrows outward so a larger pin sits deeper'.
validation: Read reference.md:1418 against metrology.rs:462 and ring.rs:378. All three should agree.

verdict.reason: reference.md:1418-1419 has the direction reversed for both kinds of gear. An external gear's tooth narrows outward, so its space widens outward, i.e. narrows inward. A ring is the mirror. The code comments, ring.rs and reference.md's own later sections all say the opposite of line 1418. The finding is also right that the sentence contradicts itself: a space that narrowed outward would seat a larger pin deeper, not higher.
verdict.evidence: reference.md:1418 says 'an external gear's space narrows outward so a larger pin rides higher, a ring's narrows inward'. Against it: metrology.rs:462-464 ('An external gear's space narrows *inward* … A ring's space narrows *outward*'), metrology.rs:484-485, ring.rs:18-20 and :378, reference.md:1510 and :1600, and corrections.md:506 all say the reverse. Physics: external tooth half-thickness angle ψ − inv α shrinks with radius, so the space angle grows outward.

title: pin_diameter_range's comment says sixty halvings of a few-module bracket; the code does 64 halvings of a bracket that starts at r_b and doubles
claim: The doc comment says 'Sixty halvings of a bracket a few modules wide is the full mantissa'. The loop runs 64 halvings. The bracket is [0, hi], where hi starts at r_b (about z/2 modules, e.g. 50 modules at z = 100) and doubles until the pin is too large, so it is not 'a few modules'. The walk's cap of 64 doublings is also an unexplained literal.
evidence: metrology.rs:181 'Sixty halvings of a bracket a few modules wide'. metrology.rs:190 `let mut hi = space.rb;`, :193 `hi *= 2.0`, :196 `if steps > 64`, :200 `for _ in 0..64 {`.
proposal: Make the comment match the code, e.g. 'bracket [0, 2^k r_b]; 64 halvings exhaust the mantissa of any such bracket'. Alternatively, derive the count from f64::MANTISSA_DIGITS plus the bracket's exponent, and name the doubling cap.
validation: Read the comment against lines 190-205.

verdict.reason: The comment says sixty halvings of a bracket a few modules wide. The code bisects [0, hi] 64 times, where hi starts at r_b (about z·m/2) and doubles until the pin is too large. The comment's count and its bracket width are both wrong. The literal 64 also appears twice with two meanings: a cap on doublings and a count of halvings. The conclusion still holds: the result is about 1-2 modules, so hi/result is about 2^5 for z around 100, and full precision needs about 53+5 halvings. 64 is enough up to hi/result of about 2^11.
verdict.evidence: metrology.rs:181 says 'Sixty halvings of a bracket a few modules wide is the full mantissa'. The code: :190 `let mut hi = space.rb;`, :193 `hi *= 2.0;`, :196 `if steps > 64 { return None; }`, :200 `for _ in 0..64 {`.
verdict.proposal_note: The simplest honest comment: 'the bracket is [0, 2^k r_b]; 64 halvings resolve it to 2^-64 of its width, finer than an ulp of any pin a space of up to ~2000 teeth measures'. Name the two 64s separately. Also, CLAUDE.md says every transcendental step routes through solve.rs's bracketed finders, and this is a hand-rolled bisection. It bisects on a categorical verdict, not a residual, so it may legitimately fall outside that rule, but the comment should say so.

title: auto.rs doc comment carries the same spur-only undercut reduction and tooth-count table
claim: The comment on the undercut-shift function states `x_min = h_w − z sin²α_t / 2` and `z ≥ 2 h_w / sin²α_t` without restricting them to β = 0. The code three screens below uses r = m z/(2 cos β). Both tests that pin the reduction use spur defaults, so a helical reading of the formula is never tested.
evidence: auto.rs:58: 'With `ρ = 0` it reduces to `x_min = h_w − z sin²α_t / 2`'. auto.rs:117: `let r = p.module / beta.cos() * f64::from(p.teeth.max(1)) / 2.0;`. The tests at :2157 and :2193 build GearParams with default helix_angle 0.
proposal: Write '/(2 cos β)' (or 'for a spur gear') in auto.rs:58 as in reference.md:239. Add one helical case to minimum_profile_shift_matches_the_closed_form_and_the_cutter_helps asserting sharp_rack == h_w − z sin²α_t/(2 cos β).
validation: cargo nextest run -p gear-core auto::

verdict.reason: The doc comment does state the spur-only reduction without saying so. The code uses r = m z/(2 cos β), so the correct helical reduction is x_min = h_w − z sin²α_t/(2 cos β) and z_min = 2 h_w cos β / sin²α_t. The two unit tests at auto.rs:2157 and :2193 are spur only. Two parts of the finding are wrong, though. First, reference.md:238-239 has the same spur-only formula, so it is a second place to fix, not the model to copy. Second, 'a helical reading is never tested' overstates it: tests/geometry_laws.rs:815 runs minimum_profile_shift over HELIX_ANGLES. That test checks the edge against the tooth's own indicator, which reads the same Rack::undercut_shift (tooth.rs:479). So no independent closed-form check of the cos β factor exists, which is the real gap.
verdict.evidence: auto.rs:58: 'With `ρ = 0` it reduces to `x_min = h_w − z sin²α_t / 2`'. auto.rs:117: `let r = p.module / beta.cos() * f64::from(p.teeth.max(1)) / 2.0;`. reference.md:238: 'it reduces to `x_min = h_w − z sin²α_t / 2`' (no cos β). geometry_laws.rs:819: `.helix_angle(HELIX_ANGLES)`. tooth.rs:479-481: `let x_min = tool.undercut_shift(m, r, alpha_t); let l = m * (x - x_min) / sa;`.
verdict.corrected_claim: auto.rs:58-59 and reference.md:238-239 both state the β = 0 reduction as general. The helical minimum shift is exercised (geometry_laws), but only against the tooth's reading of the same relation, never against an independent closed form in z, α_t and β.
verdict.proposal_note: Fix both places: '/(2 cos β)', and 'z ≥ 2 h_w cos β / sin²α_t' (the table is for spur). Add a helical case to minimum_shift_matches_the_closed_form_and_the_cutter_helps (the real test name, without 'profile_'), computing α_t independently as atan(tan α_n/cos β).

title: The corrections log's 'Where' column labels 85 rows with section numbers that no current document has
