title: A strength.rs comment names Y_S in a product that multiplies K_f
claim: The comment says the critical section is chosen by 'the largest `Y_F · Y_S · share`', but the code directly below multiplies `section.bending_factor(RootStressModel::DolanBroghamer)`, which is Y_F (less the axial term) times K_f. The code no longer computes Y_S there.
evidence: strength.rs:1501-1512: '// torque, so the worst point is the largest `Y_F · Y_S · share`.' followed by `let Some(factor) = section.bending_factor(RootStressModel::DolanBroghamer)`. state.md:827 records Y_S being replaced by K_f.
proposal: Change the comment to 'the largest bending factor (Y_F less the axial term, times K_f) · share', or to 'the largest `bending_factor · share`', so it does not name one notch model.
validation: A grep for 'Y_S' in strength.rs outside the Iso6336 arm and the matrix support finds no rating-path comment naming it.

verdict.reason: The comment at strength.rs:1502 names `Y_F · Y_S · share`, but the code below it calls bending_factor(DolanBroghamer), which bending_factor's own table (lines 1079-1082) gives as (Y_F − axial)·K_f. So the comment is wrong on the notch factor and also leaves out the axial term. The comment at line 2007 is correct, because that test uses Iso6336.
verdict.evidence: strength.rs:1097-1103: `DolanBroghamer => self.form_factor - self.axial_compression` times stress_correction(DolanBroghamer) = h + (t/ρ)^l (t/h)^m (lines 1051-1058), which is K_f. Line 1502 comment: 'the worst point is the largest `Y_F · Y_S · share`'.
verdict.proposal_note: Prefer 'the largest `bending_factor · share`', which does not tie the comment to a notch model. The same generic use of 'Y_S' also appears in the stress_correction doc at line 1015 ('The stress correction factor `Y_S` under the chosen model'), where the Dolan–Broghamer arm returns K_f. Reword it to 'the notch factor (Y_S or K_f) under the chosen model'.

title: The doc comment on the wasm smallest_tooth_count field states an unshifted formula as the design's limit
claim: The field doc says 'The fewest teeth this design could have had and still cleared its own base circle: `2 h_a cos β / (1 − cos α_t)`'. 'This design' includes its profile shift, which the formula omits. This is the documentation half of finding 0, and it is also exported to the generated TS types.
evidence: lib.rs:533-534 against ring.rs:278 `ra = r - m * (params.addendum - x)`. The probe shows x = −0.3 needs 44 teeth while the formula gives 34.
proposal: Fix it together with finding 0: have the core compute `2(h_a − x)cosβ/(1 − cos α_t)` and correct the doc to match.
validation: Same as finding 0. `tools/check_bindings.sh` is regenerated if the doc crosses into ts-rs output.

verdict.reason: smallest_tooth_count (gear-wasm/src/lib.rs:554-561) computes 2·h_a·cosβ/(1−cosα_t) without x, but the ring's tip radius is ra = r − m(h_a − x) (ring.rs:278). Setting ra ≥ rb = r·cosα_t with r = z·m/(2cosβ) gives z ≥ 2(h_a − x)cosβ/(1−cosα_t). At α = 20°, β = 0, x = −0.3 that is 2.6/0.0603 = 43.1, so 44 teeth, while the code gives 34. The doc states 'this design', so the doc and the code are wrong together. Separately, this is an engineering formula in the wasm boundary crate, not in gear-core. Rule 1 names only TypeScript, but the file map puts 'all the mathematics' in gear-core.
verdict.evidence: lib.rs:533-539 doc text; lib.rs:557 `let threshold = 2.0 * params.addendum * beta.cos() / (1.0 - alpha_t.cos());`; ring.rs:278 `let mut ra = r - m * (params.addendum - x);`; the wasm test at lib.rs:2310 asserts 34 at the default (x=0), so it cannot see the omission.
verdict.proposal_note: Move the computation into gear-core (for example a Ring or ring-module function next to the ra/ra_min logic) and include (h_a − x). Add a law: at z = smallest_tooth_count the unclamped tip is at or above the base circle, and at z − 1 it is not, swept over x, β and α. That law would also catch any remaining disagreement with ring.rs's clamp.

title: fillet_cap_guarantees_a_nonnegative_root_arc cannot catch the wrong cap it claims to guard against
claim: The test's doc comment says 'If the cap is ever rewritten, this is what catches getting it wrong.' It asserts only θ0 ≤ half_pitch, so it can only see a cap that is too large. The wrong form the code, CLAUDE.md and README all warn about, w_tip/(2 cos α), is smaller (0.532·w_tip against 0.714·w_tip at 20°): it shrinks the fillet, which keeps the root arc non-negative. The test passes under exactly the mutation it is said to catch.
evidence: In a worktree I replaced tooth.rs:914 `w_tip * ca / (2.0 * (1.0 - sa))` with `w_tip / (2.0 * ca)` and ran `cargo nextest run -p gear-core`: 604 run, 9 failed. fillet_cap_guarantees_a_nonnegative_root_arc passed. The failures were regression::matches_the_reference_implementation, gear::tests::the_root_leaves_the_fillet_without_a_kink, bending::form_factor_converges_to_the_rack_limit, extremes::the_geometric_bounds_are_exactly_where_the_generator_starts_clamping, outline::tests::the_outline_meets_the_tolerance_it_was_given, screw::tests::the_crossed_interference_verdict_meets_the_parallel_one_at_the_limit and three train tests. The fault is caught, but by the reference-implementation comparison and incidental laws, not by the test that claims to be the guard.
proposal: Add the other side to the law. Where the cap binds (CLAMP_FILLET_CAPPED fired and the limit is rho_fit), assert that the capped fillet makes the two fillets meet at mid-space: θ0 equals half_pitch to within a tolerance scaled by FILLET_FRACTION_OF_MAX, so a smaller cap fails. Or reword the comment to 'catches a cap too large; a cap too small is caught by matches_the_reference_implementation'.
validation: Re-apply the w_tip/(2 cos α) mutation: the strengthened fillet-cap law fails. It passes at HEAD.

verdict.reason: I reproduced the mutation. With tooth.rs:914 replaced by `w_tip / (2.0 * ca)`, 604 tests run and 9 fail, and geometry_laws::fillet_cap_guarantees_a_nonnegative_root_arc PASSES. At 20° the wrong cap is 0.532·w_tip against the right one's 0.714·w_tip, so it can only shrink the fillet, and the one-sided assertion θ0 ≤ half_pitch cannot see that. The fault is caught, but not by the test whose doc comment claims to be the guard.
verdict.evidence: The worktree run at HEAD with the mutation failed regression::matches_the_reference_implementation, bending::form_factor_converges_to_the_rack_limit, extremes::the_geometric_bounds_are_exactly_where_the_generator_starts_clamping, gear::tests::the_root_leaves_the_fillet_without_a_kink, outline::tests::the_outline_meets_the_tolerance_it_was_given, screw::tests::the_crossed_interference_verdict_meets_the_parallel_one_at_the_limit and three train tests. It printed 'PASS gear-core::geometry_laws fillet_cap_guarantees_a_nonnegative_root_arc'. The test is at geometry_laws.rs:115-133.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposed two-sided check ('θ0 equals half_pitch' where the cap binds) does not hold as stated. The cap binds at FILLET_FRACTION_OF_MAX·rho_fit, which is below the meeting point, so θ0 stays strictly below half_pitch by an amount that is not a simple multiple. A cleaner law tests rho_fit directly: the fillet of radius rho_fit is tangent to the tool flank and the tool centreline at once (the closed form ac/R = π/z holds with equality at ρ = rho_fit). That needs rho_fit exposed as pub(crate) or a unit test inside tooth.rs. Rewording the comment is the fallback.

title: Stale intra-doc links to retired items; no check runs rustdoc
claim: `cargo doc` reports 17 unresolved intra-doc links. Several name items that no longer exist, so the prose describes an API that is gone: `Tooth::profile` (twice), `gear_core::Tooth::outline` (dxf.rs; outlines are Gear::outline/Ring::outline), `Gear::span` (`Self::span`), `Wiring::mounts`, `stated_helix`, `Port`, and `MeshError::note`, `MeasurementError::note` and `TrainError::note` (a trait method, `Note`, not inherent). Others are only wrong paths (`crate::Ring`, `GROUND`, `kinematics::System::play`, `minimum_profile_shift`, `rolling_curvature_radius`, `Freedom`, `Train::relieve_case`). check_doc_links covers only docs/*.md#anchor pointers, and no CI check runs rustdoc, so these are invisible. gear-core also has several private_intra_doc_links warnings (34 rustdoc warnings in all).
evidence: `CARGO_TARGET_DIR=<cache> gc /home/user/gearcalc cargo doc --offline -p gear-core|gear-io|gear-wasm|gear-cli --no-deps` output is saved at /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/notes/verify-lens-docs-accuracy-1-3/rustdoc.txt: 'gear-core (lib doc) generated 34 warnings', 'gear-io generated 1', 'gear-wasm generated 6'; 17 'unresolved link' lines. Example: outline.rs:3 '//! Two things distinguish this from [`Tooth::profile`]' gives 'the struct `Tooth` has no field or associated item named `profile`'. `grep -rn 'fn profile' crates/gear-core/src` finds only gear.rs:544 and ring.rs:827. `grep -rn 'fn mounts\|fn stated_helix'` finds nothing.
proposal: Fix each link: point to Gear::profile/Gear::outline or Ring::outline, or delete the dead references (span, mounts, stated_helix, Port). Qualify the path-only ones (crate::ring::Ring, crate::kinematics::GROUND, Note::note, etc.). Then add `RUSTDOCFLAGS='-D warnings' cargo doc --no-deps --workspace` (or `-D rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links`) to the flake checks, and list it in CLAUDE.md's check table.
validation: cargo doc --no-deps --workspace with -D rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links passes after the fix and fails at HEAD.

verdict.reason: I reran `cargo doc --offline --no-deps --workspace` in a clean worktree. It reports gear-core 34 warnings, gear-io 1 and gear-wasm 6, with exactly the 17 unresolved links listed. The retired names really are absent: there is no fn span, fn mounts, fn stated_helix or Port type. `outline` is defined on Ring (outline.rs:263) and Gear (gear.rs:611), not on Tooth. MeshError::note and MeasurementError::note are implementations of a trait method (note.rs:415), not inherent methods. No flake or tools check runs rustdoc (grep for 'rustdoc' and 'cargo doc' in flake.nix and tools/ finds nothing).
verdict.evidence: Saved output: /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/notes/verify-last-12-rustdoc.txt. Example: outline.rs:3 '[`Tooth::profile`]'; dxf.rs:35 '[`gear_core::Tooth::outline`]'.
verdict.proposal_note: A gate of `-D rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links` alone is safer than `-D warnings`, which would also make the private_intra_doc_links warnings fatal. Those need either fixing or `--document-private-items`, which is a separate choice. Add the gate to flake checks and to CLAUDE.md's check table.

title: The layout table exists three times, and state.md's copy carries its own history
claim: README.md and docs/state.md each carry a Layout table whose gear-core row is word-for-word identical, beside CLAUDE.md's complete map. state.md's section opens with self-referential history ('This table named seven of them and read as though it named all of them, which is the same failure the harness's command list had.'). Its gear.rs row carries the stale 'only place a gear is drawn' (finding 13). Saying each thing once would leave one layout (CLAUDE.md) with a pointer from README, and would remove the row-by-row drift that produced finding 13 and finding 17(c).
evidence: `grep -n "serde. and .ts-rs., both optional" README.md docs/state.md` hits README.md:51 and docs/state.md:269 with identical text. docs/state.md:259-262 is the self-referential paragraph.
proposal: Delete state.md's Layout table and its history paragraph. Keep the rows that carry a decision (if any are not already in CLAUDE.md) as prose there. Keep README's short table as the newcomer's entry point, or reduce it to a pointer to CLAUDE.md.
validation: check_doc_links still passes; grep finds the gear-core row once.

verdict.reason: The gear-core row is word for word the same at README.md:51 and docs/state.md:269. state.md:259-262 is the self-referential history paragraph. Its gear.rs row still says 'the only place a gear is drawn', while Ring::outline exists at outline.rs:263. The copies have already drifted: README's gear-io row leaves out the string catalogue that state.md's includes. state.md also says it keeps only rows that 'carry a decision rather than a location', yet it keeps pure location rows such as web/ and gear-cli.
verdict.evidence: grep output: README.md:51 and docs/state.md:269 identical; state.md:257-275 and README.md:47-59 read.
verdict.proposal_note: Delete state.md's Layout section. Nothing links to #layout (a grep for '#layout' found no pointer), so check_doc_links is unaffected. Keep README's table short, with a pointer to CLAUDE.md.

title: Parallel-mesh efficiency weights each pair at F/ε everywhere on the path, not F/2 in double contact; it overstates tooth loss by about 15-18 % of the loss against ISO/TR 14179-2 / DIN 3990 H_V, and its own verification test shares the assumption
claim: `contact::efficiency` computes loss ∝ (ε1²+ε2²)/ε_α, the uniform path average of |ξ|. That assumes every engaged pair carries F_n/ε_α at every instant, so the total force at an instant is n(t)·F_n/ε_α. That equals F_n only on time average, although the doc says the /ε_α 'is what holds the total transmitted force at F_n'. With the force held at F_n at every instant and split equally between two pairs in double contact, the rigid-tooth assumption behind ISO/TR 14179-2 and DIN 3990 / Niemann's H_V, the loss integral is (1 − ε + ε1² + ε2²). The code cites 'DIN 3990's loss factor' for its cos β_b term while using the other weighting. The test `efficiency_matches_a_numerical_average_of_the_instantaneous_loss` averages |ξ| uniformly over the path, which is the same assumption, so it cannot tell the two apart. The choice is not disclosed as an approximation. It also shapes the shift search's objective (`efficient_split` differentiates the same integrand).
evidence: notes/verify-lens-standards-1/share.py simulates contacts one base pitch apart, with the load split equally among the n pairs engaged at each instant, time-averaged. e1=e2=0.8: equal-split 0.34001, ISO (1−ε+e1²+e2²)/2 = 0.34, tool (e1²+e2²)/(2ε) = 0.40. e1=0.9, e2=0.6: 0.33501 / 0.335 / 0.39. e1=0.3, e2=1.0: 0.39501 / 0.395 / 0.41923. So the tool's loss is 6-18 % higher. loss.py for 17/43 at ε 1.62 and the same μ: tool 1.672 %, ISO H_V 1.429 %. contact.rs:352-357: 'The /ε_α ... is what holds the total transmitted force at F_n.' contact.rs:383-385 cites DIN 3990's loss factor. The test at contact.rs:1726-1731 builds `numeric` from `mean_over_path(&path, f64::abs)`, a uniform average.
proposal: Weight the loss integral by the instantaneous load share, n(t) pairs sharing F_n, which gives the closed form (1 − ε_α + ε1² + ε2²) for 1 ≤ ε_α ≤ 2, and in general Σ over the path of |ξ|/n(ξ). Alternatively, route it through contact.rs's existing `load_fraction(xi, LoadSharing)` so one load-share model serves both stress and loss, with equal split as the rigid-tooth value. Rewrite the test to simulate discrete pairs one base pitch apart that share F_n at each instant, as share.py does, so it can fail on the uniform weighting. Re-derive `efficient_split`'s residual from the new integrand. Update reference.md, the Buckingham attribution and the golden and figures outputs (canary 98.345 % moves).
validation: The new closed form matches the discrete-pair simulation to 1e-9 on the existing five meshes × three helix angles. It equals ISO/TR 14179-2's H_V for ε ≤ 2. check_golden and check_figures diffs move only the efficiency lines and the shifts searches.

verdict.reason: The arithmetic is right, and it is right for spur gears. Weighting every engaged pair at F/eps_alpha satisfies force balance only on time average, and the contact.rs:352-357 comment claims it holds the total force at F_n. The numerical test shares that uniform weighting, so it cannot tell the two apart. But the claim goes wrong once it becomes universal. For a helical mesh with uniform load per unit contact-line length, the tool's uniform-path average is the exact answer once the overlap ratio eps_beta is an integer, and it is within about 0.5 % for eps_beta >= 1. ISO's (1-eps+e1^2+e2^2) is exact only at eps_beta = 0. The proposal to swap in the ISO closed form everywhere would make high-overlap helical meshes about 15 % too efficient in loss terms. That repeats the error the code's own eps_gamma paragraph warns about, in the other direction.
verdict.corrected_claim: contact::efficiency is exact under uniform line load only when the total contact-line length is constant (eps_beta an integer). For spur and low-overlap helical meshes it overstates tooth loss by up to about 18 % against the instantaneous equal-split value (ISO/TR 14179-2 H_V). The comment at contact.rs:352-357 wrongly says the /eps_alpha holds the instantaneous force at F_n. The test at contact.rs:1709-1740 uses the same uniform average, so it cannot detect the difference.
verdict.evidence: Re-derived by hand: e1 = e2 = 0.8 gives 0.04 in the single-contact zone plus 2 x 0.5 x 0.30 in the double-contact zones = 0.34, against the tool's 1.28/3.2 = 0.40. A simulation of the field of action with load F/L(t) per unit length (notes/verify-last-13/helix.py) gives, as mean |xi| per base pitch: e1 = e2 = 0.8: eps_beta 0 -> 0.340 (ISO), 0.5 -> 0.384, 1.0 -> 0.400, 1.5 -> 0.398, 2.0 -> 0.400 (tool). e1 = 0.9, e2 = 0.6: 0.335 / 0.372 / 0.390 / 0.388 / 0.390. e1 = 0.3, e2 = 1.0: 0.395 / 0.4115 / 0.4195 / 0.4184 / 0.4192. The test at contact.rs:1726-1731 builds numeric from mean_over_path(&path, f64::abs), which is the uniform assumption. LoadSharing (contact.rs:937) has only None and LinearRamp, and the LinearRamp is not constrained to sum to 1, so no equal-split model exists to route through.
verdict.proposal_note: Use one model that holds in both limits: load per unit contact-line length equals F_n / L(t), time-averaged over the rectangular field of action (eps_alpha by eps_beta). It is closed-form and piecewise in e1, e2 and eps_beta. It reduces to ISO's (1-eps+e1^2+e2^2) at eps_beta = 0 and to the current (e1^2+e2^2)/eps at integer eps_beta, so there is no branch on spur versus helical. Test it against a discrete contact-line simulation like helix.py over eps_beta in {0, 0.5, 1, 1.5}, and re-derive efficient_split's residual from the same integrand. Also correct the 'Buckingham recovered' and 'field of action ... does not matter' paragraphs: the spreading does matter unless L(t) is constant.

title: The 'close to locking' margin 0.8 × threshold is an unexplained literal
claim: The near-locking note fires when static μ exceeds 0.8 × the locking threshold. The 0.8 is not derived, not named and not exposed. Its effect is to decide whether a designer is warned that a worm's behaviour depends on an estimated coefficient. The note also cannot fire on a mesh that is locked (`else if`), so a lock with a 2 % margin reads the same as one with a 200 % margin.
evidence: shape.rs:2697-2705: `if *locked.get(drive) { notes.push(said(is_locked)); } else if threshold > 0.0 && static_friction > 0.8 * threshold {`. A grep of docs for 0.8 × threshold finds no rationale for the value.
proposal: Base the margin on the two coefficients the mesh already carries, not on a constant. For example, fire 'near' whenever the threshold lies between the sliding and static coefficients: the mesh then locks at rest but not once moving, or the reverse. That condition is exact and needs no literal. It also covers a locked mesh that would run backwards once moving, the case finding 1 raises.
validation: A law: the note fires exactly when min(μ_s, μ_k) < threshold < max(μ_s, μ_k). The 8.2° default worm (0.08 < 0.1327 < 0.16) fires it.

verdict.reason: The 0.8 is confirmed: it is an undocumented literal at shape.rs:2700. It is the only rationale-free margin on a note whose purpose is the uncertainty in an estimated coefficient. The `else if` also means a mesh locked by a 1 % margin reads the same as one locked by 200 %. The proposed replacement is wrong, though. Here `locked` is decided on the static coefficient (once_moving(at_rest) goes <= 0 when at_rest <= 0), and sliding < static. So 'threshold between sliding and static' can only hold when static > threshold, which is a mesh already locked and already carrying the self-locking note. On every unlocked mesh that condition is false, so the proposal would remove the near-locking warning altogether. The cited example (the default worm, 0.08 < 0.1327 < 0.16) is already locked, and `gear-cli train mixed` prints 'self-locking: static μ 0.160 against a threshold of 0.1327'.
verdict.corrected_claim: The near-locking margin 0.8 x threshold is an unexplained literal. Because of the else-if, a mesh locked by a thin margin is not told that the lock itself rests on an estimated coefficient.
verdict.evidence: shape.rs:2697-2706: `if *locked.get(drive) { notes.push(said(is_locked)); } else if threshold > 0.0 && static_friction > 0.8 * threshold {`. The efficiency at shape.rs:~3806 is `sliding[k].once_moving(&at_rest[k])`, and locked() at contact.rs:273 is efficiency <= 0. gear-cli train mixed prints only the self-locking note for the 8.2° worm. grep of docs/*.md finds no rationale for the 0.8.
verdict.proposal_note: Make the margin an explicit, stated band on mu (for example a named relative uncertainty in mu, surfaced as a mesh input next to the two coefficients). Fire 'near' in either direction when |mu_s - threshold| < band x threshold. That covers a thin-margin lock as well as a near miss. The sentence in the catalogue can then state the band.

title: The code comment justifying GearCase.torque ('the mesh force at its reference cylinder') is false for crossed and worm meshes
claim: The comment says a member's torque is 'the mesh force at its reference cylinder, which is the driver's torque read across the mesh and the one number every stress on the member is proportional to'. On a point-contact (crossed) mesh with friction, the driven member's tangential force is F_n(cos α_n cos γ − μ sin γ) = η·i·T1/r2, not i·T1/r2. The lossless referral therefore is not the wheel's reference-cylinder force, and the comment's reasoning covers line-contact meshes only. The worm's σ_H is the same on both members, so it comes from the normal force rather than from this torque; the error is in what the figure is said to be, not in a stress.
evidence: `gear-cli train mixed`: wheel T 199.0040 N·m = 4.9751·40, while the wheel's shaft reacts 122.9936 N·m and the ratio 1.618 = 1/η (η = 0.61805 printed). The worm's and the wheel's σ_H are both 4574.4 MPa in case 1, so the stress does not come from the member torque.
proposal: Restrict the comment to line-contact meshes, or compute a crossed mesh's driven-member figure from the screw model's force balance (η·i·T1). Keep this together with the doc fix for finding lens-standards[7].
validation: A test in crossed.rs asserting that a worm wheel's reported member torque equals −(its body's reacted torque) when the wheel is its body's only gear, or, if the lossless definition is kept, a doc test stating that it does not.

verdict.reason: A crossed mesh with friction does not split its force the way the comment assumes. The wheel's tooth-carried torque is eta x i x T1: the normal force's tangential component minus the friction component, r2 F_n (cos α_n cos γ - μ sin γ). The lossless referral i x T1 matches neither that nor the normal-force component alone, because it contains μ cos²γ/sin γ. The comment's 'mesh force at its reference cylinder' holds only for line contact, where i x T1 = F_n r_b2 exactly. The harness output agrees: the wheel's T is 4.9751 x 40, while its body reacts eta times that. The worm's σ_H comes from the normal force, since it is identical on both members.
verdict.evidence: gear-cli train mixed, part 2: worm case 1 T 4.9751 Nm, wheel T 199.0040 Nm (= x40). The body b3 reacts -122.9936 Nm, and 122.9936/199.0040 = 0.61805 = the printed forward efficiency 61.805 %. σ_H is 4574.4 MPa on both members. The member_torque closure at shape.rs:3729-3743 scales pressing_torque_at_a by z_b/z_a with no η, under the comment at shape.rs:3722-3727.
verdict.proposal_note: Rewording the comment is the smaller fix. If the figure is to mean 'what the teeth carry' for every mesh kind, take the driven member's torque from the screw model's force balance (η_mesh x i x T1 on a point contact), and state what line contacts report. Also check that the wheel's cycle and duty figures do not depend on this torque.

title: Rationale and reference say only ultimate contact is off by default; the code turns both contact ratings off
claim: rationale.md#a-contact-pressure-is-not-a-tensile-stress opens 'Peak contact is the one of the four ratings that is **off** by default. The other three compare like with like'. reference.md:2869 says 'Ultimate contact is off by default'. The default in train/mod.rs:2489-2507 sets contact ultimate: false and fatigue: false ('Neither contact rating sizes a width by default'), and state.md:534 agrees with the code. Two documents contradict the code and a third document. The rationale's 'other three compare like with like' also carries the false 'fatigue figure derived for flanks' sentence (finding 1).
evidence: sed of mod.rs:2489-2507 shows `contact: ByKind { ultimate: false, fatigue: false }`. git log -S finds the 'Neither contact rating' comment introduced in 499d26c ('a default that decided too much'); the rationale paragraph was not updated.
proposal: Rewrite rationale.md:1267-1275 to say both contact ratings are off by default, and give each kind's reason once: ultimate because a Hertz pressure is not a tensile stress, fatigue because the library has no contact-fatigue figure (see finding 1). Change reference.md:2869 to 'Neither contact rating is on by default'.
validation: Read mod.rs:2489-2507 against the two sentences; check_doc_links still passes.

verdict.reason: The code sets both contact kinds off. state.md:534 agrees with the code. rationale.md:1267 ('the one of the four ratings that is off by default. The other three...') and reference.md:2869 ('Ultimate contact is off by default') contradict both.
verdict.evidence: train/mod.rs:2489-2507 has `contact: ByKind { ultimate: false, fatigue: false }` with the comment 'Neither contact rating sizes a width by default'. rationale.md:1267-1269 and reference.md:2868-2869 are quoted above; state.md:534 reads 'Neither contact rating is enabled by default'.
verdict.proposal_note: Also give the fatigue kind's reason in the rationale section. It is the one mod.rs states ('the one that dominates by an order of magnitude ... a default making the design decision'), so both reasons live in the rationale and the code comment points to it rather than restating it.

title: contact_stress's lengthwise_curvature argument is zero in every production call
claim: The doc says the crossed-axis work 'adds an argument here rather than a second function chosen by stage type'. But crossed meshes are rated through BuiltContact::Point and the screw model, never through contact_stress with a nonzero lengthwise curvature. Every production caller passes PARALLEL_AXES. The unifying parameter is exercised only by a test, and the sentence suggests crossed axes use it.
evidence: grep 'PARALLEL_AXES|lengthwise_curvature' over crates/gear-core/src: the only production callers are shape.rs:3318 and :4513, both PARALLEL_AXES. The other hits are tests in ring.rs, screw.rs and strength.rs.
proposal: Either route crossed-axis contact through contact_stress with its lengthwise curvature (one model, as rule 4 asks), or change the doc to say crossed axes use hertz::peak_pressure through the point-contact seam and that this argument is 0 today except for a future crowning input (finding 5).
validation: grep shows the callers; after a doc fix nothing else changes.

verdict.reason: Every production call of contact_stress passes PARALLEL_AXES. shape.rs:4509 is inside a #[cfg(test)] module that starts at line 4190. Crossed meshes call hertz::peak_pressure / elliptical_contact directly at shape.rs:2569-2571. Unification does hold one level down, since both routes end in hertz. What is misleading is the sentence claiming the crossed-axis work adds the argument 'here'. PARALLEL_AXES's own doc ('Every mesh this crate builds today takes it') already admits the parameter is always zero.
verdict.evidence: grep over crates/gear-core/src: contact_stress( with a nonzero curvature appears only in strength.rs tests (2892, 2913). Production callers are shape.rs:3314-3318 (PARALLEL_AXES) and train/mod.rs:433 (curvature_along: PARALLEL_AXES). The point contact is at shape.rs:2571, `crate::hertz::peak_pressure(along, across, ...)`.
verdict.proposal_note: Either drop the argument, since the point route already reaches the same hertz function and a crowning input would add it back with a caller, or reword strength.rs:1766-1769 to say crossed axes reach hertz through BuiltContact::Point and this argument is kept for crowning. Dropping it fits the project's rule that what nothing reads goes.

title: A material's condition (the temperature and humidity its allowables are quoted at) crosses to the panel and is never shown
claim: The library says each entry is one material in one state, named by its `condition`: 'conditioned, 23 °C / 50 % RH', or '23 °C, as moulded' for POM. That field is the only place the state is recorded, because the names are plain 'PA6' and 'POM Delrin 100P'. The field crosses the wire, but the panel's material picker shows only m.name, and nothing in web/src reads `.condition`. A designer choosing a polyamide never sees that its stiffness and allowables are for the conditioned state at 23 °C. The library header calls that difference 'not small', since unfilled PA6 loses two thirds of its stiffness.
evidence: material.rs:238-243 defines `pub condition: String`, and Material.ts:27 carries `condition: string`. grep -rn 'condition' over web/src (excluding wire/) finds only comments, at TrainPanel.svelte:1034 and 1187-1197. TrainPanel.svelte:1644-1645 renders `<option value={m.name}>{m.name}</option>`. materials_default.toml:17-20 explains why the state matters.
proposal: Show the selected material's `condition` (and optionally `source`) as a muted line under the material select in the member card. The data arrives already formatted, so no string catalogue change is needed beyond a label key ×5 if one is wanted.
validation: cd web && npm run check, then load a PA6 member in the running app and see 'conditioned, 23 °C / 50 % RH' under the picker. tools/check_strings.py if a label key is added.

verdict.reason: `condition` (and `grade` and `source`) crosses the wire, and no .svelte or .ts outside wire/ reads it. The picker renders only m.name. The library names are plain ('PA6'), so the conditioned 23 °C / 50 % RH state is invisible in the panel.
verdict.evidence: grep -rn 'condition' web/src (excluding wire/) finds only comments, at TrainPanel.svelte:1034 and 1187-1197. There are no reads of .grade or .source for materials. TrainPanel.svelte:1643-1645 renders `<option value={m.name}>{m.name}</option>`. materials_default.toml:121/134/147/160 carry 'conditioned, 23 °C / 50 % RH'.
verdict.proposal_note: The condition text is English prose in a data file. Shown as it stands it is untranslated in four of the five languages, which sits awkwardly with the string-catalogue rule. Either accept that as data (like the names) and say so, or give the recurring states (conditioned 23 °C / 50 % RH, as moulded) a structured field with catalogue keys. Also fix the stale comment at TrainPanel.svelte:1032-1034 (see missed).

title: A worm at normal pressure angle 89-90° is solved and rated rather than refused
claim: Screw::new checks the pressure angle only for finiteness, and the shape passes normal_pressure_angle() unchecked. So a worm pair with α_n = 90° (no flank at all), or 89°, returns rated figures with only efficiency and locking notes. The Ranges invariant bound (0<α<90, open) would not stop 89° either.
evidence: Probe bin/tr.rs, Worm preset with both members' pressure_angle manual 90 and then 89: 'OK keys=[clamp.fillet_capped, mesh.forward_locking, mesh.low_efficiency, mesh.self_locking]' in both cases, and figures are reported.
proposal: Refuse α_n where the tooth has no usable flank, for example where the rack tooth's working depth has no involute between the base and tip circles, or bound α_n by what the rack can form (tan α_n · h < p/4). Do this in the input gate proposed for finding 0, with a key naming the pressure angle, and apply the same predicate to the parallel line contacts.
validation: A law over every preset: sweep α_n towards 90° and require either a refusal naming the pressure angle or a finite rating whose flank exists (base radius below tip radius and the involute non-empty).

verdict.reason: Re-ran it with my own probe. I set pressure_angle manual on every member of the Worm and Spur presets through Train::alone and solve_train. The worm at 89 and 90 degrees solves with keys {clamp.fillet_capped, mesh.forward_locking, mesh.low_efficiency, mesh.self_locking}. At 89 degrees it reports contact_stress 2276.29 MPa on both members, while bending_stress is null in every case. Only 95 degrees is refused (NoContact). The same inputs on Spur are refused from 85 degrees (NoRootSection), and at 90 degrees as Mesh(OutsideInvoluteDomain). The crossed path therefore reports a Hertz stress for a tooth with no root section and no usable flank, where the parallel path refuses. Screw::new (screw.rs:216-225) checks the pressure angle only with is_finite(). shape.rs:515-531 passes normal_pressure_angle() through unchecked. The member's Ranges bound pressure_angle to the open interval (0, 90), which admits 89.
verdict.evidence: Probe probes/verify-last-14: 'Worm pa=89: OK keys={clamp.fillet_capped, mesh.forward_locking, mesh.low_efficiency, mesh.self_locking}', 'Worm pa=90: OK ...', 'Spur pa=85: ERR InPart{cause: NoRootSection}', 'Spur pa=90: ERR Mesh(OutsideInvoluteDomain)'. notes/verify-last-14/worm89.json: /members/0/cases/0/contact_stress 2276.29, bending_stress None.
verdict.proposal_note: The simplest consistent fix is to make the crossed path meet the same predicates the parallel one does. Refuse NoRootSection when a member has no bending section, and refuse OutsideInvoluteDomain when the member's rb >= ra, rather than inventing a new rack-formability bound. The rack's tip width is already clamped (gear.addendum_held_to_tip_width fires from 60 degrees), so a tan(alpha_n)·h < p/4 bound would duplicate that clamp.

title: The ring solve ignores a ring's own shift bound: the ring tab validates x against the external gear's Ranges
claim: RingSummary has no ranges field. GearPanel.onInput takes its bound from the external-gear solve `result` even in internal mode, so every ring input (shift, dedendum, root radius) is checked against bounds that belong to an external gear. Finding 1's domain edge is one instance; the others (tip and space closure) are ring-specific as well.
evidence: GearPanel.svelte:124: `const b = "ok" in result ? boundFor(f.key, result.ok.ranges) : null;` where `result = solve(request)` is the external solve. The RingSummary fields (lib.rs:570-600) include no ranges.
proposal: Give Ring an `admissible_ranges` of its own (shift from x_min = -inv α_t (z - z_c)/(2 tan α_n) up to the space-closure limit) and return it in RingSummary. In internal mode, have GearPanel read `ring.ok.ranges`.
validation: A test that the ring's shift min equals the closed form for several (z, z_c, β), and a check that the ring tab refuses x below it.

verdict.reason: GearPanel.svelte:124 validates against result.ok.ranges, and result = solve(request) is the external-gear solve. boundNote (lines 47-79) and shiftNote (line 92) read the same external ranges in internal mode. So the ring tab shows an external gear's undercut, pointed and shallow-cut shift thresholds, and refuses input by them. RingSummary (gear-wasm lib.rs:570-600) has no ranges. This also contradicts docs/reference.md:1353, 'Own buildable range | shown | not shown — a rack's range is not a ring's'. That is true of a train's member card (state.md:634) but not of the gear tab.
verdict.evidence: GearPanel.svelte:124 `const b = "ok" in result ? boundFor(f.key, result.ok.ranges) : null;`. Lines 90-94: notesFor uses result.ok.ranges.profile_shift with no internal check. reference.md:1353 says ranges are not shown for a ring. solve_ring_impl builds no ranges field.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposed ring x_min formula (-inv α_t (z - z_c)/(2 tan α_n)) is not derived anywhere I could find, and it is not a ring's shift bound. Adopt it only with a derivation and an independent check. The immediate fix, consistent with the docs, is that in internal mode GearPanel neither shows nor validates against result.ok.ranges, keeping only structural bounds such as teeth ≥ 1 and module > 0. Ring-specific ranges built from the ring's own limits (generation_limit, tip/space closure in ring.rs) are a separate feature.

title: editTrain reports a boundary defect as a successful edit
claim: When edit_train throws anything that is not a 'ui.' refusal key (malformed JSON, serde failure, panic), editTrain returns null. null is also what it returns for a successful edit. The train is left unchanged, and neither Offers.svelte nor TrainPanel can tell the click failed. Every other boundary wrapper in core.ts either returns {error} or maps the failure to ui.train_boundary_failed.
evidence: core.ts:821-823 `const message = e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e); return message.startsWith("ui.") ? message : null;`. Offers.svelte:92 `refusal = editTrain(train, { graph: o.edit });`. TrainPanel.svelte:271/280 ignore the return entirely. solveTrain (core.ts ~773-790) shows the intended pattern: a throw becomes a ui.train_boundary_failed note.
proposal: Return a distinct value for a defect, e.g. { refused: key } | { failed: detail } | null, and have Offers show ui.train_boundary_failed on `failed`. Better still, once edit_train returns its refusal in the value (finding 11), any throw is a defect and can always be surfaced.
validation: A wasm_probe step that sends edit_train a request with a malformed edit and asserts the panel-side wrapper does not return null.

verdict.reason: core.ts:817-829 returns null both for success and for any throw whose message does not start with 'ui.'. Offers.svelte:92-97 treats null as success: it closes the menu and calls made?(o.edit, meshes) although the train is unchanged. TrainPanel's setDuty and addCaseOfKind ignore the return, and addCaseOfKind then selects case index length-1, which is the old last case. The doc comment ('swallowed as before') documents the swallow but gives no argument for it. It also contradicts solveTrain's own pattern, which maps a throw to ui.train_boundary_failed.
verdict.evidence: core.ts:821-823 `return message.startsWith("ui.") ? message : null;`. Offers.svelte:92-97 `refusal = editTrain(...); if (refusal !== null) return; over = null; open = null; made?.(o.edit, meshes);`. core.ts:768-790 solveTrain returns note key ui.train_boundary_failed on a throw.
verdict.proposal_note: Returning the ui.train_boundary_failed key (with the detail) from editTrain on a non-'ui.' throw is enough. Offers already shows whatever key comes back, so no new union type is needed.

title: Degenerate Gear::outline allocates over a million vertices instead of refusing
claim: Gear::outline(0.01) on module = 0 or a NaN module returns 1,114,146 vertices, and on z = 0 returns 65,538, where a normal gear gives a few thousand. The chord-tolerance refinement has no bound when the radii are zero or non-finite. export_dxf_impl builds a Tooth, and gear_profile_impl a Gear, from unvalidated resolved_params, so a malformed request reaching the wasm boundary costs this memory (or panics in profile) instead of being refused.
evidence: Probe probes/verify-lens-errors-policy-2 `prof`: 'z0: outline Ok(65538)', 'm0: outline Ok(1114146)', 'nan: outline Ok(1114146)', 'mneg: outline Ok(2244)'.
proposal: Validate GearParams once (finite, m > 0, z ≥ 1, α ∈ (0,90), |β| < 90) at the boundary's resolved_params and in Gear::new's callers, and refuse with an error note. Optionally make outline refuse a non-finite or zero pitch radius.
validation: A test over the invariant bounds' edges: outline() vertex count is below a bound derived from the chord tolerance and the gear's size, and profile() does not panic.

verdict.reason: The vertex counts reproduce: z=0 gives 65,538, m=0 and NaN give 1,114,146, and a normal gear gives 442. A DXF of a Tooth with m=0 took 424 ms against 0.4 ms for a normal one. The claim that the refinement 'has no bound' is wrong. MAX_SUBDIVISION_DEPTH = 14 (outline.rs:49) caps every span at 2^14, and 1.1M is exactly the bounded worst case that outline.rs's an_unreachable_tolerance_stays_bounded pins (400k-1.2M vertices, under 2 s) for a 1e-18 tolerance. The degenerate gear hits that same bounded cap: the sagitta is NaN or the tolerance floor is 0, so every span recurses to the stop. It costs about 45 MB and does not run away. The more serious defect is in the finding's own parenthesis: Gear::profile panics ('range start index 1 out of range for slice of length 0' at gear.rs:564) for z=0, m=0 and NaN. In wasm that panic is a trap in gear_profile, not a refusal.
verdict.evidence: Probe probes/verify-last-14: 'z0: profile Err(PANIC) outline Ok(65538)', 'm0: profile Err(PANIC) outline Ok(1114146)', 'nan: profile Err(PANIC) outline Ok(1114146)', 'ok: profile Ok(324) outline Ok(442)', 'dxf 424ms' vs 431µs. outline.rs:49 `const MAX_SUBDIVISION_DEPTH: u32 = 14;`. outline.rs:716-724 is the bounded-count test.
verdict.corrected_claim: A gear with a degenerate module or tooth count (0, NaN) builds without refusal. Its outline runs every span to the fixed subdivision stop, giving about 1.1M vertices (bounded, the same count as an unreachable tolerance), and its profile panics at gear.rs:564. Nothing at the wasm boundary refuses such params before the panel's own range check.
verdict.proposal_note: Put a structural GearParams gate (finite, m > 0, z ≥ 1, α and β in range) in resolved_params, returning Err, so solve_gear, gear_profile and export_dxf all refuse such params. The outline needs no change of its own, since it is already bounded.

title: Edit::Release of a body that is not held, or does not exist, succeeds silently while Edit::Hold refuses NoSuchIndex
claim: Train::edit refuses Hold on ground or on a body the shape lacks, but its Release arm calls self.release(body) and returns Ok(()) whatever the body is. release only runs held.retain. So Release(99) reports success and changes nothing, against offers.rs's principle that no edit which would change nothing is offered. Graph edits refuse where case and hold edits do not.
evidence: conditions.rs:1292-1302: Hold checks `body == GROUND || !self.shape.bodies.iter().any(..)` and returns Err(NoSuchIndex); Release does `self.release(body); Ok(())`. conditions.rs:1066: `pub fn release(&mut self, body: usize) { self.held.retain(|&b| b != body); }`.
proposal: Refuse Release with EditRefused::NoSuchIndex when !self.held.contains(&body), mirroring Hold. Extend a_refused_edit_changes_nothing (and finding 15's set_duty change) to cover it.
validation: A unit test: on the Spur preset, Edit::Release(99) and Edit::Release of an unheld body both return Err(NoSuchIndex), and the train is unchanged.

verdict.reason: conditions.rs:1292-1302: Hold refuses NoSuchIndex on ground or on a body the shape lacks, while Release calls release (retain only) and returns Ok(()) for any body. Offers only offers Release on a held body (offers.rs:185-189), so the panel cannot reach this. It is an API-level inconsistency, and a no-op reported as success. Hold of an already-held body is equally a silent no-op (hold() at 1052-1062 dedups), so the asymmetry is not only on Release.
verdict.evidence: conditions.rs:1298-1301 `Edit::Release(body) => { self.release(body); Ok(()) }`. conditions.rs:1066-1068 release is held.retain. conditions.rs:1052-1058 hold skips the push when already held. offers.rs:185-189 offers Release only if self.held.contains(&b).
verdict.proposal_note: Refuse Release with NoSuchIndex only for a body that is ground or missing from the shape, mirroring Hold. NoSuchIndex misnames an existing but unheld body. Either treat hold/release of a body already in that state as an idempotent Ok on both sides, or give both a distinct key such as 'already held' / 'not held', so the two arms stay symmetric.

title: The tip radius is raised to the base circle silently
claim: When the addendum asked for puts the tip below the base circle, Tooth changes the tip radius to r_b(1 + 1e-9) without pushing any note. That breaks rule 5 ('clamp rather than refuse, and say so'). It is also why the addendum floor at auto.rs:671 cannot be tested from its far side by key.
evidence: tooth.rs:471 reads `let ra = ra.max(rb * (1.0 + guard::TIP_ABOVE_BASE_FRACTION));`, and no clamps.push follows it, unlike the pointed-tip cap at line 468 just above. auto.rs:671 exposes the same bound as addendum.min. Reachability: admissible_ranges refuses it in the panel, but GearParams from code, the CLI or a TOML document can carry such an addendum (for example z = 17, addendum −0.9 gives ra 7.6 < r_b 7.987).
proposal: Push a keyed note (for example clamp.tip_raised_to_base, with the radius) where ra is raised. Add it to the 5 string catalogues. Extend extremes.rs's bounds test to assert that note fires at addendum.min − eps and does not fire at + eps.
validation: A Tooth with z = 17, addendum = −0.9 carries the new key. The same Tooth at addendum = admissible_ranges().addendum.min + 0.01 does not. gear_io::strings tests pass once the note fires.

verdict.reason: tooth.rs:471 raises ra to rb(1+1e-9) with no clamps.push, unlike the pointed-tip cap two lines above it (467-468), which pushes CLAMP_TIP_CAPPED_POINTED. With z=17 and α=20°, rb = 7.987387 and admissible_ranges' addendum.min = -0.51261. Addendum -0.52 and -0.9 (and ha=1 with x=-1.6) all give ra = 7.987387285 with clamps=[]. Addendum -0.51 gives ra = 7.99 and no clamp, as it should. The result is a tooth with no involute flank, reported silently. Such params are reachable from code, the CLI or a TOML document; only the panel's range check stops them.
verdict.evidence: Probe probes/verify-last-14: 'ha=-0.9 x=0: rb=7.987387 ra=7.987387285 clamps=[] addendum_min=-0.5126127', 'ha=-0.52: ra=7.987387285 clamps=[]', 'ha=1 x=-1.6: ra=7.987387285 clamps=[] addendum_min=1.0874'.
verdict.proposal_note: A tip at or below the base circle leaves no flank at all, which is arguably 'no shape' under rule 5. Refusing it (with a key naming the addendum) is at least as defensible as a clamp note. If a clamp is kept, the note should carry the requested and the used tip radius. The new note needs its key in all five catalogues, and the extremes test should check both sides of addendum.min.

title: Dangling pointers to a DESIGN.md / 'design document' that no longer exists outside docs/history
claim: The JGMA CSV header says 'see DESIGN.md 4.6.1'. There is no DESIGN.md: §4.6.1 exists only in docs/history/design-record.md, which is superseded and governs nothing. The current home of the two-scales argument is docs/rationale.md (around lines 1530-1548) and docs/reference.md#tolerance-tables. auto.rs:2153 says the tested thresholds are 'in the design document'; 17.10/21.37/12.82 appear only in docs/history/design-record.md. metrology.rs:7 also cites 'the design document'. check_doc_links.py does not catch these: it scans crates/**/*.rs, web/src/*.ts|svelte and docs/*.md (tools/check_doc_links.py:45-48), not the CSV, and the .rs mentions are prose rather than link syntax.
evidence: ls DESIGN.md -> No such file. grep -n '4.6.1' docs/history/design-record.md -> 1653 '#### 4.6.1 JGMA 116-02 — a lookup table, and two grade scales rather than one'. grep for 12.82|21.37|17.10 under docs/ -> only docs/history/design-record.md.
proposal: CSV line 10: point to docs/rationale.md (the two-scales section) or docs/reference.md#tolerance-tables. auto.rs:2153: rewrite or delete along with finding 7's fix. metrology.rs:7: name the document that now holds the case, or docs/corrections.md if it moved there. Optionally extend check_doc_links.py to scan crates/**/data/*.csv comment lines for doc references.
validation: grep -rn 'DESIGN.md\|design document' crates/ returns nothing once the fix is in; check_doc_links passes with the CSV added to its scan.

verdict.reason: All three stale pointers are real. But the claim that 17.10/21.37/12.82 appear only in docs/history/design-record.md is wrong: auto.rs's own module doc (lines 58-79) carries the same table (17.10 -> 18, 21.37 -> 22, 12.82 -> 13). So auto.rs:2153 should point at that doc and not be deleted. The textbook-figure case cited at metrology.rs:7 cannot be found in any current document, or by grep in the history either.
verdict.corrected_claim: jgma_116_02.csv:10 cites a non-existent 'DESIGN.md 4.6.1'; the argument now lives in docs/rationale.md#the-tolerance-table-has-two-grade-scales-not-one. auto.rs:2153 cites 'the design document' for thresholds that auto.rs's own module doc (lines 58-79) states. metrology.rs:7 cites 'the design document' for a case that no current document records. check_doc_links.py does not scan .csv files and matches only link-shaped pointers, so neither kind of reference is checked.
verdict.evidence: ls DESIGN.md -> no such file. grep 17.10|21.37|12.82: auto.rs:63,64,78 (doc table) and :2185-2187 (asserts), docs/history/design-record.md:446,448,4236, nothing else under docs/. check_doc_links.py:43-52 SOURCES = crates/**/*.rs, web/src ts/svelte, docs/*.md, README, CLAUDE.md, with no csv. grep -i 'textbook|remembered' over docs/*.md and docs/history finds no over-pins/span textbook-figure case.
verdict.proposal_note: auto.rs:2153: change the doc to 'The thresholds in this module's doc table ([what it exposes])' rather than deleting it. metrology.rs:7: if the case cannot be found, drop the sentence instead of redirecting it. CSV: link rationale.md#the-tolerance-table-has-two-grade-scales-not-one.

title: The JGMA transcription has been fully re-verified against the source page: all 618 values match
claim: Recorded as SOUND, so the plan does not touch the data. Every tooth-to-tooth and total value in the CSV (fine grades 0-6 × 21 cells, standard grades 4-12 × 18 cells) equals the rendered source at /home/user/gears/docs/JGMA 116-02 1983.pdf (outside the repo, a 2010 compilation from an xlsx). The one module-monotonicity anomaly (fine g1, m 0.6-1.0, d 12.01-25.00, total 28) is printed that way in the source. rationale.md:1553 still describes 'three transcription checks', but jgma.rs has five structural checks plus spot values (cell counts, preferred numbers, monotone in grade, total > t2t, contiguous coverage).
evidence: pdftoppm -r 110 on the PDF (poppler from /nix/store/80q9...-poppler-utils-26.06.0), both pages compared row by row with a python dump of the CSV in page order; no difference. jgma.rs tests at lines 433, 471, 493, 518, 556.
proposal: Update rationale.md:1553 (and the CSV header's 'three transcription checks') to list the checks that exist. Record in the CSV header that the fine g1 m0.6-1.0 d12.01 total of 28 is as printed, so a future module-monotonicity law can name it as a source exception.
validation: Read-through; a module-monotonicity law with that single documented exception passes.

All 618 values match. The fine g1, m0.6-1.0, d12.01-25.00 total of 28 (against 26 at m1.0-1.6) is printed that way. rationale.md:1553 and the CSV header (line 6) both say 'three transcription checks', but jgma.rs has five structural tests plus spot values.

Page 1 grade 1 row reads '...7.1 7.5 8.5 ... 22 25 28 28 30 30 34 25 26 ...'. jgma.rs #[test] at 434 (contiguous), 471 (cell counts), 493 (preferred numbers), 518 (monotone in grade), 556 (total > t2t), plus 200 spot values.

title: A third wall-clock assert in outline.rs, redundant with the vertex count beside it
claim: an_unreachable_tolerance_stays_bounded asserts elapsed < 2 s before it asserts the vertex count band 400k..1.2M. The doc comment states that the count is spans x 2^depth, and the time is proportional to it. The time assert therefore adds nothing the count does not catch. Because it runs first, a subdivision-depth mutant fails with the less diagnostic 'took 4.3s' message rather than the count message that names MAX_SUBDIVISION_DEPTH. Neither this finding nor the known train one mentions this test.
evidence: Measured 0.22 s in the debug build and 0.28 s under llvm-cov, against the 2 s bound. mutants.out/log/crates__gear-core__src__outline.rs_line_92_col_47.log fails with 'took 4.349649316s for 12144638 vertices'. That count is also outside the band, so the count assert would have fired too.
proposal: Drop the elapsed assert, or put it after the count assert and include n in both messages. The count band is the law. The 45-second hang the comment cites is a count that is too large, and the count catches it deterministically.
validation: Mutate MAX_SUBDIVISION_DEPTH to 15 in a worktree. The test must fail with the count message naming the depth.

verdict.reason: outline.rs:716-727 is as described. The time assert runs before the count band, and the mutants log for outline.rs:92:47 fails on 'took 4.349649316s for 12144638 vertices', a count also outside 400k..1.2M, so the count assert alone would have caught it with the diagnostic message. The doc comment says the count is spans x 2^depth, so time is a proxy for it. The wall-clock asserts in the crate are this one, gear.rs:1338 and train/mod.rs:10000, so 'third' is accurate.
verdict.evidence: sed -n 698-727 outline.rs; grep -n took mutants.out/log/crates__gear-core__src__outline.rs_line_92_col_47.log -> line 1859 'took 4.349649316s for 12144638 vertices'; grep Instant::now crates -> 3 sites.
verdict.proposal_note: Moving the time assert after the count assert keeps a coarse guard against per-vertex cost regressions, which the count cannot see. Deleting it outright loses that. Either option is fine; ordering it second is the safer choice.

title: A third test of the dead search, the_search_beats_a_scan_of_the_same_interval, sits among the train's laws and checks nothing shipped
claim: The train-level law guarding 'the path a given centre distance takes' computes `found` with `crate::auto::shifts_for_efficiency` and a `Pinned { sum }`, not with the shape's search that production runs. A fault in shape.rs's search coordinates passes it.
evidence: In a worktree I swapped shape.rs's Sum/Division `place` mapping (out[pa]=(s-d)/2, out[pb]=(s+d)/(2*sign)). `cargo nextest run -p gear-core` gave 604/604 passed, this test included. The golden `gear-cli shifts 9 37` moved its least-loss shifts from 0.6746/0.7332 to 0.6677/0.7640, with the same 97.678 %.
proposal: Keep the test's `at` closure, which solves fixed shifts through `solve_preset`. Compute `found` by solving `arr::pair(teeth)` with `set_search(true)`, the distance fixed at the one that implies each sum, and read `profile_shift` back. Drop the `shifts_for_efficiency` admissibility pre-check, since `solve_preset` refusal already defines admissibility. Delete the test's `Bounds` and `Pinned` imports with the dead code.
validation: The re-aimed test should fail when shape.rs:1829-1832's Division box is halved in width. The unmodified tree should pass it with the same 1e-5 tolerance.

verdict.reason: Reproduced: with shape.rs's Sum/Division place mapping swapped, `cargo nextest run -p gear-core` gave 604/604 passed. gear-cli shifts 9 37 moved from least-loss 0.6746/0.7332 to 0.6677/0.7640 at the same 97.678 %, and every distance-sweep row moved. The test does compute `found` and its admissibility check through auto::shifts_for_efficiency, which only tests call. The title's 'checks nothing shipped' overstates it, though. shifts_for_efficiency runs the shipped Search::maximise (auto.rs ~1558: `search.maximise(&box_, ...)`, also used at shape.rs:1893/1902), and the fault the test's doc names (the walk's first step falling below the resolution) lives in that shared walk. The corpus still catches the coordinate fault, but no unit law does.
verdict.corrected_claim: the_search_beats_a_scan_of_the_same_interval exercises the shipped Search::maximise walk only through the production-dead wrapper auto::shifts_for_efficiency/Pinned::place, and never through the shape's own Sum/Division coordinates and box (shape.rs:1786-1856). A fault there, such as a swapped division mapping, passes all 604 gear-core tests and is caught only by the golden corpus.
verdict.evidence: Worktree mutation at shape.rs:1845-1846: out[pa]=(s-d)/2, out[pb]=(s+d)/(2*sign) -> '604 tests run: 604 passed'. diff of gear-cli shifts 9 37: line 5 '0.6746 0.7332 1.4078 1.2929 97.678 %' -> '0.6677 0.7640 1.4317 1.2981 97.678 %', and rows 12-17 and 24-28 all move. grep shifts_for_efficiency crates: calls only in auto.rs tests (>=1932) and train/mod.rs:5253/5279 (test).
verdict.proposal_note: The re-aim is sound: solve arr::pair with set_search(true) and the distance fixed where it implies each sum, then read the shifts back. The auto.rs test-module callers (2764, 2850, 2876) also test the dead wrapper and should move in the same change, or be deleted with it.

title: The addendum's legacy { auto, manual } arm accepts any unknown keys, silently breaking the document's deny_unknown_fields guarantee
claim: `coefficient` deserialises `addendum` through an untagged enum whose `WasAuto { manual }` variant lacks deny_unknown_fields. Any table carrying a `manual` key is accepted, and every other key in it is dropped without a word. gear-io/src/train.rs says 'No compatibility shim, deliberately' and 'Every struct the document is made of says deny_unknown_fields now'. Both statements are false for this field.
evidence: Probe (probes/verify-ablate-features-2): serde_json::from_value::<MemberGear> with addendum = {"manual":1.2,"junk":7,"whatever":"x"} returns Ok(1.2). The same document with a top-level `junk` key is refused: 'unknown field `junk`'. TOML import goes through the same Deserialize impl.
proposal: Delete the WasAuto arm and deserialise `addendum` as a plain f64. Record the old `{auto, manual}` form among the formats gear-io/src/train.rs lists as refused. If the arm must stay, put #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)] on a named struct holding `auto: bool, manual: f64` and use that struct as the variant.
validation: Add a test in gear-io asserting that a train TOML whose member writes `addendum = { manual = 1.0, junk = 1 }` is refused and names the field. The existing `a_field_the_shape_no_longer_has_is_refused_and_named` sweep should be extended to cover it.

verdict.reason: Re-ran the probe. With addendum = {"manual":1.2,"junk":7,"whatever":"x"}, MemberGear deserialises to Ok(1.2), while a top-level `junk` key is refused with 'unknown field `junk`'. The untagged `WasAuto { manual: f64 }` variant has no deny_unknown_fields, and serde ignores unknown keys in it by default. The arm is also a compatibility shim, which contradicts gear-io/src/train.rs:249-266 ('No compatibility shim, deliberately', 'Every struct the document is made of says deny_unknown_fields').
verdict.evidence: crates/gear-core/src/train/mod.rs:1071-1081: `#[serde(untagged)] enum Either { Number(f64), WasAuto { manual: f64 } }`, used at mod.rs:1150 via `deserialize_with = "coefficient"`. Probe verify-ablate-features-2 output: `{"junk":7,"manual":1.2,"whatever":"x"} -> Ok(1.2)`; `top-level junk -> Err("unknown field `junk` ...")`. shape.rs:73/121 `ground_if_null` is a second shim of the same kind, for `carried_by: null`.
verdict.proposal_note: Prefer deleting the arm, as the document's own no-shim rule says. `ground_if_null` (shape.rs:121) is the same kind of shim and should get the same decision in the same change, so the no-shim paragraph ends up true or names both exceptions. If either shim stays, the paragraph at gear-io/src/train.rs:249-266 must name it.

title: Gear::new cuts an ordinary gear's tooth twice (mean and teeth[0] are identical at Δx=0), which contradicts 'costs what it always did'
claim: Gear::new builds `teeth` as one Tooth::cut_by per distinct shift (gear.rs:195) and then builds `mean` with a separate Tooth::cut_by(params, tool) (gear.rs:207). At Δx=0, shift_at returns profile_shift + 0·cos θ, exactly profile_shift, so the two cuts use identical inputs and give identical teeth. Every ordinary gear, and so every train member, is cut twice. The test doc at gear.rs:2615 says the zero-shift case 'costs what it always did: one tooth generated, not z … collapsing onto the old case has to be free', but the test only counts distinct teeth and cannot see the duplicate.
evidence: Probe /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/verify-ablate-features-3 (release): for z=9/17/43/200, format!("{:?}") of g.mean() equals that of the first distinct tooth, and Gear::new takes 2.06x / 2.05x / 3.38x / 8.85x the time of Tooth::tool_wanted_by + Tooth::cut_by (e.g. z=17: 3.3 µs vs 1.6 µs). At large z the extra time also includes the O(z) seat vector and the `which` loop.
proposal: Build `mean` by reusing the tooth whose shift equals params.profile_shift when one exists: `let mean = shifts.iter().position(|&s| s == params.profile_shift).map(|i| teeth[i].clone()).unwrap_or_else(|| Tooth::cut_by(params, tool))`, then add the tool's clamps as now. This also covers an eccentric gear, whose k=0 tooth sits at profile_shift + Δx and so is not the mean. Either extend an_ordinary_gear_still_generates_one_tooth to assert that the mean is the generated tooth (e.g. a construction counter under cfg(test)), or correct its doc.
validation: cargo nextest run -p gear-core gear:: stays green, check_golden shows no diff (the output is bit-identical because the inputs are identical), and the probe ratio for z=17 falls to about 1.0-1.1.

verdict.reason: At Δx=0, shift_at returns profile_shift + 0·cosθ = profile_shift exactly. So `at(x)` equals `params`, and `mean = Tooth::cut_by(params, tool)` repeats the cut already done for teeth[0]. The probe confirms the two are Debug-identical, and Gear::new takes about 2.1x a single cut (3.5 µs against 1.7 µs at z=17). The test at gear.rs:2615 counts only distinct_teeth(), so it cannot see the second cut, and its doc ('one tooth generated, not z') overstates what it checks. The absolute cost is microseconds, so low severity is right.
verdict.evidence: gear.rs:195 `let teeth ... Tooth::cut_by(at(x), tool)`; gear.rs:207 `let mut mean = Tooth::cut_by(params, tool);`; gear.rs:123-124 shift_at. Re-ran probe verify-ablate-features-3: z=9/17/43/200 mean==teeth[0] true; ratios 2.14 / 2.11 / 3.55 / 8.37 against want+cut.
verdict.proposal_note: The proposed exact-equality `position` lookup is sound: equality is exact by construction at Δx=0, and it also catches the k=z/4 tooth of an eccentric gear. Keep the clamp-merging loop after the clone.

title: The placeholder grammar is written three times in gear-io strings.rs
claim: fill() (production), a `placeholders` closure in every_language_carries_the_whole_catalogue, and a `fn placeholders` in the same test module each re-implement the '{name}' scan. The closure and the fn are the same code, and TS strings.svelte.ts:68 is a fourth copy. If the grammar changes in fill, the laws keep checking the old grammar.
evidence: strings.rs:327-336 and strings.rs:533-546 are the same find('{')/find('}') loop (one collects into a BTreeSet, the other into a Vec), and fill at 263-291 walks the same way.
proposal: Give the module one `fn placeholders(template) -> impl Iterator<Item=&str>` that fill uses to split the template and that both tests call, and delete the closure. Pair this with the grammar-pin test proposed for finding 14.
validation: cargo nextest run -p gear-io strings stays green, and a catalogue entry with an odd placeholder fails the one pinning test.

verdict.reason: There are three Rust copies of the '{' ... '}' scan: fill at 262-291, the closure at 327-336 (which shadows the module fn at 354-355), and fn placeholders at 533-546. The fourth copy, the TS one, is sharper than the finding says, because it is not the same grammar. TS uses /\{(\w+)\}/, so `{a b}`, `{}` and `{x-y}` stay literal in the UI, while Rust treats anything up to '}' as a name. Rust's fill also handles an unclosed brace differently from both test scanners: fill carries on after it, and the scanners stop.
verdict.evidence: strings.rs:327 `let placeholders = |text: &str| -> BTreeSet<String>`; strings.rs:533 `fn placeholders(message: &str) -> Vec<String>`; web/src/strings.svelte.ts `template.replace(/\{(\w+)\}/g, ...)`.
verdict.proposal_note: Besides one Rust `placeholders` iterator used by fill and both tests, the catalogue law should require every placeholder name to match `\w+`. Then the TS regex and the Rust scan agree on every message that ships.

title: Turning the search on makes the shipped Planocentric preset refuse to solve (OutsideInvoluteDomain)
claim: The Planocentric preset (planet 30, ring 33, both shifts and the distance automatic) solves with the search off. With the per-mesh search toggle on, which the panel offers at TrainPanel.svelte:678, the whole train refuses with 'part 1: no such gear pair: the profile shifts require the base circles to overlap'. The search returns, or the plan then builds, shifts outside the internal mesh's involute domain rather than being held to admissible points. No test switches the search on for every preset: every set_search(true) in the suite is on a pair, one planetary set, the hula or a crossed pair. So the gap is unguarded.
evidence: Release probe probes/verify-lens-performance-1 `plano` mode. Preset::Planocentric.build() gives teeth [30, 33], shifts Auto{auto:true, manual:0}, distance Auto{auto:true}. With search=false: solve_train ok, 1 path. With search=true: Err `part 1: no such gear pair: the profile shifts require the base circles to overlap`, InPart { part: 0, cause: Mesh(OutsideInvoluteDomain) }. The same sweep over every preset with search on: all the others solve.
proposal: Find where the searched shifts leave the internal mesh's domain. Either the search's objective must return None, not a value, for candidates whose mesh is OutsideInvoluteDomain (auto::maximise treats None as inadmissible), or the plan that closes the automatic distance must be solved inside the domain the search admitted. Then add a law beside every_arrangement_of_a_set_solves: every Preset::ALL, and every arrangement, with set_search(true), solves (or is refused only with a note naming why), and its searched objective is no worse than the unsearched one.
validation: The new every-preset-searched law fails today on Planocentric and passes after the fix. The golden corpus must be unchanged for search-off presets.

verdict.reason: Reproduced: Planocentric with search off solves (1 path). With search on, the solve fails with InPart{part:0, cause: Mesh(OutsideInvoluteDomain)}. Every other preset solves searched. I instrumented chosen_at in a worktree and found the root cause, which is more specific than the finding's guess. The search is admissible. The final closure pairs the shifts with the wrong plan.
verdict.evidence: Worktree trace of Shape::chosen_at (shape.rs ~1865-1935) for Planocentric with search on. Round 1: held [Some(1.7342)], v=[0.5235]; closed(plan, place(v)) = [0.5235, 0.8874], trial efficiency 0.99812, so admissible. Re-sizing at the chosen shifts gives held [None], and plan is replaced by plan_held(None). Round 2: this_round None, so break. After the loop: `self.closed(&plan, &place(&v), helix)` uses the round-2 plan with round-1 v and gives [0.5235, 0.0]. The ring's absorber no longer absorbs, and build_at gives Err(Mesh(OutsideInvoluteDomain)). Search off gives [0.0, 0.3639], build Ok. No test sweeps Preset::ALL with set_search(true): every set_search(true) in mod.rs, shape.rs, crossed.rs, arrangements.rs and strings.rs is on a pair, a set, a hula or a crossed stage. Candidate fix, tried in a worktree: when a later round's search finds nothing, and the latest plan's closure of v is inadmissible (trial_efficiency None), return the closure made at the plan v was found in. Result: Planocentric searched gives [0.5235, 0.8874], build Ok, and all 605 gear-core tests pass. Diff at /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/notes/verify-last-16-plano-fix.diff.
verdict.corrected_claim: The search itself admits only in-domain points. The fault is in chosen_at's post-loop closure. When the tip-sized distance is re-sized at the chosen shifts (held Some to None) and the next round finds nothing, `found` (from round k) is closed at round k+1's plan. There the automatic distance is no longer held, so the ring's absorbing shift falls back to settled 0, and the pair (0.5235, 0) is outside the internal mesh's involute domain.
verdict.proposal_note: Do not simply always close v at the plan it was found in. I tried that, and it breaks train::arrangements::hula::the_four_hula_studies_are_the_ones_this_code_prints: at d=2, α_w goes from 33.0 to 33.4° and the pair keeps 99.888 % against the tabled 99.893 %. The hula's tabled figures depend on closing v at the re-sized plan. Either keep that closure where it is admissible and fall back to the round's own pairing where it is not (tried: all tests green), or pair v with its plan throughout and deliberately re-record the hula table. Add the proposed every-preset-and-arrangement searched-solve law, and assert that the searched product of efficiencies is no worse than the unsearched one.

title: docs/reference.md says two conditions pick the physical power-flow branch; the suite shows they do not
claim: reference.md says the flow 'keeps the consistent assignment' and that the sign condition plus the energy condition decide it. With neither mesh self-locking, several assignments pass both conditions with different efficiencies (0 vs 0.42-0.48) on hula/Wolfrom and chained presets, and the code picks the maximum. The document's account of the model is therefore incomplete at exactly the point that decides the hula figures. This is the documentary half of lens-performance #11, which cited only the code comment.
evidence: See verdict 11: 671 logged disagreements across 26 tests. Replacing max with first-consistent fails 7 tests, the hula tables among them.
proposal: Add the third rule, the most output power among consistent branches, to reference.md's list with its physical argument, or replace it with a physical condition that rules out the zero-output branch. Make flow.rs's comment point to it.
validation: Instrument flow::solve as in verdict 11 and confirm that, under the stated rule(s), exactly one branch survives in every suite case.

verdict.reason: Several consistent branches with different efficiencies do exist; I reproduced it. But the finding misreads why. The 0-efficiency branch fails the document's condition 2 as the document writes it: 'the output has to absorb what the input delivers — T_out ω_out ≤ 0'. It passes only the code's weaker version of that condition. flow.rs checks the total loss (sum of body powers ≥ −ZERO), not that the output absorbs. So a branch where input and output both deliver power and friction eats all of it gets through, and the max-efficiency tie-break is what then rejects it. The document's two conditions would decide the choice; the code does not implement the second one as written, and its comment ('the first consistent one is the answer') is false. This is a code/comment/document mismatch at the decision point, not a missing third rule in the document. The answers themselves are right today because max compensates.
verdict.evidence: Worktree, flow::solve instrumented to log every consistent branch's body powers per unit input (a_path_holds_at_rest_where_no_mesh_does). In every 0-efficiency branch the output body delivers power. Example: 'eff=0 dirs=[Backward, Forward] powers=[0, 1.0, -0, 0.549, -0]' beside 'eff=0.2655 dirs=[Forward, Backward] powers=[0, 1.0, 0, -0.2655, -0]' (body 3 is the output). In the back-driven case the derived input delivers (body 1: +1.82 while the known body 3 gives 1.0). I then replaced the max with 'first branch in which some body absorbs (efficiency > 0), else the first consistent branch'. All 604 gear-core tests pass, including the 7 that fail under plain first-consistent. Among the absorbing branches the only disagreements left are 1e-13 vs 0.4836: a rounding-width absorption just above ZERO·input_power, which a strict rule would have to treat as nought. Log: /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/notes/verify-last-17/absorb.log.
verdict.corrected_claim: docs/reference.md's condition 2 ('the output absorbs', T_out ω_out ≤ 0) would pick one branch in every suite case. flow.rs implements it instead as 'total loss ≥ 0', which admits a branch where the output (or a derived load) delivers power, and it relies on an unstated max-efficiency tie-break to reject that branch. Its comment claims first-consistent.
verdict.proposal_note: Do not add a 'most output power' rule to reference.md. Make the code implement the stated condition: reject a branch in which no body absorbs more than the solve's zero; if every consistent branch is like that, the flow holds (efficiency 0, matching 'self-locking'). Then drop the max, or keep it only as a debug_assert that the surviving absorbing branches agree. Rewrite the flow.rs comment at 297-347 to say this and point to reference.md#the-graph. Check the rounding-width case (efficiency ~1e-13, seen in every_preset_in_every_pair_is_the_path_across_it_alone) against the zero threshold before replacing the max.

title: External tooth's tip radius silently raised to the base circle, with no note (the ring's equivalent has one)
claim: Tooth::build does `let ra = ra.max(rb * (1.0 + guard::TIP_ABOVE_BASE_FRACTION))` and pushes no note. A tip requested below the base circle is moved up to the base circle silently. The ring has a note for the same guard (clamp.ring_tip_raised); the external tooth does not. That is rule 5 ('clamp ... and say so') applied to one kind of member only.
evidence: Probe bin v3 at z17, 20°, h_a 1: at x = −1.6 and x = −1.7 the nominal r_a = r + m(h_a + x) = 7.9 and 7.8, but t.ra = 7.9874 = r_b and u_tip = 0, with clamps []. The admissible addendum range does flag these inputs: its min is (r_b − r)/m − x ≈ 1.087 at x = −1.6. A TOML import or a hand-built request bypasses the panel's bound.
proposal: Push a note when the max() changes ra, either the ring's key generalised (clamp.tip_raised with the radius) or a new clamp.tip_raised_to_base, in all 5 catalogues. Ideally ring and tooth share one key, since it is one guard.
validation: Law over the gear grid: whenever t.ra > r + m(h_a + x) + tolerance, and not because of the pointed cap, the clamps contain the tip-raised key. Run it against HEAD first: z17 x −1.6 fails.

verdict.reason: Reproduced. Tooth::new raises a tip requested below the base circle to r_b·(1+1e-9) and pushes no note. The ring's equivalent guard pushes clamp.ring_tip_raised. This breaks rule 5 for external gears. The panel's admissible range flags such inputs, but the core does not say so in its output.
verdict.evidence: tooth.rs:471 `let ra = ra.max(rb * (1.0 + guard::TIP_ABOVE_BASE_FRACTION));` has no clamps.push, unlike the pointed cap three lines above it. Probe /home/user/.cache/gearcalc-audit/probes/verify-last-17 (z17, 20°, h_a 1): 'x=-1.6 nominal_ra=7.9000 ra=7.9874 rb=7.9874 clamps=[]' and 'x=-1.7 nominal_ra=7.8000 ra=7.9874 clamps=[]'. The ring pushes CLAMP_RING_TIP_RAISED at ring.rs:302.
verdict.proposal_note: One key for both (clamp.tip_raised_to_base with the radius), fired where the max() changes ra. Rename the ring's key into it and update the 5 catalogues. strings.rs's fire-every-note test will then require a site that fires it, which the z17 x=-1.6 case provides.

title: Turning search on for the shipped Planocentric preset makes a train that solves refuse (OutsideInvoluteDomain); no test searches every preset
claim: `Preset::Planocentric` (planocentric(30, 33)) solves with search off. With `set_search(true)`, or search on its only mesh, `solve_train` refuses with `InPart { part: 0, cause: Mesh(OutsideInvoluteDomain) }`. The panel offers the search toggle on every mesh (TrainPanel.svelte:678), so a user asking the default planocentric to optimise its efficiency loses the whole solve. A search should only ever pick among buildable candidates, never turn a solvable design into a refusal. No test runs the search across `Preset::ALL`: the budget test and the search laws in train/mod.rs use pairs, one planetary and a hula.
evidence: probes/verify-lens-numerical-robustness-2/src/bin/presets2.rs: `Planocentric search=false 2.84ms -> ok`; `Planocentric search=true 3.63ms -> InPart { part: 0, cause: Mesh(OutsideInvoluteDomain) }`; `Planocentric search mesh 0 only -> same refusal`. The same sweep (src/bin/presets.rs) solves every other preset with search on. grep of `set_search(true)` in train/mod.rs finds only pair/planetary/hula fixtures, none iterating Preset::ALL.
proposal: Add a law: for every `Preset::ALL`, and each mesh individually, turning search on either solves or refuses exactly when search-off refuses. Then find why the internal-mesh search accepts a candidate that the subsequent mesh build puts outside the involute domain. The search's feasibility test is probably missing the internal-gear domain check that `mesh`/`ring` apply, so either add that check to the candidate filter or fall back to the unsearched design with a note when every candidate fails.
validation: The new law fails at HEAD on Planocentric and passes after the fix. The golden corpus is unchanged because search is off by default.

verdict.reason: Reproduced for Preset::ALL: only Planocentric fails with search on, and it fails with InPart{part 0, Mesh(OutsideInvoluteDomain)}. The proposal's diagnosis is wrong, though. The search's candidate filter does build each candidate: trial_efficiency calls build_cached(...).ok()?, so a candidate outside the involute domain is rejected there. The real cause is in Shape::chosen_at. After a round, the distance is re-sized at the chosen shifts and the plan is replaced. The next round finds nothing and breaks. The final Chosen then pairs the previous round's shifts with the new plan, which was never built. Here, re-sizing at the chosen shifts un-holds the distance (held goes from Some(1.734) to None), and under that plan the same shifts fail to build.
verdict.evidence: Probe over Preset::ALL: every preset ok with search on and off except 'Planocentric search=true -> InPart { part: 0, cause: Mesh(OutsideInvoluteDomain) }'. Worktree instrumentation of chosen_at (shape.rs ~1880-1930): 'DBG round chosen=[0.5235, 0.0] held=[Some(1.7342)] trial=Some(0.99812)', then 'DBG resized held=[None]', then 'DBG final held=[None] x=Some([0.5235, 0.0]) build_ok=Some(false)'. So the candidate built fine (η 0.998) under the plan it was searched in, and fails only under the replaced plan.
verdict.proposal_note: Keep (v, plan, bound_by) together as the search's best. Replace the plan only once the next round has actually found something under it, and return the plan v was scored in, or build the final Chosen and fall back to the last plan that built. Add the proposed law: for each Preset::ALL and each mesh, search on solves wherever search off solves. Duplicate of added2#94.

title: a_path_holds_at_rest_where_no_mesh_does keeps change history in its docstring
